## Preface

This book exists because the interview and the job have converged in a way they did not five years ago.
Until recently, most software engineering interviews tested general systems-design intuition: databases,
caches, load balancers, message queues. The underlying assumption was that specialized domain knowledge
could be learned on the job once a strong generalist was hired. That assumption has broken down at frontier
AI companies. A candidate who cannot reason about KV cache memory pressure, arithmetic intensity on a
GPU, or the difference between compute-bound prefill and memory-bandwidth-bound decoding will not pass a
senior-level systems interview at the teams building today’s most important models. The domain has become
so operationally specific that generalist intuition is no longer sufficient, and no single paper, blog post, or course
covers it end to end.
**The gap this book fills.** Academic courses teach the theory of transformers; they rarely explain why GQA
withNkv=N/ 8 reduces KV cache memory by 8 and how that changes the feasible batch size on a single
H100. Research papers present results; they do not explain how to answer “walk me through how you would
size the hardware for a 70B model serving 5,000 QPS” in the 45 minutes of a live interview. Engineering blogs
cover individual components in depth; they do not provide the unified arithmetic framework that lets you move
fluidly from model parameters to memory budgets to parallelism strategies to cost estimates. This book does.
**What this book is.** It is a technical reference and an interview preparation guide written for engineers who
already know how to code and who already understand basic ML. Every chapter develops the arithmetic behind
a topic from first principles, shows how that arithmetic connects to real hardware constraints, and then frames
the result as an interview question with a worked answer. The appendices collect the most important formulas
for fast reference during active preparation.
**What this book is not.** It is not an introduction to deep learning. It does not teach backpropagation or
explain what a transformer is from scratch. It does not survey the research literature comprehensively. Readers
who need that foundation first should work through a course on neural networks before returning here. It is also
not a prescriptive guide to any specific company’s interview process-the frameworks and derivations are generic
because the physics of hardware and the economics of inference are generic.
**Coverage.** The book follows a deliberate progression. Part I maps the interview landscape and introduces
the four-question framework that structures every design answer. Parts II through IV build the technical founda-
tion: transformer architecture, training hyperparameters, GPU hardware, and kernel-level performance. Parts V
and VI scale that foundation across distributed training and scaling laws. Part VII covers the inference stack
in depth, from the prefill-decode split through KV cache optimizations, speculative decoding, and compres-
sion. Parts VIII through X address the three domains that interviewers probe as differentiators-data pipelines,
evaluation design, and alignment methods. Part XI synthesizes everything into three full end-to-end design
drills.
**Using derivations, not memorization.** Every number in this book is derived, not asserted. The estimate
that a 7B model in bf16 requires approximately 13 GB of inference memory follows from 2 Pbytes, withP=
6. 7  109. The estimate that a single H100 decode step takes roughly 8 ms at batch size 1 follows from dividing
Mweightsby the HBM bandwidth. These derivations are the point. An interviewer who changes one constraint-
“now make it a 13B model”-expects a candidate who can update the arithmetic in real time, not one who has
memorized a table. First principles produce that flexibility; memorization does not.


## How to Use This Book

The book supports three distinct uses: interview preparation, on-the-job reference, and systematic study of
LLM systems. Read it linearly if you are building up the subject from scratch. Follow a targeted path if you are
preparing for a specific role or plugging specific gaps.

### Chapter Diﬀiculty

Chapters are written at three levels. The level is not labeled explicitly because the same content serves both
preparation and reference; the _depth_ at which you engage with it is the variable.
**Conceptual** (most of Parts I, II, VIII, IX, X) Develops vocabulary, mental models, and interview framing.
Suitable as first-pass reading and as review before an interview day.
**Arithmetic** (most of Parts IV, VI, VII; Appendix A) Derives quantitative estimates from first principles. Re-
quires pencil and paper. Work through the examples actively rather than reading passively.
**Implementation** (most of Parts III, V; Chapter 10) Discusses kernel-level, compiler-level, or systems-level
mechanics. Assumed background: familiarity with PyTorch, CUDA concepts, and distributed training
frameworks.

## For Candidates Preparing for Interviews

The LLM systems interview rewards candidates who derive answers, not candidates who recall them. Every
technique in this section is aimed at building that derivation habit before you sit down with an interviewer.

### What the Interview Actually Tests

A senior-level LLM systems interview has three observable signals interviewers are collecting simultane-
ously.
**First: vocabulary precision.** “The KV cache grows with sequence length” is not an answer. “At 4,
tokens, a single sequence in a 7B GQA model with 8 KV heads and head dimension 128 costs approximately
0.17 GB per sequence in bf16” is. The arithmetic formulas in Appendix A are the vocabulary; the chapters
explain where each term comes from.
**Second: constraint-driven reasoning.** Every design question has a binding constraint-usually KV cache
memory pressure for serving, usually communication overhead for training. Strong candidates name the bind-
ing constraint before proposing any optimization. Candidates who list optimizations without identifying the
bottleneck signal that they have read blog posts, not reasoned from hardware physics.
**Third: adaptability under constraint changes.** The most reliable signal in a live interview is what
happens when the interviewer says “what if context length doubles?” or “what if you now need to support
five model variants?” A candidate who derived their original answer updates the arithmetic immediately. A
candidate who memorized an architecture has to restart. This is why every technical chapter in this book teaches
derivation, not recall.

### A Four-Week Preparation Plan

This plan assumes roughly two hours of active study per day. Adjust the pacing to your timeline; the
sequence of topics is fixed, but the time budget per topic is flexible.
**Week 1 - Foundation** Read Chapters 1-5 and Appendix A fully. After each chapter, close the book and re-
derive the key formulas from memory on paper. Target: be able to estimate model memory footprint
(inference and training), forward-pass FLOPs, and KV cache size for any model configuration given to
you verbally.
**Week 2 - Hardware and Distributed Systems** Read Chapters 8-12. Work through every numerical example
with a calculator. Practice explaining the roofline model out loud to an imaginary interviewer. Spend extra
time on Chapter 12 (parallelism strategies): draw the TP/PP/DP combination diagram from memory until
it takes less than two minutes.
**Week 3 - Inference and Scaling** Read Chapters 13-19. Focus on Chapter 15 (the inference workload) and
Chapter 18 (speculative decoding and serving). For each optimization technique in Chapters 16-19, write
one sentence explaining which constraint it addresses and what it trades away. Read Appendix C (check-
lists) and internalize the ten-minute system design checklist.
**Week 4 - Integration and Drills** Read Chapters 20-28 at pace (one per day). Spend the last three days on
Part XI (Chapters 29-31), working each drill as a timed mock interview: 45 minutes, whiteboard or

### How to Drill a Chapter

Passive reading does not build the derivation habit. Use this sequence for every chapter in the arithmetic
and implementation tiers.

1. Read the chapter fully once, following along with any derivations.
2. Cover the page. Write down the key formula from memory.
3. Plug in a different model configuration (changed, changeL, changeNkv) and re-derive the result.
4. Answer the “How This Shows Up” questions from the chapter out loud, targeting 90 seconds per answer
    before expanding to the full 5-minute version.
5. Read the Key Takeaways bullet list and verify you can explain each point without the book.

### Timing Your Answers

```
A 45-minute design interview has roughly the following pacing for a strong candidate:
```
**Phase Time What you are doing**

Requirements clarification 3-5 min Name TTFT, throughput, quality, cost; ask which is binding
End-to-end pipeline sketch 5-8 min Tokenize!prefill!decode!scheduler; label bottlenecks
Binding constraint analysis 5-7 min Derive KV cache footprint or memory budget; identify the limit
Targeted optimizations 10-15 min Propose GQA, speculative decoding, quantization as constraint responses
Trade-off discussion 5-8 min Answer the interviewer’s constraint-change follow-ups
Wrap-up 2-3 min Summarize and invite feedback

The requirement clarification phase is the most commonly skipped and the most damaging to skip. Interviewers
at staff and principal level watch for it explicitly.

### Common Failure Modes

**Cargo-culting numbers without derivation** Stating “Chinchilla says 20 tokens per parameter” without being
able to derive where the 20 comes from, or what changes when inference cost is amortized over more
queries. Chapter 14 derives this ratio and explains when it does not apply.
**Conflating latency and throughput** Describing TTFT and tokens-per-second as if they optimize together.
They do not; Chapter 15 derives why and what each responds to.
**Listing optimizations before naming the bottleneck** Proposing speculative decoding, FlashAttention, and
quantization in the same breath before establishing whether the system is KV-cache-constrained, compute-
constrained, or communication-constrained. Chapter 2 provides the framework for identifying the con-
straint first.
**Treating batch size as a free variable** Failing to recognize that batch size is bounded by VRAM and that
both data parallelism and pipeline parallelism consume it as a resource. Appendix A and Chapter 12
derive the precise constraints.

**Ignoring inference economics during training design** Designing a training run without considering the serv-

straint.

### Using the Appendices

**Appendix A** (formulas) is the most important reference during active preparation. Print it. Put it next to
your desk. After two weeks of preparation you should not need to look at it; if you still do, spend another session
re-deriving each formula from scratch.
**Appendix B** (question bank) is organized by topic. Use it to simulate a 45-minute interview: pick one
design question and one deep-dive question from the same topic area, set a timer, and answer both without
references.
**Appendix C** (checklists) provides a ten-minute LLM system design checklist, a pre-training run readi-
ness checklist, and an inference deployment readiness checklist. Internalize the design checklist until you can
reproduce it verbally in under two minutes.
**Appendix D** (reading list) is for candidates preparing at the staff or principal level, where interviewers
expect familiarity with the primary literature. Papers are annotated with the specific claims you are expected to
reproduce, not just name.

## For Engineers Building LLM Systems

This book is organized around interview questions, but its technical content is not interview-specific.
The arithmetic behind batch-size constraints, the parallelism trade-offs in distributed training, the memory-
bandwidth math behind KV cache sizing-these are the same calculations you do on the job. This section maps
the book’s chapters to the decisions you encounter in production.

### When to Reach for This Book

**You are sizing a serving fleet for a new model** Start with Appendix A (KV cache formula, memory foot-
print) and Chapter 15 (the inference workload, latency-throughput trade-offs). The KV-crossover batch
sizeB∗=Mweights/Ckvis the first number to compute; it determines whether you are in the superlinear
or sublinear throughput regime before you touch any configuration.
**You are choosing a parallelism strategy for a training run** Chapter 12 derives the memory and communi-
cation cost of every combination: tensor-parallel, pipeline-parallel, data-parallel, ZeRO stages 1-3, and
FSDP. The worked examples are parameterized so you can substitute your own model size and cluster
topology.
**You are debugging a training run that is not hitting expected MFU** Chapter 8 (arithmetic intensity and the
roofline model) and Chapter 11 (collective communication bandwidth and all-reduce timing) are the di-
agnostic starting points. Low MFU is almost always communication-bound, memory-bound, or pipeline-
bubble-bound; the chapters give you the arithmetic to distinguish the three cases.
**You are evaluating a KV cache optimization (GQA, MLA, paged attention)** Chapter 16 derives the mem-
ory reduction and the resulting change in maximum batch size for each technique. The formulas let you
estimate the throughput gain on your specific hardware and model before running any experiment.
**You are designing an evaluation harness for a fine-tuned model** Chapters 23-25 cover evaluation design
from first principles: metric selection, contamination detection, benchmark validity, and the gap between
benchmark performance and deployment behavior. Chapter 25 covers domain-specific evaluation design
(medical, legal, code) and deployment telemetry.
**You are deciding between SFT, DPO, and RLVR for a post-training objective** Chapter 26 (SFT), Chapter 27
(DPO and RLHF), and Chapter 28 (GRPO and RLVR) each cover the method’s mechanics, its data re-
quirements, its failure modes, and the scenarios where it is the right choice. Chapter 31 synthesizes the
decision into an end-to-end alignment pipeline design.

### The Arithmetic Is the Point

Every number in production LLM engineering is derivable. When a colleague states that “a 70B model
needs at least 4 H100s to serve,” the correct response is to ask whether that accounts for KV cache at the target
batch size and context length, not to accept it as a fact. The derivation:Mweights= 2 70  109  140 GB in
bf16, spread acrossd 140 / 80 e= 2H100s for weights alone, but a realistic batch size and context window can
double that figure.
Chapter 15 and Appendix A derive these estimates in full, including the formulas forBmax(VRAM-limited
batch size),B∗(KV-crossover batch size), andtstep(decode step latency as a function of batch size and model
size). These are not rules of thumb; they are consequences of memory capacity and bandwidth, and they update
correctly when you change the model, the hardware, or the context length.

### Connecting the Book to the Engineering Literature

The book’s technical content is grounded in papers and engineering reports that have shaped the current
state of production LLM systems. Where a chapter’s content derives from a specific paper, the source is cited
inline. Appendix D provides an annotated reading list organized by topic, with each entry annotated to indicate
which specific claims are worth understanding in depth rather than simply citing by name.
The FlashAttention algorithm (Chapters 9 and 10), the Chinchilla scaling law (Chapter 14), continuous
batching (Chapter 18), and the GRPO training algorithm (Chapter 28) are examples where reading the original
paper alongside the corresponding chapter will deepen your understanding of the design choices behind the
method. The reading list indicates which papers repay that deeper reading and which are sufficient to know at
the result level.

### Staying Current

The LLM systems field moves fast. The core arithmetic and hardware physics in this book-memory band-
width, arithmetic intensity, roofline analysis, parallelism trade-offs-are stable. Specific techniques (attention
variants, serving schedulers, compression methods) continue to evolve. When a new technique is announced,
the most reliable way to evaluate it is to ask: which constraint does it address, and what does it trade away? That
question is the same one this book trains you to ask, and it does not go stale.

## Notation and Symbols

This chapter standardizes the symbols, abbreviations, and conventions used throughout the book. Defini-
tions are precise; where a symbol carries multiple meanings in the literature, the book’s chosen convention is
stated explicitly. Units are always written out on first use in each chapter; the table below lists the canonical
forms.

**Model and Architecture
Symbol Meaning Notes**
P Total parameter count e.g.P= 7 109 for a 7B model
L Number of transformer layers (depth)
d Hidden / residual stream dimension also writtendmodel
dmodel Hidden dimension (explicit form) synonym ford
dhead Attention head dimension typically 128
dff Feed-forward (MLP) intermediate dimension b 8 d/ 3 cfor SwiGLU; 4 dfor ReLU/GeLU
N Number of query attention heads
Nkv Number of key-value heads Nkv=N(MHA);Nkv< N(GQA/MQA)
H Head dimension; alsodhead context disambiguates
HQ Query head count used in GQA ratioHQ/HKV
HKV Key-value head count HKV= 1(MQA);HKV=HQ/G(GQA)
G GQA group size (N/Nkv) reduction factor for KV cache
V Vocabulary size tokens in the tokenizer
S Sequence length in tokens also writtenTin some chapters
T Sequence length in tokens synonym forS; also used for training tokens
Ke Expert utilization rate in MoE fraction of experts activated per token
r LoRA rank dimension of low-rank adapters

**Conventions
Tokens vs. sequences.** “Tokens” refers to individual vocabulary elements; “sequence” or “context” refers
to an ordered list of tokens. Batch sizeBcounts sequences, not tokens;NT=BTcounts tokens.
**FLOPs counting.** One multiply-accumulate (MAC) operation= 2FLOPs. The formulaCfwd 2 NTP
follows this convention. “FLOP/s” (floating-point operations per second) uses the same factor.
**Memory units.** 1 GB= 10^9 bytes throughout (SI prefix, not binary). Bandwidth is reported in GB/s or
TB/s.
**Latency units.** Milliseconds (ms) for per-token and per-request latencies; seconds (s) for end-to-end
generation time; microseconds (μs) for kernel-level timings.
**Throughput units.** Tokens per second (tok/s or tokens/s) for generation throughput; queries per second

```
xix
```

```
Notation and Symbols
```
(QPS) for request-level throughput.
**Precision notation.** Memory footprints assume bf16 (2 bytes/parameter) unless otherwise stated. The
training-memory figure of 16 Pbytes assumes AdamW in fp32.
**Prefill vs. decode.** Prefill encodes the full prompt in one parallel forward pass (compute-bound). Decode
generates tokens one at a time in an autoregressive loop (memory-bandwidth-bound). These two phases
have distinct bottlenecks and optimizations.
**Latency vs. throughput.** TTFT optimizes differently from aggregate TPS. Minimize TTFT with small
batches and fast prefill hardware; maximize TPS with large batches and high memory bandwidth. A single
serving configuration cannot simultaneously optimize both without workload-specific scheduling.
**Overloaded symbols.** Gdenotes both the GQA group size and the GRPO rollout count;T denotes
both sequence length and training token count;βdenotes both the Adam second-moment decay and the
KL penalty coefficient. In each case, context and the surrounding equation make the intended meaning
unambiguous.

## Part I

# Overview and Interview Landscape


## Chapter 1 The LLM Systems Interview

### 1.1 What Companies Actually Ask

**1.1.1 Design-an-LLM-System Questions**
You sit down across from the interviewer. After two minutes of introductions, the question lands: “Design
a serving system for a code-completion product with p95 time-to-first-token under 200 milliseconds.” You have
45 minutes. This is the open-ended design question, and it is the center of gravity for senior and staff-level LLM
system roles.
Design questions ask you to build an LLM system end to end: from hardware budget to serving scheduler,
from a one-line product requirement to a set of motivated architectural choices. They are open-ended on purpose.
The interviewer is not looking for a canonical architecture; they are watching how you structure ambiguity, which
constraints you surface first, and whether your decisions are driven by actual hardware physics or by pattern-
matching to things you have read.
The question has three phases that map directly to the framework in Chapter 2. First, you clarify require-
ments: TTFT SLO, throughput target, quality bar, and cost ceiling-because the answer to “which model size?”
and “which parallelism strategy?” changes completely depending on these. Second, you sketch the end-to-end
pipeline: tokenization, prefill (compute-bound, KV cache written), decode (memory-bandwidth-bound, KV
cache read each step), and the serving scheduler that batches concurrent requests. Third, you identify the bind-
ing constraint-almost always KV cache pressure rather than raw FLOPs-and propose optimizations as targeted
responses to that constraint rather than as a list of things you have memorized.
Staff-level and principal-level design questions add a second layer: the interviewer changes a constraint
mid-answer. “What if context length doubles?” “What if you need to serve five model variants behind the same
endpoint?” “What if cost-per-token becomes the primary SLO?” A candidate who derived their numbers from
first principles adapts in seconds. A candidate who memorized an architecture has to start over. This is why the
framework matters more than any specific configuration.
The vocabulary these questions test is introduced in Chapter 2 and derived in Parts IV through VII: arith-
metic intensity, memory-bandwidth-bound versus compute-bound regimes, KV cache footprint per sequence per
layer, batch-size-versus-latency trade-off, continuous batching, speculative decoding, grouped-query attention.
_Every strong answer to a design question is derivable from the constraints on the whiteboard; the inter-
viewer can always verify this by changing one constraint and watching what happens._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Design a production serving stack for a 7B chat model targeting p95 TTFT under 300 ms at 5,000
QPS.” A strong answer opens with requirement clarification (interactive or batch use? single or multi-
tenant?), sketches prefill and decode as separate boxes with different bottlenecks, estimates KV cache
memory at a target batch size, identifies the batch-size constraint, and proposes continuous batching before
discussing any optimization. Chapter 2 covers the framework; Chapters 15 and 18 cover the arithmetic
and serving optimizations.
“Design the training infrastructure for a 70B dense model on a 512-GPU cluster.” A strong answer
sizes the memory budget (parameters, gradients, optimizer states), picks a parallelism combination jus-
```

```
1.1 What Companies Actually Ask
```
```
tified by the hardware topology (tensor-parallel within node, pipeline-parallel or ZeRO-3 across nodes),
estimates the pipeline bubble, and names where batch size is being consumed as a resource. Chapter 12
covers parallelism strategies; Chapter 13 covers the FLOP and memory arithmetic.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Open every design answer with requirements-TTFT SLO, throughput target, quality bar, cost ceiling-
before naming any component.
In serving, the binding constraint is almost always KV cache memory pressure, not FLOPs; in training it
is usually communication overhead.
Interviewers change constraints mid-answer to distinguish first-principles reasoning from memorized
configurations-derive, do not recall.
Chapter 2 is the procedural skeleton; the technical chapters (Parts IV-VII) provide the arithmetic to fill it
in.
```
**1.1.2 Deep-Dive Component Questions**
Twenty minutes into the design question-or sometimes as the entire interview-the interviewer pivots: “Let’s
go deeper on speculative decoding. Walk me through the acceptance criterion. Why does that sampling proce-
dure give you an exact sample from the target distribution?” This is the deep-dive format: narrow, mechanism-
level, and unforgiving about gaps between vocabulary and understanding.
Deep-dive questions test whether you understand the mechanism, not just the outcome. “Grouped-query
attention reduces the KV cache” is something you can read in an abstract. “GQA replacesNindependent key-
value head pairs withGshared groups, reducing KV cache memory by a factor ofN/G, which allows a propor-
tionally larger batch size on the same hardware” is what the question is actually asking for. The follow-up will
probe the second-order consequence: a larger batch size raises arithmetic intensity in the MLP layers toward the
compute-bound regime-while attention remains memory-bandwidth-bound regardless-so GQA changes where
the bottleneck sits at different batch sizes.
The components that appear most often in deep dives map directly to the technical parts of this book:
**Architecture details** : attention variants (GQA, MLA, sliding-window attention), MoE routing, normal-
ization and positional embedding choices-Parts II and III.
**GPU and kernel mechanics** : memory hierarchy, arithmetic intensity, operator fusion, FlashAttention-
Part IV.
**Parallelism** : all-reduce versus all-gather, ZeRO stages and their communication cost, pipeline bubbles,
tensor versus pipeline trade-offs-Part V.
**Inference systems** : KV cache sizing, continuous batching, speculative decoding acceptance criterion,
quantization precision tiers and their accuracy risk-Part VII.
**Evaluation** : benchmark contamination, evaluation harness design, metric selection for instruction-following
and reasoning tasks-Part IX.
The depth expectation scales with seniority. A junior screen asks for a correct description of the mechanism.
A senior screen asks for the trade-off and the failure mode. A staff or principal screen asks for the case where
the standard answer is wrong-and how you would detect it before shipping. Calibrate your answer to the level
you are interviewing for; going too shallow loses the offer, but going deep and then being wrong about the
second-order consequence is worse.


```
1.2 Roles That Require LLM Systems Knowledge
```
_A deep-dive answer has two moves: state the mechanism precisely, then name the second-order conse-
quence that the mechanism creates or removes._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Explain why token generation is memory-bandwidth-bound even at large batch sizes.” A strong
answer works from arithmetic intensity: each decode step processes one new token per sequence, collaps-
ing the weight matrix multiplications to matrix-vector products with intensity proportional to batch size
divided by hidden dimension-a number almost always below the GPU’s compute-bandwidth ridge point
regardless of batch size. The derivation lives in Chapter 15.
“How does ZeRO stage 3 differ from ZeRO stage 1 in memory savings and communication cost?”
A strong answer traces what is sharded at each stage (optimizer state at stage 1, gradients at stage 2,
parameters at stage 3), quantifies the communication increase (roughly 3 parameter bytes per step at
stage 3 versus 1 at stage 1), and notes that overlapping the all-gather with the forward pass is what
makes stage 3 viable at scale. Chapter 12 covers this in full.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Deep dives test mechanism, not vocabulary: “it reduces memory” is the opening of an answer, not the
answer.
State the second-order consequence-what the mechanism enables, constrains, or shifts-to move from a
passing answer to a strong one.
Seniority raises the bar from correct description to trade-off to failure mode; calibrate accordingly.
The technical chapters in Parts II-IX are organized around the component questions that appear most
frequently in frontier-lab interviews.
```
### 1.2 Roles That Require LLM Systems Knowledge

**1.2.1 LLM Infrastructure and Training Engineer**
Picture the engineer who gets paged because a 512-GPU training run has stalled at step 47,000. The job is
not to design a new architecture; it is to figure out why GPU 203 is 40% slower than the rest-whether the culprit
is a straggling all-reduce, a pipeline bubble, or a dead NVLink lane. This role exists at every frontier lab and
most serious AI infrastructure teams, and its interview goes deep into hardware and distributed systems.
The infra and training engineer owns the layer between model code and the cluster. Their primary vo-
cabulary is hardware topology-NVLink bandwidth within a node versus InfiniBand across racks-collective-
communication primitives (all-reduce, all-gather, reduce-scatter), and the three axes of model parallelism: data,
tensor, and pipeline.
No single parallelism strategy dominates. Data parallelism scales compute linearly but does nothing for
per-GPU memory; ZeRO stage 3 (FSDP) reclaims memory by sharding parameters and optimizer states across
workers, but it raises total communication cost to roughly three times the parameter count per step. Tensor
parallelism demands ultra-fast intra-node links and is practical only up to the number of GPUs per machine-
typically eight-because going further triggers the slower inter-node fabric. Pipeline parallelism crosses machines
cheaply but introduces a bubble proportional to stages divided by micro-batches. Production runs combine all


```
1.2 Roles That Require LLM Systems Knowledge
```
three: tensor-parallel within a node, pipeline-parallel or FSDP across nodes, data-parallel at the outermost level.
We work through the arithmetic behind each strategy in Part III.
Batch size is not just a hyperparameter here-it is a scarce resource. Both data parallelism and pipeline
parallelism consume it, so a candidate who can articulate that trade-off signals genuine systems fluency. The
other half of the role is resilience: silent GPU corruption, checkpoint cadence, and automatic-restart logic. At
scale, hardware failures are routine, not exceptional.
_The training engineer’s job is to convert cluster-hours into useful gradient steps, not communication stalls
or idle GPUs._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“How would you distribute a 70B-parameter model across a 64-GPU cluster for training?” A strong
answer picks a parallelism combination, justifies it by the memory and bandwidth constraints of the hard-
ware (8-GPU nodes connected by NVLink internally, InfiniBand across nodes), estimates the bubble or
bandwidth overhead, and names where batch size is being spent as a resource. The derivations live in
Part III.
“Walk me through how FSDP reduces optimizer-state memory compared to naive DDP.” A strong
answer traces the three ZeRO stages-shard optimizer state (stage 1), then gradients (stage 2), then param-
eters (stage 3)-explains why stage 3 raises communication to three times the parameter count, and notes
that the overlap of communication with computation is what makes it viable in practice. Chapter 8 covers
this in full.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Parallelism is a combination problem: tensor-parallel within a node, pipeline-parallel or ZeRO-3 across
nodes, data-parallel at the outermost level.
Batch size is a scarce resource that both data parallelism and pipeline parallelism consume; surfacing this
trade-off signals systems maturity.
Communication is the bottleneck, not compute: on modern clusters, the training engineer reasons about
memory bandwidth and collective-communication cost more than raw FLOP counts.
Hardware failures at scale are routine-checkpoint strategy and fault tolerance are not afterthoughts.
```
**1.2.2 LLM Applied/Product Engineer**
The applied engineer takes a trained or fine-tuned model and turns it into a product that ten thousand users
hit every minute. Their interview is lighter on distributed-training arcana and heavier on inference economics:
how fast does the model respond, how much does it cost to serve, and what breaks first when traffic spikes?
The core abstraction the applied engineer must own is the two-phase structure of LLM inference: prefill
(encoding the prompt in parallel, compute-bound) and generation (emitting tokens one by one, memory-bound).
During generation, each step reads all model parameters plus the entire KV cache from high-bandwidth mem-
ory; arithmetic intensity drops to roughly one FLOP per byte regardless of batch size, because every sequence
maintains its own KV state. That ceiling is set by memory bandwidth, not the GPU’s peak FLOP count. We
derive this bound in Chapter 9.
From that ceiling follow all practical serving decisions. To improve throughput, you batch requests together-
larger batches amortize the parameter-read cost across more tokens, pushing arithmetic intensity toward the


```
1.2 Roles That Require LLM Systems Knowledge
```
compute-bound regime. To reduce memory pressure, you shrink the KV cache: grouped-query attention uses
fewer key-value heads, multi-head latent attention projects keys and values into a lower-dimensional space,
and local attention restricts each layer to a sliding context window. Quantization (FP8 or INT4 weights) cuts
parameter-read time directly. Speculative decoding uses a cheap draft model to generate candidate tokens that
the large model verifies in one parallel prefill pass-since prefill is fast and parallel, this can nearly double effective
generation throughput with no accuracy loss.
The applied engineer also needs fluency in batching dynamics under live traffic: continuous batching so
the GPU never idles waiting for a fixed batch to fill, KV cache eviction policies when memory is exhausted, and
the latency-throughput curve that determines where to set serving SLOs for a given user experience target.
_Inference at scale is a memory-bandwidth problem wrapped in a queueing problem._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Design a serving system for a 7B chat model that needs p95 latency under 500ms at 5,000 QPS.”
A strong answer estimates peak memory (parameters plus KV cache at the target batch size), checks
whether the system is memory-bound or compute-bound at that batch size, proposes horizontal scaling or
model sharding if a single GPU cannot hold the load, and discusses continuous batching. The quantitative
framework lives in Chapter 9.
“What are the trade-offs between serving a 70B model in FP16 versus INT4?” A strong answer
covers: memory reduction (roughly 4 versus the FP16 baseline), latency improvement proportional to
memory reduction in the memory-bound regime, and accuracy risk driven by outlier activations in large
models. Chapter 10 covers quantization schemes in depth.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Generation is memory-bound: the bottleneck is reading weights and KV cache from HBM, not performing
FLOPs.
KV cache dominates serving memory; shrinking it via GQA, quantization, or local attention is the highest-
leverage optimization.
Latency and throughput trade against each other: smaller batches favor latency, larger batches favor
throughput-know where your product’s SLO sits on that curve.
Speculative decoding can double throughput at no accuracy cost; it is the canonical example of exploiting
the asymmetry between prefill speed and generation speed.
```
**1.2.3 Research Engineer vs. Research Scientist**
At a small startup these roles blur into one person who trains models and writes papers the same week;
at a frontier lab they can be two distinct career tracks with different interview loops and different hiring bars.
Getting the distinction wrong-showing up to a research engineer screen expecting research scientist questions,
or vice versa-is a fast path to a misaligned conversation.
The research engineer (RE) is an engineer first. Their core job is to implement, debug, and scale research
ideas: modify training loops, wire up new data pipelines, profile GPU utilization, and ensure that an experiment
proposed by a scientist actually runs correctly on a thousand-GPU cluster. The RE interview tests implementa-
tion depth-can you trace through FSDP, explain why a training loss spiked at step 30,000, or spot a numerical


```
1.2 Roles That Require LLM Systems Knowledge
```
instability in a custom kernel? Systems judgment matters: the RE who cannot reason about memory budgets
and parallelism trade-offs will block every experiment they try to run.
The research scientist (RS) is a researcher first. Their core job is to generate hypotheses about what might
make models better-new architectures, training objectives, data mixtures, alignment strategies-and to design
experiments that test those hypotheses rigorously and efficiently. The RS interview tests scientific judgment:
can you critique an ablation design, identify confounders, propose a controlled experiment to isolate the effect
of a curriculum-learning schedule, or interpret a result that partially contradicts your hypothesis? Quantitative
rigor matters: the RS who cannot design a fair comparison or read a scaling-law plot will produce papers that
do not hold up.
Both roles require LLM systems fluency, just at different depths. An RE who cannot reason about inference
latency or training parallelism will be blocked on every implementation. An RS who cannot read a profiler trace
or estimate memory budgets will propose experiments that are not runnable. The technical chapters in this
book-on parallelism, inference, and evaluation-are directly relevant to both: the RE needs implementation-level
depth, the RS needs enough to communicate clearly with the engineering team and to scope experiments that fit
within a given compute budget.
_The interview distinguishes RE from RS by asking whether you built the system or designed what the system
should test._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Tell me about a training run you debugged from first symptom to resolution.” This is a research
engineer question. A strong answer traces symptoms (loss spike, low GPU utilization, OOM), lists hy-
potheses, describes diagnostic steps (profiler, log inspection, checkpoint bisection), and explains the fix.
Vague or high-level answers signal limited hands-on implementation exposure.
“Propose an experiment to determine whether grouped-query attention hurts model quality on
long-context tasks.” This is a research scientist question. A strong answer identifies confounders (train-
ing sequence length, model size, evaluation metric), defines a clean baseline, justifies the compute budget,
and discusses what a null result would mean. Chapter 5 covers grouped-query attention; Chapter 12 covers
evaluation design.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
RE interviews test implementation depth: profiling, debugging, and hands-on experience with distributed
training and inference systems.
RS interviews test research judgment: experimental design, hypothesis generation, and interpreting am-
biguous or contradictory results.
Both roles require LLM systems fluency; the difference is depth of implementation versus depth of sci-
entific reasoning.
If you are unsure which loop you are in, ask the recruiter before preparing-the prep is genuinely different.
```

## Chapter 2 How to Approach an LLM System Design Question

### 2.1 A Repeatable Framework

**2.1.1 Clarify Requirements (Latency, Throughput, Quality, Cost)**
The interview prompt arrives-“design an LLM-powered customer support system.” Before a single com-
ponent is named, a strong candidate pauses and asks four questions. At the senior and staff level, interviewers
watch specifically for this pause; candidates who skip it and dive straight into architecture are signaling that they
have memorized solutions rather than learned to think.
The four axes that every LLM system lives on are latency, throughput, quality, and cost. These are not
platitudes; each has a concrete definition that will drive every downstream decision you make.
**Latency** has two distinct flavors in LLM serving. Time-to-first-token (TTFT) measures how long a user
waits before any output appears-this is dominated by the prefill step, which processes the full prompt in one
parallel forward pass and is compute-bound. Per-token latency (decode latency) measures how quickly subse-
quent tokens arrive-this is dominated by the autoregressive decode loop, which is memory-bandwidth-bound
because model weights and the KV cache must traverse the memory hierarchy once per generated token. Con-
flating TTFT with decode latency is one of the most common interview errors; they respond to entirely different
optimizations. We derive the arithmetic behind both in Chapter 7.
**Throughput** measures tokens generated per second across all concurrent users, and it is the number that
determines your inference bill at scale. Higher throughput generally requires larger batch sizes, which increases
per-request latency. This tension-batching as the lever between latency-optimized and throughput-optimized
operating points-is the central trade-off in LLM serving.
**Quality** sets the floor below which no amount of speed matters. Quality requirements dictate model size,
which sets the memory footprint, which in turn constrains the batch size achievable on a given hardware bud-
get. A requirement for GPT-4-class output quality effectively forces you onto a large model and limits your
throughput options from the start.
**Cost** ties the other three together. A 70B model serving a 200 ms TTFT SLO on H100s implies a funda-
mentally different cost envelope than a 7B model with a two-second tolerance. Surfacing cost early prevents
designs that are technically correct but operationally unshippable.
Interviewers want to hear you name these four axes and immediately note which ones are in tension for the
specific scenario given. _Clarifying requirements is not housekeeping-it is the first technical decision, because
every architecture choice is a trade-off between latency, throughput, quality, and cost._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“We’re building a real-time coding assistant. Walk me through how you’d design the serving stack.”
A strong answer first asks: What is the TTFT SLO? Is usage interactive or batch? What quality bar? The
answer skeleton names TTFT (sub-200 ms is typical for autocomplete), per-token latency, and concurrent
user count before touching any component. The technical depth for meeting those SLOs lives in Chapter 7.
“How would you size the inference fleet for a new chat product launching with 10M daily active
users?” A strong answer immediately converts DAU to peak requests per second, estimates average
```

```
2.1 A Repeatable Framework
```
```
prompt and completion lengths to derive a tokens-per-second demand figure, then works backward to a
hardware configuration. Candidates who jump to “use an H100” without this derivation fail the follow-up.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Ask for the latency SLO before naming any architecture; TTFT and per-token decode latency are separate
problems with separate solutions.
Throughput and per-request latency trade against each other via batch size-name this tension explicitly
and early.
Quality requirements set the model size, which sets the memory budget, which constrains achievable batch
size and throughput.
Cost is the constraint that forces a choice between the above; surfacing it in the requirements phase prevents
designs that cannot be shipped.
```
**2.1.2 Sketch the End-to-End Pipeline**
After requirements are on the board, the next thing an interviewer watches for is whether you can draw the
right boxes in the right order. Many candidates jump immediately to optimizations-quantization, speculative
decoding, model compression-before they have established the baseline pipeline. That inversion signals pattern-
matching, not understanding; experienced interviewers catch it within the first minute.
Every autoregressive LLM serving system has two distinct computational phases, and your whiteboard
diagram must show both before you say anything else.
The **prefill** phase receives the raw prompt tokens and processes them in a single forward pass through the
model. Because all tokens are known upfront, this pass is fully parallelizable across the sequence dimension-
structurally identical to a training-time forward pass. Prefill is compute-bound: given a sufficiently long prompt,
the arithmetic intensity is high enough to saturate the GPU’s matrix-multiply units. The outputs of prefill are
two things: the next-token logit (from which the first generated token is sampled) and the **KV cache** -the key
and value tensors for every attention layer, written to GPU memory so that decode steps do not recompute them
from scratch.
The **decode** phase generates the response token by token. Each step takes the previously generated token,
runs it through the full model, reads the accumulated KV cache from high-bandwidth memory, and samples
the next token. Because only one new token is processed per step, the matrix multiplications against the model
weights reduce to matrix-vector products-the worst-case scenario for arithmetic intensity. Decode is memory-
bandwidth-bound: speed is gated by how fast model weights and KV cache can be streamed from HBM, not by
the GPU’s compute throughput. We derive the exact bound in Chapter 7.
The sketch should also include the **serving layer** : a scheduler that accepts incoming requests, forms batches
(continuous batching is the industry standard), routes them to prefill and decode workers, and manages KV cache
memory. The KV cache is the resource that sets the effective batch size ceiling; its size grows linearly with
sequence length, number of attention layers, and number of KV heads. Interviewers at frontier labs expect you
to know that KV cache pressure-not FLOPs-is usually the binding constraint on how many concurrent requests
you can serve. Chapter 8 covers KV cache sizing arithmetic in full.
Once the baseline pipeline is on the board, you can layer in optimizations in priority order: architecture
choices that shrink the KV cache (grouped-query attention, multi-head latent attention), quantization to reduce
memory bandwidth pressure, and speculative decoding to hide decode latency. Presenting optimizations before


```
2.2 Trade-Off Axes You Must Name
```
the pipeline is the canonical pitfall; presenting them as motivated responses to the constraints you have just
identified is what separates candidates who have built these systems from those who have only read about them.
_Draw prefill and decode as separate boxes with separate performance characteristics before you say a
single word about optimization._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Walk me through what happens when a user sends a prompt to a production LLM API.” A strong
answer covers tokenization, prefill (compute-bound, KV cache written to HBM), the autoregressive de-
code loop (memory-bound, KV cache read each step), detokenization, and the serving scheduler that
batches concurrent requests. Technical depth on each stage lives in Chapters 7 and 8.
“Where would you look first if users were reporting high latency?” A strong answer immediately asks
which latency-TTFT or per-token-then diagnoses accordingly: high TTFT points to a prefill bottleneck
(prompt too long, batch too large, insufficient compute provisioning), while high per-token latency points
to a decode bottleneck (KV cache pressure, memory bandwidth saturation, or a batch size that exceeds
what the memory hierarchy can sustain).
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) are distinct phases with different bottlenecks; al-
ways draw them as separate boxes.
The KV cache is the bridge between phases and the primary memory consumer; sizing it is a required
step in any capacity plan.
Continuous batching at the serving layer is the standard mechanism for maximizing GPU utilization across
requests with varying lengths and arrival times.
Present the baseline pipeline first, then optimizations as targeted responses to specific constraints-sequencing
signals fluency to interviewers.
```
### 2.2 Trade-Off Axes You Must Name

**2.2.1 Compute vs. Memory vs. Bandwidth**
A design interview turns on the moment you identify the real bottleneck. Most engineers, when asked how
to speed up a serving endpoint, jump to “add more GPUs” or “use a smaller model” - both potentially valid,
but both bypassing the diagnostic question that unlocks everything else: is the system limited by arithmetic
throughput, memory capacity, or memory bandwidth? Those three constraints behave differently, respond to
different interventions, and show up in different parts of the stack. Conflating them is one of the most common
ways to lose credibility in a systems round.
A GPU has two fundamental performance ceilings. The first is compute throughput, measured in floating-
point operations per second. The second is memory bandwidth, measured in bytes per second. Any given oper-
ation sits in one of two regimes: _compute-bound_ , meaning the arithmetic units are the bottleneck, or _memory-
bandwidth-bound_ , meaning the time is dominated by streaming data through HBM. The ratio of these two hard-
ware numbers - roughly 300 FLOPs per byte on a current-generation data-center GPU - defines a ridge point.


```
2.2 Trade-Off Axes You Must Name
```
Operations with arithmetic intensity above this ridge are compute-bound; operations below it are memory-bound
no matter how many FLOPs they perform. We derive this number precisely in Chapter 8.
Matrix multiplications at large batch sizes land firmly above the ridge. That is why training and prefill
are fast: the GPU’s multiplier arrays stay saturated. Token generation is the mirror image. Each decode step
processes one new token, which reduces the weight-matrix multiply to a matrix-vector product - arithmetic
intensity close to 1 FLOPs/byte, deep in memory-bound territory. This is the root cause of slow generation, and
it is structural: no amount of faster arithmetic fixes a problem caused by HBM bandwidth. The intervention has
to touch memory movement.
Memory capacity is a third, distinct constraint. KV cache grows with batch size and sequence length;
once it exhausts VRAM, you cannot increase the batch regardless of how much arithmetic headroom remains.
Techniques like grouped-query attention and quantization are as much about fitting more sequences into a fixed
memory budget as they are about raw speed.
_When a system feels slow, the first question is always: which ceiling are we hitting? The answer determines
whether the fix is a kernel rewrite, a memory layout change, or an architectural trade-off._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“GPU utilization is at 80% but token generation is still slow. Where would you look first?” A strong
answer distinguishes compute utilization from memory bandwidth utilization. High compute utilization
during generation just means the GPU is busy waiting on HBM reads - the real bottleneck is bandwidth,
and the path to improvement is reducing memory traffic, not adding FLOPs. The technical depth for this
lives in Chapter 9.
“A normalization layer consumes 25% of wall-clock time but less than 1% of total FLOPs. How do
you speed it up?” The answer requires recognizing that normalization is memory-bandwidth-bound, so
FLOP-reduction techniques are irrelevant; the leverage is in cutting parameter loads per call (RMSNorm
over LayerNorm) and fusing kernel launches to eliminate round-trips to HBM.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Every LLM operation is either compute-bound or memory-bandwidth-bound; the boundary is set by the
hardware’s arithmetic intensity ridge point, not by the number of FLOPs.
Training and prefill are compute-bound at practical batch sizes; token generation is memory-bandwidth-
bound by construction - these require different optimization strategies.
Memory capacity (fitting the model and KV cache in VRAM) is a third, separate constraint that limits
batch size independently of bandwidth or compute.
TFLOP ratings sell GPUs; memory bandwidth and capacity are the operative constraints for inference
engineering.
```
**2.2.2 Quality vs. Latency vs. Cost**
Every LLM serving decision eventually compresses to three numbers: how good the output is, how fast it
arrives, and how much it costs per token. In practice, you can aggressively optimize two of these; the third tends
to move against you. Interviewers at frontier labs want to see that you have internalized this triangle before you
draw a single box in your architecture diagram - because candidates who skip it waste fifteen minutes proposing
solutions that are technically interesting but wrong for the stated problem.


```
2.2 Trade-Off Axes You Must Name
```
Latency and throughput are not the same metric, and conflating them is the most common error in LLM
serving discussions. Latency is the wall-clock time a single user waits - time-to-first-token (TTFT) for the
prompt-encoding phase, then per-token decode latency during generation. Throughput is aggregate tokens gen-
erated per second across all concurrent users. These optimize in opposite directions: maximizing through-
put requires large batch sizes and full GPU saturation; minimizing latency often means small batches, aggres-
sive prefetching, and accepting lower utilization. A system cannot simultaneously be optimal at both without
workload-specific scheduling that separates the two traffic classes.
Quality is the axis that is easiest to accidentally sacrifice. Quantizing weights from BF16 to INT4 can
triple throughput; it also measurably degrades accuracy on multi-step reasoning, often in ways that aggregate
benchmarks do not surface. Grouped-query attention reduces the KV cache by a factor of eight with negligible
benchmark loss - but “negligible on standard benchmarks” is a claim about a distribution of tasks, not a guarantee
about your specific workload. Part IX covers how to design evaluations that catch these gaps before they reach
production.
Cost is the integrating metric. It is not the same as latency, though the two are correlated. A technique that
saves 30% of memory per sequence can double the batch size that fits on a single GPU, halving per-token cost

- a much larger lever than shaving a few milliseconds off the decode loop. The arithmetic for a specific model
and hardware configuration is in Chapter 15 ; the key habit is to always convert architectural decisions into a
per-token-cost estimate before committing to them.
    The vocabulary for this axis in interviews: TTFT (latency of the prefill phase, compute-bound, difficult to
compress beyond model size), decode latency (per-token, memory-bandwidth-bound, the target of most serving
optimizations), throughput (tokens/second aggregate, optimized by batching and hardware utilization), and cost-
per-token (the business metric that synthesizes all three). Speculative decoding (Chapter 18 ) is notable precisely
because it improves latency without degrading quality - an exact sample from the target distribution at draft-
model speed when the acceptance rate is high.
    _Name the metric you are optimizing before you propose a solution; an interviewer who has to ask “are you
optimizing latency or throughput?” has already registered a gap in your systems thinking._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“We are building a real-time coding assistant. What serving configuration would you recommend?” A
strong answer names TTFT and per-token decode latency as the primary metrics, not aggregate through-
put; proposes small batch sizes or continuous batching with tight SLOs; discusses the quality floor before
deciding quantization aggressiveness. The tradeoff details live in Chapter 19.
“How would you serve the same 70B model to both an interactive product and an overnight batch pipeline?”
A strong answer proposes separate serving paths: the interactive path optimizes latency (smaller batches,
possibly speculative decoding), the batch path optimizes throughput and cost (larger batches, more ag-
gressive quantization, relaxed TTFT SLO). A single serving configuration that tries to satisfy both will
be suboptimal on both.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Latency and throughput optimize in opposite directions; always establish which one your design is tar-
geting before proposing anything.
```

```
2.3 Common Pitfalls in Answers
```
```
Quality degradation from quantization and architectural shortcuts is real and workload-dependent - ag-
gregate benchmark numbers are an unreliable proxy for production quality on specific tasks.
Cost-per-token is the integrating metric: batch size, quantization, and model architecture all map onto
it differently, and the largest levers are usually in batch size and memory efficiency rather than kernel
micro-optimization.
TTFT, decode latency, and throughput are three distinct quantities; using them interchangeably signals a
gap in serving systems understanding.
```
### 2.3 Common Pitfalls in Answers

**2.3.1 Cargo-Culting Numbers Without Derivation**
A candidate writes “140 GB” next to their 70B model box, the interviewer nods, and then asks where that
number comes from. The candidate pauses. This moment - memorized figure, no derivation - is one of the most
reliable separators between senior candidates and everyone else in LLM system design interviews. It is worse
than not citing the number at all, because it signals that you treat estimates as incantations rather than tools.
Virtually every number worth citing in an LLM system interview flows from four first-principles chains:
bytes per parameter at a stated dtype, the 6 N Dapproximation for total training FLOPs, the per-token KV
cache footprint from layer count and key-value head geometry, and arithmetic intensity as the ratio of FLOPs
to memory bytes transferred. These four starting points, combined with the hardware specs on the whiteboard,
reproduce almost any published figure in under a minute of algebra. Candidates who own the derivation can
update their answer the instant an interviewer changes one input; candidates who memorized the output cannot.
The Chinchilla 20-to-1 token-to-parameter ratio is the most common cargo-cult target. Production scaling
teams at multiple major labs have re-derived this number and obtained answers that range from roughly 40-
to-1 to nearly 200-to-1, depending on data quality, architecture efficiency, and the serving economics of the
final model. Those teams do not inherit a ratio from a paper; they build small proxy models, vary compute
allocation across isoFLOP slices, fit the minimum, and read the answer. The derivation lives in Chapter 6; the
interview expectation is that you know the analysis exists, can name the variables that shift the answer, and are
not surprised when the answer differs from 20.
The danger of a memorized number is not that it is wrong - it is often approximately right. The danger is
that you have no idea which assumptions it rests on, so the moment the interviewer changes one you are stuck.
“How does your memory estimate change if you switch to FP8 inference?” “What if you add grouped-query
attention with eight key-value heads?” “What if context length doubles?” Each of these invalidates a memorized
answer while posing no problem for a derived one.
_A number you can derive is worth ten you have memorized._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Estimate the memory footprint of a 70B model during inference with a batch of 32 and a 4,096-
token context.” A strong answer starts from bytes per parameter at the stated dtype, then adds the KV
cache term - proportional to batch size, context length, number of key-value heads, and layer count - and
shows which term dominates. It also notes that switching from BF16 to FP8 halves the parameter footprint
but does not change the KV cache unless the cache itself is quantized, and that grouped-query attention
directly reduces the second term. The derivation for this lives in Chapter 8.
```

```
2.3 Common Pitfalls in Answers
```
```
“How many H100s do you need to train a 7B model on 1 trillion tokens in two weeks?” A strong
answer derives total training FLOPs from the 6 N Dapproximation, converts to GPU-hours using a realistic
model FLOP utilization (35-50% is typical in practice), and arrives at a card-count before ever citing a
benchmark number. Chapter 5 derives the 6 N Drule and calibrates MFU against published runs.
The technical depth for both estimates lives in Chapter 5 (training arithmetic) and Chapter 8 (inference
arithmetic).
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Know the derivation of three core estimates: parameter memory at a stated dtype, training FLOPs from
model size and token count, and KV cache memory per token per layer.
State every assumption before giving a number; when an interviewer changes one, update the answer in
thirty seconds.
The Chinchilla 20-to-1 ratio is a starting point, not a law - production teams re-derive it and get different
answers depending on data quality and serving requirements.
Approximate arithmetic done live and transparently is more persuasive than a precise number with no
reasoning attached.
```
**2.3.2 Ignoring the Inference Side of the System**
A candidate spends forty minutes on a compelling training pipeline - data mix, tokenizer, architecture
choices, parallelism strategy - then closes with “and we serve it with a standard inference server.” The inter-
viewer asks: “What is your expected time-to-first-token at P95?” Silence. This is the second major pitfall:
treating inference as a deployment detail rather than a first-class design constraint.
Training is a one-time capital expense. Inference is the operating cost you pay every day for every user,
and at production scale it routinely exceeds total training cost within months of a launch. The candidate who
designs only for training has optimized the wrong half.
The split between _prefill_ and _decode_ is the central concept. Prefill encodes the full prompt in a single parallel
pass - it is compute-bound, uses the GPU efficiently, and determines time-to-first-token. Decode generates one
token per step, reading the full set of model weights from GPU memory on every step while performing a
tiny amount of arithmetic. For a single sequence, the ratio of FLOPs to bytes transferred is approximately
one - far below the hundreds-to-one threshold at which a modern accelerator is compute-saturated. Decode is
therefore memory-bandwidth-bound no matter how large the model, and essentially nothing about the serving
stack changes that physics.
The KV cache is the primary constraint on serving batch size. Every live sequence occupies a per-layer, per-
head cache that grows with context length. As batch size increases, the cache grows proportionally and eventually
exhausts GPU memory before compute becomes the bottleneck. This is why grouped-query attention and multi-
head latent attention exist: they reduce the bytes stored per sequence, allowing more concurrent sequences and
improving throughput. These are not training-time curiosities - they are direct responses to a serving constraint,
and the decision to use them must be made before training begins, because it cannot be patched afterward.
This is the deeper trap: architecture decisions made at training time lock in your serving economics. The
number of key-value heads, the maximum context length, the parameter dtype - all are fixed before you write a
line of serving code, and all directly determine KV cache footprint, achievable batch size, and cost-per-token.


```
2.3 Common Pitfalls in Answers
```
Surfacing the inference constraint before committing to an architecture is not premature optimization; it is the
correct order of operations.
_Any system design that ends with “deploy to an inference server” is incomplete._

**How This Shows Up**

```
“Walk me through serving a 70B model to 10,000 concurrent users.” A strong answer immediately
names the latency-versus-throughput trade-off, sizes the KV cache per request, identifies how batch size
is constrained by total GPU memory, proposes continuous batching to avoid idle compute between re-
quests, and raises head-structure choices that reduce cache pressure per sequence. The arithmetic lives in
Chapter 8.
“Your architecture team wants to reduce key-value heads from 32 to 8 using grouped-query atten-
tion. What does that do to serving costs?” A strong answer derives the KV cache reduction directly:
cache per sequence shrinks by 4 , so the maximum batch size at fixed memory roughly quadruples,
cutting cost-per-token by roughly the same factor at throughput-limited operating points - while leaving
time-to-first-token essentially unchanged. Chapter 8 carries the full derivation.
The technical depth for both questions lives in Chapter 8 (inference arithmetic, KV cache sizing, batching
strategies).
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Name the prefill/decode split early; each phase is bottlenecked differently and therefore has different levers.
KV cache memory, not parameter count, is usually the binding constraint on serving batch size; size it
explicitly before finalizing the architecture.
Head structure, context length, and dtype are training-time decisions with direct serving-economics con-
sequences - raise these constraints before architecture is finalized.
State at least one latency SLO and one throughput target before ending any serving discussion; “standard
inference server” is not an answer.
```

## Chapter 3 Transformer Architecture Interview Essentials

### 3.1 The Baseline Decoder-Only Transformer

**3.1.1 Residual Stream, Attention, and MLP Blocks**
The opening question in virtually every LLM architecture deep-dive is some form of “walk me through the
forward pass of a decoder-only transformer.” At mid-level, interviewers want to hear you trace the data flow;
at senior level, they want you to estimate the parameter budget per block at a realistic model size, explain why
the two sub-blocks are sequenced the way they are, and articulate what goes wrong if you change the structure.
Getting this right is the baseline for every architecture discussion that follows.
A decoder-only transformer processesninput tokens, each represented as ad-dimensional vector. These
vectors form the _residual stream_ - a horizontal channel of activations that flows from the bottom of the network
to the top. The defining property of the residual stream is that neither attention nor the MLP writes directly over
the previous layer’s output: both read from the stream and _add_ their outputs back into it. The stream carries the
cumulative representation of each token from embedding to logit head.
Formally, a single layerℓexecutes two sequential updates:
a(ℓ)=x(ℓ−1)+Attn(ℓ)

_The residual stream is the skeleton of the network: every sub-block reads from it and adds an increment, so
a model with zero-initialized sub-block outputs is a pure identity - this is what makes stacks of 32 or 96 layers
trainable from random initialization._
Residual connections solve gradient vanishing. Without an additive skip, the gradient of the loss with
respect to the activations at layerℓrequires a chain ofLℓJacobians, which generically collapses to near-zero
at depth. With the skip, the gradient sees a direct path of ones alongside each Jacobian chain, guaranteeing a
non-vanishing lower bound. This is why transformers can sustain depths of 80 or 96 layers without the careful
cell-state engineering that LSTMs relied on.
The functional division between attention and MLP reflects a genuine computational separation. Attention
_aggregates across positions_ : it lets each token construct a weighted mixture of all other tokens’ representations,
gathering context from wherever it is most informative. The MLP _processes per-position_ : once a token has


```
3.1 The Baseline Decoder-Only Transformer
```
gathered its context, the MLP mixes information across the feature dimension of that single vector. Stacking
the two repeatedly allows the network to alternate between “gather context” and “refine representation.” This
intuition is supported by mechanistic analyses showing that factual associations tend to live in MLP weights,
while syntactic and positional relationships live in attention patterns.
The overwhelming consensus is to run attention before MLP in series. A minority of models (GPT-J,
PaLM) explored _parallel layers_ where both sub-blocks read the same normalized input simultaneously and their
outputs are summed. Parallel layout can yield a roughly 15% wall-clock speedup at large scale because both
sets of projections can be fused into a single large matrix multiply against a shared normalized input. However,
the parallel layout means the MLP never sees the attention output within the same layer - a mild expressiveness
loss. Most frontier models released after 2023 have reverted to the serial default, which I read as evidence that
the expressiveness loss is real enough to matter at the model sizes where these labs operate.
