**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through the forward pass of a 7B decoder-only model. How many parameters are in the
attention block versus the MLP?” A strong answer names all four projection matrices in attention, all
three in SwiGLU, derives the67M and135M figures, and explains why the MLP is roughly 2 larger.
A weak answer stops at “it has multi-head attention and a feed-forward network” without numbers.
“Why is the residual connection important? What breaks without it?” Strong answer: gradient
propagation. Without the additive skip, the gradient at layerℓinvolves a product ofLℓJacobians that
collapses to near-zero at depth; with the skip, there is always a direct gradient path of approximately ones
from the top to every earlier layer.
Senior follow-up: “Some models run attention and MLP in parallel instead of in series. What do
you trade off, and when would you choose parallel?” Senior answer: parallel layout fuses both sets of
projections against the same normalized input in a single large matrix multiply, saving memory round-
trips and yielding roughly 15% wall-clock speedup when kernels are properly written (as demonstrated in
PaLM). The cost is that the MLP sees the pre-attention representation rather than the post-attention one -
the MLP and attention cannot interact within the same layer. In practice, serial is the safer default unless
you have custom kernel support and have ablated quality impact at your target model size; most post-2023
frontier models have reverted to serial for exactly this reason.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The residual stream is the identity highway: every sub-block reads from it and adds an increment, enabling
clean gradient flow through networks of 32-128 layers.
Each layer contains two sub-blocks in series: multi-head attention (mixes across positions) followed by
an MLP (mixes across features at each position).
For a 7B model withd= 4096,df f 11008 : each layer holds67M attention parameters and135M
MLP parameters - the MLP is roughly 2 the attention block by parameter count.
SwiGLU MLPs use three weight matrices and requiredf f =b 8 d/ 3 cto stay parameter-matched with a
two-matrix ReLU MLP at 4 d; getting the sizing wrong inflates the model by50%.
Use serial layers and drop all bias terms by default; parallel layers require verified kernel-level speedups
and quality ablations before committing.
```
**3.1.2 Pre-Norm vs. Post-Norm and Why It Matters**
The question “where does the LayerNorm go in your transformer block?” reads like trivia until you have
watched a training run crash after a week of GPU-hours because gradient norms spiked and refused to come
back down. Normalization placement directly controls training stability at scale, and every frontier lab I am
aware of has converged on the same answer. Interviewers at these labs use this question to filter candidates who
have only read the original 2017 paper from those who have actually thought about what happens at depth.


```
3.1 The Baseline Decoder-Only Transformer
```
The original transformer applied normalization _after_ each sub-block’s output was added back to the residual
stream - the _post-norm_ convention:

x LayerNorm(x+Attn(x)), x LayerNorm(x+MLP(x))
_Pre-norm_ moves the normalization _before_ the sub-block computation, operating on the residual stream
input prior to branching off to attention or MLP:

a x+Attn(Norm(x)), x a+MLP(Norm(a))
The normalization now sits inside the non-residual branch. The residual stream itself - thexthat accumu-
lates across layers - is never touched by a normalization layer. This single repositioning is the difference between
a network that requires fragile learning-rate warmup to avoid divergence and one that trains stably from step one.
Pre-norm is the universal choice in production models: LLaMA, PaLM, Chinchilla, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek,
Gemma, and virtually every frontier model since GPT-2 uses it. The only notable exception is OPT-350M, which
used post-norm - an artifact widely attributed to an engineering oversight that was never corrected before the
run completed.
_Place the normalization inside the non-residual branch: pre-norm keeps the gradient highway clean, en-
ables stable training without warmup, and is the choice every serious practitioner makes._
The core argument is gradient behavior at depth. With post-norm, the loss gradient traveling back to layer
ℓmust pass through LayerNorm at every layer betweenℓand the top. LayerNorm rescales activations by the
inverse of their empirical standard deviation - a data-dependent quantity that is volatile in early training when
activations have not yet settled. This volatility causes the effective step size at early layers to oscillate by orders
of magnitude from batch to batch, which is why post-norm training famously required careful warmup: you
were buying time for activations to stabilize before the gradient became reliable.
Pre-norm sidesteps this entirely. The residual additionx x+f(Norm(x))means the gradient of the loss
at layerℓalways sees an additive term of 1 from the skip connection, regardless of what the sub-block gradient
looks like. The normalization sits only on the branch and does not obstruct the residual gradient path. At depth
L= 32orL= 96, this difference is the margin between a gradient norm that stays in[0. 1 ,2]throughout training
and one that spikes to 103 and triggers a loss divergence.
Empirical evidence is consistent and old enough to be well-established: training curves from pre-norm
models show lower gradient norm variance, fewer loss spikes, and equivalent or slightly better final loss com-
pared with post-norm models that used careful warmup. Several research teams demonstrated that pre-norm
models can remove the warmup phase entirely and still converge, which simplifies resuming from checkpoints
mid-run.
A newer variant, which I will call the _double-norm_ , adds a second normalization after each sub-block
(before the residual addition) as well as the pre-block norm. Grok-1 and Gemma 2 use this:

```
a x+Norm 2 (Attn(Norm 1 (x)))
```
The logic is that bounding both the input to the sub-block and its output gives two scale control checkpoints
instead of one, providing additional protection against activations exploding inside very large sub-blocks. Early
reports suggest marginal stability gains at very large model sizes (>30B parameters). It adds memory access
overhead (LayerNorm is bandwidth-bound, not compute-bound) but is otherwise a small cost. Double-norm
has not yet displaced plain pre-norm as the community default.


```
3.1 The Baseline Decoder-Only Transformer
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider a 32-layer, 1.3B-parameter model trained with AdamW, peak learning rate 3  10 −^4 , no warmup
schedule, on 100B tokens. Compare the gradient dynamics across three configurations:

Configuration Grad norm at step 500 Stability
-----------------------------------------------------------------
Post-norm, no warmup ~450 (highly variable) Diverges
Post-norm, 2k-step warmup ~12 (settling) Converges
Pre-norm, no warmup ~1.8 (stable from step 1) Converges

Post-norm without warmup diverges reliably: by layer 10, the LayerNorm denominators are fluctuating
because the activations are still in their initial transient. The effective step size at early layers swings by 5 - 10 
per step, causing gradient norms to spike past 102 - 103 within the first thousand steps.
Post-norm with 2,000-step warmup eventually converges because the warmup period allows activations
to settle before the learning rate reaches its peak. But this coupling between normalization placement and the
warmup schedule is a fragile dependency: if you need to restart from a checkpoint (e.g., after a hardware failure),
you must re-warm carefully or risk a second divergence.
Pre-norm without warmup produces gradient norms in the range 0. 1 - 2. 0 from the very first step. The
residual stream accumulates small increments from each sub-block, and the gradient back-propagates through
the skip connections without interference from normalization. You can restart from any checkpoint with a cold
optimizer and the training will resume cleanly.
The practical upshot at scale: at 7B parameters trained on 1T tokens, a single gradient divergence that
requires a rollback and rerun from the last stable checkpoint wastes days of compute on a cluster of 256 H100s.
Pre-norm eliminates an entire class of these failures.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always use pre-norm for new models. There is no empirical justification for post-norm in a fresh training
run. If you inherit a post-norm codebase, do not switch normalization placement mid-training - it changes
the loss landscape and will almost certainly cause a divergence.
Consider double-norm only above  30B parameters. The extra normalization costs additional memory
accesses (LayerNorm is bandwidth-bound; the extra norm adds0.3% wall time per step) and a small
number of additional parameters. Below 30B, plain pre-norm is stable enough that double-norm provides
no measurable benefit. Above 30B, if you are seeing persistent gradient norm spikes despite pre-norm,
double-norm is a reasonable next step before reaching for gradient clipping or modified optimizers.
Never put a normalization layer on the residual stream itself. Any norm that sits on the accumulation
path (i.e., onxbefore the skip addition rather than on the branch input) re-introduces the post-norm
pathology. The identity gradient path is the entire point.
Monitor gradient norms from step 1. With pre-norm and a sane learning rate, gradient norms should
be below 5.0 throughout the first 1,000 steps. If they are not, suspect a normalization placement bug, a
bad initialization scale, or a learning rate that is too high - not a fundamental architecture problem.
Treat pre-norm and RMSNorm as a package deal. The decision of where to place the norm and which
norm to use are distinct but nearly always made together in modern models. Pre-norm with RMSNorm is
the combination that appears in LLaMA, PaLM, Chinchilla, Mistral, and most other frontier open models.
```

```
3.2 Normalization Choices
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Where does the LayerNorm go in a modern transformer block, and why?” A strong answer places
the norm before the sub-block (pre-norm), explains that it keeps the residual stream as a clean gradient
highway, and notes this removes the need for warmup. A weak answer just says “before the block” without
explaining the gradient argument.
“What does the original 2017 transformer do differently, and what problem does that cause?”
Strong answer: post-norm places the normalization after the residual addition, which means the gra-
dient back-propagating to early layers must pass through LayerNorm at every layer. Because LayerNorm
rescales by the inverse standard deviation - a volatile quantity in early training - this corrupts the effective
step size at early layers and requires careful warmup to avoid divergence.
Senior follow-up: “Gemma 2 applies a LayerNorm both before and after each sub-block (double-
norm). What problem does that solve, and what does it cost?” Senior answer: double-norm bounds
both the input to the sub-block and its output before re-adding to the stream. At very large scale, sub-blocks
can still produce large-magnitude outputs even when their inputs are normalized; bounding the output
provides a second safety checkpoint. The cost is extra memory bandwidth (LayerNorm is bandwidth-
bound, not flop-bound - each extra norm adds one additional read/write pass over aRn×dactivation
tensor per layer), plus the additional learned scale parametersγ. At 7B parameters this cost is negligible;
at 70B or 100B, you should ablate whether the stability gain justifies it rather than adopting it by default.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Pre-norm applies normalization before each sub-block, keeping the residual stream as a clean identity path
for gradients; post-norm applies it after the residual addition, forcing gradients through a normalization
at every layer.
Post-norm requires careful learning-rate warmup to avoid divergence; pre-norm trains stably from step
one and allows cold restarts from any checkpoint.
Pre-norm is universal in modern frontier models: LLaMA, PaLM, Chinchilla, Mistral, DeepSeek, Gemma,
and essentially every open model released since GPT-2.
Double-norm (pre- and post-block norms, used in Gemma 2 and Grok-1) adds a second stability check-
point for very large models; it is not yet the default and costs extra memory bandwidth.
The gradient norm should be below 5.0 from step 1 with pre-norm and a sane learning rate; values above
that signal a normalization placement bug or initialization issue, not a fundamental architecture problem.
```
### 3.2 Normalization Choices

**3.2.1 LayerNorm vs. RMSNorm**
In a system design round at a frontier lab, you will almost certainly be asked why your training stack
uses RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm. The question sounds trivial - one formula versus another - but the real
interview signal is whether you can connect normalization choices to memory bandwidth, training stability, and
the arithmetic intensity of GPU kernels. This comes up at the mid-to-senior level whenever hardware efficiency
enters the conversation, and getting the answer right separates engineers who have profiled real training runs
from those who have only read the paper abstracts.


```
3.2 Normalization Choices
```
LayerNorm normalizes each activation vector by its empirical mean and standard deviation, then applies a
learned affine transform:
LayerNorm(x)i=γi

RMSNorm drops mean-centering entirely and eliminates the shift parameter:

```

Only one statistic (the root-mean-square) is computed, and onlyγ 2 Rdis loaded. Theβparameter vanishes.
On paper, the FLOP difference is negligible - normalization operations are less than 0.2% of the total FLOPs
in a transformer. The argument for RMSNorm is not arithmetic; it is memory. Careful profiling (Ivanov et al.,
2023) shows that normalization kernels account for roughly 25% of wall-clock runtime despite their vanishing
FLOP share, because they are _memory-bandwidth-bound_ : every scalar inγandβmust be staged through HBM
on every call. Halving the parameter count directly halves that memory traffic.
_The case for RMSNorm is a memory-bandwidth argument dressed up as a simplification argument: fewer
parameters to load per call, fewer operations per element, and empirically indistinguishable model quality._
GPU computation is dominated by two bottlenecks: arithmetic throughput (FLOPs) and memory band-
width (bytes/s). Matrix multiplies are compute-rooflined at large batch sizes - the GPU is limited by how fast
it can multiply, not by how fast it can read weights. Normalization kernels are the opposite: they touch each
activation element a small, fixed number of times, so the runtime is bounded by how fast the GPU can stream
data through HBM. On an H100, peak compute is around 989 TFLOP/s (bf16) while peak memory bandwidth
is 3.35 TB/s; the ratio is roughly 300 . Any kernel that is not doing at least 300 FLOPs per byte loaded will hit
the memory wall, not the compute ceiling. Normalization is firmly in that regime.
LayerNorm’sβparameter is small in count but adds a full load-and-multiply pass overdscalars per invo-
cation. For a model withd= 4096and 64 normalization calls per forward pass (32 layers2 norms), that is
64  4096  2 bytes 524 KB of parameter tensor loads per sample per forward pass in bf16, entirely eliminated
by RMSNorm.
The quality story is equally clean. Narang et al. (2020) ran controlled ablations on a transformer of com-
parable scale and found that RMSNorm reaches the same final cross-entropy as LayerNorm while running at
3.68 steps/second versus 3.50 - a free 5% throughput improvement. The LLaMA family, PaLM, Chinchilla,
Mistral, and DeepSeek have all converged on RMSNorm. The near-consensus explanation: when pre-norm
placement already keeps the residual stream well-conditioned before each sub-block, the mean of the activation
vector entering the norm is already close to zero, so mean-centering provides negligible correction.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B decoder-only model:d= 4096, 32 layers, batch sizeB= 4, sequence lengthT = 2048,
bf16 precision. Each transformer layer has two normalization calls (pre-attention and pre-MLP). Per call:

1. **LayerNorm:** compute mean (dadditions), compute variance ( 2 dmultiply-adds), normalize ( 2 dops),
    applyγandβ( 2 dmultiply-adds). Total: 7 dscalar ops. Memory loads: 2 dbytes forγ, 2 dbytes forβ
    (bf16).


```
3.2 Normalization Choices
```
2. **RMSNorm:** compute RMS (dsquares, one sum, one sqrt), normalize (ddivisions), applyγ(dmultiply-
    adds). Total: 3 dscalar ops. Memory loads: 2 dbytes forγonly.
Across the entire forward pass: 32 2 = 64normalization calls. Theβremoval saves 64  4096  2 bytes=
524 KB per sample per forward pass. AtB= 4, that is roughly 2 MB per training step eliminated from HBM
traffic. At 10,000 steps/hour, this is 20 GB/hour of avoided memory movement - not the dominant cost, but
meaningful when normalization is otherwise consuming 25% of wall time.
The throughput difference of 5% reported in ablations maps directly onto this: if normalization is 25% of
runtime and RMSNorm cuts its overhead in half, the net gain is 0. 25  0 .5 = 12.5%reduction in normalization
time, which translates to approximately 3-5% overall throughput improvement accounting for the compute-
rooflined portions of the forward pass.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Default to RMSNorm. Every major model family released since 2022 that publishes architecture details
uses it. Cohere Command A and Command R+ are the notable exception - they retain LayerNorm for
undisclosed reasons. Unless you have a specific compatibility constraint, there is no reason to start a new
run with LayerNorm.
Do not re-introduce β. Some codebases add a bias back to RMSNorm for “completeness.” This negates
the memory saving and provides no quality benefit - the downstream linear layers already supply the affine
freedom thatβwould add.
Watch ε at bf16. The defaultε= 10−^5 can underflow in bf16 for activation vectors with very small
magnitudes, producing a near-zero denominator. Useε= 10−^6 and monitor for NaN spikes on the first
1B tokens; if they appear, increaseεto 10 −^8 in fp32 accumulation mode before blaming the optimizer.
Fused kernels are mandatory at scale. A naive PyTorch RMSNorm implementation still issues separate
HBM transactions for each element-wise op. Production runs use Triton or cuDNN-fused kernels; unfused
implementations can cost 2 - 3 the wall time of the fused version, erasing the RMSNorm advantage
entirely.
LoRA adapters on RMSNorm backbones need explicit bias handling. When fine-tuning with LoRA
or prefix tuning, adapter layers sometimes implicitly assume aβterm exists. If your adapter introduces
a bias, verify it is absorbing the role ofβintentionally; accidental double-counting or missing shift can
cause subtle drift in generation quality that is hard to diagnose.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why do modern LLMs use RMSNorm instead of LayerNorm?” A strong answer names both the memory-
bandwidth argument (normalization is25% of runtime despite<0.2% of FLOPs) and the quality-parity
finding, and cites at least two concrete model families that made the switch. Answering only “it’s simpler”
scores mid-level at best.
“If RMSNorm drops mean-centering, doesn’t that hurt models where activation distributions are not zero-
mean?” The correct answer is that pre-norm placement ensures the residual stream entering each normal-
ization is already regulated by upstream norms, so the empirical mean is close to zero at initialization and
remains close throughout training. Mean-centering provides negligible correction in that regime, which
is exactly what the ablations confirm.
```

```
3.2 Normalization Choices
```
```
Senior follow-up: “Walk me through the arithmetic intensity of a LayerNorm kernel versus a matrix
multiply. Why does the roofline model determine how much you can save by switching to RMSNorm?”
A senior answer articulates the roofline model: LayerNorm is bandwidth-rooflined (low arithmetic inten-
sity), so reducing memory accesses directly reduces wall time proportionally. A matrix multiply at large
batch size is compute-rooflined, so an equivalent FLOP reduction there yields a much smaller real-world
speedup. The implication is that optimizing memory-bound kernels gives super-linear returns relative to
their FLOP share.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
RMSNorm drops mean-centering and the shift parameterβ; it computes only RMS(x)and applies a
single learned scaleγ.
Normalization kernels are memory-bandwidth-bound: they are0.2% of FLOPs but25% of runtime.
The win from RMSNorm is in memory traffic, not arithmetic.
Published ablations show quality parity with LayerNorm and a roughly 5% throughput improvement; the
LLaMA family, PaLM, Chinchilla, Mistral, and DeepSeek all converged on RMSNorm.
Do not addβback, and always use fused kernels - naive implementations negate both the memory and
arithmetic savings.
The deeper lesson: once a model is architecture-stable, the bottleneck often moves from FLOPs to memory
movement. Normalization is the canonical example of an operation that is cheap in FLOPs and expensive
in bandwidth.
```
**3.2.2 QK-Norm and Stability Interventions**
At some point in every large training run, you will open your monitoring dashboard and see a gradient
norm plot that looks like a seismograph during an earthquake - sudden spikes of 10 or 100 the baseline,
occasionally followed by NaN propagation that ends the run. Training instability is one of the most expensive
failure modes in LLM development, capable of wasting weeks of GPU time and hundreds of thousands of dollars
on a single diverged job. Knowing which architectural interventions actually prevent these spikes, and being
able to explain _why_ they work at a mechanistic level, is a senior-level topic that surfaces in both system design
rounds and deep technical interviews at labs actively training at scale.
The two locations in a transformer where numeric instability most commonly originates are the _attention
softmax_ and the _output softmax_. Both involve exponentiating logits that can grow without bound during train-
ing, producing either overflow, near-zero denominators, or pathologically peaked distributions that starve most
positions of gradient signal.

_In every case the goal is identical: keep inputs to any softmax bounded in magnitude so that neither the

Softmax is the only non-linear operation in the standard transformer that can be driven to numerical failure
by the surrounding linear algebra. A weight matrix with bounded spectral norm produces bounded outputs if
its inputs are bounded - but a softmax with growing logit magnitudes produces exponentially larger activations
regardless of what came before it. QK-norm breaks this dependency: regardless of howWQandWKevolve
during optimization, the vectors fed to the dot product are normalized to unit scale, bounding pre-softmax logits

The contrast with gradient clipping is instructive. Clipping intervenes in the backward pass after a spike
has already occurred; the forward-pass activations that triggered the spike are already resident in the residual
stream and will propagate to downstream layers before the next update corrects them. QK-norm and z-loss act
in the forward pass, preventing the spike from occurring in the first place. For runs longer than100B tokens,
this distinction matters: each uncaught spike degrades optimizer state in ways that take many subsequent steps
to wash out.
Z-loss and QK-norm address orthogonal failure modes. Z-loss controls the global scale of output logits
(acrossV  32 , 000 - 128 , 000 vocabulary items), where failure is typically a slow drift. QK-norm controls
attention logit magnitude (acrossTpositions), where failure is typically a sudden spike. Running both provides
defense in depth.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use QK-norm and z-loss together, not as alternatives. They target different softmaxes and different
failure modes. A model with QK-norm but no z-loss can still diverge through the output logit path as
training progresses and the output weight matrix scale drifts upward.
Set α= 10−^4 for z-loss as your starting point. This is the PaLM coefficient and has been reproduced
by DCLM and OLMo 2. Raising it above 10 −^3 will hurt token-level cross-entropy because the model
is penalized for concentrating probability mass, which it must do to make high-confidence predictions.
Lowering below 10 −^6 provides no measurable stabilization.
Do not add logit soft-capping without ablating. NVIDIA’s ablation found that soft-capping atc= 50
worsened perplexity by 0.1-0.3 points on their setup, while QK-norm improved it by a similar margin.
Gemma 2 reports benefit from soft-capping. The inconsistency likely stems from interactions with the
Adam optimizer’s second-moment estimates: tanh distorts the gradient landscape in a way that depends
on the learning rate schedule and model scale. Treat it as a model-specific knob.
Consider the double-norm pattern for very large runs. Grok and Gemma 2 place normalization both
before and after each sub-block (attention and MLP), rather than only before (standard pre-norm). The
post-block norm bounds the output magnitude entering the residual add, which is complementary to QK-
norm inside the attention. OLMo 2 uses only the post-block norms, omitting the pre-block norms. Ev-
idence so far suggests this is strictly more stable than pure pre-norm for models trained beyond 300B
tokens.
Gradient clipping at 1.0 is a floor, not a ceiling. Keep gradient clipping as a last-resort backstop, but
do not rely on it as your primary stability mechanism. At the scale where instability becomes dangerous
(30B parameters,100B tokens), the frequency of clipping events correlates with final model quality
degradation. If you clip more than 2-3% of steps, investigate the architectural root cause rather than raising
the clip threshold.
```

QK-norm for the attention path and z-loss for the output path. It also checks whether the current learning
rate is still in the cosine schedule’s stable descent region.
“What does QK-norm actually do to the attention distribution, and what is the cost?” Strong answer:
it bounds pre-softmax attention logits toO(1/
p

distribution over long training; cost is two extra RMSNorm calls per attention layer, negligible compared
to the surrounding projections.
Senior follow-up: “Z-loss controls the output softmax normalizer. But cross-entropy already backprop-
agates through the softmax. How can z-loss provide information that the cross-entropy gradient does
not?” The senior answer: cross-entropy gradient pushes the correct logit up relative to the others, but

does not constrain the absolute scale of the logit vector. Z-loss penalizes the scale directly - even a model

losses operate on orthogonal degrees of freedom in logit space (direction versus magnitude), which is why
they are complementary and not redundant.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Training instability in transformers concentrates at the two softmaxes: the attention softmax overTse-
quence positions and the output softmax over theV-token vocabulary.
QK-norm applies RMSNorm to query and key tensors before the attention dot product, bounding pre-
softmax logit magnitudes and preventing attention collapse or gradient vanishing. Gemma 2, OLMo 2,
and DCLM all use it.
Z-loss addsα[z(x)]^2 to the training objective, keeping the output softmax normalizer near 1 and pre-
venting unbounded logit growth; PaLM set the standard withα= 10−^4.
Use QK-norm and z-loss together - they target different failure modes and are complementary. Logit
soft-capping is a model-specific choice; ablate before adding it.
Gradient clipping is a backstop, not a primary stability tool; frequent clipping (>2% of steps) signals an
architectural problem that needs to be fixed at the source.
```
### 3.3 Activation Functions in Modern LLMs

**3.3.1 ReLU, GeLU, and SwiGLU Families**
Every major open-weight model released since 2022-LLaMA, PaLM, Gemma, Mistral, DeepSeek, Qwen-
uses a gated activation in its MLP blocks. If you walk into an architecture deep-dive and cannot explain what
SwiGLU is, why it replaced GeLU, and how it changes the hidden dimension sizing, you will stall on a warmup
question before the real design challenge begins. This topic appears most often at mid-to-senior level interviews
at frontier labs, where it quickly signals whether a candidate has read recent model cards or is still reasoning
from undergraduate deep learning.
The MLP block in a transformer layer projects from the residual stream dimensiondup to a wider hidden
dimensiondf f, applies a nonlinearity, then projects back down. Three activation families partition the design
space.
**ReLU.** ReLU(x) = max(0, x). The two-layer FFN is:
FFNReLU(x) = max(0, xW 1 )W 2

Fast, hardware-friendly, but a large fraction of hidden units saturate at zero during training, wasting capacity.
The hard kink at zero also creates gradient cliffs that require careful initialization.
**GeLU.** The Gaussian Error Linear Unit smooths the hinge:
GeLU(x) =xΦ(x)

whereΦis the CDF of the standard normal. In code it is approximated asxσ(1. 702 x). Differentiable every-
where, no dead-neuron regime, and empirically better than ReLU on every benchmark published for it. GPT-1
through GPT-3 all use GeLU, and it held as the dominant choice through 2021.
**Gated Linear Units (GLU) and SwiGLU.** The core idea: multiply the activated hidden representation


```
3.3 Activation Functions in Modern LLMs
```
element-wise by a second learned linear projection that acts as a soft gate:

```
GLU(x, W, V) =σ(xW) (xV)
```
**SwiGLU** replaces the sigmoid gate with Swish, where Swish(x) =xσ(x). The full SwiGLU MLP, without
bias terms as in all modern LLMs, is:

```
FFNSwiGLU(x) =
```
#### 

```
Swish(xW 1 ) (xV)
```
#### 

#### W 2

whereW 1 , V 2 Rd×dffandW 22 Rdff×d.
**GeGLU** substitutes GeLU for Swish and is used by T5v1.1, Gemma 2, and Gemma 3:
FFNGeGLU(x) =

#### 

```
GeLU(xW 1 ) (xV)
```
#### 

#### W 2

_Gated activations let the network learn to suppress or amplify each hidden dimension independently at
each token, which is strictly more expressive than a fixed pointwise nonlinearity at the same parameter budget._
TheV matrix acts as a context-dependent gain: for every hidden dimension at every token, the network
independently decides how much of the activated signal passes forward. A plain ReLU or GeLU MLP can
only gate in a binary sense-either the value is positive and passes, or it does not. A GLU variant attenuates
values softly, in a learned, input-dependent way. The empirical result is a consistent 0.3-0.8 nat improvement in
pre-training perplexity at equal parameter count.
The smooth nonlinearity in SwiGLU and GeGLU matters separately. The hard kink at zero in ReLU means
neurons near the boundary receive nearly zero gradients and stop participating in learning. Swish and GeLU both
maintain a small non-zero gradient slightly below zero, which keeps more neurons active throughout training.
The Swish curve dips very slightly below zero for large negative inputs-a property that alarmed some early
reviewers-but in practice, optimizer momentum carries activations far away from that tiny regime and it has
never been measured as a problem in production training runs.
Before GLU variants, the choice was ReLU (fast, rough) versus GeLU (smooth, slightly better). GLU
variants deliver GeLU-level expressiveness plus a multiplicative gate, at the cost of one additional weight matrix
V. The question is always whether that matrix earns its keep-the evidence consistently says yes.

Take LLaMA-2 7B:d= 4096, SwiGLU. The convention is that the total MLP parameter count should

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Round df f to a multiple of 64, preferably 128. Hardware tiling requirements mean oddly sized di-
mensions can cost 10-20% throughput on A100 and H100. LLaMA-2 uses 11008 rather than the exact
10922.7 for this reason. Some labs prefer multiples of 256 for very large models.
Default to SwiGLU. GeGLU and SwiGLU are empirically indistinguishable in pre-training loss; pick
whichever your framework has a fused kernel for. Both beat GeLU, which beats ReLU. There is no reason
to use ReLU in a new architecture today.
Drop bias terms everywhere. Modern LLMs omit biases inW 1 ,V, andW 2. Bias parameters add
optimizer state, consume memory bandwidth on every forward pass, and have been repeatedly observed
to destabilize large-scale training without any measurable quality benefit. Dropping them is free money.
The 8 / 3 factor only applies to the 4  baseline. If your startingdf fuses a different ratio-Gemma 2 uses
8 , the original T5-11B used 64 -the matching factor changes. Always derive from parameter matching,
not from memorizing ‘ 8 / 3 ’.
Profile fused kernel availability before committing. SwiGLU requires launching matmuls for bothW 1
andV before the element-wise product. Without kernel fusion, this is two separate GEMM launches.
Unfused SwiGLU can be slower in wall-clock time than fused GeLU on some inference runtimes. Verify
your serving stack has a fused GLU kernel before assuming the theoretical win materializes.
```

**3.3.2 Why GLU Variants Dominate Production Models**
If you survey the 19 dense LLM releases from 2024 alone-Command A, OLMo 2, SmolLM, Phi-4, Gemma
3, Qwen 2.5, LLaMA 3-almost every one uses SwiGLU or GeGLU. This is not groupthink or cargo-culting. It
is the result of independently run ablations at multiple labs converging on the same answer. Understanding _why_
GLU variants win tells you something more durable than a recipe: it gives you a mental model for reasoning
about future architecture changes that interviewers at senior levels will probe for.
The empirical case for GLU variants rests on two independent lines of evidence. Noam Shazeer’s 2020
paper evaluated every GLU variant-ReGLU (ReLU gate), GeGLU (GeLU gate), SwiGLU (Swish gate), and
others-against a standard GeLU baseline on CoLA and SST-2 fine-tuning tasks. The results were unambiguous:
every GLU variant outperformed the GeLU baseline, and the gains were statistically significant. GeGLU scored
84.67 on CoLA against 84.20 for the GeLU baseline, a difference that might look small until you consider these
are pre-training architecture choices where 0.5% gains are hard-won.
Narang et al. (2020) extended this to pre-training loss in a T5-style study covering a wide range of architec-
ture decisions simultaneously. The bolded top-performers in their loss comparison tables are, without exception,
the GLU variants. The non-gated activations (ReLU, GeLU, ELU) cluster together below them at every scale
tested.
The convergent evolution after 2022 seals the argument. PaLM (Google, 2022) used SwiGLU in a 540B-
parameter model-the most expensive training run of its era-after internal ablations. T5v1.1 (the improved version
of T5) switched from the original T5’s ReLU to GeGLU and achieved better downstream performance. The en-
tire LLaMA family, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, Yi, and dozens of open-weight models followed. When multiple
independent labs running trillion-token training runs independently converge on the same choice, the evidence
is about as strong as you ever get in empirical deep learning.
_GLU variants consistently win because gating is a universally useful architectural primitive: it appears in
LSTMs (forget gate), GRUs (update gate), attention (the_ V _projection scaled by softmax weights), and now in
MLP blocks._
The underlying mechanism is expressiveness for free. A standard FFN uses one matrix multiply to mix
features and one pointwise function to introduce nonlinearity. A GLU FFN uses two matrix multiplies to create
an activated branch and a linear gate, then combines them element-wise. The gate is not a fixed function of the
input magnitude; it is learned, input-dependent, and can vary across thedf fhidden dimensions independently.
This effectively gives the MLP a form of conditional computation at the feature level.
The memory bandwidth argument reinforces this. As discussed in the context of RMSNorm, the trans-
former’s bottleneck is not FLOPs-tensor contractions are 99.8% of FLOPs but not 99.8% of wall-clock time.
What matters is how often you move data between memory hierarchies. A GLU variant withdf f=^83 dmoves
the same amount of data as a standard FFN withdf f= 4d-three smaller matrices versus two larger ones at the
same total parameter count. The memory bandwidth cost is identical. The quality gain is free.


```
3.3 Activation Functions in Modern LLMs
```
The contrast with what came before clarifies the win. The pre-GLU choice was: ReLU (fast but rough, dead
neurons, gradient cliffs) versus GeLU (smooth, differentiable, better quality, slightly slower to compute). GLU
variants deliver GeLU-level gradient behavior plus conditional gating at the same memory cost. The iteration
from the Shazeer paper to PaLM to LLaMA 1 to LLaMA 3 is the clearest example of a clean architectural
improvement compounding across the field.

**A Worked Example**

To see why production models chose SwiGLU over a scaled-up GeLU FFN, consider two configurations
for a 70B model withd= 8192and 80 transformer layers.
**Option A: GeLU FFN** ,df f= 4d= 32, 768 :
params per layer= 2 8192  32 ,768 = 536, 870 , 912  537 M
total MLP params (80 layers)= 80 537 M 42. 9 B
**Option B: SwiGLU FFN** ,df f=^83 8192 = 21, 845! 21 , 888 (rounded to 128):
params per layer= 3 8192  21 ,888 = 537, 919 , 488  538 M
total MLP params (80 layers) 43. 0 B
The parameter counts are within 0.2% of each other. The memory bandwidth cost per forward pass is
essentially identical. Yet Option B (SwiGLU) consistently achieves 0.3-0.8 nat lower perplexity. This is why
every lab that ran this ablation chose SwiGLU: it is a free lunch. LLaMA-2 70B uses exactly this configuration
(d= 8192,df f= 28, 672 , which reflects a slightly larger ratio of roughly 3.5rather than 2.67, a choice that
trades slight parameter increase for wider matrices).

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
GLU is the default; exceptions require justification. GPT-3 uses GeLU and is still a strong model,
Nemotron-4 340B uses squared ReLU (ReLU^2 (x) = max(0, x)^2 ), and Falcon 2 11B uses plain ReLU.
These are competitive models. But if someone asks why you chose GeLU over SwiGLU for a new pre-
training run, “it’s simpler” is not a satisfying answer-you need an ablation or a systems constraint (e.g.,
your inference runtime has no fused GLU kernel).
SwiGLU and GeGLU are interchangeable in practice. No production paper shows a measurable dif-
ference between them at the same parameter count. Pick the one with better kernel support in your stack.
The T5 lesson: extreme df f ratios are legal but risky. The original T5-11B useddf f= 65, 536 against
d= 1, 024 , a ratio of 64. The model worked, but T5v1.1 (the improved version) dialed this back to a
standard 2.5ratio with GeGLU and got better results. Very large ratios spend parameters inefficiently
on width rather than depth; the Kaplan et al. scaling experiments show a wide basin (1to 10) but the
optimum is around 4(or 2.67with GLU).
Watch for the squared-ReLU surprise. Nemotron and some mixture-of-experts models use ReLU^2 ,
which is sparsity-inducing: most hidden units fire at exactly zero. This creates naturally sparse MLP
activations that can be exploited for inference acceleration. If your deployment stack supports sparse
kernel optimizations, squared ReLU is worth benchmarking.
Parameter matching is a convention, not a law. Some labs (Mistral, PaLM) use slightly largerdf f
ratios than 8 / 3 for their GLU models-effectively choosing to spend more parameters in the MLP. This is

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Would you ever use ReLU in a new architecture? When?” Strong answer: only with a specific
justification-squared ReLU for sparsity-based inference acceleration, or a constrained runtime with no
GLU kernel and GeLU not available either. For standard pre-training with a modern stack, there is no
reason to choose ReLU over SwiGLU.
“What does it mean that LLaMA and PaLM both independently picked SwiGLU?” Strong answer: it
validates the ablation-two groups with different data, hardware, and model scales ran independent exper-
iments and converged. When multiple frontier labs agree on an architecture choice without coordinating,
that is the strongest signal available that the choice is correct. The interviewer is testing whether you
reason from evidence, not just pattern-match on popular choices.
Senior follow-up: “You are designing a 100B-parameter model. Your inference stack runs on edge
hardware where kernel fusion is limited to a single GEMM per layer. How does that change your
activation function choice?” Sketch the answer: SwiGLU requires two back-to-back GEMMs (W 1 and
V) before the element-wise product; without fusion, this is two memory round-trips to HBM. On memory-
constrained edge hardware, this can be a throughput bottleneck. Options: (1) fall back to GeLU (one
GEMM, almost as good empirically); (2) rewrite the kernel to fuse both GEMMs into a single wider
matmul; (3) use squared ReLU (one GEMM, exploits sparsity for further gains if the hardware has sparse
execution units). The answer demonstrates that activation function choice is not isolated from systems
constraints.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Multiple independent labs-Google, Meta, Alibaba, Mistral-running ablations at scale all converged on
SwiGLU or GeGLU; that convergence is stronger evidence than any single paper.
GLU variants win because gating is a universal architectural primitive: the same element-wise multiplica-
tive gate that works in LSTMs and attention works in MLP blocks.
SwiGLU and GeGLU are empirically indistinguishable; choose based on which your runtime can fuse
efficiently.
GPT-3 (GeLU), Nemotron 340B (squared ReLU), and Falcon (ReLU) are legitimate exceptions-strong
models exist without GLU, but each exception needs a reason.
Very wide MLPs (df f> 10 d) spend parameters inefficiently; the T5-11B to T5v1.1 regression from
64 to 2. 5 ratio is the canonical cautionary example.
```
### 3.4 Position Encodings

**3.4.1 Absolute, Relative, and Sinusoidal Encodings**
Transformers are permutation-invariant by design: self-attention produces identical outputs regardless of
the order in which tokens appear. Position encoding is therefore not an optional add-on - it is a load-bearing
architectural choice, and “how does the model know token order?” is a near-universal architecture deep-dive


```
3.4 Position Encodings
```
question. The more revealing follow-up is “what breaks when you run the model on sequences longer than its
training context?” That question separates engineers who memorized the formula from those who understand
why a decade of iteration eventually converged on RoPE.
Three families of position encodings cover virtually every production model built before 2022.
**Absolute learned embeddings.** Add a dedicated vectorpi 2 Rdto the token embedding at positioni.
Thepiare free parameters trained end-to-end alongside everything else. This is exactly what GPT-1, GPT-2,
GPT-3, OPT, and BERT use. The only constraint is that the vocabulary of positionsf 0 , 1 ,... , L 1 gmust be
declared at model initialization, and any position beyondL 1 is simply undefined.
**Sinusoidal (fixed) embeddings.** The original _Attention Is All You Need_ (2017) proposed hard-coded vec-
tors built from paired sine and cosine functions at geometrically spaced frequencies:

```
PE(i, 2 k) = sin
```

```
#### 

```

```
#### 

```

```
#### 

whereiis the token position andk= 0, 1 ,... , d/ 2  1 indexes dimension pairs. The denominators form
a geometric series of wavelengths from 2 πtokens (fastest oscillating pair) up to 10000  2 πtokens (slowest).
Because a fixed rotation matrixMδmaps PE(i)to PE(i+δ)for any offsetδ, the model can in principle represent
relative distances as linear combinations of absolute embeddings.
**Relative encodings.** Rather than encoding absolute position into token representations, these schemes
inject a position-dependent term directly into the attention score. Shaw et al. (2018) added a learned biasaKij
to the query-key dot product for each pair(i, j), clipped at some maximum offset. T5 generalized this with a
scalar learned biasb(ij)shared across all positions at the same distance. Because the bias depends only on
ij, these schemes are inherently relative and do not need to define a maximum absolute position.
_The axis that matters: absolute schemes bake position into token representations before attention; relative
schemes fold position into the attention score computation itself._
Sinusoidal embeddings have no learnable parameters, which means they add nothing to the model’s mem-
ory footprint. Their multi-scale structure - fast oscillations for nearby tokens, slow oscillations for distant ones -
lets the model distinguish positional relationships across a wide range of distances with a singled-dimensional
vector. The linear-rotation property means a well-trained model can, in principle, extract relative offsets alge-
braically. In practice, performance degrades beyond the training context length because the model has never
seen those absolute position vectors during training; the degradation is softer than with learned embeddings but
still substantial.
Learned absolute embeddings are the simplest possible scheme and fast at inference (a single table lookup).
The critical failure mode is hard and immediate: any sequence position beyondL 1 maps to an uninitialized or
out-of-distribution vector. In GPT-3 withL= 2048, a 2049-token sequence causes undefined behavior. There
is no graceful degradation.
Relative schemes generalize to unseen lengths because the biasb(ij)is indexed by distance, not by
absolute index. The trade-off is memory: T5-style relative biases require a tensor of shape[batch,heads, n, n]
that isO(n^2 )in sequence length. Atn= 4096, 16 heads, batch size 8, infloat32, this tensor is 8  16 
40962  4  8. 6 GB - often the single largest activation in the forward pass. Beyond 4k tokens, relative bias
memory dominates everything else.
ALiBi (Press et al., 2022) sidesteps the memory issue by making the bias a fixed negative slope times
distance:m(ji), wheremis a head-specific constant. No parameters, noO(n^2 )tensor, and strong
empirical length generalization. The structural assumption, however, is a monotone recency bias: every token

```
always prefers recent context. This hurts tasks that require retrieving information from the beginning of a very
long document.

Pair(0,1)completes a full oscillation in 2 π/ 1. 0  6. 3 tokens; it is highly sensitive to whether two tokens

This exact multi-scale geometry is what motivated RoPE’s paired-dimension rotation design, described in

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Fixed context, no extrapolation needed. Learned absolute embeddings are the right call. They are
trivially fast (one embedding lookup), add a modestLdparameter count (forL= 2048,d= 4096that
is 8 M parameters - 0.1% of a 7B model), and have no inference overhead.
Any use case that might require sequences longer than training context. Do not use absolute learned
embeddings. The failure is not a smooth performance cliff; it is a hard crash. If you anticipate context
growth post-launch, paying the cost of RoPE from day one is always worth it.
Sinusoidal for new architectures. Generally not worth choosing over RoPE. Sinusoidal requires no
learned parameters, which is attractive, but it does not enable any of the context-extension algorithms that
RoPE does. There is no upside to picking sinusoidal in 2024 unless you are constrained to not touching
the attention layer.
T5 relative bias at context lengths above 4k. TheO(n^2 )attention bias tensor becomes the dominant
memory cost before the attention matrix itself. Profile memory before committing.
ALiBi for simple long-context baselines. Zero parameters, strong empirical generalization, and sim-
ple to implement. The recency-bias assumption fails for tasks that need long-range retrieval. Fine for
summarization or generation; risky for multi-document QA.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Explain the sinusoidal encoding formula. Why use 10000 as the base?” Strong answer: describe
the geometric series of wavelengths from 2 πto 10000  2 πcovering up to 63000 tokens, connect high-
frequency pairs to short-range discrimination and low-frequency pairs to long-range, and mention the
```

3.4 Position Encodings
```
```
rotation-matrix property that makes relative offsets linearly expressible. Weak answers quote the formula
without explaining the frequency intuition.
“What breaks when you deploy a model trained with absolute learned embeddings on a longer
context?” Strong answer: positions beyondL 1 access uninitialized or randomly initialized embedding
rows; the model produces incoherent logits, typically NaN or near-uniform distributions. Mention that
fine-tuning on longer sequences with the position table extended can fix this, but it requires continued
training, not just architecture changes.
Senior follow-up: “Relative encodings claim to generalize to unseen lengths. Show me where that guar-
antee breaks down in practice.” The catch: T5 clips relative distances at some maximum offsetk; beyond
ktokens all positions are treated identically, so the model has no signal to distinguish “100 tokens away”
from “10000 tokens away.” ALiBi does not clip, but its monotone penalty assumes recency always wins,
which is wrong for long-context retrieval. True unlimited-length generalization requires the encoding to
remain distinguishable at arbitrary distances - which is the design goal of RoPE’s continuous-frequency
rotation.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Transformers have no intrinsic sense of order; position must be injected either into token representations
(absolute) or into attention scores (relative).
Sinusoidal embeddings cover multiple frequency scales and have a linear-combination relative-offset
property, but they do not generalize to sequences longer than training context.
Learned absolute embeddings are fast and simple but fail immediately at any sequence length beyond the
declared maximum.
T5-style relative biases generalize better but imposeO(n^2 )memory overhead; ALiBi is cheaper but bakes
in a recency prior.
The entire landscape above has been superseded by RoPE in post-2023 production models; understanding
these predecessors matters primarily to explain why RoPE won.
```
```
3.4.2 Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) and Context Extension
Every frontier model released since 2022 - LLaMA 1 through 4, Mistral, Qwen, Gemma, DeepSeek, Falcon
```
- uses Rotary Position Embeddings. If you are asked to design an LLM from scratch, choosing RoPE is almost
certainly the right answer. But stating the choice is the easy part; an interviewer will immediately follow up
with “explain exactly why the inner product only sees relative position,” and then, if you are interviewing for a
senior role, “how would you extend a 4k RoPE model to 128k without retraining from scratch?” Both questions
require understanding the mathematics, not just the name.

additive embeddings (which introduce cross terms between content and absolute position) and rules out most
relative schemes (which modify attention scores but do not satisfy this exact factorization for inner products).

This is applied to queries and keys at every attention layer, immediately after the linear projections forQ

_RoPE is the only common encoding that provably makes the attention inner product a function of relative
distance alone, while requiring zero learnable parameters and no change to token embeddings._
Compared to absolute learned embeddings, RoPE adds zero parameters and produces no out-of-distribution
vectors at unseen absolute positions - the rotation angles grow continuously, so position 10001 is just a small
step beyond position 10000.
Compared to sinusoidal additive embeddings, RoPE’s rotation acts on the query and key vectors inside the
attention layer, which means the dot-product kernel sees only relative angles. Sinusoidal embeddings added to
token inputs do _not_ achieve this: the product(ei+pi)T(ej+pj)expands into four terms, two of which mix
content with absolute position - the encoding is not purely relative.
Compared to T5 relative biases, RoPE requires noO(n^2 )memory. The rotation is a per-vector operation
(costO(nd)), not a per-pair operation. Atn= 32768andd= 4096, this difference is 32768  4096  134 M
elements versus 327682  1 B elements - roughly an 8reduction in the position-related memory footprint.
The geometric spacing ofθk= 10000−^2 k/dprovides the same multi-scale frequency coverage as sinusoidal
embeddings: high-kpairs (smallθ) oscillate slowly and encode long-range position; low-kpairs oscillate quickly
and encode fine-grained adjacency. This design also enables length-extension algorithms discussed below.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
RoPE base θ. The original paper used 10000. LLaMA 3 raised it to 500 , 000. A higher base stretches
the period of the slow-frequency pairs, giving the model more resolution at long distances. Increasing
the base is the simplest and most reliable way to improve long-context performance when combined with
continued pretraining on long documents.
Context extension without retraining: position interpolation. Chen et al. (2023) showed that dividing
all absolute positions by a scale factors=Lnew/Ltrainbefore applying RoPE keeps rotation angles within
the trained range. The model sees positions that now look like scaled versions of what it trained on. This
works but produces a mild perplexity increase; 1000-2000 fine-tuning steps on long-context data almost
fully recover quality.
NTK-aware scaling (Bloc97). Instead of scaling positions, scale the base: replace 10000 with 10000 
sd/(d−2). This redistributes the frequency spectrum so that high-frequency pairs are less affected, preserv-
ing short-range sensitivity while stretching the slow pairs. Works better than naive position interpolation
out of the box, with no fine-tuning.
YaRN (Peng et al., 2023). Applies different interpolation factors per frequency group: high-frequency
pairs are left unchanged, low-frequency pairs are interpolated, mid-frequency pairs get a temperature
adjustment. The most reliable technique for large extension factors ( 4 or more) with minimal fine-
tuning. Used in several open-weight long-context derivatives.
RoPE applies only to Q and K , not V. A common implementation bug is accidentally rotating the value
projections. Values carry content, not position; rotating them corrupts them.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

“Why does RoPE make the attention score depend only on relative position?” Strong answer: the
rotationRmapplied toQandRnapplied toKmeanshRmq,Rnki=hRm−nq,kibecause the rotations
```

3.4 Position Encodings

compose asRTmRn=Rn−m. Work through this in 2D if asked on a whiteboard. Weak answers say “it
uses rotation” without the inner product cancellation argument.
“What breaks when you try to run a RoPE model trained with context 4k on an 8k input?” Strong
answer: positions 4001-8000 produce rotation angles that the model has never encountered during train-
ing. Unlike absolute embeddings (hard failure), this degrades gradually : perplexity rises as position
increases past training context, with the slow-frequency pairs (largek) being the first to degrade since
they have the least trained coverage. The fix is either NTK-aware base scaling or continued pretraining
with longer sequences.
Senior follow-up: “You have a LLaMA-2 7B checkpoint trained at 4k context and you need 32k context in
two weeks. Walk me through what you would actually do.” The strong answer sketches a two-stage recipe:
(1) apply NTK-aware base scaling (e.g., raise base to 128 , 000 for 8 extension) with no retraining as
an immediate fix; (2) collect a long-document corpus at the target length, run 1000-2000 gradient steps at
32 k sequence length on 8-16 GPUs, using sequence packing and gradient checkpointing to fit memory;
(3) evaluate on SCROLLS or LongBench to confirm perplexity recovery. Name the memory cost: atbf16
with a 7B model, a single 32k sequence activates 32  322  4096 / 109  4. 3 GB of KV activations
per layer, so activation checkpointing is not optional.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
RoPE rotatesQandKby position-dependent angles so that the attention inner product becomes a function
of relative position alone, with zero learnable parameters.
The dimension pairing with base-10000 frequencies provides multi-scale resolution, just like sinusoidal
embeddings, but applied inside the attention operation rather than at the input.
Virtually all post-2022 production models use RoPE; convergent evidence from 19+ open model releases
shows no competing scheme has beaten it at scale.
Context extension methods - position interpolation, NTK-aware base scaling, YaRN - all work by adjust-
ing how positions map to rotation angles; they differ in how aggressively they disturb the short-range
frequency pairs that the model relies on most.
The simplest production strategy for extending context: increase the RoPE base and fine-tune on long
documents; for large extension factors (> 4 ), use YaRN or NTK scaling as the starting point.
```

## Chapter 4 Hyperparameters You Will Be Asked to Justify

### 4.1 Width and Depth

**4.1.1 Aspect Ratio and the “128 Hidden Dims per Layer” Rule**
When an interviewer says “design a 7B-parameter dense decoder model,” the next question is almost al-
ways: how many layers, and how wide? This ratio-what practitioners call the _aspect ratio_ -is the single structural
decision that cascades into your parallelism strategy, your per-device memory footprint, and your inter-node
networking requirements. Mid-level engineers treat it as a free variable; senior engineers know the empirically
validated sweet spot and can argue for it on both quality and systems grounds.
The aspect ratio is the ratio of the residual stream width to the number of transformer layers:
aspect ratio=
dmodel
nlayers
It captures how a fixed parameter budget is allocated between width and depth. A model withdmodel= 4096
andnlayers= 32has aspect ratio 128 ; redistributing the same parameter count todmodel= 8192andnlayers= 16
gives aspect ratio 512.
Hyperparameter sweeps across three model scales (50M, 274M, and 1.5B parameters) show that loss is
minimized at aspect ratios between 100 and 128, and that this optimum is remarkably stable across scales.
GPT-3 (175B, ratio 128), LLaMA-2 7B (ratio 128), LLaMA-2 13B (ratio 128), and LLaMA-2 70B (ratio 102)
all land squarely in this band. That stability is the key finding: you can validate your aspect ratio at small scale
and carry it forward to full training with reasonable confidence.
Width and depth are not equivalent ways to spend parameters. Width increases the rank and represen-
tational capacity of every vector in the residual stream. Depth increases the number of sequential nonlinear
transformations applied. The aspect ratio controls their balance.
_The rule of thumb: target roughly 100-128 hidden dimensions per layer, build your_ d _modeland_ n _layersaround
that constraint, and you will be within the flat loss minimum for every scale that has been publicly studied._
Too narrow and too deep: each layer has low representational capacity, the residual stream bottlenecks
information flow, and pipeline stages become tiny-wasting GPU utilization at stage boundaries. Too wide and
too shallow: you over-invest in representation capacity at each step before enough nonlinear transformations
can process it, and the very wide matrix multiplies require aggressive tensor parallelism that strains inter-GPU
bandwidth.
The aspect ratio also directly determines which parallelism strategies are feasible. Wide models (high
dmodel) suit _tensor parallelism_ , where each weight matrix is partitioned column-wise or row-wise across GPUs
within a node. Tensor parallelism requires high-bandwidth, low-latency interconnects such as NVLink at
600 GB/s. Deep models (many layers) suit _pipeline parallelism_ , where consecutive layer groups are assigned
to different GPU nodes; pipeline parallelism tolerates slower inter-node networking (200 Gbps InfiniBand is
usually sufficient) because communication only occurs at stage boundaries. Your cluster topology therefore
constrains the aspect ratio before model quality does.
One important nuance separates pretraining loss from downstream task performance. Research comparing
depth versus width at matched parameter counts finds that pretraining perplexity is insensitive to the split-
total parameters dominate. But downstream fine-tuning accuracy can mildly favor deeper models at the same


```
4.1 Width and Depth
```
parameter count. If you optimize purely around pretraining loss, aspect ratio near 128 is well validated. If
downstream task capability is the primary target, there is a weak case for going somewhat deeper, within the
constraint that pipeline parallelism remains efficient.

**A Worked Example**

```
Consider designing a 7B-parameter dense decoder model. Three candidate configurations:
```
```
Configuration dmodel nlayers Aspect ratio
Standard (recommended) 4096 32 128
Too wide 8192 14 585
Too narrow 2048 64 32
```
The standard configuration matches LLaMA-2 7B exactly. On a single 8-GPU H100 node with NVLink, it
fits comfortably with 4-way tensor parallelism (dmodel/TP= 1024per shard, cleanly divisible). With 32 layers,
pipeline parallelism across two groups of 4 GPUs assigns 16 layers per stage-a sensible granularity.
The wide variant (dmodel= 8192, 14 layers) has very few pipeline stages, making coarse-grained pipeline
parallelism inefficient. Effective tensor parallelism would need degree 8 or 16, requiring a dense NVLink fabric
across multiple nodes-a significant hardware constraint. Attention with 64 heads at head dimension 8192 /64 =
128 is fine; the real cost is that wide matmuls do not automatically saturate hardware better unless the batch
dimension is simultaneously large.
The narrow variant (dmodel= 2048, 64 layers) creates very fine-grained pipeline stages. At 8 layers per
stage across 8 pipeline stages, activation tensors moving between stages are small, and pipeline bubbles dominate
runtime. Tensor parallelism across small matrices is unattractive because communication overhead relative to
compute grows as matrix size shrinks.
The arithmetic conclusion: for a 7B model on 8 H100s, 4096 hidden dimensions and 32 layers produces
a clean 4-way TP within each group of 4 GPUs and 2-way pipeline parallel across groups-no wasted hardware,
minimal bubble fraction.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start at aspect ratio 128. For a 7B model:dmodel= 4096,nlayers= 32. For 13B:dmodel= 5120,
nlayers= 40. For 70B:dmodel= 8192,nlayers= 80(ratio 102 , close enough). These numbers match
the released LLaMA-2 configs because the same reasoning applies.
Align d modelto hardware tile sizes. Always choosedmodeldivisible by 128 at minimum; divisible by
256 is safer for H100 and future hardware. Matmul kernels use tiles of 128 or 256 elements; misaligned
dimensions waste tile slots and silently hurt throughput by 10-20%.
Let your parallelism plan constrain the choices. If tensor-parallel degree is 8,dmodelmust be divisible
by 8 and attention head count must accommodate the split. If pipeline-parallel across 4 nodes,nlayersmust
be divisible by 4 and ideally by 8 (to allow 2-way micro-batch interleaving within a stage).
Wider favors tensor parallel; deeper favors pipeline parallel. Fast NVLink within a node ( 600 GB/s)
enables tensor parallelism at scale. Slower inter-node InfiniBand (100-400 Gbps) makes tensor parallelism
across nodes expensive. Your networking budget shapes the answer before model quality does.
```

```
4.1 Width and Depth
```
```
Downstream accuracy may mildly favor depth, but do not let it override systems constraints. The
quality argument for going deeper is real but modest. If adding depth would shatter pipeline efficiency or
require redesigning your cluster topology, the quality gain rarely justifies the operational cost.
```

must divide cleanly across pipeline stages.
“Why does aspect ratio matter beyond model quality?”
Strong answer: width determines tensor-parallel degree feasibility because you partition weight matrices
along the hidden dimension; depth determines pipeline stage count and stage granularity; both interact
with your cluster’s networking topology in ways that can dominate cost long before quality differences
appear.
“If pretraining loss is equal for a wide-shallow and a narrow-deep model, which do you ship?”
Strong answer: consider downstream task performance (deeper may win), then evaluate which is cheaper
to serve at inference. Narrower-but-deeper models have smaller KV cache per layer at a givendmodel,
which can reduce memory pressure during long-context generation; wider models may serve faster if
tensor parallelism can saturate hardware.
Senior follow-up: “Your cluster has NVLink within 8-GPU nodes but only 200 Gbps InfiniBand
between nodes. You have a 70B parameter budget. Walk through your aspect ratio and parallelism

node fabric, avoid tensor parallelism across nodes; use pipeline parallelism across nodes instead. Target
dmodel= 8192(divisible by 8 for TP-8),nlayers= 80(pipeline across 4 nodes of 20 layers each, with
8-way TP within each node). Aspect ratio 102 -inside the validated band. Total GPUs: 8 4 = 32
H100s, a plausible allocation for a 70B model.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The loss-optimal aspect ratiodmodel/nlayerssits between 100 and 128 across all publicly studied scales;
use 128 as your default and adjust only for systems reasons.
This optimum appears stable from 50M to 175B+parameters, meaning small-scale experiments can
validate your choice before committing to a full run.
Aspect ratio determines which parallelism strategies are feasible: wider models favor tensor parallelism
(needs NVLink), deeper models favor pipeline parallelism (tolerates slower inter-node links).
Always aligndmodelto multiples of 128 or 256 to avoid wasted CUDA tile slots; hardware alignment is
non-negotiable, not a nice-to-have.
Downstream accuracy may mildly favor depth at equal pretraining loss, but the systems cost of going very
deep is real and often overrides this preference in production.

**4.2.1 Head Count vs. Head Dimension Trade-Offs**
“Design attention for a 13B model withdmodel= 5120” is a standard architecture deep-dive prompt. The
answer-40 heads at 128 dimensions each-resolves instantly once you internalize the governing constraint. What
trips engineers is the follow-up: why this ratio, what breaks when you deviate from it, and how does the choice
propagate into tensor-parallelism planning and inference memory? This question appears at mid-level and staff-

attention.

GPT-3, LaMDA, PaLM, and all publicly documented LLaMA-family models follow the ratio-1 constraint.

_Pin_ d _head_ = 128 _, derive_ n _heads_ =d _model_ / 128 _, and you will match every production configuration that has
been publicly validated; departures from this rule require explicit justification in terms of quality or systems
trade-offs._
Multiple heads give attention the ability to express diverse patterns simultaneously. One head might track
adjacent-token dependencies, another follow long-range coreference, a third attend to syntactic head-modifier re-
lationships. That diversity is the core mechanism through which multi-head attention improves over single-head
attention. But each head’s output is a weighted combination of value vectors in adhead-dimensional subspace.
The smallerdheadis, the lower the rank of what any individual head can represent.
This is the low-rank bottleneck: with very smalldhead(below roughly 64), the per-head attention output
is intrinsically rank-limited, and the head cannot represent nuanced multi-directional aggregations even if the
attention weights are well-calibrated. In practice,dhead = 64is the minimum seen in any well-performing
production architecture; 128 is the empirically validated sweet spot across all publicly studied model scales.
The opposing failure mode is too few, very wide heads. Withnheads= 8anddhead= 512atdmodel= 4096,
each head is highly expressive but there are only eight distinct attention patterns to aggregate. In practice the
diversity loss dominates: fewer heads means fewer independent signals for the residual stream to combine, and
the model underperforms a 32-head configuration at identical parameter count. The empirical sweet spot is
nheadslarge enough that heads genuinely specialize-typically 16 or more at production scale-withdheadlarge
enough to avoid rank bottlenecks.

straints (aspect ratio, ratio-1, TP divisibility) interact.

grouped-query attention necessary at production scale and long contexts.
```
**4.2.2 Consensus Choices Across Frontier Models**
Multi-head attention is the right choice during training. The problem surfaces when your model enters
production: at batch size 32 and 8K context, the KV cache for a 70B MHA model can exceed the aggregate HBM
capacity of a four-H100 serving node. Grouped-query attention (GQA) is how frontier labs have resolved this
without sacrificing model quality, and it is now a prerequisite in any serious inference system design discussion.
This question appears at senior and staff level as part of a serving architecture deep-dive, and the expected answer
goes beyond naming GQA to computing the KV cache size and justifying the group count.
Three variants of multi-head attention differ only in how many distinct key-value heads exist:
**Multi-head attention (MHA):** nkv=nq. Each query head has its ownWKandWV. Full representa-
tional capacity. Full KV cache per token.
**Multi-query attention (MQA):** nkv= 1. All query heads share a singleWKandWV. KV cache reduced
by factornq. Shows measurable quality loss at large model scale.
**Grouped-query attention (GQA):** nkv=nq/Gfor group sizeG. Groups ofGquery heads shareWK
andWV. KV cache reduced by factorG. Quality loss is empirically negligible forG 8.
The KV cache per token per layer in bf16 is:
KV bytes per token per layer= 2nkvdhead 2

With the ratio-1 constraint (nqdhead=dmodel), this becomes:

```
MHA: 4 dmodelbytes
GQA-G: 4dmodel/Gbytes
MQA: 4 dheadbytes
GQA directly scales down the KV cache by the group factorGwith no change to the query projection.
```

```
4.2 Attention Head Configuration
```
_GQA at_ G= 4 _-_ 8 _is the current frontier consensus: it reduces KV cache by_ 4 _-_ 8  _with quality degradation
that is empirically indistinguishable from MHA on standard benchmarks._
The key intuition is that query diversity matters more than key-value diversity. Queries express what each
head is searching for; they need to be distinct to capture different aspects of the context simultaneously. Key
and value representations encode the information being retrieved-multiple query heads can retrieve from the
same K/V pool effectively because the queries direct where to look. GQA preserves the full query projection
(nqdistinctWQmatrices) while sharing the representation being queried.
The memory-quality Pareto is well-characterized. MQA-sharing a single KV head across all query heads-
saves the most memory but causes measurable quality degradation at large model scale: having one KV head
for 64 or more query heads is too aggressive a compression of the context representation. GQA atG= 4to
G= 8matches MHA on perplexity and downstream benchmarks when trained from scratch. GQA atG 16
begins to show degradation comparable to MQA for models above 30B parameters. The sweet spot isG= 8
for 70B-class models;G= 4is increasingly common for 7B-13B models.
The memory reduction is not just a convenience-it is what enables longer context windows and larger
serving batches. For a fixed HBM budget, GQA-8 allows either 8 more tokens in the context, 8 more requests
in a batch, or some combination of both. This has a direct and quantifiable effect on serving throughput.

**A Worked Example**

```
LLaMA-2 70B configuration:dmodel= 8192,nq= 64,nkv= 8(GQA-8),dhead= 128,nlayers= 80.
Step 1: KV cache per token per layer.
2  8  128  2 bytes= 4, 096 bytes per token per layer
Step 2: total KV cache at serving parameters (context 4096, batch 8).
4 , 096  4096  8  80  10. 7 GB
Step 3: compare with MHA ( n kv = 64 ).
10. 7 8 = 85. 7 GB of KV cache
```
At this configuration MHA KV cache alone equals or exceeds the entire 80 GB HBM of a single H100-before
a single byte of model weights.
**Step 4: model weight memory.** 70B parameters in bf16: 70  109 2 = 140GB. Across 4 H100s with
TP-4: 140 /4 = 35GB per GPU.
**Step 5: total memory per GPU (GQA-8).** Assuming KV cache is sharded by TP degree: 10. 7 / 4  2. 7
GB per GPU for KV. Total:35 + 2.7 = 37. 7 GB-well within the 80 GB limit, leaving 42 GB of headroom for
activations, longer sequences, or increased batch size.
With MHA instead: 85. 7 / 4  21. 4 GB per GPU KV cache. Total:35 + 21.4 = 56. 4 GB per GPU-still
fits, but leaves only24 GB of headroom, making 8K context or batch sizes above 8 impractical. At context
8192 with MHA the KV cache doubles to 171 GB total; GQA-8 at 8192 context is 10. 7 2 = 21. 4 GB-still
comfortable.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use MHA for models  7 B serving short contexts. At 7B (dmodel = 4096), the MHA KV cache
per token is half that of a 70B model, and memory pressure is manageable for batch sizes under 16 and
contexts under 4K. Once either dimension grows, switch to GQA-4.
```

```
4.2 Attention Head Configuration
```
```
Default to GQA-8 for 13B-70B models; GQA-4 for 7B-13B. LLaMA-2 70B, LLaMA-3 70B, and most
frontier 70B-class models usenkv= 8. LLaMA-3 8B usesnkv= 8withnq= 32(also GQA-4). These
represent the production-validated sweet spots on the memory-quality Pareto.
Reserve MQA for extreme memory constraints. MQA’s quality penalty is real and documented at
70B+scale. Use it only when even GQA-8 does not fit your HBM budget-for example, on inference
chips with 8 GB of memory or edge deployments.
n kvmust be divisible by tensor-parallel degree. This is the most common configuration error when
adapting a GQA model to a new cluster. With TP-8,nkvmust be 8 and a multiple of 8. GQA-8 on
a 64-head model givesnkv= 8-exactly 1 KV head per shard at TP-8. GQA-4 on the same model gives
nkv= 16-2 per shard, also clean. GQA-4 on a 40-head model givesnkv= 10-not divisible by 8, requiring
either a different GQA group size or a different TP degree.
GQA is a training-time decision, not an inference-time optimization. You cannot convert a trained
MHA model to GQA at inference without retraining. TheWKandWV weights are distinct per head
in MHA; merging them post-hoc by averaging degrades quality measurably. If GQA is needed for your
serving cluster, specify it before the training run starts.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```

Strong answer: KV cache memory. At 4096 context and batch size 8, MHA requires86 GB of KV
cache for a 70B model-exceeding a single H100’s HBM and leaving no headroom for weights alongside
the cache on any reasonable serving cluster. GQA-8 reduces this to11 GB, fitting comfortably within a
4-GPU serving configuration. Quality on benchmark evaluations is statistically identical.
“What is the difference between MQA and GQA-8, and when do you choose each?”
Strong answer: both reduce KV cache by sharingWKandWVacross query heads. MQA uses one KV
head (maximum reduction, by factornq); GQA-8 usesnq/ 8 KV heads (reduction by factor 8). GQA-8
shows negligible quality loss at 70B scale; MQA shows measurable degradation for large models. Choose
GQA-8 as the default; use MQA only when even GQA-8 exceeds your HBM budget.

32  80  85. 9 GB. Sharded by TP-4: 85. 9 / 4  21. 5 GB per GPU. Model weights: 140 /4 = 35GB
