### 4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact

**4.3.1 Monolingual vs. Multilingual Vocab Sizing**
An interviewer asks you to justify your tokenizer vocabulary size. You say 32,768. They follow up: the
model will serve 50 languages and handle code. The number sounds embarrassingly small. Vocabulary size
is one of those hyperparameters that feels like an implementation detail until you realize it directly controls
sequence length, embedding matrix cost, and whether speakers of minority languages pay a three-to-four times
token tax compared to English speakers. This question appears at every seniority level, but the depth of expected
answer scales sharply with the role.
The vocabulary is the set of distinct token identifiers the model recognizes. A BPE tokenizer builds this
set by starting from raw bytes (256 elements) and greedily merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new
token, repeating until a target vocabulary size is reached. Each merge compresses the corpus: two common
adjacent tokens become one. The vocabulary sizeV is therefore both a compression budget and a coverage
budget simultaneously.
The compression quality of a tokenizer is captured by its _compression ratio_ : the average number of bytes
encoded per token. If a tokenizer achieves a ratio ofcon a given corpus, then a document ofBbytes produces
L=B/ctokens. For GPT-2’s 50,257-token BPE vocabulary trained on English web text, this ratio is roughly
1.6 bytes per token on English prose. Byte-level tokenization achieves exactly 1.0 by definition, which forces
sequences to be four to eight times longer than BPE for the same text-a prohibitive cost for any attention-based
model.
A larger vocabulary lets BPE find and merge higher-frequency multi-character patterns, raising the com-
pression ratio. A smaller vocabulary forces rare character sequences to survive as many short tokens, inflating
sequence lengths. The cost side: each extra vocabulary element adds one row to the input embedding matrix
and one row to the output unembedding matrix, contributing 2 Vdmodelparameters total. For a model with
dmodel= 4096, moving fromV = 32, 768 toV = 131, 072 adds roughly 800 million parameters purely in the
embedding tables-parameters that are accessed sparsely and do not dominate training FLOPs.
_The vocabulary size is a compression-versus-embedding-cost dial: a larger_ V _shortens sequences at the
price of a heavier embedding matrix, and the right setting shifts dramatically once you add languages beyond
English._
Monolingual English models settled around 30,000-50,000 tokens (GPT-2 at 50,257; early LLaMA-1 at
32,000) because English text at those sizes achieves compression ratios comfortably above 1.5 and the embed-
ding overhead stays manageable. Once you add non-Latin scripts-Arabic, Chinese, Korean, Thai, Hindi-the
situation breaks. Those scripts contain characters underrepresented in a 50k vocabulary trained on English-
dominant web text. A single CJK character that appears infrequently in the tokenizer training corpus may not
survive to become its own merge and must instead be encoded as three or four byte-level fragments. This _fertility
problem_ means a 50-character Chinese sentence may tokenize to 150-200 tokens while its English translation
of 60 characters tokenizes to 70. The model runs an invisible length tax on non-English users.


```
4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact
```
The resolution is to train the tokenizer on a multilingual corpus with controlled per-language sampling,
then expandVto 100,000-250,000. The extra merge budget provides enough operations to build high-frequency
multi-character tokens for each language. The compression ratio for previously underserved languages improves
substantially: multilingual-aware tokenizers can reduce token counts for many non-English languages by 30-
60% compared to an English-only 50k vocabulary at the same model size. The embedding overhead is real-
roughly 800M to 1.6B extra parameters for a 4k-7k hidden dimension at 128k-256k vocab-but those parameters
are cheap: sparse access means they never dominate compute.
A secondary benefit of a larger vocabulary is reduced sequence length for code. Tokenizers that recognize
programming language keywords, operators, and common identifiers as single tokens cut token counts for source
files by 20-40% versus generic text tokenizers, which matters when processing long files near context limits.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a multilingual assistant withdmodel= 4096and 32 transformer layers.
**Option A: 50,000-token English-centric BPE vocabulary.**
Embedding and unembedding parameter cost: 2  50 , 000  4096  410 M parameters.
A 128-character Hindi sentence tokenizes to roughly 160-200 tokens (many Devanagari characters split
into byte pairs).
At a context budget of 2,048 tokens, practical Hindi context is limited to around 1,300 characters.
Compression ratio on Hindi: approximately 0.6-0.8 bytes per token-well below 1.0, meaning bytes per
token is less than one because multibyte characters get split.
**Option B: 128,000-token multilingual BPE vocabulary.**
Embedding and unembedding cost: 2  128 , 000  4096  1 , 048 M parameters-an increase of roughly
640M parameters, or about 1.2 GB in bf16.
The same 128-character Hindi sentence tokenizes to roughly 60-80 tokens, a 2.5x improvement.
Under the same 2,048-token budget, Hindi context expands to around 3,300 characters.
English compression ratio is largely unchanged at1.6 bytes/token.
The embedding table grows by 640M parameters-negligible relative to the 28B+ non-embedding parame-
ters in a typical production model of this size. The gain in usable context for underserved languages is substantial
and directly observable in downstream task quality on non-English benchmarks.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
English-only or narrow-domain model: 32k-64k tokens is sufficient. Early LLaMA at 32k, GPT-2
at 50k, and Mistral 7B at 32k all demonstrate strong English performance at these sizes. Adding more
vocabulary for a monolingual English use case yields diminishing returns past 64k.
Multilingual or production assistant: Target 100k-200k. GPT-4’s tiktoken vocabulary is 100,277;
LLaMA-3 expanded to 128,256; Qwen2 uses 151,936. These numbers reflect the point where per-language
compression ratios plateau for the major world languages plus code.
Tokenizer training corpus balance matters as much as vocabulary size: A 128k vocabulary trained
on 95% English data will still underserve minority languages. When training the tokenizer, oversample
rare languages-if your pre-training corpus is 80% English and 20% other, train the tokenizer on a corpus
that is 60% English and 40% other to force more merge budget toward non-English character patterns.
```

```
4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact
```
```
Embedding parameter cost is rarely the bottleneck: A 128k vocabulary atd= 4096costs about 1 GB
in bf16. A 70B parameter model has roughly 130 GB of total weights. The embedding fraction is under
1%. Do not sacrifice multilingual coverage to save embedding memory.
The vocabulary is frozen after pre-training: This is the most expensive mistake to fix. If you launch
with a 32k vocabulary and later discover poor Korean performance, you cannot surgically add Korean
tokens without retraining. Vocabulary extension via continued pre-training is imperfect and requires sub-
stantial additional compute. Pick the right vocabulary size before the first GPU-hour of pre-training runs.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why did you pick that vocabulary size, and how did you decide?” A strong answer names the target
language mix, the compression ratio measured on held-out samples per language, the embedding param-
eter budget, and the irreversibility of the decision. Weak answers pick 32k because “that is what LLaMA
used.”
“If I tell you the model will serve users in 40 languages, what changes?” Cover the fertility problem
for non-Latin scripts, the need to train the tokenizer on a balanced multilingual corpus, and the target
range of 100k-200k tokens. Note that sampling strategy for tokenizer training matters: training on an
English-dominant corpus defeats the purpose of a larger vocabulary.
Senior follow-up: “We are doing continued pre-training to improve Hindi on an existing 32k-vocab
model. Walk me through the risks.” The strong answer addresses: (1) vocabulary extension requires
adding new embedding rows initialized randomly while existing rows carry trained representations-new
and old parameters need separate learning rate treatment; (2) the model’s output distribution encodes
assumptions about token probability that conflict with the new vocabulary’s statistics; (3) extended con-
tinued pre-training is required before the new tokens contribute meaningfully; and (4) the correct engi-
neering decision is to train from scratch with the right vocabulary upfront, and vocabulary extension is
an expensive compromise accepted only under strong resource constraints.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Monolingual models: 32k-64k tokens. Multilingual or production systems: 100k-200k tokens. The jump
is driven by the fertility problem in non-Latin scripts, where English-centric vocabularies produce 2-4x
more tokens per character.
A larger vocabulary reduces sequence length for underserved languages by 2-3x, directly expanding usable
context and reducing inference cost per query.
Embedding parameter overhead from 50k to 128k atd= 4096is roughly 640M parameters (1.2 GB in
bf16)-under 1% of total weight in a 70B model and not a meaningful constraint.
Tokenizer training corpus balance matters as much as vocabulary size: a large vocabulary trained on
English-dominant data will still underserve minority languages.
The vocabulary is frozen at pre-training. There is no cheap fix after the fact.
```
**4.3.2 Tokenizer Selection and Downstream Cost**
A product manager asks why API costs for Japanese users are running three times higher than for English
users, and your engineering lead cannot explain it in the next five minutes. This is a tokenization fertility


```
4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact
```
problem, and understanding it completely requires tracing the path from raw bytes to billed tokens. Tokenizer
selection is also one of the few decisions that constrains every downstream system: sequence length budgets, KV-
cache memory, training FLOPs, and per-query billing all live downstream of the tokenizer. The inability to swap
tokenizers after pre-training makes this decision unusually high-stakes for an apparently low-level component.
Every token costs compute. At training time, the forward-backward pass cost scales roughly linearly with
sequence length (ignoring the quadratic attention term). At inference time, prefill latency, decode cost, and KV-
cache memory all scale with token count. Hosted API pricing is quoted per token, so the tokenizer’s compression
quality directly determines the dollar cost of a given piece of text.
The key measurement is the _fertility_ of a tokenizer on a specific text domain: the average number of tokens
produced per unit of input (per word, per character, or per byte). Low fertility means high compression-fewer
tokens, lower cost, longer effective context window. Fertility is not a fixed property of the tokenizer; it is a
joint property of the tokenizer and the input distribution. A tokenizer trained on English web text will have low
fertility on English and high fertility on Arabic or Thai.
Formally, if a tokenizer achieves a compression ratiocbytes per token on a given domain, a document of
Bbytes produces

```
L=Bc
```
tokens. Since inference cost scales asO(L)for prefill andO(L^2 )for full attention over a sequence, the com-
pression ratio has a multiplicative effect on total compute. A tokenizer withc= 2. 0 bytes per token generates
50% fewer tokens than one withc= 1. 0 on the same input-cutting prefill cost in half and allowing twice as
much text to fit in the same context window.
_The tokenizer is a silent cost multiplier: every downstream metric-sequence length, memory footprint,
training FLOPs, inference billing-scales with the inverse of the compression ratio on the target domain._
BPE remains the dominant tokenization algorithm at production scale not because it is theoretically optimal
but because it is simple, invertible, fast, and empirically effective. Its adaptive nature-merging pairs from the
actual training corpus-means the vocabulary becomes a compact statistical summary of whatever text it was
trained on. This is exactly the right property: a tokenizer that does maximum compression work per token on
the specific data distribution it will encounter.
The failure mode is distribution mismatch between the tokenizer training corpus and the inference domain.
An English-centric BPE tokenizer processes Arabic as a stream of bytes or very short byte-pair fragments be-
cause Arabic characters appear rarely enough in an English corpus that they never accumulate merge frequency.
For a 100-character Arabic sentence, an English-only 50k BPE tokenizer might produce 150 tokens while a
properly trained multilingual tokenizer produces 40-a 3.75x cost difference on that query alone.
A secondary cost that often goes unnoticed is the _unembedding projection_ at inference time. For each
generated output token, the model must compute a full matrix-vector product against the unembedding matrix
of shapeVdmodel. AtV = 128, 000 anddmodel= 4096in bf16, this matrix occupies roughly 1 GB of memory
and must be accessed on every decode step. In small models (sub-1B parameters), the unembedding projection
can represent 30-50% of the total parameter count and becomes a meaningful memory-bandwidth bottleneck
during autoregressive decode.
Alternatives to BPE-character-level, byte-level, unigram language model-have been studied but have not
displaced BPE at frontier scale. Byte-level models eliminate the fertility problem entirely but produce sequences
four to eight times longer than BPE for typical English text, making quadratic attention costs prohibitive. Uni-
gram LM tokenizers (used by SentencePiece) achieve similar compression ratios to BPE and are more principled


```
4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact
```
statistically, but have not demonstrated consistent downstream quality advantages. Until architectures that pro-
cess bytes efficiently at frontier scale are proven, BPE variants remain the practical default.

**A Worked Example**

You are building an API for legal document summarization. Documents average 4,000 bytes of English
legal prose. Evaluate two tokenizer options.
**Option A: Generic English BPE,** V = 50, 257 **(GPT-2 style)**
Compression ratio on legal text:c 1. 4 bytes/token. Legal text uses many long Latin-derived words
(“indemnification,” “notwithstanding,” “hereinafter”) that appear rarely enough in the tokenizer training
corpus to not have been fully merged.
Tokens per document: 4 , 000 / 1. 4  2 , 857 tokens.
At a hosted model price of $2.00 per million input tokens: cost per document$0. 0057.
**Option B: Domain-adapted BPE trained on legal corpora,** V = 64, 000
Compression ratio on legal text:c 2. 0 bytes/token. Frequent legal phrases now appear as single tokens.
Tokens per document: 4 , 000 / 2 .0 = 2, 000 tokens.
Cost per document:$0. 0040.
Savings: 30% lower per-document cost, and 30% more legal content fits in the same context window.
The tradeoff is that Option B requires training a custom tokenizer and pre-training or continued pre-training
of the model with the new vocabulary. Option A allows immediate use of an existing foundation model. The
domain-specific tokenizer makes economic sense only when document volume is large enough to amortize the
re-training cost. At a million documents per day, the cost difference is$1, 700 /day-a breakeven point reached
quickly at scale.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Reusing an existing tokenizer: If you are fine-tuning or adapting a pretrained model, use its tokenizer
without modification. Changing the vocabulary invalidates the entire embedding and unembedding matrix
and forces a full pre-training run. The cost of tokenizer-domain mismatch-higher fertility, more tokens-is
almost always lower than the cost of a wasted pre-training run.
Training a new tokenizer: Justified only when building a new model from scratch. Train BPE on a
representative sample of the target corpus-200M to 1B characters is typically sufficient for merge statistics
to stabilize. Oversample underrepresented domains and languages relative to their share in the pre-training
corpus: a 70/30 English/other split in the tokenizer training data when the pre-training corpus is 90/10
gives minority languages better coverage without hurting English compression quality materially.
Measure fertility before committing: Before finalizing vocabulary size and training the tokenizer, com-
pute compression ratios on held-out samples from every domain and language you care about. Any do-
main producing a ratio below 1.2 bytes/token is a red flag-fertility will be very high and costs will be
disproportionately elevated for users in that domain. Fix the tokenizer, not the model.
Context window arithmetic is token arithmetic: When users report fitting fewer documents than ex-
pected in the context window, check the tokenizer fertility on their specific input type. A model with
a 128k-token context window effectively provides a much shorter context for high-fertility text such as
dense mathematical notation, structured data, or low-resource language scripts.
```

```
4.3 Vocabulary Size and Tokenization Impact
```
```
Embedding weight tying: Many models tie the input embedding matrix and the output unembedding
matrix (they share the same weights), savingV dmodelparameters at no measured quality cost. At
V = 128, 000 andd= 4096, that is 524M parameters-about 1 GB in bf16. Always verify whether weight
tying is used before reporting total parameter counts; the difference between tied and untied vocabularies
at this size is significant.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why are our API costs higher for Japanese users than for English users?” A strong answer imme-
diately names the tokenizer fertility problem: Japanese text produces more tokens per character under an
English-trained vocabulary because Japanese character patterns were underrepresented in the tokenizer
training corpus and did not accumulate enough merge frequency. The answer quantifies the expected
multiplier (2-4x for CJK versus English) and outlines the fix: measure compression ratios per language,
and if the model is being rebuilt, address vocabulary balance in the new tokenizer training data.
“Can we retrain the tokenizer and swap it into our existing model?” No, not without full re-pretraining.
The embedding and unembedding matrices are indexed by token ID; a new vocabulary means new IDs,
which means the embedding rows no longer correspond to the trained representations. A strong answer
explains this clearly and then discusses the cost of alternatives: continuing pre-training with vocabulary
extension (imperfect, expensive), serving a separate model for high-fertility languages, or accepting the
cost differential.
Senior follow-up: “Your team is proposing a byte-level model to eliminate tokenization entirely.
What would you need to see before committing to that architecture at production scale?” The senior
answer names three things: (1) a credible solution to the 4-8x sequence length inflation-either subquadratic
attention, very efficient sliding window attention, or a hierarchical architecture that first groups bytes
before processing; (2) empirical evidence at scale that byte-level models match BPE models on standard
benchmarks, which has not yet been demonstrated at frontier sizes; and (3) a plan for the inference serving
infrastructure, since the KV-cache size scales with sequence length and a 5x sequence length increase
dramatically changes memory requirements per concurrent request.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Tokenizer compression ratio is a direct multiplier on inference cost, training FLOPs, and effective context
length. A domain mismatch that cuts fertility by 2x doubles your token count and your cost on that domain.
BPE fertility is not a fixed property of the tokenizer-it is a function of how well the tokenizer training
corpus matched the inference domain. Measure fertility on held-out samples before finalizing vocabulary
choices.
Never change the tokenizer of an existing pretrained model. The embedding and unembedding matrices
are tied to token IDs; a vocabulary swap requires full re-pretraining from scratch.
Embedding weight tying (sharing input embedding and output unembedding weights) savesVdmodel
parameters at no quality cost-roughly 1 GB atV = 128k,d= 4096in bf16. Verify whether it is used
before counting parameters.
Byte-level tokenization is architecturally elegant but produces 4-8x longer sequences than BPE for typical
text; it has not been proven viable at frontier scale and requires either subquadratic attention or hierarchical
architectures to become practical.
```

```
4.4 Regularization in Pre-Training
```
### 4.4 Regularization in Pre-Training

**4.4.1 Why Dropout Went Out of Fashion**
When an interviewer asks how you regularize a pre-training run, the answer that separates practitioners
from textbook readers is: you almost certainly do not use dropout. This question surfaces regularly at mid-to-
senior LLM engineer interviews whenever the conversation moves from architecture into training configuration.
Getting it wrong signals that you are importing fine-tuning intuitions into a fundamentally different regime - and
that you have not thought carefully about what pre-training actually is at a systems level. The stakes are higher
than they appear: understanding _why_ dropout is inappropriate leads directly to understanding what regularization
tools _do_ apply, and when.
Dropout randomly zeros a fractionpof activations during each forward pass. During training, each activa-
tion unit is retained with probability(1p), and in inverted dropout (the standard modern implementation), ac-
tivations are rescaled by 1 −^1 pso that the expected magnitude is preserved at test time. The objective is to prevent
co-adaptation: no single neuron can rely on the persistent presence of a specific upstream neuron, because that
upstream unit may be zeroed on the next step. The network must learn redundant, distributed representations,
and the ensemble of all exponentially many thinned sub-networks produces a model with lower generalization
error.
This argument rests on one critical assumption: the model can overfit the training data. Given sufficient
capacity and insufficient data, the model will memorize training examples and fail to generalize. Dropout in-
troduces stochastic noise during training that prevents this memorization. In image classification with tens of
thousands of examples, in question answering with carefully curated datasets, this assumption is almost always
valid.
Pre-training for LLMs violates this assumption completely. A 7B-parameter model trained on 1T tokens
sees approximately 143 tokens per parameter over the entire training run. Each individual training example -
a web page, a book passage, a code file - is seen exactly once. There is no mechanism by which the model
can memorize specific examples, because each example occupies a negligible fraction of the parameter update
history. Overfitting, in the classical sense, does not occur.
_Dropout is a regularizer that prevents overfitting; LLM pre-training is a regime where overfitting cannot
occur; therefore dropout is solving a problem that does not exist._
The empirical evidence is unambiguous. When you measure the gap between training loss and validation
loss with and without dropout across pre-training runs at multiple scales, the gap is negligible in both conditions.
Neither run overfits. The difference between the two conditions is not in generalization but in optimization
efficiency: the run with dropout shows a consistently higher training loss throughout, because each gradient
step is computed on a stochastically degraded view of the network.
At high learning rates with large-batch training - the standard regime for pre-training frontier models -
the gradient signal is already averaged over thousands of tokens per step. Adding dropout atop this introduces
additional variance without providing any compensating benefit. The network takes longer to converge to any
given loss level, and the final training loss is worse. The validation loss tracks the training loss, confirming that
the degradation is not a regularization win but a pure optimization loss.
The contrast with fine-tuning is worth making explicit. When you fine-tune a pre-trained model on a
task-specific corpus of tens of thousands of examples and run for multiple epochs, the model can absolutely
overfit. The architecture is identical; the training regime is completely different. Dropout atp= 0. 05 - 0. 1 is


```
4.4 Regularization in Pre-Training
```
often beneficial in that setting, particularly in the later transformer layers where task-specific representations are
being adapted. Applying the same treatment to pre-training is a category error that conflates two regimes with
fundamentally different statistical properties.
There is also a hardware efficiency argument. Dropout requires generating a random binary mask at every
dropout site per forward pass. With 32 layers, two dropout sites per layer (post-attention and post-FFN), and a
batch of 4  106 tokens per step, that is 2. 56  108 random number generations per step. This is not the dominant
cost, but it is nonzero, and across 200,000-500,000 training steps on thousands of accelerators, it accumulates
into compute that could be spent elsewhere.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B-parameter decoder-only model trained for one epoch on 1T tokens, with global batch size
4096 sequences of length 4096 tokens ( 4  106 tokens per step), running for approximately 245,000 steps on
H100s.
Configure two runs: Run A withdropout=0.0, Run B withdropout=0.1applied at all post-attention
and post-FFN sites across 32 layers.
At step 50,000 (roughly 20% through training), Run B has a loss 0. 03 - 0. 05 nats higher than Run A. This
deficit is not because Run A is overfitting - the validation losses track training losses identically in both runs.
Run B’s gradient updates are simply less informative: each step sees a different stochastic degradation of the
network, injecting variance that the optimizer must average out over subsequent steps.
At the end of training, the train-to-validation loss gap in both runs is< 0. 01 nats - confirming that neither
run is overfitting. But Run B’s final training loss is 0. 02 - 0. 05 nats worse than Run A’s. That delta, small in abso-
lute terms, translates into measurable downstream degradation on benchmarks such as MMLU and HellaSwag.
You paid a dropout tax and received no regularization dividend.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Set dropout to zero for pre-training, explicitly. Do not rely on defaults. Many open-source training
harnesses (Megatron-LM, NeMo, earlier versions of GPT-NeoX) have nonzero dropout defaults inherited
from supervised learning use cases. Always override withdropout=0.0in your pre-training config.
Re-enable dropout for fine-tuning on small datasets. If your fine-tuning corpus has fewer than a few
hundred thousand examples and you run more than one epoch, dropout atp= 0. 05 - 0. 1 applied to the
upper layers is a reasonable starting point. The overfitting regime has returned.
Distinguish dropout from other stochastic training techniques. Stochastic depth (dropping entire
residual blocks with some probability) and attention dropout (zeroing attention weights rather than acti-
vations) are distinct from standard dropout. Both have niche use cases in pre-training research, but neither
is standard practice for production runs.
One-epoch assumption is load-bearing. If your pre-training setup uses data repetition - for example,
a high-quality curated subset upsampled 10relative to web data - those repeated samples do create an
overfitting surface. In practice, this is handled via data-mixing ratio tuning rather than dropout, because
dropout’s effect is uniform across all tokens regardless of whether they are repeated.
Audit GPT-3 era codebases carefully. GPT-3 used residual dropout and embedding dropout during
pre-training - a choice made before the community had accumulated the ablation evidence against it.
Codebases derived from GPT-2 or GPT-3 may silently retain these settings.
```

```
4.4 Regularization in Pre-Training
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you’d configure regularization for a 7B pre-training run.” A strong answer
distinguishes pre-training from fine-tuning immediately. For pre-training: dropout zero, weight decay
enabled (see next subsection), z-loss for softmax stability, gradient clipping. For fine-tuning on small
data: dropout re-enabled in upper layers, early stopping, potentially higher weight decay.
“Why don’t modern LLMs use dropout during pre-training?” Answer skeleton: (1) pre-training is
one pass over the data - the model cannot overfit individual examples; (2) the overfitting risk that motivates
dropout does not exist; (3) dropout adds gradient noise without any compensating benefit; (4) empirically,
the train-to-val gap is negligible with or without it, but the absolute training loss is worse with dropout.
Senior follow-up: “GPT-3 used dropout during pre-training. Was that a mistake, or is there some-
thing you’re missing?” A senior answer avoids the trap of retroactively labeling it a mistake. At the
time GPT-3 was trained (early 2020), the empirical case that pre-training overfitting was a non-issue at
175B parameters had not been established through public ablations. The team also used dropout partly
as a training stability hedge, not purely for regularization. The lesson is that best practices in this field
are empirically derived and lag model scale - what was reasonable caution in 2020 became unnecessary
overhead by 2022. A senior candidate also notes that GPT-3’s dropout rates were small (p= 0. 1 ) and
their impact on the final model was likely minor compared to other training decisions.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Dropout prevents overfitting; pre-training on internet-scale data for one epoch has no overfitting risk;
therefore dropout has no benefit during pre-training.
Removing dropout is now universal consensus among frontier labs - set it explicitly to zero and verify
your codebase defaults.
Dropout re-enters the picture for fine-tuning on small corpora with multiple epochs.
The diagnostic: if adding dropout changes your train-to-val gap, overfitting is happening; if it does not
change the gap but raises training loss, dropout is only hurting you.
The broader principle: always verify that a regularization technique is solving a problem that actually
exists in your training regime before applying it.
```
**4.4.2 Weight Decay and Learning-Rate Interactions**
If the previous subsection convinced you that pre-training does not need regularization because overfitting
is not a risk, then weight decay is about to complicate your picture. Nearly every frontier LLM pre-training
run uses weight decay - and weight decay is textbook L2 regularization. This apparent contradiction catches
engineers off guard, and resolving it correctly requires understanding a mechanism that has nothing to do with
the bias-variance tradeoff. When interviewers push past “we use weight decay to prevent overfitting” and ask _why
it actually helps when overfitting is not occurring_ , the answer reveals whether you have genuinely internalized
the dynamics of large-scale optimizer behavior or are pattern-matching to supervised learning intuitions.
Weight decay adds a penalty to the loss proportional to the squared L2 norm of model parameters:
Ltotal=LCE+

```
In standard SGD, this is equivalent to subtractingλθifrom each parameter at every step - hence the name
```

```
weight decay. In AdamW, the correct implementation for adaptive optimizers, the decay is applied directly to
the parameters _after_ the Adam update rather than being folded into the gradient:

```
θt+1= (1ηλ)θtηmt/(pvt+ε)
```
wheremtandvtare the first and second moment estimates. This decoupling matters: plain Adam with an
L2 gradient penalty scales the effective decay rate per-parameter by 1 /pvt, making it non-uniform and often
counterproductive at large scale.
The standard motivation for weight decay in supervised learning is regularization: large weights signal
over-reliance on specific features, and penalizing them pushes the model toward simpler hypotheses that gener-
alize better. In LLM pre-training, this framing is wrong. When you sweep weight decay across typical values
(λ2 f 0. 01 , 0. 1 , 0. 3 g) and hold all else equal, the train-to-validation loss gap does not meaningfully change.
Overfitting is not occurring either way. What changes instead is the absolute training loss - specifically, how
much further the optimizer can descend during the learning rate cooldown phase at the end of training.
_In LLM pre-training, weight decay is not a regularizer; it is an optimizer-conditioning mechanism that
synergizes with the learning rate schedule to achieve lower final training loss._
The mechanism becomes visible when you study training loss curves under different combinations of
weight decay and learning rate schedule shape. Consider a cosine decay schedule that takes a peak learning
rateηmaxdown to a minimumηminηmax/ 10 over the full training run.
Through the high-learning-rate phase - roughly the first 80% of training - weight decay acts as a headwind.
The optimizer is making large parameter updates, and weight decay is simultaneously shrinking all parameters
toward zero. The net effect is that the model with weight decay trains more slowly during this phase: at any given
step count, its training loss is slightly higher than the zero-weight-decay baseline. This is exactly the behavior
you would expect from any regularization that conflicts with the gradient signal.
But the picture reverses in the cooldown phase. Asηdrops fromηmaxtowardηmin, the magnitude of
gradient updates shrinks, and the optimizer begins to settle into a local basin. The model without weight decay
has allowed parameters to grow large throughout training, pulled by whatever gradient directions were most
informative at high learning rates. Large parameters create sharp, irregular loss landscape curvature: the Hessian
eigenvalues in high-magnitude directions are large, making it hard for small gradient steps to traverse the terrain
cleanly.
The model with weight decay has maintained smaller parameter magnitudes throughout. Weight decay
has effectively been imposing a soft bound on the parameter scale, trading some optimization speed during the
high-LR phase for a smoother, better-conditioned parameter neighborhood at the end. When the learning rate
cools, this model sits in a flatter basin, and small gradient steps can navigate further down the loss landscape.
The result is a lower final training loss - and, critically, a lower validation loss in lockstep, since overfitting is
not occurring. The benefit is real and it is an optimization quality improvement, not a regularization artifact.

**A Worked Example**

You are training a 13B model with AdamW:β 1 = 0. 9 ,β 2 = 0. 95 ,ε= 10−^8 , peak learning rateηmax=
3  10 −^4 , cosine decay toηmin= 3 10 −^5 over 500,000 steps. Global batch size: 2048 sequences of 4096
tokens ( 8. 4  109 tokens per epoch).
Run A:λ= 0. 0. Run B:λ= 0. 1.
Steps 1-400,000 (high-LR phase): Run A loss 0. 02 - 0. 03 nats lower than Run B at each checkpoint. Run
B is paying the weight-decay headwind tax.

Steps 400,000-500,000 (cooldown phase,ηdecaying from 10 −^4 to 3  10 −^5 ): Run B begins to close the
gap. The gradient steps are now small enough that the well-conditioned parameter landscape of Run B allows
more efficient descent.
Final result: Run B ends with a training loss 0. 02 - 0. 05 nats _lower_ than Run A. The train-to-val gap in
both runs:< 0. 01 nats. The conclusion is unambiguous - weight decay improved optimizer convergence, not
generalization.
The optimalλfor a given run depends onηmaxand the schedule shape. Atηmax= 3 10 −^4 ,λ= 0. 1 is a
strong default. If you pushηmaxto 10 −^3 (aggressive but used in some runs), reduceλto 0. 05 to avoid making
the high-LR phase too slow.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use AdamW, not Adam with L2 penalty. The distinction is not cosmetic. With plain Adam and an L2
gradient term, the effective per-parameter decay isλ/
p
vi+ε. Parameters with high gradient variance get
less decay; parameters with low gradient variance get more. This breaks the intended uniform conditioning
effect. AdamW appliesλuniformly and directly to the parameter values after the Adam step. Verify your
framework is using the correct implementation - some older codebases still default to the wrong one.
Exclude embeddings and normalization parameters from weight decay. Decaying embedding ma-
trices shrinks all token vectors uniformly toward zero, collapsing the diversity of token representations
independently of their actual usage frequency. RMSNorm scale parameters and any learned bias terms
in normalization layers are scale hyperparameters, not weights in the usual sense, and should also be
excluded. Modern frameworks support parameter groups with separate hyperparameters for this purpose.
λ= 0. 1 is the empirical consensus for most configurations. Values below 0. 01 produce negligible
conditioning effects. Values above 0. 3 impose a headwind in the high-LR phase severe enough to outweigh
the tail-of-training benefit at standard learning rates. The effective range is 0. 05 - 0. 2 ; if you are uncertain,
start at 0. 1.
Weight decay interacts with schedule shape, not just magnitude. With a trapezoidal or Warmup-
Stable-Decay (WSD) schedule - long stable phase atηmaxfollowed by a sharp decay - the benefit of
weight decay is concentrated in the final decay phase. You can think of the stable phase as building up the
conditioned parameter landscape, and the decay phase as harvesting it. With cosine decay, the interaction
is more gradual but qualitatively the same.
Gradient clipping is a separate intervention and must be configured independently. Gradient clip-
ping (kgk 2 τ, typicallyτ= 1. 0 ) prevents individual catastrophic gradient steps and is standard along-
side weight decay. The two solve different problems: clipping prevents explosive single steps; weight
decay conditions the parameter space over the full training run. Never mistake one for the other in an
interview.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“If pre-training doesn’t overfit, why does every frontier model use weight decay?” The correct answer
immediately reframes: weight decay in pre-training is not preventing overfitting. It is improving final
training loss by conditioning the parameter landscape for more effective optimization during the learning
rate cooldown. The train-to-val gap does not change with or without weight decay; the absolute loss level
does. The benefit mechanism is optimizer dynamics, not regularization.
```

```
4.4 Regularization in Pre-Training
```
```
“What’s the difference between Adam and AdamW, and why does it matter?” Skeleton: In Adam
with L2, the weight decay term enters the gradient, which then passes through the adaptive scaling 1 /pvi.
The effective decay per parameter varies with gradient history, breaking the intended conditioning effect.
AdamW applies the decay directly to the parameter after the Adam update, making it uniform across all
parameters. At large model scale, this implementation difference produces measurably different training
dynamics, not just theoretical differences.
Senior follow-up: “Can you give an intuitive explanation for why weight decay and cosine LR decay
interact the way they do - beyond just citing empirical results?” A senior answer builds the following
chain: weight decay maintains a tighter distribution of parameter magnitudes throughout training, which
constrains the loss landscape curvature around the current parameter values. At high learning rates, the
optimizer is taking large steps and the curvature constraint matters less - gradient direction dominates.
As the learning rate decreases, the optimizer’s step size falls into the regime where local curvature is the
binding constraint. A model sitting in a smoother neighborhood (achieved through weight decay) can take
those small steps more efficiently and descend further. Formally, this connects to the relationship between
weight regularization and implicit sharpness reduction: weight decay is known to reduce the dominant
eigenvalue of the Hessian in over-parameterized models, and low-sharpness minima are exactly the basins
that small-step optimizers can most effectively exploit.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Weight decay in LLM pre-training is an optimizer-conditioning mechanism, not a regularizer - it improves
final training loss, not the train-to-val gap.
Always use AdamW with explicitλ; never use plain Adam with an L2 gradient penalty for large-scale
pre-training.
Exclude token embeddings and normalization parameters from weight decay; apply it only to projection
weights and attention matrices.
Standard value isλ= 0. 1 for most configurations; reduce to 0. 05 if using an aggressive peak learning
rate above 10 −^3.
The benefit concentrates in the tail of training, during LR cooldown - the diagnostic is that a model trained
with weight decay should finish lower in training loss than one without it, while both should show the same
negligible train-to-val gap.
```

## Chapter 5 Stability Tricks in Large-Scale Training

### 5.1 Softmax Instabilities

**5.1.1 Output-Side Z-Loss**
When a training run at 50B tokens shows periodic loss spikes that slowly recover before eventually cas-
cading into full divergence, the post-mortem almost always circles back to the output softmax normalizer. This
topic surfaces at the senior and staff level whenever the interview pivots from architecture to training stability:
“How do you stabilize a pre-training run at scale?” Getting the answer right requires understanding not just that
the z-loss exists but precisely what it is regularizing and why the problem compounds as model scale grows. It
is one of those interventions where the mechanism is simple, the cost is negligible, and not knowing about it is
an immediate signal that you have not shipped a large training run.

The alternative - relying on gradient clipping alone - fails for runs longer than a few hundred billion tokens.
Gradient clipping controls the global gradient norm but does not preventZfrom drifting. A model can accumu-
late a slowly increasinglogZthat stays below the clipping threshold at each individual step but compounds over
tens of thousands of steps until a single bad batch tips it into a spike. The z-loss prevents this drift by applying
a persistent, differentiable pressure that grows proportionally with the drift itself.
The compute cost of the z-loss is essentially zero.logZ(x)is already computed as part of the softmax
during the forward pass. The auxiliary loss requires only a squaring, a scaling byα, and the gradient correction
during the backward pass. Across 500k training steps on 4096 H100s, this contributes nothing measurable to
wall-clock time.

Consider a 70B-parameter model: vocabulary 128k, trained in bfloat16, global batch 4M tokens per step,
α= 10−^4 for the z-loss.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Set α= 10−^4 as your starting point. This is PaLM’s value, independently validated by OLMo 2 and
DCLM. Values above 10 −^3 visibly hurt training loss by over-constraining the logit scale. Values below
10 −^5 have negligible effect onlogZdrift.
Apply z-loss from step zero, not as a retrofit. OncelogZhas drifted to 15-20, retroactively adding
z-loss causes a transient spike as the logit distribution is pulled back. The intervention must be proactive.
Log logZ(x) per training step as a health signal. This scalar is free to compute - it is already computed
during the forward pass. AlogZthat is monotonically increasing with no plateau is a leading indicator
of a future spike, visible days before the spike appears in the loss curve.
Do not confuse z-loss with label smoothing. Label smoothing changes the target distribution, training
the model to be less confident. Z-loss does not change what the model is trained to predict - it only
constrains the logit scale. They solve different problems and can be used together.
Treat z-loss as mandatory above 30B parameters. At 7B,logZdrift is slow enough that training often
completes before a spike occurs. At 70B trained for 2T tokens, the cumulative drift is substantial. At 100B
and beyond, in my experience, running without z-loss is gambling on the absence of a known failure mode.

in 1-2k steps) from a structural drift issue (which recovers slowly and recurrs). Check gradient norms for
correlated spikes. Then inspectlogZ(x)- if it has been trending upward for tens of thousands of steps

does not change target predictions, only logit scale.

(7 decimal digits of precision); bfloat16 has 7 mantissa bits (3 decimal digits). WhenZ(x) = 10^7 and
a token’s probability is 10 −^8 , fp32 represents this as a denormal but nonzero; bfloat16 rounds it to exact

QK-norm is the more principled intervention. By controlling the norms ofqandkbefore the inner product,

to, because the learnedγparameters adjust the effective temperature of the attention distribution. Critically,

is broken, the optimizer can push harder without triggering instability. NVIDIA’s ablation on training stability
confirms this - adding QK-norm improves final perplexity relative to the baseline, specifically because it permits
higher peak learning rates.
Soft-capping is simpler to implement and requires no additional learned parameters, but it introduces a
nonlinearity with a gradient-killing property: the derivative ofstanh(l/s)with respect tolis 1 tanh^2 (l/s),
which approaches zero asjlj! 1. This means that logits which have already grown past roughly 2 sreceive
vanishingly small gradients through the capping operation. Soft-capping prevents softmax collapse but does not
force the model to represent attention distributions compactly - it merely hides the symptoms from the softmax
while the underlying logit norms continue to drift. The same NVIDIA study finds that soft-capping ats 2
[30,50]either matches or slightly worsens baseline perplexity, because the tanh distortion changes the relative
contrast between large logits, impeding the model’s ability to express sharply peaked attention distributions
when they are genuinely needed.
Both QK-norm and soft-capping originated outside pure language model training. QK-norm was intro-
duced for training ViT-22B (a 22-billion parameter vision transformer), where large-scale instability first be-
came a pressing practical problem. It migrated into language through multimodal models - Chameleon, Idefics

- before being adopted in pure-text production runs at DCLM and OLMo 2. Soft-capping was developed within
the Gemma 2 training effort. This lineage matters: both techniques were motivated by empirical failure modes

at scale, not by theoretical arguments.

compressed.

the softmax is now only moderately larger than the cap value.

guishable.

is no longer numerically degenerate.
**QK-norm behavior at initialization:** Withγq=γk= 1, the RMS of each normalized query component

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Choose QK-norm for new production runs. It addresses the root cause of logit explosion rather than
the symptom. Implement it as a standard LayerNorm applied to the query and key projections before the
dot product, withγinitialized to 1.0 and no bias term. The additional parameter count is 2 scalars per
head per layer - negligible.
If using soft-capping, use s= 30 - 50. Gemma 2 usess= 50for local attention layers ands= 30
for global attention layers. Belows= 10, the tanh nonlinearity distorts attention patterns throughout
training, not just for pathological logits, hurting quality from early on.
Do not stack QK-norm and soft-capping without ablating. They are not additive - you are restricting
logit magnitude through two mechanisms simultaneously, and the interaction can over-constrain attention
heads during early training when the model needs to form its initial routing patterns. Pick one.
Monitor per-head 99th-percentile logit magnitude as a training health metric. A logit distribution
that is monotonically increasing with no plateau signals incipient collapse, often 5k-20k steps before it
manifests as a loss spike. Log this scalar per layer per checkpoint.
Apply whichever technique you choose from step one. Retrofitting QK-norm mid-run causes a dis-
tribution shift in the attention patterns that spikes the loss; the model must re-learn its routing structure
under the new normalization regime. Retrofitting soft-capping is less disruptive but still causes a transient
perturbation. Neither is a viable mid-run rescue operation.
```

“You’re seeing attention heads collapse to attending a single position after 20B tokens. What’s

“Compare QK-norm and soft-capping. When would you choose each?” Answer skeleton: QK-norm
is preferred - it addresses root cause, adds minimal parameters, improves perplexity, and enables higher
learning rates; soft-capping is simpler (no learned parameters) and can be retrofitted into existing attention
implementations without changing the projection layers, but it can worsen perplexity due to tanh distortion
of logit ordering; choose QK-norm for greenfield runs; soft-capping if you need to stabilize an existing
architecture with minimal code changes.
Senior follow-up: “Logit soft-capping’s gradient through the tanh vanishes for large logits. Doesn’t
that prevent the model from learning to reduce a logit that’s already past the cap?” A senior answer

attenuated by(1tanh^2 (l/s)) 0 , meaning the optimizer receives almost no signal to reduce it. The
soft-cap prevents the softmax from seeing the extreme value, but the underlying logit norm can continue
to grow unchecked. This is why soft-capping addresses the symptom but not the cause: in a run without
any QK-norm, raw logit norms may still drift upward over the training horizon even with soft-capping
in place. QK-norm avoids this by preventing norm growth at the source, maintaining well-conditioned
gradients throughout.

Both techniques originate from large-scale vision and multimodal training (QK-norm from ViT-22B, soft-

### 5.2 Numerical Precision and Training Health

**5.2.1 BF16, FP16, and Mixed-Precision Pitfalls**
Every pre-training run on modern hardware mixes at least two floating-point formats, and the assignment of
tensors to formats is not arbitrary. Interviewers at infrastructure-focused roles ask about mixed precision because
getting it wrong produces either silent numerical failures that look like architecture bugs or unnecessary memory
bloat that limits achievable model scale. The question surfaces at the mid-level as “walk me through your mixed-
precision training setup,” and at the senior level as “why do you sometimes see NaN values propagate even in a
bfloat16 run that has gradient clipping enabled.”
Three floating-point formats dominate LLM training today. Each trades dynamic range against mantissa
precision:
**FP32** (float32): 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 mantissa = 4 bytes. Dynamic range 1. 2  10 −^38 to 3. 4  1038.
Roughly 7 decimal digits of precision. The traditional default; now reserved for optimizer state and master
weights.
**FP16** (float16): 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 mantissa = 2 bytes. Maximum representable value: 65504.
Minimum positive normal: 6  10 −^5. Roughly 3 decimal digits of precision. The narrow 5-bit exponent
is the critical limitation for large-model training.
**BF16** (bfloat16): 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 mantissa = 2 bytes. Dynamic range identical to FP32 (
3. 4  1038 ). Roughly 3 decimal digits of precision. Developed by Google Brain in 2018 specifically
because deep learning training needs dynamic range more than it needs mantissa resolution.
An 8-bit format, **FP8** , exists in two variants on H100 hardware: E4M3 (4 exponent bits, 3 mantissa bits,
used for weights and forward-pass activations, maximum 448 ) and E5M2 (5 exponent bits, 2 mantissa bits,
used for gradients, maximum 57344 ). FP8 requires per-tensor dynamic scale factors and is production-viable
on H100s via NVIDIA Transformer Engine, but it is not yet the default at most organizations.
The standard production recipe is _BF16 mixed precision_ :
**Forward and backward compute** (all matrix multiplications): BF16. Tensor cores accumulate partial
sums internally in FP32 and return a BF16 result.
**Master parameters** : FP32.
**Optimizer states** (Adam’s first momentmtand second momentvt): FP32.
**Gradient accumulation** across micro-batches: FP32; per-step gradients passed to the optimizer are FP32.
This asymmetry follows from a key observation: per-layer matmuls are robust to the rounding noise in-
troduced by 7 mantissa bits, but optimizer momentum terms that accumulate small corrections over hundreds
of thousands of steps require 23 mantissa bits to avoid signal loss. Under AdamW, the per-parameter update is
proportional tomt/
p
vt+ε. Whenmt 10 −^5 andvt 10 −^4 , the ratio is approximately 0. 03. In BF16, a
value of 10 −^5 rounds to zero. In FP32, it is preserved.
_Use BF16 where you need throughput; keep FP32 wherever you accumulate over time._
The core argument against FP16 for large-model training is dynamic range. FP16’s maximum representable
value is 65504. During training, gradient magnitudes, activation outputs, and pre-softmax logits can easily ex-
ceed this threshold. In naive attention (without FlashAttention’s safe-softmax), a pre-softmax score of 12 con-
tributese^12  162000 to the partition function before the log-sum-exp normalization step. If that intermediate
exponentiation happens in FP16, it overflows toinf. Onceinfenters the compute graph, any subsequent mul-
tiplication producesNaN, which propagates forward and backward through every layer in that batch. The run is


```
5.2 Numerical Precision and Training Health
```
dead.
BF16 avoids this entirely. Its 8 exponent bits match FP32’s ceiling. The precision sacrifice - 7 mantissa bits
versus 23 - means values are rounded to approximately 0.7% of their true magnitude, which has no measurable
effect on the final quality of a 10B-parameter model trained on a trillion tokens. The same 0.7% rounding
applied to an optimizer state accumulated over 500k steps would progressively corrupt the effective learning
signal, which is why optimizer states stay in FP32.
Loss scaling is the standard workaround for training in FP16: scale the loss by a constant ( 215 to 220 )
before the backward pass to lift gradient magnitudes into FP16’s representable range, then unscale before the
optimizer step. Dynamic loss scaling adjusts this factor step by step to prevent both overflow and underflow.
This works, but it adds a second failure mode: if the scale is too large, gradients still overflow; if too small,
they underflow to zero silently. BF16 eliminates the need for loss scaling entirely, removing an entire class of
training instability.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 13B-parameter model:d= 5120, 40 layers, 40 attention heads,dhead = 128, trained with
AdamW in BF16 mixed precision on 8 H100 80 GB GPUs.
**Static memory footprint (per the 16-bytes-per-parameter rule):**
FP32 master parameters: 13  109 4 = 52GB
FP32 gradients: 13  109 4 = 52GB
FP32 Adammt: 13  109 4 = 52GB
FP32 Adamvt: 13  109 4 = 52GB
BF16 compute copy of parameters: 13  109 2 = 26GB
Total static tensors: 234 GB. This far exceeds a single H100’s 80 GB. With ZeRO stage-3 across 8 GPUs, the
static footprint per GPU drops to 29 GB, leaving 50 GB per GPU for activations. The often-cited “16 bytes
per parameter” accounts for the four FP32 copies (params, gradients,mt,vt) but not the BF16 compute copy;
the true figure under BF16 mixed precision is 18 bytes per parameter.
**FP16 overflow scenario:** Suppose we use FP16 for compute without loss scaling. At step 1,500, a long-
document batch pushes attention logits tosij= 11. 9 before the 1 /

p
dheadscaling at one head. Withgrad_clip
set to 1.0 but the overflow occurring in the forward pass, no gradient norm check saves us. The raw exponent
e^11.^9  147000 exceeds FP16’s ceiling of 65504 ; the result isinf. The attention softmax for that row returns
NaN. The NaN propagates through all 40 layers in the backward pass. After the optimizer step, the affected
parameters containNaN. At step 1,501, the loss readsNaN. The run is unrecoverable without a rollback.
**BF16 with the same batch:** BF16’s exponent range extends to 3. 4  1038. The valuee^11.^9  147000 is
represented without overflow. FlashAttention’s tiled online-softmax further avoids materializing the full expo-
nentiated row in any single buffer. Training continues uninterrupted.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Default to BF16 for all compute; never use FP16 for LLM training without dynamic loss scaling.
On H100s, BF16 tensor core throughput is roughly 10 faster than FP32 and comparable to FP16, with
none of FP16’s overflow risk. The choice is effectively free.
Optimizer states and master parameters must stay in FP32. Switching Adam’smtandvtto BF16
causes visible training quality degradation above 7B parameters, even in short 100B-token runs. The 3-

```
digit mantissa precision rounds away the small per-step corrections that build up meaningful parameter
movement over 500k steps.
Use FlashAttention for numerically stable attention in BF16. Naive attention that materializes the full
NNattention matrix in BF16 can produce catastrophic cancellation at sequence lengths above 4k.
FlashAttention’s tiled algorithm maintains the running softmax max and sum in FP32 within each CUDA
kernel tile, avoiding this without a format switch.
Consider FP8 for inference-side quantization before adopting it for training. FP8 inference (quan-
tizing a trained BF16 model) is low-risk and well-supported. FP8 training requires Transformer Engine,
per-tensor scale factor calibration, and empirical validation against a BF16 baseline for 10k steps before
committing. The throughput gain ( 1. 5 - 2 over BF16) is real but the engineering overhead is substan-
tial.
Monitoractivation_maxand the pre-clip gradient norm from step zero. These two scalars are
your early-warning system for format overflow. Aactivation_maxthat is trending toward 104 in BF16
(still far from overflow, but growing) combined with an elevated gradient norm signals that the model is
entering a regime where even BF16’s range may be stressed; in FP8 mode, the same trend would indicate
imminent scale-factor miscalibration.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through your mixed-precision training setup for a 70B model run.” Answer skeleton:
BF16 for all forward and backward matmuls; FP32 master weights, gradients, and Adam optimizer states;
FlashAttention for numerically stable attention; gradient clipping at 1.0. Explain that FP16 requires dy-
namic loss scaling and is avoided for this exact reason. Mention the 16-18 bytes per parameter static
footprint and why ZeRO stage-2 or -3 is required at 70B.
“Why does training with FP16 sometimes produce NaN values that BF16 does not?” Answer skele-
ton: FP16 has a 5-bit exponent capping representable values at 65504. Attention logits, pre-softmax ac-
tivation values, or backward-pass gradient products can exceed this threshold, overflowing toinf, which
any subsequent multiplication converts toNaN. BF16’s 8-bit exponent matches FP32’s dynamic range and
eliminates this overflow path; the loss in mantissa precision (7 bits vs. 23) does not matter for per-layer
computation.
Senior follow-up: “Your team wants to enable FP8 training end-to-end on H100s to improve through-
put. What is your rollout plan and what failure modes do you specifically instrument?” A senior
answer covers: (1) start with FP8 only in the feed-forward matmuls, leaving attention, layer norm, and
softmax in BF16/FP32; (2) instrument per-tensoramax_historyto detect scale-factor miscalibration -
if the rolling maximum underestimates by 2 , overflow occurs silently; (3) run a parallel BF16 baseline
for 10k steps at small scale to confirm loss curves match within 0.1 nats; (4) expand to full FP8 only after
the subset is validated; (5) flag any step wherenan_frac> 0 for immediate investigation - in FP8 mode
a single miscalibrated tensor contaminates the entire forward pass.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
FP16 is dangerous for LLM training above 7B parameters without dynamic loss scaling; its 5-bit exponent
overflows toinfat values above 65504 , which multiplies toNaNand propagates through every downstream
tensor in the batch.
```

BF16 matches FP32’s dynamic range with half the memory, making it the standard compute dtype for
frontier training runs; the mantissa precision loss is inconsequential for per-layer computation.
Optimizer states and master weights must stay in FP32; the 23-bit mantissa precision is required to accu-
mulate small per-step corrections faithfully over hundreds of thousands of optimizer steps.
The standard static memory budget under AdamW BF16 mixed precision is approximately 18 bytes per
parameter: 4 (FP32 params) + 4 (FP32 gradients) + 4 (Adammt) + 4 (Adamvt) + 2 (BF16 compute
copy); activations scale separately with batch size and sequence length.
FP8 training on H100s with Transformer Engine yields roughly 1. 5 - 2 throughput gains over BF16 but
requires per-tensor scale factor calibration and careful monitoring ofamax_history; most teams adopt
it only after the BF16 pipeline is stable and throughput-limited.

**5.2.2 Loss Spikes: Detection and Mitigation**
A loss spike that goes undetected for 3,000 steps forces a checkpoint rollback that costs several GPU-hours
and invalidates the data-mix accounting for that training window. Staff-level interviewers expect a concrete
playbook: not “watch the loss curve” but a named set of metrics, specific alert thresholds, and tiered responses
that distinguish recoverable anomalies from structural damage. The topic surfaces as “walk me through your
training health monitoring setup” or directly as “your 70B run spiked at 150B tokens and isn’t recovering - what
do you do?”
A loss spike is a sudden increase of 0.1 nats or more in training loss that persists for more than 50 consec-
utive steps. Three root causes account for nearly all production instances, and they are distinguishable by which
diagnostic metric moves first.

1. **Data batch anomaly.** A batch containing corrupted tokens, binary-encoded text, heavily duplicated con-
    tent, or extreme-length documents with out-of-distribution statistics produces a locally very large loss
    gradient. The gradient is large but non-destructive: the model absorbs the update and the loss recovers
    within 100-500 steps as subsequent normal batches dilute the optimizer state.
2. **Gradient explosion or logit drift.** The global gradient norm persistently exceeds the clip threshold (or
    the clip threshold is set too loosely), causing large parameter updates that overshoot the loss basin over
    multiple steps. Alternatively, the softmax logit scale drifts upward as described in the z-loss subsection,
    gradually destabilizing the gradient signal until a threshold is crossed. Both sub-causes share the signature
    of a non-recovering spike with no single obvious culprit batch.
3. **Numerical precision failure.** FP16 or FP8 overflow introducesinforNaNvalues into the compute graph.
    The loss may jump to extreme values (tens of nats or literalNaN) and does not recover without a rollback
    and configuration change.
The practical monitoring set is five scalars logged every training step at negligible overhead:
loss: the primary signal, evaluated on the current batch.
grad_norm: the globalℓ 2 norm of all gradients _before_ clipping. A clipped norm tells you nothing about
whether an explosion occurred; the pre-clip norm does.
log_Z: the mean log-partition-function across the batch, already computed during the forward pass as
part of the cross-entropy loss. The leading indicator for logit drift.
loss_ema_ratio: current loss divided by an exponential moving average of the previous 1,000 steps. A
ratio above 1. 5 triggers a Tier 1 alert; above 2. 5 triggers Tier 2.
nan_frac: fraction of gradient elements that areNaNorInf. Any nonzero value triggers an immediate


```
5.2 Numerical Precision and Training Health
```
halt.
_Root cause determines the correct response; treating all spikes as identical wastes GPU hours on rollbacks
that are unnecessary and misses interventions that are urgent._
The value of the triage protocol is specificity. Three response tiers map onto the three root causes:
**Tier 1 - skip and continue.** Applied whengrad_normspikes to more than 3 its running median in a
single step,loss_ema_ratiois above 1. 5 , and the loss begins returning toward the baseline within 200 steps.
This pattern is consistent with a data anomaly. The correct action is to log the shard index of the offending batch,
optionally skip the optimizer update for that step (retain the gradient for accounting purposes), and continue
without rollback. Introducing a full rollback for a self-correcting anomaly destroys training throughput with no
benefit.
**Tier 2 - rollback to checkpoint.** Applied when the loss rises for more than 500 steps without returning
below the pre-spike level, or whenlog_Zhas increased by more than 3 units in a 300-step window. This
pattern indicates structural damage to the model or optimizer state. Roll back to the checkpoint immediately
preceding the onset of the gradient norm elevation, remove the offending data range from the training sequence,
and resume. Iflog_Zwas the leading signal, add or increase the z-loss coefficient before resuming.
**Tier 3 - rollback and reconfigure.** Applied whennan_fracexceeds zero, or the loss jumps to values
above 10 nats without gradient norm explanation. This indicates a numerical precision failure. Roll back and
identify the source tensor (activation monitoring or a per-layernan_fracbreakdown will localize it), then
adjust the precision configuration - switching a problematic layer back from FP8 to BF16, or from BF16 to
FP32 - before resuming.
The prior approach of relying on gradient clipping alone addresses only Tier 1 partially. Gradient clipping
caps the norm of each update but does not prevent logit scale drift, does not flag data quality issues upstream of
the gradient computation, and does not detect NaN propagation that originates in the forward pass.

**A Worked Example**

A 13B-parameter model:d= 5120, 40 layers, BF16 compute, AdamW, global batch 2M tokens per step,
base learning rate 3  10 −^4 , cosine decay,grad_clip= 1. 0. The run is at step 60,000 when two anomalies
occur.
**Scenario 1 - data anomaly at step 42,100:**
loss: 2. 41! 2. 89 (single step,+0. 48 nats)
Pre-clipgrad_normat step 42,100: 7. 3 (running median over prior 5,000 steps: 1. 1 ; ratio= 6. 6 )
lossover next 400 steps: 2. 89! 2. 72! 2. 58! 2. 44 (recovering)
log_Z: stable at 8. 3  0. 2 before and after the spike
nan_frac: 0 throughout
Diagnosis: data anomaly (Tier 1). The gradient norm is 6. 6 the median at a single step; the loss is
recovering. Action: log the batch shard index for data quality inspection, skip the optimizer update at step
42,100, continue training. No rollback. Estimated cost: zero additional GPU time; one flagged shard for offline
investigation.
**Scenario 2 - logit drift at step 58,500:**
log_Ztrend: 8. 1 at step 57,000, 9. 6 at step 57,500, 11. 9 at step 58,000, 15. 2 at step 58,500 (rising for
1,500 steps)
lossat steps 58,200 onward: 2. 38! 2. 65! 2. 99! 3. 41! 3. 88 (diverging)

```
grad_norm: elevated but not extreme, 1. 8 - 2. 6 (only 1. 7 median, not a single-step spike)
nan_frac: 0
Diagnosis: logit scale drift (Tier 2). The run was not configured with z-loss and the softmax normalizer
has grown toe^15.^2  4  106. At this scale, BF16’s 7-bit mantissa rounds most token probabilities to zero,
collapsing the gradient signal for the majority of the vocabulary. Action: roll back to the checkpoint at step
57,000 (the last checkpoint before thelog_Zacceleration began), add z-loss withα= 10−^4 , resume. The
log_Zstabilizes below 10 within 3,000 steps; the loss returns to the pre-spike trajectory by step 5,000 after
resumption.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Save checkpoints every 1,000 steps; retain the last 10. On a 512-GPU cluster training a 70B model
with a 4M-token global batch, 1,000 steps represents roughly 20-30 minutes of wall time. Retaining 10
checkpoints provides a three-to-five-hour rollback window for diagnosing slowly developing issues at the
cost of approximately 400 GB of checkpoint storage per saved snapshot.
Setgrad_clip = 1. 0 for 7B-70B models and log the pre-clip norm every step. The clipped norm is
uninformative. The pre-clip norm distribution tells you when something is structurally wrong: a median
around 0. 8 - 1. 2 with an occasional 5 outlier is normal; a median that steadily rises from 1. 0 to 3. 0 over
10,000 steps is an early signal of logit drift or an overheated learning rate.
Loglog_Zfrom step zero as a first-class health metric. As detailed in the z-loss subsection, a mono-
tonically increasinglog_Zis the clearest multi-step leading indicator of a future divergent spike. Iflog_Z
has exceeded 12 and has been rising for 5,000 steps, add or increase the z-loss coefficient immediately;
do not wait for the spike.
Implement skip-batch logic for Tier 1 events. Ifloss_ema_ratioexceeds 2.0 at any step, skip the
optimizer update for that step. Still run the forward and backward passes to compute the gradient norm for
diagnostic purposes, then discard the gradient beforeoptimizer.step(). This prevents a single catas-
trophic batch from damaging the Adam momentum estimates while the data shard investigation proceeds.
Stop the run immediately onnan_frac > 0 and do not attempt to continue. A single NaN in the
gradient contaminates every parameter touched by that gradient through subsequent momentum accumu-
lation. The affected optimizer state cannot be repaired; only a rollback to a clean checkpoint resolves it.
Continuing through NaN values corrupts the master weight copy in a way that may not be visible in the
loss for hundreds of steps.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Your 70B pre-training run develops a loss spike at 150B tokens that has not recovered after 3,000
steps. How do you diagnose and fix it?” Answer skeleton: first check whethergrad_normshowed a
single-step extreme outlier before the spike (data anomaly) or a gradual elevation (logit drift or LR issue).
Check whetherlog_Zhas been rising for thousands of steps before the visible spike - if so, the root
cause is logit scale instability. Roll back to the last checkpoint before thelog_Zacceleration, add z-loss
withα= 10−^4 if not already present, and resume. If neither the gradient norm norlog_Zexplains the
spike, inspect the data shard window for corrupted documents or a pipeline error that changed the data
distribution.
```

```
```
“What training health metrics do you log beyond the loss curve?” Answer skeleton: the five-metric
set -loss, pre-clipgrad_norm,log_Z,loss_ema_ratio, andnan_frac. Explain what each indicates
and at what threshold it triggers an action. Mention that per-layer gradient norm histograms (sampled
every 100 steps rather than every step to limit overhead) are added when a run is exhibiting unexplained
instability and you need to localize which layer is the source.
Senior follow-up: “Design an automated spike detection and rollback system for a production pre-
training run. What would you automate versus leave to human judgment?” A senior answer covers:
automate Tier 1 skip-batch onloss_ema_ratio> 2. 0 ; automate immediate halt onnan_frac> 0 ;
automate paging the on-call engineer for Tier 2 events with a pre-populated diagnostic summary (log_Z
trend over the prior 5,000 steps, gradient norm percentile history, data shard identifier for the steps around
the spike onset). Explain why fully automated Tier 2 rollback is risky: the rollback destination requires
understanding whether the spike is a data anomaly that already passed (in which case you roll back past
it) or a configuration deficiency that persists (in which case rolling back without configuration change is
pointless). The human judgment step is cheap; the cost of a wrong automated rollback is not.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Loss spikes fall into three tiers by root cause - data anomaly (self-recovers within 500 steps, skip-batch
response), logit drift or gradient explosion (requires rollback to last stable checkpoint), and numerical
precision failure (requires rollback and configuration change) - and each demands a different response.
The pre-clip gradient norm,log_Z, andnan_fracare the three non-loss metrics that distinguish these
tiers; log all five health metrics at every training step.
Save checkpoints every 1,000 steps and retain at least 10; this bounds the rollback cost at one to three
hours of compute while providing a multi-hour diagnostic window.
Alog_Zthat is monotonically rising and has exceeded 12 is a reliable multi-thousand-step leading indi-
cator of a divergent spike; the correct response is to add z-loss before the spike occurs, not to roll back
after it does.
Fully automated skip-batch (Tier 1) is safe and worth implementing; automated Tier 2 rollbacks require
human sign-off because the correct rollback destination depends on diagnosing the root cause, not just
detecting that a spike occurred.
```

## Part III

# Mixture of Experts and Sparse Architectures


## Chapter 6 Why MoE Is Now Standard in Frontier Systems

### 6.1 Dense vs. Sparse Models for Fixed FLOPs.

**6.1.1 Parameters for Free: The Core MoE Argument**
When an interviewer asks why you would choose a mixture-of-experts architecture over a dense model, the
answer is not simply “more parameters.” The precise answer is more parameters at the same FLOPs budget.
This single idea is what has convinced every major frontier lab to adopt MoE, and it is tested at every seniority
level once you are interviewing for roles that touch training infrastructure or model architecture. At the senior
level you need to be able to quantify it: explain why perplexity curves diverge at identical training compute and
what that implies for how you spend a fixed GPU budget.
A standard dense transformer sends every token through the same feedforward network at every layer. A
sparse MoE transformer replaces each FFN block withNexpert FFNs but activates onlyKof them per token.
If each expert is the same size as the original FFN andK= 1, the forward-pass arithmetic is identical to the
dense model-the same number of multiply-accumulate operations-but the model now storesNtimes as many
FFN parameters in memory.
The MoE layer output for tokentwith residual-stream inputuis:

```
MoE(u) =

#### XN

```
```
