```
wheregi(u) = 0for all but the top-Kexperts by router score. The nonzero gates are derived from a softmax
over the selected indices and combine the chosen experts’ outputs as a weighted average. WhenK = 1this
collapses to a single FFN evaluation with the residual added back: identical FLOPs to the dense case,Nthe
stored parameters.
The empirical case is now settled. Switch Transformer showed that at a fixed training FLOP budget, in-
creasing the expert count from 1 to 256 monotonically reduced language-modeling loss. OlMoE replicated the
result on a modern architecture: the MoE training curve decays faster and reaches a better floor than a compute-
matched dense baseline. DeepSeek’s early MoE ablations compared dense, naive-MoE, and improved-MoE
variants across multiple benchmarks and found consistent improvement as routing quality rose. The same pat-
tern reappears in the DeepSeek-V2 serving results: remarkably low error rates at activated-parameter counts far
below what a comparable dense model would require.
_At a fixed compute budget, sparse MoE models consistently outperform dense models because they pack
more parameters into the same FLOPs, and language models use those extra parameters productively._
Language modeling has two separable demands: computing good representations of context (which re-
quires FLOPs) and memorizing factual associations, vocabulary patterns, and domain idioms (which requires
parameter capacity). Dense architectures must serve both demands with the same parameter budget. MoE de-
couples them: the activated experts handle computation while the dormant ones hold capacity the model can
draw on when the right inputs arrive.
This is not an abstract argument. It is the reason that hashing-based routing-a fixed deterministic function
with no semantic content-still provides performance gains over a single FFN at the same activated FLOPs. The
capacity benefit is real and does not require perfectly learned routing to appear.
The costs are also real. More total parameters means more memory: even if your activated FLOPs are


```
6.1 Dense vs. Sparse Models for Fixed FLOPs
```
modest, you must store the full weight tensor for every expert somewhere in your serving cluster. Routing
introduces systems complexity-token dispatching, all-to-all communication in expert-parallel configurations,
and load-balancing machinery to prevent expert collapse. Dense models are simpler to checkpoint, replicate,
and fine-tune. But for any setting where training compute is the binding constraint and memory plus engineering
overhead are tractable, the FLOPs-per-loss advantage of MoE is now essentially settled empirical fact.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B-parameter dense baseline withdmodel= 4096, FFN hidden dimension 11008 (SwiGLU,
 2. 7 dmodel), and 32 layers. Each FFN block has roughly 3  4096  11008  135 M parameters (three
projections in the gated network), giving about 4.3B FFN parameters across the full model.
Now design a FLOP-matched MoE: 8 experts per layer, each expert at one-quarter the hidden dimension
(2752), top-2 routing:
Parameters per expert: 3  4096  2752  34 M
Total expert parameters per layer: 8  34 M= 272M
Total expert parameters across 32 layers: 32  272 M 8. 7 B (2the dense FFN budget)
Activated per token per layer: 2  34 M= 68M, roughly half the dense FFN per layer
For an exact FLOPs match, use top-1 routing with full-size experts: 8 experts each at 135M parameters,
activating 1. The activated compute is identical to the dense baseline; the stored FFN parameters jump from
135M to 8  135 M= 1. 08 B per layer.
Training both variants for 1T tokens at identical compute budget: empirical results typically show a 0.1-0.2
nats/token improvement in perplexity for the MoE, translating to meaningfully better downstream benchmark
scores. The memory cost for the 8-expert MoE is approximately 8 the dense FFN footprint-that is the price
paid for those gains.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use MoE when training compute is the bottleneck, not memory. If you are already memory-limited
at inference and cannot shard experts across devices, dormant parameters become dead weight that yields
no performance return.
Fine-grained experts beat fewer large ones. Ablations in both DeepSeek MoE and OlMoE consistently
show that 64 quarter-size experts outperform 16 full-size experts at the same activated-FLOPs budget.
Default to fine-grained experts when you have the routing infrastructure to support them.
K= 2 is the canonical starting point. Top-1 routing is maximally compute-efficient but gives the router
no gradient signal to compare alternatives. Top-2 provides that comparison at the cost of doubling per-
token FFN FLOPs relative to top-1. Most production systems (Mixtral, DeepSeek, Grok) useK= 2or
a fine-grained equivalent.
Expert specialization is less semantic than the name implies. Hashing-based routing provides real
gains without any learned affinity between tokens and experts. If a reviewer tells you MoE works because
experts specialize by domain, that framing is not wrong but it is incomplete: the parameter-capacity
benefit alone explains the FLOPs-matched quality gap.
Every-layer MoE is now standard at frontier scale. Earlier designs alternated dense and MoE layers
to reduce fine-tuning instability. Modern production systems that absorb the engineering overhead apply
MoE at every FFN layer.
```

```
6.1 Dense vs. Sparse Models for Fixed FLOPs
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does a sparse MoE outperform a dense model trained on the same compute?” Strong answer: the
MoE decouples parameter capacity from compute. At equal FLOPs, the activated experts do the same
arithmetic as the dense FFN, but the model holds additional capacity in dormant experts that it exploits
for memorization. Empirically, that capacity is productive across diverse tasks.
“What engineering costs do you accept when switching from dense to MoE?” Strong answer: three cate-
gories. Memory: total parameter count grows by up toN, requiring expert-parallel sharding. Routing:
non-differentiable top-Kselection requires auxiliary load-balancing losses to prevent collapse. Stability:
MoE models are more prone to loss spikes and fine-tuning divergence; z-loss on router logits and float32
router computation are standard mitigations.
Senior follow-up: “How does the MoE FLOPs advantage interact with compute-optimal scaling?” Compute-
optimal reasoning applies to activated parameters and training FLOPs. Dormant MoE parameters are
essentially free from a training-compute standpoint-you are not paying for them in multiply-accumulate
operations. This means a MoE can simultaneously be compute-optimal in its activated parameter count
and parameter-rich in its total count. The catch is that serving cost scales with total parameters, not
activated ones, so the efficiency argument flips at inference time.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
At identical training FLOPs, MoE models consistently achieve lower perplexity than dense models-this
has been replicated across architectures, scales, and labs.
The mechanism is decoupling: activated parameters set compute cost; total parameters set capacity. MoE
scales capacity without scaling compute.
Fine-grained experts (many small ones over few large ones) andK= 2routing are the dominant produc-
tion defaults.
Primary costs are aggregate memory (Nthe dense FFN footprint), routing infrastructure, and load-
balancing complexity to prevent expert collapse.
Expert specialization is real but secondary; the parameter-capacity argument alone explains the FLOPs-
matched quality gain.
```
**6.1.2 Activated vs. Total Parameters**
When a candidate describes a mixture-of-experts model as a “70B model” without qualifying which 70B
they mean, they have already lost the thread of the economics. Understanding the difference between activated
and total parameters is the single most important framing skill for reasoning about MoE systems: it determines
training compute, serving memory, hardware topology, and how to interpret the benchmark plots that labs pub-
lish. Interviewers test this at every seniority level; senior engineers must derive concrete infrastructure numbers
from both quantities on the spot.
In a dense transformer every parameter participates in every forward pass. The model hasPtotalparameters
and uses all of them to process each token, soPactivated=Ptotal.
A sparse MoE transformer breaks this coupling. For each token, the router activates onlyKof theN
available experts per MoE layer. The rest are stored in memory but contribute zero FLOPs during that token’s
forward pass. The two quantities are:


```
6.1 Dense vs. Sparse Models for Fixed FLOPs
```
**Total parameters** : all weights in the model, including every expert that will never fire for a given input.
This determines the memory required to host the model.
**Activated parameters** : the subset of weights that execute per token per forward pass. This determines
per-token FLOPs and, by extension, training compute and inference latency.
For a model withLMoE layers,Nexperts per layer, each expert containingPeparameters, andKexperts
activated per token, the two quantities are:

Ptotal=Pnon-FFN+LNPe
Pactivated=Pnon-FFN+LKPe
The ratioN/Kis the _sparsity factor_ : it describes how many times larger the total FFN parameter count is
relative to the activated FFN parameter count. A model with 64 experts and top-4 routing has a sparsity factor
of 16. Training compute scales withPactivated; hosting cost scales withPtotal.
_Activated parameters set the compute price; total parameters set the memory price-and for MoE these two
prices are decoupled by the sparsity factor._
For training, the activated-parameter count is all that matters for FLOPs. Compute-optimal reasoning fol-
lowing Chinchilla-style analysis should tune token count and activated model capacity together-dormant expert
weights cost nothing in training compute. A 70B-total MoE model with 7B activated parameters trains at the
FLOPs cost of a 7B dense model. If the resulting quality matches a 13B or 20B dense model-which empirical
results from Switch Transformer, OlMoE, and the DeepSeek MoE line suggest it can-the MoE is simply a better
use of a fixed training budget.
For serving, total-parameter count dominates. Every weight tensor, including experts that fire rarely or
never for a particular query, must live somewhere in memory at inference time. The router’s decision is data-
dependent; you cannot know in advance which expert will be needed for each token, so all experts must be
resident. A 70B-total MoE costs the same inference-time memory as a 70B dense model, even if only 7B
parameters contribute arithmetic per token. Latency per token is low (7B worth of FLOPs), but the weight
memory bill is high.
This asymmetry explains why labs publish benchmark results with “activated parameters” on the x-axis.
On that axis MoE looks spectacular: DeepSeek-V2’s MMLU results plotted against activated parameters sit far
above comparably activated dense models at the same compute. That framing is not misleading-it accurately
captures compute efficiency-but it does not tell the hosting story. An interviewer who asks “what is the catch?”
is probing exactly this gap.

**A Worked Example**

32 transformer layers; FFN total: 32  135 M 4. 3 B
Non-FFN (attention, embeddings, norms): 2. 7 B
Total 7 B, activated 7 B
Now design a FLOP-matched MoE that targets the same per-token compute:
64 experts per layer, each at one-quarter the FFN hidden dimension (deff= 2752)
```

Top-4 routing; activated FFN per layer: 4  34 M= 136M (matches dense)
Total FFN per layer: 64  34 M= 2. 18 B
Total FFN across 32 layers: 32  2. 18 B 70 B
Total model: 70 B+ 2. 7 B 73 B; activated: 7 B

This is identical for the dense and MoE variants by construction.
Serving memory in BF16:
Dense: 7 B 2 bytes= 14GB-fits on a single A100-40GB.
MoE: 73 B 2 bytes 146 GB-requires at least two H100-80GB GPUs for weights alone, with expert-

The sparsity factor isN/K= 64/4 = 16. The MoE stores 16more FFN parameters than the FLOP-
matched dense model. You pay for all 73B weights in memory but compute with only 7B of them per token.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use activated parameters for training budget planning. When computing your compute-optimal
token-to-parameter ratio, plug in activated parameters. Sizing by total parameters overstates your training
FLOPs and produces a model that is undertrained relative to its capacity.
Use total parameters for serving infrastructure planning. When provisioning GPUs for inference,
total parameters set the memory floor. Expert parallelism is mandatory once total parameters exceed a
single node’s HBM capacity (typically 640 GB for an 8-way H100 NVLink node at BF16 weights before
activations and KV cache).
High sparsity factors amplify both the benefit and the hosting cost. A sparsity factor of 32-as in
DeepSeek-V3’s 256 routed experts with top-8 routing-gives 32more FFN parameters than a FLOP-
matched dense baseline. The quality gain is real; the memory bill is proportionally real.
Know which inference regime you are in. In memory-bound inference (small batches, long context),
latency is dominated by weight loading, not arithmetic. A dense 7B model can outperform a 73B-total
/ 7B-activated MoE on latency in this regime because it loads far fewer bytes from HBM per token. In
compute-bound inference (large batches), activated parameters dominate and the MoE and dense models
have comparable throughput-the MoE wins on quality at that compute level.
Benchmark comparisons require the right denominator. Before accepting a “quality vs. activated
parameters” claim, verify what the total-parameter hosting cost is. A fair head-to-head for practitioners
is either equal activated parameters (same training cost) or equal total parameters (same serving cost).
Equal total parameters is the test the MoE must also pass at inference time.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A lab claims their MoE model has 70B parameters and matches a 13B dense model in quality. What
would you ask before accepting that comparison?” Strong answer: first, clarify whether 70B is total or
activated. If it is 70B total with 7B activated, the training compute comparison is coherent-it trained at
7B FLOPs cost. But 70B total means roughly 10the memory of a 7B dense model, which changes the
```

### 6.2 Routing: The Heart of Every MoE

```
serving calculus entirely. Second, ask whether the quality comparison is FLOP-controlled (same training
compute) or size-controlled (same total parameters): beating a 13B dense at equal training FLOPs is
expected; beating a 70B dense at equal total parameters would be a much stronger result.
“How do you provision inference hardware for a 70B-total / 7B-activated MoE?” Strong answer: start
with total parameters to set the memory floor. At BF16 that is140 GB, requiring at minimum two H100-
80GB GPUs with expert-parallel sharding. Latency per token is set by activated-parameter FLOPs (7B
worth), not total. Batch throughput is limited by the all-to-all communication dispatch added by expert
routing, so benchmark throughput degradation against a purely dense serving stack before committing.
Senior follow-up: “When does a dense model win at inference even if the MoE wins at training?” The
senior answer requires distinguishing inference regimes. In memory-bandwidth-bound serving (single-
user or small-batch), each token forces the hardware to stream weight bytes from HBM regardless of
whether those bytes are used for arithmetic. A 73B-total MoE streams 10more bytes per token than a
7B dense model even though the arithmetic is identical. Time-to-first-token and per-token latency both
suffer in this regime. Only at large batch sizes, where the hardware is arithmetic-bound, do the two
models converge on latency-at that point the MoE wins because its quality is higher at the same activated-
parameter count.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Activated parameters set per-token FLOPs and training compute; total parameters set memory footprint
and hosting cost-MoE decouples these two quantities by the sparsity factorN/K.
Training budget reasoning must use activated parameters; infrastructure provisioning must use total pa-
rameters. Mixing these up leads to hardware surprises in either direction.
The sparsity factor quantifies the memory-to-compute leverage of a MoE design: a factor of 16 means
16 more FFN parameters in storage than in any single token’s forward pass.
Benchmark plots that place “activated parameters” on the x-axis are accurate for compute efficiency com-
parisons but obscure the full memory cost of hosting all dormant expert weights.
In memory-bandwidth-bound inference regimes, total parameter count governs latency; in compute-bound
regimes, activated parameter count governs throughput-know which regime applies before choosing MoE
over dense.
```
### 6.2 Routing: The Heart of Every MoE

**6.2.1 Token-Choice Top-K Routing**
Every MoE interview question eventually lands on the routing function. An interviewer at a frontier lab

panies running production MoE systems, and a strong answer requires knowing the mechanics cold, the design
rationale, and where the gradient actually flows. Getting any of these wrong signals that you have read about

Token-choice top-Krouting directly answers the question the model cares about: given this token’s repre-

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Co-design K with expert granularity. UseK= 2when each expert is full-sized (dense FFN equiva-
lent), as in Mixtral and DBRX. IncreaseKproportionally when you halve or quarter expert size. If each
expert is 1 /mthe dense FFN size, activatingm/ 2 experts keeps the per-token FLOP cost near parity with
the dense model while maximizing the parameter-to-FLOP ratio.
Compute router logits in float32. Even in bfloat16 training runs, compute the affinity scores and the
softmax in float32. The softmax exponential can underflow rare-expert logits to zero in bfloat16, causing
those experts to never receive tokens and never recover - effectively zeroing out parameters. The float32
cast is one line of code and costs nothing at scale.
Do not invest in a heavier router. There is a tempting idea that a two-layer MLP router would route more
intelligently than a linear inner product. In practice the gradient signal to the router is weak - you only
observe gradients through theKselected experts - so a more complex router does not learn a meaningfully
better routing policy. The systems cost of additional router FLOPs is real; the quality benefit is not.
Decide on renormalization after top-K. Renormalizing the selected gate weights to sum to 1 makes the
output a proper convex combination and is slightly more interpretable. Not renormalizing is also fine; the
next layer norm absorbs the scale. Some architectures (DeepSeek-V3 with sigmoid gates) renormalize;
others (early DeepSeek MoE with softmax gates) do not. Pick one and be consistent.
Sigmoid at the gate vs. softmax before top-K. Softmax before top-K creates competitive suppression: a
single dominant expert can concentrate most of the probability mass before the discrete cut even happens,
starving the other selected experts of meaningful gate weight. Sigmoid scores are independent per expert,
so the top-Kselection is less distorted by outlier logits. DeepSeek-V3’s switch to sigmoid with post-
selection renormalization reflects this reasoning.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through the forward pass of a MoE layer.” A strong answer describes the four steps (affinity
scoring, top-Kselection, expert forward passes, weighted aggregation with residual) and gives the key
equations. Bonus: mention the FLOP count breakdown and why routing cost is negligible.
“Why not use a soft gate over all experts instead of top-K?” Activating allNexperts on every token
multiplies the FFN FLOP cost byN. Top-Kis the mechanism that preserves the FLOP budget of the
dense baseline while expanding the parameter count. Without it, you have a dense model withNFFNs
and no efficiency advantage.
```

```
6.2 Routing: The Heart of Every MoE
```
```
Senior follow-up: “How does the router learn, given that top-K is not differentiable?” The short
answer: gradients flow only through theKselected experts. The gate weightsi,tis differentiable with
respect to the router embeddingsei, so the model does learn to rank experts correctly on routed tokens.
But experts that are never selected receive no gradient signal and never improve. This is precisely why
auxiliary load-balancing losses are not optional - without them, one or two high-scoring experts absorb
all traffic, the remaining experts atrophy, and you effectively have a one-expert model with a lot of wasted
parameters.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The router is a(Nd)learned embedding matrix plus an inner product, softmax (or sigmoid), and top-K
gate. Total routing cost per token is negligible relative to the expert FFN forward passes.
Token-choice top-Kis the industry-standard routing mechanism in virtually every major production MoE:
Mixtral, all DeepSeek variants, Grok, Llama 4, Qwen MoE, OlMoE.
Kand expert size are co-designed: fine-grained (quarter-sized) experts require higherKto maintain
FLOP parity with a dense baseline; coarse-grained (full-sized) experts useK= 2.
Always compute router logits in float32, even in bfloat16 training runs, to prevent rare-expert underflow.
Top-Kis non-differentiable; the auxiliary load-balancing loss is what prevents router collapse and keeps
all experts active throughout training.
```

```
whereWnoisecontrols per-expert noise magnitude and is itself learned. The noise forces exploration: even
non-top-Kexperts receive tokens occasionally, enabling gradient signal to flow to all experts.
_All three alternatives sacrifice the token’s agency - the guarantee that each token reaches its highest-aﬀinity
experts - to achieve load balance or exploration, and that trade-off costs measurably in model quality or infer-
ence compatibility._
Expert-choice routing has one compelling advantage - perfect expert utilization - and two serious drawbacks
that together make it impractical.
The first drawback is inference incompatibility. At inference time you process one or a few requests, not
a large batch. The “each expert picks top-Ketokens from a batch” formulation breaks down forT= 1: every
expert would try to selectKe = 1/Nof a single token, which is undefined. You are forced either to revert
to token-choice at inference (creating a train-test mismatch the model has never seen during training) or to
construct an artificial batch at inference and accept the latency cost. Token-choice has no such issue; each token
independently selectsKexperts regardless of batch size.
The second drawback is variable per-token coverage. In expert-choice, a token is processed by however
many experts happen to select it, which can be zero. A token with a diffuse affinity vector (high entropy, low
peak) may be skipped entirely, with its hidden state propagating through the layer via the residual connection
only, receiving no MoE computation at all. Token-choice guarantees every token is processed by exactlyK
experts, no exceptions.
OlMoE ran the definitive comparison under controlled conditions: the same 7B-class MoE architecture,
same training data, same compute budget, only the routing direction differing. Token-choice achieved substan-
tially better validation loss at every measured checkpoint. The gap was consistent and not noise - expert-choice’s
load-balance advantage did not compensate for its coverage disadvantage.
Global assignment achieves better affinity coverage than greedy token-choice (the globally optimal assign-
ment, not a per-token greedy one) and better balance than naive token-choice without an auxiliary loss. But
solving even an approximate linear program on every forward pass is prohibitively slow. Sinkhorn iterations
on a 64  4096 affinity matrix (64 experts, 4096 tokens per batch) at 10 iterations add roughly 5.2M FLOPs
per layer per step. Across 64 layers and millions of training steps, this cost is non-trivial, and the quality gains
over token-choice with a simple auxiliary balancing loss are marginal. No production MoE system uses global
assignment.
Noisy top-Kwas ultimately abandoned for a simpler reason: auxiliary-loss balancing achieves comparable
exploration with no train-test mismatch. The noise added during training is removed at inference (to be deter-
ministic), but the model has learned routing distributions shaped by noisy training. Auxiliary-loss balancing
applies the same uniform-load pressure without introducing any inference divergence.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a batch ofT = 4096tokens processed byN = 8experts, with token-choiceK = 2versus
expert-choiceKe= 1024(each expert selects 1024 of 4096 tokens). Hidden dimensiond= 2048.
**Token-choice** : For each of 4096 tokens, compute 8 dot products with router embeddings, take top-2. Rout-
ing cost: 4096  8  2048  2  134 M FLOPs for the affinity matrix (shared by both methods). Result: every
token processed by exactly 2 experts; 8192 total expert invocations across the batch.


```
6.2 Routing: The Heart of Every MoE
```
**Expert-choice** : Same affinity matrix. Each of 8 experts sorts 4096 scores and selects top-1024. In the
ideally balanced case, each token is selected by 8  1024 /4096 = 2experts on average - identical throughput
to token-choice. But consider a skewed batch where 512 tokens are from a single domain that all 8 experts
prefer. Each expert fills most of its 1024 slots with those tokens. The remaining 3584 tokens compete for 8
512  4096 remaining slots; some get 2 expert invocations, others get 0. A token that gets 0 expert invocations
passes through the MoE layer unchanged. In a 32-layer model, that token may miss many expert computations,
degrading output quality on an input that contained no unusual or out-of-distribution content.
At inference time withT = 1: token-choice routes to exactlyK = 2experts, always. Expert-choice
requires definingKefor a batch of size 1;Ke = 1/ 8 is not an integer. The method is undefined without
patching.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Never use expert-choice if you need single-query inference. This is not a performance trade-off - it is an
architectural incompatibility. Any system that serves user requests one at a time cannot use expert-choice
routing without a structural workaround that reintroduces token-choice at inference.
Cite global assignment to show depth, but never ship it. S-BASE and Sinkhorn-based routing are useful
interview references demonstrating that you know the design space. Follow immediately with the reason
they are not in production: the approximate solver cost is not justified by quality gains over token-choice
plus auxiliary loss.
Hashing is a useful null hypothesis for ablations. Routing tokens to experts by a fixed hash function (no
learned affinity, no gradient) still outperforms a dense model at the same FLOP count. This benchmark
reveals that the gains from MoE come primarily from having more total parameters and from the implicit
data parallelism over the token stream, not from intelligent routing. A weak router that merely prevents
collapse is sufficient; heroic routing engineering has diminishing returns.
Noisy top- K was abandoned in favor of auxiliary-loss balancing. If your concern is expert collapse
(all tokens routing to one expert), the auxiliary loss is simpler, more stable, and has no inference-time side
effects. Noisy top-Kwas a reasonable early attempt but is not used in modern releases.
RL-based routing is principled but impractical. Discrete routing decisions are a natural RL target
(the routing choice is an action; the loss improvement is the reward). Clark et al. (2020) benchmarked
RL-based routing and found it roughly on par with hashing - not better than top-Kwith balancing. The
gradient variance and compute overhead rule it out for large-scale training.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What is the difference between token-choice and expert-choice routing?” Token-choice: each token
selectsKbest experts (variable per-expert load). Expert-choice: each expert selectsKebest tokens
(perfect expert utilization, variable per-token coverage). Token-choice wins empirically and is inference-
compatible. Expert-choice is inference-incompatible for single-query serving.
“Why not solve for the globally optimal routing assignment?” Global assignment (Sinkhorn, linear
program) adds a solver step that costsO(NT)per layer per forward pass. At training scale, this over-
head is non-trivial, and the quality gain over token-choice with auxiliary-loss balancing is marginal. No
production system uses it.
```

```
6.2 Routing: The Heart of Every MoE
```
```
Senior follow-up: “If you had to use expert-choice for some reason, how would you handle infer-
ence?” The cleanest approach is to train with expert-choice and switch to token-choice at inference, ac-
cepting the train-test distribution shift. To reduce that shift, constrain the expert-choice training objective
so that every token is guaranteed at leastKexpert invocations (solve a minimum-coverage assignment
rather than a top-Kper expert). In practice this requires a more expensive constrained solver and still
produces inference behavior the model has not seen during training. The honest answer is: if you need
single-query inference, do not use expert-choice - this is exactly why the field did not adopt it.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Expert-choice routing guarantees load balance but cannot be used for single-query inference, making it
incompatible with the vast majority of LLM serving systems.
Global assignment (Sinkhorn, linear program) is theoretically optimal routing but too slow for production;
its quality gains over token-choice with auxiliary balancing are marginal.
OlMoE ablations confirm token-choice produces cleaner loss curves and better final perplexity than expert-
choice under the same compute budget.
Hashing outperforms dense models even with no learned routing, which tells you the benefit of MoE
comes from parameter count and token-stream parallelism, not routing intelligence.
RL-based and noisy top-Krouting were early principled explorations; both were abandoned in favor of
the much simpler auxiliary-loss balancing approach that is now universal.
```

## Chapter 7 MoE Training and Systems Considerations

### 7.1 Fine-Grained and Shared Experts.

**7.1.1 The DeepSeek MoE Blueprint**
When an interviewer asks you to design the FFN structure for a large MoE, the right starting point is not
an empty whiteboard - it is the configuration that DeepSeek published and that every subsequent open MoE
has copied. The fine-grained expert blueprint from DeepSeek MoE has become the de facto standard because
it solves a specific parameter-efficiency problem with a clean arithmetic argument. Knowing the configuration,
the numbers, and the FLOP trade-offs cold is the difference between sketching an architecture and actually
defending one at the senior engineer level.
The vanilla MoE is straightforward: copy a dense FFNNtimes and activateKcopies per token. If each
copy is the same size as the dense FFN andK= 1, the forward FLOP count is unchanged while total parameters
multiply byN. The catch is that with a smallN(say, 8), the parameter multiplier is modest. If you want more
parameters, you need more experts - but more full-size experts means more memory, more communication, and
diminishing returns once you have more experts than training tokens can specialize them.
Fine-grained experts cut through this directly. The insight: shrink each expert to 1 /mof the standard FFN
intermediate dimension and havemtimes as many experts. Total parameter count stays the same, but now you
havemtimes more distinct expert FFNs. You then activateKof them per token, settingKlarge enough so that
the activated FFN capacity stays near the dense baseline.
Formally, letdmodelbe the hidden dimension anddffn= 4dmodelbe the standard intermediate dimension.
With granularity factorm, each fine-grained expert has intermediate dimensiondexpert=dffn/m. Total experts:
Nrouted = mNdense, whereNdenseis however many full-size experts you would otherwise have. Activated
routed experts:K. To maintain roughly the same activated FLOP count as the dense model:

```
Kdexpertdffn =) Km.
```
In practiceKis set slightly belowm(because shared experts, covered in the next subsection, absorb part of the
capacity), but this relation is the governing design equation.
_Fine-grained experts trade expert size for expert count at fixed activated FLOP cost, giving a multiplicative
parameter expansion that scales as the granularity factor_ m _while leaving the per-token computation budget
nearly unchanged._
More distinct FFN parameter matrices mean more distinct processing pathways. The scaling argument is
empirical but robust: at fixed training FLOPs, adding more expert parameters consistently lowers validation
loss, and fine-grained experts are the mechanism that lets you add those parameters without inflating activated
compute.
There is also a combinatorial argument. WithN= 8full-size experts andK = 2, the model can form

The architecture also scales cleanly. DeepSeek MoE v1 (16B total, 2.8B active), DeepSeek-V2 (236B
total, 21B active), and DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B active) all use the same structural blueprint: fine-grained

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start at m= 4 (quarter-size experts) as your baseline. Finer granularity (m= 8,m= 16) gives
more total parameters but shrinks the per-expert matrix below the efficient tile size for H100 tensor cores
(roughly 128  128 in bfloat16). Below an intermediate dimension of512 fordmodel= 4096, matrix
multiply efficiency degrades measurably. OlMoE, Llama 4, and DeepSeek all operate atm= 4or close
to it.

experts pushes you to 1.5-2. Staying below 2 keeps the MoE competitive with a dense model of the
same total training compute.
Keep all fine-grained experts the same size. Mixed expert sizes force variable-length matrix multiply
kernels that kill GPU utilization. Every expert in the routed pool and every shared expert should have the
samedexpert. Uniform expert size is a hard engineering requirement, not an aesthetic preference.
Scale total experts with model size, not just parameter count. DeepSeek MoE v1 uses 64 routed
experts at 16B total parameters; DeepSeek-V3 uses 256 routed experts at 671B. The ratio is sub-linear,
not proportional. Expert count is bounded by memory (each expert’s weights must fit on some device) and
communication overhead (more experts)more all-to-all traffic). A practical ceiling around 256 experts
appears in current large-scale deployments.

Fine-grained experts shrink each FFN to 1 /mof the standard intermediate dimension and multiply expert

token.
The canonical configuration from DeepSeek MoE:m= 4(quarter-size experts), 64 routed + 2 shared,
K = 6active routed. This blueprint is used verbatim or with minor variation in OlMoE, Llama 4,
MiniMax, and DeepSeek-V2/V3.
Activated FLOP overhead: roughly 2 the dense FFN cost with the canonical configuration - a small
premium for a large parameter expansion.
Expert granularity is hardware-constrained: belowdexpert 512 for typical hidden dimensions, tensor
core utilization degrades and expert parallelism communication overhead grows.
The MoE architecture was fixed at DeepSeek MoE v1; scaling to 671B total parameters in V3 required
only changing expert count and model width, not restructuring the blueprint.

**7.1.2 When Shared Experts Help and When They Don’t**
An interviewer will ask you to defend adding a shared expert to your MoE design, and the honest answer
is nuanced: the DeepSeek MoE paper showed gains; the OlMoE independent replication found none. If you


```
7.1 Fine-Grained and Shared Experts
```
answer with a confident “shared experts always help” or “shared experts don’t matter,” you reveal that you
read one paper without understanding what the disagreement tells you about the mechanism. The right answer
explains when the gain appears and gives a principled decision rule for a new architecture.
A shared expert is an MLP that processes every token, unconditionally, in addition to whatever routed
experts the router selects. In a standard fine-grained MoE layer, the output is:

```
ht=ut+
```

There is no gate on the shared experts. Every token, regardless of content, passes through allnsshared MLPs.
The shared experts are the same size as the fine-grained routed experts, so all active computation uses uniform
matrices - important for kernel efficiency.
The gradient structure differs fundamentally from routed experts. A routed expert receives gradient signal
only from the tokens the router sends to it, which under balanced routing isK/Ntotalof all tokens. A shared
expert receives gradient from every token in every batch - a dense, high-signal gradient at every step. This means
shared experts converge faster and to a more stable minimum than any individual routed expert.
_A shared expert is a fully trained dense FFN embedded inside a sparse MoE layer; it handles whatever
processing is needed for every token, leaving the routed pool to specialize on the residual token-specific trans-
formation._
The hypothesis is that some MLP transformations are genuinely universal across all token types - com-
mon syntactic structures, frequency-heavy vocabulary items, low-level pattern normalization - that every routed
expert would otherwise need to partially replicate. By factoring this shared component out, routed experts can
specialize more cleanly on the remaining token-specific work, improving effective capacity per routing decision.
This argument is compelling in theory. The empirical record is split. The original DeepSeek MoE paper
reports consistent benchmark improvements from adding one shared expert (orange bars) versus no shared expert
(blue bars), with further gains on some tasks from a second shared expert. But these are not controlled ablations
over a single variable; the shared expert configuration also affects how the authors setKandN.
OlMoE ran a cleaner ablation: same architecture, same training run, only varying the presence of shared
experts. Their result (comparing purple versus teal validation loss curves across training) shows no significant
difference at their scale - roughly a 7B total parameter model. This is a careful third-party test with no confounds,
and it found zero gain.
The reconciliation is likely scale and data. At DeepSeek’s pre-training scale (hundreds of billions of to-
kens, models with 16B-671B total parameters), routed experts are heavily underfit early in training. An expert
receiving 1 / 64 of all tokens takes far longer to converge than a shared expert seeing 100% of tokens. The shared
expert acts as a well-converged baseline that stabilizes learning for the underfitted routed experts. At OlMoE’s
smaller scale, routed experts converge faster relative to training time, and the stabilizing benefit disappears.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B active-parameter MoE withdmodel= 4096,dexpert= 1024(quarter-size experts), 64 routed
experts, andK= 6active routed. Compare three configurations:
**Config A: 0 shared experts,** K = 6 **routed.** Activated FLOPs per token (FFN component): 6  2 


```

```
4096  1024  2  100 M. Total FFN parameters: 64  2  4096 1024 = 536M.
**Config B: 1 shared expert,** K= 6 **routed (7 active total).** Activated FLOPs: 7  100 M/ 6  117 M
(+17%). Total FFN parameters: 65  8. 4 M= 546M (+2%).

That is 1 exaFLOP of training compute - roughly 10% of the total compute for a mid-size training run. If that
exaFLOP delivers measurably better validation loss, it is well spent. If it does not (OlMoE’s finding), it is a 10%
tax with no return.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Default to 0 shared experts; add 1 only if ablations show favorable gain-per-FLOP. OlMoE’s result is
a strong null hypothesis. Do not start with shared experts because DeepSeek used them. Run a 1B-scale
ablation for 100B tokens comparing 0 shared vs. 1 shared vs. “1 more routed expert” at the same total
FLOP cost. If the shared expert wins the gain-per-FLOP comparison, add it. If adding a routed expert
wins, add that instead.
Size shared experts identically to routed experts. If your routed experts havedexpert= 1024, the shared
experts should also havedexpert= 1024. Matching sizes means the same matrix multiply kernel handles
all active experts uniformly. A differently-sized shared expert creates a two-kernel path that complicates
the implementation with no clear upside.
The 2-shared configuration in DeepSeek MoE is partly motivated by accounting symmetry. With 2
shared + 6 routed, all 8 active experts are equal-size, and the total activated capacity is 8 dexpert= 2dffn
```
- exactly twice the dense FFN capacity. This is convenient bookkeeping but not a principled reason to
prefer 2 over 1. Llama 4 uses 1 shared expert; some Chinese releases tried more and retreated to 0 or 1.
**At**  100 **B total parameters, shared experts become more worth testing.** The mechanism - stabilizing
slow-to-converge routed experts - is proportionally stronger when experts see fewer tokens relative to their
parameter count. A model with 256 routed experts and 1T training tokens has each expert seeing roughly
1012 / 256  4  109 tokens, which is already tight for full convergence of an MLP. A shared expert seeing
all 1012 tokens provides a well-converged anchor.
**Do not freeze or treat shared experts differently from routed experts.** They are standard parameters
trained with the same optimizer, learning rate, and weight decay as every other weight in the model. The
only difference is the absence of a routing gate. Freezing shared experts after warm-up, or using a different
learning rate, introduces complexity with no theoretical justification.

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why would you add a shared expert to a MoE layer?” The hypothesis: some MLP-level transfor-
mations are universal across token types; factoring them into a dedicated always-on expert allows routed
experts to specialize more purely. Shared experts also receive a dense gradient (every token, every step),
so they converge faster and act as a stable baseline during early training when routed experts are underfit.
```

### 7.2 Load Balancing and Stability

```
“OlMoE found no gain from shared experts but DeepSeek did. How do you reconcile that?” Scale
and training budget. DeepSeek’s models are 16B-671B total parameters trained on hundreds of billions of
tokens; OlMoE is7B total. At larger scale, each routed expert sees fewer tokens relative to its capacity,
leaving more useful gradient for a shared expert to absorb. At OlMoE’s scale, routed experts converge
fast enough that a shared component adds nothing net. This is an empirically testable hypothesis: the
crossover point is somewhere between 7B and 16B total parameters.
Senior follow-up: “How would you run the ablation to decide whether to include a shared expert in
a new MoE?” Train three 1B-parameter models for 100B tokens each, holding all hyperparameters fixed
and varying only: (a) 0 shared, 64 routed,K= 6; (b) 1 shared, 64 routed,K= 6(+17%FFN FLOPs);
(c) 0 shared, 64 routed,K= 7(same+17%FLOPs via one extra active routed expert). Compare held-out
perplexity against the FLOP budget. If (b) beats (c), the shared expert is worth its cost. If (c) beats (b),
adding a routed expert is the better use of that compute, and you skip the shared expert. This design is the
right frame because it controls for the FLOP budget change, which the original DeepSeek ablation did
not cleanly do.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
A shared expert is an MLP that always fires for every token, with no routing gate; it receives dense gradient
signal at every training step, unlike routed experts which are each gated by the top-Kselection.
Empirical evidence is split: DeepSeek MoE reports gains; OlMoE’s controlled ablation finds none. The
likely explanation is scale - shared experts help when routed experts are underfit relative to training token
budget.
Each shared expert unconditionally adds 2 dmodeldexpert 2 FLOPs per token; at 1T training tokens
and 32 layers, that is1 exaFLOP per shared expert for typical model sizes. Budget this explicitly.
Default recommendation: start with 0 shared experts; ablate against the equivalent FLOP spent on an
additional active routed expert before committing to a shared expert.
Size shared experts identically to routed experts for kernel uniformity; train them end-to-end with no
special treatment.
```
### 7.2 Load Balancing and Stability

**7.2.1 Auxiliary Balancing Losses**
Every MoE training run I have been involved with hit the same failure mode within the first few thousand
steps when load balancing was omitted: one or two experts absorbed almost all the tokens, the rest went dark,
and the model ended up as a very expensive dense model wearing a MoE costume. The auxiliary balance loss
is the mechanism that prevents this collapse, and understanding its gradient mechanics - why it is differentiable
when the routing decision is not, and why it must be tuned carefully - is the core MoE training question at the
research engineer level.
Without any intervention, token-choice top-Krouting falls into a degenerate local minimum. A randomly
initialized router has slightly different affinities for each expert. One expert wins marginally, gets routed more
tokens, receives more gradient signal, improves faster, attracts even more tokens, and the cycle compounds. The
OlMoE ablation is definitive: with 8 experts and no balancing, 2 experts absorbed roughly50%of all tokens


```
7.2 Load Balancing and Stability
```
within early training; the remaining 6 were effectively dormant. The model had silently reduced itself to a
2-expert MoE while paying for 8.

**7.2.2 Auxiliary-Loss-Free Balancing (DeepSeek-V3)**
After running long MoE pre-training jobs, a pattern becomes clear: the auxiliary balance loss is doing
something uncomfortable. Every gradient step, it actively penalizes the routing the language model would
naturally prefer, pushing away from the best expert and toward the least-loaded one. DeepSeek-V3’s bias update
scheme decouples load control from loss minimization entirely - the optimizer sees only the language modeling
gradient, while a separate online controller handles balance. This design shows up in senior-level interviews as
the question that distinguishes engineers who understand auxiliary losses from those who have thought about
what they actually cost.
The standard auxiliary loss creates a constant tension between two objectives: route to the best expert
(language modeling) and route uniformly (balance). These objectives are not aligned, and every training step
the balance loss gradient steers the router away from whatever distribution the language model would prefer. At
large scale with many experts, this interference becomes harder to tune and can destabilize training.
DeepSeek-V3 replaces batch-level auxiliary balancing with a per-expert biasbi 2 Rfor each experti=
1 ,... , N. The routing decision uses the biased score:

```

```

the output sum usessi,tonly, not ̃si,t:

```

```
#### X

```

```
whereTt=TopK(f ̃si,tg, K). The bias adjusts who gets selected; the gate weight is determined by the unbiased
learned affinity. Output quality is therefore governed by the model’s actual competence estimates, not by load
corrections.
Thebivalues are updated by a simple online rule at the end of each batch, outside of backpropagation:

```

```

```

bi+γ if expertireceived fewer thanT /Ntokens
```
whereγ > 0 is a fixed step size. This is not gradient descent. It is a feedback controller: track load, increment
the bias of underloaded experts, decrement the bias of overloaded experts. No loss term, no interaction with the
optimizer, no gradient interference.
Despite claiming to be “auxiliary loss-free,” DeepSeek-V3 also includes a complementary sequence-wise
auxiliary loss with a small coefficientβseq. The batch-level controller handles average balance across the training
corpus; the sequence-wise loss ensures that within a single sequence, no expert is overwhelmed by an unusual
token distribution. At inference time, a single long sequence with atypical content can still saturate an expert
even when batch-level balance is perfect. The sequence-wise loss provides this per-inference guarantee.
_The key innovation is treating load balancing as an operations problem solved by a feedback controller,
not as a learning problem penalized through the loss, leaving the gradient optimizer free to find the best routing
distribution without a conflicting balance objective._
The standard auxiliary loss conflates two objectives with fundamentally different structures. Language
modeling is a differentiable learning problem with a clear signal: minimize prediction error. Load balancing is
a logistics problem: equalize throughput acrossNparallel compute units. Conflating them means the optimizer
receives a gradient that is a mixture of these two objectives, and the mixture coefficientαmust be tuned across
every model size, expert count, and data distribution.


```
7.2 Load Balancing and Stability
```
The bias controller handles the logistics problem with a logistics tool - a feedback control loop that observes
the current state (token counts), measures the error (deviation fromT /N), and applies a corrective signal (γ).
This is more appropriate than gradient descent for a problem with no loss landscape to optimize, just a constraint
to satisfy.
The practical benefit is cleaner gradient signal for the router. The router embeddingseiare trained exclu-
sively by language modeling gradients; every gradient step is an improvement in routing quality, not a compro-
mise between quality and balance. The controller handles balance externally, so the optimizer is free to find the
best routing distribution the data supports.
There is a cost: the online controller introduces a step size hyperparameterγand requires global visibility of
per-expert token counts (an all-reduce over data-parallel replicas). These are manageable engineering concerns.
The bigger limitation is that the controller responds to average load over time; a single batch with extreme
imbalance is not corrected within that batch - only subsequent batches benefit. This is why the sequence-wise
auxiliary loss is retained: it provides within-sequence balance that the controller cannot supply.

**A Worked Example**

ConsiderN = 64experts, a batch ofT = 2048tokens, target loadT /N = 32tokens per expert, and

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How does DeepSeek-V3 achieve load balance without an auxiliary loss?” Per-expert bias scalars

updatesbibyγeach step based on whether expertiwas over or under-loaded in the previous batch. No
gradient flows through this update; the optimizer sees only language modeling gradients.
“Why is it important to exclude the bias from the gate weight computation?” The bias is a load-
control signal, not a quality signal. If it were included in the gate weight, an expert with inflatedbi
(promoted to compensate for low affinity) would also receive a high gate weight, amplifying its output
regardless of whether its FFN has learned anything useful for those tokens. Keeping the gate weight=si,t
ensures that output quality is governed by learned competence, not load management history.
Senior follow-up: “DeepSeek-V3 claims to be auxiliary loss-free but still includes a sequence-wise
auxiliary loss. Is this a meaningful distinction or marketing?” It is a meaningful engineering distinc-
tion, though the terminology overstates the case. The batch-level auxiliary loss is what causes gradient
interference: it has a large coefficient, acts every batch, and its gradient direction conflicts with the lan-
guage modeling gradient in proportion tofi. Removing it cleanly separates the two objectives. The
sequence-wise loss has a coefficient 3 - 10 smaller, targets a different failure mode (within-sequence im-
balance at inference time), and creates far less interference because routing distributions within a single
sequence are already partially balanced by the learned router. The claim is accurate in engineering terms
even if incomplete in literal terms.

**Key Takeaways**

```
DeepSeek-V3 replaces the batch-level auxiliary loss with per-expert bias scalarsbiupdated by an online
feedback controller (bi biγbased on token load), with no gradient flowing through the update.
The bias adjusts top-Kselection but is excluded from gate weights; output quality is determined by learned
affinitysi,t, not by load corrections.
The method retains a sequence-wise auxiliary loss with a small coefficient for within-inference balance
robustness; the improvement is specifically the elimination of batch-level gradient interference, not the
removal of all balance objectives.
Bias-based control is most valuable atN 64 experts; for smaller MoEs the standard auxiliary loss is
simpler and well-understood.
Implementation requires a global all-reduce over per-expert token counts before each controller update to
prevent divergence across data-parallel replicas.
```
### 7.3 Expert Parallelism Gotchas for Interviews

**7.3.1 Token Dropping and Capacity Factors**
The question “why does our MoE API return different outputs for the same prompt at temperature zero?”
is one of those interview traps that separates engineers who have run MoE in production from those who have
only read about it. The answer is almost always token dropping - the mechanism that prevents any single expert
from being overwhelmed. Understanding capacity factors and what happens to dropped tokens is a staple of
senior MoE system design questions, sitting at the intersection of routing correctness, memory management,
and serving reliability.
Expert parallelism works by dispatching tokens to different devices via an all-to-all collective. Each expert
lives on one or a few GPUs and can process only a bounded number of tokens before its on-device buffer fills.
The _capacity factor_ Cdefines this bound:

```
capacity=
```
#### 

#### CT

#### N

#### 

whereTis the total number of tokens in the current dispatch batch andNis the number of experts. Each
expert is pre-allocated a slot buffer of exactly this size. If more tokens route to an expert than the buffer allows,
the excess tokens are dropped.
A dropped token is not erased from the sequence. Its hidden-state vector passes unchanged through the
residual connection, completely bypassing the MLP. The MoE layer contributes nothing to that token’s repre-
sentation at this layer; the output is numerically identical to the input for that position. The sequence length and
causal mask are unaffected - the token is still there, just unprocessed.
Capacity factors in practice range fromC= 1. 0 (zero tolerance for imbalance) toC= 2. 0 (buffer twice
the fair-share load). Switch Transformer and most production systems useC 1. 25 to 1. 5 as the default range.
_The capacity factor is the MoE’s circuit breaker: it trades a small number of under-processed tokens for a
guarantee that every expert finishes in bounded, predictable time._
The alternative to capacity-capped dispatch is allowing arbitrarily deep per-expert queues. Under token-
choice top-Krouting, popular experts can attract several times their fair share of tokens in a single batch -
especially early in training when the router has collapsed onto a small set of preferred experts. Without a cap,


```
7.3 Expert Parallelism Gotchas for Interviews
```
that GPU stalls draining the queue, creating a latency tail that ruins batch efficiency for every other expert on the
device. With a fixed capacity, every expert’s forward pass takes the same wall-clock time regardless of routing
decisions, which is exactly the property you need to keep GPUs synchronized, saturate tensor cores, and hide
all-to-all latency.
The cost is representation quality for the dropped tokens. A token dropped from its top-ranked expert falls
back to the residual only. If the routing has learned to rely on a specific expert for specific token types - which
it does, given sufficient training - those tokens receive a degraded representation at that layer. Empirically,
per-batch drop rates above roughly 5% consistently correlate with measurable perplexity increases.
The stochasticity angle is the subtler point. At inference time, whether a particular token gets dropped
depends on who else is in the same dispatch batch. A prompt running in isolation may have zero drops; the
same prompt batched with other high-traffic sequences may lose tokens to overloaded experts. The token’s
position in the batch, and therefore its output representation, changes based on which other requests arrived
concurrently - producing different completions even at temperature zero, with no randomness introduced by
sampling.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B-parameter MoE with 64 fine-grained experts (each one-quarter the size of a standard FFN)
spread across 8 H100s, 8 experts per GPU. An inference batch contains 1024 tokens. WithC= 1. 25 :

```
capacity=

#### 1024

#### 64

#### 

```
=b 20 c= 20tokens per expert
```
Total slot buffers: 64 20 = 1280slots. The system can absorb up to 25% routing imbalance before any
drops occur.
Now suppose the batch is heavy with English function words - “the,” “a,” “of” - whose hidden states cluster
together, routing them all toward expert 3. Expert 3 receives 35 tokens but its buffer holds only 20; 15 tokens
are dropped. Those 15 positions pass through the MoE layer unchanged.
Memory cost of the buffers: 64  20  4096  2 bytes 10. 5 MB, negligible. RaisingCto 2. 0 doubles
the buffer to 21 MB but reduces the drop rate to near zero for typical routing distributions, a clear win unless
the system is severely memory-constrained.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Set C= 1. 0 only when memory is critically constrained and your balance loss is mature. A capacity
of 1.0 guarantees no extra buffer memory but drops tokens the moment any imbalance exists. Accept it
only if per-expert drop rates stay consistently below 1%.
Default to C= 1. 25 - 1. 5 in most production serving deployments. This absorbs typical hot-expert
bursts from mildly skewed batches without materially increasing buffer memory.
Monitor drop rate as a first-class training metric. A per-expert drop rate above 5% averaged over a
training run is a load-balancing failure, not a capacity-factor failure. RaisingCpapers over the symptom;
the correct fix is re-tuning the balance loss coefficient.
Consider no-drop inference routing for latency-sensitive APIs. Route overflow tokens to their second-
ranked expert rather than dropping them. This eliminates batch-dependent non-determinism at tempera-
ture zero. Accept the mild training-inference distribution mismatch - in practice, the effect is small when
```

```
7.3 Expert Parallelism Gotchas for Interviews
```
```
overflow rates are low.
Fine-grained experts reduce drop pressure naturally. Smaller experts mean each expert handles fewer
tokens on average, so the same capacity factor tolerates a larger absolute routing imbalance before the
buffer fills. This is one of the underappreciated systems benefits of the DeepSeek fine-grained expert
design.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A user reports that your MoE API returns different outputs for the same prompt at temperature zero. You
have confirmed there is no sampling involved. What could cause this?” Strong answer: token dropping
is batch-dependent. The same prompt, batched with other requests, may share expert buffers with high-
traffic sequences. If a hot expert is saturated by other sequences in the batch, tokens from this prompt are
dropped at that layer, changing the representation and thus the output. The fix is either no-drop inference
routing or request isolation.
“What is the capacity factor in a mixture-of-experts model, and what trade-off does it control?” Strong
answer: capacity=bCT /Ncsets the maximum number of tokens any expert processes in one dispatch
round.Ctrades representation quality (fewer drops at higherC) against memory and buffer latency (larger
pre-allocated buffers at higherC). SettingCtoo low causes frequent drops on imbalanced batches; setting
it too high wastes memory that could hold activations or KV cache entries.
Senior follow-up: “If you eliminate token dropping at inference time by routing overflow tokens to their
next-ranked expert, what new problem might arise and when does it matter?” Senior answer: the model
trained under a regime where overflow tokens were dropped, not re-routed. Re-routing changes the effec-
tive per-expert load distribution seen at inference, shifting the activation statistics that downstream layers
were calibrated on. For mildly imbalanced batches this discrepancy is small enough to ignore. For heavily
skewed batches - such as a batch of all-code prompts on a model trained on mixed data - the effect can be
meaningful. One mitigation is to include some no-drop re-routing during fine-tuning so the model sees
both modes.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Each expert has a fixed slot buffer of capacity=bCT /Nctokens; tokens exceeding the cap are dropped
and receive only the residual-stream pass-through with no MLP contribution.
Token dropping is batch-dependent: whether a given token is dropped depends on which other requests
occupy the same dispatch batch, making it the primary source of non-determinism in MoE serving at
temperature zero.
Production capacity factors of 1. 25 - 1. 5 absorb typical routing imbalance; persistent drop rates above 5%
signal a load-balancing failure that requires fixing the balance loss, not just raisingC.
No-drop inference routing eliminates serving non-determinism at the cost of a tolerable training-inference
distribution mismatch.
Fine-grained experts (smaller size, more count) reduce the per-expert token variance and therefore reduce
drop rates at any given capacity factor.
```

```
7.3 Expert Parallelism Gotchas for Interviews
```
**7.3.2 Device-Level vs. Expert-Level Balancing**
Once an interviewer is satisfied that you understand expert collapse, the pivot is almost immediate: “but
what if your experts are perfectly balanced and your GPUs still aren’t?” That question targets device-level
balancing - the second tier of the two-layer hierarchy that every serious MoE training system implements. Con-
flating expert-level and device-level balancing is one of the most common mistakes I see in system design
conversations about MoE at scale, and at senior level it is a reliable differentiator.
MoE training systems maintain two distinct load-balancing objectives that operate at different granularities
of the parallelism stack.
**Expert-level balancing** targets the routing distribution itself. The Switch Transformer auxiliary loss is:

```
Lexpert=N
```
#### XN

```
i=1
```
```
fiPi
```
whereNis the number of experts,fiis the fraction of tokens dispatched to expertiin the batch (a hard
routing count), andPiis the mean router probability assigned to expertiacross the same batch (a soft, differen-
tiable quantity). The productfiPicouples the discrete routing decision to the continuous router output, giving
useful gradients while penalizing load concentration. MinimizingLexpertdrives the router toward a uniform
distribution over experts.
**Device-level balancing** has the same algebraic structure but redefines the summation unit from individual
experts to device groups:

```
Ldevice=D
```
#### XD

```
d=1
```
```
FdPd
```
whereDis the number of devices,Fdis the fraction of tokens dispatched to deviced, andPdis the total
router probability directed toward all experts residing on deviced. Minimizing this term discourages the router
from routing a disproportionate share of tokens to a single GPU, which would saturate that device’s inbound
all-to-all bandwidth regardless of how evenly the load is distributed among the experts on that device.
_Expert-level balancing prevents expert collapse; device-level balancing prevents network hotspots - they
are complementary constraints at different granularities of the parallelism hierarchy._
The two objectives can be satisfied simultaneously or independently, and that is exactly the problem. Con-
sider 64 experts on 8 GPUs (8 experts per GPU). Expert-level balancing can be perfectly satisfied with every
expert receiving exactlyT / 64 tokens. But if the routing is correlated - say, high-frequency English function
words all cluster toward experts on GPUs 0 and 1 - those two GPUs still receive double the inbound all-to-all
traffic of GPUs 2-7. The expert-level loss sees balance at the per-expert granularity; the device-level loss fires
a separate penalty for the bandwidth hotspot.
Before device-level losses were standard, practitioners would observe mysteriously variable step times and
diagnose the culprit as imbalanced communication rather than imbalanced compute. The fix of addingLdevice
with a smaller coefficient (typically 10-50smaller than the expert-level coefficient) is cheap and dramatically
stabilizes per-step time variance on multi-node runs. The DeepSeek training reports note exactly this kind of
per-device communication balancing as a necessary addition when scaling beyond 16 billion active parameters.
DeepSeek-V2 also introduced a complementary structural mechanism: **top-** M **device selection**. Before
picking the top-Kexperts for a token, the router first restricts its candidate pool to the top-Mdevices by ag-
gregated affinity score. This hard constraint bounds the number of distinct all-to-all hops any single token can

```
generate, making worst-case communication cost predictable even with hundreds of experts spread across many
devices. The loss-based approach and the structural approach are complementary: the loss gently guides the
router during training; the device cap provides a hard budget guarantee at both training and inference time.

**A Worked Example**

A 16B-parameter MoE has 64 routed experts spread across 16 H100s (4 experts per GPU). A training batch
dispatches 4096 tokens.
Ideal per-expert load: 4096 /64 = 64tokens. Ideal per-device load: 4096 /16 = 256tokens.
Suppose the router concentrates traffic toward experts 0-7 (GPUs 0 and 1) because these experts handle

remaining 56 experts average 48 tokens.

experts downward. Improvement is gradual because the loss signal is shared across all 64 experts.

level concentration, pushing the router to diversify across devices even when no single expert appears badly

Without the device-level loss, the expert-level loss alone would require many gradient steps to redistribute

time shows high variance.

since routing to a seventh or eighth device almost never helps representation quality.

when batches are large and representative. At inference, request batches are small and user-controlled

- a single unusual query can dominate a batch. A sequence-wise loss that balances routing within each

**Instrument per-GPU inbound token count, not just per-expert token count.** A per-expert utilization
dashboard can show perfect balance while two GPUs are starving for bandwidth. Add a per-device token
histogram to your training dashboard from day one.
**Understand what DeepSeek-V3’s online bias update** bi **actually controls.** The bias terms increment or
decrement based on running per-expert load, replacing the batch-level expert-load auxiliary loss. They do

system is not “auxiliary-loss-free” at the device level.


```
7.3 Expert Parallelism Gotchas for Interviews

## Part IV

# GPUs, Kernels, and Single-Device

# Performance


## Chapter 8 GPU Architecture for LLM Engineers

### 8.1 The Compute and Memory Hierarchy

**8.1.1 SMs, Warps, Threads, and Blocks**
An interviewer designing a custom CUDA kernel or probing your understanding of FlashAttention will
not ask “what is an SM?” - they will ask you to walk through what happens when a warp executes a matrix
multiply, why warp divergence tanks throughput, and why tile counts that are not multiples of the SM count
cause a cliff drop in utilization. Getting this right requires internalizing the three-level execution hierarchy cold.
This question appears at the ML infrastructure engineer and systems engineer level, and confidently deriving
performance predictions from first principles is what separates a strong answer from a mediocre one.
A GPU is a throughput machine, not a latency machine. A CPU is designed to finish any single task
as fast as possible - its die area goes to branch predictors, out-of-order execution engines, and large caches that
minimize single-thread latency. A GPU sacrifices per-thread latency to maximize the total number of operations
completed per second across thousands of concurrent threads. If you give a CPU four tasks, it finishes the first
quickly, then the second, and so on. A GPU finishes all four simultaneously - later in wall-clock time than the
CPU’s first task, but far sooner in aggregate.
The atomic unit of GPU computation is the _Streaming Multiprocessor_ (SM). An SM is a self-contained
engine: it has its own control logic, register file, shared memory, and specialized arithmetic units including
tensor cores. An A100 SXM4 has 108 SMs; an H100 SXM5 has 132. Each SM can hold up to 2048 threads in
flight simultaneously, which it uses to hide memory latency by switching between warps while some are stalled.
The execution hierarchy has three levels:
**Block.** A block is a group of threads assigned to a single SM for the duration of its execution. All threads
in a block share the SM’s shared memory and can synchronize with barriers. A block cannot span SMs. The
programmer chooses how many threads are in each block (must be a multiple of 32) and how many blocks to
launch (the _grid_ ).
**Warp.** A warp is 32 consecutively numbered threads within a block. This is the unit at which the SM
dispatches instructions. All 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction simultaneously, each on different
data. This execution model is called SIMT: Single Instruction, Multiple Threads. The SM maintains many
warps concurrently; when one warp stalls on a memory read, the SM instantly switches to another ready warp
with zero overhead (each warp’s live state is stored in registers, not on a call stack).
**Thread.** A thread is the individual execution lane. Each thread has its own registers and runs its own
instance of the kernel code. Threads within a warp are always in lockstep; threads in different warps are inde-
pendent.
The performance consequence of SIMT is _warp divergence_ : if threads within a warp take different branches
through anif-else, the SM must execute both branches serially, masking off the inactive threads for each. A
50/50 branch split halves effective throughput. Kernels should be written to avoid conditional logic that splits
warps.
_The SM is the atom of GPU computation: blocks are assigned to SMs, warps are the 32-thread instruction-
dispatch units within a block, and any branch that splits a warp forces serial execution - design kernels to
maintain warp uniformity._


```
8.1 The Compute and Memory Hierarchy
```
The SIMT model wins because matrix multiplies and tensor operations are perfectly amenable to it: every
thread does exactly the same arithmetic on a different slice of the matrix. The GPU dedicates the vast majority
of its die area to arithmetic units rather than control logic, which is why an H100 delivers 2 , 000 TFLOP/s of
bfloat16 tensor-core throughput while a CPU core delivers 1 TFLOP/s at most - not because the GPU runs at
a higher clock, but because it runs the same instruction across thousands of parallel threads at once.
The lightweight thread model is also central to the design. A CPU thread requires a full stack, OS schedul-
ing, and context switch overhead measured in microseconds. A GPU thread’s entire state is a fixed-size register
file entry; switching between warps takes zero cycles because the SM simply picks up where the other warp left
off. This is how an SM with 2048 in-flight threads achieves high utilization despite the 300-cycle latency of a
global memory access: 300 cycles is enough time to cycle through many other warps and keep the arithmetic
units fed.
The alternative - a CPU-style design with a small number of heavy threads and large caches - would give
low latency on a single problem but would not scale to the thousands of simultaneous accumulators that a large
matrix multiply requires.

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What is a warp and why does its size matter?” A warp is 32 threads that execute the same instruction
simultaneously on different data. Its size matters because (1) it is the unit of instruction dispatch, so
thread block sizes that are not multiples of 32 waste compute, and (2) branches within a warp cause serial
execution (warp divergence), reducing throughput by the fraction of threads on the minority branch.
“How does an SM hide memory latency?” By maintaining many warps in flight simultaneously. When
one warp issues a memory read and stalls for 300+ cycles, the SM instantly switches to another ready
warp. No context switch overhead because each warp’s register state is always live in the register file.
This is why occupancy (ratio of active warps to the SM’s maximum) matters: higher occupancy means
more warps to switch to, and the SM stays busy even with long-latency memory operations.
Senior follow-up: “An A100 has 108 SMs. Your kernel launches 109 thread blocks. Quantify the

Block 109 executes alone in wave 2, using 1/108 of the SM capacity. Total GPU time 2 the single-
wave time rather than 109 / 108  1. 009 . The fix: either reduce the problem to 108 blocks (coarsen
the tile size), or pad to 216 blocks (the next multiple of 108) and ensure the added work is trivial (zero-
padding the output matrix). In practice this means choosing tile dimensions that make the grid size 0
(mod 108), which often requires rounding the problem dimension up by a small amount.
```

A100 has 108 SMs, H100 has 132. Each SM can hold up to 64 warps (2048 threads) in flight simultane-

SIMT means all 32 threads in a warp execute the same instruction; any branch that splits a warp serializes
execution for the two groups, reducing throughput proportionally.

Tensor core operations require input dimensions to be multiples of 16 (ideally 128) in bfloat16; misaligned
