**8.1.2 HBM, L2, Shared Memory, and Registers**
When an interviewer asks why FlashAttention is roughly 3faster than a naive PyTorch attention imple-
mentation, the correct answer is not “it avoids materializing the full attention matrix” - the correct answer is
“it moves roughly 7less data through HBM.” GPU compute throughput has scaled10,000from K20 to
H100; HBM bandwidth has scaled 100 . Every generation, the gap widens, and every generation, the domi-
nant bottleneck in LLM kernels is memory movement, not arithmetic. Understanding the memory hierarchy in
numbers - latency ratios, bandwidth, capacity at each level - is foundational for any performance conversation
at the research engineer or systems engineer level.
A GPU has five distinct levels of memory, organized from fastest and smallest near the compute units to
slowest and largest farther away:
**Registers** (fastest,1 cycle): per-thread,255 32-bit registers available per thread on an A100. Holds
live scalar values during execution. No programmer overhead to use them - the compiler allocates registers
automatically. Spilling to local memory (HBM) when register pressure is too high is a serious performance
hazard.
**Shared memory / L1 cache** (20 cycles, per-SM): configurable up to 164 KB total per SM on an A100,
split between shared memory and L1 cache. The programmer explicitly controls shared memory by declaring
__shared__arrays. Shared by all threads in a block; not visible to other blocks. This is the primary staging
area for data that multiple threads will reuse.
**L2 cache** (200-300 cycles): 40 MB on the A100, shared across all 108 SMs. Hardware-managed; the
programmer cannot directly address it. Acts as a buffer between repeated HBM reads and the SMs. Effective
for weight matrices in batched inference where the same weights are reused across many requests.
**HBM (High Bandwidth Memory) / global memory** (300-600 cycles latency, 2 TB/s bandwidth on
A100, 3.35 TB/s on H100 SXM): 40-80 GB capacity. This is what CUDA programmers call “global memory.”
All inter-block communication must go through HBM. This is also where model parameters, activations, and
KV caches live.
**Host DRAM** (CPU side, via PCIe 4.0):64 GB/s in each direction on a PCIe 4.016 link - roughly 30
slower than HBM. This level matters for data loading, model transfers, and CPU-GPU coordination, but is too
slow to be in the critical path of any compute-intensive kernel.
The critical ratio is between compute throughput and HBM bandwidth. An A100 delivers 312 TFLOP/s
of bfloat16 tensor-core throughput and 2 TB/s of HBM bandwidth. A bfloat16 element is 2 bytes, so HBM
delivers 1012 elements/second. The compute unit can consume 312  1012 / 1012 = 312FLOPs per element
delivered. A kernel is compute-bound only if its arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte loaded from HBM)
exceeds 312 /2 = 156FLOP/byte. Most element-wise operations (softmax, layer norm, ReLU) have arithmetic
intensity below 5 FLOP/byte - they are deeply memory-bound.
HBM uses _burst-mode_ access. When a read is issued to any address, the DRAM controller moves a full
128-byte cache line (one burst section) to the L2 or SM. If the thread only needed 2 bytes, the remaining 126
bytes are either cached or discarded. Memory _coalescing_ exploits burst mode: when 32 threads in a warp issue


```
8.1 The Compute and Memory Hierarchy
```
reads to 32 consecutive 2-byte addresses that together span one 64-byte or 128-byte aligned burst section, the
hardware services all 32 reads with a single HBM transaction. Non-coalesced access - 32 threads reading 32
scattered addresses - requires up to 32 separate transactions, each fetching 128 bytes and using only 2. Effective
bandwidth drops by up to 32.
_The performance gap between compute throughput and HBM bandwidth grows with every hardware gen-
eration; every optimization strategy for GPU kernels ultimately reduces to minimizing data movement through
HBM._
The memory hierarchy is not a design choice - it is physics. Faster memory requires transistors physically
closer to the compute units and costs exponentially more die area per bit. Registers and shared memory live
on-SM because the SM needs sub-nanosecond access (1 ns at 1 GHz). HBM is a stack of DRAM dies bonded
adjacent to the GPU package; it trades latency for large capacity. Host DRAM sits on the CPU board and is an
order of magnitude further away.
The strategic consequence is that compute has become so abundant that it is nearly free compared to data
movement. Moving a bfloat16 value from HBM to an SM costs roughly 30more energy per operation than
performing a multiply-add on it. Kernels that move data unnecessarily waste almost all of their energy and time
waiting, not computing. This is why kernel fusion - combining multiple operations into a single kernel that
keeps data in registers and shared memory across all operations - is one of the highest-leverage optimizations
available. A fused operation that applies 5 element-wise transformations reads and writes HBM once; the
unfused equivalent reads and writes HBM 5 times for the same arithmetic result.
The contrast with the memory-bound profile of CPU workloads is instructive. CPU caches are hardware-
managed and opaque to the programmer. On a GPU, shared memory is programmer-managed and explicit - you
load a tile, compute over it, and write back. This explicitness is a burden during development but enables the
precise control needed to achieve 80-90% of peak HBM bandwidth on well-structured kernels.

**A Worked Example**

A100 SXM4. Layer normalization over a tensor of shape(T, D) = (2048,4096)in bfloat16.

xagain, compute variance per row (1 HBM read, 1 HBM write of variance). Pass 3: readx, read mean, read
variance, compute normalized output, write output (3 HBM reads, 1 HBM write). Total HBM traffic: 5  16. 8

Total HBM traffic: 1 read+1 write= 2 16. 8 MB= 33. 6 MB. Speedup: 84 / 33. 6  2. 5 from eliminating
HBM traffic alone, at zero change in arithmetic.

```
“What is the difference between shared memory and global memory, and why does it matter?”
Shared memory is on-SM,20 cycle latency, 96 KB per SM on A100. Global memory (HBM) is off-
chip,300-600 cycle latency, 80 GB, 2 TB/s bandwidth. The 15 - 30 latency ratio means any kernel that
reads the same data from HBM multiple times instead of caching it in shared memory wastes most of its
time waiting. The key design pattern: load from HBM once into shared memory, compute over the tile in
registers/shared memory, write back once.
“What is memory coalescing and when does it fail?” When 32 threads in a warp read 32 consecutive
addresses that together fit in one 128-byte HBM burst section, the hardware issues a single transaction

elements with strideD(the row width), touching 32 different cache lines.


### 8.2 Arithmetic Intensity and the Roofline Model.

```
Senior follow-up: “Compute throughput scales 10,000  from K20 to H100 but HBM bandwidth
scales only  100 . What does this imply for algorithm design going forward?” The arithmetic inten-
sity threshold for being compute-bound (FLOPs per byte) increases by 100over this span. Operations
that were memory-bound on K20 are even more memory-bound on H100. Three concrete implications:
(1) kernel fusion has compounding value - each fused operation eliminates a full HBM round-trip at a
penalty that grows 100over this hardware range; (2) quantization (INT8, FP8) reduces bytes moved
by 2-4and its benefit grows proportionally as the memory wall tightens; (3) any new architecture that
requires sequential operations with no fusion opportunity (e.g., state-space models with per-element re-
currence) will be increasingly penalized relative to block-structured operations like attention. Designing
for memory efficiency is not a current concern - it is an evergreen constraint that only becomes more
important.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Memory hierarchy latency ladder: registers (1 cycle)!shared memory/L1 (20 cycles, 96 KB per
SM)!L2 (200-300 cycles, 40 MB)!HBM (300-600 cycles, 2 TB/s, 40-80 GB)!host DRAM
(PCIe,64 GB/s).
An A100 delivers 312 TFLOP/s bfloat16 compute and 2 TB/s HBM bandwidth; a kernel is compute-
bound only when its arithmetic intensity exceeds 156 FLOP/byte. Most LLM non-GEMM operations are
at< 5 FLOP/byte - deeply memory-bound.
Memory coalescing: 32-thread warps reading 128-byte-aligned consecutive addresses get one HBM trans-
action; strided or random access requires up to 32 transactions for the same data volume.
Compute scales10,000from K20 to H100; HBM bandwidth scales 100 ; the gap grows every
generation, making kernel fusion and quantization increasingly high-leverage.
Shared memory is the programmer-controlled fast cache: load from HBM once, compute in shared mem-
ory, write back once. This is the design principle behind FlashAttention and every high-performance
transformer operator.
```
### 8.2 Arithmetic Intensity and the Roofline Model

**8.2.1 Compute-Bound vs. Memory-Bound Regimes**
The most common GPU performance question in an LLM systems interview is some variant of “why
is autoregressive decoding slow, and what can you do about it?” Candidates who answer purely in terms of
algorithmic complexity-“it isO(n^2 )attention”-miss the real bottleneck. During generation the constraint is
almost never FLOPs; it is memory bandwidth. Internalizing this requires two concepts: _arithmetic intensity_ and
the _roofline model_. This pair of ideas shows up at every seniority level; senior answers add numbers instead of
stopping at the qualitative claim.
Arithmetic intensity is the ratio of floating-point operations performed to bytes transferred between the
accelerator’s compute units and its main memory (HBM on a GPU):

AI= FLOPs
Bytes transferred from HBM
The roofline model says a kernel’s achievable throughput in FLOPs/sec is bounded by two separate ceilings.
The memory ceiling is bandwidthAI: regardless of how many tensor cores you have, you cannot process data


```

A kernel is _memory-bound_ when AI<peak compute/bandwidth and _compute-bound_ when the reverse holds.
The crossover is the _ridge point_ :

ridge point=

On an H100 SXM5 running BF16 tensor-core operations:
Peak tensor-core throughput: 989 TFLOPs/s

Ridge point: 989  1012 / 3. 35  1012  295 FLOPs/byte
_To saturate the H100’s compute, a kernel must execute at least 295 floating-point operations per byte
fetched from HBM-and most LLM operations during inference do not come close._
GPU generations scale compute throughput far faster than memory bandwidth. From the V100 to the H100,
BF16 tensor-core peak grew roughly 10 while HBM bandwidth grew roughly 3 . The ridge point climbs with
every generation: operations that were barely compute-bound in 2018 are memory-bound today, and the trend
continues. Designing an efficient kernel means understanding which side of this ridge your operation sits on,
because the optimization lever is completely different in each regime.
Below the ridge point the GPU is starved for data. An SM loads a tile from HBM, executes a handful of
arithmetic instructions, and stalls waiting for the next load. Tensor cores sit dark. Adding more FLOPs to the
kernel does not help; only raising AI does. The productive levers are: fuse kernels to eliminate intermediate
HBM round-trips, lower numerical precision to cut bytes per element, and restructure data access to maximise
reuse within SRAM.
Above the ridge point the opposite holds. Instruction throughput is the constraint. The levers are tile-size
tuning, register allocation, and ensuring the tensor cores have a continuous stream of work with no pipeline
bubbles. Reducing bytes transferred has no effect if compute is the bottleneck.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Identify your regime before optimizing. Run a profiler and check whether the kernel is bandwidth-
limited or compute-limited. Spending hours tuning tile sizes on a memory-bound softmax yields nothing;
spending hours fusing element-wise ops on a compute-bound matmul is equally wasted.
Rule of thumb for inference: ifBT < 300 on an H100, assume your linear layers are memory-bound.
Budget latency as bytes-transferred / bandwidth, not FLOPs / peak-compute.
Halving precision doubles AI. Going from FP32 to BF16 cuts bytes per element from 4 to 2, doubling
AI for any memory-bound kernel. This is one of the highest-leverage single changes for inference perfor-
mance and costs almost nothing in quality for the weight and activation tensors that dominate bandwidth.
Every HBM round-trip is expensive. An elementwise activation written to HBM and read back for
the next layer pays the full 295 FLOPs/byte tax twice for zero additional compute. Fuse it. PyTorch’s
torch.compileand custom Triton kernels both eliminate this by keeping intermediate results in registers
or shared memory.
Attention during decode is the worst-case scenario. For a single decode step, the attention kernel must
load the entire KV cache ( 2 LTpastNkvHbytes) from HBM and doO(Tpast)dot products
per head. The AI for this is essentially 1 regardless of batch size-batch size does not help because each
sequence has its own KV cache. This is the structural reason GQA, MLA, and local attention reduce
decode latency: they shrink the bytes, not the FLOPs.

**8.2.2 Why Matrix Multiplies Are “Blessed” Operations**
When an interviewer asks why every production LLM architecture concentrates its computation in matrix
multiplications, the answer is not “GPUs are fast at matmuls.” The precise answer is that matrix multiplies are
the only common deep-learning operation whose arithmetic intensity grows with problem size. Every other
operation you might add-elementwise activations, layer norms, softmax, attention masking-has AI that isO(1)
orO(1/N): it is memory-bound at any scale and stays memory-bound no matter how large you make the tensor.
Matmuls have AI=O(N). This geometric fact, combined with dedicated hardware that delivers 10-14the
FLOPs/s of general ALUs, means non-matmul FLOPs are not just slower-they are categorically slower. This
topic tests at the senior level whenever architecture or kernel design is on the table.
For a squareNNmatrix multiplyC=ABin BF16:
FLOPs: 2 N^3 (one multiply plus one add per output element,N^2 outputs each needing a dot product of
lengthN)
Bytes transferred: 3  2 N^2 = 6N^2 (readA,B, writeC)
AI= 2N^3 /(6N^2 ) =N/ 3
AtN= 885the AI crosses the H100 ridge point of 295 FLOPs/byte. AtN= 4096(a typical model width),
AI 1365 -more than 4 above the ridge, solidly compute-bound.
The contrast with elementwise operations is stark. A ReLU on anNNtensor hasN^2 FLOPs and
4 N^2 bytes (AI= 0. 25 ) regardless ofN. Softmax on anN-element vector has 3 NFLOPs and 4 Nbytes
(AI 0. 75 ). These operations will never be compute-bound on any conceivable GPU because their FLOPs and
bytes scale at the same rate.
Modern GPUs reinforce this asymmetry with hardware specialization. On an H100, general-purpose FP32
ALUs deliver 67 TFLOPs/s. BF16 tensor-core throughput is 989 TFLOPs/s-a 14. 8 gap. A kernel that
cannot use tensor cores (because it performs something other than a matrix multiply-accumulate) runs at 1 / 14
the FLOPs/s of one that can.
_Matrix multiplies are “blessed” because they are the only common DL operation where making the problem
larger raises the GPU’s eﬀiciency, and the only one with dedicated hardware that delivers_ 14  _higher FLOPs/s
than every other operation class._
The geometric intuition is data reuse. AnNNmatmul hasO(N^2 )input data butO(N^3 )work. If you
load a tile ofAand a tile ofBinto fast shared memory, you can perform allO(N)dot products that involve

while the FLOPs grow asO(N^3 ), so the ratio AI=O(N).
No other operation has this structure. Layer normalization computes a mean and variance over each row-
O(N)work onO(N)data, AI=O(1). Attention score accumulation (the softmax and weighted sum) has
O(T^2 )FLOPs andO(T^2 )bytes for sequence lengthT, so AI=O(1). Depth-wise convolution with kernel size
kachieves AIk/ 2 -bounded by a small constant.
The implication for architecture design is direct: if you add a non-matmul component that processes the
same activations as a matmul, you are adding a memory-bound bottleneck alongside a compute-bound one.
The new component runs at 1 / 14 the throughput per FLOPs, and if it touches the same bytes as the matmul it
“replaces,” you have paid the bandwidth cost twice.
The performance gap between matmul-dominant and non-matmul-dominant architectures is empirically
large. The same compute budget spent on a matmul-based FFN versus a recurrent or convolutional alternative
generally yields worse wall-clock performance for the alternative, even when the alternative has fewer theoretical
FLOPs-because those FLOPs are running at 1 / 14 the hardware speed.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Target >80% of FLOPs in matmuls. If your architecture allocates more than20%of FLOPs to
non-matmul operations, profile immediately. Those operations run at 1 / 14 the hardware speed and
will dominate latency despite their minority share of theoretical FLOPs.
Use dimensions that are multiples of 128 (minimum 64). Matmul tile sizes on H100 are typically
128  128 or 256  128. A matrix dimension of 4097 requires the same number of tiles as 4224 but
leaves the edge tile almost empty. Padding the vocabulary from 50,257 to 50,304 (nearest multiple of 64)
is documented to yield a 25% throughput gain-the tile alignment effect is not academic.
B= 295 is the practical break-even for linear layers on H100 BF16. Below that, optimize for band-
width (GQA, quantization, fewer HBM reads). Above that, optimize for compute (better tile sizes, higher
occupancy). Do not conflate the two regimes.
Fuse non-matmul work into adjacent matmul kernels. Activations, scales, biases, and residual adds
should never be standalone kernels in a throughput-sensitive path.torch.compilehandles this auto-
matically for simple cases; Triton is the right tool when you need custom fusion boundaries.
FlashAttention improves attention throughput by reducing bytes, not FLOPs. The attention score
matrix (TT in FP32) is never materialized in HBM; instead the softmax is computed tile-by-tile
in SRAM. Attention FLOPs areO(T^2 )in both cases-FlashAttention moves attention from bandwidth-
limited to closer to compute-limited by eliminating most HBM traffic.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

Additionally, tensor cores deliver 14 more FLOPs/s than general ALUs-non-matmul operations cannot

replaces was compute-bound at batch size> 300. Even if it has half the FLOPs, it may well be slower,

running any code.
Senior follow-up: “Why does nanoGPT’s throughput increase by 25% after increasing vocab size from
50,257 to 50,304?” Sketch the answer: the vocabulary embedding lookup and the final unembedding
projection are both matmuls with one dimension equal to the vocab size. When that dimension is not
a multiple of the tile size (64 or 128), the last tile is sparsely populated, meaning the assigned SM exe-
cutes a full tile’s worth of instructions for a fraction of useful work. Padding to the nearest multiple of 64
eliminates this waste. At the scale of an unembedding matmul (DmodelV), even a 0 .1%alignment im-
provement propagates into the entire forward and backward pass because this is the largest single matmul
in the model.

## Chapter 9 Making a Single GPU Go Fast

### 9.1 Reducing Memory Movement

**9.1.1 Operator Fusion and Kernel Launch Overhead**
Nearly every time I have profiled an LLM training run and found an unexpected bottleneck, it was not in
the matmuls but in the surrounding glue: activations, layer norms, residual adds, and masking operations, all
running as separate CUDA kernels and each one paying a full round-trip to HBM. The fix is kernel fusion:
combining sequential operations into a single kernel so intermediate results never leave the compute unit. This
concept appears at the mid level as “what is operator fusion,” and at the senior level as “design a fast custom
kernel for this attention variant” or “why is this activation function showing up in your profile?”
Think of the GPU as a factory on an island. HBM is the warehouse on the mainland. Every time a PyTorch
operation produces an intermediate result in eager mode, the result gets shipped back to the warehouse, and the
next operation has to ship it back over again. If five operations run sequentially without fusion, you have paid
five round-trips for data that could have stayed in the factory the whole time.
Kernel fusion eliminates those round-trips. A fused kernel reads the input from HBM once, performs all
chained operations entirely in registers and shared memory, then writes the final output to HBM once. For
memory-bound operations-those with arithmetic intensity (AI) well below the ridge point-this directly reduces
runtime. The HBM bandwidth, not compute throughput, is the bottleneck, so cutting the number of passes
through HBM cuts the wall-clock time proportionally.
There is a second, smaller benefit: kernel launch overhead. Each CUDA kernel launch incurs a fixed
dispatch cost: the CPU traverses theatenC interface, the CUDA runtime queues the kernel, and the GPU
drains its pipeline before starting. This overhead is typically 5-20μs per launch regardless of tensor size. For
small tensors or simple operations, this fixed cost dominates actual compute time. FusingNkernels into one
eliminatesN 1 launch overheads.
_Kernel fusion cuts HBM traﬀic by keeping intermediate results in registers across the fused operations, and
removes per-kernel launch overhead as a secondary benefit._
The memory hierarchy makes the arithmetic unavoidable. Registers are zero-latency for the thread that
owns them; L1 and shared memory have about 20 clock cycles latency within an SM; HBM has about 300 clock
cycles. An unfused chain of elementwise operations reads from and writes to HBM between every step, paying
300 cycles of stall time for each intermediate. A fused kernel holds every intermediate value in registers and
only touches HBM at the start and end.
The alternative-letting each intermediate write back to HBM-has one apparent advantage: simplicity. Py-
Torch eager mode does exactly this, and it is fine for large matmuls, which are compute-bound and spend little
time on relative memory traffic. But activation functions, residual additions, and normalization layers all have
AI well below 1 FLOPs/byte. On those operations, every extra HBM round-trip is paid at the full bandwidth
cost for zero additional arithmetic.
Modern JIT compilers automate straightforward fusion.torch.compileidentifies sequences of elemen-
twise operations with no cross-thread dependencies, emits a single Triton kernel, and eliminates intermediate
allocations. This is production-grade fusion at essentially zero engineering effort.


```

```

Written naively in PyTorch as separate tensor expressions, this decomposes into at least five distinct CUDA

hidden states of a 7 B model at batch size 512 and hidden dimension 11 008, stored in BF16. Each intermediate

Empirically, on an A100 at this scale:

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Reach fortorch.compilefirst. For standard elementwise chains-activations, bias adds, scaling, residuals-
torch.compilewill auto-fuse them and close most of the gap. Confirm it is actually fusing by checking
the profiler for a single kernel launch rather than multiplevectorized_elementwise_kernelcalls.
Only move to hand-written Triton when the compiler misses a fusion you expect.
Fuse activations into adjacent matmul epilogues. The output of a tiled matmul is already in SRAM;
applying a bias add or activation in the same kernel avoids writing the pre-activation to HBM. Cutlass and
cuBLAS wrappers expose epilogue fusion for this purpose. In Triton, you can add these steps directly at
the end of the matmul loop.
Kernel launch overhead dominates at small batch sizes. At the batch sizes used in speculative decoding
(1-4 sequences), a chain of ten elementwise ops can spend more time in kernel launch overhead than in
actual compute. At these scales, fusing into one kernel is especially important.
Do not fuse across operations that change memory layout. If fusion forces the matmul output into
a non-power-of-2 leading dimension, tile alignment breaks and the resulting performance loss can ex-
ceed the fusion gain. Fuse activations; be cautious with dimension-reshaping ops that affect downstream
matmul tile selection.
Always profile before and after. The profiler trace for the unfused GELU shows five separatevectorized_elementwise_kernel
launches. For the fused version you see exactly one. If you are not checking the trace, you do not know
whether the compiler has fused your ops or left them separate.

Senior follow-up: “Under what conditions does kernel fusion not help, or even hurt?” Senior answer:
if the bottleneck is compute-bound (AI above the ridge point), fusing memory-bound ops around it does
not change the binding constraint-you are waiting on compute, not bandwidth, so fewer HBM accesses
save nothing. Fusion can also hurt if it increases register pressure within a warp to the point of register
spilling to local memory, adding latency that was not present before. Always validate with a profiler; a
rule-of-thumb answer about AI first, then empirical confirmation.

**9.1.2 Recomputation vs. Storage Trade-Offs**
Activation checkpointing is well known as a memory-saving technique: you discard most forward-pass
activations and recompute them during the backward pass to stay within a GPU’s memory budget. What is less
well known, and what comes up frequently in senior kernel-design interviews, is that recomputation can also
make execution _faster_ -not just cheaper in memory. The logic is a direct consequence of the roofline model: if a
kernel is memory-bound, you have idle compute cycles burning while the kernel waits for HBM. Spending those
idle cycles to recompute intermediate values instead of loading them from HBM is free in terms of wall-clock
time, and it removes the HBM read that was the bottleneck. FlashAttention’s backward pass is the canonical
production example of this technique applied at scale.
The standard backward pass stores every forward-pass intermediate in HBM so gradient computation can
read them back. For an operationf:x7!ywith intermediatess 1 ,... , sk, this means:
**Standard** : writes 1 ,... , skto HBM during forward; read them back during backward.
**Recompute** : discards 1 ,... , skafter forward; recompute them fromxduring backward.
The recompute approach eliminateskHBM reads at the cost ofkextra arithmetic passes. That exchange


```
9.1 Reducing Memory Movement
```
is profitable whenever the kernel is memory-bound, because the compute units were already idle waiting for
HBM-the recomputed arithmetic consumes cycles that were wasted otherwise.
Concretely, the decision boundary is the roofline ridge point (approximately 295 FLOPs/byte on H100
BF16). Below that arithmetic intensity, compute is excess capacity. Above it, you are compute-bound, and
adding recomputation extends the runtime by consuming cycles that were not free.
The same principle, applied at large scale, underlies FlashAttention. The attention score matrixS =
QKT/

p
dhas shapeTTin FP32. Storing and reloading it during the backward pass costsO(T^2 )HBM
traffic-quadratic in sequence length. FlashAttention instead recomputesStile by tile during the backward pass
usingQandKthat are already being read for gradient computation, keeping theO(T^2 )materialization entirely
out of HBM.
_Recomputation turns excess compute into saved HBM bandwidth: for memory-bound kernels, arithmetic
that replaces an HBM read is free, because those compute cycles were idle anyway._
The roofline model quantifies the exchange rate. On an H100 at BF16, for every 295 FLOPs you can
compute, you are entitled to transfer 1 byte from HBM. Below the ridge point, the FLOPs side of the ratio is
underutilized: you are getting fewer than 295 FLOPs per byte because compute finishes faster than the memory
can deliver the next byte.
When you recompute a sigmoid or a running maximum rather than loading it from HBM, you are spending
FLOPs from the underutilized side to avoid spending bytes from the overutilized side. The exchange is one-
sided in your favor for any memory-bound kernel. The more memory-bound the kernel-the lower its AI-the
more recomputation you can afford before adding any latency.
This distinguishes recomputation-for-speed from the more familiar gradient checkpointing. Checkpointing
is applied to compute-bound operations (matmuls, full attention blocks) to reclaim peak memory at the cost of
paying the compute again. That cost is real because those operations are not memory-bound. Recomputation-
for-speed is applied to memory-bound operations where the compute cost is zero against the roofline.

**A Worked Example**

Consider three stacked sigmoid activations:s 1 =σ(x),s 2 =σ(s 1 ), out=σ(s 2 ). All values are BF16 (2
bytes per element). Count the HBM operations in each approach.
**Standard approach (store intermediates):**
Forward: readx(1 read), compute and writes 1 ,s 2 , out (3 writes).
Backward: reads 1 ,s 2 ,dout(3 reads), writedx(1 write).
Total: **8 HBM operations**.
**Recomputation approach (discard intermediates):**
Forward: readx(1 read), write out only-discards 1 ,s 2 (1 write).
Backward: readdoutandx(2 reads), recomputes 1 ,s 2 , out fromxentirely in SM registers (0 HBM),
writedx(1 write).
Total: **5 HBM operations**.
That is 5/8 = 62.5% of the original HBM traffic. The price is three sigmoid evaluations during the backward

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

Recomputation for speed requires confirming memory-bound regime first. Profile the kernel with
Nsight Systems ortorch.profiler. If the kernel’s GPU time is dominated by memory stalls (visible
as low SM utilization and high HBM read bandwidth), it is a candidate. If SM utilization is near 100%
and CUDA cores are the bottleneck, adding recomputation will extend the runtime linearly.
Apply to any activation with AI < 1 FLOPs/byte. Sigmoid, ReLU, GELU, SiLU, layer norm statistics
(mean and variance), and softmax exponentials all fall into this category. Dropping their intermediate
values and recomputing during backward is almost always a net win on H100 or A100 hardware. This is
the kernel-level form of the technique; it is separate from the layer-level gradient checkpointing decision.
Do not conflate with gradient checkpointing. Checkpointing (e.g.,torch.utils.checkpoint) is ap-
plied at the boundary of compute-bound layers to reduce peak memory at a throughput cost. Recomputation-
for-speed is applied inside memory-bound kernels at no throughput cost. The two levers operate at differ-
ent granularities and are both usable simultaneously.
Fuse the recomputed path. Recomputings 1 ,s 2 , out during backward only avoids HBM traffic if those
recomputations happen inside the same kernel as the gradient accumulation. Launching separate kernels
for the recomputed intermediates adds HBM traffic back and defeats the purpose entirely. Recomputation
and fusion must be applied together.
The break-even point depends on the recompute cost. For cheap operations (sigmoid, ReLU), a single
sigmoid is3 FLOPs and costs nothing against the 295 FLOPs/byte ridge. For expensive operations (full
softmax over a long sequence, layer norm with large hidden dimension), the recompute cost can itself
push the kernel toward compute-bound. Measure before assuming the trade is free.
```

### 9.2 Exploiting Memory Layout

**9.2.1 Memory Coalescing and Burst Sections**
Implement a naive matrix transpose in CUDA and watch effective HBM bandwidth drop to 1-2% of peak.
The computation is trivial - one read, one write per element - but the access pattern is column-major on a
row-major matrix, and that single design choice costs two orders of magnitude of bandwidth. Interviewers at
GPU-focused companies will ask why a “simple” kernel runs at a fraction of peak bandwidth, and the answer
lives entirely in how your warp’s 32 threads hit DRAM. Memory coalescing is the most impactful low-level
GPU optimization, and understanding it means understanding burst-mode DRAM at the hardware level. This
topic appears at the systems engineer and ML infrastructure engineer level.
When a warp of 32 threads issues memory reads, the hardware does not process them sequentially one by
one. DRAM is physically organized into _burst sections_ : contiguous address blocks, typically 128 bytes, that the
DRAM array delivers together in a single sensing operation. The physics: accessing DRAM requires activating
a row of memory cells (a sense amplifier step), which is the expensive operation. Once a row is open, reading
any subset of that row’s bits is nearly free. The hardware exposes this as: request any single address, receive the
full 128-byte cache line.
Memory coalescing exploits this directly. When 32 threads in a warp all read addresses that fall within a
small number of burst sections, the memory controller merges them into that many transactions rather than 32
separate ones:
**Fully coalesced** : Threadkreads address base+k 2 (consecutive bfloat16 elements from a 128-byte-
aligned base). All 32 reads map to one 64-byte burst section. One HBM transaction returns 64 bytes; all
64 useful bytes are consumed. Utilization:100%.
**Fully non-coalesced** : Threadkreads address base+kSwhereSis the row stride in bytes (e.g.,
4096 2 = 8192bytes for a 4096-wide matrix). Each thread’s address is 8192 bytes from the next: 128
separate burst sections. Hardware issues 32 transactions. Bytes fetched: 32 128 = 4096bytes. Useful
bytes: 32 2 = 64bytes. Utilization: 1 .6%.


```
9.2 Exploiting Memory Layout
```
The utilization ratio equals useful_bytes / fetched_bytes. For stride-Saccess, utilization= 2/min(128, S)
for bfloat16. At stride = 4096, that is 2 / 128  1 .6%- a 64waste.
_Coalesced access is not a software trick: it exploits a fixed DRAM hardware property (burst mode) that
already exists; non-coalesced access wastes the free bytes that burst mode delivers, cutting effective bandwidth
by up to the number of warp threads._
The reason burst mode exists is that the dominant cost in DRAM access is activating a row of cells (the
sense amplifier step), not transferring the bits. Once the row is energized, reading 128 bytes costs almost the
same as reading 1 byte. The hardware exposes this by delivering a full cache line on every access - whether you
asked for 1 byte or 128.
Coalescing turns this into a benefit: 32 threads’ reads for 64 bytes of useful data require one row activation
instead of 32. Non-coalescing turns it into a penalty: 32 row activations for 64 bytes of useful data, fetching 4
KB and discarding 63 of every 64 bytes fetched.
CPUs partially compensate for non-coalesced access via hardware stride prefetchers that detect strided
patterns and prefetch cache lines proactively. GPUs have no equivalent adaptive prefetcher. The programmer
must arrange accesses correctly, or the performance cliff materializes silently. Profiling tools like Nsight Com-
pute expose the coalescing ratio vial1tex__t_sectors / l1tex__t_requests; a ratio near 32 means fully
non-coalesced access.

**A Worked Example**

A 2 R^4096 ×^4096 in bfloat16, stored row-major. One warp (32 threads) loads one row’s first 32 elements vs.
one column’s first 32 elements.
**Row access (coalesced).** ThreadkreadsA[0, k]. Address: base+k 2 bytes.
Address span= 322 = 64bytes=one HBM cache line.

Transactions: 1. Bytes fetched: 128 (one cache line). Useful: 64. Utilization: 50% (slightly under if stride 6 =
cache line size; exactly 1 transaction in practice with 128-byte alignment).
**Column access (non-coalesced).** ThreadkreadsA[k,0]. Address: base+k 4096 2 =base+k 8192
bytes.
Distance between consecutive threads= 8192bytes= 64(cache line size).

Each thread touches a different cache line 64 lines apart. Transactions: 32. Bytes fetched: 32 128 = 4096.
Useful: 32 2 = 64. Utilization: 64 /4096 = 1.56%.
At 2 TB/s HBM bandwidth on an A100:
Effective row bandwidth 2 TB/s 0 .5 = 1TB/s (full-rate coalesced)
Effective column bandwidth 2 TB/s 0. 0156  31 GB/s.
A kernel doing nothing but column reads of this matrix would run at 31 GB/s instead of 2 TB/s - a 64
degradation. For a bfloat16 element-wise operation with 1 FLOP per element, this column-read version would
be so memory-starved that even a single arithmetic instruction per cycle cannot fill the gap.
**The fix.** Stage through shared memory:

1. Load aTTtile from HBM into shared memory in row-major order (coalesced - each block of 32 threads
    reads 32 consecutive elements from the same row).
2. Access the tile in shared memory in column order (fast - shared memory is banked, not burst-mode;
    column access incurs bank conflicts but not the 64bandwidth penalty of HBM column access).

Embedding lookups are structurally non-coalesced; mitigate at the batch level. Token embedding
tables are indexed by token ID (random integers up to vocab size). Each lookup hits a different row, with
no spatial locality. Effective bandwidth is limited. Two mitigations: (1) sort requests by token ID within
each microbatch so nearby GPU threads access nearby rows; (2) use INT8 or FP8 embeddings to double
or quadruple the useful bytes per fetched cache line.
```

“A kernel loads a 2D tensor and runs at 3% of peak HBM bandwidth. How do you diagnose and fix

access is non-coalesced. Fix: either stage through shared memory (load tile coalesced, use within shared
memory), or restructure the algorithm to access the tensor in row order.

bandwidth regardless of batch size. Coalescing is structurally impossible because token indices are

(2) Quantize the embedding table to INT8 or INT4: halves or quarters the bytes per row, so each 128-
byte burst section delivers 2-4more embedding elements; effective bandwidth in elements/sec doubles
even if bytes/sec is the same. (3) Cache hot embeddings in L2 by structuring the training loop to repeat
frequent-token batches before evicting: for a Zipfian token distribution where the top 1% of tokens appear

**9.2.2 Tiling for Matrix Multiplies**
Add one column to your matrix and watch GEMM throughput drop 30%. The FLOP count barely changed,
yet the GPU is suddenly running two execution waves instead of one, with the second wave consuming 90%
of its time on 12 tiles while 96 of 108 SMs sit idle. This is the “wavy” matrix multiply performance plot that
puzzles every GPU engineer who first encounters it, and tiling is the concept that explains every feature on that
plot. Understanding tiling is what lets you justify vocabulary size choices, explain FlashAttention’s performance
model, and design kernels that sustain high throughput under interview conditions. This topic appears at the
ML infrastructure engineer and systems engineer level.

Each output tile is one thread block, assigned to one SM. The total number of blocks isdN/Te^2. With 108
SMs on an A100, blocks execute in waves of 108. If the total block count is not a multiple of 108, the last wave
is partially populated: most SMs idle while the remaining blocks finish. This is _wave quantization_.
_Tiling reduces HBM reads by a factor of_ T _by staging the inner reduction loop in shared memory; wave
quantization causes throughput cliffs whenever the tile count crosses a multiple of the SM count._
The fundamental insight behind tiling is that matrix multiply has reuse: each element ofAparticipates in
Ndot products (one per output column), and each element ofBparticipates inNdot products (one per output
row). If you can arrange to perform allNof those dot products while the element is in shared memory, you only
pay the HBM latency once. Tiling is the mechanism that groups thoseNuses spatially: a singleTTtile of
Ais used in allTdot products for the corresponding output tile row before being evicted.
The arithmetic intensity increases proportionally toT. Naive: 2 N^3 FLOPs, 2 N^3 element HBM reads)
1 FLOP/element read. Tiled (T): 2 N^3 FLOPs, 2 N^3 /Telement HBM reads)TFLOPs/element read. For

well above the A100’s roofline threshold of 156 FLOP/byte for bfloat16, but much closer to the compute-bound
regime than the naive algorithm.
Tiling also subsumes coalescing: when a block loads a tile from HBM into shared memory, the 32 threads
in a warp each read consecutive elements from the same row (row-major, one row of the tile per warp). This
is perfectly coalesced. Subsequent intra-tile computation uses shared memory, where access order does not
matter for bandwidth. Tiling thus handles both the HBM redundancy problem and the coalescing problem
simultaneously.

### 9.3 Lower Precision and Quantization-Aware Training.

### 9.3 Lower Precision and Quantization-Aware Training

**9.3.1 FP16 and BF16 in Practice**
Cutting numerical precision in half is the highest-leverage single change you can make to LLM training
throughput, and it requires zero custom kernel code. The choice between FP16, BF16, and FP32 for each tensor
in the training graph is one of the first things an interviewer will probe once you claim to understand efficient
training. At the mid-level this surfaces as “why is BF16 faster than FP32”; at the senior level it escalates to
“walk me through every place you keep FP32 in a mixed-precision run and explain why.”
Three formats matter for LLM training. FP32 uses 32 bits (1 sign, 8 exponent, 23 mantissa) and supports
values up to 3. 4  1038. FP16 uses 16 bits (1 sign, 5 exponent, 10 mantissa) with a maximum representable
value of only 65,504-four orders of magnitude smaller. BF16, the format used by almost every production LLM
training run today, also uses 16 bits but allocates 8 bits to the exponent (matching FP32) and only 7 bits to
the mantissa. BF16 deliberately trades mantissa precision for dynamic range, keeping the same maximum and
minimum values as FP32.
The performance argument is direct. For any memory-bound kernel, wall-clock time equals bytes trans-
ferred divided by bandwidth. Halving the bits per element halves the bytes transferred, halving the kernel run-
time without changing a single arithmetic operation. A ReLU onnBF16 elements reads 2 nbytes and writes 2 n
bytes- 4 ntotal-at AI= 0. 25 FLOPs/byte. The same ReLU in FP32 moves 8 nbytes at AI= 0. 125 FLOPs/byte.
The AI ratio is the same ( 0. 25 / 0 .125 = 2), but the absolute bytes are halved, so the kernel completes twice
as fast.
Matrix multiplications gain a second effect. On H100, BF16 inputs unlock the tensor-core path at
989 TFLOPs/s. FP32 inputs fall back to general ALUs at 67 TFLOPs/s-a 14. 8 peak throughput gap. The
standard mixed-precision matmul pattern exploits both: BF16 inputs are fed to the tensor cores; each tile ac-
cumulates dot-product partial sums in FP32 accumulator registers; the FP32 result is cast back to BF16 be-
fore writing to HBM. This is the default behavior of cuBLAS andtorch.autocastwhen the target dtype is
bfloat16.
_Halving numerical precision halves HBM traﬀic for memory-bound ops and unlocks tensor cores for
compute-bound ones; BF16 is the right default for weights and activations in LLM training, not FP16._
FP16’s 5-bit exponent limits its maximum representable value to 65,504. Gradient norms in large-scale
LLM training regularly exceed this threshold during warmup, around sharp loss changes, and in embedding
tables for rare tokens. When an FP16 value overflows toInfor underflows to zero, the optimizer step either
corrupts the weight or silently does nothing. The standard workaround is loss scaling: multiply the scalar loss
by a large constantSbefore the backward pass so that gradient tensors are scaled up bySand stay in range, then
divide the accumulated gradients bySbefore the optimizer step. The machinery works but requires dynamic
tuning ofS-too small and underflow still occurs; too large and overflow reappears. Practitioners invest real
engineering effort managing this.
BF16 eliminates loss scaling entirely. Because it shares the 8-bit exponent with FP32, its representable
range matches FP32 exactly. Gradient values that overflow FP16 are representable in BF16 without any ad-
justment. The trade-off is lower mantissa precision-7 bits instead of 23 in FP32 or 10 in FP16, giving relative
rounding errors of roughly 0 .78%of the value. For weights, activations, and gradient tensors in an LLM
forward-backward pass, this rounding is empirically inconsequential. For the accumulation step inside a tile of
a matmul, it is not-which is why accumulation stays in FP32 even in a BF16 training run.


```
9.3 Lower Precision and Quantization-Aware Training
```

512 in training.
**SwiGLU activation (memory-bound):** The kernel reads two input tensors of size 512  11 , 008 and writes
one output, for three tensors total.
FP32: 3  512  11 , 008 4 = 67. 7 MB; runtime= 67. 7 / 3 , 350  20. 2 μs.
BF16: 3  512  11 , 008 2 = 33. 8 MB; runtime 10. 1 μs.
Speedup: 2 from halved bytes; zero quality loss.
**Gate projection matmul (compute-bound at** B = 512 **):** FLOPs= 2 512  4096  11 , 008 
46. 1 GFLOPs.
BF16 tensor cores at 989 TFLOPs/s: 46. 1  109 / 989  1012  46. 6 μs theoretical.

Switching from FP32 ALUs to BF16 tensor cores: 14. 8 peak throughput advantage for the dominant
operation class.
**Single decode (** B= 1 **):** The bottleneck is weight-loading, not arithmetic. Gate projection weights: 4096 
11 , 008 2 = 90. 2 MB in BF16 vs 180. 4 MB in FP32.
BF16 load time: 90. 2 / 3 , 350  26. 9 μs.
FP32 load time: 53. 8 μs.
Summed over all projection layers in a 7 B model, the 2 weight-load savings directly doubles per-token
decode throughput.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use BF16 for weights, activations, and gradients; never use FP16 for LLM training without loss scal-
ing. Wrap the forward and backward pass withtorch.autocast(device_type='cuda', dtype=torch.bfloat16);
it automatically dispatches BF16 for matmuls and FP32 accumulation for reductions. On hardware pre-
dating BF16 support (Volta, Turing), FP16 with dynamic loss scaling is the only option-but on A100 or
H100, BF16 is strictly better and simpler.
Keep optimizer state in FP32. Adam’s first moment (mt) and second moment (vt) are running estimates
of the gradient mean and variance. The weight update∆w=ηmt/
p
vt+εinvolves dividing two near-
zero BF16 quantities, producing a result that BF16’s 0 .78%relative error rounds to zero at small learning
rates or near-converged weights. FP32 master weights and optimizer state are the universal standard; the
memory overhead is acceptable because they are not on the HBM bandwidth critical path during forward
and backward.
Keep layer norm and softmax reductions in FP32 accumulation. Computing the mean and variance of
a row for layer normalization requires accurate summation of up to several thousand elements; BF16 accu-
mulation introduces a systematic bias that shifts the normalized output. PyTorch’s built-innn.LayerNorm
upcasts to FP32 internally when inputs are BF16. Do not override this with a manual BF16 implementa-
tion unless you have measured that it makes no quality difference on your specific training run.
Never store embedding gradients in FP16 on large vocabularies. Embedding gradients for rare tokens
are sparse and can be large; FP16 overflows without loss scaling. With BF16 this is not an issue. If an
older checkpoint or library forces FP16 embeddings, add per-parameter loss scaling for the embedding
table and monitor gradient norms separately.

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why is BF16 faster than FP32 for LLM training?” Strong answer: two mechanisms. First, halving bytes
per element halves HBM traffic for memory-bound kernels (activations, norms, elementwise ops), directly
halving their runtime. Second, BF16 inputs unlock H100 tensor cores at 989 TFLOPs/s vs general
FP32 ALUs at 67 TFLOPs/s-a 14. 8 peak advantage on matrix multiplications, which dominate total
FLOPs.
“Why does production LLM training use BF16 instead of FP16?” Strong answer: FP16’s 5-bit exponent
limits its maximum representable value to 65,504; gradient norms in large-scale training regularly exceed
this, causing overflow without loss scaling. BF16 matches FP32’s 8-bit exponent and hence its full dy-
namic range, eliminating overflow at the cost of lower mantissa precision-a trade that is empirically safe
for LLM weights, activations, and gradients.
Senior follow-up: “Walk me through every place in a BF16 training run where you keep FP32 and why.”
Senior answer: (1) Matmul accumulation-tensor-core tiles accumulate in FP32 register buffers before
writing BF16 to HBM; handled transparently by cuBLAS. (2) Adam optimizer state (mt,vt, master
weights)-weight updates involve small increments that BF16 rounds to zero near convergence. (3) Layer-
Norm and softmax reductions-summation over wide dimensions accumulates rounding bias in BF16. (4)
Loss scalar-used for logging and numerical debugging. Everything on the HBM bandwidth critical path
(weight matrices, activation tensors, gradient tensors) is BF16.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
BF16 (1+8+7 bits) matches FP32’s dynamic range at half the storage; FP16 (1+5+10) has higher mantissa
precision but a 65,504 maximum that overflows in LLM training without loss scaling.
Halving bits per element halves HBM traffic; for memory-bound kernels (activations, norms), this halves
runtime directly at no quality cost.
BF16 unlocks H100 tensor cores at 989 TFLOPs/s vs FP32 general ALUs at 67 TFLOPs/s-a 14. 8 
peak advantage for matmuls, the dominant operation class.
Keep FP32 for Adam optimizer state, master weights, layer norm and softmax reductions; usetorch.autocast
to dispatch the rest automatically.
AtB= 1inference, BF16 halves decode latency vs FP32 by halving weight-load bytes; the next gain
comes from INT8 or FP8, which halve again.
```
**9.3.2 FP8 and INT8 for Inference-Oriented Training**
BF16 is the floor of precision for training stability, but it is not the floor of what the hardware supports.
INT8 has been standard for inference deployment for several years; FP8 is now native to H100 and has moved
into production training pipelines. Both formats halve the bytes per element again versus BF16, and both require
decisions that go wrong in distinct ways. Senior interviews probe this territory when the topic is serving cost,


```
9.3 Lower Precision and Quantization-Aware Training
```
large-model inference on minimal hardware, or the next-generation training infrastructure that frontier labs are
deploying today.
INT8 represents values as signed 8-bit integers in the range[ 128 ,127]. Mapping a floating-point tensor
Xinto this range requires a calibrated scalesand zero-pointz:

```
xq=round
```
```
x
s
```
#### 

```
+z, ˆx= (xqz)s
```
Per-tensor quantization uses one(s, z)pair for the entire tensor-fast but coarse. Per-channel quantization assigns
one pair per output channel of a weight matrix-more bookkeeping, but it preserves the dynamic range of channels
with outlier magnitudes. H100 INT8 tensor-core throughput is 1 , 979 INT8 TOPS-exactly 2 the BF16 rate of
989 TFLOPs/s. This arithmetic benefit is only realizable when the kernel is compute-bound; atB= 1inference
the value of INT8 is purely in the halved weight-load bytes.
FP8 arrives on H100 in two hardware formats. **E4M3** (1 sign, 4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits) has a maximum
value of 448 and good per-element resolution; it is suited for weights and activations in the forward pass where
the dynamic range is relatively narrow. **E5M2** (1 sign, 5 exponent, 2 mantissa bits) has a maximum of 57,344
and wider dynamic range at the cost of lower precision; it is suited for gradients in the backward pass, which have
heavier distribution tails. Each FP8 tensor carries a companion FP32 scaling factor that maps the full floating-
point range into the narrow FP8 window. H100 FP8 GEMM throughput is 1 , 979 TFLOPs/s, matching INT8
TOPS and delivering 2 the BF16 rate on compute-bound matmuls.
Post-training quantization (PTQ) calibrates scale factors on a small representative dataset after training
completes; no re-training is required. Quantization-aware training (QAT) inserts fake-quantize operations dur-
ing the training loop that round values and pass straight-through gradients, letting the model learn to compensate
for rounding errors before deployment.
_FP8 and INT8 each halve memory footprint relative to BF16; the engineering challenge is managing scale
calibration and knowing which tensors absorb rounding without accuracy loss and which do not._
AtB= 1inference, every decode step requires loading the full weight tensor for each layer from HBM
before the arithmetic can begin. Token generation rate is therefore bytes per second, not FLOPs per second.
INT8 weights occupy half the bytes of BF16 weights. With everything else equal, loading half the bytes takes
half the time, and per-token decode throughput approximately doubles-independent of whether INT8 tensor
cores are used for the arithmetic. This is the dominant reason production serving systems quantize weights: the
decode-bound regime atB= 1means you are buying throughput by reducing bytes, not by improving peak
FLOP rate.
FP8 training offers a compound gain. Halving weight and activation storage reduces HBM pressure through-
out the forward and backward pass, not just during weight loading. FP8 GEMMs run at 2 the BF16 tensor-
core rate on H100, shifting the compute-bound threshold to lower batch sizes and directly cutting per-step wall
time. DeepSeek-V3 reported roughly 2 end-to-end training throughput improvement versus BF16 on the same
hardware using FP8 mixed precision, with no measurable quality degradation after careful per-tensor scale man-
agement.
The accuracy risk is real but concentrated. Weight quantization with per-channel INT8 scales loses almost
nothing on standard benchmarks: weight distributions in trained LLMs are approximately Gaussian and map
cleanly into[ 128 ,127]. Activation quantization is harder because activations have outlier channels whose
magnitudes can be 10 the median channel value; per-tensor INT8 scales clip these outliers into the quantized
range. Gradient quantization is hardest of all, which is why E5M2 (wider range) rather than E4M3 is the H100
hardware format for backward-pass tensors.

```
**A Worked Example**

Consider a 70 B parameter model deployed for autoregressive generation atB= 1.
**Memory footprint:**
BF16 weights: 70  109  2 bytes= 140GB. This requires two H100 SXM5 80 GB to hold weights
alone, before KV cache or activation buffers.
Weight-only INT8 (W8A16-weights in INT8, activations in BF16): 70  109  1 byte= 70GB. Fits in
a single H100 SXM5 80 GB with 10 GB available for KV cache.
FP8 weights (E4M3): same 70 GB footprint as INT8. One GPU required.
**Decode latency at** B= 1 **:**
BF16: dominant cost is loading 140 GB of weights at H100 HBM3 bandwidth 3.35 TB/s: 140 / 3 , 350 
41. 8 ms per forward pass.
W8A16 INT8: load 70 GB of INT8 weights. Load time= 70/ 3 , 350  20. 9 ms. Dequantization to BF16
before each GEMM adds< 1 ms across all layers. Net: 2 faster per-token throughput.
**Calibration overhead:** Running 512 forward passes on a representative dataset to compute per-channel
INT8 scales takes roughly 5 minutes for a 70 B model. This one-time cost is irrelevant at deployment scale and
does not require touching the original training code.
**FP8 training throughput:** For a matmul of 2  512  4096  11 , 008  46. 1 GFLOPs in BF16 at
989 TFLOPs/s: 46. 7 μs. The same GEMM in FP8 at 1,979 TFLOPs/s: 23. 3 μs. Across all layers and all
matmuls in a training step, this 2 reduction compounds to a roughly 1. 5 - 2 end-to-end step time improvement,
with the remainder of step time consumed by non-GEMM operations that remain in BF16.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start with weight-only INT8 (W8A16). Quantize weights per output channel after training; keep ac-
tivations in BF16. Libraries likebitsandbytesimplement this in one line. Quality loss is typically
unmeasurable on 7 B-70 B checkpoints, the weight-load halving gives 2 decode throughput atB= 1,
and nothing in the serving stack changes except the weight storage format.
Upgrade to full INT8 (W8A8) only after running your full eval suite. W8A8 uses INT8 tensor cores
and provides arithmetic speedup at higher batch sizes, but activation quantization requires handling outlier
channels. Per-tensor activation scales cause clipping; per-channel activation scales add synchronization
overhead in the kernel. Measure on the specific tasks your deployment serves-perplexity alone is insuffi-
cient.
Never quantize these tensors. Embedding lookup tables: rare tokens have large weight magnitudes that
get clipped under per-tensor INT8 scales, silently degrading handling of infrequent vocabulary. Layer
norm scale and bias parameters: these are tiny tensors where rounding has outsized effect on normal-
ized outputs. Softmax normalizers: numerical stability of the log-sum-exp computation is sensitive to
precision. The final unembedding projection output logits if they feed directly into sampling without a
temperature rescaling step.
FP8 training requires H100 and the Transformer Engine library. NVIDIA’stransformer_engine
handles E4M3/E5M2 format dispatch, delayed per-tensor scale updates (updating scales every 16 steps is
the standard default), and FP8 GEMM scheduling. Do not attempt to write FP8 GEMMs manually; the
hardware requirements and scale management are non-trivial. The key knob is the scale update frequency:
more frequent updates improve numerical stability at a small runtime overhead; 16-step delayed scaling
```

```

```
```
is the practical default used by production deployments.
PTQ is suﬀicient for INT8; QAT is for 4-bit and below. For INT8, calibrating per-channel weight scales
and per-tensor activation scales on a 512-sample in-domain dataset closes essentially all the quality gap
relative to BF16. QAT-simulating quantization noise during the training loop-is worth the engineering
cost only when PTQ quality becomes unacceptable, which empirically happens below 4-bit precision (the
domain of GPTQ, AWQ, and QLoRA-style methods).

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why is INT8 inference faster than BF16 inference at batch size 1?” Strong answer: atB= 1, decode
is weight-loading-bound, not compute-bound. INT8 weights occupy half the bytes of BF16 weights, so
the GPU loads the same parameters in half the time. The 2 arithmetic throughput advantage of INT8
tensor cores is irrelevant because the operation is memory-bound regardless of peak TOPS-the compute
units finish the arithmetic before the next tile arrives from HBM.
“Walk me through the memory implications of weight-only INT8 for a 70 B model.” Strong answer: INT8
halves weight bytes from 140 GB to 70 GB, reducing the serving requirement from two H100 80 GB
GPUs to one. Activations stay in BF16, so the KV cache and intermediate tensors are unchanged. Per-
token decode latency approximately halves because the dominant runtime atB= 1is weight-load time
= weight bytes / bandwidth.
Senior follow-up: “When would you choose W8A8 over W8A16 for production, and what are the risks?”
Senior answer: W8A8 is worth investigating when the batch size is high enough that the linear layers
are compute-bound-above the W8A16 ridge point of 295 FLOPs/byte, which at a single 4096 11008
projection corresponds to roughlyB > 295. Below that threshold, activation quantization adds calibration
complexity and accuracy risk without delivering the INT8 tensor-core throughput gain, because the kernel
is still memory-bound. The specific risk to measure is outlier-channel clipping: check the per-channel
activation distributions before and after quantization; if more than 0 .1%of values are clipped, per-
channel activation scales are required.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
INT8 and FP8 each halve weight bytes versus BF16; atB = 1inference, this halves decode latency
because the bottleneck is weight-load time, not arithmetic throughput.
W8A16 (INT8 weights, BF16 activations) is the safest quantization tier: near-zero quality loss on 7 B-70 B
models, 2 decode throughput, calibrated offline with 512 samples.
W8A8 uses INT8 tensor cores at 1 , 979 TOPS (H100), delivering 2 arithmetic speedup versus BF16-
but only when the kernel is compute-bound; activation quantization adds accuracy risk that must be mea-
sured.
FP8 training on H100 uses E4M3 (forward pass) and E5M2 (backward pass) with per-tensor FP32 scale
factors; the Transformer Engine handles dispatch and delayed scaling; end-to-end training throughput
improvement versus BF16 is roughly 1. 5 - 2 .
PTQ on a 512-sample calibration set is sufficient for INT8; QAT is warranted only below 4-bit, where
PTQ accuracy loss becomes non-negligible.
```

## Chapter 10 Writing and Benchmarking Custom Kernels

### 10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline.

**10.1.1 Warm-Up, CUDA Synchronization, and Wall-Clock Traps**
I have watched engineers spend three days optimizing a kernel and then present timing results showing it is
10 faster than PyTorch. The kernel was not faster. They forgot to calltorch.cuda.synchronize(), so they
measured how long the CPU took to queue the CUDA command - microseconds - instead of how long the GPU
took to execute it - milliseconds. Getting benchmarking right is a prerequisite for any GPU kernel work, and
getting it wrong produces numbers that are confidently, silently wrong. This topic appears at every level from
junior ML engineer to staff systems engineer; the mistake is embarrassingly common and the fix takes three
lines.
GPU benchmarking has exactly two mandatory steps that developers consistently miss.
**Step 1: Warm-up iterations.** The first time PyTorch dispatches a CUDA kernel, it performs just-in-time
compilation, loads shared libraries, allocates internal caches, and primes the GPU’s state. These startup costs
are one-time artifacts - not representative of steady-state performance. If you benchmark the first invocation,
you measure initialization, not computation. Always discard the first 5-10 iterations before timing.
**Step 2: CUDA synchronization.** The GPU and CPU are independent compute devices connected by a
command queue. When Python calls a CUDA operation, the CPU adds the kernel descriptor to the queue and
_immediately returns_ - it does not wait for the GPU to finish. If you calltime.perf_counter()before and after
a GPU operation without synchronizing, you measure how long the CPU spent dispatching the command: typi-
cally 10-100 microseconds. The actual GPU execution - the number you care about - completes asynchronously
and may take 100longer.
torch.cuda.synchronize()blocks the CPU until all queued GPU kernels have completed. Call it once
immediately before starting the timer and once immediately after the timed code to drain the queue and measure
true GPU execution time.
The complete benchmark pattern:

import time, torch

def benchmark(fn, n_warmup=5, n_trials=20):
for _ in range(n_warmup):
fn()

```
times = []
for _ in range(n_trials):
torch.cuda.synchronize() # drain queue; mark t=0
t0 = time.perf_counter()
fn()
torch.cuda.synchronize() # wait for GPU to finish
t1 = time.perf_counter()
times.append(t1 - t0)
```

```
10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline
```
```
return sum(times) / len(times) # mean over trials
```
Average over trials rather than taking the minimum. GPU clock speeds drop under thermal load; individual
measurements vary by 5-10%. The mean reflects steady-state production performance better than the best-case
minimum.
_Without warm-up you measure initialization cost; withoutcuda.synchronize()you measure dispatch
cost; only with both do you measure actual GPU execution time._
The GPU’s asynchronous execution model is a feature. It lets the CPU run far ahead of the GPU, filling the
command queue and keeping the GPU continuously fed without waiting for each kernel to finish. This is one of
the primary reasons Python - a slow interpreted language - can drive GPU computations at near-full utilization.
Python is never the bottleneck because the CPU is always running one full training step ahead of the GPU.
But this same asynchrony is what makes naive wall-clock measurement wrong. When the CPU calls
torch.matmul(), it takes roughly 10-50 microseconds to construct and enqueue the kernel descriptor. The
actual matrix multiply on a 4096  4096 bfloat16 matrix takes roughly 40-60 milliseconds on an A100. A
benchmark without synchronization reports 0.01 ms; with synchronization it reports 50 ms. The 5000 dis-
crepancy is entirely due to missing the sync.
The JIT warm-up trap is equally insidious but less well known. PyTorch compiles CUDA code on first use,
selects optimal cuBLAS kernels by running micro-benchmarks internally, and allocates persistent workspace
buffers. All of this happens transparently in the background and takes 100-1000 ms per unique operation shape.
The steady-state cost is zero. Benchmarking without warm-up inflates the reported cost by orders of magnitude.

**A Worked Example**

Benchmarking a manual (unfused) GELU vs. the fused PyTorch implementation on an A100, on a 64 , 000 , 000 -
element bfloat16 tensor.
**Wrong benchmark (no warmup, no sync):**

t0 = time.time()
y = manual_gelu(x) # x.shape = (64_000_000,), device='cuda'
t1 = time.time()
print(f"{(t1-t0)*1e3:.2f} ms") # prints ~0.1 ms

```
Correct benchmark:
```
manual_time = benchmark(lambda: manual_gelu(x)) # 8.1 ms
pytorch_time = benchmark(lambda: torch.nn.functional.gelu(x)) # 1.1 ms

The wrong benchmark reportsmanual_geluat 0.1 ms, apparently 11 faster than PyTorch. The cor-
rect benchmark reports 8.1 ms - 7. 4  _slower_ than PyTorch. The 80disagreement is entirely due to missing
synchronization.
The manual GELU dispatches 6 separate CUDA kernels (one each forx^3 , three multiplications, thetanh,
and one addition). Each kernel reads and writes the full 128 MB tensor from HBM. The fused PyTorch GELU
dispatches 1 kernel that reads the tensor once and writes it once. Correct benchmarking is what reveals this
7. 4 gap; without it you would optimize in the wrong direction.


```
10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline
```
Scaling sanity check: for a 256-dim, 4-layer MLP on batch size 256, time per step is approximately 5
seconds. Scaling from 2 to 5 steps gives 2, 3, 4, 5of single-step time - exactly linear, as expected. If
scaling is non-linear when it should be linear, something is wrong: memory fragmentation, thermal throttling,
or a synchronization barrier that was not there before.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Usetime.perf_counter(), nottime.time(). perf_counterhas nanosecond resolution.time.time()
has millisecond or worse resolution on some systems, which means all sub-millisecond GPU operations
look identical.
Set n_warmup  5 , n_trials  20 for production benchmarks. Five warm-up iterations is enough for
PyTorch’s JIT to complete on most operations. Twenty trials gives a stable mean. For kernels faster than
100 μs, increase to 100+ trials because individual measurement noise becomes significant.
Report the mean, not the minimum. The minimum filters out thermal throttling and cache misses,
producing best-case numbers that do not reflect production behavior. If you want to separate kernel exe-
cution from scheduling jitter, use CUDA events (torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)) which
measure inside the GPU’s own clock.
Benchmark end-to-end, not individual kernels in isolation. A kernel that is fast in isolation may be
slow when integrated because it changes memory access patterns for subsequent kernels, triggers memory
reallocation, or alters the GPU’s warp scheduler state. Always benchmark the realistic workload, then drill
down to identify the bottleneck.
Never call.item(),.cpu(), orprint(tensor)inside a benchmark loop. All three force a CUDA
synchronize, making your GPU and CPU effectively synchronous and eliminating the asynchrony advan-
tage. This also applies to training loops: aprint(loss.item())after each step can double step time
by serializing CPU and GPU execution.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you correctly benchmark a custom CUDA kernel’s performance?” Two mandatory
steps: (1) warm-up iterations to prime JIT compilation and caches; (2)torch.cuda.synchronize()
before and after the timed region to drain the GPU command queue and measure actual GPU execution
time. Average over 20+ trials usingtime.perf_counter().
“A colleague benchmarks their kernel and claims it is 500  faster than the reference implemen-
tation. What is the most likely explanation?” Missingcuda.synchronize(). The CPU timer is
measuring how long it took to queue the CUDA command, not how long the GPU took to execute it.
Typical dispatch time is 10-100μs; the actual kernel may take 50+ ms.
Senior follow-up: “Your benchmark shows a 10  speedup over PyTorch on a simple fused opera-
tion. What would you verify before claiming the result is real?” (1) Correctness: run an assertion that
both implementations produce numerically equivalent outputs. A kernel returning garbage can appear
arbitrarily fast. (2) Input size: for very small inputs, PyTorch’s dispatch overhead may dominate both
paths, making the ratio meaningless. (3) Profile both: usetorch.profilerto verify each dispatches
what you think it does - PyTorch may dispatch to a slower kernel path for the specific shape tested. (4)
Measure memory traffic: a 10 speedup on a memory-bound operation is legitimate if you reduced HBM
round-trips by 10 ; on a compute-bound operation it would require 10 more FLOPs/second than the
```

```
10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline
```
```
hardware provides, which is a red flag.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
CUDA operations are asynchronous: the CPU returns immediately after dispatch; withouttorch.cuda.synchronize()
you measure dispatch time (10-100μs), not GPU execution time (ms to seconds).
Warm-up iterations (minimum 5) are mandatory: first iterations trigger JIT compilation and internal
cuBLAS micro-benchmarking that inflates the reported cost by orders of magnitude.
The correct benchmark pattern: warm up!sync!start timer!fn()!sync!stop timer!mean
over 20+ trials.
Usetime.perf_counter(), report the mean (not min), and always verify correctness before interpreting
any timing.
Never call.item(),.cpu(), orprint(tensor)inside training loops or benchmark loops: all three
force an implicit CPU-GPU sync, serializing what should be asynchronous execution.
```
**10.1.2 Reading an NVIDIA Nsight Systems Trace**
A benchmark tells you your training step takes 500 ms. A profiler trace tells you 300 ms of that is the GPU
idle because aprint(loss.item())call is forcing a synchronization barrier that eliminates every CPU-ahead
scheduling advantage. These are different problems requiring different solutions, and you will never find the
second one from benchmarks alone. Reading profiler traces fluently is the skill that separates engineers who
know _that_ their system is slow from engineers who know _why_ and can fix it. This shows up at the senior engineer
and above level in any role involving training system performance.
GPU profiling operates at two levels of resolution.
**PyTorch Profiler (quick, no external tools).** Instrumentsaten::operations via C++ hooks and records
CPU and CUDA execution times per operation:

with torch.profiler.profile(

The output table shows: operation name (Python!aten::!CUDA kernel), self CPU time, self CUDA

selected for your matrix shape on the CUDA side. For a compound operation liketorch.cdist, it decomposes
into constituent kernels:aten::matmul(78% of GPU time),aten::pow(5%),aten::sum(3%),aten::cat
(6%). This tells you exactly where to focus optimization effort.
**NVIDIA Nsight Systems (detailed, requiresnsysbinary).** Produces a.nsys-repfile for the Nsight

```
10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline
```
**GPU lane (“CUDA HW”)** : every kernel that ran on device, its start time, duration, and name.
**CPU lanes (per thread)** : Python and C++ execution, kernel launches, memory copies.
**Memory lane** : allocation and deallocation events.
The most important feature: the GPU and CPU lanes are shown side by side on the same timeline. You
can directly observe whether the GPU is idle (no kernel running) and what the CPU was doing during that gap.
NVTX annotations mark code regions that appear as colored bands in the CPU lane:

import torch.cuda.nvtx as nvtx

for step in range(n_steps):
nvtx.range_push(f"step_{step}")
nvtx.range_push("forward"); loss = model(x); nvtx.range_pop()
nvtx.range_push("backward"); loss.backward(); nvtx.range_pop()
nvtx.range_push("optimizer"); opt.step(); nvtx.range_pop()
nvtx.range_pop() # step

These cost microseconds and make the trace immediately interpretable.
_A profiler trace tells you exactly which CUDA kernel ran, for how long, and whether the GPU was actually
busy - everything benchmarks cannot tell you._
The PyTorch Profiler costs 1-5% runtime overhead and requires zero external setup. It is the right first tool
for identifying which operations dominate GPU time and verifying that kernels dispatched are the kernels you
intended.
Nsight Systems operates at the hardware level: it instruments the CUDA driver directly, recording every
kernel launch, memory copy, and synchronization event with sub-microsecond precision. This is the right second
tool when you need to understand the relationship between CPU and GPU execution - specifically, whether the
GPU is idle and what the CPU is doing during that idle period.
The key asymmetry that traces reveal: different matrix shapes dispatch to completely different CUDA
kernels. A 4096  4096 matmul dispatches to a Cutlass large-tile kernel; a 128  128 matmul dispatches to a
different XMMA kernel. These have entirely different performance characteristics. A benchmark reports one
number per implementation; a trace shows which internal path was taken for each call.
The CPU-ahead pattern is visible in any healthy Nsight trace: the CPU timeline shows the Python code
for stepN+ 1running while the GPU timeline shows stepNstill executing. The CPU queues kernels faster
than the GPU executes them. This is correct behavior. A trace where CPU and GPU steps are perfectly aligned
is a warning sign: it means a synchronization barrier - usually a.item()call or a Python-level loss print - is
forcing the CPU to wait for the GPU at every step. Adding oneprint(loss.item())to a tight training loop
can serialize what was asynchronous execution and reduce throughput by up to 50%.

**A Worked Example**

```
Profiling a 16-layer MLP (256 dimensions, batch 256) with the PyTorch Profiler.
The top-10 table by CUDA time shows (approximate numbers on A100):
aten::mm(forward): 31% of GPU time, 16 calls per step.
aten::mm(backward dL/dX + dL/dW): 61% of GPU time, 32 calls per step.
aten::add: 3% GPU time (bias additions).
```

```
10.1 Benchmarking and Profiling Discipline
```
aten::relu: 2% GPU time.
CudaDeviceSynchronize: 2% (the profiler’s own barrier).
The immediate conclusion: 92% of GPU time is matrix multiplies. Optimizing the ReLU or bias operations
is wasted effort. The profiler answered “where should I spend three hours?” in thirty seconds.
Now compare the Nsight Systems trace for the same model in two configurations:
**Configuration A (no print):** CPU timeline shows step 0 Python running for 20 ms; GPU timeline shows
step 0 executing for 180 ms starting att= 400ms (after JIT startup). By step 1, the CPU is already dispatching
step 2’s kernels while the GPU runs step 1. The CPU runs one full step ahead. GPU utilization is continuous -
no idle gaps.
**Configuration B (withprint(loss.item())after each step):** Step 1 CPU duration is now 180 ms.
The CPU-step boundary aligns with the GPU-step boundary. The reason:loss.item()transfers a scalar from
GPU to CPU, which internally callstorch.cuda.synchronize(). The CPU blocks for 180 ms waiting for
the GPU to finish, then prints, then launches step 2. The CPU-ahead advantage is gone. Step time goes from
180 ms (GPU-paced) to 360 ms (CPU-blocked): a 2 slowdown from oneprintstatement.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Add NVTX annotations to every training loop before profiling. Do it once, keep it in the code per-
manently. The overhead is under 10μs per annotation pair. Without them, a Nsight trace of a multi-step
training loop is almost unreadable - you cannot tell where step boundaries are.
Never call.item(),.numpy(),.cpu(), orprint(tensor)inside the training loop. All four force a
CUDA synchronize that serializes CPU and GPU. For loss logging, accumulate values in a GPU tensor
and transfer once every 100 steps, or use a framework likewandbwith asynchronous logging.
Use PyTorch Profiler first; escalate to Nsight Systems when you need CPU/GPU timeline alignment.
The Profiler answers “which operation is slow?”. Nsight Systems answers “is the GPU idle, and why?”.
They are complementary. Start with the fast tool.
When you see different CUDA kernels for different matrix shapes, benchmark both shapes sepa-
rately. PyTorch dispatches to different Cutlass kernels based on matrix dimensions (and hardware). A
matmul that is fast at 4096  4096 may dispatch to a less optimal path at 512  512. Profiling reveals
this; benchmarking only the happy-path size hides it.
Profile with warm-up excluded using the schedule API:
```

wait=2, warmup=2, active=3),
on_trace_ready=torch.profiler.tensorboard_trace_handler('./log'))
```

This skips the first two steps (JIT), warms up for two steps, and records three steps. Without this, the

“How would you use the PyTorch Profiler to identify which operation to optimize in an MLP?”
Wrap the training step intorch.profiler.profilewith CPU and CUDA activities enabled. Call
