wrong operation.
Senior follow-up: “A profiler shows 60% of GPU time is inCudaLaunchKernel(the kernel launch
overhead) rather than in actual computation kernels. What causes this and how do you fix it?” This
happens when the model has many small operations instead of a few large ones. Example: an unfused
GELU implemented as 6 separate element-wise operations dispatches 6 kernels; each kernel launch takes
5-20μs. At 100 GPU kernels per step, that is 0.5-2 ms of pure launch overhead per step. In a fast model
with 50 ms steps, launch overhead is 1-4% of runtime. In a very fast model with 3 ms steps, it is 17-67%.
The fixes: (1)torch.compilefuses element-wise chains automatically and eliminates most of this. (2)
Write a Triton or CUDA kernel that fuses the compound operation. (3) Increase batch size or hidden
dimension so each kernel has more useful work to amortize the fixed launch cost.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The PyTorch Profiler reveals which operations dominate GPU time and which CUDA kernel is dispatched
per operation; use it first, as it requires no external tools.
Nsight Systems shows the GPU and CPU timelines side by side: CPU-ahead scheduling is healthy; a
CPU/GPU timeline that is perfectly aligned indicates a synchronization barrier (usually a.item()call)
that serializes what should be asynchronous execution.
A singleprint(loss.item())per step can double step time by forcing a CUDA synchronize at every
iteration, eliminating all CPU-ahead scheduling benefit.
Different matrix shapes dispatch to different CUDA kernels; only a profiler reveals this; a single bench-
mark number hides kernel selection differences.
Add NVTX annotations (nvtx.range_push/pop) to training loops before profiling; they cost microsec-
onds and make traces immediately readable.

### 10.2 Implementing Kernels

**10.2.1 A Minimal Custom CUDA Kernel (GeLU Case Study)**
Your new architecture uses a custom activation function. The naive PyTorch implementation dispatches
six CUDA kernels and runs at 8.1 ms. PyTorch’s built-in fused version runs at 1.1 ms. Writing a minimal
custom CUDA kernel in C++ fuses all operations into a single kernel launch and cuts runtime to 1.8 ms - an
80% improvement without changing any math. Every ML infrastructure role at a frontier lab expects you to
be able to sketch this pattern, explain why the fusion matters, and know where the remaining gap to PyTorch’s
implementation comes from.
A CUDA kernel is a C function marked__global__that the GPU executes on thousands of threads si-
multaneously. Each thread computes its global index and handles one (or a few) elements of your data. The


```
10.2 Implementing Kernels
```
CPU side is a thin wrapper that validates inputs, allocates the output, computes grid dimensions, and fires off
the kernel.
Every CUDA kernel for element-wise operations follows the same skeleton:

// GPU side: runs on device
__global__ void gelu_kernel(const float* in, float* out, int n) {
int i = blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;
if (i < n) {
float x = in[i];
float y = 0.5f * x * (1.0f + tanhf(
sqrtf(2.0f / M_PI) * (x + 0.044715f * x * x * x)));
out[i] = y;
}
}

// CPU side: orchestrates the launch
torch::Tensor gelu_cuda(torch::Tensor x) {
TORCH_CHECK(x.device().is_cuda(), "input must be on GPU");
TORCH_CHECK(x.is_contiguous(), "input must be contiguous");
auto y = torch::empty_like(x); // not zeros_like
int n = x.numel();
int blocksize = 1024;
int num_blocks = (n + blocksize - 1) / blocksize; // ceiling division
gelu_kernel<<<num_blocks, blocksize>>>(
x.data_ptr<float>(), y.data_ptr<float>(), n);
return y;
}

The naive PyTorch implementation of this formula dispatches six separate CUDA kernels (one each forx^3 ,
a scale, an add, atanh, a multiply, and a final scale). Each kernel reads and writes the full tensor to HBM. The
custom kernel reads once and writes once. That is the entire reason for the speedup.
_A CUDA kernel is just a C function in which each thread computes its global indexi = blockIdx.x *
blockDim.x + threadIdx.x, does a bounds check, and performs its element’s computation - everything else
is ordinary C._
Kernel fusion eliminates redundant HBM traffic. For a 64M-element float32 tensor (256 MB), each HBM
round-trip costs roughly 256 MB/ 2 TB/s 128 μs, plus a kernel launch overhead of10-50μs. Six round-
trips: 768 μs minimum bandwidth cost plus six launch overheads. The fused kernel: one read, one write, one
launch - the minimum possible HBM traffic.
The contrast withtorch.compileis instructive: the JIT compiler achieves 1.47 ms on the same operation
(vs. our 1.8 ms) by generating a Triton kernel with vectorized loads (4 float32 values per thread instead of 1)
and better inlining. For simple element-wise fusions, the compiler wins on convenience and nearly wins on

pattern, or (b) you need hardware-specific intrinsics not exposed through Triton.
The remaining 0.7 ms gap between our kernel (1.8 ms) and PyTorch’s (1.1 ms) comes from two sources:
our kernel processes one float32 element per thread (2HBM bytes vs. bfloat16), and it lacks the vector load
instructions (float4) that allow loading 4 values per transaction and better utilizing the HBM burst width.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Useempty_like, neverzeros_like, for output allocation. zeros_likezeros every element before
you write to it - an extra HBM round-trip for a tensor you are about to overwrite. For 256 MB this costs
 128 μs. Useempty_likewhen you will write every output element.
Always check device and contiguousness at the wrapper level. A tensor that has been transposed or
sliced may be non-contiguous: its elements are not laid out consecutively in memory, soin[i]does not
give you elementi. Assertx.is_contiguous()and callx.contiguous()if needed. Failing to do this
silently reads the wrong memory.
SetCUDA_LAUNCH_BLOCKING=1during development. Without it, CUDA errors are deferred and surface
in unrelated calls, making the error message point to the wrong line. With it, errors appear immediately
at the kernel launch. Remove it before benchmarking (it adds 5-15% overhead).
blocksize = 1024 is a safe default for element-wise kernels. An A100 SM supports up to 2048 threads
per SM (64 warps). With blocksize = 1024 (32 warps per block), two blocks fit per SM, giving 64 active
warps - full capacity. If register pressure is high (many temporaries), reduce to 512.

**10.2.2 Triton: Block-Level Programming in Python**
You need a fused softmax kernel for your inference server. Writing it in raw CUDA means tracking warp
shuffle instructions, shared memory barrier placement, and hand-coded memory coalescing - easily a day of


```
10.2 Implementing Kernels
```
brittle C++. Triton lets you write the same kernel in Python at the thread-block level, while the compiler handles
coalescing, shared memory, and thread synchronization automatically. For most ML infrastructure engineers
I have worked alongside, Triton is the practical answer to “I need a custom kernel”: it delivers CUDA-class
performance with Python ergonomics and a debugger that actually works. At senior-level interviews for kernel-
writing roles, interviewers expect you to sketch a Triton GeLU or softmax from memory and explain the block-
centric mental model that drives the design.
Triton is a Python domain-specific language first released by OpenAI in 2021. The key conceptual shift
from raw CUDA: you no longer think in _threads_ , you think in _thread blocks_. In CUDA, each function invocation
is a single thread computing one element. In Triton, each function invocation is one program instance - one
thread block - operating on a contiguous _tile_ of elements simultaneously. The Triton compiler maps that tile to
individual threads and automatically generates:
Coalesced memory access: adjacent tile elements map to adjacent threads, which map to adjacent ad-
dresses, fully utilizing the 128-byte HBM cache line per transaction.
Vectorized loads: the PTX output uses 4-element load instructions (ld.global.v4.f32), moving 4
float32 values per thread per transaction without any programmer annotation.
Masked boundary handling: tl.load(ptr + offsets, mask=mask, other=0.0)suppresses out-
of-bounds accesses cleanly, replacing the manualif (i < n)that every CUDA kernel requires.
What Triton does _not_ manage: scheduling across SMs. You choose the grid (number of blocks and block
size), and the GPU dispatcher decides placement. This is the one degree of freedom you retain.
A complete Triton GeLU kernel:

import triton
import triton.language as tl
import torch

@triton.jit
def gelu_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
offsets = pid * BLOCK_SIZE + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
mask = offsets < n_elements
x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
c = tl.sqrt(2.0 / 3.141592653589793)
inner = c * (x + 0.044715 * x * x * x)
y = 0.5 * x * (1.0 + tl.libdevice.tanh(inner))
tl.store(y_ptr + offsets, y, mask=mask)

def triton_gelu(x: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
assert x.is_cuda and x.is_contiguous()
y = torch.empty_like(x)
n = x.numel()
BLOCK_SIZE = 1024
grid = ((n + BLOCK_SIZE - 1) // BLOCK_SIZE,)
gelu_kernel[grid](x, y, n, BLOCK_SIZE=BLOCK_SIZE)


```
10.2 Implementing Kernels
```
```
return y
```
Compare this to the raw CUDA version from the previous subsection: the element-wise computation is
identical, buttl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)replaces the per-thread index arithmetic, andmask=maskreplaces
the explicit bounds check. The result: 1.85 ms runtime versus 1.80 ms for hand-written CUDA, with Python
code that a debugger can step through.
_Triton is CUDA where you write the block and the compiler writes the threads._
Against raw CUDA, Triton wins on development speed and correctness. Memory coalescing bugs are
among the most common and hardest-to-diagnose sources of GPU underperformance in hand-written kernels.
Triton makes them structurally impossible: thetl.arangepattern guarantees adjacent offsets for adjacent
threads, which guarantees coalesced access. Shared memory management and warp barriers are generated by
the compiler, not by the programmer.
Againsttorch.compile, Triton wins when the JIT cannot infer the right fusion pattern. For simple
element-wise ops like GeLU,torch.compilealready generates Triton internally and achieves 1.47 ms with
no kernel code at all. The case for hand-written Triton is algorithmic novelty: online reductions over tiles,
non-standard attention masking patterns, fused quantization and dequantization, or any computation where the
compiler would need to understand the mathematical structure of your operation to fuse it correctly.
The trade-off Triton does not eliminate is arithmetic intensity. A GeLU is memory-bound regardless of
whether it is written in Python or C++. Fusion cuts HBM round-trips from six to one - that is the large win. No
amount of Triton tuning changes the roofline for an inherently bandwidth-limited kernel.

**A Worked Example**

Row-wise softmax over a 4096  4096 float32 matrix on an A100 (HBM bandwidth: 2 TB/s). The natural
Triton design assigns one block per row, loading the entire row into an SM in a single vectorized pass.
**Grid.** One block per row, block size padded to the next power of two:
BLOCK_SIZE= 4096, num_blocks= 4096.
**Kernel:**

@triton.jit
def softmax_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, x_stride, y_stride,
n_cols, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
row = tl.program_id(axis=0)
cols = tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
mask = cols < n_cols
x = tl.load(x_ptr + row * x_stride + cols,
mask=mask, other=-float('inf'))
x = x - tl.max(x, axis=0) # numerical stability
x_exp = tl.exp(x)
y = x_exp / tl.sum(x_exp, axis=0)
tl.store(y_ptr + row * y_stride + cols, y, mask=mask)

```
HBM traﬀic. Each row is read once (16 KB) and written once:
2  4096  4096  4 bytes= 128MB.
```

```
10.2 Implementing Kernels
```
At 2 TB/s: 128 MB/ 2 TB/s= 64μs minimum. Measured:1.9 ms. The gap comes from the sequential
dependency within each row - max must complete before exp can begin, exp must complete before sum, sum
before normalization - so each block has an irreducible sequential fraction that no amount of parallelism can
eliminate.
**Comparison across implementations:**
Manual (6-kernel PyTorch decomposition): 3.7 ms (five HBM round-trips).
This Triton kernel: 1.9 ms (one read, one write, sequential within-block reduction).
PyTorch built-in softmax: 1.5 ms (fused CUDA kernel with online normalization).
torch.compile: 1.3 ms (Triton + online normalization, shape-specialized).
The 0.6 ms gap between this kernel andtorch.compilecloses with online (one-pass) softmax - the topic
of the FlashAttention section that follows.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Trytorch.compilebefore writing any Triton. For element-wise ops and standard reductions, the JIT
generates a fused Triton kernel automatically. Profile withtorch.profilerfirst: if you see a single
triton_kernel in the CUDA trace, the compiler already did the work.
DeclareBLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr. This tells the Triton compiler the block size is a compile-time
constant, enabling loop unrolling and better register allocation. PassingBLOCK_SIZEas a runtime integer
disables these optimizations silently.
Choose block size as a power of two. Triton’stl.arangerequires power-of-two sizes. For row-wise
operations, setBLOCK_SIZEto the next power of two above your column count. If a row does not fit in
SRAM (>96 KB shared memory per SM on an A100), tile across the row in a loop instead.
Always subtract the max before exponentiating in reductions. The linex = x - tl.max(x, axis=0)
is not optional. Without it, logits in the hundreds produceinffromtl.exp, which propagates to NaN
in the division. This is one of the easiest ways to silently break a custom attention kernel.
Reserve raw CUDA for hardware-specific intrinsics. FlashAttention-3’s gains on H100 come from
warpgroup matrix-accumulate (WGMMA) and asynchronous copy instructions that Triton’s abstraction
cannot yet express. For everything else - element-wise ops, reductions, tiled attention - Triton is within
5-10% of hand-written CUDA in my experience and is far less likely to contain silent memory bugs.
```

and thread management are handled by the compiler.
“When would you use Triton instead of torch.compile?” When the JIT cannot infer the right fusion:
non-standard memory layouts, online reductions over tiles, fused quantization-dequantization, or custom
attention masking patterns. torch.compilewins for standard element-wise ops and matmuls; Triton
wins when you need to encode algorithmic knowledge the compiler does not have.
Senior follow-up: “Your Triton softmax runs at 1.9 ms but torch.compile achieves 1.3 ms. What
accounts for the gap and how do you close it?” The naive two-pass softmax (pass 1: find max; pass 2:
exp and normalize) reads the row twice. Online softmax reduces this to a single pass: maintain running

### 10.3 FlashAttention as a Case Study.

```
maximummand running sumdacross tiles, and at each new tile apply the correctionemprev−mnewto the
accumulated sum before adding new terms. This halves HBM reads and is the foundational technique
in FlashAttention’s tiled attention kernel. Implementing it in Triton requires tracking(m, d)as scalar
accumulators across a loop over column tiles.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Triton programs in blocks:pid = tl.program_id(0)gives the block index,tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
gives the tile,mask = offsets < nhandles boundaries - three lines replace all thread-level index arith-
metic.
The compiler generates coalesced vectorized loads automatically, moving 4 float32 values per thread per
transaction without programmer annotation.

## Part V

# Distributed Training: Parallelism at Scale


## Chapter 11 Multi-GPU and Multi-Node Fundamentals

### 11.1 Interconnect Topologies.

**11.1.1 PCIe, NVLink, and NVSwitch**
Every parallelism strategy you design for a real training run starts with one question: which GPUs can afford
to communicate with each other? That question is answered by the interconnect fabric, not your algorithm.
Engineers at the mid-to-senior level are expected to know the three layers of intra-node connectivity-PCIe,
NVLink, and NVSwitch-and to justify choices like “tensor parallel up to 8” or “allreduce is fast enough here”
by pointing at concrete bandwidth numbers. If you answer that question with a vague reference to “fast GPU
networking,” you have skipped the most performance-critical part of the system.
Three interconnect technologies govern how GPUs talk to each other inside a single machine, and they sit
in a strict bandwidth hierarchy.
**PCIe** (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) is the original path between CPU and GPU. A PCIe
Gen 4 x16 slot delivers 32 GB/s unidirectional, or 64 GB/s bidirectional. Gen 5 doubles that to 128 GB/s
bidirectional. This sounds reasonable until you note that an H100 reads from its own HBM at 3.35 TB/s-PCIe is
roughly 26slower than the GPU’s own memory bus. GPU-to-GPU communication bridged through the CPU
over PCIe rarely exceeds 30-40 GB/s effective and adds CPU-side synchronization latency.
**NVLink** is NVIDIA’s direct GPU-to-GPU interconnect, bypassing the CPU entirely. Each NVLink lane
runs at far higher bandwidth than a PCIe lane. An H100 SXM5 GPU exposes 18 NVLink 4.0 lanes, delivering
900 GB/s of aggregate bidirectional bandwidth per GPU. An A100 SXM4 offers 600 GB/s per GPU via NVLink
3.0.
**NVSwitch** is the piece that makes NVLink scale beyond point-to-point links. Without it, NVLink connec-
tions are bilateral: GPU 0 might directly link to GPUs 1, 2, and 3, but not GPU 7. NVSwitch is a non-blocking
crossbar chip-every pair of GPUs in the node sees the full NVLink bandwidth simultaneously, with no con-
tention. A DGX H100 node ships with four NVSwitch 3.0 chips connecting all eight H100 GPUs, providing a
full 900 GB/s all-to-all fabric.
The three levels together form a clear mental model:

(^128) | {zGB/s}
PCIe Gen 5
 (^900) | GB/s per GPU{z }
NVLink 4.0
, non-blocking via NVSwitch| {z }
crossbar
_PCIe is the CPU highway, NVLink is the GPU express lane, and NVSwitch turns that lane into a non-
blocking switchboard so every GPU can talk to every other GPU at full speed simultaneously._
The hierarchy exists because different operations have different bandwidth tolerance. CPU-GPU data trans-
fers (loading a checkpoint, streaming host-side data) are infrequent and can tolerate PCIe latency. But collective
operations like allreduce-which fire every training step across the tensor-parallel group-happen dozens of times
per second and must complete in single-digit milliseconds to stay off the critical path of compute.
NVSwitch’s non-blocking crossbar is the enabling property for tensor parallelism. A tensor-parallel allre-
duce requires every GPU to simultaneously send and receive partial activation sums. A point-to-point NVLink
ring would serialize transfers and create contention at intermediate hops; NVSwitch eliminates both. All eight
GPUs in a node can participate in a single allreduce at near-peak wire bandwidth.
The alternative before NVSwitch was a hybrid cube-mesh NVLink topology where bandwidth between


```
11.1 Interconnect Topologies
```
non-directly-connected GPUs was lower and asymmetric. NVSwitch replaced that with a flat, predictable band-
width guarantee between any two GPUs, making performance analysis far simpler and tensor-parallel scaling
far more reliable.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 70B-parameter model with hidden dimensionh= 8192, trained with tensor parallelism across
8 H100 SXM5 GPUs in a single DGX H100 node. Batch sizeb= 4, sequence lengths= 2048, BF16 precision.
At each transformer layer, the tensor-parallel allreduce synchronizes the output activations. The activation
tensor has shape(b, s, h)with size:

4  2048  8192  2 bytes= 134MB
A ring allreduce overn= 8GPUs transfers approximately 2 n−n^1 times the data per GPU, so about
268 MB.
**On NVSwitch** at 900 GB/s bidirectional (effective allreduce bandwidth450 GB/s per GPU after protocol
overhead):
268 MB
450 GB/s^0.^6 ms
**On PCIe Gen 5 only** (128 GB/s bidirectional, shared across all eight GPUs contending for the same CPU-
side bandwidth):
268 MB
128 GB/s/ 8
 16. 8 ms

A large matmul in a single 70B transformer layer on an H100 takes roughly 1-3 ms. The NVSwitch-backed
allreduce at 0.6 ms sits safely below compute and can be overlapped with the next layer’s matrix multiply. The
PCIe-backed allreduce at 17 ms is 5-17slower than the compute itself and completely dominates step time.
Tensor parallelism becomes impractical.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Cap tensor parallelism at 8 on current hardware. Apply tensor parallelism only within a single
NVSwitch domain-almost always 8 GPUs on DGX-class nodes. Extending to 16 or 32 requires cross-
ing InfiniBand, where effective allreduce bandwidth collapses by 10-20. Published benchmarks show a
42% throughput drop at TP=16 and a 65% drop at TP=32 relative to TP=8, on the same number of GPUs.
These are not edge cases; they are the expected result of the bandwidth cliff.
Verify topology before assuming crossbar bandwidth. Not all NVIDIA nodes ship with NVSwitch.
RTX consumer cards have no NVLink at all. A100 and H100 PCIe variants have NVLink but no NVSwitch-
bandwidth between non-directly-connected GPUs is lower and non-uniform. Always runnvidia-smi
topo -mbefore assuming full crossbar performance. Two GPUs shown as connected via “SYS” (system-
level) instead of “NVL” (NVLink) will communicate at PCIe speeds.
Budget allreduce cost explicitly. For a full-model allreduce overPparameters in BF16, budget approx-
imately 2 P/Beff, whereBeff 0. 5 Bpeak NVLink. For a 7B-parameter model: 2  14 GB/ 450 GB/s
62 ms. This is large enough to matter and must be overlapped with gradient computation in the backward
pass rather than serialized after it.
When PCIe-only machines are all you have. Use data parallelism with large micro-batches to amortize
communication over more compute per synchronization. Avoid tensor parallelism entirely-the communication-
```

```
11.1 Interconnect Topologies
```
```
to-compute ratio is always unfavorable. Pipeline parallelism is permissible if point-to-point activation
transfers (not allreduces) can fit within the PCIe budget.
NVSwitch failure handling. A four-chip NVSwitch configuration has redundancy. If one chip fails,
NCCL reroutes over the remaining three, dropping peak crossbar bandwidth by roughly 25%. Effective
allreduce bandwidth can fall 20-30%. Monitor NVSwitch health viadcgmihealth checks before launching
multi-day training runs.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why do practitioners limit tensor parallelism to 8 GPUs?” A strong answer names NVSwitch as the fast
all-to-all fabric that makes layer-level allreduce cheap within a node, explains that crossing to a second
node requires InfiniBand with 10-20lower bandwidth, and cites the 42% throughput loss at TP=16 as
a concrete consequence. Weaker answers say “bandwidth” without quantifying it.
“Walk me through the bandwidth hierarchy inside a DGX H100 node.” The answer covers three levels:
PCIe Gen 5 at 128 GB/s bidirectional for CPU-GPU, NVLink 4.0 at 900 GB/s per GPU for GPU-GPU,
and NVSwitch providing the non-blocking all-to-all crossbar. Mention that NVSwitch is what makes the
bandwidth non-blocking -without it, GPU pairs that don’t share a direct NVLink lane contend.
“How would you measure the actual allreduce bandwidth available on a node?” Run NCCL’sall_reduce_perf
benchmark sweeping message sizes from 1 MB to 10 GB. Look for two regimes: latency-bound at small
messages (below100 MB) and bandwidth-bound above. The peak bandwidth-bound number is what
you should use for step-time estimates. Senior-level follow-up: “What happens to allreduce performance
if one NVSwitch chip in the node fails?” The remaining three chips reroute traffic, effective crossbar
bandwidth drops by25%, and allreduce latency for large tensors rises proportionally. NCCL falls back
to a partial ring and peak throughput may degrade 20-30%-enough to extend a 30-day training run by
several days.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
PCIe Gen 5 delivers 128 GB/s bidirectional; NVLink 4.0 delivers 900 GB/s per GPU; NVSwitch makes
that bandwidth non-blocking across all 8 GPUs in a node.
Tensor parallelism is practical only within a single NVSwitch domain. Crossing InfiniBand for TP in-
creases allreduce cost by 10-20and kills throughput.
Always verify node topology withnvidia-smi topo -m. PCIe-only nodes and NVLink-without-NVSwitch
nodes have non-uniform bandwidth that breaks the flat-bandwidth assumption.
Allreduce cost is approximately 2 P/(0. 5 BNVLink); for a 7B model on NVSwitch, this is62 ms-
significant but overlappable with compute in a correctly pipelined backward pass.
When NVSwitch hardware is unavailable, drop tensor parallelism from the strategy and rely on data
parallelism with large batches or pipeline parallelism with point-to-point sends.
```
**11.1.2 GPU Clusters vs. TPU Pods**
The moment your model requires more than one node, the question stops being “which interconnect?” and
starts being “what network topology?” The answer determines which parallelism strategies remain efficient
and, critically, where you will hit a wall as you scale. Senior engineers at frontier labs are expected to explain


```
11.1 Interconnect Topologies
```
why a training run switches from tensor parallelism to pipeline parallelism above a certain node count, and why
Google’s TPU-based runs can sustain tensor parallelism at larger group sizes than comparable GPU clusters.
The GPU fat-tree cluster and the TPU toroidal mesh are the two dominant answers to this topology question,
and they make starkly different trade-offs.
**GPU clusters** use a fat-tree or dragonfly network topology. Each node-typically 8 GPUs connected by
NVSwitch-attaches to a Top-of-Rack (ToR) switch via InfiniBand. Multiple ToR switches connect upward to
leaf switches, and leaf switches connect to spine switches. Within a rack of roughly 32 nodes (256 GPUs),
any two nodes can reach each other in at most two switch hops, giving all-to-all communication at near-wire
bandwidth. Beyond approximately 256 GPUs spanning multiple racks, traffic traverses spine switches shared by
many racks. Those uplinks are often the oversubscribed bottleneck, and effective per-node bandwidth for large
collectives can drop by 50-80%.
**TPU pods** use a multi-dimensional toroidal mesh. In a v4 TPU pod, each chip connects directly to six
immediate neighbors in a 3D torus via Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) at approximately 340 GB/s bidirectional
per chip. The topology is physically uniform-there is no hierarchy, no “within-rack” vs. “cross-rack” distinction,
and no bandwidth cliff as you scale beyond 256 chips. Allreduce is implemented as a sequence of ring operations
along each torus axis, and effective collective bandwidth approaches wire bandwidth regardless of pod size.
The constraint is the opposite: communication between distant non-adjacent chips requires multi-hop routing
through neighbors, and irregular all-to-all patterns (such as load-imbalanced expert routing) pay a higher penalty
than on a fat-tree.
_GPU fat-tree clusters give any-to-any communication at full speed up to a topology-dependent threshold,
then degrade; TPU toroidal meshes provide uniform, topology-aware bandwidth that scales gracefully but re-
wards algorithms aligned with nearest-neighbor communication patterns._
For GPU fat-tree clusters, the strength is communication flexibility. Expert parallelism with dynamic to-
ken routing, irregular pipeline schedules, and ad-hoc all-to-all operations all work without topology-specific
optimization because any two GPUs can communicate directly. The weakness is the bandwidth cliff. When
collective operations cross spine switches under 2:1 or 4:1 oversubscription, the effective allreduce bandwidth
halves or quarters. This is why standard GPU training recipes switch from tensor parallelism (which demands
high-bandwidth allreduce every layer) to pipeline parallelism (which requires only point-to-point activation
transfers between adjacent stages) as runs scale across multiple racks.
For TPU pods, the strength is bandwidth uniformity. An allreduce decomposed into per-axis ring operations
achieves near-wire bandwidth across the entire pod-the same effective rate at 64 chips and at 4096 chips. This
is the hardware reason TPU-based training can sustain tensor-parallel groups of 16 or more chips without the
throughput collapse seen on GPU clusters. The weakness is pattern sensitivity: the torus topology is optimized
for structured, axis-aligned communication. Expert parallelism with uneven loads or arbitrary point-to-point
sends require multi-hop routing that lowers effective bandwidth relative to what a fully non-blocking GPU fat-
tree would provide for the same operation.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 70B-parameter model in BF16 trained across 1,024 H100 GPUs organized as 128 nodes of 8
GPUs each, with tensor parallelism degreet= 8within each node and data parallelism across all 128 nodes.
**Within-rack data-parallel allreduce (32 nodes, 256 GPUs, single fat-tree rack):**
The gradient allreduce must synchronize 14 GB of BF16 parameters across 32 nodes. Each node must

each, giving 100 GB/s bidirectional per node:

At H100 with 50% MFU on a 70B model, a forward-backward pass takes roughly 600-900 ms. The allre-
duce at 136 ms is15-23% of step time-significant but maskable with overlapped gradient communication.
**Cross-rack allreduce (128 nodes spanning 4 racks, 2:1 oversubscribed spine):**

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
The 256-GPU threshold on GPU clusters. Within a single non-oversubscribed fat-tree rack of 256
H100s, you can sustain tensor plus data parallelism without pipeline overhead. Beyond 256 GPUs span-
ning multiple racks, add pipeline parallelism to reduce cross-rack traffic from full-model allreduces to
per-stage point-to-point sends. The rule is not 256 exactly-it is the boundary at which your fabric be-
comes oversubscribed-but 256 is the practical default for a single rack of NVIDIA DGX nodes.
Always measure fabric oversubscription before designing the parallelism strategy. Run NCCL’s
all_reduce_perfacrossN, 2 N, and 4 Nnodes. A bandwidth drop larger than 15% when doubling
node count signals oversubscription at the next switch level. Design your cross-node parallelism to mini-
mize volume at that boundary.
InfiniBand port count per node drives cross-node bandwidth. A node with a single HDR port at 25
GB/s has a 36bandwidth asymmetry with its NVSwitch fabric (900 GB/s). A node with four NDR ports
at 50 GB/s each gets 200 GB/s cross-node, a 4.5asymmetry. The number of InfiniBand ports per node
is often the single most important number for estimating cross-node allreduce feasibility.
Pipeline parallelism is the cross-rack workaround on GPU clusters. Point-to-point activation sends
in pipeline parallelism scale asbshbytes per microbatch-roughly 200 MB to 1 GB for typical
configurations-far smaller than the 14 GB allreduce for a 7B model. Pipeline parallelism tolerates the
higher latency of cross-rack InfiniBand because it is sequential and easily overlapped with microbatch
compute.
Designing for TPU topology. When partitioning a model across a TPU torus, map the highest-bandwidth
collective (typically tensor-parallel allreduce) to a single torus axis, and map data parallelism to another
axis. Mixed-axis communication requires multi-hop routing and lowers effective bandwidth. Misaligned
layouts can turn a theoretically 340 GB/s fabric into a 100 GB/s effective one for your specific collective
pattern.
```

### 11.2 Collective Communication Primitives

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does the standard recipe use tensor parallelism within a node and pipeline parallelism across
nodes?” A complete answer: tensor parallelism requires allreduce every layer; NVSwitch provides 900
GB/s all-to-all within a node; InfiniBand provides 25-100 GB/s between nodes. The 10-36bandwidth
gap means cross-node tensor parallelism is almost always bandwidth-bound. Pipeline parallelism substi-
tutes point-to-point activation sends for allreduces, dramatically reducing cross-node traffic volume.
“How does Google sustain larger tensor-parallel groups on TPUs than is typical on GPU clusters?” The
answer is ICI topology: each TPU chip has340 GB/s to its neighbors uniformly, with no spine-switch
bottleneck. Tensor-parallel allreduce implemented as torus rings approaches wire bandwidth at any pod
size. On GPU clusters, crossing the rack boundary with allreduce introduces a 2-4bandwidth penalty
that makes large tensor-parallel groups impractical.
“You have a 4,096-GPU budget. Walk me through your parallelism assignment.” A strong answer: (1)
sett= 8tensor parallel within each NVSwitch node; (2) assess whether 4,096 / 8 = 512 nodes fit in
a single non-oversubscribed fabric-probably not, so add pipeline parallelism across racks with enough
microbatches to keep bubble fraction below 5%; (3) fill remaining capacity with data parallelism up to
the batch size limit. Senior follow-up: “Your InfiniBand fabric is 4:1 oversubscribed at the spine. What
changes?” Effective cross-rack bandwidth drops to 25% of peak. Increase pipeline microbatch count to
keep bubble fraction acceptable, and reduce data-parallel node count to decrease spine traffic. Consider
whether model sharding via ZeRO stage 3 can consolidate the run onto fewer racks to stay within a single
non-oversubscribed fat-tree domain.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
GPU fat-tree clusters provide any-to-any full-bandwidth communication up to256 GPUs within a rack;
beyond that, spine-switch oversubscription cuts effective bandwidth by 50-80% for collective operations.
TPU toroidal meshes deliver uniform340 GB/s ICI per chip with no topology cliff, making tensor-
parallel allreduce feasible at large group sizes-but irregular all-to-all patterns pay multi-hop penalties.
The 256-GPU rack boundary is where pipeline parallelism typically enters the GPU cluster strategy, re-
placing full-model allreduces with small point-to-point activation sends.
InfiniBand bandwidth per node (25-100 GB/s depending on port count) is 10-36lower than NVSwitch
bandwidth (900 GB/s); this is the defining asymmetry for all cross-node parallelism decisions.
Measure actual fabric oversubscription before finalizing any parallelism plan. Published peak bandwidth
and realized collective bandwidth routinely differ by 2-4on production clusters.
```
### 11.2 Collective Communication Primitives

**11.2.1 AllReduce, ReduceScatter, and AllGather**
When a system design interviewer asks how you synchronize gradients across 64 GPUs, naming “AllRe-
duce” is the floor, not the ceiling. The follow-up-what does it cost, which ring algorithm is used, when would
you choose ReduceScatter instead, and how does NVLink bandwidth differ from InfiniBand-is where mid-level
and senior answers diverge. Collective communication primitives are the atomic operations from which every
parallelism strategy in distributed training is built, and interviewers at frontier labs expect you to reason about


```

```

A _collective operation_ is any communication pattern in which allNparticipating processes (called _ranks_ ,
indexed 0 throughN 1 , with the full set called the _process group_ ) must cooperate to complete. The six
primitives you need are:
**Broadcast** : Rankrsends an identicalP-byte tensor to every other rank. All ranks end with the same
tensor. Total bytes transferredP.
**Scatter** : Rankrsplits a tensor of total sizePintoNequal chunks and sends chunkito ranki. Total
bytes transferredP.
**Gather** : Each rankiholds aP/N-byte chunk; rankrcollects allNchunks into oneP-byte tensor. Total
bytes transferredP.
**Reduce** : Same as Gather, but rankrapplies a commutative associative operation (sum, max, min) across
corresponding positions as chunks arrive. Total bytes transferredPto the root.
**AllGather** : Each rank holdsP/Nbytes; after the operation, every rank holds allPbytes concatenated.
Using a bandwidth-optimal ring, each rank sends(N1)/NPbytes.
**ReduceScatter** : Each rank holds a fullP-byte tensor; after the operation, rankiholds only the reduction
(e.g., sum) of thei-th slice across all ranks. Each rank ends withP/Nbytes. Per-rank cost (N
1)/NPPfor largeN.
**AllReduce** is the operation every ML engineer names first. Every rank starts withPbytes, and every
rank ends with the fully-reducedP-byte result. In the bandwidth-optimal ring implementation the per-rank
communication cost is:

can do better in the bandwidth-limited regime.
_AllReduce, ReduceScatter, and AllGather are the three primitives from which every distributed training
communication schedule is constructed; the costs_ 2 P _,_ P _, and_ P _per rank should be immediate._
These primitives exist because point-to-point communication is topology-dependent and error-prone at
scale. Writing explicit send/receive pairs for a ring of 64 GPUs produces brittle code; a singleall_reducecall
lets NCCL choose the optimal topology-aware algorithm and pipeline multiple operations over available links

The ring algorithm achieves near-perfect link saturation regardless of world size. AtN= 8the per-rank

and insert optimizer computation in the gap without spending any extra bandwidth.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use AllReduce for gradient sync when each rank holds a full copy of the model. Calldist.all_reduce(param.grad,
op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)after the backward pass. Divide by world size in the optimizer, not in the

cost is identical to AllReduce, so there is no reason to use plain AllReduce once you have the ZeRO-1
infrastructure in place.

sync against 500 ms of forward+backward compute for a 7B model is under 15% overhead. Across nodes
at 138 ms, it may dominate and justify tensor parallelism or gradient compression.

executes asynchronously on the GPU; callingall_reducebeforeoptimizer.step()lets communica-
tion and compute pipeline if they target different parameter groups.
Do not confuse AllGather with Broadcast. AllGather assembles distinct per-rank chunks into one con-
catenated tensor; Broadcast replicates the same tensor from one sender. Using Broadcast where AllGather
is needed silently produces wrong results and is a common copy-paste bug when building FSDP-style code
from scratch.
```

**11.2.2 Why AllReduce Equals ReduceScatter Plus AllGather**
The identity AllReduce=ReduceScatter+AllGather is the single algebraic fact that makes ZeRO’s “zero
overhead” claim true. When an interviewer asks why sharding the optimizer state is free in the bandwidth-limited
regime, this equivalence is the complete answer. It surfaces in senior-level system design questions and-more
importantly-it is the reasoning you need to correctly evaluate any claim that a particular communication schedule
is bandwidth-optimal. Missing it means you will accept hand-wavy performance numbers without being able
to verify them on a whiteboard.
In the ring algorithm, AllReduce already executes as two sequential phases internally:

1. **ReduceScatter phase.** The tensor of sizePis logically split intoNequal slices of sizeP/N. OverN 1
    ring steps, each rank passes one slice clockwise and accumulates the incoming slice with its local copy.
    AfterN 1 steps, rankiholds the fully-reduced (summed) value of sliceiacross allNranks-and nothing
    else. Per-rank bytes transmitted:(N1)/NP.
2. **AllGather phase.** Over anotherN 1 ring steps, each rank propagates its fully-reduced slice to the rest
    of the ring. AfterN 1 steps, every rank holds allNfully-reduced slices-the complete AllReduce result.
    Per-rank bytes transmitted: another(N1)/NP.

_Any computation that operates independently on each rank’s shard and produces a same-sized shard can

The naive mental model for data-parallel gradient sync is: run backward!AllReduce!optimizer step.
The implicit assumption is that every GPU needs the full reduced gradient before updating any parameter. That
assumption is wrong, and the decomposition exposes why.
After ReduceScatter, rankiholds the exact, fully-summed gradients for its assignedP/Nparameters. That
is sufficient information to run a complete Adam step on those parameters-it does not need the gradients for any
other parameter. The AllGather is required only to redistribute the updated parameter values so all ranks agree
on the full model before the next forward pass.
Because the total bytes transferred equals the AllReduce baseline ( 2 P), there is no bandwidth penalty. The
optimizer state-first moment, second moment, master weights-can now be sharded: rankionly ever needs the
optimizer state for itsP/Nslice. On a 7B model in BF16, naive DDP carries 16 Pbytes of optimizer state
per rank (full Adam in mixed precision); ZeRO stage 1 reduces that by a factor ofN. ForN= 64, that is a 64 
reduction in optimizer memory at zero communication cost.
The contrast with the obvious alternative-gather all gradients to one rank, run the full optimizer, broadcast-
is stark. That approach costs(N1)Pto gather and(N1)Pto broadcast, totalling2(N1)P, which isN
times worse than the ring for largeN. More importantly, it also creates anNmemory bottleneck on the root
rank. The ring decomposition eliminates both problems.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
ZeRO stage 1 is always worth enabling. The bandwidth is identical to naive DDP AllReduce. The only
implementation cost is maintaining per-rank optimizer state slices and callingdist.reduce_scatter
anddist.all_gatherinstead ofdist.all_reduce. PyTorch’s FSDP automates this; if you are rolling
your own, the two-call sequence is five lines of code.
ZeRO stage 3 is not free: it costs 3 P per rank, not 2 P. The extraPis a forward-pass AllGather needed
to materialize each layer’s sharded parameters before the forward computation. This has no counterpart
in ZeRO stage 1, where parameters remain replicated. Measure the 50% communication increase against
your memory savings before committing to stage 3.
The optimizer step between ReduceScatter and AllGather is a hard serial dependency. AllGather
cannot begin until every rank has finished its Adam step on its shard. If your optimizer has pathologically
slow kernels (e.g., due to BF16-FP32 casting loops), it adds directly to latency. Fuse or kernel-optimize
the optimizer step if it exceeds5 ms per layer.
Verify your ReduceScatter + AllGather pair uses the same ring topology as your AllReduce. NCCL
selects algorithms based on message size and world size; if you call the two operations separately, NCCL
may choose a tree algorithm for one and a ring for the other, breaking the bandwidth-equivalence assump-
tion. Force the ring algorithm via environment variableNCCL_ALGO=Ringwhen benchmarking.
The equivalence holds only in the bandwidth-limited regime. For small tensors (< 1 MB), the
latency of two ring passes exceeds a single fused AllReduce kernel. Do not decompose gradient sync for
the embedding layer or small classification heads; the latency overhead will exceed the memory savings.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why is ZeRO stage 1 claimed to have zero communication overhead compared to DDP?” Strong answer:
AllReduce already decomposes into ReduceScatter+AllGather internally. ZeRO stage 1 just inserts the
per-rank optimizer step between those two phases. The bandwidth is 2 Pin both cases; the optimizer state
is sharded at no additional cost.
“What is the communication cost of ZeRO stage 3 compared to ZeRO stage 1?” Strong answer: ZeRO
stage 3 costs 3 Pper rank versus 2 Pfor ZeRO stage 1. The extraPis a per-layer parameter AllGather in
the forward pass that does not exist in ZeRO stage 1 (where parameters remain replicated). The tradeoff
is 1. 5 more communication in exchange forNparameter memory savings.
Senior follow-up: “Measured throughput on an 8-GPU FSDP run is 25% lower than DDP for the same
7B model. You know ZeRO 3 should cost 3 P versus 2 P = 50% more communication. Why is the through-
put hit only 25%?” Strong answer: three reasons. First, communication and computation overlap sig-
nificantly: FSDP prefetches the next layer’s AllGather while the GPU is computing the current layer’s
forward, so the extraPis partly hidden. Second, FSDP enables larger effective batch sizes per GPU by
```

```

the forward and backward flops dominate and the relative communication fraction is smaller than the raw

```
**Key Takeaways**

```
AllReduce=ReduceScatter+AllGather: total bandwidth is 2 Pper rank in both cases; the decomposition
is bandwidth-neutral.
ZeRO stage 1 inserts the optimizer step into the gap that already exists between ReduceScatter and All-
Gather, achievingNoptimizer memory reduction at zero bandwidth cost.
ZeRO stage 3 adds a thirdP-byte AllGather per layer in the forward pass, raising total communication to
3 Pper rank-not free, but often worth it for very large models.
The equivalence is bandwidth-based; for small tensors in the latency-dominated regime, a fused AllRe-
duce kernel beats two separate ring passes.
The key invariant: after ReduceScatter, each rank owns a fully-summed gradient shard; after AllGather,
each rank owns the fully-updated parameter tensor.
```
### 11.3 The Software Stack

**11.3.1 NCCL and torch.distributed**
An interviewer at a frontier lab will frequently ask you to trace a singledist.all_reduce()call from
your Python training loop all the way down to the NVLink packets leaving the GPU. This question appears at the
senior level because it separates engineers who have usedtorch.distributedas a black box from those who
understand the contract each layer provides. Getting this right matters in production: a misunderstood backend
choice causes either correctness failures (wrong gradients silently) or catastrophic hangs that waste hours of
cluster time.
The distributed communication stack for GPU training consists of two layers sitting between your Python
gradient tensors and the NVLink wires. The bottom layer is NVIDIA’s Collective Communications Library
(NCCL), a closed-source C library that owns the problem of routing multi-GPU collective operations as ef-
ficiently as possible on NVIDIA hardware. The top layer istorch.distributed, a Python API that wraps
NCCL-and alternative backends-behind a single, hardware-agnostic interface.
NCCL’s job starts at process-group initialization. When you calldist.init_process_group(backend="nccl"),
NCCL runs a topology discovery phase: it queries which GPUs are connected via NVLink, which are con-
nected only via PCIe, and which sit on remote nodes reachable over InfiniBand or Ethernet. From that topology
it precomputes optimal reduction trees and ring schedules for every collective. Critically, the rendezvous at
init_process_groupis a lightweight coordination step-it uses a small TCP or shared-filesystem handshake
just so ranks can find each other. No tensor data ever flows through that channel. All actual payload moves via
NCCL kernels launched directly on the GPU, bypassing the host CPU entirely once the operation is underway.
When your code reachesdist.all_reduce(tensor, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM), the CPU thread calls
into NCCL throughtorch.distributed’s nccl backend shim. NCCL enqueues a CUDA kernel on the device
stream; that kernel manages point-to-point NVLink transfers between peers, performs the partial reductions on-
chip, and writes the final result back intotensorin place on every rank-all without the CPU being involved in


```
11.3 The Software Stack
```
the data movement.
The second role oftorch.distributedis backend portability. The same collective API acceptsbackend="gloo"
to run on CPU using Ethernet, orbackend="mpi"for MPI-based clusters. For debugging on a laptop, switch-
ing togloolets you verify correctness of your distributed logic without needing a GPU. Performance will be
dramatically lower, but logical correctness transfers cleanly.
_The contract is: NCCL owns topology-aware routing and kernel eﬀiciency; torch.distributed owns the
Python API and backend portability-you operate at the torch.distributed level and trust NCCL to saturate your
NVLink bandwidth._
The alternative to this stack-manual point-to-point sends and receives through a general-purpose network
library-requires every programmer to reason about reduction trees, ring topologies, and hardware-specific band-
width asymmetries. NCCL abstracts all of that. Its topology-aware ring-allreduce or recursive halving-doubling
schedules extract close to peak NVLink bandwidth without requiring the caller to know whether the GPUs are
on the same NVLink switch or spread across two nodes.
The key trade-off thattorch.distributedmakes is that it couples correctness to strict collective-call
symmetry. Every rank in the process group must execute the same collective operations in the same order. If
one rank diverges-say, a conditional branch that skips anall_reduceon rank 3 while ranks 0-2 are waiting-
all the other ranks block indefinitely. This synchronous-collective model simplifies reasoning about gradient
consistency but is an operational hazard: a one-line Python exception on a single rank will hang the entire job.
Before NVLink-based stacks existed, multi-GPU communication had to stage data through host memory,
copy it across PCIe to the CPU, retransmit over Ethernet to another node’s CPU, copy back over PCIe, and finally
land it on the target GPU. NCCL on NVLink-equipped nodes eliminates every intermediate hop for intra-node
communication. The bandwidth difference is roughly an order of magnitude: PCIe gen 4 delivers64 GB/s
bidirectional per slot; H100 NVLink 4 delivers900 GB/s aggregate across all 18 links.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a data-parallel training job: 4 H100s on one node, each holding a copy of a model whose gradient
tensor is 400 MB (100 million float32 parameters, 100  106 4 = 400MB). After the backward pass, each
rank calls:

dist.all_reduce(grad_tensor, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)

Step 1: NCCL selects a ring-allreduce schedule over 4 ranks. In a ring-allreduce, the operation proceeds in two
phases-reduce-scatter then all-gather-each requiring(N1)steps of message passing around the ring.
Step 2: Bytes transferred per rank. Each rank sends and receives data equal to:

```
Ballreduce= 2N^1

whereS= 400MB andN= 4:

```

4

```
The factor of 2 accounts for the reduce-scatter phase (data flows in) and the all-gather phase (result flows out).
Step 3: Expected wall-clock time at effective NVLink bandwidth of 300 GB/s (a realistic single-link utilization
on a 4-GPU node, not the full 900 GB/s aggregate):

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always usencclfor GPU training; useglooonly for CPU debugging. glooover Ethernet is 10-50
slower thanncclover NVLink and will make your job communication-bound even at small scale. Never
accidentally shipglooto a GPU cluster.
Treat collective calls as global barriers. Every rank must call the same collective in the same order.
Structure your code so conditionals never cause a rank to skip or add a collective. A common bug:
wrapping a loggingall_gatherinsideif rank == 0on only one rank-this will hang the job.
Useasync_op=Trueto overlap communication with computation. dist.all_reduce(tensor,
async_op=True)returns a handle immediately; the CPU can dispatch the next backward layer while
NCCL drains the previous gradient bucket over the wire. DDP’s gradient bucketing relies on exactly this
pattern.
SetNCCL_DEBUG=INFOwhen diagnosing hangs or low bandwidth. NCCL will log its topology discov-
ery, selected algorithm, and ring schedule. If you see NCCL picking a PCIe path instead of NVLink, the
GPU placement on the node is wrong.
For cross-node jobs, InfiniBand backend matters as much as NVLink. NCCL supports GPUDirect
RDMA to write directly from GPU memory to InfiniBand without staging through host RAM. Without it,
cross-node bandwidth drops by 2-3. Verify RDMA is enabled withnccl_p2p_disable=0and confirm
withNCCL_DEBUG=TRACE.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through what happens when your training loop callsdist.all_reduce()on a gradient
tensor.” A strong answer traces the path: Python API!torch.distributed nccl shim!NCCL enqueues
a CUDA kernel!GPU executes ring-allreduce over NVLink!result written back in-place on all ranks.
Mention that the CPU is not in the data path after kernel launch.
“Why might you chooseglooovernccl?” The one valid reason: running on CPU, typically for debug-
ging or CI environments without GPUs. On a GPU node,gloois never the right production choice.
“If rank 2 throws a Python exception mid-training, what happens to the other 7 ranks?” They hang
at the next collective call waiting for rank 2 to arrive. Recovery requires catching the exception on rank 2,
broadcasting an error signal to all ranks, and having everyone calldist.destroy_process_group()
cleanly-or just letting the job manager detect the dead process and restart.
Senior follow-up: “How does DDP overlap gradient communication with the backward pass, and
what are the limits of that overlap?” DDP partitions parameters into buckets (default 25 MB). When
the backward hook fires for the last parameter in a bucket, it immediately launches an asyncall_reduce
for that bucket while the backward pass continues computing earlier-layer gradients. The limit: the first
bucket’s allreduce must complete before the optimizer step, so the final bucket on the critical path is not
overlapped. For very large models with few parameters per layer, buckets serialize and overlap collapses.
```

Tensor data never flows through the rendezvous channel;init_process_groupis only coordination.
All payload moves GPU-to-GPU via NCCL kernels on NVLink or InfiniBand.
Every rank must execute identical collectives in identical order; a single rank skipping one collective
hangs the entire job.
Useasync_op=Trueto overlap gradient communication with backward computation; this is the founda-
tion of DDP’s gradient bucketing.
On H100 NVLink 4, expect250-300 GB/s effective allreduce bandwidth per rank for large tensors;

**11.3.2 Benchmarking Bandwidth in Practice**
When an interviewer asks “how long will the gradient allreduce take for a 70B model?” they are really
asking two questions at once: do you know the formula for bytes transferred, and do you know that your answer
is only meaningful if you have validated it with a real measurement? I have seen senior engineers confidently
quote NVLink’s theoretical 900 GB/s peak in response to this question-and have that answer immediately under-
mined when the interviewer asks why production jobs run at 30% of that number. Knowing how to benchmark
collective bandwidth correctly, and knowing what causes the gap between peak and achieved, is a genuine dif-
ferentiator at the staff level.
Measuring collective bandwidth requires getting three things right: the timing methodology, the synchro-
nization model, and the byte-count formula. Each is independently easy to get wrong.
**Timing.** GPU operations are asynchronous from the CPU. When you calldist.all_reduce()and im-
mediately readtime.time(), you are measuring the time to _submit_ the kernel, not to _complete_ it. The correct
idiom is:

torch.cuda.synchronize()
dist.barrier()
t0 = time.time()
dist.all_reduce(tensor, op=dist.ReduceOp.SUM)
torch.cuda.synchronize()
dist.barrier()
t1 = time.time()
elapsed = t1 - t0

torch.cuda.synchronize()blocks the CPU until all pending CUDA kernels on the current device have
completed.dist.barrier()ensures all ranks have reached the same point before the clock starts and after it
stops, so you are measuring the slowest rank’s time-which is the correct quantity for a collective that requires
all participants.
**Warm-up.** The first execution of an NCCL kernel involves just-in-time compilation, peer-to-peer con-
nection setup, and CUDA context initialization. Run at least one-preferably three-warm-up iterations before
recording any timing. Otherwise your first measurement is dominated by one-time overhead that will never
appear again in steady-state training.

_Effective bandwidth is the agreed-upon convention for comparing hardware utilization across configura-

The alternative-trusting spec sheets-fails for two reasons. First, NVLink’s 900 GB/s aggregate is the sum
across all 18 links on an H100; any single rank-to-rank transfer uses a subset. Second, real workloads suffer from
contention, buffer setup latency, and algorithmic overhead (e.g., ring-allreduce is not embarrassingly parallel).
Benchmarking gives you the actual operating point. When the measured bandwidth is dramatically below peak,
you have actionable information: check NCCL topology selection (NCCL_DEBUG=INFO), verify NVLink vs PCIe
path, test different tensor sizes to identify the knee in the bandwidth curve.
The explicit warm-up requirement mirrors everything we know about GPU performance measurement
from single-device profiling: the first kernel launch is never representative. The same principle that demands
warm-up fortorch.compileor FlashAttention applies here.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always warm up at least 3 iterations before recording. One warm-up is often not enough if NCCL
needs to establish peer connections on first use. Three iterations is conservative but reliable.
Apply bothtorch.cuda.synchronize()anddist.barrier()around your timer. Synchronize
alone measures your own rank’s completion; barrier ensures you capture the slowest rank, which deter-
mines real step time.
Sweep tensor sizes across 1 MB to 10 GB. NCCL has a latency-dominated regime (small tensors, typ-
ically below1 MB) and a bandwidth-dominated regime. The knee is usually between 10-100 MB.
Gradient tensors from large models land firmly in the bandwidth-dominated regime.
Do not assume reduce-scatter and allreduce achieve the same bandwidth. As the worked example
shows, the ratio can be 4in favor of allreduce due to in-network compute. If your FSDP or ZeRO plan
hinges on reduce-scatter bandwidth, measure it directly.
Cross-node bandwidth is typically 5-10  lower than intra-node NVLink. An 8-GPU node connected
to another 8-GPU node via InfiniBand HDR (200 Gb/s,25 GB/s) has a cross-node bottleneck that
is 36narrower than NVLink per node. Parallelism strategies must respect this asymmetry: pipeline
parallelism across nodes, tensor parallelism within nodes.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Estimate how long the gradient sync takes for a 70B parameter model in bf16 across 8 H100s.”

At 250 GB/s effective bandwidth: 1 second. A strong answer gives the formula, plugs in realistic

pass-so raw sync time overstates the wall-clock cost.
“Why do you need to calltorch.cuda.synchronize()before stopping the timer?” Because CUDA
kernel dispatch is asynchronous; the CPU returns fromdist.all_reduce()before the GPU has fin-
ished. Without synchronize, you measure submission latency (μs), not transfer time (ms).
“You benchmarked allreduce and got 100 GB/s on a 4-GPU H100 node. NVLink peak is 900
GB/s. What do you check?” First, confirm NCCL is using NVLink and not falling back to PCIe
(NCCL_DEBUG=INFO). Second, check tensor size-below10 MB, latency dominates and bandwidth ap-
pears low. Third, verify warm-up was done and synchronization is correct. Fourth, check whether SHARP
in-network compute is enabled, which can boost allreduce specifically.
Senior follow-up: “How would you benchmark whether your pipeline-parallel job is compute-bound
or communication-bound across nodes?” Instrument both the forward/backward compute time per
microbatch and the inter-node send/recv latency. Compute is bound if the GPU utilization on inter-
mediate ranks stays near 100% while the first and last ranks are idle. Communication is bound if you
see the pipeline bubble shrink when you reduce the tensor size sent between stages. Concretely: add
torch.cuda.Eventtimers bracketing the compute and send/recv separately, record them on each rank,
and aggregate across steps.

## Chapter 12 Parallelism Strategies

### 12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO.

**12.1.1 Naive DDP and Its Memory Blow-Up**
Data parallelism is the first strategy any interviewer reaches for when probing multi-GPU training, and the
expected answer at the mid-level is straightforward: split the batch, sync the gradients, repeat. What separates a
strong answer from a mediocre one is the memory accounting. Candidates who cannot explain why naive DDP
requires 16 bytes per parameter-and why that number dwarfs the model weights themselves-have not thought se-
riously about scaling. This topic surfaces in every distributed training conversation, and the memory breakdown
is the part that gets people.
Distributed Data Parallel training is a parallelization of minibatch gradient descent along the batch dimen-
sion. Given a global batch of sizeBandMGPU workers, each worker receivesB/Mexamples, computes a
local gradient, and then synchronizes with every other worker before the optimizer step. The parameter update
rule is unchanged:

```
θt+1=θt η
B
```
#### XB

```

```
```

```
The synchronization step is an _AllReduce_ over the gradient vectors. Each worker holds a locally computed partial
sumgk = B/M^1

#### P

i∈shardkriℓ, and AllReduce produces the global average on every worker simultaneously.
Ring-AllReduce, the standard implementation, moves a total of 2 jθjbytes across the network per step (each
element travels around the ring once in the scatter phase and once in the gather phase).
The memory concern is where the analysis becomes uncomfortable. In BF16 training, the naive accounting
goes:

```
Component Dtype Bytes/param
Model weights BF16 2
Gradients BF16 2
Master weights (FP32) FP32 4
Adam first moment (m) FP32 4
Adam second moment (v) FP32 4
Total 16
```
Every GPU in a naive DDP run carries all 16 bytes per parameter. Adding more GPUs does not reduce this
burden; it just means more machines each pinning 16the parameter count in HBM.
_In naive DDP, the optimizer states-not the model weights-are the dominant memory cost, and they do not
shrink as you add more GPUs._
On the compute side, DDP scales well. Each GPU processesB/Mindependent examples, and as long as
the micro-batch is large enough to saturate the tensor cores, adding more GPUs gives near-linear throughput
scaling. The AllReduce cost is 2 jθjbytes per step, but this is paid once per batch regardless ofMin the ring
implementation, so larger batches amortize it effectively.
The memory side tells the opposite story. Every worker is a full replica: parameters, gradients, master
weights, and both Adam moments are each copiedMtimes across the cluster. Total cluster memory grows


```
12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO
```
as 16 jθjM-linear inMbut with no improvement per device. Contrast this with the ideal: if memory scaled
inversely withM, a cluster twice as large would need half the per-GPU memory. Naive DDP never achieves
that.
The practical implication is that batch size becomes the lever that makes DDP viable. Large batches mean
the AllReduce overhead is small relative to useful compute, and they improve GPU utilization. But batch size is
a resource with diminishing returns: beyond what researchers call the _critical batch size_ , increasingBreduces
gradient noise without meaningfully accelerating convergence, because the training is no longer noise-limited
but step-count-limited. Naive DDP therefore hits a wall: it cannot scale memory, and the batch size resource
needed to keep it efficient is finite.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7.5 billion parameter model trained on a cluster of 64 A100 80 GB GPUs with the AdamW
optimizer in BF16 mixed precision.
**Memory per GPU under naive DDP:**
7. 5  109 params 16 bytes/param= 120GB per GPU

An A100 has 80 GB of HBM. This does not fit. Even ignoring activations (which add another10-30 GB
depending on batch size and sequence length), the model state alone exceeds the device by 50%.
**Communication per step:**
The AllReduce moves 2 jθjbytes. With BF16 gradients:
2  7. 5  109  2 bytes= 30GB

Over an NVLink-connected 8-GPU node (effective bisection bandwidth600 GB/s aggregate), a single AllRe-
duce on gradients takes roughly 50 ms. Over InfiniBand at200 GB/s, the same exchange takes150 ms-longer
than a typical forward-backward pass on a short sequence. Without large batch sizes to hide that latency, DDP
over slow interconnects is communication-bound.
**Breakdown of the 120 GB:**
Model weights (BF16): 15 GB
Gradients (BF16): 15 GB
Master weights (FP32): 30 GB
Adamm(FP32): 30 GB
Adamv(FP32): 30 GB
The optimizer states (master weights + moments) account for 90 GB out of 120 GB-75% of the total. This
is the observation that motivates ZeRO: most of the per-GPU memory is redundant replication of optimizer state
that only one GPU needs at a time.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use naive DDP when the model fits. If 16 jθj<HBM with headroom for activations, naive DDP is the
simplest path. For a 1B parameter model on A100 80 GB, the model state is 16 GB-fine. For anything
above roughly 4-5B parameters on 80 GB devices, you are already tight before counting activations.
AllReduce bandwidth determines your minimum batch size. The rule of thumb: the compute time
for one step should be at least 2-3the AllReduce time. If you cannot achieve that with your hardware
```

```
12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO
```
```
bandwidth and model size, DDP over slow links will be communication-bound no matter how many GPUs
you add.
Gradients dominate peak memory mid-backward. The peak memory during a training step occurs
partway through the backward pass, when accumulated gradients and surviving activations overlap. Pro-
filing this rather than just the steady-state model size reveals the true memory ceiling.
The critical batch size is model- and task-dependent, typically 105 - 106 tokens. OpenAI’s batch size
scaling analysis showed that past the critical batch size, each additional example contributes negligibly to
gradient signal. If your global batch already saturates this threshold, adding more data-parallel workers
buys compute but wastes gradient diversity.
Gradient accumulation is not free. Accumulating gradients over multiple micro-batches to simulate a
larger effective batch does not reduce peak gradient memory-each micro-batch’s gradients still accumulate
into a full-size gradient tensor. It reduces communication frequency but not per-step memory overhead.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how DDP works and what its limitations are.” A strong answer covers: batch
splitting, local forward-backward, AllReduce cost ( 2 jθj), and the memory accounting that gives 16 bytes
per parameter. The limitation is that memory does not scale with GPU count.
“You have a 13B parameter model and 8  A100 80 GB GPUs. Can you train it with naive DDP?”
Calculate: 13  109 16 = 208GB per GPU. No. Even before activations this is 2. 6 over budget. The
answer should then pivot to what you would do instead (ZeRO stage 3 / FSDP).
“Why does Adam make memory worse than SGD?” SGD requires parameters + gradients = 4 bytes/-
param (BF16). Adam adds first moment (4 bytes FP32) + second moment (4 bytes FP32) + master weights
(4 bytes FP32) = 12 additional bytes. Total becomes 16 vs. 4-a 4 blow-up attributable entirely to the
optimizer.
Senior follow-up: “At what point does the AllReduce become the bottleneck, and how would you
restructure training to hide it?” The senior answer identifies the compute-to-communication ratio:
when one forward-backward pass takes less time than the AllReduce, you are communication-bound.
Remedies include gradient compression (lossy, hurts convergence), asynchronous SGD (staleness issues),
or switching to a ZeRO stage that interleaves communication with computation layer by layer-which is
exactly what ZeRO Stage 2 does.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Naive DDP uses 16 bytes per parameter: 2 for weights, 2 for gradients, and 12 for Adam optimizer state
(FP32 master weights, first moment, second moment).
AllReduce moves 2 jθjbytes per step regardless of the number of workers in a ring implementation.
Memory does not scale with GPU count in naive DDP-every device carries the full 16 bytes per parameter.
Optimizer states (master weights + Adam moments) account for roughly 75% of per-GPU memory in
mixed-precision training.
Batch size is a finite resource: past the critical batch size ( 105 - 106 tokens for most LLMs), adding
data-parallel workers does not improve sample efficiency.
```

```
12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO
```
**12.1.2 ZeRO Stages 1, 2, and 3 (FSDP)**
The moment you see that 75% of a DDP node’s memory is optimizer state that every GPU duplicates
identically, the fix becomes obvious: shard it. ZeRO-the Zero Redundancy Optimizer-is that fix, structured into
three progressive stages that trade implementation complexity for decreasing per-device memory. Interview-
ers at AI labs ask about ZeRO not because it is obscure, but because understanding it requires you to reason
simultaneously about collective communication primitives, memory layout, and backward-pass scheduling. If
you can explain all three stages and the identity that makes Stage 1 cost-free, you have demonstrated the kind of
systems fluency the job requires.
ZeRO begins with one algebraic observation: AllReduce is equivalent to ReduceScatter followed by All-
Gather.
In a ring-AllReduce overMworkers, each element of the gradient travels around the ring in a scatter phase
(each worker accumulates 1 /Mof the total) and then in a gather phase (each worker distributes its accumulated
slice to every other). The total data movement is 2 jθjbytes. ReduceScatter alone movesjθjbytes and leaves
workerkholding the fully reduced sum for thek-th shard. AllGather moves anotherjθjbytes to propagate those
shards everywhere. The bandwidth budget is identical, but the intermediate state after ReduceScatter-where
each worker holds only 1 /Mof the gradients in reduced form-is the hook ZeRO exploits.
**Stage 1 (optimizer state sharding).** After the forward and backward passes, every worker has a full
gradient vector. A ReduceScatter distributes the summed gradients so that workerkholds the reduced gradient
for parameter shardk. Each worker then applies the Adam update to its own shard using the optimizer state it
owns locally (first moment, second moment, master weights). An AllGather propagates the updated parameters
to all workers. The result is a complete synchronized parameter vector on every device, achieved with the same
2 jθjcommunication as naive DDP-but optimizer state is divided byM.
**Stage 2 (gradient sharding).** The problem with Stage 1 is that the full gradient vector must be material-
ized before ReduceScatter. For large models this is still a memory spike. Stage 2 eliminates it by issuing the
reduce operation layer by layer during the backward pass: as soon as the gradient for a layer is computed, it is
immediately reduced to the responsible worker and freed on all others. Peak gradient memory becomesjθj/M
rather thanjθj.
**Stage 3 (parameter sharding / FSDP).** Stages 1 and 2 still replicate the parameters on every GPU. Stage 3
shards the parameters themselves: each worker owns 1 /Mof the model weights at rest. During the forward pass,
the worker gathers the parameters it needs for each layer (AllGather), computes the layer, then immediately frees
the gathered weights. During the backward pass, the same AllGather-compute-free pattern applies, followed by a
ReduceScatter on gradients. PyTorch’sFullyShardedDataParallel(FSDP) is a production implementation
of Stage 3.
_ZeRO Stage 1 is algebraically free relative to naive DDP; Stages 2 and 3 pay modest overhead in exchange
for memory that scales inversely with the number of workers._
The key insight is that the optimizer update is embarrassingly parallel across parameter shards. Workerk
does not need workers 0... k 1 ork+1... M 1 to be finished with their Adam steps in order to compute its
own. All it needs is the fully reduced gradient for its shard (delivered by ReduceScatter) and its own optimizer
state. This local update is independent, so the communication required to distribute and collect shards matches
exactly what a naive AllReduce would have spent-no extra bandwidth for Stage 1.
Stages 2 and 3 do add overhead. Stage 2 requires synchronizing gradients layer by layer during the back-
ward pass, introducing fine-grained reduce operations that cannot be batched into one large AllReduce. The


```
12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO
```
total bandwidth is still 2 jθjbut the latency profile is less regular. Stage 3 is more expensive: the forward pass
AllGathers add anotherjθjbytes, pushing total communication to 3 jθj. In return, per-device memory drops to
roughly 16 jθj/Mfor model state, making it possible to fit models that would be impossible otherwise.
Compared to naive DDP, Stage 3 sacrifices 50% more network bandwidth to achieve memory that scales
linearly with the number of GPUs-a compelling trade whenever memory is the binding constraint.

**ZeRO Stage 3 (FSDP)** shards everything:

**Overlapping communication and computation in FSDP:**
FSDP achieves acceptable efficiency by prefetching. While GPUkis computing layerl’s forward pass, the

compute time-a condition that holds on NVLink-connected intra-node workers but can fail on slow inter-node

Prefer Stage 2 over Stage 3 when the model fits. Stage 2 keeps parameters on every device, which means
each layer’s forward pass requires no AllGather. The per-layer gradient reductions add overhead, but it
is a small constant penalty. Stage 3 addsjθjbytes of network traffic per step and introduces AllGather
bubbles in every layer. Use Stage 3 only when the model state does not fit even with Stage 2.

12.1 Data Parallelism and ZeRO
```
```
Stage 3 (FSDP) requires fast intra-node interconnects. The AllGather per layer is latency-sensitive.
On NVLink (600 GB/s aggregate across 8 GPUs on an H100 node), the overhead is acceptable. Across
InfiniBand (200 GB/s), prefetching can fail to fully hide the gather latency, and GPU utilization drops.
The practical rule: use FSDP within a node, and consider pipeline or tensor parallelism for cross-node
sharding of very large models.
Activation memory is not reduced by any ZeRO stage. ZeRO 1, 2, and 3 operate on model state.
The activation memory footprint-which scales asO(sbdL)for sequence lengths, batch sizeb,
hidden dimensiond, and layersL-remains fully replicated on each data-parallel worker. For long-context
training or very large hidden dimensions, activation recomputation (gradient checkpointing) or sequence
parallelism is necessary on top of ZeRO.
Gradient accumulation interacts with Stage 2. With Stage 2, per-layer gradient reductions happen
during the backward pass. If you accumulate gradients over multiple micro-batches before applying the
optimizer, you must ensure that the per-layer reduces are deferred to the end of the accumulation window-
otherwise you reduce partial gradients prematurely. PyTorch FSDP handles this with ano_sync()context
manager that suppresses gradient synchronization during accumulation steps.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Explain ZeRO Stage 1 and why it doesn’t cost more bandwidth than naive DDP.” The answer turns
on the AllReduce decomposition: ReduceScatter (jθjbytes) delivers per-shard reduced gradients; each
worker runs its Adam update locally; AllGather (jθjbytes) redistributes updated parameters. Total: 2 jθj-
same as a ring-AllReduce. The insight is that the optimizer step fits cleanly between the two halves of the
AllReduce without adding communication.
“What is FSDP and when would you use it instead of DDP?” FSDP is ZeRO Stage 3: parameters,
gradients, and optimizer state are all sharded. Use it when the model state ( 16 jθjbytes) exceeds available
HBM even after stages 1 and 2. The cost is 3 network utilization versus 2 for DDP and potential
compute bubbles if AllGather latency is not hidden by prefetching.
“Does ZeRO reduce activation memory?” No. ZeRO only shards model state (parameters, gradients,
optimizer state). Activations are local to each data-parallel worker and scale with batch size and sequence
length. The interviewer is probing whether you conflate model state with activation memory-a common
mistake.
Senior follow-up: “At 1024 GPUs, would you use FSDP alone or combine it with tensor parallelism?
Why?” The senior answer is: combine them. FSDP over 1024 GPUs means every AllGather for a layer’s
parameters crosses the full cluster, which at inter-node InfiniBand speeds is brutally slow. Instead, apply
tensor parallelism within each 8-GPU node (using NVLink) and FSDP or pipeline parallelism across
nodes (using InfiniBand). This matches the communication pattern to the available bandwidth at each
level of the hierarchy-a principle that underpins every practical large-scale training configuration.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
AllReduce=ReduceScatter+AllGather; this identity is why ZeRO Stage 1 adds zero communication
overhead relative to naive DDP.
Stage 1 shards optimizer state (M); Stage 2 additionally shards gradients; Stage 3 (FSDP) shards ev-
erything including parameters, reducing per-device model state to 16 jθj/M.
```

```
FSDP increases total communication from 2 jθjto 3 jθjper step; it masks this overhead by prefetching
parameter AllGathers while the previous layer computes.
ZeRO does not reduce activation memory; gradient checkpointing and sequence parallelism handle that
separately.
The practical rule: use Stage 1 unconditionally, Stage 2 when gradients pressure memory, Stage 3 only
when the model itself does not fit-and pair Stage 3 with tensor parallelism on fast intra-node links rather
than running it flat across the whole cluster.
