**12.2.1 Tensor Parallelism (Megatron-Style)**
When a model’s weight matrices individually exceed a single GPU’s HBM-and ZeRO-style sharding is not
enough because gathering those weights per layer costs too much bandwidth-you need to split the matrix multi-
plications themselves across GPUs. Tensor parallelism does exactly this. It shows up at senior-level interviews
the moment the conversation turns to training 70B or larger models on a single node, and the question that sep-
arates candidates is whether they can name the two synchronization points per transformer layer, explain why
the column-parallel/row-parallel split requires no communication at the first projection, and give the bandwidth
rule that caps tensor parallel degree at eight GPUs.
The foundation is that matrix-multiply outputs are sums of partial products, and those partial products can
live on different devices. Consider the dense MLP block:Y =Dropout(GeLU(XA)B), whereX 2 Rs×h,

Unlike data parallelism, tensor parallelism does not consume batch size. Every tensor-parallel GPU pro-

global batch size is already at or near its optimal value.
Unlike pipeline parallelism, tensor parallelism introduces no pipeline bubble. AlltGPUs execute every
layer in lockstep, just on different parameter shards. There is no stage sequencing, no micro-batch scheduling,

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

Cap tensor parallel degree at 8 (or the NVLink-connected GPU count for your node). Beyond that,

```
```
Tensor parallelism does not consume batch size. This distinguishes it from data parallelism and pipeline
parallelism, both of which require large batches to hide their respective overheads. If your global batch
size is already at the critical batch size threshold and you cannot increase it, tensor parallelism is the
correct memory-scaling tool.
Pair with sequence parallelism to eliminate the residual activation memory. Tensor parallelism leaves
LayerNorm and Dropout unsharded-they operate on the fullsbhactivation. Sequence parallelism
distributes these operations along the sequence dimension and replaces the MLP/attention AllReduce
with AllGather and ReduceScatter pairs of equal total cost. The combination reduces the non-matmul
activation memory by a factor oft.
Do not extend tensor parallelism cross-node to compensate for a model that is too wide. If TP-8
within a node cannot fit the model, the answer is to combine TP-8 intra-node with pipeline parallelism
inter-node-not to stretch tensor parallelism across InfiniBand. The activation AllReduce pattern of tensor
parallelism is uniquely hostile to high-latency links.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you fit a 70B model on a single 8  H100 node?” Use tensor parallelism witht= 8:

“Why is tensor parallel degree capped at 8 in most production systems?” Beyond 8 GPUs on a
standard NVIDIA node, AllReduces cross InfiniBand. For a 70B model with batch 32, sequence 2048,
each AllReduce is 1.87 GB; at 25 GB/s InfiniBand that is 75 ms versus 31 ms of compute-the GPU stalls
more than it runs. Empirically: 10-12% overhead at degree 8 (intra-node NVLink), 42% at degree 16,
65% at degree 32.
“What determines the AllReduce size in tensor parallelism?” The output activation of each projection:
sbhelements per layer, not the weight matrix size. This is why tensor parallelism traffic scales with
sequence length and batch size, not with model depth.
Senior follow-up: “If you had to scale to 1024 GPUs for a single model, how would you combine
tensor parallelism with other strategies?” Apply TP-8 within each 8-GPU NVLink node, consuming
the fast intra-node bandwidth for the activation AllReduces. Then apply pipeline parallelism across nodes
to extend model depth coverage, with InfiniBand carrying only the small activation handoffs between
pipeline stages. Data parallelism handles the remaining parallelism once the model fits. Never extend TP
beyond the NVLink boundary. The senior insight is that each interconnect tier dictates which parallelism
strategy uses it.
```

Tensor parallelism splits weight matrices width-wise: column-parallel for the first projection (input is
replicated; no upfront communication), row-parallel for the second projection (partial sums merged by
one AllReduce).
Cost is two AllReduces per transformer layer (forward and backward), each of sizesbhactivations-

**12.2.2 Pipeline Parallelism and Bubble Reduction**
Pipeline parallelism becomes necessary when a model is too large to fit even after slicing all weight matrices
across the GPUs within a node using tensor parallelism, or when you must extend to a second node and cannot
afford tensor parallelism’s AllReduce traffic over InfiniBand. Rather than splitting matrices width-wise, pipeline
parallelism cuts the network depth-wise: each device owns a contiguous group of layers and passes activations
forward to the next stage in sequence. Every serious interview on large-scale training eventually asks about
the pipeline bubble, and the answer that separates mid-level from senior is knowing the formula, knowing how
to suppress the bubble with micro-batches, and knowing why zero-bubble scheduling is hard enough that two
people at a frontier lab may be the only ones who understand their own implementation.
PartitionLtransformer layers intopequal _pipeline stages_ , each assigned to one device. Device 0 runs layers
0... L/p 1 ; device 1 runs layersL/p... 2 L/p 1 ; and so on. The forward pass is strictly sequential: device
0 finishes its layers for one micro-batch, sends the output activations to device 1 via a point-to-point send, then
immediately begins the next micro-batch. The backward pass flows in reverse-gradients of activations travel
from devicep 1 back to device 0.
The _pipeline bubble_ is the idle time that arises during startup and teardown. In the startup phase, devices
1... p 1 are idle while device 0 processes the first micro-batch. In the teardown phase, device 0 is idle while
devicep 1 finishes. The ratio of wasted time to useful time is:

bubble fraction=

wheremis the number of micro-batches that partition the global batch. Withp= 8stages andm= 1, the
bubble fraction is 7-seven eighths of the wall-clock step is wasted. Withp = 8andm = 32, it drops to
7 / 32 22%-still significant but workable.
The standard production schedule is **1F1B** (one-forward-one-backward): each device interleaves one for-
ward micro-batch with one backward micro-batch. This keeps the number of live activation tensors bounded at
pregardless ofm, preventing activation memory from growing linearly with the micro-batch count.
_Pipeline parallelism tiles the model across depth; the bubble fraction_ (p1)/m _is the price, and micro-
batch count is the only handle that reduces it without adding complexity._
The decisive advantage over tensor parallelism is communication volume. Tensor parallelism AllReduces
the full activation tensor at every layer boundary-proportional tosbhper layer per direction. Pipeline
parallelism transmits activations only at stage transitions: a single point-to-point send of sizesμbμhper
micro-batch, wherebμis the micro-batch size. For a large model with small micro-batches this is one to two
orders of magnitude less inter-device traffic per step, and critically, this communication is a one-time handoff-not
repeated per layer.
This makes pipeline parallelism viable over InfiniBand where tensor parallelism fails. A 201 MB activation
handoff at 25 GB/s takes about 8 ms. A single pipeline stage’s compute for a 175B model takes hundreds of
milliseconds. The communication cost is well under 5% of compute time, compared to tensor parallelism’s

they shard model state but leave activations fully on each data-parallel worker. For long-sequence training where

Zero-bubble scheduling (DualPipe) fills bubble slots with weight-gradient work. The standard back-
ward pass has two independent phases: computing activation gradients (B, which is a serial dependency-
earlier layers need it before they can proceed) and computing weight gradients (W, which has no serial
dependency and can run any time after the corresponding forward pass). By deferringWcomputations
into the idle bubble slots, you approach 100% GPU utilization. DeepSeek-V3 uses a variant of this called
DualPipe in production. The catch: interposing on autograd to separate theBandWphases requires
custom gradient hooks, a scheduling queue forWoperations, and careful management of intermediate
activations that must be kept alive between theBandWsteps. The anecdote I keep hearing from en-

switch) can cost 30+ ms. Design stages so that each stage lives entirely within one node, and the handoffs
stay on the lowest-latency inter-node link available.
Batch size is a shared resource between data parallelism and pipeline parallelism. If you run 8-way

Prefer FSDP over pipeline parallelism whenever the model fits. FSDP is far simpler to implement,
has no bubble, and is architecture-agnostic. Pipeline parallelism is the right answer only when (a) the
model cannot fit per-node even with FSDP and TP-8, or (b) inter-node bandwidth is too low for FSDP’s

### 12.3 Activation and Sequence Parallelism

**12.3.1 Sequence Parallelism for LayerNorm and Dropout**
After you’ve walked an interviewer through Megatron-style tensor parallelism-column-parallel first projec-
tion, row-parallel second projection, one AllReduce per layer boundary-the senior follow-up is almost always:
“Those AllReduces shard the matmul outputs across GPUs. But what about LayerNorm and Dropout? Those
operators see the full activation, right?” Most candidates who prepped TP can’t answer this without hesitation.
The unsharded pointwise operations are the hole in the tensor-parallel memory story, and at sequence lengths
above 4096 they can consume more HBM than the weight matrices you just worked so hard to shard. Sequence
parallelism, introduced alongside the Megatron-LM tensor-parallel formulation, closes the gap at exactly zero
additional bandwidth cost.
LayerNorm and Dropout are embarrassingly parallel along the sequence dimension. Each position normal-
izes independently of every other position; Dropout applies a per-element mask with no cross-position depen-
dency. This means we can partition thes-length sequence across the samettensor-parallel GPUs and run these
pointwise ops on ans/t-token slice, exactly as if we had cut the batch into micro-batches but along the sequence
axis instead.
The wrinkle is that the column-parallel matmul that follows each LayerNorm needs the full-sequence ac-
tivation on every GPU. The synchronization point must therefore change. Standard tensor parallelism issues
a single AllReduce after the row-parallel matmul to merge partial sums and replicate the result everywhere.
Sequence parallelism replaces this with a two-part operation:

1. **ReduceScatter** after the row-parallel matmul: partial sums are reduced across the group, and the result
    is _scattered_ so that GPUkholds the fully-reduced rows for sequence positions[ks/t,(k+ 1)s/t). No
    other GPU holds those rows.
2. LayerNorm, Dropout, and any other pointwise op run on the locals/t-token slice.
3. **AllGather** before the next column-parallel matmul: each GPU’s slice is concatenated so that every GPU
    sees the fulls-length sequence for the subsequent projection.
By the identity AllReduceReduceScatter+AllGather in the bandwidth-limited regime, the total bytes
transferred are unchanged. The ReduceScatter ships the same data as the first half of an AllReduce ring; the
AllGather ships the same data as the second half. Sequence parallelism is literally a rearrangement of when the
data moves, not an addition of new communication. The only change visible in the memory profile is that the
activation tensor between the ReduceScatter and the AllGather has shape(s/t)bhinstead ofsbh-a
factor-of-treduction for every byte spent on LayerNorm input, LayerNorm output, Dropout, and the residual
add.


```
12.3 Activation and Sequence Parallelism
```
The net activation memory per transformer layer, after applying both tensor parallelism and sequence par-
allelism and using FlashAttention to eliminate the quadratic softmax term, is:

```
Activation memory per layer=sbh^34
t
bytes (BF16)
```
Without sequence parallelism the formula wassbh 34 /t+sbh 10 : the second term, representing LayerNorm,
Dropout, and input embeddings, stayed constant regardless oft. Sequence parallelism removes that stranded
term.
_Sequence parallelism converts the one part of the activation that tensor parallelism could not touch into a
term that scales with_ t _-at zero bandwidth cost._
The AllReduce in vanilla tensor parallelism does the work of reduce-and-scatter and then immediately
throws away the scattered structure by copying the result to all GPUs. Sequence parallelism simply stops dis-
carding that structure. The ReduceScatter leaves each GPU holding exactly the rows it needs to run LayerNorm
on its sequence slice; the AllGather restores the full tensor before the next matmul requires it. The data travels
the same physical distance over the same wires; the only difference is how the receive buffer is allocated.
The alternative, running LayerNorm on the full sequence on every GPU and then AllReducing, is what you
get by default with TP but without SP. It is not incorrect-the gradients compute cleanly-but it wastessbh 10
bytes per layer per GPU, regardless of how aggressively you parallelized the weight matrices. For a 13B model
at sequence 4096 andt= 8, that stranded term is over 60 GB of HBM. Sequence parallelism costs nothing to
recover it.
A second advantage is composability. Because TP and SP operate on the same communicator group with
the same degree, adding SP requires no new topology decisions, no new process groups, and no change to the
pipeline or data-parallel configuration. In Megatron-LM, enabling SP is a single flag. Frameworks that expose
TP without SP are leaving memory on the table.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always enable SP whenever you enable TP. There is no scenario where you want tensor parallelism
without sequence parallelism: SP is strictly better for memory and has identical communication cost.
Frameworks that separate the two flags default SP to off; always check.
SP degree equals TP degree-they share a communicator. If TP is 8, SP is 8. They are not independently
configurable, and there is no benefit to mismatching them.
Sequence length must be divisible by t. A 4096-token sequence witht= 8gives exactly 512 tokens per
GPU. If your sequence length is not a multiple oft, pad to the next multiple. Uneven partitions require
masked gather operations and add significant implementation complexity.
The stranded sbh 10 term is the right diagnostic when TP memory savings disappoint. If you
apply TP-8 and memory usage drops by less than 8 , the culprit is almost always the unsharded pointwise
activations. Confirm by enabling SP and measuring again.
After TP+SP+FlashAttention, further memory reduction requires activation recomputation. The
minimum activation footprint issbh 34 /tper layer. Reducing below this floor means discarding and
recomputing activations during the backward pass at a cost of roughly 33% more forward-pass FLOPs.
That trade is often worth it when the alternative is a smaller batch size that hurts data-parallel efficiency.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Tensor parallelism divides your parameter memory by t. Does it also divide your activation mem-
ory by t ?” Strong answer: not entirely. The matmul activations (FFN intermediate, attention projections)
divide byt. The pointwise activations-LayerNorm input and output, Dropout-stay full-size on every GPU
in vanilla TP. Sequence parallelism fixes this by replacing the row-parallel AllReduce with ReduceScatter
+ AllGather; GPUkthen holds onlys/trows through the pointwise ops, and the memory for those layers
divides bytas well. Total communication cost is unchanged.
“Why is sequence parallelism said to be free?” The AllReduce and the ReduceScatter + AllGather
pair are bandwidth-equivalent in the ring-based implementation: both move the same number of bytes
per device. SP rearranges when the scatter happens but does not increase the total data transferred.
Senior follow-up: “Walk me through the exact communication ops for one transformer layer under
TP+SP.” Strong answer: (1) Input arrives ass/trows on each GPU (scattered from the previous layer’s
ReduceScatter). (2) AllGather before the column-parallel QKV or FFN projection: each GPU now holds
the fullshactivation. (3) Column-parallel matmul: each GPU computes its 4 h/tcolumns, no com-
munication. (4) Row-parallel matmul: each GPU holds a partial sum over the fullh-dim output. (5)
ReduceScatter: partial sums merged, GPUkkeeps itss/trows. (6) LayerNorm and Dropout ons/trows.
(7) Residual add with the correspondings/t-row slice held from before step (2). Repeat per layer. Two
collective ops-AllGather and ReduceScatter-per MLP and per attention block, identical total bytes to the
AllReduce they replace.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Tensor parallelism leaves LayerNorm and Dropout unsharded: their per-layer activation cost issbh 10  2
bytes per GPU, independent oft.
```

Sequence parallelism distributes these pointwise ops along the sequence dimension by replacing the TP
AllReduce with ReduceScatter + AllGather-same bandwidth, 1 /tactivation memory for the pointwise
ops.
After TP + SP + FlashAttention, the minimum per-layer activation footprint issbh 34 /tbytes per GPU.
SP degree always equals TP degree; sequence length must be divisible byt.
For a 13B model ats= 4096,b= 4,t= 8, enabling SP recovers 55 GB per GPU-the difference
between fitting comfortably on an H100 and running out of memory before the optimizer state is even

Context parallelism, also called ring attention, distributes the attention computation itself acrosspdevices and
is the last activation-memory tool you need to understand before discussing long-context training at the design-

_Ring attention converts the_ O(s^2 ) _attention memory problem into an_ O(s) _communication problem that is
independent of_ p _, leaving the sequence-length scaling entirely in the network rather than in HBM._
FlashAttention eliminates the fullsssoftmax matrix from SRAM by tiling the key-query computation
in blocks, but it still requires allskeys and values to be reachable from the GPU’s HBM within a single forward
pass. Ats= 128K, the K and V matrices per layer already consume several gigabytes per device, and they
must be replicated for the backward pass. Ring attention removes this requirement: each GPU holdss/pkeys
and values permanently and receives the remaining(p1)/pfraction as a transient stream, one chunk at a time,
overlapping communication with the attention tile computation for the chunk it just received. The peak local
KV footprint is therefores/p, nots.
The alternative-splitting the sequence with sequence parallelism and hoping FlashAttention’s block loop
handles the rest-breaks down because the block loop still iterates over allskey positions. Sequence parallelism
distributes the _query_ dimension but does not distribute the _key-value_ dimension. Ring attention distributes both.
Compared to a naive all-to-all approach where every GPU first AllGathers the full KV and then runs local
FlashAttention, ring attention is strictly more memory-efficient: the all-to-all approach requires each GPU to
hold allskeys in memory simultaneously, defeating the purpose. The ring rotates through chunks that can be
freed as soon as the corresponding attention tile is accumulated.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Enable context parallelism only at s≳ 32 K. Below that threshold, FlashAttention within a TP group
handles the attention memory without the ring-communication overhead. LLaMA-3 used CP only in the
final long-context fine-tuning phase; the main pre-training run did not need it.
Causal attention requires a striped sequence partition. In contiguous partitioning (GPUkholds tokens
[ks/p,(k+1)s/p)), GPUp 1 holds only the last block of tokens, which must attend to all earlier tokens
held by all other GPUs. This creates severe load imbalance: GPU 0 computes a nearly zero attention
matrix (only self-attention, all future tokens masked), while GPUp 1 computes a nearly full triangle.
The standard fix is striped or interleaved partitioning: GPUkholds everyp-th token, distributing causal
load evenly. Stripe partitioning is the default in production ring-attention implementations.
Variable-length batches require padding or sequence packing. Ring attention assumes uniform se-
quence length within the CP group. If sequences vary, pad each to the next multiple ofp, or use sequence
packing with separate attention masks per document. Packing is significantly more complex to implement
correctly and requires masked attention kernels that are aware of document boundaries within the padded
token stream.
CP and TP use separate process groups. Thepring-rotation peers form a CP communicator; thet
tensor-parallel peers form a TP communicator. In LLaMA-3 witht= 8andp= 8, a batch item involves
64 GPUs in combined TPCP parallelism. The two communicators do not interfere, but scheduling their
collective operations without stalling requires careful overlap planning in the training loop.
Allocate two KV buffers per device. At any ring step, a GPU holds its own outgoing KV chunk and the
incoming chunk from its neighbor simultaneously. Ping-pong buffering between two HBM allocations-
one for send, one for receive-is standard. Forgetting this doubles the apparent per-GPU KV overhead in
memory estimates.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you design a training system for 128K context?” Strong answer: within each 8-GPU
NVLink node, apply TP=8 for weight sharding and SP=8 for LayerNorm activation sharding. For the
attention computation, apply CP=8 across the same node group (TP and CP share the NVLink fabric
via separate communicators), rotating KV in a ring while each GPU holds 16K queries and uses online-
softmax tile accumulation. Use pipeline parallelism across nodes for model depth. The CP ring adds
roughly one AllGather-equivalent of communication per attention layer per device, maskable by overlap-
ping ring sends with tile computation.
“Why doesn’t sequence parallelism alone solve the 128K context memory problem?” SP splits the
sequence for LayerNorm and Dropout. Each GPU still needs to iterate over allskeys during FlashAtten-
tion’s tile loop, so the KV tensors must be accessible from every device’s HBM-O(s)per tensor,O(s)per
layer, blowing up ats= 128K. Ring attention extends the sequence split into the attention computation
itself, so no GPU ever holds more thans/pKV positions in its local memory at once.
Senior follow-up: “Why is ring attention mathematically exact?” Strong answer: the online-softmax
accumulator maintains three statistics per attention head: running maximum logitm, running log-sum-
exp denominatorℓ, and weighted output sumO. When a new KV chunk arrives, these three values can be
merged from two partial results using the update equations above, which are associative and commutative
over any partitioning of the key dimension. Ring attention applies this merge protocol overpring steps
```

```
instead of over SRAM tiles; since the same merge rule applies in both cases, the output is bit-identical to
single-GPU full-sequence attention.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Context parallelism (ring attention) distributes the attention computation acrosspGPUs by rotating K
and V through a logical ring while each GPU keeps its own Q shard fixed.
The online-softmax merge rule (from FlashAttention) guarantees mathematical exactness: the accumu-
lated output acrosspring steps is identical to single-GPU attention.
Local KV memory per GPU per layer scales asO(s/p); ring communication cost scales asO(s)bytes
per device-linear, not quadratic.
Causal attention requires a striped (interleaved) sequence partition to avoid severe load imbalance across
ring members.
CP stacks with TP and SP on separate process groups; LLaMA-3 usesp= 8,t= 8, engaging 64 GPUs
in combined attention-and-weight parallelism for a single 128K-token batch item.
```
### 12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism

**12.4.1 Rules of Thumb for Choosing a Mix**
Once you have all the parallelism strategies in hand-tensor, pipeline, data, and sequence-the question that
separates a strong interview answer from a great one is: in what order do you apply them, and why? This
composition question appears at senior and staff-level interviews at frontier labs, typically framed as “walk me
through how you would set up training for a 100B model on a thousand GPUs.” The answer is not a free choice.
It is constrained by hardware topology, model size, and a finite batch-size budget, and those constraints resolve
into a repeatable recipe that practitioners call _3D parallelism_ -tensor, pipeline, and data-optionally extended to
_4D_ by adding sequence or expert parallelism.
The central insight is that different parallelism strategies impose different communication patterns and
tolerate different network bandwidths. A GPU cluster is not a flat network: GPUs within a single machine
communicate via NVLink or NVSwitch at roughly 600 GB/s aggregate per GPU (on H100s), while GPUs on
different machines communicate over InfiniBand at roughly 25-50 GB/s per GPU-an 8-20gap. Applying a
high-bandwidth-hungry strategy across the slower link wastes throughput; the converse is merely suboptimal.
Tensor parallelism requires an all-reduce per transformer layer, carrying activation tensors proportional to
sbh(sequence length, micro-batch size, hidden dimension). At hidden size 8192 and sequence length 4096,
a single all-reduce moves hundreds of megabytes. NVLink saturates this in under a millisecond; InfiniBand
would take tens of milliseconds, dominating compute time entirely. Tensor parallelism must stay inside a single
NVSwitch domain, typically 8 GPUs.
Pipeline parallelism transfers activations point-to-point between consecutive stages-tensors of sizesbh
per stage boundary-and tolerates InfiniBand latency reasonably well. Its cost comes from the pipeline bubble:
the fraction of time GPUs sit idle waiting for earlier stages. The bubble ratio is(p1)/m, wherepis the number
of pipeline stages andmis the number of micro-batches in a step. Largemhides the bubble; smallmwastes
compute.
Data parallelism synchronizes gradients once per training step. With ZeRO stage 1, that is a reduce-scatter
plus an all-gather over the full parameter countP(total cost: 2 Pbytes); with ZeRO stage 3, it is 3 Pbytes spread


```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
across many small operations that can be overlapped with computation. Amortized over a full forward-backward
pass, this communication tolerates slow inter-node links-provided the batch is large enough for compute to
dominate.
The composition follows directly:

1. **Tensor parallelism first** , up to the GPU count per machine (typically 8), exploiting NVLink bandwidth.
2. **Pipeline parallelism or ZeRO-3 (FSDP) second** , across nodes, until the model fits in aggregate GPU
    memory.
3. **Data parallelism third** , across all remaining GPUs, scaling throughput until the batch-size budget is
    exhausted.
Adding a fourth dimension-sequence parallelism (SP), context parallelism (CP), or expert parallelism (EP)-
handles long-context activations or sparse MoE routing within this framework.
_Match the most communication-intensive strategy to the fastest link; let data parallelism absorb the slow
tail of the network hierarchy._
The _batch size as resource_ framing makes the trade-offs concrete. A fixed global batch sizeBis dictated
by optimization stability-the critical batch size beyond which per-step sample efficiency saturates rapidly. Every
parallelism dimension that requires micro-batches competes for that budget.
Pipeline parallelism needsm 4 pmicro-batches to keep the bubble below roughly 20%. Withp= 8
pipeline stages, you needm 32 micro-batches per DP replica per step. If your global batch is 2048 sequences
and DP degree is 64, each replica has 32 sequences-exactly 32 micro-batches of size 1. Increasingpto 16
demandsm 64 , but the batch budget may be exhausted.
Data parallelism has no bubble, but without ZeRO it does not reduce per-GPU parameter memory. Pure
DP on a 100B model requires every GPU to hold the full model; at bf16 that is 200 GB, exceeding any current
GPU’s HBM. ZeRO-3 shards parameters across all DP ranks but adds 3 Pcommunication overhead. For large
DP degree and sufficient compute time per step, this communication is overlapped and affordable.
A useful mental picture from the TPU literature: plot compute efficiency against the ratio of batch size to
GPU count. At low ratios, any strategy is communication-bound. At high ratios, pure data parallelism reaches
the compute-bound regime on its own. The mixed TP + PP + DP regime occupies the middle, where no single
strategy suffices and composition is the only path to high utilization.
Compared to pipeline parallelism, ZeRO-3 (FSDP) offers a simpler trade-off: 3 Pcommunication per step
regardless of model depth, no bubble, but higher parameter communication volume. For models whose batch
budget cannot sustain a large pipeline, ZeRO-3 is almost always the right choice over PP.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 70B dense transformer (h= 8192, 80 layers, 64 attention heads) on 256 H100 80 GB GPUs
arranged as 32 nodes of 8 GPUs each. Target global batch: 2048 sequences of 4096 tokens, bf16 mixed precision.
**Step 1 - Tensor parallelism.** Set TP= 8within each node. Parameter memory per GPU drops from
70 B 2 bytes= 140GB to 140 /8 = 17. 5 GB. The model fits on a single node after TP.
**Step 2 - Pipeline check.** With TP= 8sufficient to fit parameters, pipeline parallelism is not required.
Each 8-GPU node holds one TP-sharded model replica.
**Step 3 - Data parallelism.** With 32 nodes and one model replica per node, DP degreeD= 32. Each
replica processes 2048 /32 = 64sequences per step.
**Step 4 - Optimizer state.** With ZeRO stage 1, first and second moment tensors (fp32, 560 GB total for


```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
the model) are sharded across 32 DP ranks: each rank stores 17. 5 GB of optimizer state. Per-GPU total: 17. 5
(params)+ 17. 5 (optimizer)+ 17. 5 (gradients in bf16) 52. 5 GB-comfortably below 80 GB before activations.
**Step 5 - Gradient sync cost.** After the backward pass, a reduce-scatter plus all-gather over 140 GB of
gradients (DP degree 32) moves 140 / 32  4. 4 GB per rank. At 25 GB/s effective InfiniBand bandwidth, this
completes in 175 ms. A full forward-backward pass for a 70B model at this batch size runs on the order of
200-250 ms on H100s, so gradient synchronization is almost fully overlapped with the tail of the backward pass.
Now scale to 405B: parameters at bf16 are 810 GB. After TP= 8, each GPU still needs 810 /8 = 101GB
for parameters alone, exceeding HBM. Adding PP= 8splits 80 layers into 8 pipeline stages of 10 layers each;
per-GPU parameter memory drops to 12. 6 GB. Pipeline parallelism was not chosen-it was forced by memory.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Cap TP at 8, always. Crossing a node boundary for tensor parallelism forces per-layer all-reduces over
InfiniBand. Published benchmarks show 40%+ throughput degradation going from TP= 8(intra-node)
to TP= 16(cross-node). This is a consequence of bandwidth physics, not software; it holds across GPU
generations.
Size the pipeline to keep the bubble under 20%. Usem 4 pas a starting point. With PP= 8, target
at least 32 micro-batches per DP replica per step. If your global batch cannot support this, prefer ZeRO-3
over pipeline parallelism.
Choose ZeRO-3 over PP when batch sizes are tight. ZeRO-3’s overhead ( 3 Pbytes per step, partially
overlapped with computation) is predictable and independent of model depth. Pipeline parallelism’s bub-
ble grows with stage count regardless of tuning, and its scheduling complexity is non-trivial-production
teams have described situations where a single engineer understands the pipeline scheduler.
Add sequence parallelism alongside TP at no extra bandwidth cost. SP replaces the TP all-reduce
on activation tensors with a reduce-scatter/all-gather pair of equivalent total cost, while also partitioning
LayerNorm and Dropout activations across the TP group. Minimum activation memory per GPU drops
by a factor of the TP degree; use it whenever TP 4.
Use gradient accumulation to rescue a tight micro-batch budget. If each DP replica can hold only
micro-batch size 1 after TP and PP, accumulatekbackward passes before syncing. Effective micro-batch
count becomesk, shrinking the bubble from(p1)/mto(p1)/(km)at the cost ofk-fold longer steps.
This is preferable to reducing DP degree and cutting overall throughput.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Design the parallelism strategy for a 100B dense transformer on 512 H100s.” Strong answer: set
TP= 8within each 8-GPU node (64 nodes total, 64 TP groups). A 100B model at bf16 is 200 GB; after
TP= 8, 25 GB per GPU-fits without PP. Set DP= 64. With global batch 2048, each replica gets 32
sequences. Add ZeRO-1 to shard optimizer state across DP ranks. Explain why TP stays at 8, why PP is
unnecessary here, and how gradient sync overlaps with computation.
“Why can’t you just scale data parallelism to 10,000 GPUs?” Strong answer: DP alone does not
reduce per-GPU parameter memory without ZeRO-3. Beyond the critical batch size, adding more DP
replicas does not improve sample efficiency-you run out of useful batch-size budget before you run out
of GPUs. ZeRO-3 adds 3 Psynchronization cost that becomes harder to overlap at very high DP degree,
and parameter communication across spine switches introduces topology-dependent latency.
```

```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
```
Senior follow-up: “A 400B+ training run spans multiple rack spine switches. How does this affect
your PP assignment?” Strong answer: assign consecutive pipeline stages to physically adjacent nodes
within the same rack or pod. PP’s point-to-point activation transfers stay on high-bandwidth leaf switch
fabric; DP’s gradient all-reduces must traverse spines but happen once per step and tolerate additional
latency through asynchronous overlap. Modern cluster schedulers expose rack-locality hints; use them to
constrain the PP group placement before setting DP. The failure to do this is one of the common causes
of unexplained throughput variance at large scale.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Apply TP first (cap at 8, within a single NVSwitch domain), then PP or ZeRO-3 until the model fits in
memory, then DP for remaining GPUs.
Batch size is a finite resource: micro-batches spent hiding the pipeline bubble are not available for data-
parallel scaling.
Communication costs: DP 2 Pper step, ZeRO-3 3 Pper step, TPactivation-size all-reduce per
layer-compare each to the step’s compute time to locate the bottleneck.
TP beyond 8 GPUs on current GPU hardware causes 40%+ throughput degradation and should not be
used.
Extending to 4D by adding SP or CP alongside TP costs no additional bandwidth and is the default choice
for sequence lengths above 4-8K tokens.
```
**12.4.2 Case Studies: Llama, DeepSeek-V3, Gemma**
Training reports from frontier labs are among the most information-dense documents in the field-each par-
allelism configuration table is the compressed output of thousands of hours of ablations. Three public examples
span the design space usefully: Llama 3, which sets the canonical template for dense models on GPU clusters;
DeepSeek-V3, which deliberately departs from that template for a large MoE model; and Gemma 2, which
shows how TPU network topology reshapes the same trade-offs. Reading these side by side reveals how the
rules of thumb hold across hardware and architecture-and exactly where they bend.
Every configuration in these reports is traceable to one of three constraints: model memory, network topol-
ogy, or batch-size budget. The useful mental model is to read the TP setting as the intra-node memory reduction
strategy, the PP setting as the cross-node model-fit strategy, and the DP setting as the throughput-scaling strat-
egy. When those three are set, whatever remains-CP, EP, SP-is driven by architecture-specific demands: long
sequences, sparse experts, quadratic attention memory.
The three case studies share a common thread. Each configuration minimizes idle time: PP bubble, com-
munication stalls, and memory-bound micro-batch stalls are all forms of idle time. A configuration is correct
when the matrix-multiply units are busy essentially continuously.
_If you can read a parallelism table and explain why each dimension is set to its specific value, you can
answer most senior-level design questions about distributed training._
The three examples collectively demonstrate the universality of the bandwidth-hierarchy argument even as
specific choices differ. On GPU clusters, NVLink forces TP 8. On TPU pods with toroidal-mesh networking-
where every chip can reach every neighbor at similar bandwidth-model parallelism can scale further without
hitting the same cliff. For MoE models, expert parallelism collapses the TP/PP distinction: routing tokens to
expert GPUs is effectively tensor parallelism in the MLP block, implemented via all-to-all rather than all-reduce.


```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
The GPU case also illustrates a hardware-topology argument that rarely appears in textbooks: pipeline
parallelism is used not just to fit models, but to route around the slow spine switches that connect GPU racks
above 256 GPUs. PP’s point-to-point activation transfers are directional and predictable, degrading far more
gracefully than all-to-all operations when crossing network hierarchy boundaries.

**A Worked Example**

**Llama 3 (405B, dense, GPU)** is the closest to the canonical recipe and the most instructive to decode step
by step.
The model has 405 B parameters, 126 transformer layers, hidden dimension 16,384. Training used clus-
ters of H100 80 GB GPUs. The parallelism configuration for the standard pre-training phase:
TP= 8: one full TP group per 8-GPU node (NVLink). At bf16, 405B parameters across 8 GPUs gives
 101 GB per GPU for parameters alone-still over the 80 GB HBM limit. TP alone cannot fit the model;
PP is necessary.
PP= 16: 126 layers split across 16 pipeline stages of 8 layers each. Per-GPU parameter memory drops
to 12. 6 GB, well within budget. TPPP= 128GPUs constitutes one full model instance.
DP=(total GPUs) / 128: on a cluster of roughly 16,000 GPUs, DP 125 replicas. Global batch: 125  4
micro-batches4096 tokens 2 M tokens per step.
CP= 8: added specifically for the long-context fine-tuning phase (128K token sequences). Attention
computation distributes across 8 devices via ring-style KV passing, keeping the quadratic attention acti-
vation memory tractable. This dimension is disabled for standard pre-training.
The key lesson: PP was forced by memory, not preferred. The team would have avoided it if 80 GB HBM
were sufficient after TP= 8. The long-context CP dimension illustrates the 4D pattern: a fifth dimension would
be needed if the model were also MoE (expert parallelism), which it is not.
At this scale, Llama 3’s training report logged 148 interruptions from faulty GPUs and additional incidents
from unplanned network maintenance. The parallelism configuration is only part of the engineering; checkpoint
frequency, automatic restart logic, and silent data-corruption detection are equally critical once you cross 10 K
GPUs.
**DeepSeek-V3 (671B total, 37B active, MoE, GPU)** is the most interesting departure from the canonical
recipe. The model uses 256 routed experts with top-8 routing per token, so only 37B parameters are active for
any given forward pass.
Published configuration:
PP= 16: 61 transformer layers split across 16 pipeline stages.
EP= 64: 64-way expert parallelism. Each GPU holds a subset of experts. Tokens are dispatched to the
GPU holding the selected expert via all-to-all communication. This substitutes for the role TP plays in
dense models.
ZeRO stage 1 for DP: optimizer states sharded across DP ranks. DP degree fills remaining GPU capacity.
**No tensor parallelism.**
The absence of TP is the key departure and worth understanding precisely. In a 671B MoE model, the
expert MLP layers dominate parameter count. Expert parallelism distributes those parameters across 64 GPUs
via token routing-achieving the same memory reduction that TP provides in dense models, but through a dif-
ferent communication primitive (all-to-all for routing versus all-reduce for TP). Adding TP on top of EP would
introduce per-layer all-reduces on the attention and dense MLP blocks, which are relatively small in a MoE


```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
model, while providing little incremental memory benefit. The net effect would be increased communication
overhead for negligible memory gain-a straightforward throughput loss.
The lesson: the canonical TP-first rule assumes a dense model. For MoE, EP substitutes for TP. The
bandwidth-hierarchy argument still applies-EP’s all-to-all also benefits from fast intra-pod networking-but the
primitive changes.
**Gemma 2 (dense, TPU)** illustrates how topology reshapes every decision. TPU pods use a toroidal mesh:
each chip connects to a small number of spatial neighbors, but collective bandwidth across the full mesh is high
and symmetric for any global operation. There is no hard bandwidth cliff at a node boundary analogous to the
NVSwitch-to-InfiniBand transition on GPU clusters.
Published configuration: ZeRO-3 (FSDP)+model parallelism+data parallelism. Model parallelism can
extend well beyond 8 devices on TPUs because all inter-chip links are comparable in bandwidth; there is no
architectural reason to cap at 8. ZeRO-3 is the primary vehicle for memory efficiency, sharding parameters,
gradients, and optimizer state across all model-parallel ranks. The report does not feature pipeline parallelism,
for two reasons: the toroidal mesh has no slow inter-rack spine to route around, and ZeRO-3 handles the memory
constraint without the scheduling complexity of PP.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Dense GPU training (Llama-style): TP= 8, PP only when forced by memory (roughly above 100B
at 80 GB HBM), DP for the rest. Add CP only for the long-context fine-tuning phase; it adds pipeline
complexity and should be disabled for standard pre-training.
MoE GPU training (DeepSeek-style): replace TP with EP sized to the expert count. PP still handles
the dense attention and embedding layers. Expect the all-to-all routing to be a communication bottle-
neck at high expert count; token dropping and expert-capacity buffers control variance but add algorithm
complexity that must be tested carefully.
TPU training (Gemma-style): lean on ZeRO-3 and model parallelism beyond 8 chips. Pipeline paral-
lelism is less commonly needed because there is no hard bandwidth cliff at a hardware boundary. Collec-
tive operations scale to the full pod size without topology-driven restrictions.
At production scale, fault tolerance is a first-class concern. Llama 3 counted 148 GPU failures during
a single training run. The correct response is aggressive checkpointing (every 30-60 minutes at this scale),
automatic job restart, and silent-error detection via periodic gradient norm checks and loss spike monitors.
The parallelism configuration alone does not determine success.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“DeepSeek-V3 has no tensor parallelism. Why not?” Strong answer: in a 671B MoE model, expert
MLP layers dominate parameters. Expert parallelism distributes those parameters across 64 GPUs via
token routing, providing the same memory reduction that TP gives in dense models. Adding TP would
introduce per-layer all-reduces on the smaller attention and dense MLP layers with minimal memory
benefit-net throughput loss.
“Why does Llama 3 use context parallelism only for the long-context phase?” Strong answer: CP
distributes attention computation by passing KV blocks in a ring across multiple devices. It is necessary
only when the quadratics^2 hactivation memory from attention exceeds per-GPU HBM. At standard pre-
training sequence lengths (4096 tokens), TP+SP already keeps activation memory tractable. At 128K
```

```
12.4 Putting It All Together: 3D and 4D Parallelism
```
```
tokens, the quadratic term exceeds any mitigation from SP alone, making CP unavoidable.
Senior follow-up: “If you had to train a 1T dense model on GPUs today, what configuration would
you propose, and what would you be most worried about?” Strong answer: TP= 8, PP sized to fit the
model (likely PP= 32+), DP for remaining capacity. The primary concern is pipeline bubble: at PP= 32,
the bubble ratio(31)/mdemandsm 128 micro-batches per replica to stay under 20% idle time, which
strains the global batch budget severely. Secondary concerns: checkpoint and restart time scales with
the run duration; a single mid-step GPU failure at 32K GPUs wastes hours. The engineering response is
zero-bubble pipeline scheduling (filling idle slots with weight-gradient computation) and a battle-tested
fault-tolerant checkpoint infrastructure-both are as important as the parallelism configuration itself.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Dense GPU models follow the canonical recipe: TP= 8within a node, PP only when forced by memory,
DP for throughput. CP is a 4th dimension added only for long-context phases.
MoE models substitute EP for TP; the bandwidth-hierarchy argument still applies, but the communication
primitive changes from all-reduce to all-to-all.
TPU topology removes the 8-device NVLink cliff, allowing model parallelism to scale further and reduc-
ing reliance on pipeline parallelism.
At production scale (>10K GPUs), fault tolerance, silent-error detection, and checkpoint infrastructure
are as critical as the parallelism configuration itself.
Reading a published parallelism table backward-inferring why each dimension is set to its specific value
from memory, topology, and batch-size constraints-is the core skill this interview topic tests.
```

### 13.1 The Three Canonical Scaling Laws.

**13.1.1 Data Scaling and Non-Parametric Rates**
An interviewer at a frontier lab will often open the scaling-laws deep-dive with a deceptively simple ques-
tion: “If I double my training data, how much does the loss drop?” The answer is not “a lot” or “it depends.”
The answer is a precise power-law relationship, and if you can derive the exponent from first principles on a
whiteboard, you immediately signal a level of understanding that separates senior candidates from the pack.
This topic appears at the staff and principal level, but even L5 candidates are expected to know the empirical
fact; the derivation is what earns you the senior signal.
Data scaling is the observation that, on a log-log plot, test loss decreases linearly as a function of dataset
size. Formally, if we denote the dataset size in tokens asDand the cross-entropy loss asL, then in the scaling
regime we find:

magnitude of data, across different model architectures, and across domains including language, speech, and
machine translation. The exponentαis typically in the range[0. 05 , 0 .35]depending on the task-much smaller

_Log-log linearity between dataset size and test loss is the most robustly observed empirical fact in large-
scale language modeling, and its exponent encodes the effective intrinsic dimensionality of the learning task._

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Model size must exceed data saturation. When running data-only scaling experiments, fix the model
large enough that the scaling curve stays in the power-law region. A rule of thumb: for every doubling of
data, you want roughly 10 more parameters than what would be “Chinchilla-optimal” for that data size,
so the model cannot overfit to the finite dataset.
Data composition shifts the offset, not the slope. Kaplan et al. show that changing training data mix-
ture (domain proportions) changes the vertical intercept of the log-log line but leaves the slopeαnearly
unchanged. This means data selection experiments-which source to mix in, what weight-can be validly
run on small models and small data; the relative rankings transfer to scale.
Repeated data hurts after roughly 4 epochs. When you have exhausted unique tokens, repeating the
corpus has rapidly diminishing returns. Empirically the effective sample size grows much more slowly
than the raw token count past 4 epochs of repetition. If your corpus allows only 2 epochs before saturation,
adding lower-quality unique data is almost always better than a third pass over high-quality data.
```

```
13.1 The Three Canonical Scaling Laws
```
```
Do not confuse perplexity scaling with downstream-task scaling. The power-law relationship is clean
and reliable for cross-entropy loss. Benchmark accuracy can be non-monotone, can show emergent jumps,
and can rank architectures differently than perplexity does. Use perplexity scaling to make engineering
decisions; validate on downstream tasks before committing resources at scale.
The irreducible floor exists. Every task has an entropy floor below which no amount of data will push the
loss-the Bayes error of the task. In practice, you will rarely be close to it for language, but in low-entropy
domains (e.g., heavily templated text), you can hit it surprisingly early.
```

**13.1.2 Model and Compute Scaling**
“If I give you a fixed compute budget, how would you split it between model size and training data?” is the
single most commonly asked quantitative question in frontier-lab LLM design interviews. The answer comes


```

from the Chinchilla analysis, and getting it right-including why Kaplan’s earlier estimate was off and what the
three estimation methods actually measure-is what separates a candidate who memorized a ratio from one who
understands the underlying machinery. This question appears at every seniority level; the senior version asks
you to derive the optimal trade-off from scratch rather than recite it.
Model and compute scaling extends data scaling to a two-variable problem. The lossLdepends jointly on
model sizeN(non-embedding parameters) and dataset sizeD(tokens):

L(N, D)NAα+DBβ+L∞
HereA,B,α,βare empirically fitted constants andL∞is the irreducible entropy of the data distribu-
tion. This functional form is additive: the model-size term and the data-size term contribute independently to
reducible loss. The key insight is that for a fixed compute budgetC(in FLOPs), training cost scales approxi-
mately asC 6 N D(the factor of 6 counts both forward and backward passes per token per parameter). Given
that constraint, you want to minimizeL(N, D)subject toN D=C/ 6.
Taking the gradient of the Lagrangian and setting it to zero yields the _compute-optimal_ or _Chinchilla-
optimal_ scaling:

N∗/Ca, D∗/Cb
where the Chinchilla estimates giveab 0. 5 , implying thatNandDshould be scaled in equal pro-
portion as compute grows. The resulting rule of thumb is roughly **20 tokens per parameter** : a 70B-parameter
model is compute-optimal when trained on1.4 trillion tokens.
_Compute-optimal training balances model size and token count in a roughly 1:20 parameter-to-token ratio;
skewing either way wastes FLOPs._
Kaplan et al. (2020) were the first to analyze joint model-data scaling, but they significantly underestimated
the optimal token-to-parameter ratio-their estimate was closer to 5-10 tokens per parameter. The primary culprit
was cosine learning rate schedules. A cosine schedule cannot be truncated mid-run; if you stop training early
(before the full cosine cooldown), the model’s effective loss is higher than it would be at the same number of
steps with a properly completed schedule. Kaplan’s experiments used runs truncated at various compute levels
for comparison, which systematically overestimated the performance of large models trained on little data and
underestimated small models trained longer. Chinchilla used isoFLOP profiles-multiple models trained to the
same total compute budget, each completing its full learning rate schedule-which avoids this artifact.
The additive functional form ofL(N, D)also encodes a crucial architectural observation: not all param-
eters count equally. Embedding parameters (the token embedding matrix and positional embeddings) do not
follow the same power-law behavior as non-embedding parameters. When embedding parameters are included
inN, the scaling curve bends and loses its clean log-log linearity. Kaplan reports this explicitly: analysis
should be conducted on non-embedding parameter counts. Similarly, in sparse models like mixture-of-experts,
the number of activated parameters per token, not the total parameter count, governs the effectiveNin the
scaling law.
