That gives roughly 1 token per parameter-but this is for the abstract mathematical optimum ignoring the
20:1 convention. The discrepancy is because the 20:1 rule comes from the Chinchilla paper’s actual constant fits
(A,B,α,β), not from theα=βsimplification alone. With Chinchilla’s fitted constants, the compute-optimal
line for a 7B-parameter model falls at approximately 140B tokens, and for a 70B model at approximately 1.4T
tokens-the 20:1 ratio.
The three methods Chinchilla uses to estimate this ratio are: (1) _minimum-envelope_ over training curves
across compute levels, which finds the lower envelope of loss vs. compute for models of varying size; (2)
_isoFLOP profiles_ , which sweep model size at each fixed compute level and find the minimum of a fitted quadratic;
and (3) _parametric fit_ to the fullL(N, D)surface via least-squares. Methods 1 and 2 agree closely (0.50, 0.50
exponents); method 3 originally gave anomalous results because of an off-center residual in the curve fitting, a
flaw later identified by Epoch AI’s forensic replication of the plots.
**What You Actually Decide in Practice
Training-optimal is not inference-optimal.** Chinchilla optimizes training FLOPs. Production systems
care about inference cost-a smaller model with the same quality at deploy time is far cheaper to run at
scale. This is why modern models have drifted far from 20 tokens per parameter: Llama 3 (8B) was
trained on 15 trillion tokens (1875 tokens per parameter), and Qwen models have reached 30 trillion
tokens. When your product serves millions of requests per day, the right ratio is determined by inference
cost, not training cost.
**Exclude embedding parameters from** N**.** Always use non-embedding parameter counts when fitting
scaling laws or comparing model sizes. Embedding tables can be very large (e.g., a 128k vocabulary
at 4096 dimensions adds500M parameters) and do not improve loss at the same rate as attention and
feedforward parameters.
**For MoE models, use activated-parameter count.** In sparse mixture-of-experts architectures, only a
fraction of parameters are active per token. The effectiveNfor scaling-law purposes is the number
of activated parameters per token, not the total parameter count. Several papers have proposed “dense
equivalents” to normalize MoE model sizes for comparison.
**Learning rate schedules must complete.** When running scaling-law pilot experiments with cosine
schedules, train each run to completion (full cooldown) before comparing. Truncated runs systemati-
cally misrank large-model versus long-training options. Constant or linear decay schedules sidestep this
problem and are increasingly preferred for scaling experiments.


```
13.1 The Three Canonical Scaling Laws
```
```
Downstream task scaling is noisier than perplexity scaling. The compute-optimal analysis applies
cleanly to cross-entropy loss. If you are trying to optimize for a specific benchmark, scaling predictions
become unreliable-emergence effects and saturation are common. Use perplexity scaling to allocate re-
sources and downstream benchmarks to validate the final model.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“If you had a fixed compute budget, how would you split it between model size and training tokens?”
The strong answer names Chinchilla: roughly 20 tokens per parameter is training-optimal. Then the
candidate immediately qualifies it: if the model will be deployed at high request volume, you should
overtrain a smaller model-the inference savings over the model’s lifetime dominate the extra training cost.
This distinction is what separates rote recall from engineering judgment.
“Why did Kaplan underestimate the optimal token count compared to Chinchilla?” Strong answer:
cosine learning rate schedules require completing the full cooldown to yield a valid checkpoint. Kaplan’s
multi-model comparison used truncated runs, which made large models trained on little data look artifi-
cially better. Chinchilla’s isoFLOP method trained all runs to completion before comparing, removing
the artifact.
Senior follow-up: “Walk me through how you would run an isoFLOP experiment to estimate the
compute-optimal model size for your team’s next training run.” The senior answer sketches: (1) pick
5-7 compute budgets spanning 2-3 orders of magnitude below your target; (2) at each budget, train 5-8
model sizes ranging from0.3to 3 the Chinchilla-optimal size for that budget; (3) fit a quadratic
to the loss-vs.-model-size curve at each fixed compute; (4) extract the minimum and plot optimalNvs.
Con a log-log axis; (5) fit a power law and extrapolate to your target compute. Emphasize that the entire
pilot study uses<1% of the target compute budget and should complete in days, not weeks.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The Chinchilla functional formL(N, D) =A/Nα+B/Dβ+L∞describes joint model-data scaling;
minimizing it subject to a fixed compute budgetC 6 N Dgives the training-optimal allocation.
Chinchilla’s result is approximately 20 tokens per parameter for training-optimal runs; this is far below
what modern production models use because inference cost dominates at deployment scale.
Kaplan’s earlier (lower) estimate of the optimal token count was biased by truncated cosine learning rate
schedules; isoFLOP experiments that complete the full cooldown correct this.
Exclude embedding parameters fromNin all scaling analyses; they do not follow the same power law as
attention and feedforward parameters.
The isoFLOP method-sweeping model size at each fixed compute budget and extracting the minimum-
is the most reliable and conceptually cleanest approach to estimating compute-optimal ratios for your
specific task and architecture.
```

```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
### 13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions

**13.2.1 Architecture Comparisons at Small Scale**
Every year brings a new architecture claiming to beat the transformer. The interview question that follows
is always the same: “How would you decide whether to adopt this for your next production training run?” The
naive answer-train both at full scale and compare-is economically absurd. The right answer uses scaling laws
to make that comparison at a fraction of the cost. This question appears at the senior level and above, and the
candidate who can describe the procedure cold, with the right caveats, signals genuine production experience.
The scaling-law comparison procedure works as follows. You pick two or more candidate architectures and
train instances of each across a range of compute budgets spanning two to three orders of magnitude-say, from
1018 to 1021 FLOPs. For each architecture, you measure the best achievable validation loss at each compute
level (holding the other architecture fixed and sweeping over model sizes to get the optimal point). You then
plot both curves on a log-log axis: log compute on thex-axis, log loss on they-axis.
The crucial diagnostic is the relationship between the two curves:
**Parallel curves with a constant vertical gap** : the better architecture is compute-efficient by a fixed
multiplicative factor at every scale. If architecture A sits∆log-loss units below architecture B across
all compute levels, that translates to a constant factor speedup-architecture A achieves the same loss as B
with ak-fold smaller compute budget, wherek= 10∆/αandαis the common scaling slope.
**Crossing curves** : the ranking reverses at some compute level. The cheaper architecture may look better
at small scale but lose at large scale, or vice versa. Crossing curves require extrapolation before you can
make a decision.
_A constant-factor offset in log-log scaling curves is the signature that an architecture advantage is real and
will survive to your target compute budget._
The reason this procedure is reliable is that the slope of a scaling curve-the rate at which loss decreases
per unit of log-compute-is largely determined by the task and data, not the architecture. What the architecture
controls is the efficiency constant: how many FLOPs are needed to reach a given loss. A better architecture
shifts the whole curve down (lower loss at every compute level) or equivalently left (same loss at lower compute).
Because the slope is preserved, a gap measured at 1019 FLOPs extrapolates cleanly to 1023 FLOPs.
Contrast this with the alternative of just training at small scale and comparing accuracy numbers. A model
with 10M parameters and 50M tokens trained on a narrow benchmark tells you almost nothing about relative
quality at 70B parameters and 2T tokens. The scaling-law approach is cheap precisely because the parallelism
of curves means small-scale information is informative about large-scale rankings.
The transformer-vs-LSTM comparison is the canonical example of this working well. LSTMs consistently
sit1 log-perplexity unit above transformers at every compute level, on a log scale. That gap corresponds to
roughly a 10-15compute penalty: to match a transformer trained on a given budget, an LSTM needs 10-15
times more FLOPs. Knowing this at the 1018 FLOP level means you never need to run the 1023 FLOP LSTM
experiment to know the answer. Similarly, gated linear units and mixture-of-experts architectures showed reli-
able parallel downward shifts relative to the standard transformer baseline, which is precisely why they became
the dominant modifications at frontier labs.


```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
**A Worked Example**

Suppose you want to evaluate a new state-space model architecture against a standard transformer. You
train both at five compute budgets:C2f 1018 , 3  1018 , 1019 , 3  1019 , 1020 gFLOPs. At eachC, you sweep
over five model sizes (varying width and depth) and select the lowest validation loss achieved.
After plotting on a log-log axis, you observe:
Both curves have approximately the same slope,α  0. 08 (consistent with language modeling data
scaling).
The transformer curve sits∆  0. 05 log-loss units below the SSM curve consistently across all five
budgets.
The curves are parallel-no crossing.
Interpreting the gap: a constant offset of∆ = 0. 05 in log-loss means the SSM needs a compute multiplier
ofk= 10∆/α= 10^0.^05 /^0.^08  100.^625  4. 2 times more FLOPs to match the transformer at any target loss. For
a $5M training run, the SSM would require an equivalent $21M run to achieve the same quality-a clear decision
signal obtained for roughly 0.01% of the target budget.
Total pilot cost: five compute levels, two architectures, five model sizes each = 50 training runs. If your
target run isCtarget= 10^23 FLOPs, your pilot spans 1018 - 1020 , which is at most 1020 / 1023 = 0.1%of the target.
In practice, the pilot consumes even less because the small runs dominate compute.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Require at least two to three orders of magnitude of compute coverage in your pilot. A single data
point per architecture is not a scaling law; you need enough range to confirm linearity and detect potential
crossings. In my experience, five compute levels spanning three orders of magnitude is the minimum to
feel confident.
Crossing curves are a stop sign, not an answer. If the curves cross within your pilot range, you need to
extrapolate carefully-fit power laws to each segment, determine where they diverge, and assess whether
your target compute falls before or after the crossing. Extrapolation beyond the pilot range is unreliable
unless the curves are clearly parallel by the end.
Always compare on validation perplexity, not downstream benchmarks. Perplexity scales cleanly and
predictably. Benchmark accuracy is noisy, nonlinear, and subject to emergence effects that can make a
better architecture look worse at small scale. Use perplexity to select the architecture; validate downstream
performance only after committing to the winner.
The two modifications that reliably beat the standard transformer at every scale are gated linear
units and mixture of experts. All other alternatives (linear attention, state-space models, recurrent vari-
ants) show either no reliable gap or task-specific wins that do not generalize. This is exactly what large-
scale architecture sweep papers found, and it directly explains the architectural choices in current frontier
models.
Exclude embedding parameters from all comparisons. Embedding matrices do not follow the same
power-law scaling as attention and feedforward parameters. If you include them, the scaling curves bend
and you lose the clean log-log linearity that makes the comparison reliable. Always report and compare
on non-embedding parameter counts.
```

```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A researcher proposes a new attention variant. How do you decide whether it is worth scaling
up?” A strong answer describes the scaling-law comparison: train both architectures at 3-5 compute
levels spanning 2-3 orders of magnitude, check whether the new variant shows a consistent parallel offset
below the baseline. If yes, quantify the compute-efficiency gain. If curves cross, extrapolate and determine
whether the advantage emerges before or after your target compute.
“Why not just train the new architecture at a small scale and compare accuracy on a benchmark?”
The strong answer explains why benchmark accuracy is an unreliable signal at small scale: architectures
can rank differently on perplexity versus benchmarks, and emergent capabilities can appear discontinu-
ously. Perplexity scaling is the reliable channel; benchmark validation comes only after the architecture
decision is made.
Senior follow-up: “What would you do if the scaling curves for two architectures crossed within
your pilot range?” The senior answer goes beyond “extrapolate.” It explains that crossing curves mean
one architecture is better in the data-limited regime and the other in the compute-rich regime; you need to
characterize where your target compute falls relative to the crossing point. If the crossing happens before
your target, the extrapolation is more reliable; if after, you may need to push your pilot to larger scale
before committing. The candidate should also ask why the curves cross-is it a depth-width interaction? A
saturation artifact? Understanding the mechanism determines whether the crossing is robust or an artifact
of the comparison setup.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Train each candidate architecture at 3-5 compute levels spanning 2-3 orders of magnitude; compare on
validation perplexity, not benchmark accuracy.
Parallel curves with a constant vertical gap confirm that the better architecture’s advantage will survive to
your target compute; the gap size gives you the compute-efficiency multiplier.
Crossing curves require extrapolation and deeper investigation before committing.
The two architecture modifications with the strongest and most consistent evidence of compute-efficiency
improvement are gated linear units and mixture of experts.
Always use non-embedding parameter counts; embedding parameters break log-log linearity and skew
comparisons.
```
**13.2.2 Optimizer and Hyperparameter Selection**
Choosing the wrong learning rate for a 70B model is not a minor inconvenience-it can cost weeks of H100
time and produce a model that is meaningfully worse than it should be. The right way to pick learning rates,
batch sizes, and depth-to-width ratios is not to tune them at large scale; it is to verify at small scale that these
hyperparameters either transfer directly or follow a predictable scaling law of their own. Understanding when
each case applies is a senior-level topic that shows up in both design and deep-dive interviews.
The scaling-law mindset applied to hyperparameters rests on one observation: if the optimal value of a
hyperparameter produces scaling curves that are _parallel and non-crossing_ across model sizes, then the optimal
value at small scale is the optimal value at large scale. You train a grid of small models varying the hyperpa-
rameter of interest, identify the optimal value at several compute levels, and check whether that optimum is


```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
stable.
Three hyperparameters deserve special treatment:
**Aspect ratio (depth-to-width).** Kaplan et al. show that for models between 50M and 1.5B parameters, the
loss difference between aspect ratios from10 to100 is small-well under 5% relative. The basin is wide and
flat. A single layer is genuinely bad; all reasonable aspect ratios above that are approximately equivalent. The
practical upshot: pick anything in the rangedmodel/nlayers 2 [64,256]and you are in the safe zone at all scales.
**Batch size and critical batch size.** Doubling the batch size is equivalent to taking two gradient steps-but
only below the _critical batch size_ B∗. AboveB∗, additional samples in the batch reduce useful gradient noise at
a diminishing rate, and you are effectively paying full parallelism cost for less than full optimization benefit. The
critical batch size itself scales with the loss target: lower loss (later in training) implies largerB∗, because the
gradient landscape becomes smoother and you need more samples to reduce noise to a useful level. Empirically,
B∗follows a power law:

B∗/L−γ
for some task-dependentγ > 0 , whereLis the current validation loss. This is why production training runs
(Llama 3 is a public example) ramp batch size during training: early in training, loss is high andB∗is small;
later, loss is lower andB∗is larger, so you can increase parallelism without sacrificing optimization efficiency.
**Learning rate.** Under the standard parametrization, the optimal learning rate decays with model widthd
roughly asη∗/ 1 /d. This means every time you double the width, you need to re-tune the learning rate. The
alternative, _maximal update parametrization_ (μP), reparametrizes the model so that the optimal learning rate is
exactly stable across width. You tune it once at a small model (say, 50M parameters) and apply the same value
to a 70B model.
_Hyperparameter tuning and architecture selection should be done at small scale and extrapolated; the only
reliable signal is whether the optimal value is stable across compute levels on a log-log plot._
The critical insight about hyperparameter stability is that it is not universal. Some hyperparameters-aspect
ratio, feedforward ratio, attention head dimension-have wide, flat loss basins that barely move as scale increases.
Others-learning rate under standard parametrization, batch size-require active management as you scale. Know-
ing which is which saves enormous amounts of compute.
The optimizer comparison follows the same logic as architecture comparison. Adam versus SGD produces
a roughly constant-factor compute efficiency gap across scales, with Adam consistently requiring roughly 10 
fewer FLOPs to reach the same loss. Since the gap is parallel (constant offset on log-log axes), you don’t need
to run SGD at full scale to know the answer-a small-scale pilot is sufficient.
The μP approach deserves particular attention because it eliminates one of the most expensive unknowns
in scaling: the learning-rate transfer problem. Standard parametrization initializes attention projection weights
withN(0, 1 /d)variance and applies the same learning rate to all layers regardless of width. As width grows,
the gradient signal through the attention layers blows up without the 1 /dcorrection, forcing the learning rate
down. μP corrects this by scaling initialization variance, per-layer learning rates, and the forward-pass output
multiplier by appropriate powers ofd. The result is a model where every layer’s activation magnitude is invariant
to width, and consequently the optimal global learning rate does not change as you scale.


```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider selecting the optimal learning rate for a standard transformer withdmodel2f 256 , 512 , 1024 , 2048 , 4096 g
(corresponding roughly to 15M, 55M, 220M, 900M, and 3.5B non-embedding parameters). For each width, you
run a grid of seven learning rates spaced in log scale from 10 −^4 to 10 −^1 , train for a fixed number of tokens (say
10B), and record the minimum validation loss.
The optimal learning rate at each width:

```
d= 256 η∗ 3  10 −^3
d= 512 η∗ 1. 5  10 −^3
d= 1024 η∗ 8  10 −^4
d= 2048 η∗ 4  10 −^4
d= 4096 η∗ 2  10 −^4
```
Fitting a power law: η∗ / d−^1.^0 , exactly the 1 /drule. Extrapolating tod= 8192(a 14B-parameter
model), you predictη∗ 10 −^4. This is reliable enough to use as a starting point, but still requires a validation
run because the learning-rate surface is narrow enough that being off by 3 costs you real loss.
Under μP, the same pilot atd= 256withη∗ = 3 10 −^3 gives you the value to use atd= 8192-no
extrapolation required. The computational cost of the pilot is the same; the benefit is that you eliminate the
large-scale validation run.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Treat aspect ratio as a low-stakes decision. Pick a depth-to-width configuration that keeps you in the
range of 10-64 layers and admodelthat gives reasonable hardware utilization (multiples of 128 for tensor-
core alignment). The loss basin is wide enough that you will not see a meaningful degradation from
non-optimal aspect ratios-spend your tuning budget elsewhere.
Set your starting batch size at or below the critical batch size, then ramp. A practical heuristic: at the
beginning of training (loss 3 -4 nats for language modeling), start with a batch size of 0.5-2M tokens.
As loss drops to2 nats (mid-training), double the batch size. As loss approaches your target (e.g., 1.5
nats), double again. This mirrors what Llama 3 and similar runs do and keeps you in the efficient regime
throughout.
Use Adam (or AdamW) by default; only switch if you have a scaling-law pilot showing a competing
optimizer wins. The empirical gap between Adam and SGD is approximately a 10 compute factor in
favor of Adam, consistent across task types and model sizes. There is no strong evidence that alternatives
(Adafactor, Lion, etc.) reliably beat Adam across all scales; run a small pilot before committing.
Adopt μP if your team has the engineering bandwidth. The payoff is largest when you expect to train
many models at different scales-hyperparameter transfer eliminates re-tuning costs that compound across
experiments. The cost is implementation complexity: μP requires modifying initialization variance, per-
layer learning rate multipliers, and output scaling, all as functions of width. Mistakes are subtle. If your
team is running a one-off training run, standard parametrization with a careful scaling law fit for learning
rate is lower risk.
Verify parallelism before extrapolating any hyperparameter. The scaling-law approach is only valid
if the loss curves for different hyperparameter values are parallel. Run your pilot, plot loss-vs-compute
```

```
13.2 Using Scaling Laws to Make Design Decisions
```
```
for each hyperparameter value, and confirm visually that the curves do not cross. If they cross, you cannot
safely extrapolate the small-scale optimum to large scale.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How do you pick the learning rate for a new 70B model?” A strong answer gives two paths: (1)
standard parametrization-fit a power law onη∗vs.dfrom a small-scale pilot, extrapolate to the target width
usingη∗/ 1 /d, then validate with a short 1B-token warmup run; (2) μP-tuneη∗once on a 50M model,
apply directly at 70B, skip the large-scale validation run. The candidate should note the engineering trade-
off: path (1) is simpler but requires re-tuning at each scale; path (2) eliminates re-tuning but requires
careful implementation.
“What is the critical batch size and how do you use it in practice?” The strong answer defines it as
the batch size above which marginal gradient steps become less efficient than ideal (gradient noise no
longer decreasing proportionally with batch size), explains that it scales inversely with loss (lower loss!
larger critical batch size), and describes the ramp strategy: start small and increase batch size as training
progresses, matching the growingB∗.
Senior follow-up: “Explain μP and why it solves the learning-rate transfer problem.” The senior
answer explains the mechanics: standard parametrization initializes weights with variance/ 1 /din at-
tention layers but applies a width-independent learning rate, causing gradient signal magnitude to scale
withdand forcingη∗ / 1 /dto compensate. μP explicitly scales initialization variance and per-layer
update rates by powers ofdso that forward-pass activations and weight updates remainO(1)regardless
of width. The consequence: the gradient update magnitude is invariant to width, so the global learning
rate that minimizes loss at width 256 is numerically the same that minimizes loss at width 8192. The
limitation: μP guarantees this in the infinite-width limit; in practice, there are finite-width corrections,
and labs still run short validation runs to confirm transfer.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Hyperparameter stability (optimal value constant across scale) or predictable scaling (optimal value fol-
lows its own power law) can both be established cheaply with a small-scale pilot; never tune at large scale
without this prior.
Aspect ratio has a wide, flat loss basin-anything between 10 and 100 layers at a reasonable width is
approximately optimal at every model size.
Batch size should stay at or below the critical batch sizeB∗, which grows as training loss decreases; ramp
batch size progressively during training to stay efficient.
Under standard parametrization, optimal learning rate scales as 1 /d; μP eliminates this dependence,
allowing exact learning-rate transfer from a tiny pilot model to the full-scale run.
Adam outperforms SGD by roughly 10 in compute efficiency across scales; this gap is consistent enough
that it does not need to be re-validated for each new task.
```

**14.1.1 IsoFLOP Analysis Step by Step**

_IsoFLOP analysis converts the joint question of model size and training duration into a single-variable

The practical IsoFLOP procedure is:

1. Fix a compute budgetC(in FLOPs).
2. Train several models of varyingNeach to its matched token countD=C/(6N), holdingCconstant
    across all runs in the sweep.
3. Plot final loss againstN; identify the minimizingN∗empirically for this budget.

5. Repeat the sweep at several values ofCspanning at least two orders of magnitude to obtain a reliable

The Kaplan et al. (2020) scaling laws preceded Chinchilla and reached a different conclusion: optimal
model size grows faster than token count, suggestingN∗/C^0.^73 and a ratio of roughly 1-2 tokens per parameter.
The discrepancy traces to a methodological artifact.
Kaplan’s experiments used _truncated_ cosine learning-rate schedules. When a model trains for more steps,
the cosine schedule decays the learning rate further and yields a lower final loss-not because the larger model
is inherently better, but because the schedule is better calibrated to longer runs. The comparison confounds
model capacity with schedule quality: models trained longer appear better because they also experience a more
favorable schedule.
Chinchilla used complete cosine schedules matched to each run’s actual training length. With that confound
removed, the token-count benefit became visible: the data-scaling exponentβis not substantially smaller than the
model-scaling exponentα, so the optimal recipe requires far more tokens per parameter than Kaplan suggested.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Count non-embedding parameters only. TheC 6 N Didentity applies to parameters that participate

model size that must serve those requests. Section 14.2 addresses this inference-aware regime explicitly.
```

**14.1.2 Replications, Corrections, and the Epoch AI Re-Fit**
The Chinchilla paper presented three independent methods for estimating compute-optimal scaling, and
all three appeared to agree. When Epoch AI forensically re-digitized the data behind Method 3 in 2023, they
found non-zero-mean residuals in the published nonlinear regression-a numerical artifact of local-minimum
convergence that drove the fitted exponents away from those returned by Methods 1 and 2. A 0.03 shift in the
scaling exponent is invisible in a log-log plot of a single experiment; extrapolated over four to five decades
of compute, it predicts a meaningfully different optimal model size. Understanding this episode tells you how
scaling-law estimates fail in practice and what diagnostics to run before trusting a published fit.
The Chinchilla paper estimated the parameters of the joint loss model:

#### L(N, D) =E+

#### A

```
Nα+
```
#### B

```
Dβ
using three distinct approaches applied to the same set of training runs:
```
1. **Method 1: empirical envelope.** For each FLOP budgetC, identify the model that achieves the lowest
    final loss across all runs at that budget. Read offN∗(C)directly from the observed loss envelope. Fit
    logN∗vs.logCto obtain the scaling exponent.
2. **Method 2: optimal-allocation regression.** Use theD∗/N∗ratio implied by Method 1. Fit a power law
    relatingD∗/N∗toCacross all budget levels. This method uses the full set of runs but targets only the
    ratio, not the full loss surface.
3. **Method 3: full nonlinear regression.** Fit all five parametersfE, A, B, α, βgsimultaneously to all
    (N, D, L)observations by minimizing the sum of squared residuals between predicted and observed loss.
Methods 1 and 2 are robust: they require only that the empirical minimum is identifiable, and they are
insensitive to the shape of the loss surface far from the optimum. Method 3 is statistically more efficient-it uses


```
14.1 Compute-Optimal Training
```
all the data and jointly identifies all parameters-but nonlinear regression over a five-dimensional curved surface
has multiple local minima, and the optimizer can converge to the wrong one.
The Epoch AI finding was that the Method 3 regression in the Chinchilla paper had converged to a local
minimum. The diagnostic was straightforward: in a well-fitted regression, residualsLˆLobsshould have ap-
proximately zero mean across all subgroups of the data. The published Method 3 fit had residuals that were
systematically positive for small models and negative for large models-evidence that the fitted model was at-
tributing too much benefit to model size (overestimatingα). Reinitializing the nonlinear optimizer from the
Method 1 and Method 2 estimates and rerunning the regression converged to a different solution with near-
zero-mean residuals that agreed closely with both earlier methods.
_The Epoch AI re-fit showed that the three Chinchilla methods do agree when Method 3 is initialized cor-
rectly. The discrepancy was a numerical artifact of local-minimum convergence, diagnosable by checking that
regression residuals have zero mean across regimes of_ N _,_ D _, and_ C _-the standard first diagnostic for any scaling-
law fit._
Two systematic risks in fitting scaling laws become concrete in this episode.
The first is initialization sensitivity in nonlinear regression. The five-parameter Chinchilla loss surface is
highly curved and has many local minima; a starting point far from the global minimum reliably produces a
biased fit. Standard practice-run from multiple starting points (grid search or random initialization) and accept
only solutions for which residuals are approximately zero-mean across all data subgroups-would have caught
the problem before publication.
The second is exponent compounding at scale. Scaling laws are power laws:N∗(C)/Cβ/(α+β). A small
error in the exponent amplifies with every decade of compute extrapolation. At the scale of Chinchilla’s own
experiments, Methods 1, 2, and the biased Method 3 gave similar enough predictions that the error was unde-
tectable empirically. Extrapolating to frontier runs-four to five decades beyond the calibration range-produces
a compounding gap that translates directly into mis-sized models.
The re-fit ultimately strengthened confidence in the main Chinchilla result. Once the local-minimum ar-
tifact was corrected, all three methods agreed onα  β  0. 5 andD∗/N∗  20 , providing independent
validation from three methodologically different approaches.

```
14.1 Compute-Optimal Training
```

Bottom quintile (N < 1 B):LˆLobs> 0 (fit over-predicts loss for small models-too pessimistic about
their quality).
Top quintile (N > 10 B):LˆLobs< 0 (fit under-predicts loss for large models-too optimistic).
This monotone sign pattern-positive residuals at smallN, negative at largeN-is the fingerprint of an over-
estimated capacity exponentα. The fitted model is more confident in large models than the data warrants, and
uses the non-zero-mean residuals to absorb the bias. Checking for this pattern costs one group-by on the residual
dataframe and takes under a minute.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always check that residuals are zero-mean across data subgroups. For scaling-law fits, bin residuals
bylogN,logD, andlogCseparately. A monotone sign pattern in any of these signals local-minimum
convergence or model misspecification. Both are fixable; neither is detectable without this check.
Run the nonlinear regression from multiple initializations. Initialize from the Method 1 / Method
2 estimates, from random perturbations of that estimate, and from naive starting points. Accept only
fits in which all initializations converge to the same parameter values. If they disagree, the loss surface
has multiple competing minima and you need a broader search (Nelder-Mead from a grid of starts, or
basin-hopping).
Methods 1 and 2 are more robust and should be reported alongside Method 3. The envelope approach
and the optimal-ratio fit do not require solving a five-dimensional non-convex problem; they are less
statistically efficient but less prone to local-minimum failure. If your Method 3 disagrees with both, trust
Methods 1 and 2 as the sanity check.
Treat published exponents as point estimates with uncertainty. The Chinchilla exponents were fitted
on a specific dataset (MassiveText), architecture (decoder-only transformer), and compute range ( 6  1018
to 3  1023 FLOPs). Applying them to a different modality, architecture, or compute regime larger than
the training range requires either refitting or explicitly widening your uncertainty interval onN∗.
Report confidence intervals on scaling exponents when making resource decisions. A 95% interval on
αandβtranslates directly into a confidence interval onN∗(C). Reporting only point estimates conceals
the prediction uncertainty that grows with each decade of compute extrapolation.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Did the three Chinchilla methods agree with each other?” Strong answer: Methods 1 and 2 agreed
closely. Method 3, as originally published, produced slightly different exponents because the nonlinear
regression converged to a local minimum. Epoch AI’s 2023 re-analysis found non-zero-mean residuals
split by model size in the Method 3 fit. Reinitializing from the Method 1 and 2 estimates brought Method
3 into agreement with the others, strengthening confidence inD∗/N∗ 20 andN∗/C^0.^5.
“How would you detect that a scaling-law fit is wrong?” Strong answer: check residuals. In a well-fitted
regression,LˆLobsshould be zero-mean and uncorrelated withlogN,logD, andlogC. A monotone
sign pattern in any of these-positive residuals for small models and negative for large, or vice versa-means
the fitted model is misspecified or the optimizer found a local minimum. The fix is multi-start nonlinear
regression initialized near the Method 1 / 2 estimate, and verification that all starts converge to the same
parameter values.
```

### 14.2 Inference-Aware Token-to-Parameter Ratios

```
Senior follow-up: “By how much does a 0.03 exponent error affect a frontier model recommenda-
tion, and when does it become practically significant?” Strong answer: the error grows as(C/C 0 )^0.^03
whereC 0 is the calibration point. At 1,000the calibration compute (Chinchilla scale) the error is
19%. At 105 the calibration (frontier training runs) it reaches41%-enough to shift a 300B-parameter
recommendation to 425B, which has architectural and hardware implications. The error grows slowly but
monotonically with log-compute extrapolation, so small exponent inaccuracies matter more the further
you push beyond the data used to fit the law.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The Chinchilla paper’s three methods did not agree internally because Method 3’s nonlinear regression
converged to a local minimum; Epoch AI’s re-fit corrected this by using better initialization and checking
residual zero-mean.
The diagnostic for local-minimum convergence is non-zero-mean residuals binned bylogN: system-
atic over-prediction for small models and under-prediction for large models identifies an over-estimated
capacity exponentα.
A 0.03 exponent shift produces a19% error inN∗at Chinchilla-scale compute and a41% error
at frontier scale ( 105 the calibration range)-practically significant when sizing a multi-billion-dollar
training run.
The corrected re-fit strengthened, not weakened, confidence in the main Chinchilla result:N∗/C^0.^5
andD∗/N∗ 20.
Standard practice for any scaling-law fit: multi-start nonlinear regression, residual zero-mean check across
all data subgroups (logN,logD,logC), and exponent confidence intervals on any prediction that extrap-
olates beyond the fitted compute range.
```
### 14.2 Inference-Aware Token-to-Parameter Ratios

**14.2.1 Why Modern Models Overtrain on Tokens**
Every serious training run eventually hits the same question: given a fixed compute budget, should you
scale up model size or token count? Chinchilla answered this for the case of minimizing training loss per FLOP,
and the answer was 20 tokens per parameter. But that answer optimizes the wrong objective for production. A
model you serve to millions of users accumulates inference FLOPs that will dwarf the one-time training cost
within weeks. Practitioners at every major lab have quietly moved the ratio far above 20, and the empirical
record from Llama 3, MiniCPM, and Hunyuan makes clear that the 20:1 figure is a floor, not a target. This topic
appears in senior system design interviews whenever the conversation shifts from “how do you train?” to “why
did you make this model that size?”
Chinchilla defines the _compute-optimal_ point: given a training FLOP budgetC, the model sizeN∗and
dataset sizeD∗that minimize loss satisfyN∗/C^0.^5 andD∗/C^0.^5 , givingD∗/N∗ 20. This is a Pareto
frontier for the specific objective of minimizing loss for a fixed training spend. It says nothing about what
happens after training ends.
Inference cost scales withN: every token generated passes through the full model. If you will serveM


```
14.2 Inference-Aware Token-to-Parameter Ratios
```
inference tokens after training, total system cost is approximately:

```
Ctotal 6 N D+ 2N M,
```
where 6 N Dis training cost and 2 N Mis cumulative inference cost (both in FLOPs). For any deployment at
scale,M Dwithin weeks, and the second term dominates. The right question then is: given a fixedN
(bounded by serving budget), what is the bestD? The answer is: pushDas high as data quality allows. A
smaller, more-trained model is cheaper to serve indefinitely.
A separate empirical question is how much worse the model gets as you pushDbeyond the compute-
optimal point. Researchers from the University of Washington and Apple studied this directly, framing it as the
_Chinchilla penalty_ : given a compute-optimal baseline atD∗= 20N, how much does validation loss increase
if you instead train withD=cNforc 20? Their finding is that the penalty follows a roughly log-linear
curve-small and predictable at moderate overtraining, not catastrophic. Training a 7B model at 640 tokens per
parameter inflates loss by only a few percent compared to a freshly trained Chinchilla-optimal model of the same
size, yet halves the compute and memory required at inference time compared to a Chinchilla-optimal model
trained on the same total FLOP budget.
_Compute-optimal and inference-optimal are different objectives; production ML optimizes the latter, which
consistently pushes the token-to-parameter ratio well above 20._
Three independent forces push modern labs toward higher token-to-parameter ratios.
First, **data quality has improved**. The original Chinchilla experiments were run on the Pile, a relatively
noisy web-scraped corpus. Modern training sets apply aggressive deduplication, quality filtering, and domain
reweighting. Cleaner data means each token carries more signal, effectively shifting the isoFLOP curve so the
compute-optimal ratio rises. Llama 3’s own replication of the Chinchilla analysis finds roughly 39:1 as the
compute-optimal ratio for their data mixture-already double the original figure.
Second, **architectural eﬀiciency has improved**. Better tokenizers, grouped-query attention, and improved
normalization schemes all increase the information extracted per training FLOP. If your architecture learns
faster from the same tokens, the compute-optimal point shifts further toward tokens and away from parame-
ters. MiniCPM’s curve-fit estimates 192:1, a number the authors themselves note is at the far end of published
estimates and likely reflects both data quality and their architectural choices.
Third, **serving economics are asymmetric**. Training is paid once; inference is paid on every request. For
a 7B model at 200 tokens per parameter versus a 70B model at 20 tokens per parameter-both costing the same
to train-the 7B model generates tokens at 10 lower inference cost. At the scale of a product serving millions
of daily active users, that asymmetry dominates every training-efficiency argument.

**A Worked Example**

```
Suppose your compute budget isC= 10^23 FLOPs. You are choosing between two configurations:
Config A (Chinchilla-optimal) :N= 8B,D= 160B tokens (20:1 ratio). Training cost: 6  8  109 
1. 6  1011  7. 7  1021 FLOPs.
Config B (inference-aware) :N= 1B,D= 1. 3 T tokens (1300:1 ratio). Training cost: 6  109  1. 3 
1012  7. 8  1021 FLOPs.
Both consume roughly the same training budget. Now consider 1 trillion inference tokens served:
Cinfer, A= 2 8 B 1012 = 1. 6  1022 FLOPs,
Cinfer, B= 2 1 B 1012 = 2 1021 FLOPs.
```

```
14.2 Inference-Aware Token-to-Parameter Ratios
```
Config B costs 8 less per inference token. Across 1T served tokens, the saving is 1. 4  1022 FLOPs-roughly
double the original training budget. Config A’s superiority in raw loss (it was compute-optimal) is wiped out at
any deployment scale above a few billion inference queries.
At the Chinchilla penalty curve’s typical slope, Config B’s loss inflation relative to A is 3-5% in perplex-
ity. For most downstream tasks, that difference is smaller than the variance from data mixture changes. The
deployment math is not even close.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Do not cargo-cult 20:1. The Chinchilla 20:1 ratio was fit on a specific dataset at a specific time. Run
your own isoFLOP analysis on your data mixture; labs routinely find 30-100:1 as the compute-optimal
point, before adjusting for inference.
Estimate your inference-to-training ratio before choosing N. If your deployment will serveMinfer-
ence tokens, andM > 3 D∗, the inference-optimalNis strictly smaller than the Chinchilla-optimalNat
the same training budget.
Cap repetition at 2-3 epochs. Data quality bounds how far you can pushD. Repeating data beyond
about 2 epochs on web-scale corpora measurably hurts loss; the penalty curve steepens sharply past this
point. Unique high-quality tokens are always preferable to repeated lower-quality ones.
Cite the right ratio for MoE models. Hunyuan-Large finds 96:1 for active parameters, but the total
parameter count is far higher due to the mixture-of-experts routing. When comparing ratios across archi-
tectures, always clarify whether the denominator is total or active parameters.
Validate with small-scale proxies before committing. Run 10-20 proxy model pairs spanning 1017 - 1020
FLOPs to fit your own Chinchilla curve. Add 3-5 points at the overtrained end to empirically measure the
penalty slope before you scale up.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Chinchilla says 20 tokens per parameter is optimal. Llama 3 trained a 70B model on roughly 15T
tokens-over 200:1. Was that wasteful?” Strong answer: compute-optimal and deployment-optimal are
different objectives. Chinchilla minimizes training loss per FLOP spent in training; Llama 3’s choice
minimizes total cost across training and serving. At a production scale of billions of daily requests, a
70B model at 200:1 is far cheaper to operate than a Chinchilla-optimal 700B model trained on the same
budget-and the loss difference is empirically small due to improved data quality.
“How would you decide the right token-to-parameter ratio for a new model?” Strong answer: first,
run isoFLOP analysis on small proxies at your data distribution to find the compute-optimal ratio; sec-
ond, estimate your projected inference-to-training ratio from product requirements; third, adjust the ratio
upward from compute-optimal accordingly; fourth, check the overtrained region empirically with a few
small pilot runs before committing the large budget.
Senior follow-up: “Your isoFLOP analysis says 40:1 is optimal, but you only have 500B tokens of
clean licensed data and a 30B-parameter budget. Walk me through your options.” The constrained
ratio is 500 B/ 30 B17 : 1, below compute-optimal. Option 1: shrink the model to 25B parameters
to reach 20:1; you sacrifice some model capacity but achieve compute optimality for the available data.
Option 2: accept the undertrained 30B model-if inference volume is low, the larger model’s quality ad-
vantage may be worth the training inefficiency. Option 3: invest in data acquisition to raise the token
```

```
budget. The right call depends on whether serving cost or model quality is the binding constraint; frame
that trade-off explicitly in the interview.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Chinchilla’s 20:1 optimizes training efficiency; inference-optimal training consistently pushes the ratio to
40:1, 100:1, or higher because serving cost-not training cost-dominates total system spend at production
scale.
Llama 3 finds 39 :1 compute-optimal on modern data; MiniCPM estimates 192:1; Hunyuan uses 96:1
for active parameters. None suffer catastrophic degradation.
The excess-token penalty is real but log-linear and small at moderate overtraining; catastrophic degrada-
tion sets in only after heavy data repetition, typically beyond 2-3 epochs.
Always rerun isoFLOP analysis on your own data mixture; the 20:1 figure is a historical reference point
from one study on one dataset.
When citing token-to-parameter ratios for MoE models, specify whether the denominator is total or active
parameters.
```
**14.2.2 Learning-Rate Schedules: Cosine vs. WSD**
To fit Chinchilla-style scaling curves, you need validation loss as a function of both model size and dataset
size. The dataset-size axis requires training each model to multiple data targets. With a standard cosine learning
rate schedule, every distinct data target demands its own training run from scratch-checkpoints from an ongoing
run are not a valid substitute. At even moderate scales, that requirement is ruinously expensive. MiniCPM
popularized a schedule that reduces thisO(N^2 )cost to roughlyO(1): the Warmup-Stable-Decay schedule, now
so widely copied that training loss curves with sharp late-stage drops have become a recognizable fingerprint of
the approach. The schedule also clarifies something fundamental about why learning rate annealing works at
all-a question with direct relevance to optimizer design interviews at senior and staff level.
A cosine schedule defines a learning rate at steptas:

phase at stept∗is a valid starting point for a fresh decay of lengthTd. The resulting terminal loss is equivalent

This property transforms the Chinchilla analysis procedure. Instead ofKseparate runs from scratch, you
run one stable phase to the maximum token budget, save checkpoints throughout, and applyKshort independent
decays-one per data target. Total compute: stable run+KTdsteps.
_WSD makes the learning rate annealing separable from the data accumulation phase, enabling cheap
Chinchilla-style analysis without sacrificing terminal model quality._
The efficiency gain is intuitive once you understand why the decay phase matters so much. During the stable
phase, the optimizer is taking large, noisy steps through the loss landscape. The model improves steadily but
slowly; the high learning rate prevents settling into any local basin. During the decay phase, the step size shrinks,
and the optimizer converges into a nearby low-loss region. Almost all of the gap between “undertrained stable”
and “fully converged” model quality closes during the decay. This is not unique to WSD: the same phenomenon
happens in cosine schedules, where the final 20-30% of training-when the cosine drops steeply-accounts for a
disproportionate share of the total loss reduction.
The practical implication is that the stable phase is nearly interchangeable across checkpoint positions: a
model at step 50B and a model at step 80B of a stable phase differ in loss by roughly the amount they would
differ on any training run, but they will both converge to approximately the same loss quality after a standard
decay. The stable phase is a continuous bank of launching pads; the decay is the final landing.
This contrasts with cosine, where the learning rate is falling throughout, meaning each step has a slightly
different effective annealing budget. WSD makes the transition sharp and cleanly separated, which is why it
enables checkpoint reuse while cosine does not.
DeepSeek LLM adopted WSD with a two-stage decay (two consecutive decays of roughly 10% of total
compute each), finding the results largely insensitive to the exact decay shape. Their empirical conclusion,
consistent with MiniCPM’s, is that cosine and WSD reach comparable final losses, but WSD’s reusable stable
phase is worth more than any marginal quality difference between the two schedules.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use 10-20% of total compute for the decay phase. MiniCPM and DeepSeek both land in this range. Be-
low 5%, the model fails to fully anneal; you leave several percent of loss improvement on the table. Above
20%, you are running the decay for longer than necessary-returns diminish rapidly after the optimizer has
settled.
Save stable-phase checkpoints at least every 5-10% of total tokens. Coarse checkpointing limits the
granularity of your scaling curve and forces you to interpolate between sparse data points. Dense check-
points are cheap storage relative to the training cost; save them.
Never use early cosine checkpoints for scaling analysis. This is the single most common mistake in
in-house scaling studies. A checkpoint at 25% of a long cosine run has a higher LR than a dedicated
short run fully annealed to that point. The losses are not comparable. If you see published results that use
mid-run cosine checkpoints as data-scale proxies, treat them skeptically.
WSD and cosine are quality-equivalent at the final checkpoint. The advantage of WSD is flexibility,
not quality. If you are training a single model to a fixed token count with no plans to run scaling analysis,
cosine is fine. Choose WSD when you need checkpoint reuse.
The decay phase is the optimizer settling into a basin. If you cut the training run short before the decay
completes, you will see a significant loss elevation. Budget the decay before you commit the training run:
it is not optional.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“You want to fit a Chinchilla scaling law for your model family. A teammate suggests saving check-
points from a single long cosine training run to get multiple data-scale points. What’s wrong with
this?” Strong answer: terminal loss depends on the full learning rate schedule, not just tokens seen. An
early checkpoint in a long cosine run has a higher LR than a dedicated shorter run that fully anneals-the
two models are not equivalent data points on the scaling curve. You will systematically underestimate
loss for short training runs, producing a biased fit. The correct approach is either independent runs or
WSD with checkpoint branching.
“What is the WSD learning rate schedule and why did MiniCPM introduce it?” Strong answer:
WSD separates training into a warmup phase, a flat stable phase, and a short steep decay. The stable
phase is reusable: any stable-phase checkpoint can be branched into an independent decay to produce a
terminal-quality model equivalent to a dedicated shorter training run. MiniCPM introduced it to enable
cheap Chinchilla-style scaling analysis-gettingKdata-scale data points at the cost of one long stable run
plusKshort decays, versusKseparate training runs from scratch.
Senior follow-up: “Why does the decay phase recover so much loss so quickly? What is the optimizer
doing during the stable phase?” The stable phase takes large steps, exploring a wide region of the
loss landscape. High learning rate prevents convergence into any single basin-the model is in a noisy
```

### 14.3 Maximal Update Parameterization (muP)

```
equilibrium between gradient signal and step size. The decay phase gradually reduces step size, allowing
the optimizer to follow the gradient toward the basin bottom. Virtually all the loss improvement relative
to no-cooldown is attributable to the decay. This is why cosine schedules that terminate early (before
the cosine reaches its minimum) produce significantly worse models: the annealing step-not the data
accumulation-drives the final loss improvement.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Cosine LR schedules are training-length-dependent: early checkpoints from a long cosine run are not
equivalent to dedicated shorter runs, making them invalid proxies for Chinchilla scaling analysis.
WSD (Warmup-Stable-Decay) separates data accumulation from annealing: the flat stable phase produces
reusable checkpoints; branching a decay from any stable checkpoint yields terminal-quality results.
WSD reduces the cost ofK-point Chinchilla analysis to one stable run plusK10%of that run’s cost-a
factor of3-5cheaper thanKindependent cosine runs.
The decay phase accounts for nearly all the loss improvement over an unannealed checkpoint; budget
10-20% of total compute for it and never cut it short.
WSD and cosine converge to equivalent final quality; the advantage of WSD is the flexibility of checkpoint
reuse, not intrinsic quality superiority.
```
### 14.3 Maximal Update Parameterization (muP)

**14.3.1 Initialization and Per-Layer Learning Rates**
You carefully tune a learning rate on a 200M proxy run, scale up to 7B, and discover the optimal rate has
shifted by a factor of four. That is the standard parameterization (SP) tax: as models grow wider, the optimal
learning rate migrates predictably downward, forcing expensive re-tuning at every new scale. Maximal Update
Parameterization (μP) eliminates this by choosing initialization variances and per-layer learning rates so that
activation magnitudes and gradient update sizes stayΘ(1)per coordinate regardless of width. At senior MLE
and research engineer interviews you will be expected to explain both why the optimal LR drifts in SP and
exactly howμP fixes it.

2. **Update stability (A2):** After a single gradient step, the change in each activation coordinate is alsoΘ(1),
    i.e.,k∆h(l)k 2 = Θ(pnl).

**14.3.2 What** μ **P Is Robust To and What Breaks It**
Knowing theμP derivation is table stakes. The question that separates practitioners from theorists is: which
production modifications actually break LR transfer, and which ones are safe to apply freely? An interviewer
asking “when would you not useμP” expects a concrete list of failure modes, not a wave of the hand. The
empirical record from Cerebras-GPT, MiniCPM, and a careful third-party ablation study gives a mostly positive
answer with four well-defined caveats you need to know cold.
TheμP promise is that you run a learning-rate sweep over widthsf 128 , 256 , 512 gon a cheap proxy model,
identify the optimalηbaseat the smallest scale, and that sameηbaseremains optimal when you scale to 7B or
70B. The sweep costs a few hundred GPU-hours; the transfer replaces a multi-million-GPU-hour re-tune.
Empirically, Cerebras-GPT demonstrated this end to end across models from 111M to 13B parameters.
Under SP, predicted and actual test loss oscillate because LR must shift at each scale; underμP, the deviation
between the scaling-law prediction and the measured loss collapses substantially. MiniCPM shows the analogous
result on their 30M-1B range: the optimalηbasestays flat near 10 −^2 across an order of magnitude in model size.
The optimal point inηbasespace does not shift.
μ _P does not improve model quality relative to a perfectly tuned SP run-it eliminates the cost of achieving
that perfect tuning at scale._
The LR transfer property survives most architectural variations because those variations do not violate
conditions A1 or A2. Nonlinearities (ReLU, GELU, SwiGLU, squared-ReLU) preserve theΘ(1)per-coordinate
activation property as long as the linear layers are correctly initialized. Batch-size changes rescale the gradient
noise but do not alter the width dependence of the update magnitude. Variations in query initialization (zeroing
WQfor uniform initial attention) also turn out to be harmless because they do not change how activations scale
with width.
WhereμP breaks, the failure modes share a common structure: a new free parameter is introduced whose
magnitude changes with model size, violating theΘ(1)update assumption without a corresponding correction
in the per-layer LR table. The result is a drift in the optimalηbaseacross widths that, if undetected, means your
proxy sweep is steering you to the wrong LR.

**A Worked Example**

Consider the Cerebras-GPT width-sweep experiment. Models of widths 128, 512, and 2048 are trained
under both SP andμP across a grid of learning rates. Under SP, the loss minimum occurs atη 6  10 −^4
for width 128, atη 2  10 −^4 for width 512, and shifts again at width 2048. If you had locked in the width-
128 optimum for the width-2048 run, you would train at 3 the optimal LR and suffer instability or degraded
terminal loss.
UnderμP, the same three widths show a flat optimum: the loss valley sits atηbase 3  10 −^3 regardless
of width. At width 2048 the actual MLP up-projection LR is 3  10 −^3 / 2048  1. 5  10 −^6 , butηbaseitself does

not shift. The proxy sweep transfers exactly.
The Cerebras team also reports that scaling law predictions align much more tightly with measured loss
underμP than SP, because under SP the LR adjustment between scales introduces scatter around the predicted
scaling line.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Remove learnable gains from normalization layers, or set their LR to zero. If your RMSNorm in-
cludes a learnable scalarγinitialized to 1, it acts as an implicit per-layer LR amplifier whose magnitude
can grow during training.μP’s per-layer LR table does not account for this, so LR transfer breaks. Re-
movingγ(or freezing it) restores the invariant. This is the most common production failure mode.
Keep weight decay at or below  0.1. Large-scale ablations show that weight decay above roughly 0.1-
0.3 disrupts LR transfer. The likely mechanism is that strong decay changes the effective learning rate seen
by each layer as a function of weight magnitude, which is itself width-dependent. Standard pretraining
values ofλ= 0. 1 are safe;λ= 0. 3 and above introduce drift.
μ P is optimizer-specific; do not mix and match. The per-layer formulaηl/ 1 /ninis derived for Adam.
Lion (which uses the sign of a momentum-weighted gradient) and Adafactor both alter the update scaling
in width-dependent ways that are not covered by the Adam derivation. If you switch optimizers, re-derive
the correction or expect LR transfer to fail.
Consider the DeepSeek alternative. DeepSeek LLM did not useμP. They instead trained a grid of
models at two small scales, measured the optimal LR and batch size at each scale, fitted a power-law
relationship across FLOPs, and extrapolated to their 7B and 67B targets. The fitted LR curve is visibly
noisier than aμP sweep but gets the order of magnitude right. This approach requires no implementation
complexity, but it costs the grid training runs and assumes that LR follows a clean power law in FLOPs-
an assumption that is somewhat less principled. For a single fixed-target training run where you will not
re-run at multiple scales, direct fitting is a defensible and simpler choice.
μ P is growing but is not yet consensus. As of 2025,μP (or the closely relatedμTransfer variant) is in
use at several frontier labs and was confirmed for Llama 4. Cerebras and MiniCPM published positive
results. Other major runs (DeepSeek, Llama 2, Mistral) did not use it and still achieved high quality
by direct tuning. In an interview, present both strategies and their trade-offs rather than claiming one is
universally correct.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Under what conditions does μ P fail to transfer the learning rate?” Strong answer: three main failure
modes-learnable gains in normalization layers (introduce a scale-dependent implicit LR amplification),
weight decay above0.1-0.3 (disrupts the update-size invariant), and non-Adam optimizers (the per-layer
correction is derived specifically for Adam and does not generalize without re-derivation).
“Cerebras uses μ P, DeepSeek does not. How would you choose for a new 70B training run?” Strong
answer:μP requires clean implementation (per-layer LRs, 1 /dattention scale, no learnable norm gains)
but amortizes the LR sweep cost across all future scaling experiments. Direct fitting is simpler but requires
training a grid at multiple scales, which may cost comparable compute. If you plan to train multiple models
at different scales-a research lab scenario-μP pays off quickly. If you are training one model at a fixed
target scale with a well-understood architecture, direct fitting is equally defensible.
```

## Part VII

# Inference Systems


## Chapter 15 The Inference Workload

### 15.1 Prefill vs. Generation

**15.1.1 Compute-Bound Prefill**
When an interviewer asks you to design a low-latency chat system and then asks “what determines your
time-to-first-token?”, the answer bottoms out in prefill. This phase is what runs before the model emits a single
output token: you feed the entire prompt through the transformer, computing all the intermediate activations
and caching the key and value tensors for every layer. Getting this phase right is the central lever for TTFT,
and understanding _why_ it behaves differently from generation is a foundational piece of inference architecture
knowledge that shows up at every seniority level.
Prefill is the phase in which allSprompt tokens are processed in a single forward pass. Because all
input tokens are known before execution begins, the attention computation can be fully parallelized across the
sequence dimension-exactly as in training. The transformer reads an input matrixX 2 RS×d, passes it through
Llayers of attention and MLP, and produces two outputs: the logit distribution over the vocabulary for the _next_
token, and the KV cache that will be consumed by every subsequent generation step.
The key metric for understanding whether a computation is hardware-limited is _arithmetic intensity_ : the
ratio of floating-point operations to bytes transferred from high-bandwidth memory (HBM).

Arithmetic Intensity= FLOPs
Bytes transferred
For an MLP layer during prefill, the dominant operation is two matrix multiplications (up-projection and
down-projection). With batch sizeBandT=Stokens, the intensity evaluates toBS. For the attention layers,
the QK⊤V computation gives an intensity of roughlyST /(S+T), which simplifies toS/ 2 whenT=S(as it
is during prefill). Both expressions grow with sequence length. On an H100 the roofline crossover for a standard
matrix multiply sits around 295 FLOPs/byte; prefill crosses that line comfortably onceSis even modestly long.
_Prefill is compute-bound: the GPU’s arithmetic units are the bottleneck, not the memory bus, which means
you are extracting close to peak FLOP/s from the hardware._
The reason prefill gets to be compute-bound is structural: every token’s query, key, and value projections
involve the same weight matrices, and withStokens in flight simultaneously you are executing a true matrix-
matrix multiply (X 2 RS×d,W 2 Rd×f). Matrix-matrix multiplies have arithmetic intensity proportional
to the matrix dimensions, so asSgrows you can fully hide the cost of loading weights from HBM behind
arithmetic.
Compare this to the alternative-naive recomputation where you feed one token at a time, recomputing all
prior context from scratch. The complexity per output token would beO(S^2 )in FLOPs because you’d re-attend
over the full prefix. The KV cache removes this redundancy: you payO(S)FLOPs during prefill to populate
it, and thereafter each generation step costsO(1)additional attention FLOPs per prior token. You are trading
memory (storing the KV tensors) for computation (not recomputing them). At inference time, where you have
no gradient bookkeeping, this trade is always worth it.
The practical consequence is that TTFT scales approximately linearly withSunder fixed batch size, and
reducing batch size during prefill gives you better latency at the cost of throughput. Unlike generation, adding
sequences to a prefill batch genuinely helps because the arithmetic intensity scales withBS.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Prefill batch size governs TTFT. ReducingBduring prefill directly lowers TTFT because the compute
time scales withBS. If your SLA is TTFT< 200 ms, you may need to cap concurrent prefill requests
to 1-2, accepting lower GPU utilization during this phase.
Long prompts become the bottleneck faster than you expect. AtS= 8, 192 tokens, prefill on a 13B
model takes 640 ms atB= 1. AtS= 32, 768 it is over 2.5 seconds. If your application has retrieval-
augmented prompts or long system instructions, prefill latency will dominate your TTFT budget even
before generation starts.
Chunked prefill allows interleaving with generation. Some production serving systems split a long
prompt into chunks (e.g., 512 tokens each) and interleave prefill chunks with ongoing generation steps for
other requests. This smooths TTFT distribution at the cost of slightly higher per-request latency variance.
Use it when your tail latency SLA is tight and you have concurrent requests.
Model parallelism affects prefill differently than generation. Tensor parallelism acrossTGPUs cuts
prefill time by roughlyTbecause you are splitting a compute-bound operation. For generation, the
same parallelism provides less benefit because the bottleneck shifts to memory bandwidth.
Flash Attention changes the constant, not the asymptotic bound. Using FlashAttention-2 during prefill
reduces HBM traffic by fusing the attention kernel and avoiding materializing the fullSSattention
matrix. It improves prefill throughput by roughly 2-3on long sequences, but the operation remains
compute-bound; it does not change the fundamental scaling behavior.
```

```
15.1 Prefill vs. Generation
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A user sends a 10,000-token system prompt. Your TTFT is 4 seconds. How do you fix it?” A strong
answer covers: (1) chunked prefill to interleave with ongoing decode; (2) prompt caching-if multiple
requests share the same system prompt prefix, compute the KV cache once and reuse it; (3) reducing tensor
parallelism overhead by verifying all-reduce latency is not dominating; (4) checking GPU utilization to
confirm you are actually compute-bound.
“Why is prefill compute-bound but generation memory-bound?” Strong answer: during prefill you
processStokens simultaneously, so weight reads are amortized overScompute ops per weight element.
During generation you process one token at a time, so each weight matrix is read from HBM to perform
only a matrix-vector multiply-one compute op per weight element loaded.
Senior follow-up: “Suppose you disaggregate prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools. What
are the implications?” The senior answer covers: prefill-optimized hardware can favor high-FLOP-count
GPUs (H100 SXM); decode-optimized hardware benefits more from high memory bandwidth per GPU
(or more GPUs per parameter shard). Disaggregation also lets you scale each pool independently based on
prompt-length distribution and output-length distribution, and eliminates the head-of-line blocking where
a long prefill stalls ongoing decode steps.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel, making it a matrix-matrix multiply with arithmetic intensity
/BS-compute-bound on modern accelerators for any reasonable prompt length.
The output of prefill is the populated KV cache; every generation step that follows reads from this cache,
so prefill is a one-time amortized cost.
TTFT scales linearly with prompt length and batch size. A 4longer prompt means 4 longer TTFT.
Prompt caching (reusing KV tensors across requests sharing a common prefix) can eliminate prefill cost
entirely for repeated system prompts-a high-leverage optimization in production.
Disaggregating prefill and decode onto separate GPU pools lets each be tuned for its regime: compute-
intensive vs. memory-bandwidth-intensive.
```
**15.1.2 Memory-Bound Generation and the KV Cache**
Generation is the phase that breaks most engineers’ intuition the first time they benchmark an LLM in pro-
duction. You have a massively parallel GPU with hundreds of tensor cores and 3.3 TB/s of memory bandwidth,
and yet it is sitting at 5% compute utilization while producing tokens one by one at 80 milliseconds each. The
culprit is arithmetic intensity: generating a single token is a sequence of matrix-vector multiplies, and matrix-
vector multiplies are almost always memory-bound on modern hardware. This bottleneck is the central fact
around which every inference optimization-larger batches, grouped-query attention, quantization, speculative
decoding-is organized. Understanding it at the arithmetic level is what separates a surface-level interview answer
from a strong one.
After prefill, the model enters the _autoregressive generation loop_ : at each step it takes one new token
embedding, runs it through allLtransformer layers, and samples the next token. Crucially, only one new token
is processed per step. The attention layers need to attend over _all_ prior tokens, but the key and value projections
for those prior tokens were already computed during prefill and cached in HBM-the _KV cache_.


```
15.1 Prefill vs. Generation
```

processed so far. Its total size is:

_Generation is memory-bound because producing each token reduces the transformer to a series of matrix-

The KV cache is still the right trade-off despite introducing the memory bottleneck. Without it, each
generation step would recompute the key and value projections for allSprior tokens from scratch, costingO(S)
attention FLOPs per step. With the cache, attention per step costsO(S)bytes read (to load the cache) plus
O(S)FLOPs for the dot products-but the prefill amortized the projection cost. You are trading computation for
memory bandwidth, and for autoregressive generation this trade is always favorable: compute is the constrained
resource during prefill, memory bandwidth is the constraint during generation, and the cache lets each resource
be the binding constraint during its respective phase.
The MLP layers behave differently from attention in an important way. Their arithmetic intensity isB
(the batch size), not 1. This means that by processingBrequests simultaneously, you amortize the cost of
loading each weight matrix overBactivation vectors-you getBuseful FLOPs per byte loaded. AtB= 295on
an H100 you cross the roofline and the MLP becomes compute-bound. Attention, however, gives you no such
relief: because each sequence has its own KV cache, batching does not reduce the bytes loaded per sequence.
The KV cache bytes and FLOPs both scale linearly withB, so the intensity stays pinned near 1 no matter how
large the batch.
This asymmetry has a practical consequence that trips up engineers who only look at MLP utilization:
even if your batch size is large enough to saturate the MLP layers, the attention layers remain memory-bound
throughout generation. The attention layers are therefore the harder constraint to escape.

```
Batch size is your primary throughput knob, up to the memory wall. Every doubling ofBroughly
```
