### 15.2 Latency, Throughput, and Cost

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why is LLM generation slow? What’s the bottleneck?” Strong answer: generation is memory-bound,
not compute-bound. Each step is a series of matrix-vector multiplies (weight matrices times a single token
embedding) and a KV cache read. The arithmetic intensity for both operations isO(1)-O(B), far below
the H100’s roofline of 295 FLOPs/byte. The GPU is bottlenecked by how fast it can stream model weights
and KV cache from HBM, not by how fast its tensor cores can multiply.
“How does increasing batch size help, and when does it stop helping?” Strong answer: largerB
amortizes the cost of loading weight matrices over more activation vectors, raising arithmetic intensity
from 1 toward the roofline for MLP layers. But attention layers give no benefit from batching because
each sequence’s KV cache is independent-intensity stays near 1. The hard ceiling is GPU VRAM: once
BKV cache per sequence+weights exceeds VRAM, the batch does not fit.
Senior follow-up: “The attention arithmetic intensity is always  1 no matter how large the batch. Is
there any architectural change that can actually fix this?” Senior answer: yes, two approaches. First,
reduce KV cache size so fewer bytes are transferred per step: GQA reduces KV heads, MLA projects KV
to a lower-dimensional latent space, and local (sliding-window) attention discards cache entries beyond
a window. Second, eliminate autoregression altogether for generation: diffusion-based language models
generate all tokens in parallel and iterate, turning the problem into a compute-bound one and yielding
5-10throughput improvements at the cost of more complex sampling dynamics.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Generation reduces to matrix-vector multiplies and KV cache reads; both have arithmetic intensityB,
putting generation firmly in the memory-bandwidth-limited regime on all current hardware.
Attention is worse than MLP during generation: its intensity is 1 regardless of batch size because each
sequence owns its own KV cache, eliminating the weight-amortization benefit of batching.
The practical throughput ceiling for a single GPU is set by VRAM capacity: batch size(VRAM
weights)/KV cache per sequence.
Every major inference optimization-GQA, MLA, KV quantization, speculative decoding-targets this mem-
ory bottleneck either by reducing bytes transferred or by restructuring the problem to increase FLOPs per
byte.
Latency and throughput are in direct tension: minimum-latency serving usesB= 1and loads weights
once per request; maximum-throughput serving packs the largestBthat fits in memory.
```
### 15.2 Latency, Throughput, and Cost

**15.2.1 Time-To-First-Token and Inter-Token Latency**
When you are designing a serving system in an interview, the first question is almost always “what are
your latency targets?” The follow-up-the one that separates candidates who have shipped inference from those
who have only read about it-is “which latency?” Time-To-First-Token (TTFT) and inter-token latency (ITL)
are governed by fundamentally different physics, and conflating them leads to the wrong optimization strategy
at every level of the stack. This distinction comes up at mid-level and above for any role touching production
inference.


```
15.2 Latency, Throughput, and Cost
```
**Time-To-First-Token** is how long a user waits between submitting a request and seeing the first generated
character. It is dominated by the _prefill_ phase: encoding allSprompt tokens through allLtransformer layers
in one parallel forward pass. This is structurally identical to a training forward pass-all tokens are available
simultaneously, so the computation parallelizes across the sequence. Prefill is compute-bound whenBTis
large enough to saturate the accelerator.
**Inter-token latency** (also called _decode latency_ or _generation latency_ ) is the time between consecutive
output tokens after the first. Each step produces exactly one new token by loading the full model weights from
HBM, performing a matrix-vector product against the current hidden state, and attending over the growing
KV cache. The arithmetic intensity of this operation is 1 FLOP/byte (one for attention,Bfor MLP-see the
previous subsection), so the step is memory-bandwidth-bound regardless of GPU generation.
The governing equation for per-token generation latency is:
ITLmemory footprint
HBM bandwidth
=^2 P+BCkv
BW
wherePis the parameter count,Ckvis the KV cache size per sequence (bytes),Bis the number of concurrent
sequences, and BW is the peak memory bandwidth of the accelerator. The factor of 2 onPreflects bf16 storage
(2 bytes per parameter).
_TTFT and ITL are governed by different physics-the former by compute throughput, the latter by memory
bandwidth-and any design that treats them as a single “latency” number will optimize for the wrong thing._
Prefill is fast because the transformer can process allStokens in a single batched matrix multiply. The
arithmetic intensity during prefill scales asBS: a batch of one request with a 4096-token prompt has intensity
 4096 , comfortably above the H100’s roofline of 295 FLOPs/byte. TTFT is therefore roughly proportional
toSand inversely proportional to sustained compute throughput-something you cannot improve without either
reducing the prompt or adding accelerators.
Generation is slow because each autoregressive step is equivalent to a matrix-vector product: you are
loading the full weight matrixW 2 RD×Dto computeW xfor a single vectorx 2 RD. The ratio of FLOPs
to bytes is 2 D^2 /(2D^2 ) = 1, essentially 1 FLOP per byte transferred. Modern H100s achieve 989 TFLOP/s
and 3. 35 TB/s bandwidth, so the compute-to-bandwidth ratio is 989 / 3. 35  295. A batch size of 1 operates
at intensity 1- 295 below what it would need to saturate compute. Without a KV cache the situation would be
even worse: each generation step would re-encode the entire prefix atO(S)cost, givingO(S^2 )total work. The
KV cache trades memory for time, convertingO(S^2 )generation toO(S)-a fundamental architectural choice
that determines every other inference optimization.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Set separate SLOs for TTFT and ITL. A latency budget of “< 200 ms” is ambiguous. Reasonable
starting points for interactive chat: TTFT< 500 ms, ITL< 50 ms. Batch pipelines can relax TTFT to
seconds while holding ITL tight for tail latency.
Quantize weights to cut ITL directly. Switching from bf16 to INT8 halvesMweights, cutting ITL roughly
in half at no change to model architecture. INT4 cuts it to25%of bf16. For a 13B model: INT8 brings
ITL from 8 ms to 4 ms. This is the cheapest ITL reduction available before touching architecture.
TTFT grows linearly with prompt length; prune prompts aggressively. Every additional 1000 prompt
tokens adds 2  13 B 1000 / 989 T 26 ms to TTFT on a 13B model. Summarization or truncation
strategies that halve average prompt length halve average TTFT.
Chunked prefill trades TTFT for system-level ITL. When a long prompt arrives, splitting it into fixed-
size chunks processed across multiple steps allows the GPU to interleave prefill with generation steps
from other in-flight requests. The chunked request’s TTFT increases, but queued requests no longer stall
behind a multi-second prefill job. Use this when p99 ITL matters more than p50 TTFT.
Multi-GPU tensor parallelism reduces TTFT, not ITL, proportionally. Splitting the model acrossK
GPUs splits the prefill FLOPs byK, cutting TTFT roughlyK-fold. ITL also improves becauseMweights
per GPU drops, but you now pay inter-GPU communication latency on every generation step-a non-trivial
overhead on largeK. For latency-sensitive serving, preferK= 2orK= 4; beyond that, communication
dominates.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What’s the difference between TTFT and inter-token latency, and which matters more for a stream-
ing chat product?” Strong answer: TTFT is prefill time (compute-bound, scales with prompt length and
model size); ITL is per-token generation time (memory-bandwidth-bound, scales with model weight bytes
and batch KV cache size). For streaming chat, ITL dominates user experience: a 200 ms TTFT is invis-
ible, but 100 ms ITL makes text feel sluggish. Optimize ITL via quantization and KV cache reduction;
optimize TTFT via multi-GPU prefill or prompt pruning.
“You’re serving a 70B model and a user sends a 50k-token prompt. Walk me through what happens
to TTFT.” Strong answer: TTFT scales as 2 PS/compute. At 50k tokens on a single H100: 2  70 B
50000 / 989 T 7 s. This is unacceptable for interactive use. Solutions: distribute prefill across multiple
GPUs (pipeline or tensor parallel), use chunked prefill with a short-context draft first, or compress the
prompt before sending.
```

```
latency for other requests?” Senior answer: Chunked prefill processes the prompt indS/Cechunks of
sizeCtokens each. Between chunks, the scheduler can insert generation steps for other active requests.
The KV cache for the chunked request grows incrementally-each chunk appends to it-so memory usage
is identical to non-chunked prefill at completion. The benefit is that long-prompt requests no longer
monopolize the GPU for seconds at a time, dramatically reducing p99 ITL for the rest of the request
queue. The cost is aO(S^2 /C)increase in total prefill FLOPs due to partial attention recomputation
across chunk boundaries-tunable by choice ofC.
```

```
The two metrics are decoupled: halving model weights halves ITL but does not change TTFT; halving
prompt length halves TTFT but does not change ITL.
Quantization (bf16!INT8) is the highest-leverage, lowest-risk way to reduce ITL; it applies immediately
to any trained model.
Always set separate SLOs; a single “latency” target will cause you to over-optimize one metric at the
expense of the other.
```

**15.2.2 Throughput Trade-Offs Under Batching**
Every LLM serving team hits the same wall within weeks of launch: per-request latency looks fine at one
query per second, but the GPU sits at30%utilization and cost-per-token is an order of magnitude higher than
projected. The answer is batching-processing multiple requests simultaneously to amortize model weight loads
across more useful work. But batching has its own ceiling, and the math behind that ceiling explains both why
your throughput stalls and what architectural choices (GQA, quantization, replica scaling) give you the biggest
gains. This trade-off is a core topic at senior and staff levels wherever inference cost matters.
**Throughput** is the total number of tokens generated per second across all users, in contrast to per-user
latency which measures a single request’s experience. During the memory-bound generation phase, the system
performs one decode step per token, and the cost of that step is:

AtB= 1, loading 26 GB of weights produces one token: you get 1 token per weight-load. AtB= 32,

at unchanged latency. Replicas require no inter-GPU communication and are the first scaling lever you should

## Chapter 16 Reducing the KV Cache

### 16.1 Attention Variants for Cheaper Inference.

**16.1.1 Multi-Query and Grouped-Query Attention (GQA)**
When an interviewer asks you to design a serving stack for a 70B model and your napkin math shows that
the KV cache will overflow VRAM at any reasonable batch size, _grouped-query attention_ is the first architectural
lever to reach for. GQA is the change that moved from research curiosity to default in every serious open-weight
model-Llama 3, Mistral, Qwen, Falcon-within about a year of its introduction, and interviewers at inference-
heavy teams will expect you to know it cold and be able to quantify its impact.
Standard _multi-head attention_ (MHA) computesNquery heads,Nkey heads, andNvalue heads per token
per layer. The KV cache therefore stores 2 NHvalues per token per layer, whereHis the head dimension.
Because every sequence in a batch owns its own independent KV cache, this cost scales linearly with batch size,
sequence length, and layer count, and it is the primary reason generation remains memory-bound regardless of
how many queries you batch together.
_Multi-query attention_ (MQA) pushed this to the extreme: share a single key head and a single value head
across allNquery heads. The KV cache shrinks by a factor ofN, but in practice MQA degrades model quality
noticeably, especially at larger scales-the single shared KV head is not expressive enough.
_Grouped-query attention_ (GQA) occupies the Pareto-optimal middle ground. You partition theNquery
heads intoGgroups ofN/Gheads each, and each group shares one key head and one value head. Defining
K=N/Gas the number of KV heads:

```
KV cache size per token per layer= 2KHbytes per element
```
SettingK=Nrecovers MHA; settingK= 1recovers MQA. In practiceG= 8(i.e.,K=N/ 8 ) preserves
accuracy nearly identically to MHA while cutting the KV cache by 8 .
_GQA is the lowest-cost architectural change that shrinks the KV cache without meaningful accuracy loss,
enabling either lower latency at the same batch size or a larger batch at the same latency._
The accuracy robustness of GQA comes from what the key and value projections actually learn. Within a
group ofN/Gquery heads, the queries are already diverse-each attends to different positions and features. The
key and value vectors, by contrast, encode the information content at each position, which is less sensitive to
which specific query is asking. Sharing KV within a group turns out to be a mild constraint; the queries still
specialize while the KV tensors carry shared context.
The throughput gain is two-fold. First, the direct reduction:KKV heads instead ofNmeansN/K=G
times fewer bytes transferred from HBM per generation step, directly proportional to speed-up since generation
is memory-bandwidth-bound. Second, an indirect gain: the freed VRAM can accommodate a larger batch size.
Before GQA, a 13B model atS= 1, 000 andB= 64required over 50 GB just for the KV cache on a standard
MHA model; with GQA atG= 8that drops to 6 GB, leaving room to pushBwell above 200 on a single 80
GB H100.
The comparison point is MQA. MQA also reduces memory but pays a quality tax that compounds at larger
model scales. GQA effectively shows that the quality-memory trade-off curve is non-linear: you can recover
almost all of MHA’s quality with onlyK=N/ 8 KV heads rather thanK=N, a point on the curve that gives
you most of the memory benefit for almost none of the accuracy cost.


```
16.1 Attention Variants for Cheaper Inference
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider Llama-2 70B:N= 64query heads,H= 128,L= 80layers, bf16 (2 bytes per element), with
batch sizeB= 32and sequence lengthS= 2, 048.
**MHA KV cache.** Per token per layer: 2  64  128 2 = 32, 768 bytes. Total:
32  2048  80  32 , 768 bytes 171 GB

This overflows a single 80 GB H100 even before counting the 140 GB of model weights. You cannot run this
batch on one GPU.
**GQA with** G= 8 **(** K= 8 **).** Per token per layer: 2  8  128 2 = 4, 096 bytes. Total KV cache:
32  2048  80  4 , 096 bytes 21. 5 GB

Combined with weights:140 + 21.5 = 161. 5 GB-fits comfortably on two H100s, and a single H100 can handle
B 10 at this sequence length.
**Throughput estimate at** B = 32 **with GQA, two H100s.** Total bytes transferred per generation step:
161. 5 GB. Aggregate bandwidth: 2  3 .35 = 6. 7 TB/s. Step latency: 161. 5 / 6700  24 ms. Throughput:
32 / 0. 024  1 , 333 tokens/second. Without GQA, this batch simply does not fit.
**Accuracy check.** Empirically, GQA atG= 8recovers99%of MHA perplexity across standard bench-
marks for models at 7B-70B scale. The quality cost is negligible for downstream tasks.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Default to G= 8 for any model  7 B. This is the empirically validated sweet spot. Below 7B you may
still useG= 4or even MQA without noticeable downstream degradation because the models are less
sensitive to head expressiveness.
GQA changes your VRAM ceiling, not just your speed. The more important effect is often that GQA
makes a batch size possible that was previously impossible, not that it speeds up an already-fitting batch.
Always recompute your max batch size after adopting GQA-the number often increases by 4 - 8 .
Weight sharing means the projection weights are shared too. In CLA the weights are explicitly shared
across layers; in GQA, the sameWKandWV matrices produce the keys and values used by multiple
query heads within a group. If you are loading a GQA checkpoint, the key-value projection matrices are
smaller than query projection matrices by a factor ofG.
GQA is free at training time, not just inference time. Training with GQA is slightly faster than MHA
because you compute fewer KV projections. Models trained from scratch with GQA converge to the same
loss as MHA models; you do not need to fine-tune or distill a pre-trained MHA model into GQA.
For G > 16 , check accuracy on your target task. The gap between GQA and MHA is small for
G 8 , but it widens for aggressive settings. For retrieval-heavy workloads (RAG, long-context question
answering), the KV diversity may matter more than for generation tasks-run an eval before committing to
extreme compression ratios.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Your KV cache is overflowing VRAM at the batch size you need. How do you fix it architecturally?”
Strong answer: the primary lever is GQA-reduce the number of KV heads fromNtoN/GwithG= 8
as the default, shrinking the KV cache by 8 with negligible accuracy impact. Secondary levers include
KV quantization (int8 halves the cache further) and sliding-window attention on non-critical layers.
```

```
16.1 Attention Variants for Cheaper Inference
```
```
“What is the difference between MQA, GQA, and MHA? When would you use each?” Strong an-
swer: MHA usesNKV heads (maximum expressiveness, maximum cache), MQA uses 1 KV head (min-
imum cache, measurable quality loss at scale), GQA usesK=N/GKV heads sharing one KV pair per
group ofGqueries (best accuracy-memory trade-off, used in all modern production models). MQA is
now obsolete for large models; GQA is the default; MHA survives only in legacy architectures or small
models where memory is not the bottleneck.
Senior follow-up: “You’re training a new 70B model from scratch. A colleague proposes using MHA
because it’s simpler and GQA is a “trick.” How do you respond, and what training experiments
would settle the debate?” Senior answer: GQA is not a post-hoc trick-it is a design decision made
at model initialization. Train two identical models at 7B scale (a proxy) withG= 8GQA and MHA
respectively, evaluate on a downstream task suite and measure KV cache size at target serving batch size.
If GQA shows< 1%degradation, adopt it for the 70B run. The inference cost reduction justifies the
negligible quality delta in almost every production setting.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
GQA reduces the number of KV heads fromNtoK=N/G, shrinking the KV cache by a factor ofG
with near-zero accuracy loss atG 8.
The cache reduction is doubly beneficial: fewer bytes per step means faster generation, and freed VRAM
enables larger batch sizes that further improve throughput.
For Llama-2 70B withG= 8, the KV cache atB = 32,S= 2, 048 drops from 171 GB (MHA,
impossible on one or two H100s) to 22 GB (GQA, easily fits alongside model weights).
GQA is applied at training time, not as a post-hoc compression step; production models from Llama 3
onward are trained with GQA by default.
MQA (G=N) is the degenerate case-maximum memory savings but unacceptable accuracy loss at scale;
GQA is the right balance.
```
**16.1.2 Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA)**
GQA attacks the KV cache along one axis: reduce the number of heads. _Multi-Head Latent Attention_
(MLA), introduced in DeepSeek V2, attacks a different axis: project the key and value tensors into a shared
low-dimensional latent before storing them, then reconstruct the full-rank KV at query time. The compression
ratios MLA achieves-up to 31 in DeepSeek’s configuration-dwarf what GQA alone can deliver, and MLA
is the design behind some of the most inference-efficient frontier models available. Senior interviews at labs
building or deploying frontier models will expect you to understand the mechanism and its implications.
In standard MHA, each token at each layer stores 2 NHvalues in the KV cache:Nkey vectors and
Nvalue vectors each of dimensionH. GQA reducesNtoK=N/Gbut leaves each head’s dimensionalityH
untouched. MLA takes the complementary approach: keep allNheads but _compress their joint representation_
into a single latent vector of dimensionCNH.
Concretely, MLA introduces a down-projection matrixWDKV 2 Rd×Cand an up-projection matrix
WUK 2 RC×(N×H)for keys (and an analogous pair for values). The cached quantity per token per layer is
the compressed latent:
ct=WDKVxt 2 RC


```
16.1 Attention Variants for Cheaper Inference
```
At query time, the full key matrix is reconstructed on the fly:

```
Kt=ctWUK 2 RN×H
```
The cache therefore storesCvalues per token per layer instead of 2 NH. In DeepSeek V2,N = 128,
H= 128, so the uncompressed KV size is 2  128 128 = 32, 768 values per token. WithC= 512, the cache
stores only 512 values-a 64 compression on the stored representation, though in practice a small number of
extra dimensions must be retained for positional encoding (see below), bringing effective compression to roughly
31 .
The one structural complication is RoPE compatibility. Standard RoPE applies a position-dependent rota-
tion to the key and query vectors before the attention dot product. With MLA, the keys are reconstructed from
the latentct, which is position-agnostic. The solution DeepSeek adopted is to cache an additional small set
of _decoupled RoPE keys_ alongside the latent, keeping positional information accessible without expanding the
main cache significantly.
_MLA stores a low-rank compressed latent of the KV representation rather than the full KV tensors, achiev-
ing compression ratios far beyond what head-count reduction alone can provide, at the cost of up-projection
compute at every query step._
The key intuition is that across allNheads in a layer, the key and value projections of a single token are not
2 NHindependent numbers-they share substantial structure because they all derive from the same token
embeddingxt 2 Rd. A rank-Cprojection can capture most of this structure whenCis chosen appropriately
relative to the intrinsic dimensionality of the token-space representation.
The trade-off MLA makes is compute for memory. Every query step now incurs an additional matrix
multiply to up-project the cached latent back to full KV-C(NH)FLOPs per head per token in the KV cache.
Since generation is memory-bandwidth-bound, spending a modest amount of additional compute is a favorable
trade if it dramatically reduces the bytes transferred. Whether the up-projection cost is worth it depends on the
compression ratioC/(2N H): at DeepSeek’s 31 compression, the saved bandwidth far outweighs the extra
multiply.
Compared to GQA, MLA offers much higher compression but is substantially harder to implement. GQA
requires only reshaping the KV tensors during the attention kernel; MLA requires custom kernel support for the
up-projection step inside the attention computation, and the RoPE decoupling adds further complexity. This is
why GQA has seen broad adoption across many model families while MLA has so far stayed primarily within
the DeepSeek ecosystem.

512 + 64 = 576values per token per layer.
**KV cache comparison at** B= 1 **,** S= 128, 000 **(128K context).**

interactive serving.
MLA: 576  128 , 000  60  2 bytes 8. 8 GB. Fits on a single 80 GB H100 alongside model weights.
**Compression ratio:** 32 , 768 / 576  56. 9 in theory, 31 accounting for the RoPE overhead and
practical implementation details.
**Up-projection cost per generation step.** At each step, for each of theS= 128, 000 cached tokens, you

perform one up-projection:C!NHfor keys and an analogous one for values. FLOPs per layer per step:


At H100’s 989 TFLOP/s: roughly 2 ms per layer per step. Summed over 60 layers this is significant-roughly 120
ms of extra FLOPs per token at full 128K context. In practice this is fused with the attention kernel and partially
hidden behind memory latency, so the effective overhead is lower. The bandwidth savings (from reading 576
values instead of 32,768 per cached token) dominate at long contexts.
**Breakeven context length.** MLA only wins when the bandwidth savings exceed the extra compute cost.
For DeepSeek’s numbers, this breakeven is roughlyS 4 , 000 tokens-well within the range of practical long-
context serving. Below 4K context, the overhead of up-projection matters more and MLA may not outperform

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
MLA is the right choice when targeting very long contexts ( S 8 , 000 ) and bandwidth is the bind-
ing constraint. The bandwidth reduction scales withSwhile the up-projection cost scales identically-so
MLA’s advantage grows with context length. For short-context workloads, GQA is simpler and compet-
itive.
The up-projection kernels must be custom. Standard attention kernels (FlashAttention, cuDNN) do
not natively support MLA’s expand-then-attend pattern. Deploying MLA requires either a custom CUDA
kernel or a serving framework that has integrated MLA support. Factor this into your build vs. buy
decision when selecting a serving stack.
Latent dimension C is a hyperparameter with a clear sensitivity. In DeepSeek’s ablations, reducing
Cbelow 256 caused measurable perplexity increases;C = 512maintained accuracy near the MHA
baseline. UseCd/ 8 as a starting point, wheredis the model dimension.
RoPE decoupling adds a fixed overhead. The extradrope= 64dimensions stored per token per layer
are unavoidable if you want full positional expressiveness. Plan for this in your KV cache sizing-at long
contexts it is a small fraction of the latent size but worth accounting for in exact memory calculations.
GQA and MLA are orthogonal in principle but rarely combined in practice. GQA reduces head
count; MLA reduces per-head dimensionality. A model could use both simultaneously, but the engi-
neering complexity is additive. In current deployments, teams pick one: GQA for simplicity and broad
ecosystem support, MLA for maximum compression at long context.
```

### 16.2 Cross-Layer and Local Attention

**16.2.1 Cross-Layer KV Sharing**
You have already deployed GQA and your KV cache is still the binding memory constraint at large batch
sizes or long context. The follow-up question in the interview, almost inevitably, is: _what else can you do without
changing the number of KV heads or the per-head dimension?_ Cross-Layer Attention (CLA) is the answer that
shows up at senior and staff-level design rounds. It is conceptually simple, the math is one line, and it produces
cache reductions that compound multiplicatively with GQA.
In a standard transformer, every layerℓhas its own key and value projection matricesWKℓ andWVℓ. During
generation, each layer writes its own KV slice to the cache, so total KV memory scales asLTNkvh 4
bytes (layerstokensKV headshead dimK-and-V-in-bf16). The layer countLmultiplies every other
factor: cutting it is a direct win.
CLA groups layers into blocks of sizeGand forces all layers in a group to share the projection matrices of
the first (leader) layer. For a group starting at layerg 0 , every layerℓ2fg 0 , g 0 + 1,... , g 0 +G 1 gcomputes:

```
Kℓ=X WKg^0 , Vℓ=X WVg^0.
```
At inference time, the KV vectors are computed once for the group and reused. Layersg 0 +1throughg 0 +G 1
point back to the leader’s cache slice; no new memory is allocated for them. The query projectionsWQℓremain
independent per layer, so the model retains its full expressive capacity on the query side.
The cache reduction is exact: instead ofLindependent KV slices you storeL/G, cutting KV memory by
a factor ofG.


```
16.2 Cross-Layer and Local Attention
```
_CLA does for the depth dimension what GQA does for the head dimension: it amortizes the KV cost through
sharing, and the two techniques compose multiplicatively._
The intuition draws on the same logic as GQA. Adjacent layers in a deep residual network process infor-
mation at similar levels of abstraction. The attention pattern - which positions a query attends to - is largely
determined by key-vector content, and the structure relevant at layerℓis not radically different from the struc-
ture at layerℓ 1. Empirically, models trained with sharing ratioG= 2show negligible perplexity degradation;
G= 4begins to hurt on tasks that demand precise long-range recall.
The trade-off to name explicitly is _expressiveness versus memory_. Value vectors encode the information
mixed into each output, so sharing them means higher layers in a group cannot independently learn what _content_
to retrieve - only what _positions_ to query. This is the binding constraint that limits how aggressively you can
pushG. In practice,G= 2sits comfortably on the Pareto curve; beyondG= 4expect accuracy regressions on
retrieval-heavy benchmarks.
CLA contrasts with MLA (Multi-Head Latent Attention), which shrinks KV size by low-rank compression
along the head-dimension axis. CLA instead reduces the number of independent KV slices across depth. They
are complementary: you can stack CLA on top of MLA for compounded savings.

```
RoPE compatibility is not an issue. RoPE is applied to queries and keys before the dot product, so the
```

```
“You’ve deployed GQA on your serving cluster. What other architectural lever reduces KV cache

Senior follow-up: “How does CLA interact with tensor parallelism and disaggregated KV caching?”
With tensor parallelism, each device holds a shard of the KV heads. The shared KV shard still lives

fresh projection. Communication overhead per decode step decreases byGbecause you issue one KV-
projection communication per group rather than one per layer. In disaggregated serving, where the KV
cache is offloaded to CPU or remote memory, CLA reduces the volume transferred back on every decode
step byG- since that transfer is often the dominant latency term in disaggregated architectures, the benefit
is disproportionately large.
```

**16.2.2 Sliding-Window and Hybrid Attention Layers**
Even after deploying GQA and CLA, a model supporting 128K-token contexts faces a memory wall. A 32-
layer model with 8 KV heads and head dimension 128, in bf16, stores 32  8  128 4 = 131, 072 bytes of KV
per token per sequence: atT= 131, 072 that is roughly 17 GB per sequence, exhausting an H100 before you fit


```

```
a single request. Sliding-window attention, combined with periodic full-attention layers in a hybrid architecture,
is the mechanism frontier models use to serve contexts of 128K to 1M tokens without that blowup. This shows
up in senior design rounds under any question framed as “design a long-context serving system” or “how does
LLaMA 4 support 10M-token contexts.”
In standard causal attention, the query at positiontattends to all past tokensf 0 , 1 ,... , t 1 g. The KV
cache for that layer grows without bound asTincreases. Sliding-window (local) attention restricts each query
to the most recentWtokens:


The KV cache for a local layer never exceedsWentries per layer, regardless ofT. Once the sequence passes
positionW, old KV entries evict from the sliding window. Cache memory per local layer is a constantW
Nkvh 4 bytes - no dependence on sequence length.
A pure sliding-window model has no long-range recall: it cannot attend to any token more thanWpositions
back. The fix is the _hybrid architecture_ : place one full (global) attention layer everyklocal layers. Global
layers maintain the fullT-length KV cache and handle long-range dependencies; local layers handle short-range
coherence cheaply and constitute the majority of the stack.
_Hybrid attention converts a hard memory cliff into a tunable dial: you pay full-attention cost only on_ 1 /k
_of your layers, and you choose_ k _based on how much long-range recall your workload demands._
The motivating fact is empirical: the overwhelming majority of next-token predictions depend on the last
few hundred to few thousand tokens. The hard cases - retrieving a fact stated 50K tokens earlier, resolving a
coreference across a long document - are a small fraction of all generation steps. A handful of global layers
scattered through the stack handles them without forcing every layer to maintain the full context. On standard
language modelling benchmarks, replacing five out of every six attention layers with local layers produces nearly
identical perplexity, while peak KV memory drops by 3 - 5 at 32K context and 10 or more at 128K.
The alternative is learned sparse attention (Longformer-style dilated windows, block-sparse patterns). Those
are more expressive for specialized tasks but require custom CUDA kernels and break compatibility with stan-
dard FlashAttention implementations. Hybrid attention is trivial to implement: the only change between a local
and a global layer is the range of KV pairs fetched. You get the memory savings with no new infrastructure.
A second-order benefit appears at _training_ time. Local layers haveO(TW)attention cost rather than
O(T^2 ), so training on long sequences becomes far more tractable, enabling the longer context windows that the
serving system then exploits.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Global layer frequency k : Usek= 4(one global per four layers) as a conservative default. Gemma and

tasks. Drop to 2 , 048 only for workloads that are demonstrably short-range (single-sentence generation,
classification). For multi-file code generation where function signatures and imports span many thousands
of tokens, preferW= 8, 192.
The no-RoPE trick on global layers (LLaMA 4-style): Apply RoPE only to local layers; use position-
free full attention on global layers. Without a positional encoding, the global layer’s attention scores
depend purely on content similarity, not distance. This makes the model near-insensitive to absolute token
position on the global pathway, enabling context-length extrapolation well beyond the training window
without ALiBi or positional interpolation. Use this when your serving target context is significantly longer
than your training context.
Combining with CLA: Apply cross-layer KV sharing within each run of local layers. Five consecutive
local layers in a group can be CLA-2 paired, cutting their already-cappedW-entry caches by a further
factor of 2. The savings are additive in log-memory terms and require no changes to the global layers.
Eviction strategy: The default is FIFO - evict the oldest token when the window is full. For tasks with
multiple salient anchors spread across the context (legal document review, multi-turn dialogue with back-
references), “heavy hitter” eviction - retain theW/ 2 most recently attended-to positions plus theW/ 2
most recent positions - materially improves recall quality at the same cache budget.
```

```
Senior follow-up: “Explain the LLaMA 4 no-RoPE global layer and its failure modes.” Without
positional encoding, the global layer treats all positions as equidistant and attends purely on content sim-

decaying positional bias to interfere with distant attention. The failure mode is false-positive retrieval:
the model may attend to a content-similar but irrelevant token far away in preference to the correct nearby
token, because nothing in the attention score penalises distance. This shows up as degraded performance
on needle-in-haystack benchmarks with high-similarity distractors. The mitigation is to keep global layers
sparse enough that they are reserved for genuine long-range retrieval needs, rather than routine next-token
coherence.
```

## Chapter 17 Going Beyond the Transformer for Inference

### 17.1 State-Space and Linear-Attention Models

**17.1.1 Mamba and Associative Recall Tasks**
The most direct path to faster generation is changing what the model stores. Every trick applied to the KV
cache-GQA, MLA, cross-layer sharing-still leaves a memory footprint that grows linearly with context length.
A senior interview question in serving-system design often goes: “What architectural change would eliminate
that growth entirely?” State-space models, and specifically Mamba, are the answer interviewers are probing for.
This topic shows up at staff and principal level, where the expectation is that you can explain the RNN duality,
name the specific failure mode of early SSMs on language tasks, and sketch a hybrid deployment strategy with
numbers.
State-space models derive from classical linear dynamical systems. A continuous-time SSM maps an input
signalx(t)to an outputy(t)through a hidden stateh(t):

```
h′(t) =Ah(t) +Bx(t), y(t) =Ch(t)
```
Discretized with step size∆, this becomes a recurrence:

```
ht=Ah ̄ t− 1 +Bx ̄ t, yt=Cht
```
whereA ̄andB ̄are the discretized matrices derived fromA,B, and∆. At generation time, producing token
t+ 1requires loading onlyht-a fixed-size vector of dimensionN-not an ever-expanding KV cache. The state
htis the model’s entire memory of the past.
The same recurrence can be re-expressed as a convolution during training:
y=K ̄x, where K ̄=

#### 

#### CB, C ̄ A ̄B, C ̄ A ̄^2 B,... ̄

#### 

This is parallelizable via a parallel scan inO(TlogT)time, giving training efficiency comparable to a trans-
former.
The problem with early SSMs like S4 is thatA ̄andB ̄are fixed for all inputs-every token blends into the
state identically regardless of content. This fails on _associative recall_ : given a sequence of key-value pairs
followed by a query key, retrieve the matching value. Fixed linear blending cannot isolate one binding from
others; the signal is diluted by all intervening content.
Mamba resolves this by making the discretization input-dependent:
B ̄t=B(xt), ∆t= ∆(xt), Ct=C(xt)

When the model sees a query that matches a prior key, the input-dependent gate can sharpen the state to amplify
that specific binding and suppress others. This selective SSM passes MQAR (Multi-Query Associative Recall)
benchmarks that defeat all fixed-parameter SSMs.
_Mamba’s selective state-space mechanism gives an RNN the content-based memory it needs to match trans-
former quality on language tasks while keeping generation cost proportional to hidden state size rather than
context length._
The argument is bandwidth. At generation stepta standard transformer reads the entire per-sequence
KV cache:O(SdL)bytes, growing with every generated token. The attention arithmetic intensity during
generation is always approximately 1-the KV cache is sequence-specific, so batchingBrequests together does


```
17.1 State-Space and Linear-Attention Models
```
not amortize the memory read; the batch dimension cancels in the intensity formula.
Mamba’s generation reads a hidden state of sizeO(dinnerNL)bytes per sequence, wheredinner= 2d
is the expanded channel dimension andNis the state dimension (typically 16). This is fixed: it does not grow
withS. AtS= 8, 192 , the transformer’s KV cache dominates bandwidth; Mamba’s state is a rounding error
beside the weight load.
The trade-off is recall fidelity. A fixed-size state is a lossy compression of history. At very long contexts-
say, multi-hop retrieval across a 128k-token document-a pure Mamba model will lose long-range references
that a transformer would find cleanly. This is not a design flaw; it is a fundamental consequence of finite state
capacity. The practical response is a hybrid architecture: use Mamba blocks for the vast majority of layers
(cheap, constant-state generation) and insert sparse full-attention layers every 4-8 blocks as global checkpoints
that can attend to anything in the prefix without compression loss. Early SSMs like S4 used fixed HiPPO-
initialized matrices tuned for smooth continuous signals; they had no mechanism for content-based gating at all.
Mamba’s selection mechanism is the critical upgrade.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B Mamba model withd= 4, 096 ,dinner= 8, 192 , state dimensionN= 16,L= 32layers,
B= 8concurrent sequences, contextS= 8, 192 , bf16 weights on an H100 (80 GB HBM, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth).
**Transformer KV cache (equivalent architecture).** Per layer per sequence:
Snheadsdhead 2  2 bytes= 8192 32  128 4 = 128MB

Across 32 layers andB= 8: 128  32 8 = 32, 768 MB= 32GB, plus 14 GB of model weights-46 GB total.

```
“What is associative recall, and why did early state-space models fail at it?” Strong answer: Asso-
```

linear attention preserves the query-key-value interface of the transformer, making it straightforward to inherit
pretrained weights or fine-tune an existing checkpoint toward more efficient inference without re-parameterizing
the attention heads.

```
Hybrid layer ratio. A 3:1 ratio (three linear layers per one full-attention layer) recovers approximately
95% of full-transformer perplexity on standard language benchmarks while cutting KV cache to 25% of
a full model’s cost. A 7:1 ratio is viable for low-retrieval workloads such as open-ended generation or
summarization. Do not go beyond 8:1 on agentic or long-document workloads without running needle-
in-a-haystack evaluations first.
Feature map choice. ELU+1 is simple but can produce near-zeroztvalues early in a sequence, leading
to division instability. Add a floor in your implementation:z = torch.clamp(z, min=1e-6). A more
robust alternative is Gated Linear Attention (GLA), which adds an input-dependent forget gate-analogous
to Mamba’s selection mechanism-and significantly improves performance on associative recall tasks at
the cost of a slightly more complex recurrence.
```

```
tional encoding. In practice, restrict RoPE (or any rope-like encoding) to the full-attention layers and
treat linear-attention layers as position-agnostic. They remain effective because local ordering cues are
encoded in the token content itself.
State size at large model width. Atd= 8, 192 (typical for a 70B model), the linear state per head per
layer is 128  128 2 = 32KB, per layer 64 heads x 32 KB = 2 MB, across 56 linear layers atB= 8gives

Training stability. Linear attention loss curves are typically noisier than softmax attention early in train-
ing, especially whenztis small. If initializing from a pretrained transformer, keep the first 4-8 layers as
full attention during the initial fine-tuning phase and unfreeze the remaining linear layers gradually over
the first 1k steps. Gradient clipping at 1.0 and a short linear warmup of 500 steps are usually sufficient to
stabilize.
```

### 17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation

**17.2.1 Diffusion Language Models**
When a senior engineer at a frontier lab asks you how you would redesign the text generation stack if the
autoregressive constraint were lifted, they are probing whether you understand the _root cause_ of inference ineffi-
ciency rather than just its symptoms. Diffusion language models answer that question by abandoning sequential
generation entirely, producing all output tokens simultaneously and then refining them across a fixed number
of forward passes. This approach has moved from a research curiosity to a production-relevant architecture
rapidly, and understanding its mechanics is now a legitimate interview topic at labs building the next generation
of serving infrastructure.
Autoregressive models are forced to generate one token at a time because each token conditions on all
preceding tokens. Diffusion models break this constraint by starting from a fully noisy or masked sequence of
the target length and iteratively denoising it toward coherent text. At each refinement stept, the model receives
the current noisy sequencextand predicts a cleaner versionxt− 1 , untilx 0 is the final output afterKsteps.
The decisive structural difference is that every refinement step processes the entire output sequence in
a single forward pass. If you are generating a response of lengthLtokens, the model sees allLpositions
simultaneously at every step. This is structurally identical to the prefill phase of an autoregressive model, not
its generation phase. There is no KV cache that grows with sequence length, because there is no sequential
dependency to cache. Every step is a dense matrix multiply across the full sequence.
Formally, letq(xtjx 0 )be a fixed forward noising process (masking or Gaussian corruption) andpθ(xt− 1 j
xt)the learned denoising model. Training minimizes a denoising objective:

```
L=Et, x 0 , ε
```
#### 

```
kx 0 pθ(xt)k^2
```
#### 

#### .

Inference drawsxKfrom the prior and runs the chainxK!xK− 1 !!x 0 using a fixed number of steps,
typically 10-50 in practice.
_The payoff is that by paying the cost of a prefill-like forward pass_ K _times instead of paying the cost of
a sequential memory-bottlenecked pass_ L _times, diffusion models trade a small number of expensive parallel
steps for a large number of cheap-but-idle sequential steps._
The arithmetic intensity argument is decisive. During autoregressive generation, the effective arithmetic
intensity per token is approximately 1 for the attention layers andBfor the MLP layers. At batch size 1, both
collapse to the floor, and memory bandwidth - not compute - limits throughput. You spend most of every GPU
cycle waiting for HBM reads.
In a diffusion model, each forward pass processes allLoutput tokens at once. The arithmetic intensity of
the MLP layers becomesBL. For a sequence of 1024 tokens and batch size 1, that is 1024 versus 1 - three


```
17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation
```
orders of magnitude better GPU utilization per pass. The model is compute-limited for any reasonably long
sequence, meaning you are doing useful arithmetic on every cycle of the accelerator.
The trade-off is quality. Autoregressive generation samples each token from its exact conditional distri-
bution given the full prefix. Diffusion models make a weaker guarantee: the global distribution over output
sequences is approximately correct afterKsteps, but individual token predictions mid-chain are noisy. Early
diffusion LMs struggled on tasks requiring precise factual recall or tight long-range consistency. On coding
tasks, where correctness is mechanically verifiable, results are already competitive with similarly-sized AR
models. The open question is whether more refinement steps or better training objectives will close the gap on
harder tasks.

**A Worked Example**

Consider generating a 1024-token response using a 7B-parameter model on a single H100 (3.35 TB/s HBM
bandwidth, 989 TFLOPS BF16).
**Autoregressive baseline, batch size 1.** Each generation step reads approximately the full parameter set:
7  109  2 bytes (BF16)= 14GB. Latency per token 14 GB 3. 35 TB/s 4. 2 ms. Total for 1024 tokens:
4. 2  1024  4. 3 seconds. Throughput: approximately 238 tokens/second.
**Diffusion model, 20 refinement steps.** Each step is a full forward pass over 1024 tokens. FLOPs per pass:
2  7  109  1024  1. 43  1013 FLOPs.

Time per pass on H100: 1. 43  1013  9. 89  1014  14. 5 ms. Total for 20 steps: 20  14 .5 = 290ms.
Throughput: 1024  0. 29  3 , 500 tokens/second.
That is roughly a 15 throughput improvement while generating the same number of tokens from a similarly-
sized model. The 20 refinement steps can be reduced to 10 for another 2 speedup at some quality cost, or raised
to 50 for better quality at reduced throughput. The operating point is a continuous dial, not a fixed cost, which
is qualitatively different from autoregressive generation where the step count equals the token count and is non-
negotiable.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Refinement step count is a quality-latency dial, not a constant. Start at 20 steps as a reasonable default
for production. Below 10, quality degrades sharply on long-form generation. Above 50, returns diminish
and you approach the throughput of a small autoregressive model. Sweep this on your task distribution
and set it per request tier, not globally.
Output length must be committed at request time. Unlike AR models that stop at an EOS token,
diffusion models require knowing the target sequence length upfront. Wasted padding positions cost
compute proportionally. Build your serving layer to bucket requests by expected output length (powers of
two: 128, 256, 512, 1024 work well) to keep average padding below 2 .
Architecture uses bidirectional attention. Because all positions are visible at every step, there is no
causal mask. This means flash attention applies, prefix caching does not, and the attention FLOPs per
step areO(L^2 )rather thanO(1)per new token. For very short outputs (L < 64 ), the quadratic cost
erodes the throughput advantage rapidly.
Quality gaps are real on recall-heavy tasks. In my experience testing diffusion LMs on tasks requiring
exact entity lookup or precise numerical computation, quality drops noticeably compared to AR models of
```

```
17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation
```
```
the same parameter count. Routing recall-heavy requests to an AR model and generation-heavy requests
to a diffusion model is a production-viable strategy, but it requires a lightweight classifier at the request
boundary.
The draft model in speculative decoding is a natural fit. A small diffusion model can serve as the draft
proposal generator in a speculative decoding setup, because it produces multiple tokens per forward pass
natively. If the acceptance rate is reasonable, this combines the quality guarantee of the AR target model
with the throughput of a diffusion draft.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Autoregressive generation is memory-bottlenecked at batch size 1. What are the fundamental
architectural alternatives?” Strong answer: contrast AR generation (arithmetic intensity 1 , memory-
limited) with diffusion (all tokens in parallel, compute-limited, intensity BL). Name the trade-off
explicitly: throughput advantage is large for long outputs but shrinks for short ones; quality lags on recall
tasks.
“Walk me through how a diffusion language model generates text.” Strong answer: describe the iter-
ative denoising chain fromxKtox 0 , emphasize that every step is a full-sequence forward pass (identical
to prefill), explain the absence of a KV cache, and note that output length must be specified upfront. Give
the arithmetic: 20 stepsprefill cost versusLstepsgeneration cost.
“If diffusion models are so much faster, why isn’t everyone using them?” Strong answer: the quality
gap on factual recall and instruction following is real. Fixed output length at request time creates padding
waste and serving complexity. The compute advantage only materializes at output lengths long enough to
amortize per-step cost, roughlyL 200 tokens. Frontier labs are using them for high-throughput batch
workloads, not interactive chat.
Senior follow-up: “How would you use a diffusion model as the draft component in a speculative
decoding pipeline serving a 70B AR target?” Senior answer: the diffusion draft generatesKtoken
proposals in a single forward pass (no sequential sampling loop), which is faster than an AR draft gener-
atingKtokens one-by-one. The AR target verifies allKin parallel via prefill. Acceptance rate depends
on distribution alignment; fine-tune the draft on the target model’s output distribution to improve it. The
diffusion draft’s fixed-length constraint requires knowing the speculative lookahead windowKahead of
time, which is compatible with standard speculative decoding whereKis a fixed hyperparameter.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Diffusion language models generate all output tokens in parallel at each refinement step, shifting inference
from memory-limited (arithmetic intensity 1 ) to compute-limited (intensityBL).
A 7B diffusion model with 20 refinement steps achieves approximately 3,500 tokens/second on an H100
versus approximately 238 tokens/second for a 7B autoregressive model at batch size 1 - roughly a 15 
throughput advantage atL= 1024.
The advantage shrinks for short outputs and disappears below roughlyL= 64; build output-length buck-
eting into the serving scheduler to protect efficiency.
Quality lags AR models on recall-heavy tasks; the refinement step count is the quality-latency dial to tune
per task tier.
```

```
17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation
```
```
There is no KV cache, which eliminates the most complex part of AR serving infrastructure but requires
output length to be committed at request time.
```

**17.2.2 Implications for Serving Cost**
When inference costs are growing faster than revenue, the honest engineering question is not “which
model is fastest in a benchmark?” but “what changes when I swap from an autoregressive backend to a non-
autoregressive one, and which parts of my serving stack need to be redesigned?” Non-autoregressive generation
does not just produce tokens faster - it changes the memory model, the scheduler contract, and the capacity plan-
ning calculus in ways that compound across a large deployment. Knowing these second-order effects is what
separates a staff-level system design answer from a mid-level one.
The serving cost of an autoregressive model has two structurally different components: the model weights,
which are static and shared across all requests, and the KV cache, which grows per-request and per-generated-
token. Managing that growth requires PagedAttention-style virtual memory, copy-on-write prefix sharing, and
eviction policies - all of which add engineering overhead and introduce fragmentation.
Non-autoregressive models collapse this structure. Because there is no sequential dependency across re-
finement steps, there is no KV cache to accumulate. Each step reads the model weights and the current noisy
sequence, writes the refined sequence, and exits. Memory consumption per request is a flatO(Ld)bytes where
Lis the committed output length anddis the model hidden dimension - constant across allKrefinement steps.
The total HBM footprint for a diffusion serving deployment is:
Mtotal=Mweights+BLd 2 bytes (BF16)

whereBis the batch size andLis the fixed output length. Compare this to an AR deployment whereMKV
grows as the sequence extends and must be tracked dynamically. The diffusion model’s memory budget is fully
computable before a single token is generated, which makes capacity planning a spreadsheet exercise rather than
a runtime estimation problem.
_Eliminating the KV cache turns the serving stack’s hardest dynamic-memory problem into a static alloca-
tion, at the cost of requiring output length to be committed at request time._
The economic argument is clearest when you look at cost per output token. Autoregressive generation is
memory-bandwidth-limited: every token costs one full HBM sweep of the parameter set. For a 7B model in
BF16, that is 14 GB of data movement per token. At 3.35 TB/s on an H100, the hardware-imposed minimum is
4.2 ms per token regardless of software optimization. No kernel tuning removes this floor.
Diffusion generation amortizes weight-sweep cost across allLoutput tokens in a step. The effective band-
width cost per output token acrossKrefinement steps is:

BW cost per token=
KMweights
L
ForK= 20andL= 512, this is 20 / 512  0. 04 the per-token cost of AR generation. Compute, not memory
bandwidth, becomes the binding constraint - which is a far healthier operating regime because compute is easier
to scale horizontally.
The catch is fixed output length. Autoregressive models can stream tokens and stop at any EOS, adapting
response length to content at runtime. Diffusion models commit toLupfront. Positions that go unused are
wasted compute. In my experience, the serving system must either predict output length accurately or accept
efficiency losses from padding; neither is free, but length bucketing at powers of two keeps average waste below
2 .


```
17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider 100 concurrent requests, each expecting up to 512 output tokens, served on a single H100 with
80 GB HBM.
**Autoregressive backend (13B model, BF16):**
Weight memory: 13  109 2 = 26GB.
KV cache per sequence (40 layers, 32 KV heads,dhead= 128, 512 tokens): 512  32  128  40  2  2 
3. 4 GB.
At batch size 16: 16  3 .4 + 26 = 80. 4 GB - already at the memory limit.
Maximum practical batch size: 15-16 requests.
**Diffusion backend (comparable model scale, BF16):**
Weight memory: 26 GB (same).
Sequence buffer per request (L= 512,d= 5, 120 ): 512  5 , 120  2  5 MB.
At batch size 100: 100  5 MB+ 26GB= 26. 5 GB total.
53 GB remain free for larger batches or additional model shards.
Maximum practical batch size: limited by compute throughput, not memory - exactly the operating point
you want.
The memory freed by eliminating the KV cache allows a batch size of 100 versus 16 on identical hardware,
a 6 improvement that directly multiplies throughput before any algorithmic changes. Combined with the per-
token compute advantage from the previous subsection, the end-to-end throughput difference for long outputs
is striking.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Output length prediction is a first-class infrastructure problem. Build a lightweight length predictor
(a small classification head on a pooled prefix embedding works) that bins requests into length buckets
before routing. Rounding up to the nearest power of two (128, 256, 512, 1024) keeps padding waste below
2 on most real distributions. Avoid variable-length padding within a batch; pad all requests in a batch
to the sameLand process them together.
Maintain separate queuing lanes per output-length bucket. Pack requests of similar expected length
into batches; flush each lane when the batch is full or a timeout fires. This is simpler than AR continuous
batching because there is no mid-sequence request admission: all requests in a batch start and finish
together, so the scheduler contract is identical to training.
Expose refinement step count as a per-request parameter. Low-stakes requests (short-form Q&A,
autocompletion) can use 10-15 steps. High-stakes requests (long-form document generation, code for
production) benefit from 30-50 steps. Implementing this as a tier enum in your request proto gives the
product team a quality-cost lever without infrastructure changes.
Route by task type, not just model size. Deploy AR backends for time-to-first-token-sensitive workloads
(interactive chat, function calls, streaming responses) and diffusion backends for throughput-sensitive
batch workloads (document summarization, bulk code generation, offline evaluation). A lightweight
router that classifies on task type plus expected output length outperforms a single-model strategy on
both cost and quality.
Prefix caching does not apply; but prompt conditioning is cheaper. Because diffusion models use
bidirectional attention, there is no causal prefix whose KV vectors can be cached across requests. The
```

```
17.2 Non-Autoregressive Generation
```
```
cost of conditioning on a long system prompt is paid again at every refinement step. If your serving traffic
has a shared system prompt, this eliminates one of the major cost-saving mechanisms of modern AR
serving systems. Design around it by keeping prompts short or by absorbing prompt information into the
model at training time via instruction tuning.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How does eliminating the KV cache change your serving infrastructure?” Strong answer: memory
becomes static and fully predictable before generation begins; batch size is set by compute budget rather
than memory budget; the scheduler no longer needs eviction policies or copy-on-write prefix sharing; but
output length must be committed upfront, introducing a new length-prediction requirement.
“What are the limits of the diffusion serving cost advantage?” Strong answer: three limits. First,
short outputs (L < 64 ) do not amortize the per-step weight-sweep cost, shrinking or eliminating the
advantage. Second, padding waste from poor length prediction can erode the memory savings. Third,
prefix caching disappears, which hurts workloads with long shared system prompts. Name the cross-over
point quantitatively: the diffusion backend breaks even with AR roughly whenK/L < 1 , i.e., the number
of refinement steps is smaller than the output length.
“How would you operate a mixed AR-diffusion cluster to minimize cost per quality point?” Strong
answer: profile your request distribution by task type, expected output length, and quality sensitivity.
Assign AR capacity to the interactive, recall-heavy, and short-output tail; assign diffusion capacity to the
long-output, throughput-sensitive bulk. Size each backend to its SLA: AR optimized for P95 latency,
diffusion optimized for tokens/second. Rebalance allocation weekly as the request mix shifts.
Senior follow-up: “How does the capacity planning model change when the serving SLA is throughput-
per-dollar rather than latency?” Senior answer: AR throughput is bounded by memory bandwidth:
tokens/second BW/(2Nparams), independent of batch size once memory is saturated. Diffusion
throughput scales with compute: tokens/second TFLOPSL/(2NparamsK), meaning it im-
proves with longer outputs and fewer steps. The cost-per-token crossover is atL= K(output length
equals refinement step count); above that, diffusion dominates per dollar. Model this in your capacity
plan and provision diffusion GPUs for the long-output tail of your distribution while using AR GPUs for
the short-output head.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Diffusion models have a flat, predictable per-request memory footprint (O(Ld)bytes, constant across
all refinement steps) versus an AR model’s linearly growing KV cache, enabling 6 larger batch sizes
on identical hardware for 512-token outputs.
The effective per-token bandwidth cost isK/Ltimes the AR cost; atK= 20,L= 512, this is4%of
the AR figure, shifting the bottleneck from memory bandwidth to compute.
Output length must be committed at request time; build output-length bucketing (powers of two) into the
scheduler to hold padding waste below 2 .
Prefix caching does not apply to diffusion models (bidirectional attention, no causal KV cache); workloads
with long shared system prompts lose a major AR cost-saving mechanism.
Route by task type and expected output length: diffusion for long-output batch workloads, AR for inter-
active or recall-heavy short-output workloads.
```

## Chapter 18 Speculative Decoding and Serving Optimizations

### 18.1 Speculative Sampling

**18.1.1 The Draft/Target Algorithm and Its Math**
Speculative sampling comes up in nearly every inference-focused system design interview because it is the
rare technique that cuts latency without any approximation: the output distribution is provably identical to that
of the target model. Interviewers at frontier labs ask about it both to probe whether a candidate understands
_why_ generation is slow (it is memory-bound, not compute-bound) and to test whether they can reason about
probabilistic correction schemes under pressure. Expect it at the senior to staff level, where the follow-up is
almost always “prove the acceptance step is unbiased” or “how would you choose the draft model?”
Autoregressive generation produces one token per forward pass, and each pass is dominated by loading the
model weights from HBM-not by arithmetic. For a 70 B parameter model inbf16on an H100 with 3.35 TB/s
memory bandwidth, a single generation step requires moving roughly 2  70  109  140 GB of weights,
which takes about 42 ms regardless of batch size. Prefill, by contrast, processes all prompt tokens in parallel
and is compute-bound: you pay the weight-load cost once and amortise it over the whole sequence. Speculative
sampling exploits this asymmetry directly.
The algorithm uses two models: a small, fast _draft model_ pand the large, accurate _target model_ q. Given a
prefixx1:t, the draft model autoregressively producesKcandidate tokensx ̃t+1,... ,x ̃t+Kunder its own distri-
bution. The target model then scores allKtokens in a single forward pass-this is just a prefill over the extended
sequence, so it runs in parallel and is fast. For each positioni2f 1 ,... , Kgthe candidatex ̃t+iis accepted with
probability

_The central insight is that verifying a proposed token under the target model is identical to prefill, which is
cheap; only generating the_ next _token requires a fresh, expensive decode step._
The acceptance-rejection correction is not a heuristic-it is an exact importance-sampling step borrowed
from the Metropolis-Hastings framework. The proposal distribution isp; the target isq. When the draft agrees
with the target (p( ̃x)q( ̃x)), the token is accepted unconditionally. When the draft is overconfident relative
to the target, the excess probability mass is redistributed via the residualq′, ensuring the marginal distribution
of every emitted token matchesqexactly. No temperature adjustment, no post-hoc filtering-the samples are
mathematically identical to what you would get from greedy-free sampling the target model alone.

latency wall from weight-loading is amortised across those tokens, reducing wall-clock time per output token
proportionally.
The key trade-off is draft quality versus draft cost. A stronger draft model pushesα ̄higher but also con-
sumes more memory and FLOPs, narrowing the gap to the target model. A weaker draft is cheaper but drops
acceptance rates; ifα ̄falls below roughly 1 /Kthe overhead of running the draft outweighs the savings. The
sweet spot in production is typically a draft 5-10smaller than the target, from the same model family and
ideally distilled from the target.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a setup with Llama 3 70B as the target and a 7B draft, both inbf16on a single H100 (80 GB
HBM, 3.35 TB/s bandwidth).
**Baseline latency per token (target only).** Weight size: 2  70  109 = 140GB. Time to load weights:
140 / 3350  42 ms per step. AtK = 5lookahead tokens the target model is called once for every 5-step
window.
**Draft cost.** The 7B draft weighs 2  7  109 = 14GB. Loading time: 14 / 3350  4. 2 ms per step. Five
draft steps cost 5  4 .2 = 21ms total.
**Verification cost.** The target scores all 5 candidates in one prefill call. Prefill is compute-bound, not
bandwidth-bound; at reasonable sequence lengths this is roughly equivalent to one generation step: 42 ms.
**Effective throughput with** α ̄= 0. 75**.** Expected accepted tokens per round:1 + 5 0 .75 = 4. 75. Total
time per round:21 + 42 = 63ms. Effective latency per output token: 63 / 4. 75  13 ms, versus the 42 ms
baseline. That is a 3. 2 wall-clock speed-up with zero change in output quality.
**Whiteboard summary:**

For each round of K draft steps:

1. Draft model: generate x_{t+1} ... x_{t+K} [K * draft_cost ms]
2. Target model: one prefill over the K tokens [~1 decode step ms]
3. Accept/reject each token, emit 1 + K*alpha tokens on average
Speedup = (1 + K*alpha) / (1 + K * draft_cost / target_cost)

```
a 70B target leaves roughly 10 GB for the draft after KV caches-enough for a 4-5B model inbf16or a
7B model quantized to INT4. If you cannot fit both models, consider offloading the draft weights to CPU
and streaming them in; the CPU-GPU transfer cost is often less than the savings on generation steps.
```

**18.1.2 Medusa, EAGLE, and Draft Model Design**
When you ship speculative decoding to production, the single hardest engineering decision is the draft
model itself-how to build it, where to host it, and how tightly to couple it to the target. This question shows up
in system design interviews at exactly the point where a candidate has explained the basic algorithm and the
interviewer pivots to: “OK, but how would you actually build the draft model for a 70B serving system you
own?” Getting this right separates candidates who have thought about the operational reality from those who
have only memorized the algorithm.
The draft model’s sole job is to proposeKtokens fast enough that the target model’s verification step-a
single prefill-recovers more wall-clock time than the draft cost. Three architectures dominate in practice.
**Standalone draft model.** A fully independent, smaller model from the same family as the target. It has its
own weights, its own KV cache, and runs its own autoregressive decode loop to produceKtokens. Acceptance
rates are highest here because the draft sees the full autoregressive context at each step. The cost is memory: on
an 80 GB H100 with a 70B target, a standalone 7B draft inbf16consumes 14 GB, leaving barely enough room
for KV caches at non-trivial sequence lengths.
**Medusa.** Medusa attachesKindependent prediction heads directly on top of the target model’s last hid-
den state. Headkpredicts the tokenksteps ahead of the current position without any autoregressive rollout.
There is no separate model and no additional memory for weights beyond the heads themselves (each head is a
single linear projection of sizedmodelV, roughly 0.5 GB per head for a 4096-dimensional model and 128 K
vocabulary). The draft cost per round collapses to a single forward pass through theKheads in parallel. The
downside is expressive power: headksees only the hidden state at positiont, not the predicted tokens at posi-
tionst+ 1,... , t+k 1 , so the heads are conditionally independent. In practice this cuts acceptance rates by
10-20 percentage points relative to a well-tuned standalone draft.
**EAGLE (Extrapolation Algorithm for Greater Language-model Eﬀiciency).** EAGLE threads a middle
path. It trains a lightweight autoregressive draft module-typically a single transformer layer-that takes as input
the _feature vectors_ from the target model’s final layer concatenated with the token embeddings of the previously
accepted tokens. The draft module is therefore not standalone; it is a thin attachment that rides on the target’s
residual stream. Because the draft sees the target’s own high-level representations, it has far more signal than
Medusa’s static hidden state, and acceptance rates recover to within 5-10 percentage points of a standalone draft.
The draft module is also small-one transformer layer for a LLaMA-sized target is roughly 500 M parameters or
1 GB inbf16-so memory pressure is minimal.
_The design spectrum runs from standalone (highest acceptance rate, highest memory cost) through EAGLE
(near-standalone quality, low memory cost) to Medusa (lowest cost, lowest acceptance rate); the right choice
depends on how much GPU memory the target leaves unclaimed after KV caches._
The memory argument is decisive at the 70B scale. A standalone 7B draft eats 14 GB; EAGLE’s single-
layer module eats 1 GB; Medusa’sK= 5heads eat 2.5 GB. For a 70B target inbf16(140 GB) sharded across
two H100s (160 GB total), the KV cache budget for a batch of 16 sequences at sequence length 2,048 is roughly
10 GB, leaving only 10 GB spare. EAGLE or Medusa fit easily; a standalone 7B draft does not without aggressive
quantisation.
The co-location advantage of EAGLE over a standalone draft is not just memory. Because the draft module
ingests the target model’s feature vectors, those vectors only need to be computed once per token position-
they are produced by the target during verification and cached. The draft therefore uses information that the
standalone model would have to independently re-derive, which is why EAGLE’s acceptance rates are high


```
18.1 Speculative Sampling
```
despite the module being tiny.
The residual between Medusa and EAGLE is conditional independence. When generating code or struc-
tured output where tokent+ 2strongly depends on tokent+ 1, Medusa’s heads-each conditioned only on
positiont-systematically underestimate the entropy of later positions and generate plausible-looking but lo-
cally inconsistent proposals. EAGLE’s autoregressive rollout within the draft module preserves this conditional
structure.

(same family, distilled). Tokens per target call:1 + 5 0 .80 = 5. 0.

### 18.2 Serving System Design

**18.2.1 Continuous Batching and Selective Batching**
Production serving of LLMs looks nothing like the clean batched inference your benchmarks describe. Real
traffic is chaotic: requests arrive at random intervals, prompts span 50 to 50,000 tokens, and generations finish
at unpredictable times. An interview question like “how would you serve a 70B model at high throughput with
low latency?” is really asking whether you understand the scheduling and batching machinery that separates
a demo from a production system. This topic appears consistently at senior and staff levels wherever teams
own inference infrastructure, and the two mechanisms here-continuous batching and selective batching-are the
architectural foundation of every serious open-source serving system today.
The naive approach is _static batching_ : collect requests until the batch is full, run all sequences in lockstep
until every one of them finishes, then start the next batch. The problem is obvious once stated: a request that
generates 5 tokens holds a batch slot hostage for the full 512-step budget, and the GPU sits idle between batch
arrivals while you wait for enough requests to form a full batch.
_Continuous batching_ (also called iteration-level scheduling) fixes this by making the generation step the
atomic scheduling unit. The worker generates one token for every active sequence, then yields control back to the
scheduler. The scheduler inspects the waiting queue: any sequence that just generated an end-of-sequence token
frees its slot, and a new request can be inserted immediately. The GPU is never blocked waiting for stragglers
or for a batch to fill.
Selective batching addresses the second problem: variable-length sequences cannot be naively padded into
a rectangular tensor when the length variance is large, because attention compute scales quadratically with se-
quence length and most of that padding is wasted work. The key observation is that attention and the feed-forward
(MLP) layers behave differently. Attention is inherently per-sequence-each sequence has its own KV cache-so
it must be dispatched separately for each sequence (or handled with variable-length kernels like FlashAttention-
2’scu_seqlensinterface). MLP layers, however, apply the same weight matrices to every token regardless
of which sequence the token belongs to. Given tokens from sequences of different lengths, you can simply
flatten the batch dimension: reshape inputs from[B, Ti, D]into[

#### P

iTi, D]and process all tokens together as
one large matrix multiply. Because the tokens from different sequences do not interact inside an MLP, this is
mathematically identical to processing them separately but with much higher arithmetic intensity.
_The key principle: continuously schedule at the granularity of individual generation steps, and batch MLP
computation across all active tokens regardless of their sequence boundaries._
The throughput gains from continuous batching are compound. First, you eliminate idle GPU time from
batch formation. Second, you eliminate the slot-wasting effect of stragglers: a 20-token request that finishes
early frees its KV cache and batch slot after exactly 20 steps, not 512. Third, continuous batching naturally


```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
increases the average number of concurrent sequences in steady-state, which raises the arithmetic intensity of
MLP layers and drives the GPU toward its compute-bound regime.
Selective batching amplifies this by ensuring that the bulk of the computation-MLP layers constitute roughly
two-thirds of total FLOPs in a standard transformer-is batched at maximum efficiency even when sequence
lengths vary wildly. Without selective batching, a variable-length batch either suffers quadratic padding waste
in attention or requires an inefficient loop over individual sequences in the MLP.
The alternative-waiting for a fixed batch and running to completion-gives lower memory pressure per step
because fewer sequences are active at once, but it produces dramatically worse GPU utilization and higher
latency variance. In practice, static batching delivers 20-30% GPU utilization for typical interactive workloads;
continuous batching pushes that to 70-85%.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B model on an H100, with a KV cache budget of 512 concurrent sequence slots, each pre-
allocated to 2048 tokens maximum.
Under **static batching** with batch sizeB= 16: the batch is padded to the longest sequence in the batch. If
the distribution of actual generation lengths is geometric with mean 256 tokens but maximum 2048, then at least
one sequence in every batch of 16 will be near the maximum, so all 16 are padded to 2048 tokens. A request that
actually generates 30 tokens occupies a slot for the full 2048 steps. Average slot utilization: 256 / 2048  12 .5%.
Under **continuous batching** with the same memory budget: slots free as sequences finish. In steady state,
the scheduler keeps 16 sequences running simultaneously. When sequenceigenerates its EOS at step 30, sloti
is immediately assigned to the next waiting request. Effective throughput is:
