with batch size). AtB= 16,tstep 12 ms, giving a steady-state throughput of 16 / 0. 012  1333 tokens/s,
compared to 160 tokens/s with static batching at 12.5% slot utilization.
For selective batching, suppose active sequences have lengths[128, 512 , 64 ,256]tokens in their KV caches.
The MLP forward pass flattens these into a single tensor of shape[960, D]and runs two large matrix multiplies
of size[960, D][D, 4 D]and[960, 4 D][4D, D]. Arithmetic intensity is/ 960 , comfortably compute-bound
on an H100 (threshold 300 for bf16). Attention is dispatched per-sequence with per-sequence KV lengths,
using variable-length flash attention kernels.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Schedule in token budget, not sequence count. Set a maximum of, say, 8,192 active tokens across all
sequences rather than a fixed batch size. This bounds both memory usage and per-step latency regardless
of sequence length distribution. A batch of 64 short sequences and a batch of 4 long sequences both
consume the same compute.
Chunk long prefills. A single request with a 32,768-token prompt will monopolize the GPU for the entire
prefill, stalling all ongoing generation steps and spiking inter-token latency for other users. Chunked prefill
breaks the prompt into pieces of, say, 512 tokens per step, interleaving them with generation steps. This
bounds prefill latency per step at the cost of slightly slower time-to-first-token for the long-prompt request.
Use chunk sizes of 512-2048 tokens; smaller chunks hurt MLP efficiency.
```

```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
```
Preemption when memory fills. If a high-priority request arrives but there are no free KV cache slots,
preempt the lowest-priority active sequence: save its KV cache to CPU DRAM (swap) or simply discard
it and restart the sequence from scratch when a slot frees. Swap is preferable for long sequences (large KV
cache already built); restart is preferable for short sequences (cheap to redo). The crossover is typically
around 500-1000 tokens of context.
Priority tiers for multi-tenant serving. Continuous batching makes priority trivially composable: each
step, the scheduler fills available token budget starting from the highest-priority queue. Latency-sensitive
interactive requests get first pick; batch-processing jobs fill remaining capacity. This is simpler to imple-
ment than priority in static batching because slots turn over every step.
Flash attention with variable-length support is non-negotiable. Without FlashAttention-2’svarlen
kernels (or equivalent), selective batching for attention requires either a Python loop over sequences (ter-
rible) or padding to the max length in the batch (defeats the purpose). Verify your serving stack uses
flash_attn_varlen_funcor equivalent before deploying.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How does vLLM achieve higher throughput than naive batching?” Strong answer: iteration-level
continuous batching reclaims slots as soon as a sequence finishes, eliminating straggler waste. Selective
batching ensures MLP computation is always batched at full efficiency across all active tokens. Page-
dAttention (the next subsection) then eliminates KV cache fragmentation to maximize the number of
concurrent sequences.
“Why can’t you just pad all sequences to the same length and run a standard batch?” Strong answer:
padding wastes compute quadratically in attention (padded positions still participate inQK⊤), wastes
memory for the padded KV cache, and lets long stragglers hold batch slots for all shorter sequences. At
mean generation length of 256 and max 2048, effective utilization is12%.
Senior follow-up: “If prefill is compute-limited and generation is memory-limited, what happens
to generation latency when a large-batch prefill lands?” Senior answer: a large prefill dominates the
GPU for many steps, stalling all generation steps and causing inter-token latency (ITL) spikes for other
users. The fix is chunked prefill: bound the prefill tokens per step to, say, 512, so that each step is a mix of
prefill and generation. FlashAttention-2 supports this via thevarleninterface, which handles sequences
of mixed prefill and generation tokens in a single kernel call. The trade-off is slightly higher TTFT for the
long-prompt request, which is acceptable if TTFT SLOs are looser than ITL SLOs.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Continuous batching reclaims GPU slots every generation step, eliminating straggler waste and idle time
between batches.
Selective batching separates attention (per-sequence, variable-length kernels) from MLP (all tokens flat-
tened into one large matrix multiply), keeping MLP compute-bound.
Schedule by token budget, not sequence count, to bound per-step latency regardless of sequence length
distribution.
Chunked prefill prevents long prompts from monopolizing the GPU and spiking inter-token latency for
concurrent generation requests.
```

```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
```
FlashAttention-2 variable-length kernels are the prerequisite for practical selective batching; confirm your
stack supports them before benchmarking.
```
**18.2.2 Paged Attention and Memory Fragmentation**
The KV cache is the dominant consumer of GPU memory in inference, often eclipsing model parameter
storage once you scale to reasonable batch sizes. A naive allocator that pre-reserves a contiguous chunk for
each request wastes 20-40% of KV cache capacity to fragmentation-directly capping the number of concurrent
sequences you can run and therefore your throughput ceiling. If you are interviewing for any role that touches
inference infrastructure, expect to explain exactly how PagedAttention works and why it matters: this is the
core mechanism behind vLLM and the design pattern that every serious serving system has since adopted or
reimplemented. The concept is worth understanding deeply not just for interviews but because it reveals how
much of systems work is rediscovering operating-system ideas in new contexts.
The fundamental problem is that you do not know how many tokens a request will generate before it starts.
A pre-emptive allocator that reserves the maximum possible sequence length (say, 2048 tokens) wastes GPU
memory proportional to the gap between that maximum and the actual generation. An allocator that starts small
and grows dynamically requires copying the KV cache each time it outgrows its current allocation-expensive
and disruptive.
PagedAttention borrows the solution that operating systems developed for process memory: virtual mem-
ory with paging. Physical DRAM is divided into fixed-size pages; a page table maps virtual addresses to scat-
tered physical pages. A process sees a contiguous virtual address space, but the underlying physical layout is
fragmented.
Applied to the KV cache, the translation is direct. The KV cache is divided into fixed-size _blocks_ , each
storingbtokens of KV state for all layers and all KV heads. A _block table_ maps each sequence to an ordered list
of physical block indices. When a sequence needs more KV storage, the allocator assigns the next free physical
block from a pool-no contiguity requirement. When a sequence finishes, all its blocks are returned to the free
pool immediately.
The memory cost of a single block is:
bytes per block= 2bLNkvH 2

wherebis the block size in tokens,Lis the number of layers,Nkvis the number of KV heads,His the head
dimension, and the final factor of 2 accounts for bf16 precision. The factor beforebdoubles for key and value.
Copy-on-write enables the second major feature: _prefix caching_. Many requests share a common prefix-
a system prompt, a few-shot example block, or a retrieved document chunk. Without sharing, every request
independently computes and stores the KV cache for that prefix, paying both compute and memory costs that
scale linearly with the number of concurrent requests. PagedAttention gives each physical block a reference
count. Blocks in a shared prefix region have reference count equal to the number of sequences using them;
those sequences read from the block but never write to it. When a sequence generates its first token past the
shared prefix, the scheduler forks it: new blocks are allocated for the diverging suffix, and the shared prefix
blocks remain intact and untouched. This is copy-on-write, and it makes the KV cache cost of a repeated system
prompt a one-time allocation regardless of how many requests share it.
_Eliminate fragmentation first, then exploit prefix sharing: together these two mechanisms double or triple
the effective batch size you can sustain within a fixed GPU memory budget._
Pre-PagedAttention serving systems suffered two kinds of fragmentation. _Internal fragmentation_ : you


```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
reserve 2048 tokens for a request that generates 80, wasting 1968 / 2048  96%of its allocation. _External
fragmentation_ : the gaps between allocations that no single request can use, analogous to heap fragmentation in
a long-running process. The vLLM paper measured 20-40% total KV cache waste from these effects on realistic
workloads.
With block-based allocation, internal fragmentation is bounded by at mostb 1 tokens per sequence-at a
block size of 16 tokens, that is at most 15 wasted token slots per sequence, negligible at any reasonable sequence
length. External fragmentation is eliminated because blocks are fungible: any free block can be assigned to any
sequence.
Prefix caching compounds the benefit. A 1,000-token system prompt on a 7B model (32 layers, 8 KV
heads, head dimension 128, bf16) costs:

```
1000  32  8  128  2 2 = 131MB
```
per request. With 100 concurrent requests all using the same system prompt, the naive cost is 13.1 GB-a sig-
nificant fraction of the entire KV budget on an 80 GB GPU. Prefix caching reduces this to 131 MB, a 100
reduction in KV memory for the shared prefix. This frees space for more concurrent sequences, which directly
improves throughput.
The alternative-a bump allocator with padding-is simpler to implement but puts a hard ceiling on batch size
that degrades with sequence length variance. A slab allocator (fixed-size objects) partially addresses external
fragmentation but does not support prefix sharing.

**A Worked Example**

**Setup:** 7B model, H100 80 GB GPU, model weights in bf16: approximately 14 GB. KV cache budget:
roughly 60 GB. Block sizeb= 16tokens,L= 32layers,Nkv= 8KV heads,H= 128.
**Bytes per block:**
2  16  32  8  128 2 = 2, 097 , 152 bytes 2. 1 MB
**Total physical blocks:** 60 GB/ 2. 1 MB 28 , 500 blocks, representing 28 , 500 16 = 456, 000 token slots
of KV capacity.
**Without PagedAttention (pre-allocation):** Reserved 2048 / 16 e= 128blocks per sequence at request
start. Maximum concurrent sequences: 28 , 500 / 128  222. If actual generation length averages 256 tokens
(needing 16 blocks), then 128 16 = 112blocks per sequence are reserved but unused: internal fragmentation
= 112/ 128  87 .5%. Effective concurrent sequences at the 256-token average:  28 sequences actually
needed simultaneously (22waste factor).
**With PagedAttention (on-demand allocation):** Each sequence holds exactlydT / 16 eblocks at any given
step. At 256-token average generation: 16 blocks per sequence. Maximum concurrent sequences given 28,500
blocks: 28 , 500 / 16  1 , 781. Practical limit is set by other memory constraints and scheduling, but the point is
that fragmentation no longer caps batch size at 28 sequences.
**With prefix caching:** If all 100 concurrent requests share a 512-token system prompt:d 512 / 16 e= 32
blocks, reference count 100. Those 32 blocks serve all 100 sequences. Without prefix caching: 100 32 = 3, 200
blocks. Savings: 3 , 168 blocks 6. 6 GB freed for generation context.


```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Block size is a tunable constant with real trade-offs. Smaller blocks (8 tokens) reduce internal frag-
mentation but multiply the size of the block table and increase pointer-chasing overhead during attention,
which must now gather non-contiguous blocks. Larger blocks (32 tokens) are more cache-friendly and
reduce metadata overhead but waste up to 31 token slots per sequence. In practice, 16 tokens per block
is the right default for mixed-length workloads; adjust toward 32 if your sequence length distribution is
long-tailed and toward 8 if you serve many very short requests.
Prefix cache eviction needs a policy. Shared prefix blocks are held in cache indefinitely under the as-
sumption that the prefix is fixed. For multi-tenant serving where each tenant has a different system prompt,
you need LRU eviction on prefix blocks, triggered when the free block pool drops below a watermark (e.g.,
10% of total blocks). Evicting a prefix block invalidates all sequences that depend on it-force a KV re-
compute for those sequences or preempt them. Radix attention (used in SGLang) automates this with a
prefix trie and LRU eviction at the subtree level.
CPU swap is a last resort, not a primary strategy. When the free block pool is exhausted, the scheduler
can swap a paused sequence’s KV blocks to CPU DRAM over PCIe or NVLink. NVLink bandwidth
is roughly 900 GB/s bidirectional (H100 SXM); PCIe 4.0 is roughly 32 GB/s. At 2. 1 MB per block
and 16 blocks for a 256-token context: 33. 6 MB transferred over PCIe takes 1 ms-tolerable once but
not repeatedly. Prefer preemption-and-restart for short sequences (under 500 tokens) and swap for long
sequences where the recompute cost exceeds the transfer cost.
Block table lookup is on the critical path in the attention kernel. The attention kernel must translate
logical block indices to physical addresses for each sequence. This adds one level of indirection per
block boundary. Verify that your attention kernel handles non-contiguous blocks natively (as vLLM’s
paged_attentionkernel does) rather than copying KV blocks into a contiguous staging buffer before
attention-the latter negates the memory savings.
Chunked prefill interacts with block allocation. When a 1,024-token prompt arrives and is chunked
into 512-token pieces, the first chunk allocatesd 512 / 16 e= 32blocks at step one, and the second chunk
allocates another 32 blocks at step two, before any generation blocks are needed. Account for this prefill
block reservation in your watermark-based eviction policy, otherwise a burst of long-prompt requests can
exhaust the block pool before generation even starts.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Explain how PagedAttention works and why it matters.” Strong answer: describe block-based KV
cache allocation, the block table mapping logical to physical blocks, copy-on-write for prefix sharing,
and quantify the fragmentation reduction. Concrete numbers matter: pre-PagedAttention systems waste
20-40% of KV cache; with block size 16, internal fragmentation is at most 15 tokens per sequence.
“Why does KV cache fragmentation hurt throughput?” Strong answer: fragmentation reduces the
number of concurrent sequences you can hold in GPU memory. Fewer concurrent sequences means lower
arithmetic intensity for MLP layers, pushing the GPU toward its memory-bound regime. The throughput
loss is multiplicative: halving the effective batch size roughly halves throughput at the operating point
where the system is memory-bound.
Senior follow-up: “How does SGLang’s radix attention extend PagedAttention, and when does it
help most?” Senior answer: radix attention maintains a prefix trie over all KV-cached sequences across
```

```
18.2 Serving System Design
```
```
all current and recent requests, not just those that share the same system prompt. Any common prefix
subtree-including multi-turn conversation history and RAG-retrieved context-is automatically dedupli-
cated. LRU eviction at the subtree level keeps the trie bounded. The gain is largest in multi-turn chat
(where conversation history grows and is shared across turns) and RAG applications (where the same
retrieved documents recur across users). The trade-off is trie management overhead and the risk of cache
thrashing if prefix diversity is high relative to the block pool size.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
PagedAttention divides the KV cache into fixed-size blocks (typically 16 tokens), allocated on demand and
returned immediately when a sequence finishes-eliminating fragmentation that previously wasted 20-40%
of KV cache capacity.
Copy-on-write lets multiple sequences share KV blocks for a common prefix at no extra memory cost;
prefix caching turns a repeated system prompt from a per-request allocation to a single shared allocation.
The block table lookup adds one level of indirection in the attention kernel; use a kernel that handles
non-contiguous blocks natively rather than copying to a staging buffer.
Block size, prefix eviction policy, and CPU-swap thresholds are the three key tunable parameters in pro-
duction; defaults of 16 tokens/block, LRU eviction at 10% free watermark, and swap-for-long/restart-for-
short cover most workloads.
Radix attention (SGLang) extends prefix caching to a full prefix trie, maximizing cache hits for multi-turn
conversations and RAG pipelines where prefix overlap spans multiple users.
```

## Chapter 19 Compression Techniques for Deployment

### 19.1 Quantization.

**19.1.1 INT8 Quantization with Outlier Handling (LLM.int8())**
Imagine you have trained a 70B parameter model and now you need to serve it. At BF16, those weights
consume 140 GB of memory-more than a single H100’s 80 GB HBM. INT8 would halve that to 70 GB, letting
you serve on a single node. But every engineer who has tried naively packing a large transformer into INT8 has
watched perplexity spike and downstream task accuracy collapse. Understanding why that happens, and how to
fix it, is a question I have seen asked at nearly every frontier lab interview touching inference or deployment.
Quantization maps a floating-point tensor to a lower-precision integer representation. The simplest scheme,
_absmax quantization_ , works as follows: given a weight vectorw 2 Rnstored in FP16, compute the scale
s= max(jwj)and produce the INT8 vector

```
wq= round
```
```
w
s ^127
```
#### 

, wq 2 [ 127 ,127].
To dequantize:wˆ =wqs/ 127. Memory shrinks by 2 (2 bytes per weight in BF16, 1 byte in INT8).
Bandwidth shrinks by the same factor, which directly translates to lower generation latency in the memory-bound
regime.
The catch is _outlier activations_. Research has shown that in transformer models at or above 6.7B parame-
ters, a small fraction of hidden-dimension channels-typically fewer than 1% of all feature dimensions-develop
systematically large magnitudes, often 10-100larger than the median channel. These outliers emerge consis-
tently across every token processed by the model. When you include even one such outlier in the absmax scale
computation, the quantization grid becomes too coarse for every other channel, and the accumulated rounding
error destroys model quality.
The LLM.int8() paper addresses this with a _mixed-precision decomposition_. Given the weight matrixW 2
Rdout×dinand the activation matrixX 2 RB×din, partition the columns corresponding to outlier channels into an
index setO(typicallyjOj< 0. 01 din). Then:

XW=XOWO⊤+XO ̄WO⊤ ̄,
where the first term is computed in FP16 (covering outlier columns) and the second in INT8 (covering the
vast majority). The two partial products are accumulated back into FP16. Because outlier columns are identified
offline from a small calibration set, no runtime search is required.
_INT8 quantization at scale requires explicit outlier handling: a tiny fraction of channels disrupts the entire
quantization grid, and the fix is to route those channels through a separate FP16 compute path._
The key property that makes the decomposition practical is that outlier channels are _consistent across
tokens_. The same handful of columns that blow up in activation magnitude for one input tend to blow up for
all inputs processed by a given layer. That means you can profile a few hundred calibration samples, identify
the outlier channel indices once, and bake the decomposition into your serving kernel. There is no per-token
routing overhead.
The trade-off is speed versus capacity. Because the FP16 path involves a sparse scatter-gather across out-


```
19.1 Quantization
```
lier columns, LLM.int8() is typically 10-20% slower at runtime than a native BF16 forward pass on the same
hardware. It is not a speed optimization-it is a memory-capacity optimization. The value proposition is: run a
175B model on 880 GB A100s instead of 16, or a 70B model on a single 880 GB node instead of two.
Compared to pure INT8 without outlier handling, mixed-precision decomposition recovers most of the
quality loss (within 1-2 points on common benchmarks) at the cost of that modest throughput penalty. Compared
to staying in BF16, you trade 10-20% throughput for a 2reduction in memory footprint and the ability to fit a
larger model or serve a larger batch.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a single linear layer in a 13B model:din=dout= 5120, batch sizeB= 16, BF16. The weight
matrixWis 5120  5120 , consuming 5120  5120  2  52 MB per layer. Across 40 transformer layers (MLP
up-projection, down-projection, and the three attention projections-roughly five large matrices per layer), total
weight memory is around 26 GB, consistent with a 13B BF16 model.
After profiling 128 calibration samples, we identify 26 outlier columns (roughly 0.5% of 5120). These 26
columns remain in BF16: 26  5120 2 = 0. 27 MB per matrix. The remaining 5094 columns are quantized to
INT8: 5094  5120 1 = 26MB. Total per-matrix: 26. 3 MB versus the original 52 MB-a near 2 reduction
with 99.5% of the compute running in INT8.
At inference, the forward pass for this layer does:

1. Load the 26-column FP16 slice ofWand the corresponding slice ofX; computeXOWO⊤in FP16.
2. Load the remaining 5094 columns as INT8; dequantize on-the-fly; computeXO ̄WO⊤ ̄in INT8.
3. Add the two partial products in FP16 to produce the output.
    Total bytes transferred per token: 26 MB (INT8 path dominates), versus 52 MB in BF16-halving memory
bandwidth, which maps directly to halved generation latency per layer at batch size 1.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Outlier threshold. A practical heuristic is to flag columns whose maximum absolute activation magni-
tude exceeds 6 standard deviations above the layer mean across your calibration set. Too low a threshold
wastes compute on FP16; too high and you leave genuine outliers in the INT8 path.
LLM.int8() is a capacity tool, not a speed tool. If your model fits comfortably in BF16, do not use it.
Use it when you are trying to serve a model on fewer GPUs or to increase maximum batch size.
Calibration data quality matters. Outlier detection is distribution-sensitive. A calibration set drawn
only from short chat exchanges will misidentify outliers when the model processes long code contexts.
Use diverse calibration data representative of your actual traffic.
Kernel support. The mixed-precision path requires custom CUDA kernels (bitsandbytes is the canoni-
cal open-source implementation). Naively implementing this in standard PyTorch will not give you the
memory savings because PyTorch may still keep the original FP16 weights around.
Interaction with GQA and MLA. Outlier patterns differ across projection types. KV projections in
models using grouped-query attention typically have fewer outliers than the value projections in the MLP.
Profiling each projection separately rather than using a single global threshold improves quality.
```

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A 70B model is too large for your H100 fleet. How do you fit it?” A strong answer names three
levers: model parallelism (tensor or pipeline), lower precision (INT8, INT4), and quantization schemes
(LLM.int8() for memory-safe INT8). The candidate should quantify: 70B at BF16 is 140 GB; at INT8 it
is 70 GB, fitting on one 8-way H100 node.
“What goes wrong when you naively quantize a large transformer to INT8?” Strong answer: outlier
activations in 1% of channels inflate the absmax scale, making the INT8 grid too coarse for the remaining
99% of channels. The fix is mixed-precision decomposition for outlier columns.
“Why do outliers appear more in larger models?” This is the senior follow-up. The empirical finding
is that outlier channels emerge at model scales of roughly 6.7B parameters and above, growing more
extreme with scale. The intuition is that larger models rely on specific feature dimensions to carry sharp,
high-magnitude signals-a form of emergent specialization. A senior answer connects this to the phase
transitions observed in scaling laws and notes that the outlier columns correspond to attention heads or
MLP neurons that have learned to function as routing or gating mechanisms.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
INT8 absmax quantization halves weight memory but causes severe accuracy degradation in models at or
above 6.7B parameters due to outlier activation channels.
LLM.int8() uses mixed-precision decomposition:1% of columns in FP16, the rest in INT8, identified
offline from a calibration set.
The method is a capacity optimization-it enables fitting larger models in GPU memory-not a throughput
optimization; it typically runs 10-20% slower than native BF16.
Outlier channels are stable across inputs, making offline profiling viable for production deployments.
Use LLM.int8() when memory is the binding constraint; move to AWQ or INT4 schemes when you also
need throughput gains.
```
**19.1.2 Activation-Aware Weight Quantization (AWQ) and INT4**
Once LLM.int8() gets your 70B model into memory, the next interviewer question is: “Now make it fast.”
LLM.int8() is a capacity tool-it typically runs 10-20% slower than BF16 because the mixed-precision scatter-
gather adds overhead. AWQ (Activation-Aware Weight Quantization) targets a different objective: squeezing
throughput by going to INT4, which halves memory bandwidth again relative to INT8 and delivers 2-3end-
to-end generation speedup over BF16 with minimal accuracy loss. This question shows up when an interviewer
has already confirmed you can fit the model and wants to know whether you understand the path to production
throughput targets.
The core insight of AWQ is that weights are not equally important for quantization error. Given a linear
layerY =XW, a small fraction of input channels-those multiplied by large activation magnitudes-contribute
disproportionately to the output. When you quantize a salient weight channeljcoarsely, the output error is
∆Yj=xj∆wj. Ifxjis large, even a small per-weight quantization noise∆wjcauses significant output error.
Non-salient channels with smallxjcan absorb much larger∆wjwithout visible effect.
AWQ identifies salient channels by running a small calibration set through the model. For each input

In practice, weights are quantized in _groups_ : every 128 consecutive weights share one FP16 scale and zero-
point, a scheme called group quantization withg= 128. This prevents a single outlier weight from degrading an
entire row and is the dominant production choice. The effective bit-width is slightly above 4 (128 INT4 values
plus one FP16 scale and zero-point per group4.25 bits per weight) but the storage overhead is negligible.
_AWQ finds which weights matter most, scales them up before INT4 quantization so the grid is finer where
errors count, and absorbs the correction into adjacent layers for free._
The bandwidth argument is direct. Inference generation is bandwidth-bound: every generation step loads
the full weight matrix once to multiply against a single token. Cutting weight precision from BF16 (2 bytes) to
INT4 (0.5 bytes) reduces bytes transferred per layer by 4 . In the pure bandwidth limit that translates to 4 
lower latency per token. Real systems achieve 2-3because of kernel launch overhead, the cost of dequantizing
INT4 to FP16 on the fly, and the residual bandwidth of FP16 group scales.
AWQ’s accuracy advantage over naive INT4 comes from the weighted error reduction. Scalingwjby
sjbefore quantization makes the post-dequantization noise∆wj′ = ∆wj/sj, so the output error for salient
channeljdrops fromxj∆wjtoxj∆wj/sj-reduced by exactly the scale factor. Non-salient channels with small
xjare unaffected because their output error was already small. AWQ searches the exponentαover a coarse
grid (0.0 to 1.0 in steps of 0.1) to minimize calibration-set quantization error, making the procedure fast and
calibration-data-efficient.
The design contrast with LLM.int8() is worth internalizing. LLM.int8() targets INT8 weights _and_ handles
activation-outlier channels with a separate FP16 compute path; the result is a model that fits in memory but does
not run faster. AWQ targets INT4 weights only, leaving activations in FP16 (the W4A16 regime). W4A16 is
simpler-weight quantization is far more tractable than activation quantization because weights are static-and it
targets throughput rather than just capacity.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Group size is your accuracy-vs-speed knob. Group size 128 is the standard: it limits scale overhead to
<2%of total weight storage and keeps accuracy within 1-2 points of BF16 on most benchmarks. For
models under 3B parameters, tighten to group size 64 to compensate for the stronger relative compression.
Widening to 256 saves a bit more memory but hurts accuracy noticeably on code and math tasks where
precision matters.
W4A16 before W4A8. Quantizing activations (W4A8) further reduces compute cost but requires per-
token activation scales that must be computed at runtime, adds latency at low batch sizes, and is sensitive
to input distribution shifts. Start with W4A16, validate accuracy on your eval suite, and consider W4A8
only if you have a hardware-specific reason (e.g., INT8 tensor cores running at 2 the FLOP rate of FP16
on your device).
Do not quantize embedding tables or the LM head. These layers are accessed once per forward pass
in a different access pattern and are small relative to the total parameter count. Quantizing them saves
negligible bandwidth and carries real accuracy risk for low-frequency tokens whose embeddings can be
hard to represent in INT4.
Calibration data should match your serving distribution. AWQ activation magnitude estimates stabi-
lize at 128-512 samples. Use diverse data spanning your expected input types-chat, code, documents-so
salient channels are correctly identified for all input modes. A calibration set drawn purely from short
chat turns will misidentify salience for long-context or structured-output use cases.
Stack AWQ on top of GQA for maximum throughput gain. GQA already reduced KV-projection head
counts; AWQ cuts the projection weight bandwidth by another 4 . The two compose multiplicatively on
the KV projection layers and are independent on MLP layers. A LLaMA-3-70B model with GQA and
AWQ INT4 can serve on a single 880 GB H100 node with throughput competitive with a BF16 LLaMA-
3-7B on the same hardware.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“We need 3  throughput improvement on a production 7B model without retraining. What is
your plan?” Strong answer: quantize weights to INT4 using AWQ with group size 128. Generation is
bandwidth-bound; INT4 cuts weight bandwidth by 4 relative to BF16; AWQ’s activation-magnitude-
based scaling preserves accuracy within 1-2 points. Expect 2-3real-world speedup with near-zero ac-
curacy loss on standard benchmarks.
“What is the difference between LLM.int8() and AWQ?” Strong answer: LLM.int8() is a capacity
tool-it targets INT8 with a mixed FP16/INT8 split on activation-outlier channels; it fits models that do
```

### 19.2 Pruning and Distillation.

```
not otherwise fit in memory but typically runs slightly slower than BF16. AWQ is a throughput tool-it
targets INT4 weight-only quantization guided by activation magnitudes; it genuinely makes generation
faster by reducing bandwidth. They solve different problems and can coexist (though INT4 alone usually
dominates once both goals are met).
Senior follow-up: “Why does scaling weights by activation magnitude before quantization actually
reduce output error? Walk me through the math.” Strong senior answer: the per-token quantization
output error for channeljisεj = xj∆wj, where∆wj  kwjk∞/ 127 (the INT8 step size). By
premultiplyingwjbysj> 1 before quantization, the post-dequantization weight error becomes∆wj′=
∆wj/sj, reducing output error toε′j = xj∆wj/sj. Settingsj /s ̄jαwithα 0. 5 balances error
reduction for salient channels against the distortion imposed on non-salient channels. Theαsearch is
cheap: it is a 1D grid search over ten values using only the calibration set, taking seconds per layer.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
AWQ identifies weight channels that matter most by their corresponding activation magnitudes, scales
them up before INT4 quantization for finer resolution, and absorbs the inverse scale into the preceding
layer at zero runtime cost.
INT4 weight quantization with group size 128 (W4A16) cuts weight memory by 4 versus BF16 and
delivers 2-3practical generation throughput improvement by reducing bandwidth in the memory-bound
generation regime.
Group quantization is non-negotiable at INT4: without it, a single outlier weight degrades the entire row’s
resolution, causing accuracy collapse on long-tail tokens.
AWQ is a throughput optimization; LLM.int8() is a capacity optimization. Use AWQ when you need
faster tokens per second from a model that already fits in memory; use LLM.int8() when memory is the
binding constraint.
AWQ and GQA compose multiplicatively on KV projections; combining both is a practical path to serving
70B-class models at 7B-class latency on a single node.
```
### 19.2 Pruning and Distillation

**19.2.1 Structured Pruning of Layers, Heads, and Channels**
In production, the pressure to cut serving costs often arrives after a model is already deployed and has real
traffic. The question is not “can we train a smaller model?” but “can we make this specific 15B checkpoint
cheaper without starting over?” Structured pruning is the tool that answers yes: remove entire transformer
layers, attention heads, or MLP hidden channels from a trained model and hand back a smaller, denser model
that runs on unmodified kernels with genuine latency and memory savings. This topic comes up regularly in
senior inference interviews because it sits at the intersection of model architecture, importance estimation, and
deployment economics.
_Unstructured_ pruning zeros individual weights scattered throughout a weight matrix. Modern hardware
cannot exploit that sparsity efficiently-you still load every weight from HBM before zeroing it in registers, so
you get no memory bandwidth reduction and no throughput gain. Structured pruning removes entire contiguous
blocks: a full transformer layer, all positions of one attention head, or a set of MLP hidden-dim channels. The


```
19.2 Pruning and Distillation
```
result is a model with genuinely smaller dense matrices, producing linear reductions in parameter count, memory
footprint, and compute.
The standard three-step pipeline is:

1. **Score.** Run a small calibration set (typically 128-512 representative sequences) through the model and
    compute an importance score for each structural unit.
2. **Remove.** Zero out or drop the lowest-scoring units until you reach the target parameter budget.
3. **Repair.** Recover lost accuracy by fine-tuning or distillation from the original model (covered in the next
    subsection).
Several importance criteria are used in practice. The simplest is _activation magnitude_ : compute the mean
ℓ 2 norm of a unit’s output across the calibration set-low-magnitude units contribute little to downstream residuals
and are safe to remove. A more principled criterion is the first-order Taylor approximation to the loss increase
caused by removing unitu:
∆Lu

#### X

```
i∈u
```
```
jgiwij,
```
wheregiis the gradient andwithe weight at positioni. For _layer removal_ specifically, a cheap proxy is the
cosine similarity between a layer’s input and output activation vectors: a layer whose output is nearly identical
to its input adds almost nothing to the residual stream and is the first candidate for deletion.
_Structured pruning converts a trained model into a smaller one that runs on unmodified kernels, trading a
controlled accuracy loss for proportional reductions in parameter count, memory, and inference latency._
The alternative-training a smaller model from scratch-requires the full pre-training compute budget. A 15B
model that took weeks on hundreds of GPUs cannot be reproduced in the time a product team has. Structured
pruning plus distillation recovery delivers a comparable result in one to two orders of magnitude less compute.
Structured pruning also composes naturally with quantization. Quantization reduces bytes per weight (e.g.,
BF16 to INT4) but leaves the number of matrix operations unchanged. Pruning reduces the number of operations
outright. Applying both-prune first to shrink layer dimensions, then quantize the surviving weights-stacks the
gains without interference, as long as you run quantization calibration after pruning and not before.
The drawback compared to unstructured pruning is that structured pruning is coarser: you must remove
entire heads or layers even if only a fraction of their weights are dispensable. This means a given parameter
reduction target costs more accuracy points than unstructured pruning on the same model. The tradeoff is
that hardware speedup from structured pruning is real and immediate, whereas the theoretical speedup from
unstructured pruning is largely unrealized on current accelerators.

**A Worked Example**

Consider an NVIDIA-style compression of a 15B Llama-family model: 32 layers,dmodel = 5120, 40
attention heads, MLP hidden dimdff= 13, 696.
**Step 1 - score layers.** Run 256 sequences from a mixed pre-training corpus. For each of the 32 layers
compute the mean cosine similarity between the residual stream at the layer’s input and output. Layers 14-18
(mid-network) consistently show cosine similarity above 0.97-nearly identity transformations. These are flagged
for removal.
**Step 2 - score heads and channels.** For each attention head compute the mean output norm; for each MLP
hidden channel compute the mean activation norm. Rank both globally.
**Step 3 - remove to target.** Remove 8 of the 32 layers (the 8 with highest input-output cosine similarity).


```
19.2 Pruning and Distillation
```
Trim the MLP hidden dim from 13,696 to 9,216 by dropping the lowest-norm channels. Optionally reduce KV
heads from 40 to 8 (GQA-style) for additional KV cache savings.
After pruning: approximately 8.1B parameters. MMLU immediately after pruning drops from 65% to
roughly 58%-a 7-point raw gap. Memory for weights in BF16 shrinks from 30 GB to 16 GB, and generation
throughput at batch size 32 on an H100 increases from 3 , 200 tokens/s to 5 , 800 tokens/s, a 1. 8 improve-
ment, before any distillation recovery.
After a short distillation pass (covered in the next subsection), MMLU recovers to roughly 64.5%-within
half a point of the original 15B, at 53% of the parameter count and 1. 8 the throughput.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Prune layers before heads or channels. Layer removal is the highest-leverage decision: each removed
layer eliminates 2 dmodeldffparameters in one cut. Score layers first, remove them, then re-score
heads and channels on the surviving architecture. Pruning all dimensions simultaneously compounds
errors.
Score on calibration data that matches your deployment distribution. A calibration set that is too
short (< 128 sequences) or domain-mismatched produces noisy importance scores. If you prune a coding
model with web-text calibration data, you will over-prune heads that are important for code structure and
miss heads that are dead weight for your actual traffic.
Use cosine similarity for layer removal, Taylor sensitivity for head and channel removal. Cosine
similarity is fast and requires no gradients. Taylor sensitivity is more accurate for fine-grained removal
but requires a backward pass. This split gives you the best of both at reasonable cost.
Keep a validation set of diﬀicult prompts and check it after each pruning step. Accuracy on standard
benchmarks like MMLU is not sensitive enough to catch regressions in long-context or multi-step rea-
soning tasks. Run at least one specialized eval (e.g., a chain-of-thought benchmark) before committing to
the pruned structure.
Never quantize before pruning. Some quantization calibration methods (AWQ-style) compute per-
channel weight scales from activation statistics. If you prune channels after calibration, those scales are
stale. The correct order is always: prune!distill!quantize.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you compress a 70B model to fit on a single 80 GB H100?” The 70B model in BF16 is
 140 GB, which does not fit. Structured pruning to35B active parameters brings the weight footprint
to70 GB; add INT4 quantization to land at35 GB with room for KV cache. Distill from the 70B
teacher to recover accuracy. A strong answer names this sequence and gives the memory arithmetic.
“What is the difference between structured and unstructured pruning, and why does it matter for
inference?” Unstructured pruning produces sparse weight matrices that do not reduce memory bandwidth
on dense-matrix hardware. Structured pruning removes whole rows, columns, heads, or layers, producing
smaller dense tensors with proportional speedup on standard kernels. This is the answer that separates a
candidate who has thought about hardware from one who has only read papers.
Senior follow-up: “You removed 8 of 32 layers from a 15B model and see a 10-point MMLU drop.
Before running distillation, what do you investigate?” First, break down the MMLU drop by category:
if it is uniform, the issue is capacity loss that distillation can recover. If it is concentrated in world knowl-
```

```
19.2 Pruning and Distillation
```
```
edge or multi-hop reasoning questions, you may have removed layers that serve as key associative recall
steps. In that case, swap in the two or three layers with the highest Taylor sensitivity scores instead of the
ones with the highest cosine similarity. Cosine similarity is a coarse proxy; for reasoning-heavy tasks,
sensitivity-based scoring is more reliable.
```
**19.2.2 Distillation Recovery from a Pruned Initialization**
Structured pruning always leaves you with a model that is noticeably worse than the original. The question
every interview panel eventually asks is: how do you get the accuracy back, and what does it cost? Knowledge
distillation from the pruned initialization is the standard answer, and it shows up at every seniority level in LLM
inference interviews because it bridges the architectural decision to prune and the quality guarantee you owe a
product team. What separates a strong answer from a weak one is understanding why distillation from a pruned
init is fundamentally different from-and cheaper than-training a small model from scratch.
Standard cross-entropy fine-tuning trains a model against hard one-hot labels: at each token position,
only the ground-truth token contributes gradient. Knowledge distillation instead trains the student to match
the teacher’s full probability distribution over the vocabulary. The training loss is the forward KL divergence
between the teacher’s next-token distributionpTand the student’spS:


entirely:
L=LKD+λLCE, λ 0. 1.
The key insight is not the loss function-it is the initialization. When you prune a 15B model to produce an
8B student, the surviving weights are already the best 8B-worth of weights the teacher had. The student starts
with a loss that is already near the pruning-induced gap, not at random initialization. Training from that point
requires only a small correction, not a full optimization trajectory from scratch.
An optional extension is _feature-level distillation_ : for each student layerlpaired with a corresponding
teacher layerl′, add a loss term
