whereWprojis a learnable linear projection to align dimensions when the teacher and student hidden sizes differ.
This aligns intermediate representations and accelerates accuracy recovery but requires the teacher to remain
resident in GPU memory for every training step.
_Distilling from a pruned initialization is strictly better than training a small model from scratch because
you are correcting a small perturbation in an already-converged loss landscape, not optimizing from a random
starting point._
Training a fresh 8B model from scratch requires hundreds of billions to a trillion tokens-roughly the same
scale as pre-training the original. Distillation from a pruned 15B initialization recovers most of the accuracy
loss with far fewer tokens, because the student has already seen the effective gradient signal accumulated over
the teacher’s full pre-training. NVIDIA’s Minitron experiments show recovery to within one MMLU point using
roughly 128B tokens of distillation, compared to1T tokens for scratch training to equivalent quality-a 8 
reduction in the recovery budget alone.
The soft probability targets from the teacher provide a dense per-step gradient signal. A one-hot label


```
19.2 Pruning and Distillation
```
on a 32,000-token vocabulary gives exactly one nonzero gradient component per position. The teacher’s dis-
tribution typically assigns non-negligible probability to dozens of plausible continuations, each contributing
gradient. This richness is especially helpful for recovering the student’s early layers, which must now handle
token interactions that the pruned architecture routes differently than the original.
Versus other recovery strategies-continued pre-training, LoRA fine-tuning, task-specific fine-tuning-distillation
is the only approach that recovers general-purpose capability rather than task-specific accuracy. Fine-tuning on
a downstream task recovers performance on that task but does not restore the broad capability distribution of
the original model. If you need a general-purpose compressed model, distillation is the right tool.

**A Worked Example**

Setup: teacher is a 15B Llama-family model; student is the 8.1B model produced by structured pruning as
described in the previous subsection. Pre-pruning MMLU: 65%. Post-pruning MMLU: 58%. Target: recover
to within 1 point of 65%.

1. **Assemble the calibration corpus.** Sample 128B tokens from the same distribution as pre-training-mixed
    web text, code, multilingual data-in the original mixture ratios. Do not use only downstream task data;
    you want to recover general capability, not overfit to a benchmark.
2. **Configure the loss.** Use output-level KD with temperatureτ= 2(softer distributions help the student
    learn inter-token relationships). Setλ= 0. 1 for the cross-entropy term.
3. **Estimate the compute cost.** Each distillation step requires:
    One teacher forward pass: 2  15 BTFLOPs per batch
    One student forward pass and backward pass: 6  8 BTFLOPs per batch
    Over 128B tokens with sequence length 4,096, total compute is roughly 6  8  109  128  109  6  1021
    FLOPs for the student, plus 2  1021 for teacher inference. Compare to scratch training an 8B model
    on 1T tokens: 6  8  109  1012  5  1022 FLOPs-roughly 6 more compute for the scratch run.
4. **Results.** After the 128B-token distillation pass:
    MMLU: 64.5% (recovered 6.5 of the 7-point pruning gap)
    Coding benchmark (MBPP): recovers from 47% to 54% against teacher 55%
    Generation throughput at batch size 32: 5 , 800 tokens/s vs. 3 , 200 tokens/s for the original
    15B-an 1. 8 improvement
    The remaining 0.5-point MMLU gap is the irreducible cost of reduced capacity. Extending distillation to
    256B tokens closes it by another 0.2 points but with sharply diminishing returns.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start with output-level KD; add feature-level distillation only for persistent gaps. Feature-level dis-
tillation keeps the teacher resident in memory for every training step, roughly doubling GPU memory
pressure. In most cases, output-level KD over 50-100B tokens recovers 85-90% of the pruning loss. Only
add the feature-level term if you see a systematic gap on specific capability categories that does not close
with more output-level tokens.
Use temperature τ = 2 - 4 for the KD loss. Temperatureτ = 1(raw logits) produces a distribution
that is too peaked on the argmax, reducing the soft-label information. A temperature of 2-4 flattens the
distribution enough that secondary tokens contribute meaningful gradient. A practical default isτ= 2
with a linear warmup of the KD loss weight over the first 5% of training steps.
```

```
19.2 Pruning and Distillation
```
```
Match calibration data to your deployment traﬀic. The distillation step is short enough that domain-
targeted data is tractable. If your compressed model will primarily serve code generation, distill on a
code-heavy corpus. A general-purpose distillation that underperforms on your actual request distribution
costs user quality on every inference for the model’s lifetime.
Expect 90% accuracy recovery in 10-100B tokens for models above 7B. Returns diminish sharply
after 100B tokens because the student has effectively exhausted its capacity; additional tokens are not
adding new gradient directions. If you are still seeing a large gap at 100B tokens, the gap is structural (too
aggressive a pruning ratio), not a training-budget problem.
The prune-then-distill recipe breaks down above  50% parameter reduction. Removing more than
half the parameters leaves the pruned initialization with too little useful structure. A fresh 8B model
trained on the same data as a pruned-and-distilled 7.5B-from-15B will typically be competitive or better
because it is not constrained to a damaged architecture. Treat 50% as the rough ceiling; beyond it, con-
sider training a new small model from scratch using the large model’s outputs as training labels (offline
distillation) rather than starting from a pruned checkpoint.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through producing an 8B model from a 15B checkpoint without full retraining.” Strong
answer: run structured pruning to remove layers and channels using importance scores on a calibration
set, then run output-level knowledge distillation from the 15B teacher over 50-100B tokens withτ= 2.
Name the compute saving (6-8vs. scratch training) and the expected accuracy gap (within 1 MMLU
point for a 15B!8B compression).
“Why is distilling from a pruned initialization better than training a small model from scratch?”
Strong answer: the pruned model starts with weights already optimized over the teacher’s full pre-training;
it begins near the target loss rather than at random initialization. The distillation step corrects a small
perturbation, not the full optimization problem. This translates to 6-8fewer training tokens to reach
equivalent quality.
“What loss function do you use and why not just cross-entropy?” Strong answer: forward KL diver-
gence between teacher and student distributions. Cross-entropy against hard one-hot labels discards the
teacher’s uncertainty information; the soft distribution provides gradient from all high-probability tokens,
not just the argmax. The richness of the signal is especially important in the early distillation steps when
the student’s distribution is still far from the teacher’s.
Senior follow-up: “After distillation your 8B model recovers MMLU well but regresses significantly
on multi-step reasoning. What is the most likely cause and how do you fix it?” Multi-step reasoning
relies on the residual stream accumulating state across specific layers. If you removed layers uniformly
by cosine similarity, you may have deleted layers that specialize in intermediate reasoning steps even
if their input-output similarity happened to be high on general calibration data. Diagnosis: re-run the
importance scoring using a calibration set that includes chain-of-thought traces and compare which layers
are now flagged. Fix: restore the two or three reasoning-critical layers and re-prune a different set of less-
critical layers to maintain the parameter budget, then re-distill with a calibration corpus weighted toward
reasoning-heavy tasks.
```

## Part VIII

# Data: The Real Differentiator


## Chapter 20 Pre-Training Data Pipelines

### 20.1 Where Training Data Comes From

**20.1.1 Common Crawl, WET vs. WARC, and Extraction Tools**
When an interviewer asks “where does your pre-training data come from?”, the honest answer for most large
models is: mostly Common Crawl, with a lot of careful processing on top of it. Common Crawl is the closest
thing the open world has to a snapshot of the web, and understanding its internals-specifically the difference
between the WARC and WET formats, and what extraction tool you apply to convert HTML to text-is the kind
of detail that separates an engineer who has built a real data pipeline from one who has only read about it. This
topic shows up in senior ML engineer and research scientist interviews whenever the conversation gets into data
quality or pipeline design.
Common Crawl is a nonprofit that has been running monthly web crawls since 2007. Each crawl visits
billions of URLs using a seeded breadth-first traversal of the web, starting from hundreds of millions of seed
URLs and respectingrobots.txtdirectives. The result of each crawl is stored in two primary formats:
**WARC** (Web ARChive): the raw HTTP response, including headers and the original HTML. This is the
ground truth and can be tens of terabytes per snapshot.
**WET** : a pre-extracted plaintext version produced by Common Crawl itself. The conversion from HTML
to text is lossy-structure, links, and metadata are stripped-and the extraction quality is modest by modern
standards.
As of 2024, there are roughly 100 crawl snapshots, each adding approximately 2-3 billion pages. Naively,
this looks enormous:240 trillion tokens if you take all snapshots and run minimal filtering (as DCLM-pool
does). But the raw quality of random Common Crawl pages is low-boilerplate, spam, near-duplicate content,
and non-English text dominate a random sample.
The HTML-to-text conversion step matters more than it looks. Starting from the WARC files and applying
a high-quality extractor produces substantially better text than using the WET files directly. The DataComp-LM
paper ran a controlled ablation across extraction methods and found that using Trafilatura instead of the raw
WET files improved downstream benchmark scores by roughly four points. _Your choice of HTML extraction
tool is a hyperparameter with measurable impact on model quality._
The appeal of WARC over WET is information density. WET is a blunt conversion: it strips away HTML
structure and applies a simple heuristic to identify the “main content” of a page. WARC lets you apply a modern,
ML-informed extractor like Trafilatura or jusText, which use statistical models to distinguish article body text
from navigation bars, footers, and ads. On a real web corpus, this distinction is not trivial-a significant fraction
of WET tokens are boilerplate that would never appear in a well-written document.
The trade-off is cost. Processing WARCs yourself requires storing or streaming tens of terabytes per snap-
shot, running an extractor at scale, and managing failures in a distributed pipeline. WET is turnkey: download
and tokenize. For many teams prototyping a new filtering algorithm, starting with WET is fine. For a production
corpus where per-point improvements on benchmarks matter, WET is a ceiling.
There is also a secondary effect: different extractors make different coverage-quality trade-offs. Trafilatura
is aggressive at removing boilerplate and retains fewer tokens; jusText is more permissive and retains more,
which is important when you are trying to sustain a very large training run. NVIDIA’s Nemotron-CC work


```
20.1 Where Training Data Comes From
```
explicitly chose jusText over Trafilatura to maximize the token yield for training runs that require well above 6
trillion tokens, accepting slightly noisier extractions in exchange for coverage.

**A Worked Example**

Consider the DCLM-pool construction: all Common Crawl snapshots up to 2024 are taken, WARC files are
processed with Trafilatura, language identification is run to keep primarily English pages, and basic heuristics
(minimum document length, removal of mostly non-alphabetic content) are applied. The result is approximately
240 trillion tokens.
Now apply the DCLM-baseline quality filter (a fastText classifier trained to distinguish instruction-like
data from generic web text): the pool shrinks to roughly 3.8 trillion tokens-about 1.6% of the original. This
aggressive filtering yields high benchmark scores per token, but a 70B model trained for 2 epochs on 3.8 trillion
tokens only sees 7. 6  1012 training tokens, which is already reaching the data ceiling for that corpus.
Compare to Nemotron-CC starting from the same Common Crawl dumps: by using jusText (more per-
missive extraction) and a softer ensemble of classifiers rather than a single hard threshold, NVIDIA recovered
approximately 6.3 trillion tokens while maintaining quality that outperforms DCLM-baseline on most bench-
marks. The arithmetic is simple: same source, different extraction and filtering strategy, 66% more usable
tokens.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
WET vs. WARC: Use WET for prototyping and research where you need fast iteration. Use WARC with
a modern extractor (Trafilatura or jusText) for any corpus that will be used to train a model above 7B
parameters, where the four-point quality gap is significant.
Extractor choice: If maximizing benchmark scores per token is the goal, prefer Trafilatura. If you need
more tokens to fill a longer training run (e.g.,>10 trillion tokens), prefer jusText and accept marginally
noisier extractions.
How many snapshots to use: Newer snapshots have more overlap with newer web content. Older snap-
shots have higher duplicate rates across themselves. Deduplication cost grows super-linearly with the
number of snapshots, so most pipelines start with 5-15 recent snapshots and add more only when data
quantity becomes the bottleneck.
robots.txt compliance: Common Crawl does respect robots.txt in principle, but coverage is imperfect.
If you are building a corpus for a commercial product, spot-check robots.txt compliance on high-volume
domains to avoid legal exposure.
Incomplete coverage is real: Common Crawl is not the internet. Even applying the same Reddit karma
filter used to construct OpenWebText against all of Common Crawl yields only about half the tokens that
a direct crawl of those Reddit-linked pages would produce. For domains that matter to your application,
augment with targeted crawls.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how Common Crawl becomes training tokens.” A strong answer covers: raw crawl
produces WARC and WET; you extract text from WARC using a tool like Trafilatura; apply language ID
and heuristic filters; deduplicate; optionally apply a quality classifier. Name the 4-point gap between
extraction tools.
```

```
20.1 Where Training Data Comes From
```
```
“Why not just use the WET files Common Crawl provides?” Key points: WET is a lossy conversion
with low-quality boilerplate extraction; modern extractors applied to WARC produce measurably better
text; the cost is pipeline complexity and storage, which is worth it above prototype scale.
Senior follow-up: “DCLM-baseline filters 240 trillion tokens down to 3.8 trillion. Is that a prob-
lem?” A senior answer acknowledges the data ceiling this creates for large-model training runs, explains
the Nemotron-CC approach of using a softer classifier ensemble to recover 6.3 trillion tokens from the
same source, and discusses the coverage-quality trade-off in classifier design. The deeper point is that
aggressive quality filtering can become a capacity constraint before compute does.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Common Crawl produces WARC (raw HTML) and WET (pre-extracted text); always prefer WARC with
a quality extractor for production corpora.
Extraction tool choice is a measurable hyperparameter: Trafilatura vs. raw WET is worth roughly four
benchmark points in controlled ablations.
Trafilatura maximizes quality per token; jusText maximizes token yield-choose based on whether your
bottleneck is quality or quantity.
Common Crawl is not a complete snapshot of the web; targeted domain crawls are necessary for coverage
of high-value sources.
Aggressive quality filtering that reduces 240 trillion tokens to 3.8 trillion creates a data ceiling for large
training runs; ensemble-based filtering recovers more tokens at comparable quality.
```
**20.1.2 Books, Code, Papers, and Forums**
Every serious pre-training mix reserves dedicated weight for curated domain corpora-books, code reposi-
tories, academic papers, and Q&A forums-even when web data already totals trillions of tokens. An interviewer
asking “why not just filter Common Crawl more aggressively?” is testing whether you understand what these
domains provide that filtered web text cannot. This question surfaces regularly in ML infrastructure and re-
search scientist interviews, especially when the topic is domain-specific capability, long-context extension, or
instruction-following ability.
Web text is wide but shallow. A typical web page is short, self-contained, and stylistically generic. The
corpora described in this subsection are valuable because they provide signal that web pages structurally cannot:
**Books** : long-range coherence and narrative structure. A single book can span hundreds of thousands
of tokens with thematic continuity, making book corpora the primary tool for long-context extension
training. BooksCorpus (7,000 self-published works, now defunct) was used for BERT. Project Gutenberg
(75,000 public-domain books) is the clean open alternative. Books3, drawn from shadow libraries, was
used in the Pile and the original Llama but has since generated substantial copyright litigation.
**Code** : formal structure, precise semantics, and executable reasoning chains. The dominant source is
GitHub. The Stack (from BigCode) is the open replication: 137 million repositories git-cloned, filtered
to permissively licensed files, deduplicated, yielding 3.1 TB of code in over 300 programming languages.
Code is commonly cited as improving reasoning and tool-use capabilities beyond programming tasks,
though the mechanism is not fully understood.
**Academic papers** : dense factual knowledge and structured argumentation. arXiv provides open-access
preprints across STEM fields. PubMed Central provides biomedical papers under an NIH open-access


```
20.1 Where Training Data Comes From
```
mandate. Together they add tens of billions of tokens of high-information-density text that is underrepre-
sented in general web crawls.
**Forums (Stack Exchange, Reddit, Wikipedia)** : question-answer structure that closely mirrors how users
interact with a deployed chat model. Stack Exchange is particularly valuable because votes and comments
provide a quality signal that lets you filter aggressively. Wikipedia is used both as a direct training source
and as a quality reference (via n-gram language models) to score other documents.
_Each domain corpus provides a structural signal-long coherence, formal correctness, QA format, or ency-
clopedic density-that filtered web text approximates poorly at any reasonable scale._
The core argument is coverage of distributions that web text undersamples. Consider what a random Com-
mon Crawl page looks like: short, often list-formatted, frequently e-commerce or news. The long-tail of tech-
nical, literary, and mathematical knowledge that makes a model broadly capable lives in books, papers, and
specialized forums. A quality classifier trained to select “Wikipedia-like” text from Common Crawl will re-
cover some of this, but it will miss the structural properties (multi-page coherence, formal proof style, multi-turn
Q&A) that domain corpora provide natively.
Stack Exchange deserves special attention. A Stack Overflow thread-question, accepted answer, commu-
nity comments-looks almost identical to a user-assistant chat exchange. Models trained on substantial Stack
Exchange data have, in a sense, seen instruction-following examples during pre-training. This is one reason
the line between pre-training and post-training data is blurry: the instruction-following distribution is already
present in the pre-training mix, just unlabeled.
Code has a different but equally important property: it is almost always semantically valid (it compiles or it
doesn’t), it is heavily deduplicated by nature (copy-paste code is easy to detect), and it carries explicit structure
(function signatures, docstrings, tests) that exposes relationships between specification and implementation.
Training on code improves performance on tasks that require multi-step planning and precise output formatting,
even when code itself is not the target.

**A Worked Example**

The Dolma corpus used to train OLMo (AI2) illustrates how these domains compose in practice. The
reported breakdown across3 trillion tokens is approximately:

Source Tokens Notes
Common Crawl 2.0T processed via CCNet-style rules
The Stack (code) 0.4T permissive licenses only
C4 0.2T used as a clean web supplement
Reddit 0.1T submissions and comments separately
Semantic Scholar 0.08T 40M academic papers
Project Gutenberg 0.006T public-domain books
Wikipedia 0.004T monthly dump, all languages
Web text dominates by volume, but code (13%) and academic papers (3%) punch above their weight:
models trained without these domains show notably degraded performance on programming tasks and technical
Q&A even though they represent a small fraction of total tokens.
The token counts also reveal a practical constraint: Project Gutenberg at 6 billion tokens is tiny relative to
the corpus. It is included not for scale but for structural diversity-long-form text with high coherence that no
other source provides at equivalent quality.


```
20.1 Where Training Data Comes From
```
**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
License filtering for code is mandatory. The Stack and similar pipelines filter to permissive licenses
(MIT, Apache, BSD) before any other step. Training on GPL code and releasing the model exposes you to
viral license claims; the legal landscape is unsettled enough that teams err on the side of permissive-only.
This drops coverage from all of GitHub to roughly one-third of public repositories.
Wikipedia as a quality anchor vs. training source. Wikipedia is small (<0.2% of a typical corpus)
but appears in almost every mix. Its dual role-as a direct source of high-quality text and as the reference
distribution for quality classifiers-means removing it from training to avoid license concerns would also
break most model-based quality filters.
Books3 and shadow libraries are off the table for commercial models. Meta’s use of LibGen (4M
books) is the subject of ongoing litigation. Project Gutenberg (75,000 public-domain books) is the safe
alternative; the quality is high but the volume is 50smaller.
Stack Exchange and Reddit licensing changed around 2023. Both platforms moved to require paid
licenses for commercial model training. Budget for this or find community-sourced snapshots taken before
the policy change. Datasets like Dolma used pre-2023 Reddit dumps; replicating this for a new corpus
requires negotiation or a substitute.
Domain upsampling at mid-training. Even if a domain is well-represented at pre-training scale, it is
common to upsample math, code, and long-context data at mid-training to strengthen specific capabili-
ties. The Tulu and OLMo-2 pipelines both do this explicitly, applying 5-20upsampling on math and
reasoning data relative to their natural frequency in the web corpus.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why include Stack Exchange in a pre-training corpus? It’s only a few billion tokens.” Key points:
volume is not the reason; it is the QA structure, which pre-exposes the model to instruction-following
format, and the quality signal from votes that enables aggressive filtering. Contrast with raw Common
Crawl where no comparable quality signal exists per document.
“How do you handle code licensing in a pre-training corpus?” A strong answer covers: filter to
permissive licenses (MIT, Apache, BSD) at repository level before extraction; deduplicate aggressively
because copy-paste code is common; note that GPL code creates viral license risk that most teams avoid
for production models. Mention The Stack as the open benchmark for this approach.
Senior follow-up: “If you had to cut your corpus from 15 trillion tokens to 3 trillion due to a compute
budget reduction, which domains would you preserve and at what ratios?” A senior answer reasons
from capability impact rather than volume: preserve code (10-15%), academic papers (5%), and high-
quality filtered web (75-80%); cut general Reddit and unfiltered Common Crawl first. Justify by pointing
to ablations (Dolma, DCLM) showing that code and papers have outsized impact per token on benchmark
performance, while generic web text is the most substitutable component.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Books, code, papers, and forums each provide structural signals-long coherence, formal correctness, QA
format, encyclopedic density-that filtered web text cannot replicate at any scale.
Stack Exchange and Wikipedia appear in nearly every mix not for volume but for structural quality;
```

### 20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora.

```
Wikipedia also doubles as the reference distribution for quality classifiers.
Code must be filtered to permissive licenses before training; GPL and other copyleft licenses create legal
exposure in commercial models.
Shadow library books (Books3, LibGen) offer substantial volume but are subject to active litigation;
Project Gutenberg is the safe 75,000-book alternative.
Domain data is typically upsampled 5-20at mid-training to strengthen targeted capabilities, even when
the domain was already present at pre-training scale.
```
### 20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora

**20.2.1 From C4 and The Pile to RefinedWeb and FineWeb**
Every serious interview question about pre-training eventually comes down to one uncomfortable truth:
“the internet” is not a dataset. When you first start building corpus pipelines, the naive assumption is that you
download Common Crawl, shuffle it, and feed it to the model. What you actually get is mostly boilerplate,
spam, and machine-generated SEO text. The history of open pre-training corpora is the history of the commu-
nity figuring out, dataset by dataset, how to turn Common Crawl into something trainable. Understanding the
milestones-C4, The Pile, RefinedWeb, FineWeb-tells you what decisions matter, what mistakes were made, and
what the current defaults are. This progression shows up in senior interviews as a framing question: “How did
the community’s approach to corpus construction evolve, and why?”
The central challenge is that Common Crawl is simultaneously enormous and noisy. A single monthly
snapshot contains roughly 1.4 trillion tokens, but most of it fails to qualify as coherent natural language by any
reasonable measure. The filtration problem is: given a very large, very cheap pool of text, how do you maximize
the quality-per-token of the subset you actually train on?
The early answer, introduced by **C4** (Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus, from the T5 paper in 2019), was
purely heuristic: keep lines ending in terminal punctuation, require at least three sentences per document, strip
pages containing certain keywords, and discard any text containing curly braces-which removed most code.
Starting from one snapshot of approximately 1.4 trillion tokens, these rules yielded roughly 156 billion tokens
of English text. The approach is fast, deterministic, and interpretable. Its limitation is equally obvious: well-
formed spam still passes, and legitimate domain-specific text (technical documentation, structured prose) often
fails.
EleutherAI’s **The Pile** (2020) took the opposite stance: instead of filtering a single noisy source aggres-
sively, curate 22 deliberately chosen high-quality domains and mix them. The result is an 825 GB dataset
(roughly 400 billion tokens) spanning Common Crawl subsets, Books3, arXiv, PubMed Central, GitHub, Stack
Exchange, Wikipedia, and others. Each source was selected because domain experts believed it carried signal-
not because a classifier said so.
**RefinedWeb** (2023, from TII) reversed the Pile’s philosophy: it bet that Common Crawl alone, filtered well
enough, outperforms any handpicked multi-source blend. Using Trafilatura for HTML extraction, Gopher-style
heuristic quality rules, and aggressive fuzzy deduplication, TII produced a 5 trillion token corpus without any
model-based classifier. **FineWeb** from Hugging Face extended this approach to all available Common Crawl
dumps, yielding 15 trillion tokens with additional deduplication and light anonymization.
_The core progression is from heuristics-on-one-dump, to multi-source curation, to aggressive-heuristics-
on-all-dumps-each step trading a different dial between volume, coverage, and quality._


```
20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora
```
Rule-based filtering has one decisive advantage over model-based filtering: it cannot overfit to a proxy.
A classifier trained to find Wikipedia-like text will produce more Wikipedia-like text, not necessarily better
pre-training data. In 2020, this was a genuine concern-the models available for filtering were too weak to be
trusted for semantic judgments, and aggressive model-based filtering risked stripping out legitimate content
from underrepresented dialects and domains that simply did not look like encyclopedia articles.
The Pile’s multi-source design solved coverage differently. Instead of filtering a noisy pool, it sourced
directly from known-good repositories: arXiv for scientific reasoning, PubMed for biomedical language, Stack
Exchange for technical QA. The trade-off is that assembling and licensing 22 separate sources is expensive and
fragile-several Pile sources (Books3, Reddit) have since been removed or restricted due to copyright and API
policy changes.
RefinedWeb and FineWeb took the pragmatic position: if you deduplicate thoroughly and apply heuristic
rules carefully, you can extract more quality from Common Crawl than any curated multi-source mix, because
Common Crawl is simply larger. FineWeb’s 15 trillion tokens dwarfs The Pile by 37. The deduplication
step deserves particular emphasis: fuzzy deduplication using MinHash to find near-duplicate documents con-
sistently improves downstream model quality even when it reduces token count. Models that memorize repeated
boilerplate instead of learning novel patterns pay a quality tax that raw token volume cannot compensate for.

**A Worked Example**

Walk through building a C4-equivalent pipeline from a single Common Crawl snapshot,CC-MAIN-2019-18,
which contains approximately 1.4 trillion tokens in WET format.

1. **Language filter.** Run fastText language identification; keep only documents classified as English with
    confidencep > 0. 65. This drops roughly 50% of documents. Remaining:700 billion tokens.
2. **Heuristic rules.** Apply C4 rules: drop lines not ending in terminal punctuation, drop documents with
    fewer than three sentences, drop documents containing{or}, drop documents matching a 400-word
    blocklist. Remaining:165 billion tokens.
3. **Exact deduplication.** Hash each 3-sentence window with SHA-1; drop any document where more than
    30% of windows appeared before. Remaining:156 billion tokens.
That is the C4 slice: one snapshot, three passes, 11% retention. Now extend to FineWeb: repeat across
all 100 Common Crawl snapshots (roughly 140 trillion token raw pool), replace step 2 with Gopher rules, add
MinHash fuzzy dedup with a Jaccard threshold of 0.8, and you converge toward 15 trillion tokens of retained
text-the FineWeb baseline.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
WET vs. WARC extraction. Using pre-extracted WET files is faster but delivers 3-4 benchmark points
lower than re-extracting HTML with Trafilatura or jusText. Pay the compute cost of WARC extraction
once; you will not redo the corpus every month, and the quality gain is permanent.
Deduplication scope. Within-snapshot exact dedup is cheap. Cross-snapshot dedup catches repeated
boilerplate (news syndication, Wikipedia mirrors) but requires storing hundreds of billions of hashes. For
most teams, within-snapshot exact dedup plus cross-snapshot MinHash fuzzy dedup is the right balance.
Multi-source vs. single-source. If your targets are domain-specific (biomedical, legal, scientific), include
those sources explicitly-web data undersamples technical literature by roughly 10 relative to professional
usage. For general language, FineWeb or a filtered Common Crawl is sufficient.
```

```
20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora
```
```
Rule-based vs. model-based. Pure heuristics are reproducible and fast; use FineWeb as your base and
layer model-based filters on top for targeted quality improvements. Mixing both is now standard in pro-
duction.
Token budget alignment. At 7B parameters, roughly 1 trillion high-quality tokens hits the Chinchilla-
optimal frontier. At 70B, that rises to 10 trillion. Choosing a dataset with fewer tokens than your compute
budget forces multi-epoch training, which hurts quality; an oversized dataset means you stop before the
model is saturated.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you would build a pre-training corpus from Common Crawl.” A strong
answer names the four stages in order: extract (WET vs. WARC, choice of tool), language filter, quality
filter (heuristic rules and/or classifier), deduplication (exact then fuzzy). Mention approximate retention
rates at each step-11% retention for C4-style filtering on a single snapshot is a concrete number worth
having.
“Why does The Pile use 22 sources instead of just filtering Common Crawl harder?” Coverage:
Common Crawl systematically underrepresents technical domains. PubMed, arXiv, and Stack Exchange
are not well-crawled, so model-filtered web data misses them regardless of filter quality. A strong answer
also notes that this advantage erodes as legal and API access to those sources becomes restricted.
“What is the difference between C4 and FineWeb? When would you use one over the other?”
C4 is a single-snapshot, heuristic-only, 156-billion-token dataset-useful for ablations and reproducibil-
ity. FineWeb is all-dumps, 15 trillion tokens, heuristic rules plus fuzzy dedup-use it for any real training
run where you want a strong general-purpose baseline with more than enough tokens for a 70B model.
Senior follow-up: “FineWeb outperforms C4 on benchmarks. Is that because of more tokens or
better deduplication?” The senior answer isolates the variables: FineWeb uses 96 more tokens
but also applies MinHash deduplication, which C4 lacks. Controlled ablations in the FineWeb release
show that deduplication alone accounts for most of the gap on knowledge-intensive benchmarks, while
the additional token volume helps primarily on few-shot generalization tasks. The practical lesson is that
deduplication is higher leverage than raw volume once a corpus exceeds a few hundred billion tokens.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
C4 established the heuristic-filtering template: punctuation rules, sentence-count thresholds, blocklists
applied to one Common Crawl snapshot, yielding 156 billion tokens at 11% retention.
The Pile showed that multi-source curation outperforms filtered web alone when domain coverage matters,
but the approach is fragile to copyright and API restrictions that have since removed several of its key
sources.
RefinedWeb and FineWeb validated the counter-bet: aggressive fuzzy deduplication plus heuristics ap-
plied to all Common Crawl dumps produces a superior general-purpose corpus without model-based
filtering, at 5-15 trillion tokens.
Fuzzy deduplication (MinHash, Jaccard0.8) is higher-leverage than additional raw tokens once a corpus
exceeds a few hundred billion tokens-it is now standard practice in every serious pipeline.
HTML extraction tool choice (Trafilatura or jusText vs. pre-extracted WET) shifts benchmark scores by
3-4 points and is one of the cheapest, highest-return decisions in the entire pipeline.
```

```
20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora
```
**20.2.2 DCLM, Nemotron-CC, and the Modern Recipe**
The 2024 DataComp-LM (DCLM) paper changed the default assumptions for every team building a serious
pre-training pipeline. Before it, the community had largely avoided machine-learning classifiers for filtering pre-
training data, on the grounds that such filters introduce hard-to-audit biases and may strip out underrepresented
content. DCLM settled the question empirically through a controlled benchmark competition: a fastText classi-
fier trained on instruction-style positive examples, applied aggressively to Common Crawl, outperforms every
prior heuristic baseline on standard evaluations. Nemotron-CC from NVIDIA followed with a complementary
finding-aggressive quality filtering preserves quality but destroys token volume, and at the scale required for a
70B-class model you need both. These two datasets now define the upper boundary of what is publicly achiev-
able in open pre-training data, and understanding their pipelines in detail is expected knowledge for any senior
ML engineer working on pre-training.
DCLM frames corpus construction as a machine-learning competition: given a fixed compute budget for
a 7B-parameter model, which data pipeline produces the best benchmark scores? To make this repeatable, the
team first processed all available Common Crawl dumps through a unified extraction and MinHash deduplication
pipeline, producing **DCLM-pool** : 240 trillion tokens of deduplicated English web text. The competition then
asks: what quality filter, applied to DCLM-pool, yields the best downstream model?
Their winning recipe is afastTextbinary classifier. The positive training set combines two sources:
**OpenHermes-2.5** : a collection of GPT-4-generated instruction-following examples covering diverse tasks-
question answering, reasoning, code, summarization.
**ELI5** : the Reddit “Explain Like I’m 5” subreddit, where community members write detailed, accessible
explanations in response to curious questions.
Negative examples are sampled uniformly from RefinedWeb-not garbage, but less curated than the positives.
The classifier score is computed for every document in DCLM-pool; keeping documents above a threshold of
0.5 produces **DCLM-baseline** :

```
3.8 trillion tokens retained
```
#### 3. 8

240 ^1 .6%of the pool
DCLM-baseline outperforms RefinedWeb by approximately 3 percentage points on the core benchmark
suite (HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU) when training a 7B model to 1 trillion tokens.
**Nemotron-CC** from NVIDIA accepted DCLM’s quality signal but rejected its extreme selectivity. Their
argument: training a 400B-parameter model to Chinchilla optimality requires on the order of 8-10 trillion tokens.
DCLM-baseline at 3.8 trillion is insufficient. Their response was to ensemble multiple quality signals-the DCLM
fastText score, an educational-value classifier distilled from a large Nemotron model, and document length-and
then _stratified-sample_ across score buckets rather than hard-thresholding at the top. The result was **Nemotron-
CC** : 6.3 trillion tokens, outperforming DCLM-baseline on benchmarks while providing 66% more training
tokens.
A further Nemotron-CC contribution was LLM-assisted document transformation. Low-quality retained
documents were rewritten into cleaner prose by an LLM. High-quality documents had synthetic instruction pairs
generated from them-for example, a Wikipedia article was converted into a “Summarize this” task, a “List the
key facts” task, and a factual question-answer pair. This deliberately blurs the boundary between pre-training and
post-training data, with the explicit goal of giving the model early exposure to instruction-following structure.
_The modern recipe is: DCLM-pool for extraction and dedup, a fastText or LLM-distilled classifier for
quality scoring, stratified sampling across score strata for volume control, and LLM rephrasing for the long tail_


```
20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora
```
_of retained documents._
Using instruction-style data as positive examples for a pre-training quality classifier is counterintuitive-you
are not training on instructions, you are looking for web documents that resemble instructions. The insight is
that well-formed question-and-answer content is a strong proxy for coherent, informative language. ELI5 posts
and OpenHermes examples are explanatory, specific, and well-structured; a document that looks like them tends
to be substantive rather than spammy.
The competing approach-using Wikipedia as the quality anchor, as CCNet and GPT-3 did-produces data
that looks like an encyclopedia. That is excellent for factual recall but underweights reasoning chains, instruc-
tional prose, and conversational question-answering. DCLM’s ablations show that the instruction-anchored
positives outperform the Wikipedia-anchored approach by 1-2 points even when controlling for token count.
Nemotron-CC’s stratified sampling strategy addresses a genuine production problem. Hard-thresholding at
a high quality score is like accepting only the top decile of candidates: you get quality, but you sacrifice diversity
in the lower nine deciles, some of which contain irreplaceable domain-specific content. Bucketing by score and
sampling proportionally preserves quality distribution while maintaining volume. The 1 trillion token high-
quality Nemotron-CC subset (the top two score buckets) outperforms the full 6.3T on per-token quality metrics,
confirming that quality and volume trade off rather than compound; the extra tokens are worth including only
when your training budget demands them.

**A Worked Example**

Walk through the DCLM pipeline for a 7B model targeting 1 trillion tokens of training.
**Step 1: Obtain DCLM-pool.** DCLM-pool is publicly available on Hugging Face. It contains 240 trillion
deduplicated English tokens, already MinHash-deduplicated across all Common Crawl dumps. Do not rebuild
this yourself; the extraction and dedup engineering is the most expensive part and is already done.
**Step 2: Train the fastText classifier.**

Positive set : 300K docs from OpenHermes-2.5
+ 50K docs from ELI5 subreddit
Negative set : 350K docs sampled from RefinedWeb
Labels : __label__positive / __label__negative
Training : fastText supervised, 5 epochs, lr=0.1
Model size : ~2 GB
Train time : <10 minutes on a single CPU machine

**Step 3: Score DCLM-pool.** Run the classifier over 240 trillion tokens. At1 million tokens per second
per CPU core, scoring the full pool requires240 million CPU-core-seconds, or roughly 2,800 CPU-core-
hours-about 28 hours on a 100-core cluster.
**Step 4: Filter.** Keep documents with fastText positive-class score> 0. 5. Empirically this retains 1.4-
1.6% of documents, yielding 3.4-3.8 trillion tokens. Sample 1 trillion uniformly from this retained set for your
training run.
**Step 5: Validate with a proxy model.** Train a 1B-parameter proxy on 10 billion token samples drawn from
(a) the retained set and (b) FineWeb. A 1-2 point improvement on HellaSwag confirms the classifier is working.
If you see no improvement, check that your positive-set format matches typical web document encoding (UTF-8,
not HTML entities).


```
20.2 Evolution of Open Pre-Training Corpora
```
Total additional cost over downloading DCLM-pool: approximately 3,000 CPU-core-hours for scoring.
This is negligible compared to GPU-hours for the actual 7B training run.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start from DCLM-pool, not raw Common Crawl. Reproducing the extraction and deduplication
pipeline from scratch takes weeks of engineering. DCLM-pool is public, covers all dumps through mid-
2024, and the only cost is download bandwidth. Reserve engineering time for the classifier.
Hard-threshold for models under 70B; stratified-sample for larger. If your token budget is under 5
trillion, a hard threshold at the DCLM fastText score of 0.5 is sufficient. Above 5 trillion-which is where
70B+models live at Chinchilla optimality-use stratified sampling or lower the threshold, consciously
trading some quality for volume.
Do not use GPT-4-generated data as positives in a production classifier. It violates OpenAI terms of
service. Use open-weight model outputs (Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral) or human-curated instruction datasets
under permissive licenses (e.g., FLAN, Dolly, OpenHermes under its Apache-2.0 variant).
LLM rephrasing is worth the cost for the bottom quartile only. Rephrasing the lowest-scoring 25%
of retained documents with a 7B model costs roughly 0. 25  3. 8 T 950 billion tokens of generation.
Budget this only if those documents cover rare domains not well-represented in the top tier; otherwise the
hallucination risk outweighs the coverage gain.
Use Nemotron-CC-1T as your default single-source option for a 7B run. It is the highest-quality public
corpus as of mid-2024 at a token count that fits comfortably within a 7B Chinchilla-optimal budget, and
its benchmark numbers are well-documented.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you use a quality classifier to filter a 200-trillion-token web corpus?” Name the pipeline:
define positive examples (instruction-style data), define negatives (lightly filtered web), train fastText (fast,
interpretable,<2 GB model), score the pool in parallel CPU jobs, threshold at a target retention rate.
Mention that 1.4-1.6% retention at a threshold of 0.5 yields3.8 trillion tokens-enough for a 7B model.
“What makes DCLM-baseline better than FineWeb if both come from Common Crawl?” The clas-
sifier. FineWeb uses only heuristic rules; DCLM adds a fastText classifier trained on instruction-like
positives. The DCLM paper shows a 3-point improvement on core benchmarks at 7B scale. Both apply
MinHash deduplication, but the classifier is the dominant factor in the quality gap.
“What is the trade-off between DCLM-baseline and Nemotron-CC?” DCLM-baseline: higher aver-
age quality per token, 3.8 trillion total tokens-constrains training runs for large models. Nemotron-CC:
slightly lower average quality per token across the full 6.3T, but includes a 1T high-quality subset that
matches or exceeds DCLM quality while providing 66% more tokens for training if needed. Choose
DCLM for 7B; choose Nemotron-CC full for 70B+where token volume limits the training run.
Senior follow-up: “Nemotron-CC uses LLM rephrasing to recover low-quality documents. What
could go wrong, and how would you detect it?” The core risk is hallucination: the rewriting model
invents facts or systematically injects its own biases into the training corpus. Three detection strategies:
(a) perplexity divergence-rephrased documents with perplexity far below their source indicate fabrication;
(b) n-gram overlap checks-if rephrased text deviates dramatically from the source, flag for review; (c)
factual benchmark regression-if adding rephrased documents degrades TriviaQA or NaturalQuestions
```

### 20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations.

```
relative to the clean baseline, the rephrasing model is corrupting factual knowledge. In production, cap
the rephrased fraction at 10-15% of total tokens and treat factual benchmarks as a canary before scaling
up.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
DCLM-pool covers all Common Crawl dumps through mid-2024 (240 trillion deduplicated tokens);
DCLM-baseline applies a fastText quality classifier to reduce it to 3.8 trillion tokens-roughly 1.6% retention-
outperforming prior heuristic baselines by 3 points at 7B scale.
Instruction-like data (OpenHermes, ELI5) as positive examples for the quality classifier outperforms
Wikipedia-anchored proxies; the intuition is that explanatory, question-answering prose is a better proxy
for useful pre-training content than encyclopedia-style writing.
Nemotron-CC addresses DCLM-baseline’s volume limitation through ensemble classifier scoring, strati-
fied sampling across score buckets, and LLM-assisted rephrasing, yielding 6.3 trillion tokens with quality
competitive with DCLM-baseline.
For a 7B model, start with DCLM-baseline or Nemotron-CC-1T; for a 70B+model, use Nemotron-CC
full (6.3T) or lower the DCLM threshold to recover token volume at the cost of some quality dilution.
The key engineering insight of the modern recipe: spend CPU cycles on classification (cheap, paralleliz-
able), spend GPU cycles only on model training-the classifier itself is a fastText model that trains in under
ten minutes.
```
### 20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations

**20.3.1 Copyright, Licenses, and Fair Use**
Copyright is the central legal friction in assembling a pre-training corpus, and it surfaces in almost every
senior-level data interview. The question “can you legally train on Common Crawl?” sounds simple, but answer-
ing it well requires understanding three distinct concepts that most engineers conflate: what copyright covers,
how licenses grant permission, and when fair use provides a defense without a license. Getting this wrong does
not just expose the company to litigation-it shapes which data sources you can include in an open-weight release
versus a closed commercial product.
Under the US Copyright Act of 1976, copyright attaches automatically to any _original work of authorship
fixed in a tangible medium of expression_. Registration is not required; the moment someone publishes a blog
post, that post is copyrighted. This means the overwhelming majority of web content that ends up in Common
Crawl is copyrighted, regardless of whether the page displays a copyright notice.
Copyright protects _expression_ , not _ideas_. You cannot copyright the algorithm for computing attention; you
can copyright the specific code implementing it. Facts-names, dates, addresses-are not copyrightable, which
is why a phone book’s content is in the public domain even though a sufficiently creative arrangement of that
content might not be. This distinction matters for training data: corpora heavy in factual encyclopedic text
(Wikipedia, arXiv abstracts) sit in a more defensible position than corpora heavy in fiction, journalism, or
creative prose.
There are two legal paths to use copyrighted material. The first is a **license** : a contract in which the rights
holder grants you permission under specified terms. Creative Commons licenses (CC-BY, CC-SA, CC-NC,
etc.) are a standardized form of pre-granted license-Wikipedia is CC-BY-SA, so anyone may use its text with


```
20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations
```
attribution and share-alike obligations. Commercial licenses negotiated directly with platforms (Reddit-Google,
Stack Exchange-OpenAI) work the same way but are bespoke and paid. The second path is **fair use** : a statutory
defense that allows use of copyrighted material without a license when four factors favor it: (1) the purpose
and character of the use (commercial vs. educational, transformative vs. reproductive); (2) the nature of the
copyrighted work (factual vs. creative); (3) the amount used relative to the whole; and (4) the effect on the
market for the original.
_Whether training an LLM on web-scraped text constitutes fair use is unresolved law, but the strongest
argument turns on the “transformative use” prong: the model extracts statistical patterns across billions of
tokens, not a copy of any particular work._
The transformative-use argument draws force from _Authors Guild v. Google_ (2d Cir. 2015), which held
that Google Books’ systematic digitization and snippet display of millions of copyrighted books was fair use
because it served a fundamentally different function than reading the books-it enabled search and discovery.
LLM training proponents argue the analogy holds: the model does not reproduce the training corpus; it com-
presses statistical regularities into weights that support generation of new text.
The tension is that LLMs can memorize. Carlini et al. showed that training data can be extracted verbatim
from GPT-2 given the right prompt, and subsequent work demonstrated the same for larger models. A model that
can regurgitate entire paragraphs of a copyrighted novel weakens the transformative-use defense considerably,
because the infringement is no longer abstract-the expression itself is reproduced. This is why deduplication
and memorization audits are now standard pipeline steps, not just quality hygiene.
The commercial/non-commercial distinction also matters asymmetrically. Academic researchers running
non-commercial experiments are more insulated than a company selling API access. Open-weight releases sit
in a legally awkward middle: the weights are “open,” but the training data disclosure that accompanies them
makes the copying more legible to plaintiffs. Closed commercial models paradoxically enjoy better legal cover
on this dimension because the training data is never disclosed.

**A Worked Example**

Consider the trajectory of **Books3** , a dataset of roughly 200,000 copyrighted books scraped from Library
Genesis, a shadow library. Books3 appeared in the Pile (2020) and was later incorporated into Llama 1’s training
mix. In 2023, a group of authors including Richard Kadrey, Sarah Silverman, and Christopher Golden sued
Meta, alleging that Llama 1’s use of Books3 constituted copyright infringement.
Meta’s primary defense was transformative use: training compresses millions of books into 7 billion param-
eters that do not store or reproduce any individual work. The plaintiffs countered that the model can reproduce
passages verbatim and that it effectively substitutes for buying the books, harming the market. The district court
dismissed several claims but allowed some to proceed. In parallel, Books3 was removed from the Pile’s hosted
version and Llama 2 quietly dropped it from its data card.
The practical lesson: the risk profile of a dataset is not just “is this copyrighted” but “is it from a source
whose rights holders are organized, motivated, and able to sue.” Published authors are a concentrated, articulate
group. Individual bloggers are not. This asymmetry-not legal principle-explains why Books3 triggered litigation
while the vast majority of Common Crawl’s copyrighted content has not.
As a contrast, **Project Gutenberg’s** 75,000 books are predominantly in the public domain (copyright has
expired, typically 95+ years after publication in the US). Using them is legally safe, and they provide long-
document text that books corpora were specifically valued for in the BERT era.


```
20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations
```
**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Public domain 6 = freely usable scans. A 19th-century novel is in the public domain, but a publisher’s
typeset PDF of that novel may carry a new copyright on the layout and OCR corrections. Use raw Project
Gutenberg text, not publisher PDFs.
Creative Commons licenses have variants. CC-BY and CC-SA allow commercial use; CC-NC (non-
commercial) does not. If your pipeline ingests CC content, track the license variant per document. Mixing
NC-licensed content into a commercial training run is a genuine legal risk.
Open-weight releases attract more scrutiny than closed products. If you publish your data card,
you are handing plaintiffs a roadmap. For open-weight models, prefer datasets with clear provenance:
FineWeb (Common Crawl, ToS-respecting crawl), DCLM-baseline, The Stack (permissively licensed
code only).
Memorization audits belong in the pipeline. Run a membership-inference probe or verbatim-extraction
test against held-out copyrighted text before a model release. A model that can reproduce more than a few
sentences of a copyrighted work verbatim is a liability.
Shadow libraries are a hard no for commercial products. LibGen has 4 million books; it also has a
litigation history. The token-per-lawsuit ratio looks attractive until the first discovery subpoena arrives.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through whether training on Common Crawl is legal.” Strong answer: most Common
Crawl content is copyrighted; the legal path is fair use, specifically the transformative-use prong from
Authors Guild v. Google ; the argument weakens if the model memorizes verbatim text; commercial vs.
non-commercial use affects the analysis; no court has definitively ruled on LLM training specifically.
“What’s the difference between a public dataset and a legally safe dataset?” Strong answer: “public”
means accessible without authentication; “legally safe” means you have a license or a defensible fair-use
argument. YouTube videos are public but scraping them violates ToS. Wikipedia is publicly licensed (CC-
BY-SA). Common Crawl is public but largely copyrighted content used under implicit fair-use reliance.
“How would you audit a proposed training dataset for legal risk before a model release?” Strong
answer: categorize each source by license type; flag shadow-library or paywalled content; run memoriza-
tion probes on high-risk sources; check whether rights holders in each category have litigation history;
produce a data card that documents provenance and any exclusions.
Senior follow-up: “What changes in your analysis if this is an open-weight release versus a closed API?”
Senior answer: open-weight releases require full data disclosure, which lowers plausible deniability and
makes it easier for plaintiffs to identify infringing sources; commercial use eliminates the educational fair-
use factor; the calculus therefore shifts toward more conservative sourcing (CC-licensed, public domain,
licensed data) for open releases, while closed commercial models rely more heavily on fair-use arguments
they never have to articulate publicly.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Nearly all web content is automatically copyrighted; the question is not whether it is copyrighted but
whether you have a license or a fair-use defense.
```

```
20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations
```
```
Fair use turns on four factors; for LLM training the strongest factor is transformative use, and the weakest
point is verbatim memorization.
Creative Commons licenses differ by variant: CC-BY and CC-SA allow commercial use; CC-NC does
not.
Shadow libraries (LibGen, Books3) carry concrete litigation risk for commercial products; public-domain
sources (Project Gutenberg) and permissively licensed code (The Stack) are the safe alternative.
Open-weight model releases face higher legal exposure than closed APIs because data provenance is
disclosed, making memorization-based claims easier to assert.
```
**20.3.2 Terms of Service and Data Governance**
Copyright is not the only legal friction in data pipelines. Even when fair use provides a plausible defense
for the content of a web page, a separate body of law-contract and computer-fraud statutes-governs how you
obtained that content. Engineers who understand copyright but treat platform terms of service as advisory text
are operating with a dangerously incomplete picture. At staff and principal level, interviewers test whether you
can reason about the full legal surface of a data decision, not just the copyright slice of it.
When you visit a website, you implicitly accept its _terms of service_ (ToS). Most platform ToS prohibit
automated scraping, redistribution of content, and use of data to train competing AI systems. Violating ToS is
not a copyright infringement-it is a breach of contract, and depending on how the data was accessed, potentially a
violation of the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (CFAA). These are distinct legal theories with distinct remedies
and different parties who can sue.
**robots.txt** is a machine-readable file at the root of a web server that signals which crawlers are permitted
to access which paths. It is not legally binding-there is no statute that makes ignoringrobots.txtillegal by
itself-but courts have treated a site’s robots.txt as evidence of the operator’s intent, which strengthens a CFAA
or breach-of-contract argument when a crawler ignores it. The major frontier-lab crawlers (GPTBot, ClaudeBot,
GoogleBot for AI training) are all explicitly named in robots.txt files across major news, publishing, and social
media sites, with access typically denied.
A **data licensing agreement** is the commercial resolution to this friction: the platform grants a contractual
right to use its data for AI training in exchange for payment or a cross-licensing deal. Examples include the
Reddit-Google agreement (2024), the OpenAI-Stack Exchange agreement, and the OpenAI-Shutterstock agree-
ment. These deals emerged as platforms recognized that their data had become a scarce input to a high-value
industry and that they could monetize it rather than watch it be scraped for free.
_The practical constraint this imposes is stark: there is no way to get a ToS license for the entire internet,
which means any corpus that relies on broad web crawl is necessarily operating under a fair-use assumption
while simultaneously accepting the contractual risk of ToS violation._
The governance structure that has emerged-frozen Common Crawl snapshots plus separately licensed high-
value verticals-reflects the only feasible way to assemble a large, legally defensible corpus at scale. Common
Crawl performs the crawl on your behalf and explicitly intends the data for research use, which provides one
layer of insulation. Separately licensing Reddit for social dialogue data, Stack Exchange for QA data, and a news
aggregator for current-events coverage fills the gaps where the high-value signal is concentrated and the rights
holders are organized enough to enforce their ToS.
Data poisoning introduces a governance dimension that is easy to underestimate. Carlini et al. demonstrated
a timing attack against Wikipedia: an adversary can inject a malicious edit to a Wikipedia article in the window


```
20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations
```
between the edit and the next editorial rollback, timed to coincide with Common Crawl’s periodic dump. The
injected text enters the dump, gets included in downstream training data, and is rolled back on Wikipedia before
anyone notices. The result is a model trained on attacker-controlled text, which can be used to steer model
behavior-for example, associating a trigger phrase with a specific sentiment or behavioral policy. The fix is
partial: Wikipedia has hardened its edit policies, and some pipeline operators now diff their Wikipedia snapshots
against a trusted reference. But the broader point stands: data provenance is a security surface, not just a legal
one.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a concrete pipeline decision around **YouTube**. Millions of YouTube videos carry Creative Com-
mons licenses (CC-BY), making the _content_ legally usable without a separate agreement. An engineer might
reasonably conclude: “I have a license to the content, so I can download and transcribe these videos for training.”
This is wrong.
YouTube’s ToS explicitly prohibits automated downloading of video or audio, regardless of the content’s
license. The Creative Commons license governs what you can do with the content once you have it lawfully;
the ToS governs how you obtain it. Downloading programmatically without YouTube’s permission is a breach
of contract, and YouTube has sent DMCA-adjacent takedown notices and pursued injunctions against services
built on this basis (e.g., _hiQ Labs v. LinkedIn_ , though that case turned on CFAA specifically).
The correct path for YouTube audio is either: (1) negotiate a data licensing agreement with Google, as some
frontier labs are rumored to have done; (2) use the official YouTube Data API within its rate limits (which are
set too low for training-scale data collection); or (3) use transcripts that were lawfully obtained and redistributed
under a license (several academic ASR datasets exist in this category). The “it’s Creative Commons” shortcut
collapses the distinction between content rights and access rights.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Treat robots.txt as legally meaningful, not just advisory. RespectingDisallowdirectives does not
give you immunity, but ignoring them is affirmative evidence against you in both CFAA and breach-of-
contract claims. Crawl engines should parse and honorrobots.txtby default; build in a crawl-delay
header to avoid overload arguments as well.
Distinguish access rights from content rights. Before adding a source, ask two separate questions: (a)
Is the content licensed for this use? (b) Did we obtain it through a channel permitted by the platform?
Both must be yes. Creative Commons answers (a); the ToS answers (b).
Use frozen snapshots to avoid ToS time-bombs. Reddit and Stack Exchange changed their APIs in 2023
mid-production for many teams. If you collected data before the ToS change, the legal exposure is frozen
at the time of collection. Snapshot-based pipelines (Common Crawl dumps, Wikipedia XML dumps with
a dated version) are more defensible than live API scraping that crosses ToS update boundaries.
Track provenance at the document level. For every document in your corpus, record the Common Crawl
snapshot ID, the retrieval date, and the source URL. This is not just good hygiene-it is the audit trail you
need if a rights holder demands removal (a “right to erasure” request under GDPR or a DMCA notice),
and it lets you exclude specific domains post-hoc without reprocessing everything.
Implement a data-poisoning audit for high-trust sources. For sources included specifically because of
their quality (Wikipedia, arXiv), maintain a checksum or diff against a reference snapshot. An edit that
```

```
20.3 Legal and Ethical Considerations
```
```
appeared only in one Common Crawl dump but not in the live site warrants manual review before that
document enters the training corpus.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you design a legally defensible data collection pipeline for a commercial LLM?” Strong
answer: layer the strategy-use Common Crawl as the broad web base (crawl performed by a third party,
data intended for research/AI use); negotiate licenses for the highest-value verticals (code, books, QA);
exclude sources whose ToS explicitly prohibit AI training use; respect robots.txt in any first-party crawl-
ing; maintain per-document provenance logs for erasure requests.
“What is data poisoning and how would you defend against it in your pipeline?” Strong answer: data
poisoning is the injection of adversarial text into training data to steer model behavior; for Wikipedia,
the attack surface is the dump-timing window between edit and rollback; mitigation is diffing snapshot
content against a trusted live reference, flagging documents that appeared transiently; for Common Crawl,
domain-level reputation signals can exclude known spam or compromised domains.
“A rights holder sends a takedown notice claiming their content is in your training set. Walk me
through how you respond.” Strong answer: use provenance logs to identify which documents origi-
nated from the claimant’s domain; assess whether a license or fair-use argument applies to that source;
if neither, remove the documents from the dataset, retrain affected checkpoints if the content contributed
meaningfully, and document the removal.
Senior follow-up: “Can you actually “unlearn” a document from a trained model, and how would you
handle this operationally at scale?” Senior answer: machine unlearning is an active research area but not
yet production-reliable-gradient-based unlearning methods exist but cannot provide the same guarantees
as simply not training on the data in the first place. In practice, the operational answer is (1) maintain mod-
ular training checkpoints keyed to data provenance so a corpus can be reconstructed without the disputed
content and a fresh training run initiated from the last clean checkpoint; (2) for models already deployed,
implement output filters that suppress verbatim reproduction of the claimed content while the longer-term
retraining proceeds; (3) accept that this is expensive, which is why upstream provenance hygiene is worth
the investment.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
ToS violations are a breach-of-contract risk distinct from copyright; both must be evaluated independently
for any data source.
robots.txt is not legally binding but is treated as evidence of intent; always honor it in first-party crawls.
Creative Commons licenses answer “can I use this content?” not “can I collect it from this platform?”-the
ToS answers the second question.
Document-level provenance logs (snapshot ID, retrieval date, source URL) are the operational prerequisite
for DMCA compliance, GDPR erasure requests, and data-poisoning audits.
Data poisoning is a real attack surface: snapshot-diffing against a trusted reference is the practical miti-
gation for high-trust sources like Wikipedia.
```

## Chapter 21 Data Filtering and Deduplication Algorithms

### 21.1 Quality Filtering Algorithms

**21.1.1 n-gram Models and KenLM**
An interviewer designing a pre-training data pipeline will almost always ask how you distinguish high-
quality web text from garbage, and the first tool you should name is a language-model perplexity filter backed
by KenLM. This question shows up at the senior engineer level because it sits at the intersection of classical NLP,
large-scale distributed processing, and model quality-getting it wrong can mean millions of wasted GPU-hours
training on near-random bytes. The n-gram approach is deliberately crude, but that crudeness is a feature: it
runs at a fraction of the cost of any neural scorer while filtering the most egregiously low-quality pages before
anything more expensive touches the data.
The abstract primitive is: given a small set of high-quality _target_ documentsTand a massive _raw_ corpus
R(e.g., a Common Crawl dump), find a subsetR′ Rwhose distribution resemblesT. All three methods
in this section-n-gram models, fastText classifiers, and importance sampling-are instances of this same recipe.
What changes is how you estimate the scoring function.
An n-gram language model estimates the probability of a tokenwngiven the precedingn 1 tokens:
P(wnjwn− 1 ,... , w 1 )CC(w(w^1 ,... , wn)

whereC()denotes corpus count. In practice, manyn-gram sequences never appear even in large corpora,
so raw maximum-likelihood estimates assign zero probability to perfectly grammatical sentences. _Kneser-Ney
smoothing_ addresses this by backing off to lower-ordern-grams when counts are sparse, interpolating between
orders rather than hard-cutoff discounting. KenLM is the standard open-source implementation: it uses on-disk
trie structures so that models with hundreds of millions ofn-grams fit in memory and score millions of tokens
per second on a single CPU.
Given a trained KenLM model, the score for a document is its _perplexity_ under the target distribution:

Low perplexity means the document looks like the target; high perplexity indicates it is out-of-distribution.
Documents are sorted by perplexity and a top fraction is retained.
_The north-star summary: train KenLM on a clean reference corpus, score every raw document by its
perplexity, and keep the low-perplexity fraction-this is the cheapest defensible filter you can run at web scale._
The key trade-off is **cost vs. sophistication**. A neural classifier can judge quality more accurately, but
scoring a trillion tokens with a BERT-scale model would cost roughly the same in FLOPs as the pre-training run
itself-you cannot spend that budget on filtering. KenLM, by contrast, is a counting procedure: fitting a 5-gram
model on Wikipedia takes minutes and produces a file of a few gigabytes. Inference is a trie lookup, not a matrix
multiply; throughput on a single core routinely exceeds 107 tokens per second.
The limitation is equally clear:n-grams are local. A document composed of individually plausible bigrams
but globally incoherent content (shuffled sentences, SEO keyword stuffing) can fool the filter. In practice this
is acceptable because the primary goal is to remove true garbage-pages filled with binary content, encoding
artifacts, or character-level noise-not to make fine-grained quality judgments. The model is intentionally crude


```
21.1 Quality Filtering Algorithms
```
so that it can be extremely fast.
Before KenLM-based filtering became widespread, pipelines relied entirely on heuristic rules: URL block-
lists, minimum word count, fraction of alphabetic characters, and so on. Rules are brittle and require constant
maintenance as the web evolves. A perplexity filter generalizes from whatever reference corpus you supply,
which makes it easy to retarget for new domains without rewriting logic.

**A Worked Example**

The CCNet pipeline-the foundation for the first LLaMA pre-training dataset-illustrates the approach con-
cretely. The setup:
**Target corpus** : Wikipedia (all languages, split by language).
**Raw corpus** : Common Crawl WET files (one monthly snapshot40B tokens after HTML stripping).
**Unit of scoring** : paragraph (not full document), to allow partial retention.
Step 1: Train one KenLM 5-gram model per language on the corresponding Wikipedia dump. For English,
this produces a model of roughly 5-8 GB.
Step 2: For each paragraph in Common Crawl, compute perplexity under the English model (or whichever
language model matches the fastText language-identification label).
Step 3: Sort paragraphs by perplexity in ascending order and retain the bottom third (lowest perplexity =
most Wikipedia-like). In CCNet’s English slice this cut reduced the token count from roughly 400B to130B
while measurably improving downstream benchmark scores.
Arithmetic check: a 5-gram lookup over a 1,000-token paragraph requires roughly 103 trie traversals. At
107 tokens per second per core, scoring a 40B-token dump completes in about 40 , 000 core-seconds-under 12
core-hours, which is negligible compared to any GPU budget.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Reference corpus choice matters more than smoothing details. If you train KenLM on Wikipedia, you
bias toward encyclopedic prose; if you train on GitHub commit messages, you bias toward code. Match
the reference to the downstream use case. Mixing reference corpora (Wikipedia + books) is fine-just
concatenate and retrain.
Score at the paragraph level, not the document level. Long documents often contain both excellent and
garbage paragraphs. Scoring paragraphs independently lets you perform surgical removal rather than dis-
carding entire pages. C4 uses three-sentence spans; CCNet uses single paragraphs. Both work; paragraph
is usually the safer default.
Set the threshold by inspection, not formula. Examine the text at the 33rd, 50th, and 67th perplexity
percentiles before committing. The right cut point varies by domain: code corpora show different per-
plexity distributions than news. CCNet’s top-third heuristic is a reasonable starting point for English web
text.
KenLM does not replace rule-based filters; it complements them. Run basic heuristics first (minimum
length, non-ASCII fraction, URL spam detection), then KenLM, then a neural classifier if budget allows.
Each stage is cheap and removes material the next stage would struggle with.
Beware of perplexity collapse on short sequences. Paragraphs under 50 tokens have high variance in
perplexity estimates; their scores are unreliable. Set a minimum token threshold (50-100 tokens is typical)
before applying the perplexity filter.
```
