**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you would filter Common Crawl to produce a high-quality English pre-
training corpus.” A strong answer names the pipeline stages in order: language identification, heuristic
rules, perplexity filtering with KenLM trained on a clean reference, then optionally a fastText or neural
quality classifier. Quantify the expected token retention at each stage.
“Why use KenLM instead of a BERT-based classifier for quality scoring?” The key point is FLOPs
budget: scoring 1012 tokens with BERT at10 ms per sentence would cost millions of GPU-hours, ex-
ceeding the training budget. KenLM runs on CPUs at 107 tokens per second; the entire web can be scored
in hours on a modest CPU cluster.
“What are the failure modes of perplexity-based filtering?” Name: (1) n-grams are local, so globally
incoherent text can pass; (2) the filter is language-model-centric, so stylistically unusual but valid text
(poetry, code-switching) is penalized; (3) the reference corpus must match the target domain or the filter
misfires.
Senior follow-up: “If your target domain is scientific papers and Wikipedia is a poor reference,
how do you adapt the pipeline?” Train KenLM on a seed set of high-quality papers (arXiv abstracts,
PubMed, Semantic Scholar). If the seed set is tiny (<1B tokens), supplement with Kneser-Ney’s backoff
to lower-ordern-grams for robustness. Alternatively, switch to an importance-sampling estimator that
explicitly models both the target and raw distributions-this gives principled weighting rather than a hard
threshold and handles small target sets more gracefully.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The universal filtering recipe: estimate a model on target data, score raw documents with it, keep high-
scoring examples-KenLM operationalizes this with near-zero compute cost.
Kneser-Ney smoothing handles unseenn-grams by interpolating with lower-order models; the implemen-
tation detail matters less than the choice of reference corpus.
KenLM throughput (> 107 tokens/sec per CPU core) makes it feasible to score an entire Common Crawl
snapshot in core-hours, not GPU-hours.
Score at the paragraph or sentence level, not the document level, to allow partial retention of otherwise
heterogeneous pages.
KenLM is a first-pass filter, not a final verdict-follow with a discriminative classifier or importance-
sampling reweighter for finer-grained quality control.
```
**21.1.2 fastText Classifiers and Importance-Sampling Filters**
Once a perplexity filter has removed the worst of the web, the next question in a data-pipeline interview
is how you build a supervised quality classifier without labeling millions of documents by hand-and how you
justify the classifier’s compute budget relative to the training run. This topic separates engineers who have built
real pipelines from those who have only read about them. The two dominant answers are fastText discriminative
classifiers and importance-sampling reweighters; each has a distinct theoretical motivation and a concrete set of
production trade-offs worth articulating on a whiteboard.
Both methods share the same abstract recipe: estimate the ratio of the target distributionpto the raw
distributionq, then use that ratio to preferentially select examples from the raw corpus. They differ in whether


```
21.1 Quality Filtering Algorithms
```
the ratio is estimated _discriminatively_ (fastText) or _generatively_ (importance sampling).
**fastText** trains a shallow log-linear classifier over hashedn-gram features. Given a vocabulary of sizeV
andKoutput classes, a naive bag-of-words classifier needs aVKweight matrix-unwieldy whenV is large.
fastText adds a bottleneck hidden layer of dimensionh(typicallyh= 16), reducing parameters fromV Kto
Vh+hK:
yˆ= softmax(W 2 mean(W 1 x))

wherexis the average of hashedn-gram embeddings over the document. To avoid an unbounded bigram vo-
cabulary, alln-grams are hashed into a fixed bucket count (e.g., 107 bins) before lookup. For quality filtering
specifically,K= 2(positive / negative), so the output is effectively a single logistic unit. Training uses asyn-
chronous SGD, and inference is a pair of dense matrix products-extremely fast even for documents measured in
thousands of tokens.
**Importance-sampling filters** take a generative approach. Fit a unigram orn-gram probability modelpˆto
the target corpusTand a second modelˆqto the raw corpusR. The importance weight for documentdis:

w(d) =pˆ(d)
qˆ(d)
Resample documents fromRwith probability proportional tow(d). Documents that look more likeTthanR
receive high weight and are sampled more often; documents that look more likeRthanTare down-weighted.
In practice, bothpˆandqˆare estimated using hashed unigram counts-exactly as in the fastText feature hashing
trick-so the whole procedure is as cheap as fastText while having a clearer distribution-matching interpretation.
_The key insight is that fastText asks “is this document in-distribution?” (a classification boundary) while
importance sampling asks “by how much is this document over- or under-represented relative to target?” (a
density ratio)-the latter is more principled for preserving diversity._
The fastText compute argument is the one interviewers probe hardest. If you are filtering a corpus to 1%
of Common Crawl, the classifier sees the full raw corpus. Every FLOP you spend on the classifier must be
amortized over the data retained. A BERT-style encoder scoring each document at10 ms per 512-token chunk
would consume 105 GPU-hours to score 1012 raw tokens-rivaling the training cost itself. fastText on the same
corpus, running on CPUs at 106 documents per second, finishes in hours. The rule of thumb: if filtering discards
99% of data, the per-token classifier cost must be under1/100th of the per-token training cost. fastText clears
that bar; BERT does not.
Importance sampling offers a diversity guarantee that fastText lacks. A discriminative classifier optimizes
the decision boundary; once most of the data cluster in the positive region, the model does not care whether it
samples uniformly from that region. An importance-sampling filter explicitly adjusts for density mismatch: rare
but target-consistent topics receive higher weights and are more likely to appear in the final corpus. Empirically,
importance-sampling-curated corpora outperform fastText-curated ones on GLUE-style benchmarks when the
target set is small, though the absolute gains are often modest (≲2-3 points).
The principal limitation of importance sampling is that the target corpusTmust be large enough to estimate
pˆreliably. WhenTis very small, the unigram estimates for rare tokens are noisy. A practical fix is Laplace or
add-εsmoothing so that zero-count tokens receive a small but nonzero probability.

**A Worked Example**

**phi-1 code quality filter** is the clearest end-to-end example because it shows how to construct the target
setTwhen none exists a priori.


```
21.1 Quality Filtering Algorithms
```
1. **Define** Tby prompting GPT-4 with a rubric: _“Rate the educational value of this Python snippet for a_
    _student learning basic coding concepts.”_ Apply this to 100,000 documents sampled from the Python
    subset of The Stack.
2. **Label** : documents with high GPT-4 educational ratings become positive examples; the rest become neg-
    atives. This produces a labeled set of100K examples-small enough that GPT-4 annotation is affordable
    (roughly $2,000-$5,000 at 2023 API prices for 100K500-token snippets).
3. **Train classifier** : embed each document with a small pre-trained code encoder, then train a random forest
    on those embeddings. A random forest is used rather than a neural classifier because the labeled set is
    small and training must be fast.
4. **Score raw corpus** : run the random forest across the full Python subset of The Stack (200B raw tokens).
    Random forest inference is CPU-bound and parallelizes trivially across shards.
5. **Retain** documents classified as high educational value (3B tokens selected).
    Result: a 1.3B-parameter model trained on this 3B-token filtered corpus reached 17% on HumanEval at
36K training steps. The same architecture trained on the unfiltered 200B-token corpus reached only 12% at 96K
steps-roughly 6 more efficient in both tokens and compute.
The compute budget check: GPT-4 annotation of 100K examples at 500 tokens each = 50M tokens at
roughly $0.03/1K tokens = $1,500. Random forest scoring of 200B tokens takes perhaps 200 CPU-hours. Both
are negligible versus a multi-day GPU training run.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use fastText when you have a natural source of positive and negative labels. GPT-3 and LLaMA
used Wikipedia-referenced pages as positives and raw Common Crawl as negatives. If your domain has
an obvious high-quality source (GitHub starred repos, arXiv accepted papers, curated forums), this is the
fastest path. Training fastText takes minutes; inference scales to the full web on a CPU cluster in hours.
Use importance sampling when diversity matters or your positive set is tiny. IfjTj< 1 B tokens,
discriminative classifiers have too little signal to learn a reliable boundary. An importance-sampling un-
igram model needs only enough data to estimate token frequencies reliably-a few hundred million tokens
suffices.
Use GPT-4 annotation to synthesize T when no natural target exists. Label 1,000-100,000 examples
(not more-beyond that cost grows without proportional gain). Train a cheap classifier (random forest,
fastText) on those labels and apply it to the full corpus. This is now the dominant approach for domain-
specific data curation.
Stochastic retention sharpens the boundary without hard cutoffs. Both GPT-3 and CCNet use a
sigmoid sharpening function: documents near the threshold are kept or dropped probabilistically rather
than by a hard threshold. This prevents the model from memorizing the exact boundary and improves
diversity at the margin.
Never skip a compute budget check before choosing a classifier architecture. If the raw corpus isN
tokens and the training compute budget isCFLOPs, the classifier can spend at mostC/(retention fraction)
FLOPs on scoring. At 1% retention, that means the classifier budget is roughlyC/ 100. fastText almost
always fits; BERT-scale almost never does.
```

```
21.1 Quality Filtering Algorithms
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How did GPT-3 build its quality classifier, and why did that approach work?” Strong answer:
positive examples came from web pages linked by Reddit with3 upvotes, negatives from raw Common
Crawl. This required no human annotation at scale-Reddit karma acts as a noisy but free quality signal.
A linear classifier (fastText) was trained on these labels and applied stochastically (not with a hard cutoff)
to retain high-scoring documents.
“What is importance sampling in the context of data filtering, and when would you use it over
fastText?” A strong answer defines the importance weightˆp(d)/ˆq(d), explains the resampling procedure,
and names when it wins: small target sets, domains where diversity is critical, or when the discriminative
boundary is ill-defined because positive and negative data overlap heavily.
“You want to add more chemistry data to a pre-training corpus. Walk me through end-to-end how
you would do it.” A complete answer: (1) defineTusing arXiv chemistry papers + textbook excerpts,
(2) train KenLM onTfor a fast first-pass perplexity filter, (3) optionally train fastText withTas positive
and raw web as negative, (4) score the full corpus and retain documents above threshold, (5) deduplicate
the result with MinHash LSH before mixing into the main corpus.
Senior follow-up: “fastText uses hashed n -grams. What are the implications of hash collisions for
quality filtering?” Collisions cause distinctn-grams to share a weight. For binary classification this
means the model learns a weight that represents the average behavior of all collidingn-grams. With 107
bins and a typical English vocabulary of 105 unigrams and 109 possible bigrams, collision probability
for any single bigram is low (10 ppm), but with enough training the model adapts. The key insight is
that importance-sampling unigram models have no collision problem because they only use single-token
counts; this is one reason importance sampling can match fastText quality on small target sets.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
fastText is a shallow log-linear model over hashedn-gram features; atK= 2it is binary classification
that runs at> 106 documents per second on CPU-the dominant choice when labeled positive/negative
data exists.
Importance-sampling reweighting estimatespˆ(d)/qˆ(d)from twon-gram models and resamples accord-
ingly; it matches distributions rather than drawing a decision boundary, which helps preserve diversity
when the target set is small.
When no naturalTexists, use a strong LLM to annotate100K examples and train a cheap classifier
(fastText or random forest) on those labels-compute cost is negligible relative to pre-training.
The compute budget rule: classifier scoring cost must be less than (training cost) divided by (raw corpus
size / retained size); this almost always rules out BERT-scale encoders and almost always clears fastText.
All three filtering methods (KenLM, fastText, importance sampling) share the same recipe: score raw
documents relative to a target, keep the high-scoring fraction-they differ only in how the score is estimated
and whether it is a hard threshold or a probabilistic retention.
```

### 21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks.

### 21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks

**21.2.1 Language Identification**
Every serious pre-training pipeline applies language identification before any other filter, because feeding
multilingual noise into a monolingual model wastes tokens and measurably hurts benchmark performance. This
topic comes up at the mid-level when interviewers ask how you would clean a Common Crawl dump, and it is a
good test of whether candidates understand that the same lightweight classification machinery used for quality
scoring can be repurposed for an entirely different dimension of the data. Getting it wrong is not catastrophic,
but getting it subtly wrong - a threshold that is too loose, a model that misclassifies code as Estonian - compounds
quietly across hundreds of billions of tokens.
Language identification (LID) is document-level multi-class classification: assign a language label and a
confidence score to a piece of text, then threshold. The dominant tool in production is the fastText LID model,
which supports 176 languages and runs at several hundred thousand paragraphs per second on a single CPU
core. Its architecture is a bag of character n-grams fed into an averaged embedding layer, then a softmax over
language classes - no non-linearity beyond that final softmax.
Formally, for a documentdwith character n-gram multisetG(d), the model computes:

```
logp(ℓjd) =w⊤ℓ
```

whereφ(g)hashes n-gramginto one ofB  107 buckets,ebis a learned bucket embedding, andZis the
partition function over all classes. The hashing trick bounds memory regardless of vocabulary size and is the
same technique fastText uses in its text classifier. The DOLMA pipeline applies this model at the paragraph
level and keeps paragraphs wherep(en)> 0. 5.
_Language identification is the same bag-of-n-gram classification machinery used for quality and toxicity
filtering - the only difference is that the label space is a set of language codes rather than a binary quality
judgment._
The obvious alternative is rule-based detection: check Unicode script ranges, use curated word lists, or
rely on HTMLlangattributes. This works well for well-separated scripts - Latin versus Cyrillic versus CJK -
but collapses on Latin-script languages that share large vocabularies (Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, Galician). A
character n-gram model implicitly encodes each language’s orthographic distribution at exactly the granularity
where the signal lives, without requiring a hand-curated lexicon per language.
The key trade-off is precision versus recall in a compute-constrained training regime. If the LID threshold is
too permissive, non-English text contaminates the corpus and steals token budget from the target language. If it is
too strict, you drop legitimate text from code-switched documents, low-resource dialects, and informal registers
that look statistically unusual to the model. BLOOM was trained with only 30% English tokens; in a compute-
limited regime, that dilution measurably hurt English benchmark scores relative to English-only models at the
same parameter count. Monolingual labs typically accept a recall penalty to guarantee high precision.
The character n-gram approach degrades gracefully on short texts: it becomes less confident, not wrong. A
single sentence might score 0.71 for English; a full paragraph by the same author might score 0.98. This is why
LID should run at the paragraph or document level, not the sentence level - longer units produce better-calibrated
scores.


```
21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider building an English pre-training corpus from a 100-billion-token Common Crawl dump. Assume
paragraphs average 200 tokens, giving roughly 5  108 paragraphs. The fastText LID model runs at 4  105
paragraphs per second on 4 CPU threads at 2.5 GHz. Total CPU-core-time:

5  108 paragraphs
4  105 paragraphs/core-s^1 ,^250 core-seconds^21 core-minutes
Distributed across 64 cores in a Spark or Ray cluster, LID finishes in under two minutes of wall time.
The compute budget is negligible compared to any downstream neural scoring step. Applying the threshold
p(en)> 0. 5 retains roughly 45-50% of Common Crawl by token volume, since the web carries substantial
non-English traffic.
Now the edge cases appear immediately. Math content scoresp(en)around 0.35-0.45 because LATEX ex-
pressions and formula tokens look like no known language to the model. Inline code (Python identifiers, function
names) is classified as Russian or Estonian 15-20% of the time due to identifier-character patterns. OpenWeb-
Math handles this with a two-tier threshold: documents that pass a LATEX heuristic (more than 5% of lines contain
\frac,\sum, or similar macros) are kept atp(en)> 0. 3 , while everything else requiresp(en)> 0. 65. The
result was a 15-billion-token math corpus that outperformed models trained on 20 times more unfiltered data on
mathematical reasoning benchmarks.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Threshold: Start at 0.5 for a general-purpose English corpus; push to 0.65 if you prioritize precision.
Drop to 0.3-0.4 for domain corpora (math, code) where the LID model is miscalibrated by design. Audit
500 randomly sampled rejections before locking the threshold - you will find surprising failures.
Classification unit: Document-level is coarser but preserves document coherence. Paragraph-level im-
proves precision on multilingual pages but can produce incoherent documents downstream if you excise
individual paragraphs. Use paragraph-level only when you are building passage-level retrieval datasets;
use document-level for general pre-training corpora.
Script-level pre-filter: Before running the neural model, check Unicode script frequency. If a document
is more than 50% CJK, Devanagari, or Arabic characters, assign the script’s dominant language directly
and skip fastText. This saves roughly 15% of inference compute and avoids weak-signal classifications
on script-heavy documents.
Code-switching: Pages that mix two languages will be classified confidently as whichever language dom-
inates by token count. If purity matters, run sentence-level LID within paragraphs and keep only para-
graphs where at least 80% of sentences agree on the majority language.
Off-the-shelf vs. fine-tuned: The public fastText LID model is sufficient for high-resource languages.
For low-resource languages with fewer than 107 training tokens in the model’s corpus, the confusion rate
with geographically proximate languages can exceed 20%. In those cases, fine-tune a new output layer on
dialect-specific data (Wikipedia, CommonVoice transcripts) while keeping the base embeddings frozen.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you isolate English documents from a 100 TB Common Crawl dump?” A strong answer
names the fastText LID classifier, describes the character n-gram architecture, proposes a threshold with
```

```
21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks
```
```
justification (0.5-0.65), and proactively raises edge cases: code, math, short texts, and languages that
look similar to English at the surface. Weaker answers jump straight to regex or Unicode ranges without
addressing Latin-script language confusion.
“What happens to model quality if you skip language filtering?” Strong answer: non-English tokens
dilute the training budget proportionally. Cites BLOOM as a concrete example: 30% English pretraining
produced noticeably weaker English benchmark scores than comparably sized English-only models under
the same compute budget. The effect scales with the fraction of off-language tokens in the corpus.
Senior follow-up - “Your LID model misclassifies Python files as non-English. How do you fix this
without retraining?” The senior answer: apply a two-tier threshold controlled by a domain heuristic.
Documents containing more than a threshold fraction of Python keywords (def,class,import) or a
high density of ASCII special characters (brackets, colons, underscores) get a relaxed LID threshold of
0.3; everything else stays at 0.65. No model retraining is needed because the heuristic compensates for
the LID model’s domain blind spot. This is the same two-tier strategy OpenWebMath applies to math
content.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Language identification reuses the same bag-of-character-n-gram classifier architecture as quality and
toxicity filtering - there is nothing architecturally special about LID.
The fastText LID model runs at 400K paragraphs per second per core, imposing negligible compute
overhead compared to any downstream neural scorer.
Training on a diluted multilingual corpus in a compute-limited regime measurably hurts target-language
performance; filtering with a precision-biased threshold is almost always the right default for monolingual
labs.
The classifier degrades on short texts, code, and math - compensate with domain heuristics that adjust the
threshold rather than retraining the model.
Classify at the document level when downstream processing must respect document boundaries; use
paragraph-level only for passage-centric datasets where intra-document coherence is not required.
```
**21.2.2 Toxicity and Safety Filtering**
Interviewers at frontier labs routinely ask how you would prevent a pre-training corpus from poisoning a
model with hate speech, graphic content, and targeted harassment. The question probes two things: whether you
understand that toxicity filtering uses the same classifier machinery as quality and language filtering, and whether
you can articulate the precision-recall trade-off when a false positive means discarding legitimate content and a
false negative means baking harmful content into a production model. This shows up at mid-to-senior level
and often comes paired with a harder follow-up about what you do when the classifier is miscalibrated on
marginalized dialects or domain-specific terminology.
Toxicity filtering is binary classification applied to a harm dimension rather than a quality or language
dimension. The standard approach trains one or more fastText classifiers on a labeled dataset of harmful text,
then scores every document in the raw corpus and discards those that exceed a threshold. The key dataset that
anchors most production pipelines is the _Jigsaw Toxic Comment Classification_ corpus: comments scraped from
Wikipedia talk pages and annotated by crowdworkers across six harm categories - toxic, severe toxic, obscene,
threat, insult, and identity hate.


```
21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks
```
The DOLMA pipeline trains two separate fastText classifiers on this data: one for hate speech (collapsing
threat, insult, and identity hate into a single positive class) and one for NSFW content (collapsing severe toxic
and obscene into a positive class). Both classifiers use the same architecture described in the quality-filtering
section - a bag of character n-grams hashed into a fixed embedding table, averaged, then classified with a linear
head. Each classifier outputs a scalar in[0,1], and documents that exceed separate per-classifier thresholds
are discarded. Using two classifiers rather than one multi-label head is a practical decision: it lets you tune
precision and recall independently across harm types, since the consequences of under-filtering hate speech
versus under-filtering NSFW content differ by deployment context.
_Toxicity filtering is harm-dimension classification with the same lightweight n-gram machinery as every
other filter - the only thing that changes is the label definition and the labeled dataset you train on._
The alternative is rule-based blocklisting: maintain a list of slurs, profanity, and explicit terms and reject
any document containing them. This has two failure modes. First, it generates high false-positive rates on
legitimate educational, journalistic, and clinical text that necessarily discusses the same terms in context. A
document explaining the history of racial slurs in American legislation and a document celebrating that history
look identical to a keyword filter. Second, it is trivially bypassed by creative spelling (letter substitutions, zero-
width characters, non-ASCII lookalikes) that a character n-gram model handles naturally because it operates
below the word level.
The fastText classifier generalizes across these surface variants because the n-gram representation captures
sub-word patterns. A model trained on the Jigsaw corpus learns that certain character sequences cluster near tox-
icity labels without being hard-coded to any specific word form. This is the same reason character n-grams work
well for LID on closely related languages: the signal is in the distributional statistics of character transitions,
not the lexicon.
The key trade-off is recall versus collateral damage to legitimate content. A conservative threshold that
catches 99% of hate speech will also remove a meaningful fraction of news articles, academic discussions of
extremism, and creative fiction that engages with dark themes. I have seen pipelines that aggressively filtered
toxicity produce models that refused to discuss historical atrocities because the training data had been scrubbed
of all documents containing relevant terminology. Tuning the threshold requires evaluating both the corpus’s
downstream task performance and the rate at which known-safe documents are incorrectly discarded.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you are building a 300-billion-token English corpus from Common Crawl and want to apply
DOLMA-style toxicity filtering. You have two classifiers: a hate-speech classifier and an NSFW classifier, each
a fastText model with a 16-dimensional hidden layer and 107 hashed n-gram buckets.
Inference throughput for each classifier is roughly 2  105 documents per second per CPU core. A 300B-
token corpus at 500 tokens per document contains 6  108 documents. Running both classifiers sequentially on
128 CPU cores:

6  108 docs
2  105 docs/core-s 128 cores
 23 seconds per classifier
Total wall time for both passes: under one minute. Compute cost is negligible relative to any neural quality
scorer.
With the DOLMA hate-speech threshold set at 0.3 and the NSFW threshold at 0.1 (both intentionally
conservative, erring toward recall), you expect to discard roughly 1-2% of the corpus. Auditing 1,000 random


```
21.2 Targeted Filtering Tasks
```
discards reveals the classifier’s failure modes: it flags medical and legal text discussing assault, removes news
articles about far-right extremism, and incorrectly labels some African American Vernacular English as toxic.
This audit is not optional - it tells you whether the precision-recall trade-off is acceptable for your deployment
context and whether you need to adjust thresholds per domain.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Threshold calibration: Never pick a threshold from the paper. Always calibrate on a human-audited
sample of 500-1,000 random positives (discards) and negatives (retains). What matters is not the classi-
fier’s accuracy on Jigsaw test data - it is the false positive rate on the domain you actually care about.
One classifier vs. multiple: A single multi-label classifier is simpler to train and maintain. Multiple
single-label classifiers let you tune thresholds independently and trace discards to specific harm categories,
which is valuable when explaining filtering decisions to policy and legal teams. Use multiple classifiers
whenever deployment context requires accountability by harm type.
Dialect and register bias: fastText classifiers trained on Jigsaw are known to over-flag African American
Vernacular English and LGBTQ+ community language. Before deploying, run the classifier on a balanced
sample that includes these dialects and measure false positive rates per demographic group. If they exceed
3-5the baseline false positive rate, either adjust the threshold or curate additional training data for those
groups.
Domain-specific thresholds: Medical corpora, legal corpora, and fiction corpora require relaxed thresh-
olds because they legitimately discuss explicit content. A single global threshold applied across all do-
mains is almost always wrong. Tag documents by domain before filtering and apply per-domain thresh-
olds.
Bootstrapping the classifier with a stronger model: If you want better recall on subtle or implicit
toxicity - dog whistles, coded language, context-dependent slurs - use a larger model (BERT-scale or
larger) to label 100K samples from your target distribution, then distill those labels into a fastText classifier.
The expensive model runs once; the fast classifier runs on the full corpus. This is the same bootstrap
strategy phi-1 used for quality filtering.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you remove toxic content from a web-scale pre-training corpus?” A strong answer
identifies the Jigsaw dataset as the standard training source, names the fastText classifier as the stan-
dard production tool, specifies that two classifiers (hate and NSFW) are typically trained separately, and
immediately raises the precision-recall trade-off. Weak answers propose rule-based blocklists without
addressing bypass mechanisms or false positive rates.
“What is the risk of over-filtering for toxicity?” Strong answer: aggressive filtering creates systematic
blind spots in the trained model. A model that has never seen text discussing violence, discrimination, or
explicit content in any context will refuse to engage with those topics - even in clearly beneficial settings
like academic analysis, clinical documentation, or counter-speech. It also produces a biased corpus if the
classifier has differential false positive rates across demographic groups.
Senior follow-up - “Your toxicity classifier was trained on Wikipedia talk-page comments. How
does that affect its performance on Reddit or Twitter-style text?” The senior answer: domain shift is
the central risk. Wikipedia talk pages are longer, more formal, and less code-switched than social media
```

### 21.3 Deduplication at Scale

```
text; the classifier’s precision on short, informal, and heavily abbreviated posts will degrade. The fix is
targeted data collection: sample 10K documents from the target domain, have annotators label them, and
either fine-tune the classifier’s output layer or use the labels to recalibrate the decision threshold. The key
insight is that the embedding layer trained on Jigsaw generalizes reasonably well; it is the classification
boundary that shifts with domain.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Toxicity filtering reuses the same fastText n-gram classifier machinery as language and quality filtering -
train on a labeled harm dataset, score the corpus, threshold.
The Jigsaw Toxic Comment corpus is the standard training source; DOLMA trains two separate classifiers
(hate speech and NSFW) to allow independent threshold control.
Always audit random samples of discarded documents before deploying a threshold - false positive rates
on legitimate content are the critical failure mode, not classifier accuracy on the training benchmark.
fastText toxicity classifiers are known to over-flag marginalized dialects; measure per-group false positive
rates before deploying and adjust thresholds or training data accordingly.
Use a stronger model (BERT or larger) to bootstrap labels on your target domain, then distill into fastText
```
- the expensive model runs once on 100K samples, the fast model runs on hundreds of billions of tokens.

### 21.3 Deduplication at Scale

**21.3.1 Exact Deduplication with Bloom Filters**
Exact deduplication is the first quality gate every serious pre-training pipeline runs, and it matters more
than most engineers expect. A 2022 audit of C4 found a single product-description sentence appearing 61,000
times; training on that corpus without dedup is equivalent to taking 61,000 gradient steps on the same data point.
Interviewers at frontier labs ask about exact dedup at every seniority level, but the senior-level question is not
“do you hash things?”-it is “how do you dedup 10 trillion tokens without running out of memory?” The answer
is Bloom filters.
Exact deduplication has a three-axis design space. First, the _unit_ : sentence, paragraph, or document. Sec-
ond, the _match criterion_ : exact character equality. Third, the _action_ : remove all copies, or keep one. The
algorithmic challenge is that duplicate detection is fundamentally pairwise: to know whether itemais a dupli-
cate, you must compare it against every other item. Fornitems that isO(n^2 )comparisons, which is infeasible
at web scale. Hashing collapses this toO(n)by converting pairwise equality into shared bucket membership:
computeh(x)for every item and group by hash value. Items in the same bucket are candidate duplicates; with
a collision-resistant hash such asMurmurHash3, same bucket means same content.
The standard distributed formulation-a MapReduce over hash buckets-is correct and parallelizable, but it
requires persisting all hashes in a random-access structure. At 100 billion items you are building a hash table
that occupies tens of gigabytes of cluster RAM. A _Bloom filter_ solves the memory problem.
A Bloom filter is a bit array ofmbits, initialized to zero, withKindependent hash functionsh 1 ,... , hK
each mapping items tof 0 ,... , m 1 g. To insert itemx: set bitsh 1 (x),... , hK(x)to 1. To query item
x: returnpresentiff allKbits are already set. The filter has _no false negatives_ -an inserted item is always

**What You Actually Decide in Practice
Unit of deduplication.** Paragraph-level is the industry default (DOLMA, RedPajama). Document-level is
faster but misses partial duplicates such as boilerplate footers, license text, and templated ads. Sentence-

```
Action: keep-first vs. remove-all. Keep-first (retain the earliest occurrence, discard later ones) is simpler
and retains the data. Remove-all is appropriate for boilerplate that should never appear-but the MIT license
is valid training signal; you just do not want 10,000 copies.
Exact vs. near. Exact dedup is high-precision but blind to near-duplicates differing by punctuation or one
substituted word. Plan to follow with a MinHash LSH pass if your corpus contains templated content,
scraped mirrors, or synthetic data.
```

```
“Walk me through how you would deduplicate a 10-trillion-token web corpus.” Strong answer:

fits dedup exactly.
Senior follow-up: “A false positive in your Bloom filter causes a unique paragraph to be discarded.
What is the impact, and how would you detect calibration drift?” A false positive silently reduces
recall with no signal-you cannot know from the output alone that a unique paragraph was lost. AtPFP=
10 −^6 you lose roughlyn 10 −^6 paragraphs. To audit calibration, run a random sample of discarded
items through an exact hash-set lookup against the corpus; if the measured false positive rate exceeds the
target, eithernhas grown beyond the designed capacity ormwas sized too small. Recalibrating requires
rebuilding the filter-there is no in-place resize.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Exact dedup reduces anO(n^2 )pairwise problem toO(n)by mapping items to hash buckets; same bucket
means same content.
A Bloom filter is a bit array withKhash functions supporting constant-time set membership with no false
negatives and tunablePFP 2 −Kat optimalK= (m/n) ln 2.
Size the filter withm nlnPFP/(ln 2)^2 ; atPFP= 10−^9 andn= 10^11 that is approximately 5 bytes
per item.
UseMurmurHash3with fixed integer seeds; never use Python’shash()in distributed pipelines.
```

```
Paragraph granularity with keep-first action is the production default; follow with a MinHash LSH pass
to catch near-duplicates.
```
**21.3.2 Near-Deduplication with MinHash and LSH**
Exact deduplication removes verbatim copies; near-deduplication removes everything else that provides
nearly zero additional signal. The web is full of templated ad copy where only a city name changes, scraped
articles where one synonym differs, and terms-of-service boilerplate that picks up or loses a comma across
a thousand mirror sites. After exact dedup, these near-duplicates can still represent 20-40% of a large crawl.
MinHash LSH is the standard algorithm for catching them at linear time complexity, and it appears in interviews
as a deep-dive on probabilistic data structures applied to ML infrastructure-the kind of question that separates
engineers who know the algorithm from those who have debugged it at scale.
The similarity measure for near-deduplication is _Jaccard similarity_. For two setsAandBof n-gram
shingles extracted from a document:

```

```
Two documents are near-duplicates ifJ(A, B)θfor some thresholdθ(typically 0.8-0.99). ComputingJ
explicitly for all pairs isO(n^2 )-infeasible at billions of documents.
_MinHash_ solves the first part. Given a hash functionhdrawn from a min-wise independent family, define
hmin(S) = minx∈Sh(x).

Then:
P(hmin(A) =hmin(B)) =J(A, B).

The argument is direct:hmin(A) =hmin(B)iff the element with the globally smallest hash value belongs to
A\B, which happens with probabilityjA\Bj/jA[Bj.
UsingKindependent MinHash functions gives aK-dimensional signature vector per document. The
expected fraction of matching positions betweenσAandσBequalsJ(A, B), but a single signature is too noisy
for a binary near-duplicate decision.
_Locality-Sensitive Hashing_ (LSH) sharpens this estimator into a binary flag. Divide theKhash functions

_MinHash LSH converts the pairwise near-duplicate problem into a linear-time bucket-collision problem
by ensuring that similar documents hash to the same bucket with high probability and dissimilar documents do

**Pipeline steps.**

1. Tokenize each document into overlapping 5-gram character shingles. A 500-word document produces
    roughly 2,400 shingles.

    hashing the result-to a 64-bit bucket key.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Threshold choice. Useθ = 0. 99 for strict near-verbatim dedup (SlimPajama, DOLMA: one word
changed per hundred words allowed). Useθ= 0. 8 when your corpus has heavy templated content and
you want aggressive repetition reduction. Belowθ= 0. 7 you risk discarding topically similar but sub-
stantively different documents-especially dangerous in domain-specific corpora such as code or medical
text.
Sizing b and r. FixKfrom the memory budget first (K= 100for 400 bytes/document). Deriverfrom
the desired sharpness: higherrsteepens the sigmoid. Computeb=K/r. Plug intoθ(1/b)^1 /rand
verify the S-curve at one similarity above and one below the threshold to confirm the transition is sharp
enough.
Shingle granularity. 5-gram character shingles are robust to tokenizer differences and language variation.
Word n-grams are faster but language-dependent. For code, use 10-gram character shingles: they catch
copy-pasted functions that differ only in variable names better than word-level n-grams do.
Verification pass. Skip it when throughput is the bottleneck-false positives from band collisions are
typically well under 1% for 64-bit bucket keys. Add it when discarding good documents is costly (domain-
specific corpora under 100 billion tokens) or when you need an accurate duplicate count for auditing
downstream.
Semantic deduplication. MinHash operates on n-gram shingles and is blind to paraphrase. If your corpus
contains synthetic data generated by rewriting existing documents, MinHash LSH will miss those near-
duplicates. In that regime, embed documents with a small encoder, index with FAISS, and threshold on
cosine similarity. Expect roughly 20 higher compute cost and careful threshold tuning to avoid over-
pruning topically related but distinct content.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why is exact deduplication not enough? What does MinHash catch that a hash set misses?” Strong
answer: exact dedup requires bit-for-bit identity. Near-duplicates-the same paragraph with one word
changed, the same article with a different byline-survive exact dedup but add no training signal. MinHash
measures Jaccard overlap over n-gram shingles; LSH converts that into a fast bucket-based collision test
with a tunable threshold.
“Explain how MinHash LSH works and why it runs in linear time.” Strong answer: MinHash gives
each document aK-dimensional signature where the expected fraction of matching positions equals Jac-
card similarity. LSH splits the signature intobbands ofrrows; two documents collide if any band is
identical. Each document performsbhash lookups inO(K)time; total work isO(nK), linear in corpus
size, with no explicit pairwise comparisons.
Senior follow-up: “How do you choose b and r to hit a specific threshold with sharp behavior? Walk
through the math.” Senior answer: the threshold formula isθ(1/b)^1 /r; the collision probability as

rates are acceptable. If the transition is too shallow, increaseKto allow a largerrwhile maintainingb.
```

## Chapter 22 Mid-Training and Post-Training Data

### 22.1 Instruction and Chat Data.

**22.1.1 Aggregated NLP Tasks (FLAN-Style)**
When an interviewer asks you to explain the difference between a base model and an instruct model, the
answer is almost entirely a data answer-and the FLAN-style approach is where that data story begins. Converting
thousands of labeled NLP benchmarks into a unified instruction format was the field’s first systematic answer
to the question “how do you teach a model to follow instructions?” It shows up in interviews at the L5-L6
range whenever the discussion reaches post-training pipelines, data mix composition, or why instruct models
generalize to tasks they were never fine-tuned on directly.
The NLP community spent two decades building task-specific labeled datasets: natural language inference,
sentiment classification, summarization, machine translation, reading comprehension, commonsense reason-
ing. Each dataset is already a collection of (input, output) pairs. The only missing piece is a natural-language
instruction that wraps the pair and tells the model what task it is performing. The FLAN approach and Super-
Natural Instructions demonstrated independently that if you templatize these datasets at scale-writing a handful
of natural-language templates per task and applying them to every example-a model fine-tuned on the result
generalizes to tasks it was never explicitly trained on.
The recipe is mechanical. For each source dataset, writeknatural-language templates, typicallyk= 2to
10 , that describe the task in different words. For a natural language inference example with premisep, hypothesis
h, and gold labely2fentailment, neutral, contradictiong, one template might be:

Premise: {p}
Hypothesis: {h}
Does the hypothesis follow from the premise?
Options: Yes / No / It's impossible to tell
Answer: {y}

A second template for the same example might ask “Is the following hypothesis true given the premise?”
with a different label mapping. SuperNatural Instructions collected 1,616 tasks from the NLP community,
each with two or more manually written templates, producing millions of examples covering classification,
generation, extraction, and structured prediction-all formatted in the same prompt-response structure.
_The fundamental move is re-framing every existing supervised dataset as an instance of instruction follow-
ing, so one fine-tuning run buys transfer across an entire task taxonomy._
The primary advantage is data leverage. Decades of annotation work in the NLP community become nearly
free training signal with minimal new human effort. A templating pass converts a 100k-example NLI dataset into
a 300k-example instruction dataset in hours. The secondary advantage is benchmark coverage: a model trained
on FLAN-style data sees labeled examples from the same task families that standard evaluation benchmarks
draw from, which is a direct contributor to strong HellaSwag, MMLU, and BIG-Bench numbers.
The weakness is that the prompts are templated and therefore artificial. If you sample randomly from a
SuperNatural Instructions mix, many examples share the same sentence skeleton and differ only in their filled
slots. Real users ask questions in idiosyncratic, messy ways: “can u explain why the EU passed that regulation”


```
22.1 Instruction and Chat Data
```
looks nothing like “Given the following passage, extract the key regulatory rationale.” Models trained only on
FLAN-style data perform well on structured benchmarks but feel robotic and brittle in open-ended conversa-
tion. The pre-training data for most models contains documents like Stack Exchange Q&A and Reddit threads
that already resemble instruction-response pairs; FLAN-style fine-tuning is unlocking that latent capability, not
installing it from scratch.
There is also a saturation effect. FLAN-style data helps enormously early in fine-tuning-it moves the model
from “coherent text continuation” to “instruction following”-but has diminishing returns past a certain coverage
threshold. The empirical consensus is that 1,000+ diverse tasks from well-curated templates is sufficient; adding
more tasks beyond that contributes less than improving the quality and diversity of examples within existing
tasks.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you are building a FLAN-style mix from three source datasets: a 400k-example NLI corpus, a
50k-example extractive QA corpus, and a 200k-example summarization corpus. Two annotators each spend a
day writing three templates per task-nine templates total.
For NLI you get400k3 = 1.2Mexamples. For QA you get50k3 = 150kexamples. For summarization
you get200k3 = 600kexamples. Total: roughly 1.95M instruction pairs before deduplication.
You fine-tune a 7B-parameter base model on this mix for one epoch-approximately 2B tokens at an average
of 1k tokens per example on an 8-GPU H100 node, which completes in under 12 hours. The model that previ-
ously generated incoherent continuations now correctly handles NLI, QA, and summarization prompts. More
importantly, if you prompt it with a paraphrase task it has never seen, the model attempts it rather than ignoring
the instruction. That zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks is precisely what FLAN-style training buys.
Now suppose you extend the mix with a commonsense reasoning dataset containing 100k examples and
three templates. You do not need to retrain from scratch: extend the mix to 2.25M examples and fine-tune for
an additional 0.5 epochs. Benchmark scores on commonsense tasks improve by 4-6 points while regression on
the original three tasks is minimal-provided you weight sampling proportional to task size and keep template
vocabulary diverse across tasks.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Template count vs. template quality. Three to five high-quality templates per task consistently out-
performs ten mediocre ones. Template quality means: varied surface forms, varied label vocabulary,
varied prompt ordering. If two templates are paraphrases of each other, they provide almost no additional
diversity signal.
Task sampling strategy. Uniform sampling over examples-not tasks-over-represents large datasets and
starves small ones of gradient signal. Temperature-based sampling, where taskiis drawn with probability
proportional tojDijTwithT  0. 7 , smooths coverage without fully equalizing tiny tasks against large
ones. Below roughly 1,000 examples per task, quality degrades because the model sees too few template
variations to internalize the task format.
When to stop and move on. FLAN-style data is the right tool for getting a base model to follow instruc-
tions at all. Once benchmark gains from adding new tasks fall below 0.3 percentage points per additional
100k examples, further improvement comes from higher-quality open-ended data-synthetic or human-
written-not more templated tasks.
```

```
22.1 Instruction and Chat Data
```
```
Replay a pre-training fraction. Fine-tuning only on instruction data with no raw-text signal causes for-
getting, especially on long-form generation. Including a 10-20% “replay” fraction of pre-training tokens
in the instruction fine-tuning batch stabilizes perplexity on held-out raw text without measurably hurting
instruction-following performance.
Label noise compounds through templating. A 15% label error rate in the source dataset becomes
a 15% error rate across all derived templates. A 10k-example NLI set with clean labels beats a 500k-
example set with 15% noise; expect roughly a 2-point downstream gap. Audit source dataset quality
before investing in templating effort.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What is the difference between a base model and an instruct model, and how does data drive
that gap?” Strong answer: a base model is trained on next-token prediction over raw text and interprets
any prompt as a document to continue. An instruct model is fine-tuned on (instruction, response) pairs-
beginning with FLAN-style templated NLP tasks-which teaches the model to interpret a user turn as a
directive and produce a targeted response rather than a free continuation. The architectural difference is
typically zero; the behavioral gap is entirely in the data.
“How would you build an instruction dataset from scratch with a small team and a limited budget?”
Strong answer: inventory existing labeled NLP datasets in your target domain, write three to five tem-
plates per task, and convert them into a unified prompt-response format. Prioritize task diversity over raw
example count-100 tasks at 10k examples each generalizes better than one task at 1M examples. Layer in
real or synthetic open-ended conversations once the model reliably follows structured instructions.
Senior follow-up: “FLAN-style models score well on benchmarks but often feel mechanical in free-
form chat. What is the root cause, and how would you fix it?” Root cause: benchmark-derived tem-
plates are structurally regular; real conversational prompts are irregular, context-dependent, and often
underspecified. To close the gap, augment the FLAN mix with open-ended conversational pairs from
human annotators, real user logs with appropriate consent, or a strong model prompted with diverse seed
questions. Weight the open-ended component so it represents at least 30-40% of the final instruction mix,
and oversample task types that exhibit the mechanical feel on a held-out conversational eval.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
FLAN-style training converts existing labeled NLP benchmarks into instruction-following data at near-
zero marginal annotation cost by wrapping each (input, output) pair in a natural-language task template.
The core benefit is cross-task generalization: a model that sees 1,000+ templated tasks acquires a general
instruction-following prior that transfers to unseen tasks at inference time.
Template rigidity is the central weakness-structured prompts do not match the messiness of real user
queries, so FLAN-style data must be supplemented with open-ended conversational data in any production
instruction mix.
Use temperature-based task sampling (T 0. 7 ) rather than uniform example sampling to balance cover-
age across tasks of different sizes.
Replay 10-20% pre-training tokens during instruction fine-tuning to prevent forgetting on long-form gen-
eration, and audit source dataset label quality before investing in large-scale templating.
```

```
22.1 Instruction and Chat Data
```
**22.1.2 Human-Written vs. AI-Generated Instruction Data**
Once instruction-following data is recognized as the lever that turns a base model into a useful assistant,
the next question is immediate and practical: where does it come from? Paying humans to write examples is
expensive and slow; prompting a stronger model to generate them is cheap and fast but carries license exposure
and a quality ceiling bounded by the teacher. Every lab I know has grappled with this trade-off explicitly, and
it surfaces in system design interviews-usually phrased as “how would you scale your SFT dataset?”-at every
level from L4 upward.
There are three production-grade sources of instruction data, each with a distinct cost and quality profile.
**Human-annotated data.** Contractors or in-house annotators write (prompt, response) pairs following
a rubric. Quality is high when the rubric is tight and the annotators are domain experts. Cost runs roughly
$10-$100 per example depending on task complexity and response length; throughput is capped by headcount.
Llama 2’s post-training data included human-authored examples, and the team reported that a modest number
of high-quality human-written pairs outperformed millions of open-source synthetic examples for instruction
following.
**Distillation from a stronger model.** A capable model is prompted to generate responses to a set of seed
questions. The resulting (question, response) pairs are used to fine-tune a smaller target model. This is the
dominant approach in the open community. Alpaca used a self-instruct loop against GPT-3 to generate 52k
examples; Vicuna was trained on ChatGPT conversations shared publicly on ShareGPT; OpenHermes is an
agglomeration of multiple GPT-4-sourced community datasets; the Llama-Nemotron post-training corpus draws
from Llama, Qwen, and other open-weight models to avoid proprietary license issues.
**Self-play and evol-instruct synthesis.** The model itself-or a sibling model-is seeded with a pool of ques-
tions and asked to both expand the pool and answer the new questions. Evol-instruct methods take existing
questions and iteratively mutate them to be more complex, more specific, or more constrained, producing a
diversity gradient from simple to hard.
The self-instruct loop from the Alpaca work is representative of the distillation approach:

1. Seed pool: ~175 hand-written (instruction, input, output) triples
2. Prompt teacher model with k=8 in-context examples sampled
    from the pool; generate a new instruction
3. Filter: drop if ROUGE-L overlap with any pooled example > 0.7,
    or if output is malformed (empty, refusal, truncated)
4. Add accepted example back to pool
5. Repeat until target corpus size is reached

_The self-instruct loop converts a few hundred seed examples into tens of thousands of training pairs; the
ceiling on quality is the teacher model’s own capability, and that ceiling descends into the student._
Human annotation wins on quality ceiling and legal cleanliness. For tasks where the teacher model is
known to be unreliable-highly regulated domains, multi-step mathematical reasoning before strong reasoning
models existed, low-resource languages-the only defensible path is a human expert who understands the failure
modes. Human-written data also carries no downstream license risk: if your annotators wrote it, you own it.
AI generation wins on cost, coverage, and throughput. A single GPU-day on a 70B model produces
100k diverse examples; the equivalent human annotation would cost tens of thousands of dollars and weeks
of turnaround. Coverage diversity is also genuinely hard to match by hand: prompting a strong model to answer


```
22.1 Instruction and Chat Data
```
questions spanning astrophysics, tax law, culinary chemistry, and software debugging gives you breadth that no
annotation workforce could deliver efficiently.
The critical failure mode for AI-generated data is confident wrongness. A teacher model does not generate
examples it is uncertain about; it generates fluent, plausible-sounding responses that happen to be incorrect.
The student model learns that confident, fluent responses are correct by construction-exactly the hallucination
problem. When you later evaluate with a judge model, you may not even catch this because the judge has the
same blind spots as the teacher. Human-written data at least has domain experts who know when to say “I don’t
know.”

**A Worked Example**

Consider building a 100k-example SFT dataset for a coding assistant. Budget: roughly $5,000 and two
weeks of engineering time.
**Option A-human annotation.** Hire 20 contractors at $25 per example, each writing Python and SQL
prompt-response pairs. At 10 examples per contractor per day, you produce 2,000 examples per day-reaching
100k in 50 working days. That is 10 weeks of calendar time and $2.5M. Clearly not viable.
**Option B-distillation from Llama 3 70B.** Write 500 seed prompts covering Python, SQL, debugging,
code review, and docstring generation. Run the self-instruct loop prompting Llama 3 70B via 8 H100s. Apply
an execution filter: run every generated code block through a Python interpreter and discard examples where
the snippet raises an uncaught exception. This filter removes roughly 15% of outputs and is the single highest-
leverage quality gate for code data. In three GPU-days you produce 100k filtered examples at a compute cost
of approximately $600. License check: Llama 3’s acceptable use policy permits training derivative models for
organizations below the commercial threshold, which covers most teams.
The resulting 7B model fine-tuned for two epochs scores 5-8 points below a model trained on premium
human-written coding data on a hard held-out benchmark. For most teams below frontier scale, that gap is the
correct economic trade-off. Human annotation is then reserved for the specific task slice-perhaps adversarial
debugging or multi-file refactoring-where AI generation is demonstrably wrong on the held-out eval.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Read the teacher model license before you generate a single example. OpenAI’s terms of service
explicitly prohibit using GPT-4 outputs to train a competing model; violation exposes you to contract
breach, not just moral awkwardness. Open-weight models-Llama, Mistral, Qwen-have more permissive
terms, but Llama still restricts commercial use above certain active-user thresholds. The right answer is
to read the actual license document, not a summary in a blog post.
Apply an automated quality gate matched to the task type. For code: execute the snippet and discard
failures. For structured outputs (JSON, SQL, function calls): parse and schema-validate. For factual QA:
optionally run a retrieval check against a known-correct source. A well-targeted filter removes 10-20% of
AI-generated examples and consistently improves downstream evaluation scores by 2-5 points relative to
raw unfiltered generation.
Diversity matters more than volume past roughly 10k examples. Generating 500k examples from
20 seed prompts produces a dataset with shallow diversity that adds little over 50k. Measure diversity
concretely: compute n-gram entropy over instructions, or cluster instruction embeddings and measure the
```

```
22.1 Instruction and Chat Data
```
```
fraction of clusters with fewer than five members. When diversity stops growing, expand the seed set
rather than generating more from existing seeds.
Reserve human annotation budget for the hard tail. Run a small held-out evaluation first. Identify
the task slices where the AI-generated model fails at rates above your threshold. Allocate annotation to
exactly those slices. Human annotation at $50 per example is only expensive if you spend it on tasks
where AI generation already works.
Defend against annotator leakage. When Llama 2’s team ran human annotation, they acknowledged
a real risk: contractors querying GPT-4 and pasting the output as their “human-written” submission.
A practical detector is to measure the perplexity of the submitted response under the suspected teacher
model. Responses that score anomalously low-lower than median responses from genuine domain experts-
are likely machine-generated. Flag them for review rather than discarding automatically, since a domain
expert might produce text that happens to look similar to GPT-4 output simply because they are both
correct.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“You have a $50k budget and six weeks to build an SFT dataset for a domain-specific assistant.
Walk me through your approach.” Strong answer: spend week one identifying the five to ten task types
the assistant must handle and running an AI-generation pilot on each to measure failure rate. Allocate hu-
man annotation to the one or two types where AI generation fails above threshold-likely domain-specific
reasoning or regulated content. Use distillation from an open-weight 70B model for the remainder with
task-appropriate quality filters. Plan for 70-90k AI-generated examples and 5-10k human-written ones;
oversample the human examples in the training batch by a factor of three to compensate for volume im-
balance.
“What are the risks of training on GPT-4-generated data?” Strong answer: three distinct risks. First,
the OpenAI terms of service prohibit using model outputs to train a competing model-this is a legal and
contractual risk, not just an ethical concern. Second, the student model inherits the teacher’s failure modes
without the teacher’s uncertainty calibration: it hallucinates confidently in the same situations GPT-4 does,
because those are precisely the situations where the training examples were wrong. Third, GPT-4’s style
and safety filters shape the data distribution in ways that may not match the deployment context-you are
distilling a general assistant when you may need a specialized one.
Senior follow-up: “Llama 2 reported that a small set of human-written examples outperformed
millions of open-source synthetic examples. Is that a general result?” Senior answer: it is regime-
and quality-dependent, not a fundamental law. The open-source synthetic datasets available at the time
Llama 2 was trained were low-diversity and generated from weaker teacher models. When the quality of
AI-generated data is controlled-strong teacher, diversity-enforced seed set, automated quality filtering-it
consistently matches or exceeds small human-written corpora at fraction of the cost. The Llama 2 paper
also noted that RLHF on top of either data source recovered much of the gap, which suggests the human-
annotation advantage was partly about capturing preference signal rather than instruction quality alone.
The operationally correct interpretation is: human annotation is worth the cost at the thin tail where the
task is genuinely beyond AI generation; everywhere else, distillation with a quality gate is the right call.
```

### 22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data

**Key Takeaways**

```
Human annotation provides the highest quality ceiling and full legal cleanliness but costs $10-$100 per
example; reserve it for the hard tail where AI generation demonstrably fails.
Distillation from open-weight models (Llama, Qwen, Mistral) is the dominant cost-effective path-but
always verify the license before generating training data, since proprietary model terms often prohibit
training competitors.
The self-instruct loop scales a few hundred seed prompts to 100k+ examples in GPU-days; quality is
bounded by the teacher model and improved most reliably by automated execution or format filters that
remove 10-20% of raw outputs.
Diversity matters more than volume past ~10k examples: measure n-gram entropy or embedding cluster
coverage and expand the seed set when diversity plateaus rather than generating more from existing seeds.
Annotator leakage-contractors querying a proprietary model to produce nominally human-written data-is
a real production risk; detect it by measuring submission perplexity under the suspected teacher model.
```
### 22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data

**22.2.1 Books and Math for Context Extension**
When an interviewer asks you to extend a 7B model’s context from 4k to 128k tokens, most candidates
immediately reach for RoPE scaling factors and overlook the data question entirely. What you actually train on
during the extension phase determines whether the model genuinely attends across the full window or merely
pattern-matches on position encodings it has never encountered. Long-context extension appears in senior and
staff-level interviews because it sits at the intersection of architecture, training schedule, and data curation-and
getting the data mix wrong wastes weeks of expensive GPU time.
The fundamental problem is cost. Full attention scales asO(L^2 )per layer in both compute and memory,
whereLis the sequence length. If standard pre-training runs atL= 4096, extending toL= 131072(128k
tokens) multiplies attention cost by a factor of(131072/4096)^2 = 1024at each layer. Training at that length from
the first step would consume the entire compute budget before the model has learned basic language patterns,
so the canonical practice is to defer long-context training to a dedicated mid-training phase once a strong 4k
checkpoint exists.
The data requirement for this phase is specific: you need documents with _genuine long-range dependen-
cies_ , not simply long documents. A 128k-token chunk assembled by concatenating 32 unrelated 4k web pages
has no dependency structure beyond each page-the model learns nothing about attending across the full window.
Books are the canonical source because they encode narrative arcs, character motivations, and thematic call-
backs that span tens of thousands of tokens. The PG-19 dataset, derived from Project Gutenberg, was specifically
constructed to benchmark long-context language models because book chapters force models to track informa-
tion from much earlier in the sequence. Mathematics and formal papers are complementary: proof steps and
derivations maintain tightly coupled variable definitions across hundreds of lines, creating a different pattern of
long-range dependency that covers reasoning chains rather than narrative continuity.
_Long-context extension is a mid-training phase, not a pre-training phase, because_ O(L^2 ) _attention cost
makes early long-context training economically irrational, and the model is not capable enough early on to
benefit from the distant context anyway._


```
22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data
```
Books force genuine cross-sentence coherence. A reference to a character’s internal conflict in chapter
15 connects back to something established in chapter 1-the only way to assign meaningful probability to that
reference is to actually use the distant context. This is precisely the training signal a context-extension phase
needs. Random web text concatenated to fill a 128k window teaches the model that context is useless beyond
4k, because it is: the adjacent documents are unrelated. You can verify this failure mode by checking attention
entropy across positions in a model trained on stitched documents-heads at position 60k are essentially ignoring
positions 1-40k.
The trade-off versus starting long-context training from scratch is purely economic. A model trained from
step zero at 128k would require hundreds of billions of tokens to reach base language quality, burning roughly
1024 the compute per token at the attention layer compared to 4k training. The mid-training approach inher-
its all the knowledge from cheap 4k pre-training and spends a much smaller budget-typically 20-50B tokens-
adapting the positional encoding and calibrating the attention patterns for the longer window.
Against the alternative of simply relying on sliding-window or sparse attention to avoid the quadratic cost:
those approaches reduce the compute burden but also reduce quality at tasks that genuinely require attending
across the full window. Full attention at mid-training, on the right data, remains the highest-quality path for
frontier models.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you have a 7B model pre-trained to 200k steps atL= 4096. Your target context length is 128k.
Hardware budget: 256 H100s (32 nodes of 8). Estimated mid-training budget: 40B tokens.
**Data mix:**
65% books (PG-19 and similar long-form corpora): average document length 80k-200k tokens, packed
contiguously by chapter.
20% arXiv and math papers: average document length 10k-40k tokens, packed contiguously per paper.
15% long-form web documents: filtered to documents with raw length>32k tokens, using the original
HTML parser (not WET) to preserve structure.
**Sequence packing rule:** fill each 128k-token training chunk from a single document or from contiguous
chapters of one book. Never pack unrelated documents into the same chunk. This is non-negotiable-mixing
documents destroys the long-range dependency signal.
**Graduated schedule:** Run 10B tokens atL= 32768, then 10B tokens atL= 65536, then 20B tokens
atL= 131072. Each transition applies a learning rate warmup of 500 steps to absorb the change in positional
encoding behavior. Jumping directly from 4k to 128k causes loss spikes because the position encodings have
never been exercised at intermediate ranges.
**RoPE adjustment:** Apply NTK-by-parts interpolation before the extension phase begins, scaling the base
frequency by a factor of(128k/ 4 k)^1 /(dim/^2 −1) 8 for a 128-dimensional head. This initializes the position
encodings to a state the optimizer can refine rather than one it must escape from.
At the end of the 40B-token schedule, perplexity on long-document benchmarks improves by 15-25%
relative to the base 4k model, while short-context benchmark scores degrade by less than 2% if you maintain
10% general web text in the mix.


```
22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data
```
**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Never skip the graduated schedule. Jumping from 4k to 128k in one step causes optimizer instability
because the gradient signal from positions 4k-128k is initially near-random. Two or three intermediate
lengths costing 10-15B tokens each are always worth the insurance.
Maintain 10% general web text throughout the extension phase. Removing short-context data entirely
for the sake of long-document purity causes capability regression on standard benchmarks. The loss on
short-context tasks climbs noticeably after 5B tokens of pure long-context training.
Use document-contiguous packing, always. If your packing code splits chapters at random boundaries,
audit it before the run starts. Splitting a 90k-token chapter at the 65k mark and continuing in the next
chunk gives the model a truncated signal. Either pack full documents or set a hard minimum document
length equal to the chunk size.
Books are not just any long text. A 128k chunk assembled from 30 news articles concatenated in order
has a document-length of 128k but a coherence length of roughly 4k per article. Use documents where
the author intended a reader to track information over the full length: books, long-form investigative
journalism, technical manuals, multi-part legal filings.
Evaluate before the extension phase ends. Run a checkpoint at 20B tokens through a long-context
needle-in-a-haystack test. If the model cannot retrieve facts from the middle of a 64k window, the data
packing is likely wrong-fix it before burning the rest of the budget.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you would design a context-extension phase for a model that currently
supports 8k tokens but needs to reach 1M.” Strong answers cover the graduated schedule, document-
contiguous packing, the choice of books and math as the primary corpus, and the architectural adjustment
(RoPE scaling). Weak answers describe only the architecture change with no mention of data.
“Why not train at long context from the beginning?” The answer is cost:O(L^2 )attention means long-
context training per token is orders of magnitude more expensive. The model is not capable enough in
early training to exploit distant context, so the compute would be wasted. Mid-training extension amortizes
that cost over a checkpoint that already has strong language priors.
Senior follow-up: “Your book corpus is 90% genre fiction. What does that mean for the model’s
long-context capability?” The senior answer identifies that the model learns long-range narrative coher-
ence patterns specific to fiction-character tracking, dialogue attribution, scene transitions-but misses the
dependency structures in technical writing, legal documents, and formal mathematics. To build general
long-context capability, you need domain-diverse long documents: books plus arXiv papers plus legal fil-
ings plus long-form technical documentation. Genre imbalance in the extension corpus produces a model
that can retrieve story facts from 80k tokens but struggles to track variable definitions across a long proof.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Long-context extension is a mid-training phase because full attention scales asO(L^2 )-deferring it to after
pre-training saves the majority of compute while preserving the quality benefit.
Books and math papers are the canonical sources because they contain genuine long-range dependencies:
narrative arcs and formal proof chains that force the model to use the full window.
```

```
22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data
```
```
Always pack documents contiguously; mixing unrelated documents into one long chunk destroys the
dependency signal and teaches the model that distant context is noise.
Use a graduated sequence-length schedule with intermediate lengths-jumping directly from 4k to 128k
causes optimizer instability and loss spikes.
Retain 10% general web text in the extension mix to prevent short-context capability regression.
```
**22.2.2 Synthetic Rephrasing and Task Conversion**
If aggressive quality filtering retains only 1-2% of your raw token pool, you face a hard arithmetic problem:
frontier models now train on 15-36 trillion tokens, and a 3.8T-token baseline like DCLM may not sustain a large
model for a full training run. Two techniques developed in recent mid-training pipelines attack this problem
directly-rephrasing low-quality documents into usable prose, and converting high-quality documents into struc-
tured instruction-following examples. Both appear in senior interviews framed as “how do you get more usable
signal out of data you already have without crawling more of the web?”
**Rephrasing** uses a capable language model to rewrite documents that fall below your quality threshold
into cleaner prose. The source document supplies the factual content; the rewrite model normalizes grammar,
removes boilerplate and template noise, and restructures run-on sentences. The resulting token is synthetic, but
the information it encodes is grounded in original text rather than hallucinated from scratch.
**Task conversion** applies a language model to high-quality source documents to generate structured input-
output pairs. Given a Wikipedia article or a math textbook passage, the conversion model produces multiple
task variants:

Source: Wikipedia article on Bernoulli numbers

Task variants generated:
QA: Q: "What is the generating function for Bernoulli numbers?"
A: "t / (e^t - 1) = sum_{n=0}^{inf} B_n * t^n / n!"

```
Summary: Input: [article text]
Output: [3-sentence summary]
```
Extract: Input: [article text]
Output: [key formulas and their names]
The general form is: given a source documentD, generatef(prompti,responsei)gfori2fQA,summarize,extract,classify,.. .g.
This is precisely the transformation that FLAN and Supernatural Instructions applied to NLP benchmark datasets
in 2022-the Nemotron-CC work extended it to raw corpora at scale.
_Rephrasing extends usable token count beyond what filtering alone allows; task conversion pre-loads
instruction-following structure before post-training begins._
The token yield argument for rephrasing is concrete. DCLM-baseline filtered 240 trillion raw tokens down
to 3.8 trillion-a 1.4% retention rate-using an aggressive fastText classifier. Nemotron-CC, operating on the same
Common Crawl pool with a combination of quality bucketing, rephrasing, and task conversion, produced 6.3
trillion tokens: roughly 1.7the DCLM yield, and Nemotron-CC achieved better average benchmark scores
than DCLM-baseline on downstream evaluations. The compute spent rephrasing borderline documents was
cheaper than the alternative of crawling additional raw data or accepting the smaller token budget.


```
22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data
```
Task conversion addresses a different problem. Standard pre-training data is overwhelmingly document-
shaped: a model trained on it learns to continue documents, not to answer questions posed by a user. The gap
between “document continuation” and “respond to an instruction” is what post-training is designed to close, but
the gap is easier to close if some instruction-following structure was already present in mid-training. Models that
see task-formatted data during mid-training require fewer post-training examples to reach the same instruction-
following quality-the gradient signal is not starting from zero.
The risk of rephrasing is error propagation: if the rewrite model makes a factual error or hallucinates, that
error enters the training corpus as if it were original text. This is why rephrasing should target only documents
that a quality classifier scores in the lower-quality band-documents already unreliable enough that the rephrase
is no worse than the original. Rephrasing high-quality sources like Wikipedia introduces risk with no gain.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose your quality classifier partitions 10 trillion filtered tokens into three tiers based on educational
value score:
