**Tier A (top 20%, score** > **0.8):** 2T tokens. Source: Wikipedia, arXiv, high-quality STEM sites. Action:
keep as-is; additionally run a 70B Nemotron-class model to generate 3 task variants per document (QA,
summarization, extraction). Estimated additional yield: 2 T 3  0. 6 k avg response tokens/ 3 k avg doc tokens
1. 2 T task tokens.
**Tier B (middle 50%, score 0.4-0.8):** 5T tokens. Source: general web pages with moderate coherence.
Action: rephrase using a distilled 7B rewrite model. Expected quality lift: score distribution shifts to
0.6-0.85. Yield after deduplication: approximately 4.5T tokens.
**Tier C (bottom 30%, score** < **0.4):** 3T tokens. Action: discard. Rephrasing severely incoherent text is
not cost-effective-the rewrite model cannot reliably recover factual content from near-nonsense.
Total yield: 2 T (Tier A original)+1. 2 T (task pairs)+4. 5 T (Tier B rephrased)= 7. 7 T usable training
tokens, compared to 2 T if you kept only Tier A or 3. 8 T if you applied aggressive filtering without rephrasing.
Compute cost estimate for rephrasing 5T tokens: at 500 output tokens per second on a single H100 in bf16,
and assuming a 3:1 input-to-output length ratio for rephrasing (each 4k document produces a 4k rewrite), you
need roughly:

5  1012 tokens
500 tokens/sec 256 GPUs
 39 , 000 GPU-hours
That is a small fraction of the pre-training GPU budget for a 7B model over 6T tokens, which runs into the
millions of GPU-hours. The yield increase justifies the rephrasing compute.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Rephrase only the middle quality tier. Tier A documents are already usable; rewriting them adds noise.
Tier C documents are too incoherent for reliable rephrasing-the rewrite model will hallucinate to fill gaps.
The 20th-70th percentile by quality score is the productive target range.
Diversify task conversion templates. If you only generate QA pairs, the model memorizes QA format
rather than developing general instruction-following. Aim for at least five distinct task types per source
document: question answering, summarization, key-point extraction, classification, and open-ended gen-
eration. Ask the conversion model to vary its phrasing rather than slot-filling a fixed template-template
```

```
22.2 Long-Context and Domain Data
```
```
memorization is a real failure mode.
Use a rewrite model significantly stronger than the target. A 7B rewrite model fine-tuned on 70B
outputs sets a quality ceiling below the 70B model’s level. A 3B rewrite model introduces systematic
errors-collapsed clauses, dropped numerical precision, consistent tense mistakes-that are subtle enough
to survive perplexity filtering but harmful at scale. The rewrite model should be at least 4the parameter
count of the target when possible.
Mix rephrased and original tokens; do not replace. Training exclusively on rephrased documents
causes distributional drift from the original web distribution. Keep at least a 1:1 mix of rephrased and
original text in the final data blend. The original anchors the distribution; the rephrase improves local
quality.
Evaluate on held-out tasks not in the conversion templates. If your only evaluation is on tasks struc-
turally similar to the generated pairs, you are measuring format memorization, not capability. Reserve a
held-out set of instruction tasks whose format was never in the training templates; improvement on those
is evidence of real generalization.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Your quality filter throws away 98% of your Common Crawl tokens. How do you get more usable
data without crawling more of the web?” Strong answers cover both rephrasing and task conversion,
with a concrete split of which documents to rephrase versus discard. Quantify the expected yield increase
and note the compute cost. Weak answers mention “synthetic data” without distinguishing rephrasing
(salvage) from task conversion (augmentation) or discussing when each applies.
“Is it circular to use a language model to generate training data for a language model?” The strong
answer: not if the rewrite model is significantly stronger than the model being trained. The quality ceiling
is the rewrite model’s quality-you are not training a model on its own outputs, you are distilling from a
stronger model. Self-distillation without an external stronger teacher does collapse over repeated itera-
tions; that is why production rephrasing pipelines use a dedicated, larger rewrite model rather than the
checkpoint being trained.
Senior follow-up: “How do you verify that rephrased tokens actually improved model quality and
did not just inflate your token count?” The senior answer: run a controlled ablation on identical token
budgets (not identical document counts). Train one model onNrephrased tokens mixed withNoriginal
tokens; train another on 2 Noriginal tokens from the next quality tier. Evaluate both on held-out bench-
marks that were not part of the rephrasing or task-conversion process. If the rephrased model wins on
held-out tasks, the quality improvement is real. If it only wins on tasks that look like the task-conversion
templates, it is overfitting to format and the templates need diversification.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Rephrasing uses a stronger LM to rewrite borderline-quality documents into cleaner prose, extending
usable token count beyond what filtering alone can achieve-Nemotron-CC nearly doubled token yield
relative to DCLM-baseline using this approach.
Task conversion generates instruction-formatted input-output pairs from high-quality documents, priming
instruction-following structure before post-training and reducing the post-training data requirement.
```

### 22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews

```
Rephrase only the quality middle band (roughly 20th-70th percentile); high-quality documents do not
benefit, and very low-quality documents cannot be reliably salvaged.
The rewrite model’s capability sets the ceiling: use a model substantially larger than the target to avoid
amplifying systematic errors into the training corpus.
Validate on held-out tasks whose format was never in the conversion templates; improvement there dis-
tinguishes real capability gain from format memorization.
```
### 22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews

**22.3.1 Length, Style, and Citation Traps**
An interviewer asks: “Walk me through how you would curate a high-quality instruction-tuning dataset.”
The candidate who answers “I would collect long, detailed, expert-written responses with citations” sounds
credible-and is describing a trap. Three systematic biases in post-training data collection-length inflation, style
mimicry, and citation hallucination-consistently degrade model quality while appearing as improvements during
collection. This topic appears at L5-L6 interviews whenever the discussion reaches SFT data curation, RLHF
reward modeling, or why instruction-tuned models hallucinate despite being trained on “correct” responses.
Instruction tuning works by showing a pre-trained model (instruction, response) pairs and fine-tuning it
to produce the response given the instruction. The model simultaneously learns two things: the _content_ of
the response and its _type signature_ -the surface structure, length, and formatting conventions that the training
distribution exhibits. These two learning signals are inseparable at the level of cross-entropy loss, which creates
three failure modes.
**Length bias.** Human evaluators prefer longer responses by roughly 60-70% in pairwise comparisons, even
when the longer response contains filler or additional hallucinations. AI judges trained on human preferences
inherit this bias. A model trained via RLHF on length-biased reward signals learns to pad rather than im-
prove accuracy. Studies have found that instruction-tuned models with dramatically different average response
lengths achieve nearly identical MMLU scores-benchmark performance is largely decoupled from length-while
chat evaluation scores such as AlpacaEval win rates track length closely. Optimizing win rate without length
normalization is optimizing for verbosity.
**Style mimicry.** SFT reliably teaches output style. If 60% of training responses use bullet-pointed lists, the
fine-tuned model uses bullet points even when prose is more appropriate. If training data ends responses with
emojis, the model learns to generate emojis at the end as a positional pattern, regardless of semantic relevance.
This is not pathological; it is exactly what next-token prediction does. The problem is that style conventions in
annotation data reflect annotator culture and time constraints, not what is actually useful to end users.
**Citation traps.** This is the subtlest failure mode. Consider a training example with the instruction “Write
an introduction to monopsony in economics” and a response ending with a formatted citation such asBivens
& Mishel (2015). Two things happen during fine-tuning simultaneously. If the model already encodes that
citation from pre-training, it learns to surface it appropriately-a genuine improvement. If it does not, it learns
something worse: whenever it encounters a complex academic prompt, it should append a plausible-looking
citation. The model has been trained to hallucinate in a structured way, and the training loss cannot distinguish
between these two outcomes.
_SFT teaches the type signature of outputs unconditionally; the model cannot distinguish between “I know
this fact and should cite it” and “I do not know this fact but the training distribution expects a citation here.”_


```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
The citation trap comes down to a mismatch between what the cross-entropy loss measures and what we
want. The loss penalizes the model equally for failing to produce a correct citation it already knows and for
failing to hallucinate a citation it does not know. From the loss’s perspective, producing any plausible citation
token is strictly better than producing nothing. A model minimizing loss on citation-heavy training data therefore
learns hallucination as a default structural behavior.
The principled fix is on-policy reinforcement learning, because RL only reinforces behaviors that were
already latent in the model. A generation that correctly cites a known fact gets rewarded; one that invents a
citation does not, regardless of stylistic plausibility. This is one of the practical arguments for why PPO and
DPO sit downstream of SFT in production pipelines-they can correct for what SFT mis-teaches.
Length and style biases have a more direct remedy: measure preference scores as a function of response
length, deconfound the two, and normalize win rates at annotation time. Presenting annotators with length-
matched pairs eliminates the bias at the source. For AI judges, running ablations that hold content fixed while
varying length-and measuring how much the preference score shifts-gives you an empirical length-bias coeffi-
cient you can subtract.

**A Worked Example**

You are building an instruction-tuning dataset for a 7B model. You use a strong teacher model to generate
50,000 responses, resulting in an average response length of 480 tokens with frequent inline citations. You
fine-tune and evaluate: Chatbot Arena win rate against the base model is 62%. Encouraged, you run MMLU-
the fine-tuned model and base model are within 0.3 percentage points. You run TruthfulQA: the fine-tuned
model is 4.1 points _worse_. You manually check 200 responses: 18% contain at least one hallucinated citation
or unsupported specific statistic.
The diagnosis is length inflation from the teacher model combined with citation mimicry. The 7B student
learned the citation structure without having the underlying factual knowledge to support it.
The fix proceeds in three steps. First, filter training examples where response length exceeds 3 the median
for that prompt category-this removes the longest-tail padding without truncating genuinely complex responses.
Second, strip inline citations from training responses, replacing specific references with non-specific language
such as “research in this area suggests.” Third, add 5,000 examples where the correct response is a calibrated
hedge-“I don’t have reliable information on that specific claim”-for prompts where the model’s pre-training
coverage is likely sparse. After retraining: TruthfulQA recovers by 3.2 points; Chatbot Arena win rate drops
from 62% to 58%. That is a real trade-off, and the correct one for any deployment that cares about factual
reliability.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Separate style from substance in your evaluation stack. Run benchmark-based evals (MMLU, Truth-
fulQA, GSM8K) in parallel with preference evals (Chatbot Arena, AlpacaEval). If they diverge, trust
benchmarks for capability claims. Use preference evals only for UX signal and style tuning.
Control length at annotation time, not post-hoc. If collecting human-written SFT data, instruct annota-
tors to target a specific length range-for example, 150-300 words for factual Q&A, 400-600 for multi-step
reasoning. Post-hoc truncation introduces artifacts; a front-loaded constraint produces more natural re-
sponses.
```

```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
```
Strip or verify citations before including them in SFT data. Either remove all inline citations from
training responses, or run a verification step that confirms the model can reproduce the cited fact from a
zero-shot prompt before including that example. Unverified citations produce a hallucination-optimized
model by construction.
Distillation from a much stronger teacher compounds the citation trap. If distilling GPT-4-quality
responses into a 7B model, the capability gap means many responses will teach behaviors the student
cannot support from its own knowledge. Prefer prompts where the student already gets the answer roughly
right, and use the teacher to improve surface quality rather than inject fundamentally new factual claims.
500 carefully chosen safety examples can dominate model behavior. Because SFT runs on relatively
few tokens, safety data has outsized influence. Use this leverage deliberately-and audit the safety data for
the same citation and length biases, because a safety response that halluccinates specifics is worse than a
vague refusal.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What makes a good instruction-tuning dataset?” A strong answer names three axes: diversity of
task types, correctness of responses relative to the model’s existing knowledge (not just surface quality),
and calibration-explicit hedges on low-confidence claims rather than confident fabrication. Weak answers
focus on response length or vague notions of “high quality.”
“Why do instruction-tuned models hallucinate more than base models on certain tasks?” The an-
swer is the citation trap: SFT teaches type signatures unconditionally. If training data contains responses
with citations, the model learns to produce citations as a stylistic pattern regardless of whether it has the
underlying knowledge. The fix requires either on-policy training that rewards only verifiable correctness,
or data hygiene that removes unverifiable factual statements before SFT.
Senior follow-up: “How would you design a pairwise annotation process that avoids length bias?” A
strong answer includes: (1) present annotators with length-matched response pairs when possible; (2) add
an explicit annotation dimension for conciseness, separate from overall quality; (3) run calibration passes
where annotators compare known-correct short responses against plausible-but-longer hallucinated ones
to train out the length heuristic; (4) for AI judges, compute preference score as a function of∆length
across the evaluation set and apply a length-normalization correction before reporting win rates.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Human and AI evaluators prefer longer responses by 60-70% in pairwise comparisons even when length
adds no factual value; always deconfound length from quality in preference evaluation pipelines.
SFT teaches output type signatures unconditionally-the model cannot distinguish between surfacing a
known fact and hallucinating to match a structural template.
Including citations or specific statistics in SFT responses trains hallucination unless the model’s pre-
training already encodes that knowledge; strip or verify them before training.
Benchmark evals (MMLU, TruthfulQA) and chat preference evals (Chatbot Arena) routinely diverge; a
model that wins on preference evals can simultaneously regress on factual accuracy.
On-policy RL is the principled remedy for the citation trap; SFT-only pipelines require aggressive data
hygiene to avoid the same failure mode.
```

```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
**22.3.2 Mid-Training as the New Annealing Phase**
Interviewers at frontier labs increasingly ask a question that trips up candidates who know only the classical
InstructGPT pipeline: “What is mid-training, and how does it differ from both pre-training and post-training?”
The question probes whether you understand that modern base model checkpoints are not the same objects
described in GPT-3 era papers-they have been partially instruction-tuned through a process invisible in the
checkpoint name. This topic appears at L6-L7 system design interviews and in any deep-dive on training pipeline
architecture, data mix composition, or evaluation methodology for open-weight models.
The classical three-stage pipeline-pre-train, then SFT, then RLHF-assumed a clean boundary between the
stage that installs knowledge (pre-training) and the stages that shape behavior (post-training). Mid-training dis-
solves that boundary. The key insight is that the learning rate schedule already contains a natural injection
point: the decay phase of WSD (Warm-up, Stable, Decay) scheduling is the period when training loss is con-
verging and small gradient steps are compressing the model into a stable attractor. Injecting high-quality and
instruction-adjacent data _during_ this decay phase produces a checkpoint that is simultaneously well-calibrated
on the pre-training objective and partially instruction-tuned.
Concretely, a WSD mid-training setup looks like this:

Stage 1 (Stable):
data: ~95% web/code/books pre-training mix
lr: cosine stable plateau
tokens: ~90-95% of total budget

Stage 2 (Decay / Annealing):
data: ~70% pre-training + ~30% high-quality/SFT mix
lr: cosine decay, stable plateau -> near 0
tokens: ~5-10% of total budget

The high-quality SFT mix in Stage 2 typically includes upsampled Wikipedia, curated domain data (math,
code, scientific papers), and a fraction of actual instruction-following pairs. The SFT-adjacent data should
remain rare enough during Stage 2 that it does not displace the pre-training distribution entirely-the goal is
shaping, not overwriting.
_Mid-training is the decay phase used as a curriculum: the model consolidates broad world knowledge from
pre-training while simultaneously acquiring the behavioral patterns required for instruction following._
When instruction tuning is applied as a completely separate post-training step, it typically runs at a mod-
erately high learning rate on a very different data distribution. This creates catastrophic forgetting pressure: the
model’s pre-trained knowledge degrades as the optimizer moves aggressively toward the instruction-following
objective. Standard remedies-tiny learning rates, LoRA adapters, KL regularization toward the pre-trained
weights-reduce forgetting at the cost of slower convergence or reduced final quality.
Injecting instruction data during decay sidesteps this trade-off because the learning rate is already small
and monotonically decreasing. The model cannot move far from its pre-trained attractor; it is forced to find a
minimal adjustment that accommodates the instruction signal. This is the same intuition behind low-learning-
rate probing in representation learning: fine-tuning near the end of training, when the model’s representations
are already rich, extracts far more instruction-following capability per token seen than a separately initialized
SFT run.


```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
The secondary advantage is data efficiency. Because the model encounters instruction data when its pre-
trained representations are already mature, a much smaller absolute token count is needed to unlock instruction-
following behavior. Published results from groups using this approach report that 5-15% instruction-adjacent
data in the decay phase produces instruction-following quality comparable to separate SFT runs that used 5-10
more instruction tokens.
The downside is interpretability: the resulting checkpoint is neither a clean base model nor a clean instruct
model. When a lab releases a “base model” checkpoint trained with decay-phase injection, few-shot evaluation
protocols that assume a clean base-model distribution give misleading scores. Benchmark comparisons across
generation boundaries require verifying the training recipe, not just the checkpoint label.

**A Worked Example**

The MiniCPM training pipeline is one of the few publicly documented examples of explicit decay-phase
data mixing.
Stage 1 uses approximately 2.4 trillion tokens from a mix of processed Common Crawl, code repositories,
The Pile, and Dolma. The learning rate holds at the stable plateau from roughly step 5k to step 200k.
Stage 2 uses approximately 130 billion additional tokens with the following approximate composition:
Wikipedia (carried over from Stage 1, upsampled 4 )
Code SFT data (verified solutions to programming problems)
UltraChat (multi-turn conversational data)
Stack Exchange QA (question-answer pairs with votes)
Evol-Instruct and OSS-Instruct (instruction-complexity evolved examples)
Instruction-adjacent sources constitute roughly 30-35% of Stage 2 tokens. The learning rate decays from
the stable plateau to near zero across Stage 2. Total training cost is dominated by Stage 1; Stage 2 adds roughly
5-6% to the token budget but contributes disproportionately to downstream instruction-following benchmark
scores.
After Stage 2, the checkpoint is released as the “base model.” Running standard few-shot evaluation on
this checkpoint produces scores that cannot be compared directly to GPT-3-era base models, which had zero
instruction-adjacent exposure. The base model here already behaves closer to a lightly instruction-tuned model;
a subsequent short SFT pass is then used for safety tuning and formatting preferences rather than foundational
instruction following.
For reference: Llama 3 was trained on 15 trillion tokens; Qwen3 on approximately 36 trillion. At these
scales, a 5-10% decay phase represents 750 billion to 3.6 trillion tokens of high-quality injection-more tokens
than many earlier complete training runs.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start mixing instruction data when the learning rate begins its final decay, not earlier. Mixing
instruction data during the stable phase displaces web-scale knowledge unnecessarily because the model
is still absorbing high-entropy pre-training signal. The decay phase is when the model is consolidating,
not exploring; that is the right moment to steer.
Target 10-30% instruction-adjacent data in the decay mix. Below 10%, the instruction signal is too
diluted to produce measurable behavioral change. Above 40%, knowledge-intensive benchmarks start
```

```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
```
degrading, indicating the pre-training distribution is being displaced. The sweet spot is empirically con-
sistent across published ablations.
The “base model” label is unreliable in modern releases. If your work requires a clean base model-
perplexity comparisons, probing studies, scaling law extrapolations-verify the training recipe of the check-
point you are using. Llama 3, Qwen2, and OLMo2 base checkpoints all contain instruction data in their
training lineage.
Long-context extension belongs in mid-training. Transformers scale quadratically with sequence length;
spending Stage 1 compute on 32k-128k contexts before the model has strong representations at shorter
contexts is wasteful. Introducing long-context data during the decay phase, after Stage 1 has built rich
short-context representations, is the dominant approach at frontier scale.
A short post-decay SFT pass is still useful, but it is lighter. Decay-phase mixing handles foundational
instruction-following behavior; a subsequent SFT pass at very low learning rate handles safety tuning,
response formatting, and capability targeting that require precise distribution control. The two stages
complement rather than duplicate each other.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What is the difference between a base model and an instruct model today?” A strong answer ac-
knowledges that the distinction has blurred: modern base models undergo instruction-adjacent training
during the decay phase of pre-training, so they are not naive text predictors. A complete answer names
the WSD annealing phase as the mechanism and explains why this produces better instruction following
with less catastrophic forgetting than a separate SFT run.
“Why would you mix instruction data into pre-training instead of doing a separate SFT run?” The
answer is threefold: (1) catastrophic forgetting is reduced because the learning rate is already decaying; (2)
data efficiency improves since the model’s pre-trained representations are already rich when the instruction
signal arrives; (3) this approach scales using pre-training infrastructure, avoiding a separate training job
with its own hyperparameter surface.
Senior follow-up: “How would you structure the data mix for a 70B model’s annealing phase, and
what would you monitor to know if it is working?” A strong answer specifies: (1) roughly 20-30%
instruction-adjacent data, starting with high-quality domain data-math, code, curated web-and adding a
smaller fraction of chat SFT pairs; (2) monitor validation loss on both the pre-training held-out set and a
held-out instruction set simultaneously-both should decrease, not trade off; (3) run intermediate capability
evals every 5-10 billion decay tokens to catch benchmark regression on knowledge-intensive tasks early;
(4) apply a KL penalty or reference-model constraint to bound distribution drift from the stable-phase
checkpoint, especially if the decay phase is long.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Mid-training is the injection of high-quality and instruction-adjacent data during the learning rate decay
phase of pre-training, exploiting the model’s consolidation dynamics to achieve instruction following with
minimal catastrophic forgetting.
The WSD schedule creates a natural two-stage curriculum: broad web-scale learning during the stable
phase, behavioral shaping during the decay phase.
Most modern “base models”-Llama 3, Qwen2, OLMo2-contain instruction data in their training lineage;
```

```
22.3 Data Quality Heuristics That Matter in Interviews
```
the base/instruct distinction now describes the post-decay SFT stage, not a clean separation of knowledge
from behavior.
Long-context extension, domain specialization (math, code), and early safety tuning all belong in mid-
training rather than as separate post-training jobs, for the same data-efficiency and forgetting-reduction
reasons.
Empirically, 10-30% instruction-adjacent data during the decay phase matches or exceeds the quality of
5-10more instruction data applied in a separate high-learning-rate SFT run.


## Part IX

# Evaluation


## Chapter 23 Designing an Evaluation

### 23.1 Goals of Evaluation.

**23.1.1 Evaluating Models vs. Systems vs. Methods**
You are asked in an interview to design an evaluation for a new LLM-powered coding assistant. Do you
benchmark the underlying model weights, the full product stack, or the novel training recipe your team just
shipped? These are not the same question, and confusing them is one of the most common evaluation mistakes
I see from engineers at all levels. Getting the object of evaluation wrong means the number you report answers
a different question than the one you are trying to answer-and that mismatch quietly propagates into bad product
decisions and misleading research claims.
There are three distinct objects you can evaluate, and each requires a different setup.
A _model evaluation_ fixes the neural network weights and a minimal, standardized inference call: no external
tools, no retrieval pipeline, no prompt engineering beyond what every competitor also gets. You are asking: what
can these weights do on their own? The input is a prompt; the output is a completion; the metric is computed
directly on that completion. This is what leaderboards like MMLU, GPQA, and HumanEval measure.
A _system evaluation_ treats the entire production stack as the unit under test-model weights, prompt tem-
plates, RAG pipeline, tool calls, re-rankers, safety filters, and any agent scaffolding that drives multi-step loops.
The user does not care which specific checkpoint sits at the center; they care whether the product solves their
problem. System evaluations answer the question a buyer or a product manager is actually asking.
A _method evaluation_ is what a research paper should be doing. Here the claim is that some algorithmic
change-a new attention variant, a different data mixture, a revised RLHF loss-causes an improvement. The
model trained with the new method is just a vehicle for demonstrating that claim. A valid method evaluation
requires an ablation that isolates the variable: same data, same compute budget, same architecture except for
the proposed change. Without that control, you are evaluating a system or a model, not a method.
_Every evaluation you design should start with one sentence that names which of these three objects you are
measuring-because that sentence determines everything else._
The distinction matters because the three objects differ in what they hold constant. Model evals hold
constant the inference protocol, so the score is portable: you can compare your checkpoint against anyone else’s
checkpoint on the same benchmark. System evals hold constant the task and the user population, so the score
is predictive of production outcomes. Method evals hold constant the training regime except for the proposed
change, so the score is attributable to the hypothesis you are testing.
Mixing these up has real consequences. If you compare System A-a retrieval-augmented pipeline built on
a mid-tier model-against a bare-model eval of System B’s underlying weights, you are largely measuring the
quality of System A’s scaffolding. I have seen this comparison made in competitive benchmarking slides, and
it always favors whoever built the better wrapper. Conversely, a method paper that reports only a system score
(“our model plus chain-of-thought plus self-consistency reaches X%”) cannot be credited with the improvement
because the chain-of-thought and self-consistency would lift any baseline similarly.
The naive alternative-just report the highest number the model achieves under any configuration-is tempting
because it looks good in a paper or press release. The problem is that it makes the number uninterpretable to
anyone trying to replicate or compare.


```
23.1 Goals of Evaluation
```
**A Worked Example**

Consider evaluating a 70B model on SWEBench, a benchmark where an agent is given a GitHub issue and
a codebase and must produce a patch that makes the unit tests pass.
**Configuration 1: model eval.** You call the model once per issue with a zero-shot prompt containing the
issue description and the relevant file contents. No tool calls, no multi-step loop, no linting pass. A strong 70B
model achieves roughly 10-15% resolve rate in this configuration.
**Configuration 2: system eval.** You wrap the same checkpoint in a scaffolded agent: the agent reads files,
runs bash commands, iterates on failing tests, and submits only when lint passes. The same 70B model now
achieves 35-45% resolve rate-a two-to-three-times lift from scaffolding alone.
**Configuration 3: method eval.** Your research question is whether adding a “verify-before-submit” step
(the agent runs the relevant unit tests before submitting the patch) improves resolve rate. You train two check-
points with identical data and compute, differing only in whether verification rewards were included during
RLHF. You evaluate both under the _same_ scaffolded system from Configuration 2, with the verification step dis-
abled at inference time for both models. If the checkpoint trained with verification rewards achieves 40% versus
36% for the baseline under identical scaffolding, you can attribute the 4-point delta to the training method.
Note what breaks if you skip the discipline: if you enable the verification step for the new model but not the
baseline, the 4-point delta is confounded-you have no idea whether the improvement comes from the training
change or the inference-time verification.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Choose model eval when reporting public benchmarks or comparing against published checkpoints.
Standardized prompting (zero-shot or fixed few-shot, no tools) keeps the playing field level. If your eval
protocol differs from the benchmark’s canonical setup, report both numbers and explain the delta.
Choose system eval when making a deployment or procurement decision. A 5-point gain on MMLU
from a new checkpoint means nothing if your production system uses RAG and the bottleneck is retrieval
recall, not model knowledge. Evaluate the full pipeline on a traffic sample from your actual users.
Choose method eval when writing a research paper or justifying a training investment. Fix compute,
data, and architecture except for the single variable under study. Reporting system improvements without
ablations is a red flag reviewers will catch.
Watch for scaffolding budget asymmetry. In agent benchmarks, “number of model calls allowed” and
“maximum context length” are parameters that can easily be tuned per model. If System A gets 50 tool-
call turns and System B gets 20, you are measuring budget allocation, not capability. Always match
scaffolding budgets when comparing systems.
Perplexity is closer to a pure model eval than task accuracy. Perplexity assigns credit at every token,
does not depend on agent scaffolding, and is difficult to game through prompt engineering. For tracking
model quality during pre-training, it is the right signal. For production decisions, it is not sufficient on its
own-a model with lower perplexity on web text can still underperform on your specific downstream task.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you evaluate your company’s new code generation assistant?” Strong answer: distin-
guish the model eval (does the checkpoint improve on HumanEval or SWEBench compared to the previous
```

```
23.1 Goals of Evaluation
```
```
checkpoint?) from the system eval (does the full product increase the fraction of user sessions where the
user accepts the suggestion?). Explain that you need both: the model eval guides training; the system eval
guides the deployment decision.
“A paper claims their new attention variant improves MMLU by 3 points. How would you assess
whether that claim is valid?” Strong answer: check whether compute and data are matched, whether
the baseline uses the same training recipe except for the attention change, and whether the improvement
holds across multiple seeds. A 3-point gain that disappears under controlled ablation is a system variation
(e.g., the new attention allowed a larger batch size), not a method result.
Senior follow-up: “Your system eval shows a 5% win rate gain over the previous release. Your VP
wants to know whether to credit the new model checkpoint or the prompt engineering rewrite your
team shipped at the same time. How do you disentangle them?” Senior answer: run a 2  2 factorial-
old model with old prompt vs. old model with new prompt vs. new model with old prompt vs. new model
with new prompt-on a held-out traffic slice. The interaction term tells you whether the prompt and model
improvements are additive or whether one dominates. If you cannot run the factorial (the old model is
decommissioned), you have a confounded result and should say so explicitly rather than attributing the
gain to the most recently shipped change.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
A model eval measures weights under a standardized inference call; a system eval measures the full pro-
duction stack; a method eval isolates a single training variable under controlled ablation. Name which
one you are running before you design anything else.
Comparing a scaffolded system against a bare-model baseline is not a model comparison-it is a scaffolding
comparison. Match inference protocols when comparing models.
Agent benchmarks like SWEBench can produce a two-to-three-times spread in resolve rate between a bare-
model call and a well-engineered scaffolded loop on the same checkpoint. That gap is system performance,
not model performance.
Method claims require controlled ablations: same compute, same data, same architecture except for the
proposed change. Reporting only the fully optimized system score is not sufficient to support a method
claim.
When you cannot disentangle variables (e.g., multiple changes shipped simultaneously), report the con-
founding explicitly. A confounded result is not useless-it tells you the system improved-but it does not let
you allocate credit to a cause.
```
**23.1.2 Ask-Style vs. Quiz-Style Prompts**
An interviewer hands you a model that scores 87% on HumanEval. You are asked to decide whether to roll
it out as the primary coding assistant for your engineering org. The number feels solid-but the question you need
answered is not “can this model solve LeetCode problems someone has already verified?” The question is “will
engineers accept its suggestions when they are stuck on real, ambiguous work at 2 am?” Those are fundamentally
different prompts, and the gap between them is where most production deployments quietly underperform their
benchmark numbers. This distinction-ask-style versus quiz-style-is one of the most practically important ideas
in LLM evaluation, and it comes up whenever an interviewer wants to probe whether you understand why
benchmark scores do not automatically transfer to product outcomes.


```
23.1 Goals of Evaluation
```
Every evaluation prompt can be classified by whether the person writing it already knows the correct answer.
A _quiz-style prompt_ is one where the evaluator holds the ground truth before the model sees the question.
Standardized benchmarks-MMLU, GPQA, HumanEval, GSM8k-are entirely quiz-style. A human expert (or
an automated pipeline) constructed the question, verified the answer, and packaged both into a data set. The
model’s job is to reproduce the known answer. The evaluator’s job is to check whether it did.
An _ask-style prompt_ originates from a user who genuinely does not know the answer and is submitting the
prompt because they need help. The user asking Claude to draft a differential diagnosis for a patient they are
currently treating, or to explain why their Kubernetes pod keeps OOMing, has no verified ground truth in hand.
They are trying to extract value from the model, not test it.
The distinction is not just philosophical. It determines what the score actually predicts. Quiz-style scores
predict performance on other quiz-style tasks drawn from the same distribution. Ask-style scores-which require
either human judges, LLM-as-judge pipelines, or downstream behavioral proxies like acceptance rate-predict
whether real users get value from the system. The two correlate weakly at best once you move outside the
model’s training distribution.
_A benchmark score tells you how well a model performs on problems where someone already knows the
answer; what matters in production is how well it performs on problems where nobody does._
Quiz-style benchmarks dominate the evaluation literature for one reason: they are cheap to construct and
cheap to score. You do not need human judges. You do not need live users. You need a question, an answer key,
and a string-matching or execution harness. That operational simplicity is why MMLU has 14,000 questions
and GPQA has 448, and why you can reproduce either in a single script.
The cost is validity. Quiz-style prompts are clean, precisely specified, and have unambiguous single correct
answers. Real user queries are underspecified-“fix my code” with no error message, “summarize this” with no
stated audience. A model trained on internet text and evaluated on quiz-style prompts derived from the same
internet can score well while failing badly on genuine user need.
Ask-style evaluation is harder operationally but more predictive. Analyses of real conversation traffic find
coding is the dominant use case, followed by writing assistance and analysis. None of those sessions look like
multiple-choice questions. The prompts are long, messy, contextual, and often span multiple turns. A benchmark
built from that traffic-with humans or calibrated LLM judges scoring helpfulness rather than correctness-tracks
production quality far better than any standardized exam.
The tension is that realistic ask-style data is often private. Clinical notes, customer service transcripts, and
internal code reviews are the highest-value ask-style prompts, and they cannot be published. This is why initia-
tives like MedHELM exist: 29 clinicians identified 121 tasks reflecting their actual practice, and the resulting
benchmark uses realistic prompts (patient note summarization, treatment plan drafting) that no multiple-choice
exam covers. The privacy-versus-realism trade-off is real, and the right answer is almost always to invest in the
ask-style eval even if it cannot be open-sourced.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you are evaluating a code completion model for internal deployment. You run two evaluations in
parallel.
**Quiz-style (HumanEval).** 164 Python function stubs with docstrings and unit tests. The model generates
a completion; you execute the tests; you report pass@1. Your new checkpoint scores 87%, up from 80% on the
previous release. The delta of 7 points looks meaningful.


```
23.1 Goals of Evaluation
```
**Ask-style (sampled production sessions).** You sample 2,000 real completions accepted or rejected by
engineers over the past two weeks. A human rater panel (or a calibrated LLM judge) scores each completion on
a 1-5 helpfulness scale, blind to which model generated it. You also instrument the IDE plugin to record whether
the engineer accepted the suggestion, modified it substantially, or discarded it. Results: mean helpfulness score
3.4 vs. 3.1 for the prior release (+0.3 points), and acceptance rate 54% vs. 51% (+3 points). Both improvements
are real but smaller in magnitude than the HumanEval delta suggests.
The gap exists because HumanEval problems have clean docstrings and self-contained scope. Real tickets
say things like “add the same caching logic we use inUserServicebut forOrderService”-which requires
reading a second file, understanding an undocumented convention, and matching a style the model has never
seen. Ground truth requires a self-contained problem; real work is rarely that. The 7-point HumanEval gain
measures something narrower than “will engineers be more productive?” The accept-rate gain of 3 points an-
swers the question that actually matters.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use quiz-style benchmarks to track training progress, not to make deployment decisions. They are
reproducible, fast, and cheap. They are the right tool for deciding whether a checkpoint is heading in the
right direction during development. They are the wrong tool for deciding whether to ship it.
Build at least one ask-style eval before launch. The minimum viable version is a few hundred real
prompts from your target user population, scored by human raters or an LLM judge calibrated against
human raters on a held-out slice. If you cannot get real prompts pre-launch, use synthetic ones drawn
from a model of your users’ tasks-but acknowledge the limitation.
Instrument for behavioral proxies when human rating is too slow. Acceptance rate, edit distance after
acceptance, session abandonment rate, and thumbs-up/thumbs-down feedback are all ask-style signals that
accumulate automatically once you are in production. Wire these up before launch so you have a baseline
to compare against when the next checkpoint ships.
Never report only quiz-style scores for a safety-sensitive deployment. A model that scores 86% on
USMLE Step 2 CK may still hallucinate drug dosages at a rate that is clinically unacceptable. Safety
evals must be ask-style, grounded in the actual failure modes that harm real users, not the failure modes
that fit neatly into a multiple-choice format.
Watch for quiz contamination in user feedback. Live traffic from a deployed model is not automatically
ask-style. A significant fraction of real sessions are engineers or researchers actively probing the model’s
limits-quiz-style behavior from real users. If your user population skews toward power users or developers,
your “live traffic” evaluation may overestimate performance on genuine end-user need. Segment by user
cohort before drawing conclusions.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Your model hits 90% on MMLU. How do you decide whether to deploy it to customers?” Strong
answer: MMLU is a quiz-style benchmark and tells you the model can retrieve factual knowledge under a
standardized prompt format. Before deployment you need an ask-style eval on a representative sample of
your actual customer tasks-measuring helpfulness, groundedness, and refusal behavior-because MMLU
accuracy does not predict those. Name a specific eval you would run (e.g., a human-judged sample of 100
realistic customer sessions) and what pass threshold you would require.
```

### 23.2 Metrics and Protocols.

```
“We’re seeing a gap between our benchmark scores and user satisfaction in production. What’s
going on?” Strong answer: the gap almost always traces to the quiz/ask mismatch. Benchmarks have
clean ground truth; production prompts are underspecified and context-dependent. Diagnose by sampling
failing production sessions and checking whether they share structural properties-long context, cross-file
references, ambiguous intent-that are absent from the benchmark. Then build a targeted ask-style eval
that captures those properties.
Senior follow-up: “How would you build an ask-style eval for a general-purpose assistant where
there is no single correct answer?” Senior answer: layer three signals. Use LLM-as-judge at scale
for triage (fast, cheap, biased toward length and verbosity). Audit a random 5% slice with human raters
and report judge calibration-if the LLM judge agrees with humans 80% of the time you know how far to
trust the automated scores. Track behavioral proxies (acceptance rate, task completion, return rate) as a
continuous production signal. A score reported without calibration metadata is not an evaluation; it is an
anecdote.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Quiz-style prompts have a known answer before the model sees the question; ask-style prompts originate
from users who genuinely need help. The distinction determines what the resulting score predicts about
production behavior.
Quiz-style benchmarks are cheap and reproducible-use them to guide training. Ask-style evals are expen-
sive but valid-use them to make deployment decisions.
The quiz/ask gap is largest when real user traffic is underspecified, context-dependent, or drawn from a
domain (clinical, legal, internal codebases) that is not well represented in public benchmarks.
Safety-critical deployments require ask-style evals grounded in realistic failure modes; a strong USMLE
or MMLU score does not substitute for them.
A production ask-style eval needs a judging layer with measured reliability: report inter-rater agreement
or LLM judge calibration alongside the helpfulness score, or the number is not trustworthy.
```
### 23.2 Metrics and Protocols

**23.2.1 Perplexity as a Universal Signal**
Every scaling law curve you have ever seen was fit against perplexity, not task accuracy. That is not an
accident. When a senior engineer asks during an interview how you would track training health across a multi-
week pre-training run, or how you would compare two architectural variants before committing to training one
at full scale, perplexity is almost always the right first answer. Understanding both what perplexity measures
and where it breaks down separates engineers who can read a training dashboard from engineers who can design
the evaluation protocol behind it.
A language model defines a probability distributionpover sequences of tokens. Given a held-out sequence
x 1 , x 2 ,... , xN, the model assigns a joint log-probability

#### PN

i=1logp(xijx<i). Perplexity is the exponential of
the average per-token negative log-likelihood:

23.2 Metrics and Protocols
```
whereDis a held-out data set andNis the total token count. A lower perplexity means the model assigns
higher probability to the observed text-it is less surprised. Perplexity of 1 is a perfect oracle; perplexity equal to
the vocabulary sizejVjis a uniform random guesser.
Mechanically, perplexity during pre-training is a monotone transformation of the training objective. The
gap between training loss and validation perplexity is the canonical sign of overfitting or distribution shift.
Perplexity on a held-out slice of web text the model has never seen is the standard signal for tracking whether
the model is learning to model language in general.
The perplexity-maximalist argument, which I find largely compelling for pre-training diagnostics, goes
like this. If the true data-generating distribution istand your model isp, then minimizing the KL divergence
DKL(tkp)is equivalent to minimizing cross-entropy, which is equivalent to minimizing perplexity. In the limit
wherep=t, the model has matched human-level text generation and, in principle, can answer any question a hu-
man can answer. Perplexity, when computed against a broad and representative corpus, is measuring proximity
to that ideal.
_Perplexity is the only metric that assigns loss to every token uniformly, making it the most data-eﬀicient
signal for detecting whether a model is learning-and the right tool for fitting and extrapolating scaling laws._
Perplexity wins for pre-training diagnostics for three concrete reasons.
First, it is smooth. Task accuracy on a multiple-choice benchmark is a step function: you either produce
the right letter or you do not. Perplexity is a continuous function of the model’s log-probabilities, which means
you can detect a small improvement from a data mixture tweak or a learning-rate schedule change before that
improvement is large enough to move a downstream accuracy number. This smoothness is why every pub-
lished scaling law-Chinchilla, GPT-4’s training curves, Llama’s ablations-is expressed in terms of cross-entropy
loss rather than MMLU scores. In the mid-2010s, the most striking result in language modeling was a paper
from Google showing that a carefully scaled architecture could push Penn Treebank perplexity from roughly 51
down to 30. That 40% reduction signaled a sea change in what neural language models could do, long before
downstream task benchmarks existed to measure it.
Second, perplexity is architecture-agnostic. If you are comparing two models that differ only in attention
variant and you want to know which is learning more efficiently per FLOP, perplexity on the same validation
set is an apples-to-apples comparison. Task accuracy would require both models to be trained long enough to
generalize to the task format, which may not happen for small ablations early in a run.
Third, perplexity is hard to game through prompt engineering. Win rates and task accuracies can be inflated
by choosing the right few-shot examples, the right chain-of-thought template, or the right decoding strategy.
Perplexity does not depend on any of these; it requires direct access to the model’s logits over the held-out text,
and as long as train and test splits are separate, it is not a quantity you can easily overfit to.
The main weakness of perplexity is that it is not always predictive of downstream task performance on any
particular task in the short run. A model can achieve lower perplexity on web text by getting better at predicting
Reddit discussions and financial news, without improving on formal mathematical reasoning. Over large scale
differences, perplexity and task performance tend to correlate because stronger models are better at most things.
Within a narrow training regime or for a specific domain, the correlation can be weak.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a pre-training ablation: you want to know whether increasing the proportion of code data from
15% to 25% of your training mixture helps a 7B model (dmodel= 4096, 32 layers, 32 heads, bf16, trained on


```
23.2 Metrics and Protocols
```
300B tokens across 64 H100s).
You train two ablation models, each for 10B tokens, on the two mixtures. After 10B tokens, Model A (15%
code) has validation perplexity 8.4 on a held-out web text slice and 12.1 on a held-out code slice. Model B (25%
code) has 8.6 on web text and 11.3 on code.
From this you conclude: the code-heavy mixture slightly hurts general web text modeling (perplexity rises
by 0.2) but improves code modeling by 0.8 perplexity points. Had you used HumanEval pass@1 instead, you
would need to run much longer before either model generates enough correct completions for a statistically
stable comparison. Perplexity gives you the direction after 10B tokens; a task-accuracy signal would require
50-100B tokens before variance is low enough to trust.
You also watch per-token loss curves during training. If validation perplexity flattens while training loss
keeps falling, you have a data contamination or overfitting signal. If perplexity spikes sharply on a particular
batch, you have a data quality issue or a bad learning-rate spike. Neither of these would show up as a task-
accuracy alarm until much later.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use perplexity for all training-time decisions and ablations. Any decision made before the model com-
pletes pre-training-data mixture, learning rate schedule, architecture tweak-should be based on perplexity,
not downstream task accuracy. Task accuracy is too noisy at small scale and too expensive to evaluate
continuously during a run.
Match tokenizers when comparing perplexities across models. Perplexity is a function of the token
sequence, not raw text. A model with a larger vocabulary will have lower perplexity on the same text
because it segments tokens more coarsely. If tokenizers differ, normalize to bits-per-byte or bits-per-
character before drawing any conclusions.
Require logit access before trusting a reported perplexity. If you are running a leaderboard that accepts
model submissions, perplexity is easy to misreport. A model that assigns 0.8 to every next-token position-
a non-distribution-will appear to have low perplexity but is meaningless. Verify that reported logits sum
to 1 over the full vocabulary, or compute perplexity yourself from open-weight checkpoints.
Use domain-stratified perplexity, not a single aggregate. One number averages over all text types.
Split your validation set into slices-web text, code, math, multilingual-and track perplexity per slice. This
is what reveals whether a data mixture change helped one domain at the cost of another, which a single
aggregate will hide.
Perplexity does not replace task evaluation at deployment time. Once you are making a deployment
decision-should we ship this checkpoint?- perplexity is necessary but not sufficient. Two models with
identical web text perplexity can differ by 10 points on HumanEval if one was trained with more code.
Use perplexity to filter candidates during training; use task accuracy to select among finalists.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you track training health during a long pre-training run?” Strong answer: monitor
validation perplexity on a domain-stratified held-out set, tracking both aggregate and per-domain curves.
Set up automated alerts for perplexity spikes (indicating data or learning-rate issues) and for validation-
training divergence (indicating overfitting or contamination). Task accuracy is too slow to provide the
real-time feedback you need during training.
```

```
23.2 Metrics and Protocols
```
```
“A colleague says their new data mixture improved MMLU by 2 points after 10B training tokens.
Is that a reliable signal?” Strong answer: almost certainly not. At 10B tokens, MMLU variance across
seeds is typically larger than 2 points. The right signal at 10B tokens is perplexity on domain-stratified
validation slices. Ask them to show the perplexity curves before treating the MMLU number as meaning-
ful.
Senior follow-up: “When is perplexity insuﬀicient as your only signal, even during pre-training?”
Senior answer: perplexity is insufficient when the capability you care about requires compositional gen-
eralization rather than next-token prediction-for example, multi-step mathematical reasoning or long-
horizon planning. A model can minimize perplexity on math corpora by learning to predict common
surface patterns without being able to solve novel problems. For these capabilities you need targeted held-
out task evaluations at training time-not as the primary optimization signal, but as a periodic diagnostic.
Some training runs at frontier labs use “canary tasks”-small, carefully constructed task suites evaluated
everyNsteps-precisely to detect when perplexity progress stops translating to capability progress.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Perplexity isexp

better; it measures how surprised the model is by held-out text.
Its smoothness and token-level granularity make it the right signal for training-time decisions: data mix-
ture ablations, learning-rate tuning, and architecture comparisons at small scale.
Perplexity requires raw logit access and is easy to misreport. Require that reported logits sum to 1 over
the full vocabulary, and normalize to bits-per-byte when comparing models with different tokenizers.
Use domain-stratified perplexity to detect trade-offs between text domains that a single aggregate number
will hide.
Perplexity is necessary but not sufficient for deployment decisions. Use it to guide training; add task-
accuracy evals to select among final checkpoint candidates.

**23.2.2 Exact Match, F1, Pass@k, and Win Rates**
Once you move past perplexity and onto measuring what a model actually produces when deployed-answers
to questions, code patches, explanations, clinical summaries- you have to choose a task-level metric. That choice
is not cosmetic. I have seen teams report a 5-point accuracy gain that evaporated when they switched from
exact match to F1, and I have seen code generation win rates swing 15 points when the evaluation moved from
pass@1 to pass@10. The metric is a design decision with real consequences, and interviewers at any lab with
a production system will probe whether you understand those consequences.
Four metric families cover the vast majority of LLM evaluation scenarios.
**Exact match (EM)** compares the model’s output, after normalization (strip punctuation, lowercase, col-
lapse whitespace), to a reference string. It scores 1 if they are identical, 0 otherwise. This is the right metric for
closed-form, unambiguous outputs: MMLU letter choices, arithmetic results, entity extraction with a canonical
form.
**Token-level F1** treats the prediction and reference as bags of tokens and computes precision and recall over
the overlap:

#### F 1 =

```

This gives partial credit for approximately correct answers. It is the standard for open-domain QA tasks
like SQuAD and TriviaQA, where a reference answer may have multiple valid phrasings and a word-for-word
match is too strict.
**Pass@k** is used for code generation and any task where the model’s output can be automatically tested
for correctness. Rather than literally drawingksamples and checking, you drawnksamples and use the
unbiased estimator:

**Win rates** are used when there is no ground-truth reference: open-ended generation, creative writing,
instruction following, summarization. You present pairs of model outputs-to human judges or to a judge LLM-
and record which output the judge prefers. Aggregating pairwise preferences via an ELO or Bradley-Terry
model yields a scalar rating that is comparable across models. Chatbot Arena applies this protocol at scale with
human judges; AlpacaEval applies it automatically with GPT-4 as judge.
_The right metric is determined by the task’s output space: closed-form answers use EM; partial-credit
spans use F1; verifiable programs use Pass@k; open-ended generation requires a judge, human or model._
Each metric trades precision against breadth of applicability in a different way.
Exact match is maximally precise but brittle. A reference of “Paris” and a prediction of “Paris, France”
score 0 under EM despite being semantically equivalent. You pay for that brittleness with simplicity: EM is
fast, requires no judge, and cannot be gamed once the answer form is fixed.
Token-level F1 buys robustness to surface variation at the cost of rewarding verbosity. A model that outputs
a very long prediction containing the correct tokens will inflate its recall while precision stays low. This is why
SQuAD-style QA systems often apply the min of prediction and reference length, or use a normalizer that strips
articles and punctuation, to reduce the surface area for gaming.
Pass@k decouples evaluation from deployment scenario in a way that matters for production. Pass@1
measures the probability that a single sample is correct-relevant if you show users one completion. Pass@10
measures the probability that at least one of 10 samples is correct-relevant if your system generates multiple
suggestions and picks the best via a reranker or test execution. The gap between pass@1 and pass@10 reveals
how much diversity the model has: high pass@10 with low pass@1 means the model generates varied samples
and benefits from sampling; nearly equal pass@1 and pass@10 means the model is low-entropy and additional
samples add little value.
Win rates via LLM judges are convenient but systematically biased. GPT-4-as-judge prefers longer, more
verbose outputs even when they are not more correct-a well-documented artifact that caused inflated win rates
for models that learned to pad responses, until length-controlled variants of AlpacaEval corrected for it. On the
human side, Chatbot Arena judges are representative of whoever visits the site, which may not match your target
user population. A leaderboard that becomes a PR target also attracts gaming: the “Leaderboard Illusion” paper
documented cases of providers gaining privileged submission access or cherry-picking model configurations,
eroding the benchmark’s integrity.

Put cost on the Pareto frontier, not in the denominator. A model with pass@1= 0. 70 that costs
10 more per token than one with pass@1= 0. 68 is not obviously better for production. Report accu-
racy at fixed latency budget or accuracy per dollar when comparing models with different serving costs.
Many public leaderboards omit cost entirely; supplement them with a Pareto frontier if you are making a
deployment decision.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you evaluate a code generation model for production deployment?” Strong answer:
use pass@1 at the system’s actual sampling temperature as the primary accuracy metric; supplement
with pass@10 to characterize ceiling capability; measure latency-to-first-token and cost per accepted
suggestion; report accuracy vs. cost on a Pareto frontier rather than a single number.
“A team reports a 5-point win rate improvement on AlpacaEval. What should you check before
trusting that number?” Strong answer: check whether the improvement survives length correction;
check whether the same improvement appears on Chatbot Arena or a human evaluation on your actual
task distribution; verify the baseline was evaluated under identical decoding parameters (temperature,
top-p, maximum tokens). A win rate that disappears after length correction is measuring verbosity, not
quality.
Senior follow-up: “Your pass@1 improved by 4 points on HumanEval, but users are not reporting
a better experience. What might explain the gap?” Senior answer: HumanEval problems are short,
self-contained, and have canonical test suites. Production code generation tasks involve existing code-
bases with implicit context and rarely have test suites. A 4-point HumanEval gain can come from better
performance on easy function-completion problems that are already mostly solved in production. Run an
evaluation on a held-out sample of real user sessions-accept rate, or user edit distance after accepting a
suggestion-to determine whether the benchmark gain translates. If it does not, the gap is in the evaluation
distribution, not the model, and you should redesign the benchmark before acting on future HumanEval
results.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Exact match is precise but brittle-use it only for closed-form, canonical outputs such as classification
labels and arithmetic results.
Token-level F1 gives partial credit for span-extraction tasks; watch for verbosity inflation and normalize
output length if the model’s responses are unconstrained.
Pass@k decouples capability from deployment scenario. Use pass@1 for single-suggestion systems,
pass@k for best-of-Nor capability research, and always apply the unbiased estimator withn 20 sam-
ples per problem.
Win rates require a judge and are systematically biased toward longer outputs. Always report a length-
controlled variant alongside the raw win rate.
Pair every accuracy or safety metric with a cost metric. Accuracy at fixed latency budget or accuracy per
dollar is the right unit for deployment decisions.
```

## Chapter 24 Benchmarks You Must Know

### 24.1 Knowledge and Reasoning Benchmarks

**24.1.1 MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA**
In a system design interview at a frontier lab, one of the first questions after you describe your evaluation
pipeline is usually: “Which benchmarks are you tracking and why?” The interviewer is not fishing for a list
of acronyms-they want to know whether you understand what each benchmark actually measures, where it
saturates, and what its failure modes are. MMLU, MMLU-Pro, and GPQA are the three rungs of the standard
knowledge-and-reasoning ladder, and misunderstanding any one of them signals a gap that mid-level candidates
routinely fall into.
_Massive Multitask Language Understanding_ (MMLU) was released in 2020, coinciding with GPT-3. The
benchmark spans 57 subjects-ranging from abstract algebra and virology to world history and foreign policy-
each formatted as a four-option multiple-choice question. Questions were scraped from the web, which already
hints at contamination risks we will return to. At the time, the dominant evaluation paradigm was few-shot
prompting on base models, so a canonical MMLU prompt looks like this:

The following are multiple choice questions about astronomy.

Q: What is the main sequence?
A) A band of galaxies
B) The period after the Big Bang
C) Stars fusing hydrogen in their cores
D) Planetary orbital zones
Answer: C

Q: ... [3 more exemplars] ...

Q: Which instrument was used to first detect gravitational waves?
A) The Hubble Space Telescope B) LIGO C) ALMA D) Chandra
Answer:

```
The model is expected to emit the letter of the correct answer. GPT-3 scored 45% under this protocol in
```
2020. Today’s frontier models score in the low 90s, which is why the benchmark has essentially lost discrimi-
native power.
    _MMLU-Pro_ addresses saturation by replacing four answer choices with ten and removing the noisiest, most
trivial questions. Chain-of-thought prompting is now the norm rather than raw next-token prediction. Frontier
model scores drop to the 65-75% range, restoring a useful spread across model families.
    _Graduate-Level Google-Proof Questions_ (GPQA) raises the bar to PhD-level. Questions were written by
domain experts, validated by a second expert, and then given to non-experts who spent up to 30 minutes on each
with full internet access-the “Google-proof” designation means the non-expert accuracy was still only around
30%, while domain experts reached 65%. GPT-4 scored 39% at launch; O3 now reaches approximately 75%.


```
24.1 Knowledge and Reasoning Benchmarks
```
_The ladder exists because knowledge benchmarks saturate in order: MMLU first, then MMLU-Pro, then
GPQA-and you should know which rung a model currently sits on before choosing your evaluation target._
Multiple-choice benchmarks have three properties that make them endure: they are automatically scorable,
they are reproducible across labs without access to proprietary human raters, and they produce a single number
that fits cleanly into a training dashboard. When you are running hundreds of evaluation checkpoints during a
training run, automatic scoring is not a convenience-it is a necessity.
The escalating difficulty across the three tiers also reflects a real property of model capability. A model
that struggles on MMLU is not ready for GPQA; a model that saturates MMLU-Pro without a gap on GPQA is
likely memorizing rather than reasoning. The gaps between tiers are diagnostic.
The main trade-off is that none of these benchmarks reflects what real users do. A user asking an LLM
to debug their deployment pipeline or draft a patient summary is not taking a standardized test. MMLU in
particular is better thought of as a proxy for base-model breadth: if a model trained on a broad web corpus can
ace questions it never explicitly studied for, that is evidence of genuine generalization. If you curate a training
set to hit MMLU specifically, you get a high score that tells you almost nothing about general capability.

**A Worked Example**

Consider evaluating a 7B model checkpoint at step 50,000 of pre-training. You want a quick signal on
whether the model is developing factual knowledge.
Set up 5-shot MMLU on the _computer science_ subset (170 questions). Feed the prompt above, sample
greedily (temperature 0), and extract the first token. If it isA,B,C, orD, record it; otherwise mark invalid.
Compute accuracy as:

Accuracy=correct answers
total questions
At 7B scale with a strong data mix, you should see roughly 55-65% on the computer science subset after
a full training run, versus 25% random baseline. If your number is below 35% at step 50,000, the data mix or
learning rate is likely off-this is the diagnostic value of tracking MMLU during training.
Now switch to GPQA for a 70B model you are preparing to deploy into a medical-information use case.
Run GPQA’s biology subset (approximately 65 questions) with chain-of-thought, 0-shot. A score below 40%
means the model cannot reliably handle expert-level biomedical questions; a score of 55% or above puts you
in territory where domain-expert human annotators are necessary to catch the remaining errors. That threshold
informs whether you can deploy without a mandatory human-in-the-loop review layer.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
MMLU for base models, not instruction-tuned models. Once you apply RLHF or supervised fine-
tuning, MMLU scores can actually drop slightly because the model becomes more cautious about out-
putting raw letters. Use MMLU-Pro or GPQA for post-training checkpoints.
MMLU-Pro is the current workhorse for frontier comparisons. Scores in the 65-75% range give real
differentiation between GPT-4-class and GPT-3.5-class models. If you see a model claiming 90%+ on
MMLU-Pro with standard prompting and no majority-vote ensembling, audit the evaluation code-it is
almost certainly using a non-standard prompt.
```

```
24.1 Knowledge and Reasoning Benchmarks
```
```
Few-shot example order is a confounder. Randomizing the order of the five exemplars and averaging
over three orderings reduces variance by 2-4 accuracy points on MMLU. Always report the protocol, not
just the number.
Chain-of-thought is now mandatory for GPQA. Without scratchpad reasoning, even 70B models under-
perform by 10-15 points because the questions require multi-step derivations. Zero-shot GPQA without
chain-of-thought is not a meaningful measurement.
Assume contamination exists. MMLU was released in 2020. Any model trained on a 2023-or-later
web crawl has almost certainly seen fragments of the test questions. A 13-gram deduplication pass can
quantify this, but it does not catch paraphrases. When you report MMLU scores for a new model, add a
contamination disclaimer to your model card-it is now a community norm, even if not universally followed.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Which benchmark would you use to evaluate a new 70B model before deployment?” Strong answer:
choose based on the deployment target. For broad factual knowledge in a general assistant, MMLU-Pro
gives meaningful signal. For a domain-expert use case like medical or legal, supplement with GPQA on
the relevant subset. Never use plain MMLU for a frontier-sized model-you will hit the ceiling.
“MMLU scores have been in the 90s for a year. Is the benchmark still useful?” Strong answer:
MMLU is still useful as a sanity check and a base-model diagnostic, but it has no discriminative power
among frontier models. The field has shifted to MMLU-Pro and GPQA precisely because saturation kills
the ranking signal. Know the saturation threshold: approximately 90% for MMLU, roughly 75% for
MMLU-Pro, somewhere above 75% for GPQA (not yet saturated as of 2025).
Senior follow-up: “A competitor claims their model beats yours by 3 points on GPQA. How do
you verify or refute this claim?” Senior answer: first, inspect the evaluation protocol-prompt format,
whether chain-of-thought was used, whether majority voting over multiple samples was applied. A 3-
point gap can easily be manufactured by switching from 0-shot to 8-shot chain-of-thought. Second, check
the subset: 3 points on the full GPQA (448 questions) is statistically meaningful, but 3 points on a 65-
question chemistry subset is within noise. Third, run your own evaluation on their model using a locked
evaluation harness like HELM or LM-Evaluation-Harness so the prompt format is identical.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
MMLU (2020) covers 57 subjects with 4-choice questions; saturated for frontier models at90%.
MMLU-Pro raises the bar to 10 choices and harder questions; current frontier scores cluster 65-75%.
GPQA targets PhD-level, Google-proof questions; domain experts score 65%, non-experts 30%, and top
models now reach75%.
Multiple-choice benchmarks are valuable precisely because they are automatic, reproducible, and cheap-
but they are proxies for knowledge, not for real-world task performance.
Evaluation protocol details-few-shot count, example order, chain-of-thought, sampling strategy-can swing
scores by 5-15 points; always report the full protocol alongside the number.
```
**24.1.2 Humanity’s Last Exam and ARC-AGI**
Every knowledge benchmark eventually gets saturated-that is the pattern, and interviewers at frontier labs
know it. When a candidate mentions GPQA, a senior interviewer often follows up with: “So what do we


```
24.1 Knowledge and Reasoning Benchmarks
```
do when O3 is at 90% on GPQA in 18 months?” Humanity’s Last Exam and ARC-AGI represent two very
different attempts to solve that problem, and understanding the philosophical difference between them is the
kind of nuance that separates a strong answer from a rehearsed one. Both have appeared in recent evaluation
discussions at top labs, and knowing the current numbers as well as the structural critiques is table stakes.
_Humanity’s Last Exam_ (HLE) is a multimodal, crowdsourced benchmark built around the premise that if
you aggregate the hardest questions that domain experts can construct-and then use frontier models themselves
to filter out anything “too easy”-you get a ceiling that will not be quickly saturated. Organizers solicited ques-
tions from researchers and practitioners, offering co-authorship to contributors and a prize pool for accepted
submissions. Each question went through a multi-stage review process. The resulting dataset contains prob-
lems in mathematics, physics, chemistry, biology, law, economics, and other fields, covering both text-only and
image-based formats. Questions are either multiple-choice or short-answer with a verifiable correct response-
there is no open-ended generation. At launch, the best-performing models scored roughly 8-10%; as of early
2025, O3 reaches approximately 20%.
_ARC-AGI_ (Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus for Artificial General Intelligence) is philosophically differ-
ent. Introduced in 2019-before large language models were the dominant paradigm-it deliberately removes both
language and world knowledge from the equation. Each task is a small grid of colored cells. You are shown two
or three input-output example pairs that illustrate a transformation rule, and then you must apply that rule to a
new input grid to produce the correct output. There are no words, no task descriptions, no domain knowledge
required. The intent is to isolate abstract reasoning: can the model induce the rule from examples and generalize
it? GPT-4o scored near 0% on ARC-AGI in standard evaluation mode. O3, using extended test-time compute,
reaches approximately 75% on ARC-AGI v1-but at a cost of several hundred dollars per task in compute.
_HLE measures the frontier of expert knowledge retrieval and multi-step reasoning; ARC-AGI measures
abstract inductive reasoning stripped of any factual prior-and these are fundamentally different capabilities
that current architectures handle very differently._
HLE’s strength is coverage depth. By recruiting experts and using adversarial filtering via frontier mod-
els, it ensures that questions are not just hard but are hard _for current LLMs specifically_. The multi-modal
component also targets a genuine gap: reasoning over diagrams, equations rendered as images, and scientific
figures is a capability that text-only benchmarks cannot probe. The benchmark’s primary weakness is selection
