```
####  96 .0%

Conversely, if the model has genuine errors on 132 clean problems but happens to match all 53 wrong
reference labels:

```
measured accuracy=(1,^266  1 , 319 132) + 53=^11 ,,^187319  90 .0%
```
Both scenarios produce 90%, yet one reflects 94.6% true accuracy on clean examples and the other reflects
89.5%. Without a data quality audit, these are indistinguishable from the score alone. The operational conse-
quence is clear: when benchmark scores reach the upper eighties and above, always audit a sample of “errors”
before concluding the model has hit a capability ceiling.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Pin three things before reporting any score: framework version, prompt template, and few-shot
count. A score reported with “we used lm-eval-harness v0.4.2, zero-shot, default template” is repro-
ducible. “We evaluated on MMLU” is not.
Require decontamination disclosure as a reporting norm, not an optional footnote. When you pub-
lish evaluation results, state explicitly: (a) what decontamination method was used, (b) the removal rate
(percentage of training documents flagged), and (c) whether the post-decontamination score differed from
the pre-decontamination score. A removal rate of 0% is informative: it tells the reader the method found
nothing, which is different from not running the method at all.
Audit benchmark label quality before using it as a decision signal. For any benchmark you intend
to use to make a deployment decision, randomly sample 100 examples and verify the reference answers
manually. For benchmarks near ceiling, sample from the “errors” the model makes - if you find mislabeled
items, the effective ceiling of the benchmark is below 100%.
Track score time-series, not point estimates. A model that improves from 85% to 87% on a benchmark
is a signal; a model that jumps from 87% to 92% in one version update warrants investigation. Sudden
large jumps more often reflect a change in evaluation protocol or a contamination event than a genuine
capability leap.
For closed-weight models evaluated externally, treat scores as approximate ordinals, not precise
quantities. A closed model can silently update between when you run an eval and when your paper is
published. Reporting the model version, the API endpoint slug, and the date of evaluation gives future
readers enough context to detect silent updates.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“A colleague says our new model got 91% on MMLU. What follow-up questions do you ask?” A strong
answer covers: which prompt format and few-shot count, which framework version, whether decontami-
nation was run and what the removal rate was, and whether this is a base model or instruction-tuned model
(since the same benchmark can behave differently for each). A weak answer says “that sounds good” or
asks only “what was last version’s score?”
“What does it mean for a benchmark to be reproducible, and what breaks it?” Protocol variance (prompt
format, decoding settings), data quality (label noise), and contamination status. Reproducibility requires
```

### 25.2 Real-World Evaluation

```
locking all three. The most actionable fix is adopting a versioned evaluation framework that pins the
protocol as code.
“A benchmark you care about shows model scores plateauing near 90% despite clear improvements on
harder tasks. What is your diagnosis?” This is the senior question. The strong answer distinguishes
three competing explanations: (1) genuine capability ceiling on the benchmark’s difficulty distribution,
(2) label noise floor - the model can no longer improve beyond the noise rate, and (3) distribution shift
between the model’s strengths and the benchmark’s coverage. The senior move is to audit 100 randomly
sampled “errors” to discriminate between explanations 1 and 2 before concluding the model has hit a real
ceiling.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
A benchmark score is only reproducible when the prompt format, few-shot count, decoding settings,
framework version, and decontamination protocol are all disclosed alongside it.
Label noise inflates apparent model accuracy near benchmark ceilings and creates ambiguity that cannot
be resolved from the score alone; auditing a sample of model errors is necessary.
Decontamination disclosure should be a community norm analogous to reporting confidence intervals:
state the method, the removal rate, and whether post-decontamination scores changed.
Standardized frameworks (lm-evaluation-harness, HELM) address protocol variance by pinning
evaluation as versioned code; always report the framework version when citing scores.
Sudden large jumps in benchmark scores warrant investigation before being attributed to capability im-
provement - they more often signal a protocol change or a contamination event.
```
### 25.2 Real-World Evaluation

**25.2.1 Deployment Telemetry and Live Traﬀic**
When a model passes every curated benchmark on your eval rack and then underperforms in production, the
problem is almost always distribution mismatch. Standardized benchmarks quiz models-the question designer
already knows the answer and the prompt is crafted to probe a specific capability. Real users _ask_ -they do not
know the answer, the phrasing is messy, the intent is sometimes ambiguous, and they care only about whether the
response actually helps them. Closing this gap is a core challenge for senior ML engineers building production
systems, and interviewers at frontier labs ask about it directly when evaluating candidates for deployment or
evaluation engineering roles.
Deployment telemetry treats live inference logs as a first-class evaluation signal. After a model is in pro-
duction, every request is a data point: what prompt arrived, what the model returned, how long it took, whether
the user continued the conversation, whether they copied the output, whether they hit the feedback button, and-if
you instrument it-whether the downstream task succeeded. Aggregating these signals gives you a distribution
of actual usage that no benchmark author could have anticipated.
The distinction between quizzing and asking is not just philosophical-it determines which metric you should
trust. A quizzing prompt (MMLU, GPQA, AMC) has a ground-truth answer baked in; you can score automat-
ically and the number is clean. An asking prompt (“help me draft an email declining this meeting”, “explain
why my Kubernetes pod keeps OOMKilling”) has no canonical answer; the only reliable judge is whether the
person who asked got what they needed.


```
25.2 Real-World Evaluation
```
Operationally, live-traffic evaluation takes two forms. _Aggregate telemetry_ clusters conversations by topic
and intent, then monitors quality proxies per cluster over time. _Shadow evaluation_ runs a candidate model in
parallel on the same traffic, compares outputs to the production model using an LLM judge or human raters, and
reports a win-rate before the candidate is promoted.
_Once you have paying or regular users, you have the best evaluation data in the world-use it._
Benchmark prompts, however carefully written, compress the tail of possible user behavior almost to zero.
Production traffic is fat-tailed: the median prompt is unremarkable, but the 99th-percentile prompt is something
the eval team never imagined. If your deployment serves millions of daily requests, the tail is enormous, and it is
precisely the tail that reveals model failures-hallucinations on uncommon domain terms, refusals on legitimate
edge-case requests, format breakdowns when the user pastes in a long document.
The alternative-relying solely on periodic offline evals-fails for two reasons. First, you discover regres-
sions after users have already experienced them. Second, the offline distribution drifts from production as user
behavior evolves; a new feature, a new user cohort, or even a seasonal shift in topics can invalidate a carefully
tuned eval suite within weeks.
The trade-off is noise. Live traffic contains spam, prompt injection attempts, benchmark probers, and
developers stress-testing the API. These dilute your quality signal. A raw thumbs-up rate across all traffic is
almost meaningless without stratification by intent cluster and user type.

**A Worked Example**

Anthropic published an analysis of real Claude usage by running their own model over a large sample
of production conversations and using it to assign soft cluster labels-essentially a scalable version of human
topic coding. Coding tasks were the single largest cluster, followed by writing and summarization. This kind
of analysis immediately tells you where to concentrate your evaluation budget: if 30% of your traffic is code
generation and your offline eval suite has 5% code tasks, you are under-measuring your most important use case.
To make this concrete: suppose you pull one week of production logs, 10 million turns. You embed each
user turn and cluster intoK= 200topics usingk-means over sentence embeddings. You then sample 50 turns
per cluster and score them with a judge model on a 1-5 scale. You now have a per-cluster quality heatmap. You
find that cluster 47 (“debugging Python asyncio code”) scores 2.1 on average while the overall mean is 3.8. That
is your next fine-tuning target-not whatever the next benchmark paper happens to benchmark.
Shadow evaluation works like a canary deployment. The new model handles, say, 1% of traffic. A judge
model scores both the shadow response and the production response on the same prompt. After 100k compar-
isons, you have a win rate with a tight confidence interval. A win rate above 55% is a meaningful signal to
promote; below 50% means do not ship.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Instrument before you launch. Logging is cheap; retroactive reconstruction of what happened is ex-
pensive. At minimum log: timestamp, prompt hash, model version, latency, output token count, and any
explicit user feedback. Add conversation-level signals (session abandonment, follow-up clarification rate)
as soon as feasible.
Stratify before you trust any aggregate metric. A single overall thumbs-up rate mixes spam with gen-
uine queries, short factual lookups with 2,000-token coding tasks. Stratify by intent cluster, prompt length
bucket, and user cohort before drawing conclusions.
```

```
25.2 Real-World Evaluation
```
```
Use shadow mode for every major model swap. Promoting a new model based solely on offline evals
without a shadow run first is how you ship regressions. Shadow for at least 24 hours to capture diurnal
patterns in traffic distribution.
Cap your spam fraction. If more than 20-30% of your logged traffic is probers, red-teamers, or clearly
synthetic test traffic, filter it before building your quality heatmap. Leaving it in will make the model look
worse on legitimate queries and better on pathological ones.
Budget for human annotation on the tail. LLM judges are fast and cheap but systematically miss certain
failure modes-subtle factual errors, culturally inappropriate outputs, responses that are technically correct
but practically useless. Reserve 2-5% of your annotation budget for human review on low-scoring cluster
tails.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you evaluate a model once it’s in production?” A strong answer describes the two-track
approach: aggregate telemetry for ongoing health monitoring and shadow evaluation for model upgrades.
Mention stratification by intent cluster and the difference between proxy metrics (thumbs-up, session
continuation) and direct quality scores.
“What’s wrong with using only Chatbot Arena or MMLU as your evaluation?” Point out that Chatbot
Arena users are self-selected (whoever visits the site, which skews toward tech-savvy users testing the
model, not using it), and MMLU is a quizzing distribution that does not resemble any deployed use case.
Both are useful leading indicators but not substitutes for production telemetry.
Senior follow-up: “How do you detect a regression in production before users complain?” The senior
answer involves anomaly detection on your quality heatmap: track the rolling mean score per cluster with
exponential smoothing, alert when any cluster drops more than 0.3 points in a 6-hour window. Pair with
latency and refusal-rate monitoring since safety over-refusals often accompany model regressions in the
same rollout.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Benchmark prompts quiz models; real users ask models-these are different distributions and require dif-
ferent evaluation strategies.
Deployment telemetry is the highest-fidelity eval signal available once a model is live; build logging
infrastructure before launch, not after.
Shadow evaluation-running a candidate model on 1-5% of live traffic and scoring against the production
model-is the standard practice for safe model promotion.
Stratify all aggregate metrics by intent cluster and user type before drawing conclusions; raw averages
over heterogeneous traffic are nearly meaningless.
Human annotation on cluster tails remains irreplaceable for catching failure modes that LLM judges sys-
tematically miss.
```
**25.2.2 Domain-Specific Evaluations (MedHELM-Style)**
General-purpose benchmarks tell you roughly how capable a model is. They tell you almost nothing about
whether it is safe and useful for a specific high-stakes domain. A model scoring 90% on MMLU and 75% on


```
25.2 Real-World Evaluation
```
GPQA may still hallucinate drug interactions, misread imaging reports, or produce legally incoherent contract
clauses-because none of those benchmarks were built from practitioner workflows. Senior engineers evaluating
models for specialized deployment are expected to understand how to move from generic leaderboard numbers
to domain-grounded assessments, and how to navigate the privacy and annotation costs that come with that
territory.
Domain-specific evaluation starts from a different question than general benchmarks: not “what can this
model do on a curated test set?” but “which tasks does this domain actually require, and how well does the
model perform on those?” The design process inverts the usual flow. Instead of researchers proposing tasks
and then recruiting subjects, you recruit domain practitioners first, extract their workflows and pain points, and
derive evaluation tasks from those.
MedHELM, a medical evaluation suite built on top of the HELM framework, is the clearest published
example of this methodology. The authors recruited 29 clinicians across specialties and asked a simple question:
where in your daily practice would a language model be useful? They identified 121 distinct clinical tasks.
These were not exam questions. They included things like synthesizing a patient’s history into a structured note,
drafting a referral letter, proposing a differential diagnosis given a case summary, and answering a patient’s
follow-up question in plain language. Those tasks were then operationalized into concrete evaluation instances-
prompts paired with rubrics or reference outputs that clinicians themselves validated.
The resulting benchmark has a fundamentally different character from MMLU. It is narrower in domain but
far deeper in ecological validity: the tasks look like what the system will actually be asked to do in deployment.
_The right evaluation asks the same questions the deployment will ask; anything else is measuring a proxy._
The failure mode of generic medical benchmarks is well-documented. For years, the standard way to evalu-
ate a model on medicine was to run it on USMLE Step 1 and Step 2 questions-the licensing exams for American
physicians. A model that aces USMLE has demonstrated that it memorized a large amount of structured medical
knowledge. It has not demonstrated that it can produce a usable clinical note, counsel a patient about medica-
tion risks in understandable language, or flag when a case summary contains internally inconsistent lab values.
Those are the tasks that create or destroy value in practice.
Practitioner-derived benchmarks close this gap by construction: the tasks were sourced from people whose
job depends on executing them correctly. They also reveal capability distributions that generic evals obscure.
A model may score 88% on a general medical knowledge benchmark but 52% on patient-facing communica-
tion tasks and 71% on clinical documentation-a profile that directly informs deployment decisions (use it for
documentation, monitor carefully for patient-facing use, do not deploy autonomously for either).
The main trade-off is cost and access. Designing a practitioner-sourced benchmark requires significant ex-
pert time, which is expensive in any high-skill domain. And once you have real clinical cases-the highest-fidelity
evaluation material-you immediately run into privacy constraints that prevent public release. This means the
community cannot independently verify scores, and model developers must run the evaluation under controlled
access agreements.

**A Worked Example**

Take the clinical note synthesis task from MedHELM. A clinician sees a patient with chest pain. After the
visit, they need to produce a structured SOAP note (Subjective, Objective, Assessment, Plan) for the electronic
health record. The evaluation instance looks like this:

Prompt:


```
25.2 Real-World Evaluation
```
```
Patient: 58-year-old male, presenting with 2-day history of
exertional chest pain, worse on inspiration. PMH: hypertension,
type 2 diabetes. Current meds: metformin 1000mg BID, lisinopril
10mg QD. Vitals: BP 148/92, HR 88, SpO2 97% on room air.
ECG: sinus rhythm, no ST changes. Troponin x2 negative.
```
```
Write a SOAP note suitable for the EHR.
```
Reference (clinician-authored):
S: Patient reports 2-day exertional chest pain, pleuritic in
character. Denies diaphoresis, radiation, or rest pain.
O: BP 148/92, HR 88, SpO2 97%. ECG NSR, no ischemic changes.
Troponin x2 negative.
A: Chest pain, likely musculoskeletal vs. pleuritis. Low
probability ACS given negative workup.
P: Ibuprofen 400mg TID x5d, follow-up in 1 week, return
precautions for worsening symptoms or rest pain.

The model output is scored on four axes by a clinician rater or a validated rubric: (1) factual accuracy-does
it reflect what was in the prompt without adding hallucinated details; (2) structural correctness-does it follow
SOAP format; (3) clinical appropriateness-is the assessment and plan medically sound; (4) usability-would the
clinician accept this note with minimal edits. A model that scores well on a generic medical benchmark but
produces a note attributing atrial fibrillation to a patient whose ECG explicitly shows sinus rhythm has a factual
accuracy failure that the benchmark exposes immediately.
Across 121 tasks scored this way, you get a capability profile, not a single number. That profile is what an
engineering team uses to scope deployment.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Source tasks from practitioners, not from existing literature. Literature-based tasks inherit the same
exam-question bias as standardized benchmarks. Ask clinicians, lawyers, or engineers what they do on a
Tuesday, then build evaluation tasks around that.
Separate public and private splits deliberately. Release a subset of tasks publicly for reproducibility
and community benchmarking. Keep the high-fidelity split (real patient records, real legal documents)
private and run it under controlled access. The public split maintains accountability; the private split
preserves validity.
Plan for multi-axis scoring from the start. A single accuracy score collapses the capability profile
that practitioners actually care about. Budget for rubric design and, ideally, clinician review of at least a
sample of model outputs. LLM judges can handle scale but require calibration against human scores in
the specific domain.
Realism and privacy are in direct tension-resolve it explicitly. The most realistic evaluation uses real
data. Real data often cannot be shared. Make this trade-off explicitly in your evaluation design documen-
tation so downstream users understand what they are and are not measuring.
```

```
25.2 Real-World Evaluation
```
```
Expect 3-6 months of practitioner engagement to build the first version. Domain-specific benchmark
construction is not a weekend project. Factor expert interview time, task validation cycles, and rubric
calibration into your project plan before committing to a launch date.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you evaluate a model for deployment in a medical or legal context?” A strong answer de-
scribes the practitioner-interview process, contrasts it with standardized exam benchmarks, identifies the
specific task types (documentation, summarization, patient communication), names the axes of evaluation
beyond simple accuracy, and addresses the privacy constraint on using real data.
“Why can’t we just use USMLE or bar exam scores to evaluate domain models?” Point out the
quizzing-versus-asking distinction: licensing exams test whether you have memorized structured knowl-
edge under exam conditions, not whether you can execute the actual workflows of the profession. A model
could pass Step 2 CK and still fail to write a usable discharge summary.
Senior follow-up: “How do you validate that your domain-specific benchmark actually predicts
deployment quality?” The senior answer involves a calibration study: deploy the model on a small pilot
with real practitioners, collect their satisfaction ratings and error reports, then measure the correlation
between your benchmark scores and those outcomes. If a model that scores 0.4 on your rubric is flagged
by clinicians 3more often than one that scores 0.7, your benchmark has predictive validity. If the
correlation is weak, you need to revise the task set or the scoring rubric.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Generic benchmarks measure capability breadth; domain-specific evaluations measure deployment fitness-
both are necessary, neither is sufficient alone.
Practitioner-interview-driven task design (as in MedHELM) produces evaluations with far higher ecolog-
ical validity than repurposing existing standardized exams.
Multi-axis scoring (factual accuracy, format compliance, clinical or legal appropriateness, usability) gives
engineering teams actionable deployment guidance; single-number scores do not.
Realism and privacy are structurally in tension in high-stakes domains: plan a public/private split from
the start to balance reproducibility and validity.
Benchmark construction in specialized domains requires months of expert engagement; build this into
project timelines before any model evaluation commitments are made.
```

## Part X

# Alignment and Post-Training


## Chapter 26 Supervised Fine-Tuning

### 26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach.

**26.1.1 Style, Format, and Task Specification**
An interviewer at a frontier lab will often open an SFT discussion with a deliberately simple question:
“GPT-3 and ChatGPT use essentially the same architecture trained on similar internet data-what does fine-
tuning actually do?” The answer is more nuanced than most candidates expect, and getting it wrong signals
that you have only ever used these models, not built them. At a mid-level this question probes whether you
understand the separation between pre-training and post-training; at a senior level it probes whether you can
reason about which desired behaviors SFT can deliver reliably and which it fundamentally cannot.
Pre-training packs the model with latent capabilities. Somewhere in a 7B parameter checkpoint trained on
two trillion tokens lives the ability to summarize, translate, write code, and answer questions-but none of it fires
reliably on a bare prompt likeSummarize this article:. The model was never trained to respond to that
framing; it was trained to predict the next token in a web-scale corpus. Supervised fine-tuning bridges that gap.
Mechanically, SFT is nothing more than continued gradient descent on a new dataset. You format each
example as an _instruction-response_ pair, concatenate them with a chat template, and compute cross-entropy loss
only on the response tokens:

```
LSFT(θ) =
```
#### XT

```
t=1
```
```
logpθ(ytjx, y<t)
```
wherexis the instruction prefix (masked out of the loss) andy 1 ,... , yTis the target response. Nothing
exotic happens algorithmically. The power comes from what the data teaches.
What SFT reliably teaches falls into three buckets. First, _output format_ : whether to respond in prose, bullet
points, markdown, code blocks, or structured JSON. Second, _task framing_ : the model learns what kinds of com-
pletions belong to what kinds of prompts-that a prompt asking for a “subject line” expects a short noun phrase,
not a paragraph. Third, _response style_ : register (formal vs. casual), length norms, whether to ask clarifying
questions, whether to hedge uncertainty. These are all properties of the output distribution’s shape-its “type
signature,” to borrow a programming term.
_SFT teaches the model what kind of token sequence to produce; whether the content of that sequence is
factually correct or deeply reasoned depends almost entirely on what the base model already knows._
The intuition is distributional. A base model has seen instruction-response pairs in pre-training-Stack
Overflow Q&A, documentation, tutorials-but they appear infrequently and inconsistently formatted. SFT con-
centrates that signal: every example in the fine-tuning set is an instruction followed by a high-quality completion,
so the model learns a strong prior that this template triggers a particular response mode.
This matters for an important reason: the cost structure is favorable. You can dramatically change how
a model presents information with far fewer examples than you might expect. Studies with early open models
showed that fine-tuning on as few as 500 to 1,000 high-quality examples moved a base model’s output distri-
bution much closer to a deployed assistant. The data quality multiplier is enormous at this scale-ten carefully
written examples often outperform a thousand noisy ones.
The trade-off is that surface behavior and underlying capability can diverge. A model fine-tuned on data


```
26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach
```
where every answer is formatted as a numbered list will produce numbered lists. It will do so even when the
question calls for a single-sentence reply, and even when the underlying reasoning is absent or wrong. Style and
correctness are trained independently. This is exactly why length and formatting biases are so persistent: human
raters and LM judges both prefer longer, list-heavy responses, so any SFT data shaped by human or AI feedback
will systematically drift toward that style regardless of whether more words mean better answers.

**A Worked Example**

Take a Llama-class 7B base model (d_model=4096, 32 layers, bfloat16, trained on roughly 2T tokens).
Feed it the raw prompt:

Explain the difference between precision and recall.

The base model might continue with something like “Precision and recall are two metrics commonly used
in... The precision of a binary classifier is defined as...” followed by a rambling continuation that drifts into
unrelated content, because the base model is completing a document, not answering a question.
After SFT on 50,000 instruction-response pairs with 3 epochs, batch size 128, learning rate 2  10 −^5
with cosine decay (total compute roughly 150 GPU-hours on 8H100s), the same prompt now elicits a clean
structured answer: a two-sentence definition of each metric, a concrete example with a confusion matrix, and a
note on when to prioritize each-because hundreds of similar prompt-response pairs in the training set established
that template.
What changed? Not the underlying knowledge of precision and recall-that was already in the base model.
What changed is the trigger: the model now recognizes a standalone instructional prompt as a signal to enter
“teaching assistant” mode, adopt an explanatory register, and terminate with a clean conclusion. The computa-
tion that produces the correct definition is largely reusing pre-trained circuits; SFT just learned the routing.
The same experiment illustrates the format ceiling. If you now ask the same SFT model to solve a novel
multi-step math problem the base model never mastered, the SFT model will confidently produce a well-
formatted wrong answer. The format is right; the substance is not. SFT cannot manufacture capability that
does not exist in the pre-trained weights.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Volume vs. quality threshold. Below roughly 1,000 examples, quality dominates; every noisy example
noticeably hurts. Above 100,000, you can tolerate some noise and diversity starts to matter more than
per-example quality. If you are resource-constrained, invest in curation, not volume.
Template coverage over domain coverage. It is more important that your SFT data covers the space of
interaction patterns (multi-turn, tool-calling, refusal, clarification) than that it covers every knowledge
domain. The base model handles domain breadth; SFT handles behavioral patterns.
Fight length bias explicitly. Human raters prefer responses approximately 60-70% of the time when
those responses are longer, all else equal. LM judges share this bias. If you use human or AI preference
signals to curate SFT data, audit response lengths and actively include short, correct answers. Failing to
do so produces a model that hedges everything and adds unnecessary preamble.
Safety data must be mixed in, not applied separately. A model SFT’d purely on capability demonstra-
tions and then separately safety-tuned often exhibits over-refusal-it refuses borderline but safe queries like
```

```
26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach
```
```
“how do I kill a Python process?” because the safety tuning had no context about the capability distribu-
tion. Mixing even 500 carefully crafted safety examples into the main SFT run dramatically reduces this
problem.
Modern pipelines blur pre-training and SFT. At frontier scale, instruction data is increasingly injected
during the learning-rate decay phase of pre-training (“mid-training”), not saved for a separate SFT pass.
This avoids catastrophic forgetting of pre-trained capabilities, gives the instruction data more gradient
steps, and allows instruction-tuning data volumes that would be prohibitively expensive in a standalone
SFT stage.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What does SFT actually change in a pre-trained model?” Strong answer: SFT reshapes the output
distribution’s surface properties-format, register, task framing-without adding new world knowledge. The
base model has latent capabilities; SFT installs the routing that triggers them on instructional prompts.
Mention that the effect is large even with small data, and that quality dominates quantity at this scale.
“Why does SFT improve benchmark performance even with very little data?” Strong answer: Bench-
marks like MMLU are multiple-choice or short-answer; the format is simple and the knowledge is already
in the base model. SFT teaches the model to emit the expected output format, which is almost all that is
needed. The jump from base to instruction-tuned model on MMLU is largely a formatting effect, not a
knowledge effect.
“A model fine-tuned on our data produces outputs that are always too long. How do you fix it?”
Strong answer: Audit your SFT data for length distribution and human/AI curation bias. Explicitly add
short-answer examples. If using preference data to filter SFT examples, control for length when computing
preference scores. Do not just add a system prompt instructing brevity-that is a band-aid.
Senior follow-up: “How would you approach SFT if your instruction data was generated by a
stronger teacher model like GPT-4?” The deeper concern is distribution mismatch: the teacher’s re-
sponses may require knowledge or reasoning ability the student model does not yet have. If the student
must produce tokens it cannot faithfully generate from its own weights, it learns to imitate the structure
of the response while potentially hallucinating the content. The mitigation is to filter teacher-generated
data to only include examples where the student, when probed, already demonstrates the underlying
knowledge-effectively conditioning SFT data on what the student can support.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
SFT reliably teaches output shape: format, style, task framing, and interaction patterns. It does not reliably
teach new factual knowledge.
The effect is large even with small data; quality dominates quantity below roughly 10,000 examples.
Length and list-formatting biases are structural artifacts of human and AI preference data; actively audit
and counteract them.
Modern pipelines inject instruction data during the decay phase of pre-training (mid-training) to scale up
without catastrophic forgetting.
SFT cannot manufacture capability the base model does not possess; it can only route and express what
is already there.
```

```
26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach
```
**26.1.2 Risks of Teaching Hallucination**
When a candidate in a systems interview says “we just need higher-quality SFT data,” the follow-up that
separates senior engineers from mid-level ones is: “what does high quality actually mean, and can SFT data
ever make a model _worse_ ?” The answer is yes, and the failure mode is counterintuitive-fully correct, richly
detailed SFT examples can actively train a model to fabricate. This is one of the most consequential and least
understood pitfalls in post-training pipelines, and it surfaces in staff-level interviews whenever the conversation
turns to hallucination, distillation, or why RL is needed at all.
Supervised fine-tuning is next-token prediction on a fixed dataset. Every token in the target response con-
tributes to the loss, and the model has no mechanism to distinguish between tokens it can faithfully generate
from its own weights and tokens it is being forced to predict without supporting knowledge. The cross-entropy
loss treats all target tokens symmetrically:

#### LSFT=

#### XT

```
t=1
```
```
logpθ(ytjx, y<t)
```
This symmetry is the source of the problem. Suppose the target response contains a factual claim or citation
that the pre-trained model does not reliably know. To minimize the loss, the model faces two competing mecha-
nisms. The first is genuine knowledge retrieval: if the model already encodes the relevant fact in its parameters,
it learns to surface that fact in the right context-a good outcome. The second is _structural imitation_ : the model
learns that completions with a certain input structure (“write an introduction to a complex economics concept”)
should end with a reference, and it learns to produce tokens that look like a citation regardless of whether those
tokens are grounded in anything. Structural imitation is always easier to learn than knowledge retrieval, because
structure is a shallower pattern and the gradient signal for it is denser.
The key insight is that from the model’s perspective, hallucinating a plausible-looking citation incurs _less
loss_ than producing nothing at the end. The structure of the response must be completed. If the model lacks the
parametric knowledge to fill the slot correctly, it fills the slot with invented content because that is the lower-loss
option. SFT does not teach the model to abstain; it teaches the model to complete.
_The deeper a model’s SFT data exceeds the model’s own knowledge, the stronger the incentive to learn
structural imitation over knowledge retrieval-and the worse the hallucination problem becomes._
The standard intuition for SFT data quality is “more knowledge, longer responses, more citations is better.”
That intuition is wrong for a model that has not already internalized the underlying facts. Consider two expla-
nations for what happens when you fine-tune on a response that cites a specific economics paper: (a) the model
learns to associate that input topic with that specific paper, surfacing it reliably at inference time; or (b) the
model learns the abstract behavioral pattern “complex concept!response!citation.” If the model genuinely
knows the citation from pre-training, (a) dominates. If it does not, (b) dominates-and (b) generalizes in the worst
possible way: it fires on every complex question and fills the citation slot with whatever token sequence has the
highest probability under the language model, typically a plausible-but-fabricated author-year pair.
The contrast with what RL-based methods do is instructive. Reinforcement learning with verifiable or
preference-based rewards provides a signal that is conditional on whether the model got something right. SFT
provides no such signal-it applies gradient descent unconditionally. This is why on-policy RL is a principled
remedy: you only reinforce completions the model itself produced and got correct, so you never update on
knowledge the model does not possess.
The same failure mode applies to knowledge distillation. When a small student model is fine-tuned on


```
26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach
```
outputs from a large teacher model, the teacher’s responses will frequently describe facts, reasoning chains, or
technical details that are simply not encoded in the student’s smaller weights. The student cannot distinguish
“I should learn this fact” from “I should learn to produce tokens that look like I know this fact.” At small
model scales, the distillation signal that appears to improve benchmark performance is often actually training
the student to pattern-match the teacher’s output structure.

**A Worked Example**

Consider fine-tuning a 7B model (d_model=4096, 32 layers, bfloat16, pre-trained on 1T tokens) on 50,000
instruction-response pairs drawn from an OpenAssistant-style dataset. A representative example in the dataset:

Instruction: Write an introduction to monopsony in labor economics.

Response: Monopsony occurs when a single employer dominates a labor
market, giving it wage-setting power over workers. Bivens and Mishel
(2013) document how this mechanism has suppressed wage growth in the
United States over the past three decades, estimating that monopsony
rents account for roughly 25% of the gap between productivity and
compensation since 1979. [Bivens, J. and Mishel, L. (2013). ...]

After 3 epochs of SFT, two things have happened simultaneously. First, if “Bivens and Mishel (2013)”
appeared in the pre-training corpus with sufficient frequency, the model may have strengthened its association
between “monopsony,” “labor economics,” and that specific citation-a genuine knowledge reinforcement. Sec-
ond, and more likely for a 7B model trained on 1T tokens where this specific paper may appear only a handful of
times, the model has learned the pattern:[economics topic]! [prose introduction]![Author
Year (Year) summary sentence]. Now run inference on a different economics question:

Instruction: Write an introduction to oligopsony in shipping markets.

The model produces a fluent, well-formatted response ending with a fabricated citation-say, “Jensen and
Kowalski (2017)”-because the citation slot must be filled and the most probable tokens for that slot given the
structural pattern are a plausible author-year pair. The model did not retrieve; it completed a template.
To verify this at development time: before adding citation-heavy examples to your SFT set, probe the base
model with the underlying claims in isolation. If the model cannot reliably reproduce “Bivens and Mishel docu-
mented monopsony rents” in a zero-shot probe, that SFT example will train structural imitation, not knowledge
retrieval. Filter it out, or replace the citation with “according to labor economists” to keep the useful instruction-
following signal without encoding a specific fabrication pattern.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Probe before you fine-tune. Before including a factual claim or citation in SFT data, test whether the base
model can produce that fact unprompted. A simple consistency check-ask the same underlying question
five times and measure agreement-takes under an hour on a batch of examples and filters out the most
dangerous cases. Examples where the model is inconsistent or confidently wrong are the highest-risk
SFT candidates.
```

```
26.1 What SFT Can and Cannot Teach
```
```
Prefer abstention patterns over forced answers. If you cannot verify that the model knows a fact,
include a paired abstention example: the same input, with a response that says “I don’t have reliable
information on this specific point.” Training models to abstain gracefully is far more valuable than training
them to answer confidently and wrong. Even 100-200 abstention examples mixed into a 50,000-example
SFT set noticeably reduces fabrication rates on out-of-distribution queries.
Cap teacher-student capability gap. When generating SFT data from a stronger teacher model (e.g.,
using a 70B or GPT-4-class model to write responses for a 7B student), restrict examples to tasks the
student can plausibly learn. A practical heuristic: if the student’s loss on the teacher response exceeds
a threshold (typically 3-4 nats per token on held-out examples), that example is likely training structural
imitation and should be dropped or simplified.
Separate knowledge from format signals. If the goal is to teach the model a new response format
(chain-of-thought, JSON, structured summaries), use examples where the content is simple and already
well within the model’s knowledge. Combining novel format with novel content in the same examples
conflates two learning signals and increases hallucination risk. Teach format first on known content, then
introduce harder content once the format is stable.
SFT cannot fully solve this; RL is the complement. No amount of SFT data curation perfectly eliminates
hallucination, because you can never fully audit which facts a model “knows reliably.” On-policy RL with
a reward that penalizes factual errors-or even simple best-of-N rejection sampling-provides the adaptive
per-example correctness signal that SFT structurally cannot. Treat SFT as installing behavioral patterns,
and RL as correcting factual reliability on top of those patterns.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does fine-tuning sometimes increase hallucination rates compared to the base model?” Strong
answer: SFT applies loss unconditionally on all target tokens. When the training data contains claims the
model does not encode, the model minimizes loss by learning to structurally imitate the response format
rather than retrieve the underlying knowledge. This is cheapest in loss terms and generalizes badly-the
model learns to confidently complete response templates even without grounding.
“You are building a medical QA assistant using SFT on doctor-written responses. What data quality
checks would you run?” Strong answer: For each doctor-written response, probe the base model for
the underlying factual claims before including the example. Filter examples where the base model is
inconsistent or fabricates on similar queries. Include explicit abstention examples for edge cases. Consider
a lower-fidelity but factually safe alternative: simplify cited claims to general attributions, rather than
training the model to pattern-match specific author-year pairs it cannot verify.
“What is the relationship between SFT data quality and hallucination, and how does it motivate
RLHF?” Strong answer: High factual depth in SFT data is only safe when the model already possesses
the underlying knowledge. If there is a capability gap between the data and the model, SFT teaches
structural completion rather than knowledge retrieval. RLHF provides a correctness-conditional signal:
in PPO, rewards are only propagated for completions the model itself generates and that are judged correct,
so the model never takes gradient steps on knowledge it does not have.
Senior follow-up: “How would you design a data curation pipeline that automatically identifies
SFT examples likely to cause hallucination, at the scale of millions of examples?” The senior answer
involves a self-consistency filter: for each candidate SFT example, samplekcompletions from the base
```

### 26.2 SFT Data in Practice

```
model on the instruction alone (without the reference response). Compute agreement across samples
using a lightweight verifier or embedding similarity. Examples where base model completions show
high agreement with the reference response are safe; examples where the base model is inconsistent or
produces completions that contradict the reference are flagged as hallucination-risk examples. At scale,
run this filter on GPU with small-ksampling (say,k= 5) to keep cost manageable-this adds roughly 5
the inference cost of the SFT dataset but is far cheaper than dealing with hallucinating deployed models.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
SFT loss is unconditional: the model takes gradient steps on every target token regardless of whether it
has the underlying knowledge, creating an incentive to learn structural imitation over factual retrieval.
Fully correct, richly detailed SFT data can increase hallucination when the model does not already possess
the referenced facts-counterintuitive but well-documented.
The capability gap between teacher and student in distillation amplifies this risk; filter or simplify exam-
ples where the student’s per-token loss on the teacher response is abnormally high.
Mixing abstention examples (“I don’t know”) into SFT data is one of the few tractable SFT-level mitiga-
tions; RL with correctness-conditional rewards is the principled long-term fix.
At interview, connect this failure mode directly to the motivation for RLHF: RL’s on-policy correctness
signal is precisely what SFT lacks.
```
### 26.2 SFT Data in Practice

**26.2.1 Aggregated, Human-Written, and Model-Generated Data**
When a team puts you in charge of building the SFT pipeline for a new model, the first concrete question is
not which optimizer to use - it is where the training examples come from. Three distinct paradigms have emerged
across the open literature, each with a different cost profile and a different failure mode. Interviewers at frontier
labs ask about this because the data composition decision is real, made early, and has outsized downstream
consequences. Expect it at mid-to-senior level when the conversation shifts from “how does SFT work” to “how
would you actually build it.”
The first paradigm is _aggregated NLP data_. The idea is to take existing supervised benchmark datasets -
summarization, question answering, classification, slot filling - and reformat each example as a natural-language
instruction followed by the expected output. A summarization pair becomes “Write highlights for the following
article: [article]” and a classification pair becomes “What topic does this text cover? Options: business, sports,
politics.” The payoff is that you can assemble millions of examples at near-zero marginal cost. The cost is that
the resulting distribution looks nothing like a real chat interface: inputs are short and formulaic, outputs are
often single words or phrases, and the whole dataset retains the fingerprints of benchmark surgery. FLAN is the
canonical example of this approach, aggregating dozens of NLP tasks into one large metadata set.
The second paradigm is _human-written crowdsourced data_. Human annotators write both the instruction
and the response from scratch. When motivated and given enough time, they produce diverse, natural, high-
quality examples. The scaling problem is severe. Writing a thorough, accurate, multi-paragraph response to
a nuanced question takes ten to fifteen minutes for a skilled annotator. At $0.10-$0.50 per example, 100,000
examples costs $10,000-$50,000 and still may not cover the tails of the prompt distribution. In practice, time-
pressured annotators produce short, low-effort completions; the long, expert-quality responses in any crowd-


```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
sourced dataset tend to trace back either to domain experts or to AI copy-paste. OpenAssistant is the clearest
public example of this paradigm’s ceiling and its floor.
The third paradigm is _model-generated data_. A seed set of a few hundred human-written instructions is used
to prompt a capable model to generate both new instructions and their responses. Stanford Alpaca demonstrated
this at scale: GPT-3 completions filled in 52,000 instruction-response pairs at a cost under $500. The trade-off
is that the student model learns the teacher’s output distribution, including any hallucination tendencies, and the
diversity of the seed set limits the diversity of the generated set.
_SFT data paradigm choice is not a one-time decision but a mixing problem: each paradigm fills a different
gap in quality, cost, and coverage._
No single paradigm dominates on all axes. Aggregated NLP data wins on volume and is excellent for
breadth across structured tasks, but models trained on it consistently underperform on open-ended chat eval-
uations because they learn a benchmark-centric output style - short, formulaic, task-conditioned rather than
conversationally grounded.
Human-written data wins on naturalness and, when collected carefully, on factual accuracy. The problem
is scale. A well-run annotation campaign at a frontier lab might produce 100,000-200,000 examples. That is
enough to establish a strong behavioral baseline, but not enough to cover the long tail of real-world prompts.
The gap between what motivated annotators write and what time-pressured crowdworkers produce is also wider
than most engineers expect when they first run a labeling project.
Model-generated data has become the workhorse of modern SFT pipelines because it occupies the right
trade-off: cheap, naturally phrased, and scalable to tens of millions of examples. The failure mode to manage is
hallucination transfer. When the teacher model is significantly stronger than the student, the student may learn
to mimic the surface form of confident, detailed responses without having the underlying factual knowledge to
support them. The practical rule: keep teacher and student within roughly two to three capability levels of each
other, and audit generated responses for claims the student model could not have seen during pre-training.
The modern synthesis is mid-training: mixing SFT examples directly into the learning-rate decay phase of
pre-training rather than treating SFT as a separate post-training step. This sidesteps catastrophic forgetting and
allows the instruction-following signal to be learned at a deeper representational level.

**A Worked Example**

MiniCPM, an openly documented small-model series, illustrates the two-stage approach with concrete data.
Their training uses a Warm-up, Stable, Decay (WSD) learning-rate schedule totaling approximately 4  1012
tokens.
During the stable phase the data mix is entirely pre-training corpora: Common Crawl, code, the Pile, and
Dolma. During the decay phase - roughly the final 10% of total compute - the mix shifts substantially:
Wikipedia and high-quality curated web text (approximately 30% of the decay mix)
Instruction-following data: UltraChat, Evol-Instruct, OSS-Instruct (approximately 30%)
Code SFT and domain-specific Q&A: Stack Exchange, structured coding exercises (approximately 20%)
Continued general pre-training data to prevent catastrophic forgetting (approximately 20%)
The training loss drops sharply at the start of the decay phase, which practitioners interpret as the model
rapidly consolidating the instruction-following signal as the learning rate falls. After the decay phase, a short
conventional SFT run of a few thousand steps on the highest-quality subset reinforces instruction-following
behavior. Ablations from this work show that models trained with the two-stage approach outperform models


```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
fine-tuned only at the end, particularly on tasks requiring factual recall combined with instruction following -
exactly the regime where late-stage SFT risks catastrophic forgetting.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Validate mix ratios before committing to scale. Build a 50,000-100,000 example pilot from all three
paradigms and run evals before assembling a million-example pipeline. Relative proportions matter more
than total volume past a few hundred thousand examples.
Length bias is a real confounder. Both human raters and LM-as-judge systems prefer longer outputs
roughly 60-70% of the time independent of content quality. Never use chatbot-arena-style win rates as
your sole quality signal. Cross-check on capability benchmarks like MMLU or GSM8K where response
length cannot inflate scores.
SFT teaches format reliably; it does not teach new facts reliably. Fine-tuning will teach a model to
always respond in bullet points, to open with a summary sentence, or to append a disclaimer. It will not
reliably teach a model a fact absent from pre-training. SFT data containing citations or specific statistics
the model has never seen will produce the format of confident citation without the correct underlying
knowledge.
Crowdsourcing quality requires explicit incentive design. Paying per example produces short exam-
ples. Audit a random sample of every batch; set a minimum substantive length that requires genuine
content, not padding. Expect that the longest, most detailed responses in any crowdsourced set were
written by a small fraction of high-effort annotators or generated by AI and submitted directly.
Mid-training is worth the infrastructure cost at scale. If you have more than approximately 1 million
SFT examples and a pre-training pipeline already in place, mixing into the decay phase almost always
outperforms late-stage SFT on chat benchmarks and shows fewer signs of capability degradation.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through the trade-offs between FLAN-style aggregated data and model-generated data
for instruction tuning.” Strong answer: FLAN is cheap and broad but unnatural, producing benchmark-
centric output styles; model-generated data is more naturally phrased and scalable but risks hallucination
transfer when the teacher is much stronger than the student. Both tend to underperform human-written
data on naturalness but scale better on volume.
“Why might a model trained on high-quality, expert-level SFT data hallucinate more than one
trained on shorter, simpler responses?” Strong answer: when SFT examples contain knowledge the
model does not have from pre-training, the model learns the output structure - confident, detailed, cited
```
- without the factual content. It fills the structural template with plausible-sounding fabrications because
the loss penalizes wrong tokens more than it rewards honesty about uncertainty.
**“You have a limited annotation budget of $50,000. How do you allocate it across data paradigms
for a 7B model SFT run?”** Strong answer: use model-generated data from a strong API model for
breadth (500,000-1,000,000 examples at near-zero marginal cost), reserve the human budget for high-
value borderline and safety examples (5,000-10,000 carefully reviewed pairs), and fill structured-task
coverage gaps with aggregated NLP data.
**Senior follow-up: “How would you detect and correct for length bias in your SFT evaluation pipeline?”**
Senior answer: disaggregate win rates by output-length bracket; run a reward model trained explicitly to be


```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
```
length-neutral; compare chatbot-arena rankings against benchmark rankings and investigate divergences;
introduce length-controlled paired comparisons where both responses are truncated to the same token
count before human or model rating.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Three paradigms exist - aggregated NLP, crowdsourced human-written, and model-generated - each trad-
ing cost, naturalness, and scalability differently; modern pipelines blend all three.
SFT reliably shapes output format and style; teaching new factual knowledge requires that knowledge to
already exist in pre-training.
Length bias inflates both human and LM-judge preference scores by 60-70%; always cross-validate against
capability benchmarks that cannot be gamed by longer outputs.
Mid-training (mixing SFT data into the learning-rate decay phase) is the current state-of-practice at scale
and largely avoids catastrophic forgetting.
Crowdsourcing quality degrades sharply under time pressure; incentive design and batch auditing are as
important as vendor selection.
```
**26.2.2 Safety Tuning and Refusal Trade-Offs**
Every LLM that ships to users has to answer a practical question: what does the model do when someone
asks it to do something it should not do? The naive implementation is to collect harmful prompts and train
the model to output refusals. The problem is that a model trained only on refusals develops the wrong decision
boundary - it pattern-matches on surface features like the word “kill” and refuses “how do I kill a Python process”
alongside genuinely harmful requests. This failure mode is as important to understand as hallucination, and it
shows up in both early-stage design questions (“what is safety tuning?”) and senior-level architecture discussions
(“build me the safety data pipeline for a production model”).
Safety tuning is a targeted SFT procedure that teaches the model two distinct behaviors: when to refuse,
and how to do so gracefully without lecturing or over-explaining. The training data comes in two structurally
critical categories.
**Harmful examples** are (prompt, refusal) pairs where the prompt requests something clearly off-limits:
detailed instructions for generating scam content, synthesis routes for dangerous materials, targeted harassment
of a specific individual. The completion is a polite, brief refusal that acknowledges the request type without
restating it in detail.
**Borderline-positive examples** are (prompt, compliant response) pairs where the prompt superficially re-
sembles a harmful request but is entirely legitimate: a security researcher asking about exploit mechanics, a
physician asking about lethal medication doses for treatment planning, a sysadmin asking how to terminate a
process. These examples define the decision boundary from the other side. Without them, the model’s refusal
behavior drifts toward surface features of the harmful examples rather than their semantic intent.
The informal but important principle is: for any vocabulary clusterVthat appears prominently in harmful
prompts, the training data needs at least as many examples of legitimate uses ofVas harmful ones, or the model
learnsV )refuse rather than harmful_intent(V))refuse.
_A safety-tuned model that over-refuses is not safe - it is broken in a different direction, and the product
experience consequences are just as real._


```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
The finding that consistently surprises engineers new to post-training is how little data safety tuning needs.
Research across multiple groups has shown that even 500-1,000 safety examples mixed into a standard SFT run
produce a measurably safer model without meaningfully degrading capability benchmarks. The reason is that
the pre-trained model already encodes a strong representation of harm, danger, and ethics from the pre-training
corpus. Safety tuning does not teach the model what harm is - it teaches the model to act on that representation
by refusing rather than complying.
This is the same leverage principle that makes SFT powerful in general: capabilities are baked in during
pre-training; post-training steers the output mode. The corollary is equally important: safety tuning cannot
fundamentally fix a model that has deeply harmful behaviors embedded in its pre-training. It can redirect surface
outputs, not reorganize deep representations.
The over-refusal failure mode is symmetric to hallucination. In both cases the model defaults to a learned
surface pattern rather than grounding its response in the actual prompt content. Hallucination fills the response
template with invented facts; over-refusal fills the response template with a refusal pattern triggered by surface
keywords. Both are the same underlying problem: the model learned a shortcut that satisfies the type signature
of the training data without performing the intended reasoning.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you are fine-tuning a 7B parameter model on a 50,000-example general SFT corpus. You have a
budget for 1,000 additional safety examples. Consider two allocation strategies.
**Strategy A** uses all 1,000 as harmful-refuse pairs, covering topics such as fraud, dangerous synthesis, and
harassment.
**Strategy B** splits the budget: 500 harmful-refuse pairs plus 500 borderline-positive pairs using the same
vocabulary in legitimate contexts (technical jargon, medical queries, security research framing).
Evaluate on three metrics before and after each strategy:

1. **Refusal recall** : fraction of genuinely harmful prompts that receive a refusal. Target: above 95%.
2. **Refusal false-positive rate** : fraction of benign domain-specific prompts that receive a spurious refusal.
    Target: below 3%.
3. **MMLU accuracy** : should not degrade more than 0.5 absolute points from baseline SFT.
    With Strategy A a typical 7B model achieves refusal recall of approximately 97% but a false-positive rate
of 12-18%: the model learned to refuse any prompt containing vocabulary associated with harmful categories.
With Strategy B recall stays at 96-97% and the false-positive rate falls to 2-4%. MMLU degrades by less than 0.3
points in both cases. The composition of the borderline-positive set is what drives the improvement: examples
must share the same surface vocabulary as the harmful set but carry clearly legitimate framing, forcing the model
to attend to framing rather than vocabulary alone.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Start at 1-2% safety data in the SFT mix. If your overall SFT corpus is 500,000 examples, start with
5,000-10,000 safety examples. Going above 5% of the total mix begins to noticeably degrade helpfulness
and general-capability benchmarks without proportional safety gains.
Match borderline-positive examples to harmful examples topic by topic. For every category of harm-
ful prompts you cover - synthesis instructions, fraud scripts, targeted harassment - write an equal number
```

```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
```
of borderline-positive examples that use the same surface vocabulary in a legitimate context. Without this
pairing, your model will over-refuse entire topic areas rather than specific intents.
Refuse at the intent level, not the topic level. A topic-level rule such as “always refuse chemistry ques-
tions” will break legitimate medical and research use cases and will visibly frustrate users. Train the
model to identify malicious intent within a topic, not the topic itself. This requires examples that make
the distinction explicit, often with a brief explanation of why the request is complied with.
Track refusal recall and false-positive rate on separate dashboard rows. An aggregate safety score
that combines recall and precision hides over-refusal regressions behind high recall numbers. A model
that refuses 99% of harmful prompts but also refuses 15% of benign technical queries is not a good model.
Both numbers need to be visible and gated on.
Safety properties degrade with continued post-training. Every subsequent SFT or RLHF round can
erode safety behavior if safety data is not re-included in proportion. Schedule red-team evaluations after
every major post-training update, not only at initial release. Safety is not a one-time certification.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How do you build safety tuning data and what is the most common mistake?” Strong answer: col-
lect both harmful-refuse pairs and borderline-positive pairs in roughly equal numbers. The most common
mistake is collecting only harmful examples, which teaches the model to pattern-match on surface vocab-
ulary rather than infer intent, causing high false-positive refusal rates on legitimate technical or domain
queries.
“A user reports that the model refuses ‘how do I kill a Python process.’ Walk me through diagnosing
and fixing this.” Strong answer: (1) confirm the issue is reproducible on a held-out eval set; (2) inspect the
safety training data for over-representation of the vocabulary cluster around “kill” in harmful-refuse pairs;
(3) add borderline-positive examples using the same technical vocabulary in clearly legitimate contexts;
(4) re-evaluate refusal recall to confirm the fix does not degrade safety recall; (5) add the repro case to the
false-positive eval set so regression is detected automatically in future runs.
Senior follow-up: “Design an eval suite that simultaneously detects regressions in safety and help-
fulness after any data update.” Senior answer: maintain a fixed red-team set of approximately 500
harmful prompts measuring recall and a fixed borderline set of approximately 500 benign-but-surface-
risky prompts measuring false-positive rate; gate model releases on both passing defined thresholds; in-
clude MMLU and a chat-style benchmark to catch capability regressions; track all four metrics on a single
release dashboard so no individual regression is absorbed by an aggregate score passing.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Even 500-1,000 safety examples produce measurable impact; the pre-trained model already encodes harm
representations - safety SFT steers the output mode, not the underlying knowledge.
Borderline-positive examples are as important as harmful examples; omitting them causes topic-level
over-refusal rather than intent-level refusal.
Track refusal recall and refusal false-positive rate independently; aggregate safety scores hide over-refusal
regressions behind high recall numbers.
Keep safety data at 1-2% of the SFT mix; above 5% measurably harms helpfulness without proportional
safety gains.
```

```
26.2 SFT Data in Practice
```
Safety behavior degrades with continued post-training; schedule red-team evaluations after every major
update, not only at initial release.


## Chapter 27 Preference-Based Alignment (RLHF)

### 27.1 The RLHF Pipeline

**27.1.1 Pairwise Preference Collection**
You are asked in a system design interview to improve a model that has already been fine-tuned on ex-
pert demonstrations. The interviewer wants to know what comes next. The canonical answer is reinforcement
learning from human feedback-and the first question you will face is where the feedback comes from. Pairwise
preference collection is the annotation backbone of the entire RLHF pipeline: the mechanism that converts
vague human preferences into a learnable scalar signal. This topic appears consistently at senior ML engineer
and research scientist interviews at any lab running a post-training pipeline, and the ability to reason about
annotation quality, cost trade-offs, and systematic biases separates a strong answer from a shallow one.
The fundamental shift from supervised fine-tuning to RLHF is a shift in what you ask humans to do. In
SFT you ask: _write the ideal completion_. In RLHF you ask: _which of these two completions is better?_ The first
question demands generation; the second demands only discrimination. Humans are systematically better at the
second task-they can reliably judge quality even when they cannot produce it themselves under time pressure or
without deep domain expertise.
The standard setup is straightforward. Given a promptx, the current model generatesk 2 candidate
responsesfy 1 ,... , ykg. An annotator reviews pairs(yA, yB)and marks a preference: A is better, B is better,
or roughly equal. Each labeled pair becomes training signal for a reward model. The InstructGPT annotation
guidelines operationalized this with three axes to judge: helpfulness, truthfulness, and harmlessness.
The optimization objective that consumes these preferences is:

```

The first term maximizes the learned reward; the KL penalty keeps the RL policy from drifting too far from
the SFT initialization, suppressing reward hacking and preserving fluent language generation. In practiceβsits
in the range 0. 01 - 0. 1 ; larger values produce more conservative, SFT-like outputs.
_Pairwise feedback exploits the generator-validator gap: humans validate far more reliably than they gen-
erate, and RLHF collects supervision by asking the easier of the two questions._
SFT has a structural bottleneck: demonstration quality is bounded by what annotators can produce under
real-world constraints. When you ask a crowd to write completions for a nuanced question about Bayesian in-
ference or macroeconomic policy, you get short, hedged, often incomplete responses-because producing expert-
level prose in five minutes under pay-per-task conditions is genuinely hard. You are paying for the full cognitive
cost of generation.
Pairwise comparison costs a fraction of that. The same annotator who would spend fifteen minutes writing
a mediocre demonstration can evaluate two strong model-generated responses in two to three minutes and give
you a reliable ranking. Empirically, inter-annotator agreement on pairwise helpfulness judgments runs around
70-80%, which is comparable to the agreement you get from a strong AI judge. That signal-cheaper to collect
and often more consistent than demonstrations on the same budget-is what reward model training runs on.
The trade-off is information density. A demonstration gives you a full token-level trajectory; a pairwise
comparison gives you one bit of relative signal. You compensate with volume: InstructGPT trained its reward


```
27.1 The RLHF Pipeline
```
model on roughly 50,000 pairwise comparisons while using only about 13,000 SFT demonstrations. Because
the model itself generates both responses, on-policy rollouts produce new pairs at near-zero marginal cost once
the infrastructure is in place.

**A Worked Example**

Suppose you are building an RLHF annotation pipeline for a 7B chat model and you have a $50,000 anno-
tation budget. Expert annotators cost roughly $25 per hour.
_Option A-SFT demonstrations:_ a high-quality multi-paragraph demonstration takes approximately twenty
minutes to write, costing about $8.33 per example. Your budget yields roughly 6,000 demonstrations.
_Option B-pairwise feedback:_ judging a pair takes approximately five minutes, costing about $2.08 per
comparison. The same budget yields roughly 24,000 comparisons. The model itself generates both responses,
so annotation cost does not scale with response length.
The quality picture is even starker. In my experience watching large-scale annotation projects, speed con-
straints destroy signal quality for anything requiring verification. Reports from a production assistant’s annota-
tion guidelines described a target rate of approximately one judgment per minute per question. At that pace an
annotator must read two responses of several hundred words each, compare them on helpfulness and safety, and
check the relevant box-leaving no time to verify embedded citations or check arithmetic. Studies of crowdworker
behavior under speed pressure confirm what you would expect: annotators correlate strongly with formatting
signals (bullet-point density, paragraph count, word count) and weakly with factual accuracy.
Consider the summarization case: expert writers asked to compare their own summaries to model-generated
ones showed a consistent preference for the AI outputs. One explanation collected in a follow-up interview:
“When I wrote, I felt pressure to use flowery language. The AI ones just read better.” Generation and evalua-
tion are different cognitive tasks, and people are often better at the latter-even when judging their own work.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Human vs. AI feedback. GPT-4-class models agree with human consensus at roughly 70-75% on ca-
pability judgments-on par with human inter-annotator agreement-at orders of magnitude lower cost. For
most helpfulness and instruction-following axes, AI feedback is the production default today. Reserve
human annotation for high-stakes safety and factual domains where a rubric cannot fully capture the
judgment required.
Control for length bias explicitly. Both humans and AI judges prefer longer responses at a 60-70% base
rate, independent of quality. If you ignore this, your reward model learns to produce verbose outputs rather
than correct ones. Fix it by including length-controlled pairs in your annotation set, by adding an explicit
conciseness criterion to the rubric, or by normalizing response length during reward model training.
On-policy data is more valuable than off-policy data for reward model training. On-policy pairs-
where both responses come from the model you are currently optimizing-anchor the reward model to
the policy distribution you actually care about. Off-policy data from unrelated models adds distributional
coverage early in training but becomes stale quickly as your model improves. Refreshing pairwise datasets
every major training iteration is the standard pattern at labs running continuous post-training.
Annotator demographics shape model values. RLHF sits at the end of the pipeline and has outsized
influence on surface behavior. When the annotator pool skews toward a particular nationality or cultural
background, the resulting model shows measurably stronger alignment with that group’s norms-detectable
```

```
27.1 The RLHF Pipeline
```
```
in controlled probing studies. Audit annotator composition before deployment, especially on topics where
cultural context affects what counts as helpful or harmful.
AI self-preference is a real confound in evals. When you use a model to judge its own outputs versus a
competitor’s, it exhibits strong self-preference at rates that do not correspond to human rankings. Always
use a judge model that is distinct from the model under evaluation; otherwise your win-rate numbers are
systematically inflated.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does RLHF outperform SFT for instruction following at scale?” Strong answer: SFT is
bounded by what annotators can generate under time and cost pressure; pairwise preference collection
exploits the generator-validator gap, extracting more usable signal per annotation dollar. The KL diver-
gence penalty in the training objective keeps the RL policy grounded in the SFT distribution, preventing
the degenerate outputs that unconstrained reward maximization produces.
“What are the main failure modes of pairwise preference collection?” Strong answer: length bias (60-
70% preference for longer responses regardless of quality), inability to verify facts under speed pressure,
AI judge self-preference bias, and annotator demographic skew that embeds cultural assumptions into the
reward model.
Senior follow-up: “How do you detect whether your reward model has learned real quality or just
superficial style?” Strong answer: hold out a set of pairwise examples where ground truth is indepen-
dently verifiable-math problems with known answers, code with executable test suites, factual QA with
reference sources. Measure reward model ranking accuracy on this set. If RM scores correlate more
strongly with response length than with ground-truth correctness, the model has overfit to style. Fix it by
augmenting the pairwise training set with verified correct-versus-incorrect pairs, adding explicit accuracy
and conciseness dimensions to the annotation rubric, and-where possible-using verifiable rewards (correct
math, passing tests) to anchor the preference signal.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Pairwise feedback exploits the generator-validator gap: judging two responses requires a fraction of the
time and expertise needed to generate a high-quality demonstration from scratch, which is why the same
annotation budget buys roughly four times as many pairwise comparisons as SFT examples.
The InstructGPT training objective couples reward maximization with a KL penalty against the SFT
model, keeping the RL policy from drifting into degenerate, reward-hacking outputs.
AI judges at the GPT-4 class match human inter-annotator agreement at roughly 70-75% on most capabil-
ity axes and are the production default at scale today; human annotation is reserved for high-stakes safety
and factual verification tasks.
Length bias is a systematic confound: both humans and AI judges show a 60-70% base preference for
longer responses independent of quality; failing to control for it trains a reward model that optimizes
verbosity.
On-policy pairwise data-pairs generated by the model currently under optimization-is more valuable than
off-policy data and should be refreshed regularly as the model improves.
```

```
27.1 The RLHF Pipeline
```
**27.1.2 Reward Modeling and the Bradley-Terry Assumption**
You have collected tens of thousands of pairwise preference labels and you need to turn them into a signal
that a neural network can optimize against. The interviewer asks: “How does a collection of binary A-vs-B
comparisons become a reward function?” The answer is a probabilistic assumption called the Bradley-Terry
model and a reward model trained by maximum likelihood on that assumption. This topic comes up at MLE
and research scientist interviews whenever RLHF is on the table, and the depth of your answer-whether you can
derive the loss from first principles, name its failure modes, and explain when you would skip the reward model
entirely-is what separates candidates at the senior and staff levels.
The Bradley-Terry model posits a latent, scalar-valued ground truth: every possible responseyto a prompt
xhas a true scalar rewardr(x, y) 2 R. We never observerdirectly. What we observe is noisy pairwise

the annotator is effectively flipping a coin.
Given a datasetD=f(xi, yiw, yil)gNi=1of pairwise labels, training a reward modelrφmeans maximizing
the log-likelihood of the observed preferences under this model. The negative log-likelihood loss is:

MinimizingLpushesrφ(x, yw)aboverφ(x, yl)for every observed preferred pair-exactly the ranking we
