In practice,rφis implemented by taking a pre-trained language model, discarding the vocabulary projection
head, and adding a single linear layer that maps the final hidden state of the last token to a scalar. The resulting
network reads the concatenation of prompt and response and outputs one number: the estimated quality of that
response.
_The reward model is the bridge between human preference data and an optimization landscape: it converts
a discrete ranking over pairs into a continuous, differentiable signal that the RL training loop can ascend._
The Bradley-Terry assumption is the minimal probabilistic model that is consistent with pairwise prefer-
ence data. It has one free parameter per sequence-the latent reward-and generates binary comparisons via a
logistic noise model. That simplicity is a feature: the loss function is convex in the reward differences and
well-understood, and the model generalizes beyond the observed pairs becauserφis parameterized by a neural
network that shares weights across all prompts and responses.
The key advantage over alternatives is coverage. If you trained only on SFT demonstrations you would
have no way to score outputs the model generates at RL time-the reward model fills that gap, acting as a proxy
judge for any(x, y)pair the policy might produce, including ones never seen during data collection.
The critical trade-off is that the reward model is a proxy, not the true objective. It is trained on a finite
sample of human comparisons, which means it has blind spots: regions of output space where it assigns high
reward to responses that humans would reject. The standard mitigation is the KL penalty in the RL objective,
which keeps the policy close enough to the SFT distribution that the reward model’s estimates remain reliable.


```
27.1 The RLHF Pipeline
```
When the policy strays too far from that distribution-a phenomenon called _reward overoptimization_ -RM scores
continue rising while actual human preference scores plateau and eventually fall.

**A Worked Example**

Consider training a reward model for a 7B chat model. You have 50,000 pairwise comparisons collected
on 10,000 distinct prompts (roughly five comparisons per prompt).
**Architecture.** Start from the 7B SFT checkpoint. Replace the final unembedding matrix (vocabulary
dimension32,000) with a single linear layer mapping from the model’s hidden dimension (d= 4, 096 ) to a
scalar. Total added parameters: 4,096. The remaining 7B parameters are fine-tuned on the reward modeling
loss.
**Batch construction.** Each training example is a triplet(x, yw, yl). Bothywandylare concatenated withx
and forward-passed through the same network in a single batch. You read off the scalar at the last token position
for each, then computeσ(rφ(x, yw)rφ(x, yl))and take the log. A batch of 64 pairs requires two forward
passes of the 7B model, so effective batch size for memory purposes is 128 sequences.
**Numbers.** With 50,000 pairs, a learning rate of 1  10 −^5 , and 1-2 epochs of training on an H100 (roughly
80 GB HBM), reward model training typically completes in a few hours. The resulting RM achieves human
preference accuracy (does the RM agree with the human annotator on held-out pairs?) of around 65-72% on
general helpfulness tasks and lower on specialized factual domains-which is the quantitative signal you use to
decide whether the RM is good enough to drive RL training.
**Calibration check.** Evaluate RM score versus ground-truth preference on a held-out factual QA set where
correct answers are known. If Spearman correlation between RM score and factual accuracy is below 0.5, the
RM is primarily scoring style and the RL run will optimize verbosity rather than correctness.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Reward model size relative to policy size. The RM does not need to be as large as the policy. In
production pipelines I have seen 3B RMs driving 70B RL runs effectively. A smaller RM trains faster
and is easier to refresh as new preference data arrives. The floor is that the RM must be large enough to
understand the semantic content it is scoring; going below roughly one quarter of the policy size tends to
hurt quality noticeably.
Margin-based loss variants. The standard Bradley-Terry loss treats all pairs equally regardless of how
clear the human preference was. Many teams add an annotation confidence score and train with a margin
term:
L=logσ
```

```
When to skip the explicit reward model (DPO). If your dataset is fixed and you do not need to run
on-policy rollouts, Direct Preference Optimization eliminates the RM entirely by reparameterizing the
reward in terms of the policy’s own log-probability ratio. DPO is simpler to implement and avoids RM
training costs. Use it when your pairwise data is off-policy and relatively small (≲100K pairs). Use an
explicit RM when you need on-policy rollouts at RL time-the RM must score live outputs that do not exist
```

```
Distribution shift is the main failure mode. The RM is calibrated on responses similar to those in the
pairwise dataset. As RL training proceeds, the policy shifts and its outputs diverge from the RM’s training
distribution. Monitor RM score versus human evaluation score on a rolling held-out set throughout RL
training; if they diverge, either stop training, refresh the RM with on-policy preference data, or tighten
the KL coefficientβ.
Ensemble or leave-one-out calibration for high-stakes deployment. A single RM can overfit to anno-
tation artifacts. Training two or three RMs from different random seeds and using their minimum score
(rather than mean) as the optimization target is a practical hedge against reward overoptimization in pro-
duction settings where you cannot run frequent human evals.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you train a reward model from pairwise preferences.” Strong answer: start
with the Bradley-Terry model-each response has a latent scalar reward, preferences are logistic in the
reward difference-then write the negative log-likelihood loss over preferred and rejected pairs. Implement
as a pretrained LM with the vocab head replaced by a scalar linear layer. Train with learning rate around
10 −^5 for 1-2 epochs; evaluate with held-out pairwise accuracy.
“What can go wrong with reward model training and how do you detect it?” Strong answer: the two
main failure modes are length bias (RM scores longer responses higher regardless of quality) and distri-
bution shift during RL (RM extrapolates incorrectly to outputs it was not trained on). Detect length bias
by measuring correlation of RM scores with response length on a neutral prompt set; detect distribution
shift by tracking the gap between RM score and human eval score as RL training progresses.
Senior follow-up: “When would you choose DPO over training an explicit reward model?” Strong
answer: DPO reparameterizes the reward in terms of the policy’s own log-ratio, eliminating the RM and
the RL training loop. It is the right choice when the pairwise dataset is static (you will not collect on-
policy preferences), the policy is moderate in size (under30B), and you want a simpler pipeline. Use an
explicit RM plus PPO when you need on-policy rollouts-live scoring of model-generated outputs that do
not exist in any precomputed dataset-or when your RM needs to be shared across multiple policy variants.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The Bradley-Terry model assumes every response has a latent scalar reward; pairwise preferences are lo-
gistic in the reward difference, giving a clean maximum-likelihood training objective: minimizelogσ(rφ(x, yw)
rφ(x, yl))over all preference pairs.
The reward model is architecturally a pretrained LM with its vocabulary head replaced by a single scalar
linear layer; it is trained on the same pairwise data and produces a continuous quality estimate for any
(x, y)the policy might generate.
The RM is a proxy, not the true objective: it generalizes poorly to outputs far from its training distribution,
so the KL penalty in the RL objective is essential for keeping the policy in-distribution for the RM.
The primary failure mode is reward overoptimization: RM scores rise while true human preference scores
plateau or fall; monitor with a rolling held-out human eval throughout RL training and refresh the RM
when divergence appears.
When pairwise data is static and on-policy rollouts are not needed, DPO eliminates the explicit RM by
```

### 27.2 Optimization Algorithms

**27.2.1 PPO for Language Models**
You are asked in an interview to design the optimization loop that turns a reward model into a better
language model policy. The moment you say “gradient descent on the reward,” the follow-up is: “what exactly
is your loss, and why do you need a value network?” PPO is the answer InstructGPT gave in 2022, and frontier
labs continued using variants of it long after DPO arrived. Understanding PPO concretely-not just as a named
algorithm but as a sequence of decisions-is the minimum bar for an RLHF deep-dive at the staff-engineer level.
The goal is to find a policyπθthat maximizes expected reward while staying close to the supervised fine-
tuned reference modelπref. The InstructGPT objective formalizes this as:

```
maxπ
θ
Ex∼D, y∼πθ(·|x)[rφ(x, y)]β DKL(πθ(jx)kπref(jx))
```
The KL term keeps the RL policy from drifting so far fromπrefthat it produces fluent-sounding but reward-
hacked outputs. The scalarβis a regularization coefficient; typical values range from 0.01 to 0.1.
Starting from the plain policy gradient, the gradient ofEπθ[r(z)]with respect toθequalsEπθ[r(z)rθlogπθ(z)].
This is _REINFORCE_ : multiply the log-probability gradient by the reward and update accordingly. It is unbiased
but high-variance. Two refinements turn it into PPO.
First, replace the raw reward with an _advantage_ At-the reward minus a learned state-value baselineVφ(st).
Subtracting any baseline that does not depend on the current action leaves the gradient unbiased while dra-
matically reducing variance. In practiceAtis computed via Generalized Advantage Estimation (GAE) with
hyperparametersλandγ; setting both to 1 collapses GAE to a simple return-minus-baseline form, which al-
ready works well.
Second, allow multiple gradient steps on a single set of rollouts using importance-weighted corrections. If
the current policy isπθbut samples came from the olderπθold, the corrected objective becomes:

LCLIP(θ) =Et[min(ρtAt,clip(ρt, 1 ε,1 +ε)At)], ρt=
πθ(atjst)
πθold(atjst)
The clip removes any incentive to push the probability ratio outside[1ε,1+ε]; a typical value isε= 0. 2.
This is the PPO-Clip objective-no KL constraint to tune, just a hard floor and ceiling on how much the policy
can shift per update.
_PPO is policy gradient with variance reduction via a value baseline, importance weighting for multi-step
updates, and a clipping constraint that naturally keeps the new policy close to the old one._
The plain policy gradient fails at scale because its gradient variance grows with sequence length-a 512-
token response has 512 token-level log-probabilities whose products create enormous variance. Subtracting the
value baseline brings that variance down to something tractable without introducing bias.
The clipping mechanism does something subtle: it makes the optimization landscape less adversarial.
Without clipping, a lucky update can send the policy into a region of high reward-model scores but low actual
quality. Clipping hard-caps how far a single update can travel, which is especially important in the first few
thousand steps when the reward model is most at risk of being exploited.


```
27.2 Optimization Algorithms
```
Compared to the alternative of using a hard KL constraint (TRPO), PPO is much simpler to implement and
tune. TRPO requires a second-order computation to enforce the constraint; PPO replaces that with a clip and
a step-size schedule. The performance tradeoff is minimal, which is why PPO absorbed TRPO’s market share
almost entirely after its 2017 release.
The cost is real, though: PPO for language models requires _four_ live models-the policy, the reference policy,
the reward model, and the value model. The value model is typically as large as the policy, so GPU memory
roughly doubles compared to SFT.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 7B parameter policy (e.g. Llama-3-7B) in bf16 on 8H100 80 GB GPUs, with a 7B reward
model and a 7B value model.
**Memory budget.** Each 7B model in bf16 uses roughly 14 GB for weights. With activations and optimizer
state, a single model consumes around 60-80 GB during a forward-backward pass. Running policy+reference
+reward+value simultaneously requires memory-efficient strategies: the reference and reward models are
frozen (no gradients), so they can be kept in inference mode at14 GB each. Total active memory:14 (ref)
+14 (reward)+70 (value, with optimizer)+70 (policy, with optimizer)168 GB, which fits across 8 80
GB with tensor parallelism.
**One PPO step, end to end.**

1. **Rollout.** SampleB= 64prompts from the dataset; run the policy autoregressively to generate responses
    of up to 512 tokens. This is the slow step: at 5,000 tokens/s on an H100 with vLLM, 64 sequences of 512
    tokens takes6.5 seconds.
2. **Reward and value computation.** Feed each (prompt, response) pair through the reward model to get
    scalarr(x, y). Feed each token through the value model to getVφ(st)at every position.
3. **KL penalty.** Compute per-token KL:klt= logπθ(atjst)logπref(atjst). Addβkltto the terminal
    reward to build a per-token reward signal.
4. **GAE.** Withγ= 1,λ= 0. 95 , compute advantagesAtbackward from the last token.
5. **Policy update.** RunK= 4mini-batch gradient steps onLCLIPwithε= 0. 2. Monitor the mean ratioρt;
    if it drifts above 1.3 consistently, reduce learning rate or decreaseK.
6. **Value update.** Run a parallel MSE loss on the value head to keepVφ(st)calibrated.
    In practice, 1,000 such PPO steps on 64K training prompts takes 6-8 hours on this hardware. Reward
usually peaks and plateaus within the first 500 steps; continuing further without increasing data diversity leads
to overoptimization.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
β , the KL coeﬀicient. Start at 0.04-0.1. If you see the KL divergence from the SFT model exceeding
10 nats after a few hundred steps, increaseβ. If reward barely moves, lower it. Some implementations
annealβduring training.
Number of PPO epochs per rollout batch ( K ). Common choices are 1-4. More epochs extract more
signal per rollout, but stale importance weights cause the clip to activate more and gradients become
increasingly biased. AtK= 1you are essentially doing online policy gradient without any staleness;
K= 4requires careful monitoring.
```

```
27.2 Optimization Algorithms
```
```
Value model initialization. Always initialize the value model from the same checkpoint as the policy,
not randomly. A poorly initialized value model produces high-variance advantages for the first thousands
of steps and can destabilize training. Add a warm-up phase of pure value training on rollouts before joint
optimization if instability appears.
Reward shaping: per-token vs. terminal. The true task reward (“did the model answer correctly?”) is
a terminal reward on the last token. The KL penalty is applied per token. Never add the terminal reward
to every token-this creates a heavily biased gradient that overweights early tokens in the response. Assign
terminal reward only at the EOS token position.
Memory vs. throughput tradeoff. If GPU memory is the bottleneck, offload the frozen reference and
reward models to CPU between rollout batches. This trades30% throughput for halving active GPU
memory. Alternatively, quantize the reference and reward models to int8 (they are frozen, so QAT is
unnecessary).
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through the PPO loop for a language model.”
Strong answer: describe the four models, the rollout step, reward computation, KL penalty construction,
GAE advantage estimation, and the clipped surrogate loss. Name the clip rangeεand the KL coefficient
βwith representative numbers. Many candidates skip the value model or the KL shaping entirely.
“Why can’t you just do gradient ascent directly on the reward model output?”
Strong answer: reward models are finite-capacity proxies; direct gradient ascent exploits their blind spots
(overoptimization). The KL term and the clip prevent the policy from moving too far into high-reward-
model-score but low-true-quality regions. Without these constraints, you get reward hacking within hun-
dreds of steps.
“What is the value model for in PPO, and can you remove it?”
Strong answer: the value model provides a variance-reducing baseline for the policy gradient. Without it,
gradient variance scales with sequence length and training is unstable. You can remove it, and GRPO does
exactly this by replacing the value baseline with a group mean reward, at the cost of requiring multiple
rollouts per prompt to compute that baseline.
Senior follow-up: “PPO for an LLM is actually a contextual bandit, not a full MDP. What changes?”
In a contextual bandit, there are no intermediate state transitions: the prompt is the context, the full
response is the action, and the reward arrives once. This means the credit assignment problem simplifies-
you do not need multi-step Bellman backups. The consequence is thatγcan safely be set to 1 without
worrying about discounting future states, and the value function only needs to estimate the expected
return of the entire completion rather than a trajectory. The KL penalty still matters as a regularizer, but
it is applied token-by-token as a reward shaping term rather than as a constraint over state transitions.
Recognizing the bandit structure is why GRPO can discard the value network entirely and use a within-
group mean as a baseline without loss of correctness.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
PPO requires four live models during training: policy, reference (frozen), reward (frozen), and value.
The value model is the primary memory and complexity cost; its role is variance reduction via advantage
estimation.
```

```
27.2 Optimization Algorithms
```
```
The clip rangeε= 0. 2 prevents any single update from moving the policy too far from its previous state,
replacing the second-order KL constraint of TRPO with a simpler and cheaper mechanism.
In the language-model setting, the reward is a terminal scalar; the KL divergence from the reference policy
is applied per token as a shaped per-step penalty, not as a hard constraint.
Reward peaks and then plateaus or declines as the policy begins to exploit the reward model’s weaknesses;
monitoring KL divergence and true human preference win-rates together is the only reliable way to catch
overoptimization early.
GRPO eliminates the value model by computing a group-mean baseline over multiple rollouts of the same
prompt, making it the practical default when memory and implementation complexity are constraints.
```
**27.2.2 DPO and Its Derivation**
At some point in any RLHF system design discussion, the interviewer will ask why you need PPO at all.
The correct answer is: you often do not. Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) removes the reward model,
the value model, and the RL loop entirely, collapsing the RLHF objective into a supervised cross-entropy loss
over preference pairs. It is the algorithm behind nearly every open-weight RLHF release between mid-2023 and
late-2024, and understanding its derivation is what separates a candidate who has “used DPO” from one who
actually understands it.

There is no reward model parameter to train, no value network, and no rollout loop. Bothπθ(the policy
being trained) andπref(the frozen SFT checkpoint) are evaluated on the already-collected preferred and rejected
completions, making every gradient step a standard forward-backward pass.


```
27.2 Optimization Algorithms
```
_DPO turns the RL problem into supervised learning by showing that the optimal policy and the reward
function are two parametrizations of the same object, so you can optimize preference likelihood directly without
ever representing the reward explicitly._
PPO requires on-policy rollouts: you must sample from your current policy, evaluate those samples with
the reward model, and update. DPO is fully offline: it consumes a static dataset of (prompt, chosen, rejected)
triples. This eliminates the slowest part of RLHF-autoregressive generation at training time-and removes the
need for a reward model and a value model, halving the GPU memory requirement compared to PPO.
The DPO gradient has an interpretable form. Letrˆθ(x, y) = βlog(πθ(yjx)/πref(yjx))be the implicit
reward. The gradient upweights the chosen completion and downweights the rejected completion, with a weight
equal toσ(ˆrθ(yl)rˆθ(yw))-the probability that the model currently gets the pair wrong. When the model
already ranks the pair correctly (weight near 0), the gradient is small; updates concentrate on hard examples.
This is analogous to focal loss in classification.
The tradeoff vs. PPO is that DPO is offline: it never generates new completions to explore the reward
landscape. If the reference policyπrefnever produced diverse enough completions during dataset construction,
DPO cannot escape that blind spot. Online variants (iterative DPO, RLHF-Flow) address this by periodically
regenerating the rejected set from the current policy, recovering much of PPO’s on-policy advantage while
keeping the simpler loss.

**A Worked Example**

Setup: a 7B model (Mistral-7B-v0.1) fine-tuned with SFT to produceπref, now trained with DPO on the
UltraFeedback dataset (60K preference pairs), in bf16 on 4A100 80 GB GPUs.
**Memory.** The policyπθrequires70 GB with optimizer states (AdamW + gradient buffers). The reference
πrefis frozen and kept in bf16 inference mode:14 GB. Total:84 GB across 480 GB GPUs with no tensor
parallelism needed-compare to PPO’s>160 GB.
**One DPO gradient step.**
Assume a mini-batch of 4 triples(xi, yw,i, yl,i)with max sequence length 512.

1. Forward passπθon all 8 sequences (ywandylconcatenated with their prompts): compute token log-
    probabilities, sum over response tokens only to getlogπθ(ywjx)andlogπθ(yljx).
2. Forward passπrefon the same 8 sequences (no gradient): getlogπref(ywjx)andlogπref(yljx).
3. Compute implicit rewards:ˆrw=β(logπθ(ywjx)logπref(ywjx)), similarlyrˆl.
4. Loss:L=logσ(ˆrwrˆl), average over the batch.
5. Backward onL; updateπθonly (ref is frozen).
    Withβ= 0. 1 and a well-initialized SFT model,rˆwˆrlstarts near 0 (the model does not yet distinguish
the pairs) and should reach3-5 nats on average after a full epoch. At a batch size of 32 and 60K examples,
one epoch is 1,875 steps; a full DPO run on 4A100 takes roughly 2-3 hours.
**Implicit reward check.** After training, verify thatβlog(πθ(ywjx)/πref(ywjx))> βlog(πθ(yljx)/πref(yljx))
on a held-out preference set. Accuracy below 65% on this proxy metric is a strong signal thatβis too large
(over-regularizing) or the SFT checkpoint was too weak to start.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
β , the temperature parameter. This controls how tightly the policy stays nearπref. Values in[0. 05 , 0 .5]
are common; start at 0.1. Too small: the policy drifts far from the reference and can produce degenerate
```

```
27.2 Optimization Algorithms
```
```
outputs. Too large: effectively no change from SFT. Monitor KL divergence fromπrefon a validation set;
target 5-15 nats after training.
Length normalization. Sum log-probabilities over response tokens without normalization biases the loss
toward shorter sequences, which receive higher per-token log-probability on average. SimPO and length-
normalized DPO divide the log-probability sum by sequence length before computing the reward margin.
This simple fix measurably reduces the model’s preference for very short responses; use it by default.
Offline vs. iterative. Static offline DPO is fast but brittle when the reject set is low-quality or the SFT
model is strong. If your rejected completions are all from an early, weak model, the policy learns to beat
a low bar and does not generalize. Regenerate the rejected set from your current policy every 1-2 epochs
(online DPO) to keep the training signal challenging and on-distribution.
Chosen completion collapse. A silent failure mode: as the policy is pushed away from the rejected com-
pletion, the log-probability of the chosen completion can also decrease. Tracklogπθ(ywjx)logπref(ywjx)
separately during training; if it goes negative and keeps falling, the model is degrading on the positive
examples, not just improving on the negative ones. Reduce learning rate or add a supervised term on
chosen completions.
Data quality beats data quantity. On 7B-scale models, 10K high-quality human preference pairs (from
annotators with explicit factuality checks) consistently outperform 200K AI-generated pairs in down-
stream benchmarks. The DPO loss is sensitive to label noise: a single flipped pair in a batch contributes
a gradient in the wrong direction with full weight.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Derive DPO from first principles.”
Strong answer: state the KL-regularized RL objective, take the non-parametric optimum, solve for the
implied reward, substitute into Bradley-Terry, and show thatZ(x)cancels. Many candidates can name
DPO; very few can reproduce the derivation under pressure. Practice the three-step: optimal policy form
!implied reward!preference loss.
“When would you use PPO instead of DPO?”
Strong answer: when rewards are verifiable (math, code), when you need on-policy exploration to escape
the static offline data distribution, or when the preference dataset is too small/noisy to provide stable
gradients. PPO’s on-policy nature lets it discover high-reward completions that were never in the original
training set. DPO is bounded by the quality of the collected pairs.
“How is DPO related to contrastive learning?”
Strong answer: the DPO loss increases the log-likelihood of chosen completions relative to rejected ones,
weighted by prediction error-closely analogous to InfoNCE / noise-contrastive estimation. The difference
is that DPO’s “negative” is a specific rejected completion from a preference dataset, not a random negative
sample.
Senior follow-up: “DPO has no explicit reward model. Where does the reward model effectively
live?”
It lives implicitly in the log-ratioβlog(πθ(yjx)/πref(yjx)). This ratio is the implied reward for any com-
pletion under the optimal DPO policy. In practice, you can extract this scalar at inference time to rank
completions just as you would with an explicit reward model-the difference is that this reward was never
trained with a classification head, so it is not calibrated in absolute terms but is well-ordered within a
```

### 27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF.

```
prompt. This is useful for best-of-nreranking and for diagnosing what the DPO model actually learned
to prefer.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
DPO derives from the same KL-regularized objective as PPO but avoids rollouts, reward models, and
value networks by showing that the optimal policy and the reward are interchangeable representations of
the same underlying quantity.
The DPO loss is a binary cross-entropy over preference pairs where the logit is the margin between implicit
rewards of chosen and rejected completions;βcontrols how far the policy can drift from the SFT reference.
A critical failure mode is chosen-completion collapse: track the log-ratio for chosen completions sepa-
rately; if it falls below zero and keeps falling, the policy is deteriorating on positive examples.
Offline DPO is bounded by the quality of the static preference dataset; iterative or online DPO (regen-
erating rejected samples from the current policy) recovers much of PPO’s benefit at a fraction of the
implementation cost.
Length normalization (dividing log-probabilities by sequence length before computing the reward margin)
eliminates the length bias that favors short completions and should be applied by default.
```
### 27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF

**27.3.1 Reward Over-Optimization**
In any RLHF deep-dive, you will eventually be asked: “what goes wrong when you optimize too hard
against the reward model?” Reward over-optimization is the canonical failure mode - the wall every production
RLHF system eventually hits. Understanding it separates engineers who can implement the algorithm from those
who can debug a live system that started producing worse outputs even though the proxy reward kept climbing.
At senior and staff level, you are expected to know not just that this happens, but why it happens mechanically
and how to detect it before it reaches users.
Reward over-optimization occurs when the RL policy gets so good at maximizing the _proxy reward_ - the
learned reward modelrφ- that it drifts away from whatrφwas actually supposed to measure: true human
preference. The reward model is a finite-sample estimator of human preferences trained on a fixed annotation
set. Like any learned model, it has gaps between its training distribution and the true underlying oracle. As
optimization pressure increases, the policy finds and exploits those gaps.
The framing I find most useful is a train-test gap in RL clothing. The reward model is your training signal;
true human preference is your test set. The RL algorithm overfits the former, and you pay the cost on the latter.
Formally, letr∗denote the true human preference oracle andrφthe fitted proxy. The PPO training objective
maximizes:
Ey∼πθ(·|x)[rφ(x, y)]β DKL(πθkπref)

but what we actually care about isE[r∗(x, y)]. These two quantities correlate whenπθstays close to the distri-
butionrφwas trained on, and diverge asπθmoves away. The KL penalty keeps the policy nearπref, but it is a
soft constraint - once the policy gradient finds directions that increaserφwhile partially circumventingDKL, it
will exploit them.
Empirically, this pattern is remarkably consistent: proxy reward climbs monotonically with RL steps while


```
27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF
```
true win-rate first increases, peaks, and then falls. Studies confirm this for human feedback and noisy AI feed-
back. It does not appear for clean, noiseless reward signals - pointing directly at label noise and finite-sample
estimation as the root causes, not RL per se.
_A reward model is a proxy, not an oracle; every RL algorithm will eventually find the gap between them._
The mechanism is Goodhart’s Law instantiated in RL: when the proxy becomes the optimization target, it
ceases to be a reliable proxy. Human preference annotations are noisy in two compounding ways. First, individ-
ual annotators disagree; a pair that one rates “clearly response A” another rates “slightly response B.” Second,
the preference data is collected on a distribution of prompts and responses that the current policy never gener-
ated, which means the reward model is queried increasingly far outside its training distribution as optimization
proceeds. A relentless RL optimizer will find exactly those out-of-distribution regions.
The alternative - optimizing directly against live human ratings - is logistically infeasible at training speed.
You cannot collect fresh human feedback fast enough for gradient updates at typical RL throughput. DPO
sidesteps reward-model fitting by directly optimizing the policy against a static preference dataset, which reduces
proxy-exploitation risk at the cost of being offline. Iterating the preference-collection loop partially recovers
freshness but adds annotation latency and engineering complexity. Neither approach eliminates the fundamental
finite-sample problem; they only slow the divergence.

**A Worked Example**

You are running PPO with a reward modelrφtrained on 100K pairwise annotations for a 7B chat model.
Your SFT baseline achieves 50% win-rate against itself (the reference point). After 500 RL steps, proxy reward
has risen 0.4 normalized units and human win-rate is 62% - a solid alignment gain worth shipping.
You continue to 2,000 steps. Proxy reward has now risen 1.1 units. But the next human evaluation returns
a win-rate of 53%. What happened?
Inspect a sample of rollouts at step 2,000. The policy has learned three consistent patterns the reward
model scores highly but humans do not: (1) responses are 2.1longer on average; (2) nearly every response
opens with “Certainly! Here is a comprehensive answer to your question”; (3) factual claims are decorated with
hedging phrases that sound authoritative but add no information. These stylistic patterns were rare in the reward
model’s training corpus - it never learned to penalize them - but after 2,000 steps of optimization they appear in
over 80% of rollouts. The reward model confidently assigns them high scores. Human raters find them grating.
Proxy and reality have diverged.
The diagnosis is clean: the proxy reward at step 2,000 measures “looks like the training distribution of
good responses” rather than “is a good response.” The RL algorithm found a different attractor.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always monitor two signals simultaneously. Track both proxy reward and an independent evaluation
signal: a held-out reward model trained on disjoint data, an automated capability benchmark, or scheduled
human spot-checks. When they diverge, stop. Do not wait for the next planned evaluation checkpoint.
Set a KL budget, not just a learning rate. A KL penaltyβin the range 0.01-0.05 is typical for 7-70B
models; largerβreduces over-optimization risk but weakens the RL signal. If the mean KL from the
reference policy climbs past 10-15 nats, you are likely in dangerous territory regardless ofβ.
Collect fresh reward data iteratively. If annotation throughput allows, retrain the reward model on
samples from the current policy everyNRL steps. This shrinks the distribution gap at each step. The
```

```
27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF
```
```
cost is engineering complexity; the benefit is a slower divergence curve.
Do not port “optimal RL step” numbers between projects. The over-optimization inflection point
depends on reward model quality, annotation noisiness, and base model capability. Typical inflection
ranges I have seen are 500-3,000 steps for instruction-tuned 7-70B models, but these numbers are not
transferable across reward model quality tiers or annotation protocols.
Verifiable rewards are the cleanest cure. Over-optimization is essentially absent when rewards are
noise-free - unit tests for code correctness, exact match for structured math answers. This is the core
motivation for the RLVR paradigm: by replacing noisy human feedback with a ground-truth oracle, the
proxy gap closes to near zero.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does RLHF sometimes make models worse even though the reward goes up?” Strong answer:
the reward model is a finite-sample proxy. As the policy optimizes against it, the policy finds stylistic and
structural patterns that score well on the proxy but were underrepresented in reward model training - a
train-test gap. Proxy reward and true win-rate diverge after a critical number of RL steps; empirically,
this inflection is consistently observed across human and noisy AI feedback settings.
“How do you detect and prevent reward over-optimization in a production training run?” Strong
answer: maintain a separate evaluation signal not used for training reward (held-out reward model, auto-
mated benchmark, human A/B), monitor both continuously throughout the run, use KL regularization to
limit policy drift, and stop when the independent signal plateaus or drops.
Senior follow-up: “If you iteratively retrain the reward model on data from the current policy, does
over-optimization disappear?” Senior answer: it is significantly reduced but not eliminated. Each iter-
ation fits a fresh finite-sample estimator on the current policy’s distribution, which closes the distribution
gap at that step. But label noise in human annotations is irreducible - you are still fitting a noisy estimator,
and the RL algorithm will still find its edges given enough steps. This is why noise-free verifiable rewards
achieve fundamentally different training dynamics: there is no proxy gap to exploit.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Reward over-optimization is the RL analog of overfitting: the policy maximizes a proxy that drifts from
the true objective.
The root cause is noise and finite-sample estimation in human preference labels, not a flaw in RL itself.
Proxy reward and true win-rate always diverge eventually; monitoring both and stopping early is non-
negotiable.
KL regularization slows but does not eliminate over-optimization; iterative reward model retraining helps
but does not fully close the gap.
The cleanest solution is verifiable rewards, where noise-free signals make over-optimization negligible -
the key insight motivating the reasoning-model generation of post-training.
```
**27.3.2 Length Bias and Calibration Degradation**
Two failure modes of RLHF are subtle enough to survive into production before anyone notices. First,
models trained with human feedback systematically grow more verbose - not because verbosity helps users,


```
27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF
```
but because the reward signal incentivizes it. Second, they become overconfident: their output probabilities no
longer track empirical accuracy in any reliable way. Neither shows up in the proxy reward metric, and neither is
caught by standard capability benchmarks. Both have been replicated across multiple labs. Understanding them
is basic literacy for any engineer running a production RLHF pipeline.
**Length bias** arises from the structure of pairwise preference annotation. When a human rater sees two
responses and must pick one, a consistent heuristic applies: the longer, more detailed response _looks_ more
thorough and helpful. This is often true - more relevant content is better - but it creates a spurious correlation
between response length and preference label that is independent of actual quality. A reward model trained on
these annotations internalizes the correlation. The RL policy, optimizing against that reward model, learns that
verbosity is profitable. Lengths climb throughout training even after task accuracy has plateaued.
**Calibration degradation** is a deeper structural consequence of abandoning distribution matching. Pre-
training and SFT train the model by minimizing cross-entropy loss, which is equivalent to minimizing KL
divergence from the data distribution. This implicitly trains the model to assign token probabilities that match
empirical frequencies - the origin of calibration. RLHF replaces this objective with a scalar reward. There
is no term in the PPO or DPO loss that requires output probabilities to remain accurate probability estimates.
The optimizer is free to, and does, push probabilities toward extremes that maximize reward while discarding
distributional accuracy.
Expected calibration error (ECE) measures the resulting gap:

```
ECE=
```
#### XB

```
b=1
```
```

n jacc(Bb)conf(Bb)j
```
whereBbis the set of predictions with confidence in bucketb,accis empirical accuracy within that bucket, and
confis mean predicted probability. RLHF models consistently show higher ECE than their SFT counterparts at
temperature 1, and the gap grows with RL training steps.
_RLHF produces a policy, not a probability model; treating its output probabilities as calibrated confidence
estimates is a category error._
Length bias exists because pairwise annotation measures overall impression, not information per token. A
300-token response with three substantive points and a polite closer tends to beat a 150-token response with the
same three points and nothing extra, even when both are equally correct. The reward model is not wrong to
learn this - it correctly fits the labels it was given - but those labels conflate quality with length. Once the reward
model internalizes the correlation, the RL loop exploits it directly.
Calibration degradation exists because pretraining instills calibration as a side effect of log-likelihood max-
imization on a diverse corpus. RLHF is an active intervention that overrides that prior. The policy gradient ob-
jective pushes the model’s distribution toward regions of high expected reward, which are not the same regions
of high empirical token frequency that calibration requires. Empirically, RLHF models at temperature 1 assign
probability0.90 to answers where actual accuracy is0.70. The models _sound_ more decisive and confident
to users. Human raters find decisive responses appealing and reward them, which means the RL loop actively
reinforces overconfidence.
Both pathologies compound with over-optimization: the longer you run RL, the longer responses get and
the worse calibration becomes, independently of whether the proxy reward is still climbing.


```
27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF
```
**A Worked Example**

Start from a 7B model fine-tuned with SFT on an instruction corpus. Run 1,000 steps of PPO against a
reward model trained on 50K pairwise annotations. Evaluate at checkpoints: SFT baseline (step 0), step 500,
and step 1,000.
**Length.** On 200 sampled open-ended questions: SFT baseline averages 118 tokens per response. At step
500: 174 tokens. At step 1,000: 231 tokens. The proxy reward has increased 0.6 normalized units over this
range. A held-out reference-based metric (ROUGE-L against human-written answers) gains 2.1 points from
step 0 to step 500 - a real quality improvement. From step 500 to step 1,000, ROUGE-L adds only 0.3 points
while mean length grows by 57 tokens. The extra tokens are padding: repeated topic sentences, redundant
closing summaries, filler phrases like “I hope this helps.”
**Calibration.** On 500 factual multiple-choice questions with verified ground truth: SFT ECE 0. 06 at
temperature 1. After 1,000 PPO steps: ECE 0. 19. The model now assigns mean confidence 0.91 to questions
where its accuracy is 0.74. To recover ECE< 0. 07 via temperature scaling, the SFT model requiresT 1. 15 ;
the RLHF model requiresT 1. 80 , indicating that probability mass has been substantially compressed toward
high-confidence predictions throughout RL training.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Log output length throughout RLHF training and compare against the SFT baseline by query category.
If mean length doubles without a corresponding quality gain on a held-out metric, you have a length bias
problem. Address it with length-normalized objectives - SimPO divides the reward by response length;
length-normalized DPO applies the same correction inside the DPO loss. Both add one division to the
loss computation and cost negligible engineering effort.
Never use an RLHF model’s raw output probabilities as confidence estimates. If your application
requires calibrated uncertainty - risk scoring, threshold-based routing, any safety-critical use - either apply
post-hoc calibration (temperature scaling, Platt scaling) at deployment time or use the SFT checkpoint for
probability estimates and the RLHF checkpoint for output generation.
Include a calibration checkpoint in your model evaluation gate. Before any RLHF checkpoint ships,
measure ECE on a factual benchmark at temperature 1. Treat it like a regression test: any checkpoint with
ECE exceeding a predefined threshold is blocked from serving. A reasonable starting threshold for a 7B
model is ECE< 0. 10 ; tighten this for high-stakes applications.
Overconfident models are a safety concern, not just a calibration metric. Users interpret confident
tone as reliable information. In medical, legal, or financial contexts, a model that expresses 90% confi-
dence when it is right only 70% of the time is actively misleading. This is worth naming explicitly in any
system design review.
Both pathologies worsen with more RL steps , which is an additional practical reason - beyond reward
over-optimization - to monitor closely, set early-stopping criteria, and not treat longer training as auto-
matically better.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What are the systemic side effects of RLHF on model behavior beyond the intended alignment?”
Strong answer: length bias (verbosity is spuriously rewarded because human annotators conflate length
```

```
27.3 Pitfalls of RLHF
```
```
with quality) and calibration degradation (RL optimizes a scalar reward rather than a distributional likeli-
hood, destroying the probabilistic interpretation of output probabilities). Both are empirically replicated
across lab settings and grow worse with more RL steps.
“How would you detect and fix length bias in a deployed RLHF model?” Strong answer: instrument
production request logs for output token count by query category; compare against the SFT baseline.
If length is inflated, fix it in the next training run with length-normalized objectives. As a short-term
mitigation, apply a maximum-token constraint in the inference server.
Senior follow-up: “Design an evaluation protocol that catches calibration degradation before a
model ships.” Senior answer: maintain a calibration benchmark of 500-1,000 factual multiple-choice
questions with verified ground truth. After each RLHF checkpoint, measure ECE at temperature 1 and
track the temperature-scaling coefficient needed to reach a target ECE. A rising coefficient signals growing
overconfidence even if post-scaling ECE looks acceptable - the model is producing increasingly peaked
distributions that require larger corrections. Treat both the raw ECE and the scaling coefficient as go/no-
go signals. Flag any checkpoint where the required scaling temperature exceeds 1.5 for explicit review
before serving.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Length bias is a systematic artifact of pairwise annotation: human raters conflate length with quality,
reward models learn this correlation, and RL exploits it. Monitor mean output length throughout training.
RLHF breaks calibration because RL optimizes a scalar reward rather than log-likelihood; output proba-
bilities from RLHF models should not be treated as calibrated confidence estimates.
Both pathologies are empirically confirmed across labs and worsen with more RL steps, providing addi-
tional practical motivation to stop early and monitor closely.
Length-normalized objectives (SimPO, length-normalized DPO) directly address length bias at the algo-
rithm level with minimal implementation cost.
Post-hoc temperature scaling can partially recover calibration for RLHF models, but the required temper-
ature coefficient grows with RL training steps - track it as a leading indicator of degradation.
```

## Chapter 28 Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

### 28.1 From RLHF to RLVR.

**28.1.1 Why Verifiable Rewards Scale Better**
When an interviewer asks you to design a post-training pipeline for a reasoning model-one capable of
solving olympiad-level math or generating working code-you will eventually be asked why RLHF alone is not
enough. The failure mode is overoptimization, and knowing its exact mechanism is what distinguishes a senior
answer from a vague one. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) is the architectural shift
powering every frontier reasoning model released in the past two years: o1, DeepSeek R1, Kimi K1.5, and Qwen
3 all rely on it. This topic appears in design-round and deep-dive interviews at virtually every lab working on
post-training.
RLHF trains a policy to maximize a learned reward model fitted on human pairwise preferences. That
reward model is a proxy: a finite neural network trained on a finite set of comparisons, approximating an un-
derlying human preference distribution that is both noisy and complex. As gradient descent pushes the policy
against this proxy, the policy learns to exploit the gaps between the proxy and the true preference function-a
phenomenon called reward overoptimization. The proxy score climbs, but real human win rates plateau and
eventually decline.
RLVR replaces the learned reward model with a deterministic, ground-truth verifier. In math, the verifier
checks whether the model’s final answer matches the reference solution, either via regex or a symbolic equiv-
alence library. In code, it executes the generated function against a hidden test suite and returns pass/fail. The
reward is binary and exact. Because the verifier is not a neural network, it cannot be gamed by the gradient-there
is no gap between the proxy and the ground truth, because they are the same object.
The formal RL objective is identical in both paradigms:
maxπ

The entire difference lives inr(x, y). In RLHF,ris a neural classifier with hundreds of millions of parameters,
updated on human labels, and subject to distributional shift. In RLVR,ris a deterministic function: a regex
match, a SymPy symbolic check, or a unit-test runner. The verifier has zero learnable parameters, evaluates in
microseconds, and cannot be overfit by gradient descent.
_RLVR succeeds where RLHF fails not because the RL algorithm changes, but because the reward signal is
ground truth rather than a learned approximation of it._
The practical ceiling of RLHF arises from two compounding problems. First, human pairwise preferences
are expensive to collect-labeler programs at scale cost roughly $1-$5 per comparison after quality control, and
a production RLHF run consumes millions of comparisons. This makes it structurally impossible to generate
reward signal online during training at the rate a GPU cluster can consume it. The reward model is trained once,
fixed, and then used as a static oracle, even as the policy drifts far from the distribution the reward model was
trained on.
Second, human preferences are noisy. Individual annotators disagree, preference labels carry positional
and length biases, and the reward model fits to these artifacts. Empirically, when researchers train RLHF reward
models on noiseless synthetic preferences, overoptimization disappears almost entirely; it reappears immediately
when noise is reintroduced. This tells you that overoptimization is not a failure of RL algorithms but a failure


```
28.1 From RLHF to RLVR
```
of the signal source.
RLVR bypasses both problems. A regex match costs a fraction of a cent per sample, so you can evaluate
reward on every rollout during training with no budget pressure. The verifier is noiseless and stationary-a correct
answer is always correct, regardless of how the policy evolved. This is the same design insight behind AlphaGo
and AlphaFold: once you have a domain where correctness is computable, RL scales in proportion to compute,
not in proportion to human annotation bandwidth.
RLHF also silently degrades calibration. Because the policy gradient optimizes expected reward rather
than log-likelihood of any distribution, the resulting model has no probabilistic grounding. Multiple indepen-
dent results-from Anthropic, from the GPT-4 technical report, from academic studies-show that RLHF models
are substantially overconfident at temperature 1 relative to their SFT checkpoints. If you are building a system
where calibrated probabilities matter (uncertainty-aware retrieval, best-of-nselection, or chain-of-thought ag-
gregation), this is a real operational liability. RLVR does not fix calibration, but it at least operates in a domain
where calibration is less central to the deployment use case.

**A Worked Example**

Consider training a 7B base model (32 layers,d= 4096, bf16) with RLVR on a curated set of competition
math problems using GRPO on 8 H100s. Group size isG= 8completions per prompt.
For a promptxsuch as “Find all real solutions tox^2  5 x+ 6 = 0”, the policy samples 8 responses. Each
is graded by a SymPy equivalence checker: responses statingx= 2andx= 3(in any equivalent form) receive
ri= 1; all others receiveri= 0.
Suppose the group rewards for one prompt are[1, 1 , 0 , 1 , 0 , 0 , 1 ,1], giving a group meanr ̄= 0. 625 and
standard deviationσr 0. 48. The GRPO advantage for each response is:

Correct responses receiveAˆi +0. 78 ; incorrect responses receiveAˆi   1. 30. The policy gradient step
increases the log-probability of tokens in correct responses and decreases it for incorrect ones-with no reward
model, no value network, and no human in the loop.
Notice what happens at the extremes. If all 8 responses are correct ( ̄r= 1,σr= 0), the advantages collapse
to zero and the gradient vanishes-this problem is too easy and contributes nothing. If all 8 are wrong ( ̄r= 0,
σr = 0), the same collapse occurs-this problem is too hard. Only problems where the group pass rate sits
between roughly 20% and 80% generate informative gradient signal. Filtering your training set to this difficulty
band is one of the highest-leverage decisions in an RLVR pipeline.
After a few thousand gradient steps across an 8-H100 run, a 7B model trained this way typically improves
15-25 percentage points on MATH-500 relative to the SFT checkpoint. A comparable RLHF run on open-ended
preferences would require careful early stopping, and the gains would be harder to reproduce across seeds.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Domain selection is the upstream constraint. RLVR only applies where you can write a verifier. Math
(symbolic equivalence via SymPy), code (unit-test execution), and formal proofs (proof-checker APIs)
qualify. Summarization, creative writing, and general instruction following do not. For those domains,
RLHF or AI-judge feedback remains the only option.
```

```
28.1 From RLHF to RLVR
```
```
Format rewards are not optional. Every production RLVR system pairs the accuracy reward with a
lightweight format reward-typically a small bonus for placing the chain of thought inside designated de-
limiters such as<think>...</think>. Without format rewards, models produce structurally inconsis-
tent outputs that are difficult to verify or display. In practice, the format reward is as operationally critical
as the accuracy reward for training stability.
Verifier quality is the new reward-model quality. Raw string matching on math answers fails on equiv-
alent but syntactically different expressions (e.g.,^12 vs. 0. 5 ). Use symbolic equivalence (SymPy) or an
LLM-as-judge for math, and hidden test cases with edge coverage for code. A leaky verifier creates exactly
the same overoptimization dynamic as a noisy reward model.
Problem diﬀiculty filtering is a first-class concern. Sample only problems where your current policy’s
group pass rate falls between 20% and 80%. Problems outside this range contribute near-zero gradient in
expectation. Kimi K1.5 explicitly excludes problems solvable by best-of-8 from their base model; Qwen 3
achieves strong reasoning gains from only about 4,000 curated problems filtered to this difficulty window.
RLHF still follows RLVR in production. RLVR sharpens domain competence; it does not produce a
well-rounded assistant. DeepSeek R1, Kimi K1.5, and Qwen 3 all apply a standard RLHF stage after
RLVR to recover helpfulness, formatting quality, and safety on open-ended tasks. The two stages are
complementary, not competitive.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does RLHF fail for reasoning tasks?” Strong answer: the reward model is a noisy, finite proxy
for human preferences. The policy exploits the gap between proxy and ground truth-reward scores rise
while real quality stagnates. This is Goodhart’s law in practice. Human feedback is also too expensive to
generate online at training scale.
“How would you design a reward function for a math RL training pipeline?” Strong answer: binary
accuracy reward using symbolic equivalence (SymPy) rather than string matching, plus a lightweight
format reward for response structure. Filter problems to a 20%-80% group pass-rate window. Do not use
multiple-choice or true/false problems-the model can random-walk to high reward without reasoning.
Senior follow-up: “If RLVR is strictly better for reasoning, why do production pipelines still run
RLHF afterward?” Senior answer: RLVR is better only within its domain. Once math and code compe-
tence are locked in, the model needs to handle open-ended tasks-writing, instruction following, multi-turn
chat-where no verifier exists. RLHF with AI-judge feedback is the only practical signal source for those
domains. The two stages address orthogonal capabilities and are used sequentially in all known production
reasoning-model pipelines.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
RLHF overoptimizes because the reward model is a noisy, learnable proxy; the policy exploits the proxy
faster than human win rates improve.
RLVR uses deterministic verifiers-regex, symbolic checkers, unit tests-eliminating the proxy and making
overoptimization structurally impossible against the reward function.
Format rewards are a critical implementation detail: without them, RLVR pipelines produce structurally
inconsistent outputs and train unstably.
```

```
28.1 From RLHF to RLVR
```
```
Only problems with a 20%-80% group pass rate generate meaningful gradient signal; filtering to this
difficulty window is one of the highest-leverage decisions in RLVR.
RLVR and RLHF are complementary: production pipelines use RLVR to build domain competence, then
RLHF to recover general-purpose alignment on open-ended tasks.
```
**28.1.2 Outcome Rewards vs. Process Rewards**
When you are designing the reward signal for a math or code RL pipeline, the most consequential decision
is not which optimization algorithm to use-it is where in the response to measure correctness. Do you score only
the final answer, or do you also score each intermediate reasoning step? This outcome-versus-process distinction
drives data cost, training stability, and the ceiling on model quality. It shows up in system design interviews as a
follow-on after the basic RLVR setup is established, and answering it precisely-with the empirical context from
R1 and DeepSeekMath-is what marks a senior answer.
An _outcome reward_ is a single scalar assigned to the entire response based solely on whether the final answer
is correct. The reward functionr(x, y)ignores all intermediate reasoning: chains of thought, intermediate
calculations, self-correction steps. It asks exactly one question: did the model produce the right final answer?

```
r(x, y) =
```
#### 8

#### <

#### :

1 if final answer matches ground truth
0 otherwise
A _process reward_ (or _process reward model_ , PRM) assigns a score to each intermediate reasoning step.
Given a problemxand a chain of thoughty= (s 1 , s 2 ,... , sT, a)wherestare reasoning steps andais the final
answer, a PRM assigns a scalarrt 2 [0,1]to each stept. The total reward is typically the minimum step score,
a product, or a running average. The key advantage is that the PRM provides gradient signal at every step in the
chain, not only at the terminal token.
_Outcome rewards are cheap to evaluate and structurally immune to overoptimization; process rewards
provide denser gradient signal but require expensive annotation and introduce a learned proxy that can itself
be exploited._
Outcome rewards dominate production systems for three concrete reasons.
First, they require no labeled data beyond the final answer, which in verifiable domains is already known
deterministically. A SymPy equivalence check or a test-suite runner costs microseconds and involves no human.
A PRM, by contrast, requires either human annotation of individual reasoning steps-which is roughly 10 more
expensive per example than annotating final answers-or a separately trained neural scorer. That scorer is itself a
learned proxy, which reintroduces the overoptimization risk that RLVR was designed to escape. A miscalibrated
PRM can penalize creative but ultimately correct reasoning, or reward plausible-looking but incorrect chains of
thought that happen to resemble training examples.
Second, PRMs are uniquely difficult to calibrate for long chains of thought. A step that appears wrong
at positiont= 3might be a deliberate detour that arrives at the correct answer byt= 15. Human annota-
tors disagree heavily on intermediate mathematical steps, and model-based PRMs trained on synthetic labels
compound their errors multiplicatively across a long chain. The effective noise of a PRM on a 64-step chain of
thought is substantially higher than the noise of a binary outcome verifier on the same problem.
Third, the large-scale empirical evidence has settled, for now, in favor of outcome rewards. DeepSeekMath
showed process supervision outperforming outcome supervision for a mid-sized base model on competition
math-the PRM line was the best-performing method in that comparison. But when DeepSeek R1 scaled to a


```
28.1 From RLHF to RLVR
```
much larger base model with careful difficulty filtering and GRPO’s group baseline, they tried extensive PRM
experiments and concluded that outcome-based rewards matched or exceeded PRM performance. R1 also eval-
uated Monte Carlo Tree Search as an alternative dense-feedback mechanism and reached the same conclusion:
neither PRMs nor search-based methods added consistent value over outcome rewards with GRPO. The result
that made PRMs look compelling in DeepSeekMath was contingent on model scale and dataset composition; it
did not transfer to the R1 setting.
The main practical failure mode of outcome rewards is _sparse reward_ : when the model is too weak to
solve any problems in a batch, every rollout receives reward zero, the GRPO group advantage collapses to zero
everywhere, gradient updates vanish, and training stalls. This is a scenario where process rewards would provide
non-zero signal on partially correct reasoning. The practical resolution, however, is difficulty filtering rather than
switching to PRMs-keep only problems where the group pass rate falls between roughly 20% and 80%, which
guarantees that at least some rollouts receive nonzero reward and the group advantage is informative.

**A Worked Example**

Consider the two-step problem: “If 3 x+ 7 = 22, what is 2 x?” Ground truth:x= 5, so 2 x= 10.
Under an **outcome reward** , the verifier reads only the final answer token. A response that correctly com-
putes 3 x= 15, thenx= 5, but writes “therefore 2 x= 9” due to an arithmetic slip receives reward 0. The
correct intermediate steps contribute nothing.
Under a **process reward** , a step scorer reads each line. Step 1: “ 3 x= 227 = 15” scores 1.0. Step 2:
“x= 5” scores 1.0. Step 3: “ 2 x= 9” scores 0.0. The minimum-step PRM gives reward 0.0, a product gives
0.0, and an average gives 0.67. All formulations agree the final step is wrong; they disagree on how much credit
the correct preceding steps deserve.
Now runG= 8rollouts. Suppose 3 correctly produce 2 x = 10(reward 1) and 5 do not (reward 0).
Under outcome rewards, the group mean is 0.375 and the GRPO advantage for a correct response is positive:
the gradient step increases the log-probability of correct completions. If instead all 8 rollouts get the final
step wrong, but 6 of them show correct intermediate algebra, a well-calibrated PRM returns non-zero group
advantages-training does not stall. This is the canonical scenario in which process rewards add value.
But building this PRM cost human annotators several hours of step-level annotation, or required training a
separate neural scorer on hundreds of thousands of labeled derivations. For a 7B model that can already solve
30% of problems at outcome level after difficulty filtering, this cost is rarely justified.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Default to outcome rewards; switch to PRMs only when filtering cannot rescue sparse rewards. If
best-of-Gon your filtered training set still yields near-zero pass rate for the current policy checkpoint,
a PRM may be necessary. This scenario is unusual for base models above 7B parameters on standard
competition math.
Treat diﬀiculty filtering as the first-pass fix for sparse outcome rewards. Before investing in a PRM,
filter problems so that the group pass rate sits between 20% and 80%. This directly addresses the sparsity
problem that motivates PRMs. Kimi K1.5 and Qwen 3 both use this filtering strategy and achieve strong
results without process supervision.
GRPO already has a process-like component through per-token KL regularization. In the full
reward-shaping setup, the per-token reward for tokentis the negative KL penalty: βlog(πθ(at j
```

```
28.1 From RLHF to RLVR
```
```
st)/πref(at jst)). The accuracy reward appears only at the terminal token. This means GRPO is al-
ready a hybrid: dense regularization signal at every position, sparse task reward only at the end. The
per-token KL is not a process reward in the supervised sense, but it prevents the model from taking arbi-
trarily divergent intermediate paths.
Remove length normalization when using outcome rewards. Dividing the reward by response length-
a choice in some early GRPO implementations-creates a perverse incentive: when reward is negative
(incorrect response), the loss is minimized by making the response as long as possible so each token’s
contribution is small. This produces models that pad incorrect responses to extreme lengths. Control
response length through a separate, decoupled length reward rather than by normalizing the accuracy
reward.
If you do build a PRM, use a model-based equivalence checker rather than human step labels. Math
shepherd-style approaches train a PRM on process annotations derived from large-scale rollouts: generate
many responses, identify which steps appear in correct versus incorrect completions, and use that signal to
train the scorer. This amortizes annotation cost but introduces its own distribution shift and noise. Budget
for a calibration evaluation before deploying the PRM in a training loop.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“What’s the difference between outcome and process rewards, and when would you use each?”
Strong answer: outcome rewards score only the final answer-deterministic, costless, no learned scorer.
Process rewards score intermediate steps-denser gradient signal, but require expensive step-level anno-
tation or a learned PRM that introduces proxy noise. Default to outcome rewards; consider PRMs only
when difficulty-filtered outcome rewards still yield near-zero group pass rates across your training set.
“Your RLVR training curve is flat and reward isn’t improving. What do you diagnose first?” Strong
answer: check the group pass-rate distribution across your training problems. If the majority of problems
have 0% or 100% group pass rate, you have a difficulty calibration problem, not an algorithm problem.
Re-filter the problem set before adding a PRM or changing the optimizer. Also verify that your verifier is
not silently accepting incorrect formats.
Senior follow-up: “DeepSeekMath showed PRMs clearly outperforming outcome rewards. DeepSeek
R1 used outcome rewards and dropped PRMs after extensive experiments. How do you reconcile
those results?” Senior answer: DeepSeekMath used a smaller base model on hard competition problems,
so outcome rewards were genuinely sparse-the model solved too few problems to receive useful signal.
At R1 scale (a large pre-trained model with strong mathematical priors), enough problems in the filtered
set receive nonzero outcome reward for GRPO’s group baseline to work well. The PRM advantage is a
function of model weakness and problem difficulty relative to the current checkpoint; as those improve,
the marginal value of a PRM decreases while its engineering cost remains constant. R1’s conclusion is
conditional on their filtering and model scale, not a universal result.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Outcome rewards assign a single binary score to the final answer; process rewards (PRMs) assign scores
to each intermediate reasoning step, providing denser gradient signal at higher annotation cost.
Outcome rewards win in production systems because they are deterministic, require no learned scorer,
and avoid the secondary overoptimization risk a PRM introduces.
```

### 28.2 Policy Gradient Methods

```
Sparse outcome rewards are best addressed by difficulty filtering (target 20%-80% group pass rate), not
by adding a PRM.
GRPO is already a hybrid: it applies per-token KL regularization at every position (dense regularization)
with the accuracy reward concentrated at the terminal token (sparse task signal).
The PRM advantage observed in smaller-scale systems diminishes as base model capability improves and
difficulty filtering is applied; PRMs remain a viable tool for bootstrapping RL on weak policies, not a
permanent fixture of mature pipelines.
```
### 28.2 Policy Gradient Methods

**28.2.1 Baselines, Advantages, and Variance Reduction**
At a senior post-training interview, after you sketch out any RL training loop-PPO, GRPO, or a custom
variant-the follow-up is almost always: “Walk me through why your gradients are noisy and what you do about
it.” Variance in policy gradient estimates is the central numerical challenge that separates working implemen-
tations from broken ones. Engineers at L5-L6 are expected to derive the baseline trick on a whiteboard, prove it
is bias-free, and explain how it connects to the advantage function that every practical algorithm uses internally.
The _policy gradient theorem_ gives the gradient of expected rewardJ(θ) =Ea∼πθ(·|s)[R(s, a)]as:
rθJ(θ) =Es,a[R(s, a)rθlogπθ(ajs)]

The derivation uses one identity:rθπθ=πθrθlogπθ. In the language model setting,sis the prompt,ais
the complete response, andRis a scalar reward-binary for verifiable tasks (correct/incorrect). Estimating this
gradient from a single rollout is unbiased but has enormous variance. If a model generates math proofs and
achieves a 5% solve rate, 95% of gradient samples are exactly zero and training makes no progress.
The _baseline trick_ is the structural fix. Any functionB(s)that depends only on the state (not the action)
can be subtracted from the reward without biasing the gradient:

```
rθJ(θ) =Es,a
```

The proof is one line:Ea∼πθ[B(s)rθlogπθ(ajs)] =B(s)Ea[rθlogπθ(ajs)] = 0, because the gradient
of a normalized log-probability sums to zero over any action space.
The optimal baseline (minimizing gradient variance) isB⋆(s) =Ea∼πθ[R(s, a)js], the expected reward
from states. Practitioners call this the _value function_ V(s). The difference between actual reward and this
baseline is the _advantage function_ :
A(s, a) =R(s, a)V(s)

A positive advantage says actionaoutperformed the policy’s average expected outcome froms; a negative
advantage says it underperformed. All practical policy gradient algorithms-PPO, GRPO, and every variant in
between-are ultimately different answers to one question: how do we estimateA(s, a)cheaply and with low
variance?
_Every working RL algorithm for language models boils down to: compute an advantage estimate, upweight
high-advantage responses, downweight low-advantage ones, and prevent the policy from moving too far in one
step._
Without a baseline, raw reward conflates two signals: how good the response was and how easy the prompt
was. A hard problem scoring 0.6 and an easy problem scoring 0.6 receive identical gradient weights, even
though the former represents an excellent response and the latter a mediocre one. The baseline removes the


```
28.2 Policy Gradient Methods
```
prompt-level expected reward, isolating only the within-prompt quality signal.
This matters because sparse rewards make the naive estimator nearly useless even at large batch sizes. In
supervised learning, every sample contributes a non-zero gradient. In sparse-reward RL, a 0-reward rollout
contributes exactly zero-scaling the batch just scales the waste. Centering by the per-prompt mean turns every
wrong answer into an active downweight signal, converting a sparse signal into a dense training signal across
all rollouts in the group.
The value function approximation also adapts to question difficulty automatically. A baseline estimated
from group rollouts is high for easy prompts (where most responses succeed) and low for hard prompts (where
most fail). The resulting advantage correctly flags when a response is surprisingly good for its difficulty level,
rather than just absolutely high-reward.

**A Worked Example**

Setup: 32 prompts,G= 4rollouts each, from a 7B model on a math benchmark. Focus on two represen-
tative prompts:
**Prompt P1 (easy):** rollout rewards= [1, 1 , 0 ,1]. Mean= 0. 75 , std 0. 43.
**Prompt P2 (hard):** rollout rewards= [0, 0 , 0 ,0]. Mean= 0, std= 0.
**Naive policy gradient:** weight each rollout’s log-probability gradient by raw reward. P1-correct rollouts
get weight+1. 0 ; P1-wrong and all P2 rollouts get weight 0. P2 contributes nothing to training even though the
model is failing on it.
**Centered advantages** (subtract per-prompt mean):

```
Rollout RawR RR ̄
P1-correct ( 3 ) 1.0 +0. 25
P1-wrong ( 1 ) 0.0  0. 75
P2-any ( 4 ) 0.0 0. 0
```
Now P1’s wrong rollout receives a downweight of 0. 75 , reinforcing the contrast between correct and
incorrect responses. P2 correctly contributes zero gradient-there is no within-group signal when every rollout
fails, and making a noisy update would only harm training.
As a concrete variance illustration: suppose two prompts contribute rewards of 11 and 9 (easy) or 0
and 2 (hard) under a uniform initial policy. Naive gradient variance across the four (state, action) pairs is
Var(f 11 , 9 , 0 , 2 g) = 21. 25. With baselinesB(easy) = 10andB(hard) = 1, effective rewards become
f+1, 1 , 1 ,+1gwith variance 1. 0 -a roughly 21reduction at zero cost to the optimization objective.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Use G 4 rollouts per prompt. With fewer samples, the empirical mean is a poor baseline estimate and
may increase variance rather than reduce it. The GRPO paper usesG= 8; in practiceG= 4- 8 balances
rollout inference cost against baseline quality.
When all G rollouts for a prompt achieve the same reward, centered advantages are zero and no
update fires. This is correct behavior, not a bug. If every rollout is correct (easy) or every rollout is wrong
(unsolvable), there is no within-group learning signal. Forcing an update from this zero-signal state only
adds noise.
```

```
28.2 Policy Gradient Methods
```
```
Dividing centered advantages by the group standard deviation is not a valid baseline operation. Sub-
tracting the group mean is bias-free (the subtracted quantity has expectation zero over actions). Dividing
byσis not-it changes gradient magnitude as a function of reward spread. Whenσis small, gradients are
amplified for prompts that are trivially easy or completely unsolvable, precisely the prompts where the
gradient signal is least informative.
A frozen initial checkpoint is a valid and cheap baseline. TreatB(s) =Ea∼π 0 [R(s, a)js], estimated
from a handful of rollouts under the pre-RL model, as a constant. No gradient flows through it. This
approximates the value function without any learned network.
Track per-prompt reward mean as a curriculum signal. Once the running success rate for a category
of prompts exceeds 90%, those prompts contribute near-zero gradient signal at full inference cost. Filter
them out and replace with harder examples.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Why does vanilla policy gradient have high variance, and what is the baseline trick?” Name sparse
rewards as the root cause. DeriverθJ= E[Rrθlogπθ]in one line via the log-derivative trick, then
show subtractingB(s)is bias-free becauseEa∼πθ[rθlogπθ(ajs)] = 0. The key constraint:Bmust
depend only on state, not action.
“What is an advantage function and how does it connect to value functions?” The advantageA(s, a) =
R(s, a)V(s)is the signed difference between actual reward and the policy’s average expected reward
from that state. In outcome-reward LM-RL,V(s)is approximated by the mean reward acrossGrollouts
for the same prompt-no future-reward bootstrapping is needed.
Senior follow-up: “GRPO divides the group advantage by the standard deviation. Is that mathe-
matically valid?” No. Subtracting the group mean is a valid baseline (zero-expectation subtraction over
actions). Dividing byσis not-it modifies gradient magnitude as a function of reward spread, which has
no justification in the policy gradient theorem. Specifically, whenσ! 0 (all rollouts score identically),
gradients explode. The practical consequence is that problems at both extremes of the difficulty spectrum-
already mastered or completely unsolvable-get disproportionate gradient weight. The “Dr. GRPO” anal-
ysis demonstrates that removing theσnormalization yields shorter responses and equal-or-better reward,
confirming this is a design flaw rather than a feature.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The policy gradientrθJ=E[R(s, a)rθlogπθ(ajs)]is unbiased but catastrophically high-variance
under sparse rewards.
Any state-dependent functionB(s)is a valid bias-free baseline; the optimal choice is the value function
V(s) =E[Rjs].
The advantageA(s, a) =R(s, a)V(s)converts sparse rewards into dense relative signals across the
rollout group, involving every rollout in training rather than only the successes.
When all rollouts for a prompt tie on reward, centered advantage is zero and no update fires-this is correct
behavior indicating no within-group learning signal.
Dividing by group standard deviation (the GRPO default) is not a valid baseline operation; it overweights
the difficulty extremes and can be safely removed without hurting performance.
```

**28.2.2 GRPO in Depth**
When you sketch an RL training loop for a 70B reasoning model and the interviewer asks, “PPO requires a
critic as large as the policy-how do you handle that?” the answer is GRPO. Group Relative Policy Optimization
removes the value network entirely, replacing it with a within-group reward normalization that fits naturally
into the language model setting. Understanding the full algorithm-objective, training loop, memory layout, and
failure modes-is now a baseline expectation for post-training roles at frontier labs, typically probed at L5 and
above.
GRPO starts from PPO and makes one structural change: replace generalized advantage estimation (GAE),
which requires a separately trained value network, with a group-level normalized reward. For each promptq,
