_GRPO is PPO with the value network deleted and the advantage replaced by within-group z-score normal-
ization; clipping, KL regularization, and the multi-step inner loop transfer directly from PPO unchanged._
The value network in PPO is typically the same architecture as the policy. A 7B policy in bf16 occupies
14 GB for parameters; with Adam optimizer states the footprint grows to roughly 56 GB. Adding a co-located
7B critic doubles the parameter memory to 112 GB before activations. On an 8H100 node with 640 GB total
GPU memory, this leaves little headroom for activation memory and rollout buffers. Eliminating the critic is
not a minor optimization-it is often the difference between a training run fitting on one node versus requiring
two.
The group structure provides a difficulty-adaptive baseline without any learned parameters. A prompt
where allGrollouts score 1.0 producesAˆi= 0for everyi: the policy has mastered it and no gradient flows. A
prompt where 1 of 8 rollouts is correct producesAˆcorrect+1. 63 (the z-score of the single success), concen-
trating gradient mass precisely on the response that worked. This adaptive difficulty weighting is implicit and
costs only a mean and standard deviation computation.
Compared to DPO, GRPO is inherently online: rollouts are sampled from the current policy at each step,
rewards are computed immediately by a deterministic verifier (regex match, unit test, symbolic solver), and
updates follow. DPO requires a static pre-collected preference dataset with an explicit pairing structure. When
your reward is a fast deterministic checker-as it is for math, code, and logic tasks-on-policy GRPO can leverage


```

**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How does GRPO differ from PPO, and when would you choose one over the other?” The core
difference is the advantage estimator: GRPO uses within-group z-score, eliminating the value network
and roughly halving memory. Choose GRPO when memory is the binding constraint or when you lack
a good value function initialization (common in new task domains). Stay with PPO when you have a
mature critic and need stronger variance reduction on long-horizon tasks where the group-mean baseline
is insufficiently accurate.
“Walk me through the GRPO training loop.” A complete answer covers: (1) rollout phase-sample
Gresponses per prompt, compute rewards andlogπoldfrom a single forward pass; (2) advantage phase-
normalize within group by subtracting mean and dividing by std plusε; (3) inner loop-compute importance
ratios with a stop-gradient onlogπold, apply clipped surrogate loss, optionally add KL penalty againstπref,
take gradient step; (4) repeat inner loopKtimes, then refresh rollouts.
Senior follow-up: “What happens to GRPO training when the model solves nearly all prompts in
the training set?” This is the curriculum collapse scenario. As best-of-Gpass rate approaches 100%
across most prompts, group standard deviation approaches zero everywhere. Advantages collapse (or
explode with 1 /σnormalization) and training stalls despite the model still having room to improve on
unseen distributions. The correct response is dynamic difficulty filtering: continuously measure pass rates,
remove prompts above roughly 90% success, and inject harder prompts. Without this, GRPO training
terminates not because the model is optimal but because the fixed training set has been exhausted.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
GRPO eliminates the PPO value network by replacing GAE with within-group reward normalization:
Aˆi= (RiR ̄)/(σR+ε), saving roughly 100% of critic parameter and optimizer-state memory.
```

### 28.3 Case Studies in Reasoning Models

**28.3.1 DeepSeek-R1 and R1-Zero**
When an interviewer asks you to design a reasoning model from scratch, they are really probing whether you
understand the interaction between supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards.
DeepSeek R1 and its controlled sibling R1-Zero are the clearest public demonstrations of this pipeline working
end-to-end: released around the same time as OpenAI o1, they matched its performance on competitive math
benchmarks using a recipe that is, in retrospect, surprisingly simple. This topic appears in senior-level design
interviews at frontier labs because the engineering decisions-reward design, training stability, the role of cold-
start data-reveal whether you can reason carefully about what each component actually contributes.
R1-Zero is the controlled experiment. Take DeepSeek V3 (the pretrained and mid-trained base model,
before any instruction tuning or RLHF), and run pure RL using GRPO with verifiable rewards. No chain-of-
thought (CoT) fine-tuning beforehand. No search or process supervision. Two rewards: a binary accuracy reward
(r2f 0 , 1 gfor correct or incorrect answers on math and coding tasks) and a format reward that incentivizes the
model to place its reasoning inside<think>.. .</think>tags. The format reward feels like a cosmetic detail
but turns out to be structurally important: without it, long CoTs do not emerge reliably from RL.
R1 is the production recipe. The pipeline has three stages:

1. SFT on long CoT data to cold-start the reasoning format.
2. RL with GRPO, using a binary accuracy reward, the format reward, and an added language consistency
    reward.
3. Standard post-training: instruction SFT combining reasoning and non-reasoning data, followed by RLHF
    using GRPO.

_The minimal viable RLVR recipe is a strong base model, binary correct/incorrect rewards on verifiable
tasks, a format reward to stabilize CoT structure, and GRPO with group-normalized advantages._
Verifiable rewards eliminate the feedback loop that causes reward overoptimization in RLHF. When the
reward is “is the math answer correct?”, it cannot be hacked: either the symbolic expression matches the refer-


```
28.3 Case Studies in Reasoning Models
```
ence, or it does not. There is no proxy reward model to overfit, and the signal does not degrade as you optimize.
This is the core reason RLVR scales where RLHF stalls.
The SFT cold-start in R1 serves a specific purpose: it gives RL a reasonable starting distribution to explore
from. Without it (R1-Zero), long CoTs do emerge eventually, but they can be incoherent and language-mixed-the
model will switch mid-reasoning from English to Chinese and back, because RL has no incentive to stay in a
single language. The language consistency reward in R1 provides that incentive explicitly. Some practitioners
have found that even 1,000 long-CoT examples for SFT cold-start are enough to stabilize the format before RL.
Two clear negative results from the R1 paper deserve equal weight. Process reward models (PRMs), which
provide intermediate per-step feedback on reasoning chains, did not outperform simple outcome-based rewards
despite earlier promising results in the DeepSeekMath work. Monte Carlo Tree Search did not help either. The
simpler, cheaper approach won: GRPO with outcome-only rewards, no tree search, no step-level annotation.

**A Worked Example**

```
Walk through the R1 training run with realistic numbers.
```

    pass.
2. **SFT stage** : Fine-tune on a set of long CoT trajectories (source not disclosed in the paper) to prime the
    model for structured reasoning.
3. **RL stage** : GRPO withG= 8rollouts per prompt. Accuracy reward is binary:r2 f 0 , 1 g. Clip ratio
    ε= 0. 2 , KL coefficientβ= 0. 001.
4. **Advantage computation example** : Suppose a math problem yields 8 rollouts, 5 correct and 3 incorrect.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Always do SFT cold-start before RL, even if it is small. R1-Zero is a research artifact; it language-
mixes and ships poorly. Even 1,000 long-CoT examples stabilize the format. Budget data collection time
before touching RL.
The format reward is load-bearing. It seems cosmetic but multiple practitioners report that without
rewarding the model for placing reasoning inside structured tags, GRPO does not reliably produce long
CoTs. Add it from the start; do not treat it as optional.
```

```
28.3 Case Studies in Reasoning Models
```
```
Add a language consistency reward. Aggressive RL on multilingual base models causes language mix-
ing in CoTs. This is an optimization pressure artifact, not a base model defect. An explicit reward signal
to stay in the user’s language is necessary for production.
Do not invest in PRMs or MCTS until outcome rewards plateau. R1 tried both extensively and found
neither improved over simple GRPO with outcome rewards. PRMs require expensive step-level annota-
tion; MCTS adds infrastructure complexity. Optimize the simple thing first.
SFT quality dominates RL algorithm choice. Empirical work (AI2’s Tulu 3) showed that improving
the SFT stage closes most of the gap between DPO and PPO. If your reasoning RL is underperforming,
check the SFT data before switching RL algorithms.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through the training pipeline for a model like DeepSeek R1.” Strong answer: (1) start
with a strong pretrained base model; (2) SFT on long CoT data to cold-start reasoning format; (3) GRPO
RL with binary accuracy reward, format reward, and language consistency reward on verifiable tasks; (4)
post-training SFT combining reasoning and general data; (5) RLHF using GRPO for instruction following.
Make explicit that the RL stage in (3) is distinct from the RLHF stage in (5).
“What reward signals would you use to train a reasoning model, and why not process rewards?”
Strong answer: binary accuracy reward (correct/incorrect), format reward (structured tags), language con-
sistency reward. PRMs require step-level human or model annotation and tend to be gamed; outcome
rewards are fully self-supervised and, in the R1 experiments, sufficient.
Senior follow-up: “R1-Zero shows CoT length growing during training and backtracking emerg-
ing. Is this evidence of genuine reasoning emergence?” Senior answer: treat this claim skeptically. The
length growth is at least partially explained by the biased GRPO objective-standard deviation normaliza-
tion upweights near-zero-variance problems (all correct or all incorrect), and the length normalization that
vanilla GRPO applies creates perverse incentives to produce longer responses when the answer is wrong.
Backtracking phrases like “wait, let me reconsider” appear in the base model at temperature above zero as
well. R1-Zero produces a strong math model; attributing the CoT behavior to emergent reasoning rather
than optimization artifacts requires stronger evidence than the paper provides.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
R1-Zero demonstrates that pure GRPO RL on verifiable rewards is sufficient for strong math reasoning;
R1 adds SFT cold-start and language consistency rewards for production stability.
The minimal reward design is binary accuracy plus format reward; language consistency reward prevents
CoT language mixing under aggressive RL.
Process reward models and Monte Carlo Tree Search both failed to outperform simple outcome-based
GRPO in the R1 experiments.
Distillation via SFT on800,000 R1 CoT traces transfers most of the reasoning gain to a smaller student
model without any RL.
SFT data quality dominates RL algorithm choice: fixing the supervised stage routinely closes gaps that
switching between RL algorithms cannot.
```

**28.3.2 Kimi K1.5 and Qwen3**
Kimi K1.5 and Qwen 3 arrived within weeks of DeepSeek R1, both independently matching OpenAI o1
on competitive benchmarks. Studying them alongside R1 is instructive precisely because they solve the same
problem with different algorithmic choices and different engineering emphases, revealing which design deci-
sions are load-bearing and which are incidental. In a system design interview, after you have described the R1
recipe, the follow-up is often: “Is there another way to do this?” or “How would you control the inference cost
of a reasoning model?” These two papers are your answer.
Kimi K1.5 derives its RL objective from the same KL-regularized reward maximization problem as DPO,
but without pairwise preferences. The Moonshot team starts from the optimality condition for the constrained
policy:

scaled by a baselined reward, plus an explicit regularization term pulling the policy toward the reference. The
key differences from GRPO are that standard deviation normalization is absent (avoiding the GRPO bias on
near-uniform reward groups) and the regularization is an explicit squared-loss penalty rather than clipping.
On top of this RL objective, Kimi adds a _length reward_ to directly control CoT verbosity:

whereLminandLmaxare the shortest and longest rollout lengths in the current batch,jojis the response length,

weakly penalized for being long.
Qwen 3 follows the R1 pipeline closely-SFT cold-start, reasoning RL, post-training RLHF-but adds _think-
ing mode fusion_ : after RL, the model is fine-tuned via SFT to respond to a<think>tag with a full CoT and to
ano_thinktag with a direct answer. A single set of model weights serves both modes. Critically, mid-CoT
generation can be interrupted by injecting a special prompt string, causing the model to emit its best current
answer before the full reasoning budget is exhausted.
_The two innovations that distinguish these papers from R1 are the length reward (Kimi) and dynamic in-
ference budget control via thinking mode fusion (Qwen 3)._
The Kimi length reward addresses the most practical objection to long-CoT reasoning models: inference
cost. Without explicit length incentives, GRPO training creates a perverse incentive-when a rollout is incorrect
and receives negative reward, the cheapest escape is to produce a longer response, diluting the per-token penalty
under length-normalized objectives. The Kimi reward breaks this by making _correct and short_ the uniquely
rewarded combination, while incorrect responses are incentivized toward batch-average length rather than al-
lowed to grow unboundedly. The reward must be introduced only after initial RL convergence; adding it at the
start traps the model in a short-answer local minimum before it has learned to solve problems at all.
Qwen 3’s thinking mode fusion is a pragmatic response to the same problem from the serving side. Rather
than training and deploying separate thinking and non-thinking models-doubling storage, serving infrastructure,
and operational complexity-a single model can serve both modes. The mid-generation interrupt is particularly
useful for latency-constrained applications: set a maximum thinking-token budget, inject the interrupt string


```

```
at that boundary, and the model produces a valid answer based on partial reasoning rather than timing out or
truncating incoherently. Qwen 3’s ablation confirms graceful degradation: performance drops smoothly as the
thinking budget shrinks from unconstrained to zero, rather than falling off a cliff.

**A Worked Example**

and 4,096 tokens. ThenLmin= 512andLmax= 4, 096.

Correct answer at 4,096 tokens:λ= 0. 5 (4096512)/(4096512) = 0. 5. Length reward= 0. 5.
Incorrect answer at 4,096 tokens:λ= 0. 5 ; sincec= 0,rlen= min( 0. 5 ,0) = 0. 5.

**Qwen 3 RL scale.** The Qwen 3 RL stage uses just 3,995 training problems-a surprisingly small number.
Despite this, the RL stage delivers measurable gains on math and STEM benchmarks relative to the SFT-only
model. This illustrates that RLVR is highly sample-efficient on verifiable tasks: the model already knows much
of the underlying reasoning; RL is refining the strategy for applying it.
**Thinking mode fusion data construction.** After the RL stage, construct two types of SFT examples:
Thinking mode:<think>[long CoT from the RL model]</think>[final answer].
Non-thinking mode:<no_think>[direct answer, no CoT].
Fine-tune the RL model on a mix of both. After this supervised stage, the model respects the tag semantics and,
when generating in thinking mode, will respond coherently to the interrupt string by emitting an answer based
on its partial reasoning.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Gate the length reward on only after RL stabilizes. Adding the Kimi length reward from step one
forces the model into a short-answer local minimum before it has learned to solve anything. In practice,
run unconstrained RL until reward curves show clear upward progress, then introduce the length reward.
A rough heuristic: wait until mean accuracy reward on the training distribution exceeds 0.3.
Use a learned judge for answer equivalence, not only regex. Kimi uses a fine-tuned reward model for
math answer comparison rather than relying solely on SymPy or regex. Notation variants (e.g.,^12 vs. 0. 5
vs.1/2) break naive string matching at scale. A model trained specifically on equivalence checking is
more robust and can be made very accurate because the task is narrow.
Separate inference and training workers. RL training requires alternating between rollout generation
(inference) and parameter updates (training). Running both on the same GPUs causes memory thrashing
and poor utilization. The standard architecture has a pool of inference workers running vLLM and a pool
of training workers, with weight updates broadcast via NCCL or by restarting the inference server. Budget
for this infrastructure; it is the hardest engineering component in reasoning model RL.
Filter data by diﬀiculty before RL. Both Kimi and Qwen 3 exclude problems where the untuned model
can solve at least one of eight rollouts (pass rate 1 / 8 ). Spending compute on problems the model
```

```
28.3 Case Studies in Reasoning Models
```
```
already handles is waste. Continually re-evaluate the training set difficulty as the model improves and
prune easy problems dynamically.
Expect RLHF post-training to trade math for instruction following. Qwen 3’s ablation shows the
general RLHF stage improves instruction-following and general tasks but slightly hurts math and STEM
scores in thinking mode. This is not a bug-the RLHF objective does not reward math accuracy-but it is a
trade-off to design for explicitly when building a multi-capability model.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How would you control the inference cost of a reasoning model?” Strong answer: add a length reward
during RL that incentivizes correct-and-short responses over correct-and-verbose ones; introduce it after
initial convergence to avoid the short-answer local minimum. For serving, add thinking mode fusion so
that operators can cap the thinking-token budget at inference time, getting graceful degradation rather
than abrupt failure.
“What are the infrastructure bottlenecks when training a reasoning model with RL?” Strong answer:
three main bottlenecks. First, rollout generation blocks training; separate inference and training worker
pools with asynchronous message passing. Second, variable CoT lengths create uneven batches and GPU
underutilization; implement sequence packing or per-length-bucket batching. Third, syncing updated
weights from the training process to the vLLM inference server is non-trivial; current approaches either
use an experimental NCCL weight-loading API or tear down and restart vLLM each iteration.
Senior follow-up: “Kimi K1.5 and DeepSeek R1 both work, but with different RL objectives. How
do you choose between them?” Senior answer: both converge to the same structure-policy gradient
scaled by a baselined reward, plus regularization toward a reference policy-and empirical differences
between them are smaller than differences introduced by data quality and reward design. The more con-
sequential choice is whether to add a length reward (Kimi has it; vanilla GRPO does not) and whether to
use standard deviation normalization in the advantage (the Dr. GRPO analysis argues against it). In prac-
tice, start with GRPO for familiarity, add a length reward after initial convergence, and remove standard
deviation normalization if you observe training instability on near-uniform reward groups.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Kimi K1.5 derives its RL objective from the DPO optimality condition without pairwise preferences,
arriving at a policy gradient update similar to GRPO but without standard deviation normalization.
A length reward is essential to prevent unbounded CoT growth; add it only after initial RL convergence,
not from the start, to avoid trapping the model in a short-answer local minimum.
Qwen 3’s thinking mode fusion trains a single model to serve both thinking and non-thinking requests,
enabling graceful performance degradation under a token budget at inference time.
RLVR is highly sample-efficient: Qwen 3 achieves strong reasoning gains from fewer than 4,000 training
problems.
The dominant infrastructure challenge in reasoning model RL is weight synchronization between training
and inference workers; allocate engineering time for this before starting large RL runs.
```

## Part XI

# End-to-End System Design Drills


## Chapter 29 Building a Production LLM Serving Stack

### 29.1 Reference Architecture

**29.1.1 Gateway, Router, and Autoscaler**
When an interviewer asks you to “design a production LLM serving system,” what they want to see is not
a single GPU running a model loop. They want the full stack: the layer that faces the internet, the layer that
decides which replica handles each request, and the layer that expands or contracts the fleet as traffic shifts. This
question appears at every senior systems or ML-infra interview at frontier labs, and candidates who conflate
“inference efficiency” with “serving architecture” rarely get the offer. The two concerns interact, but they live
at different abstraction levels, and you need to be fluent in both.
A production LLM serving stack decomposes into three collaborating planes. The _gateway_ is the public-
facing API endpoint: it authenticates callers, enforces rate limits, validates payloads, and streams tokens back
to clients using server-sent events or WebSocket connections. The _router_ sits behind the gateway and is respon-
sible for request dispatch: given an incoming prompt, it selects a backend replica (or a prefill/decode worker
pair in disaggregated setups) and hands the request off. The _autoscaler_ monitors aggregate queue depth, GPU
utilization, and SLO attainment and adjusts replica count accordingly.
The three components share a common data plane: a token stream flowing from the inference workers
back through the router and out the gateway, and a control plane: health signals, load metrics, and scheduling
decisions flowing in the other direction. In practice, the gateway is often a thin reverse proxy (Nginx, Envoy,
or a cloud load balancer), the router is a custom service aware of model-specific state (particularly KV cache
residency), and the autoscaler is a policy engine running against a metrics store.
Two metrics govern every SLO conversation at this layer. _Time-to-first-token_ (TTFT) measures the wall-
clock gap between request arrival and the moment the client receives the first generated token. TTFT is domi-
nated by prefill latency because the model must encode the entire prompt before it can emit anything. _Inter-token
latency_ (ITL), sometimes called decode latency, measures the gap between successive tokens after the first. ITL
is dominated by memory bandwidth because generation is memory-bound, not compute-bound. Throughput-
tokens generated per second across all concurrent users-is the aggregate metric the operator cares about when
planning capacity.
_Every architectural decision in the serving stack is ultimately a negotiation between TTFT, ITL, and
throughput, and you cannot improve all three simultaneously._
Separating gateway, router, and autoscaler is not bureaucratic over-engineering. Each component has a
radically different scaling profile. The gateway needs horizontal scale proportional to request rate; it is stateless
and trivially replicated. The router needs to carry soft state: knowledge of which replicas have which KV
blocks cached, what their current queue depths are, and what prefix hashes look like. Merging router logic into
the gateway produces a monolith that cannot scale the two concerns independently. The autoscaler, meanwhile,
is a control loop with a multi-minute decision horizon; it has no business sitting on the hot path of individual
requests.
The deeper argument for this decomposition comes from the physics of GPU inference. Prefill (encod-
ing the prompt) is compute-bound: given a long enough sequence the arithmetic intensity exceeds the H100’s
compute-to-bandwidth ratio of roughly 295, so the GPU stays busy. Decode (generating tokens one at a time) is


```
29.1 Reference Architecture
```
memory-bound: with batch size 1 the arithmetic intensity collapses to approximately 1 FLOP per byte, nearly
300 below what the hardware can sustain. This asymmetry means the optimal allocation of GPU time for
prefill and decode is very different, and a router that is unaware of which stage a request is in will make poor
dispatch decisions. The alternative-a single monolithic worker that handles both phases-wastes GPU-hours on
the slower decode phase and creates queuing pressure for new arrivals whose TTFT suffers while they wait
behind long decode tails.

**A Worked Example**

Consider a 13B-parameter model served on H100 SXM5 GPUs (80 GB HBM, 3.35 TB/s memory band-
width, 989 TFLOPS BF16). Model parameters in BF16 consume 13  109 2 = 26GB. Each H100 can hold
the model and leave roughly 50 GB for KV cache.
The KV cache per sequence is:
KV bytes= 2NkvHLT 2

whereNkvis the number of key/value heads (for a vanilla 13B with 40 heads,Nkv = 40),H= 128(head
dimension),L= 40layers,Tis the sequence length (1024 tokens), and the factor of 2 at the front accounts for
both key and value, and 2 bytes for BF16. This yields 2  40  128  40  1024  2  838 MB per sequence.
With 50 GB free, a single GPU can hold at most around 50 , 000 / 838  59 sequences concurrently.
At batch size 1, decode latency is:
latency=parameters bytesbandwidth+KV bytes=^26 ,000 + 838 3 , 350 GB/sMB 8 ms per token

Throughput is 1000 /8 = 125tokens/second for one sequence. At batch size 32, the memory footprint becomes
26 ,000 + 32 838  52 , 800 MB and latency is 52 , 800 / 3 , 350 , 000  15. 8 ms, but throughput is 32 / 0. 0158 
2 , 025 tokens/second-a 16 throughput gain at the cost of 2 latency. This arithmetic is what the autoscaler
must internalize: adding replicas is the right move when queue depth is climbing and per-request latency is still
within SLO; increasing per-replica batch size is the right move when replicas have headroom but throughput
targets are not met.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
TTFT SLO drives prefill isolation. If your TTFT SLO is under 500 ms and prompt lengths routinely
exceed 4k tokens, you will almost certainly need to disaggregate prefill onto dedicated high-compute
nodes and decode onto high-memory-bandwidth nodes. A single fleet trying to do both will violate TTFT
under bursty load because long decodes hold the GPU while new prefills queue.
Router state granularity matters. A stateless round-robin router wastes KV cache: the same system
prompt gets re-encoded on every replica. A prefix-hash-aware router routes requests with shared prefixes
to the replica that already holds those KV blocks, cutting TTFT for chat history, RAG context, and system
prompts to near zero for cache hits. The cost is router complexity and the need for a fast prefix-hash store
(typically a Redis or in-memory hash table).
Autoscaler lag is your biggest latency risk. GPU instances take 2-5 minutes to start and load a 13B
model. If you scale reactively, you will absorb a traffic spike entirely as latency degradation. Scale
proactively: watch the ratio of queue depth to mean decode time per step. If that ratio exceeds your
replica’s max concurrent sequence count, trigger scale-out before queues overflow.
```

```
29.1 Reference Architecture
```
```
Continuous batching, not static batching. Static batching waits until a fixed batch fills before dis-
patching. With variable-length completions this wastes GPU cycles waiting for stragglers. Continuous
batching (as implemented in vLLM) inserts new requests into a running decode step as soon as a sequence
slot frees, keeping the batch dense at all times. This is non-negotiable for production.
Model replicas scale throughput linearly; tensor parallelism does not. LaunchingMindependent
copies of the model acrossMGPUs multiplies throughput byMat constant latency. Sharding one model
acrossMGPUs via tensor parallelism reduces per-request latency but introduces all-reduce communi-
cation overhead and does not scale throughput unless you also add replicas. Use tensor parallelism only
when the model does not fit on a single GPU; prefer replicas otherwise.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through what happens when a user hits your LLM API endpoint.” Strong answers name
each layer: TLS termination and auth at the gateway, routing policy at the router, prefill on a dedicated
or shared worker, incremental token streaming back through the gateway, and where TTFT and ITL are
measured. Weak answers start at the GPU and work inward.
“How would you reduce TTFT for a system serving 10k concurrent users?” A strong answer distin-
guishes the two root causes: long prompts slow prefill (fix with disaggregated prefill workers or prompt
compression), while large queue depths slow dispatch (fix with more replicas or better scheduling priority
for new arrivals). A weak answer says “use a faster GPU.”
“How does your router avoid recomputing the same system prompt on every request?” The answer
is prefix caching: hash the system prompt tokens, store the associated KV blocks on each replica, and
route requests to the replica holding the match. State that cache eviction follows an LRU policy and that
the KV store must be block-granular (as in PagedAttention) to avoid pinning entire sequences.
Senior follow-up: “Your autoscaler is scaling in correctly but P99 TTFT is still spiking every 30
minutes. What’s happening?” The senior answer diagnoses a garbage-collection analogue: KV cache
eviction storms. As sequences complete, their blocks are freed; if the scheduler allows too many long-
context requests to pile up simultaneously, memory pressure forces the eviction of partially-warm cache
blocks mid-batch, causing re-prefill for evicted sequences and a TTFT spike. The fix is admission control
at the router: cap the number of sequences admitted based on remaining KV capacity, not just compute
capacity.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
The production serving stack has three separable planes-gateway, router, autoscaler-each with a distinct
scaling profile and state requirement.
TTFT is dominated by prefill (compute-bound); ITL is dominated by decode (memory-bound); these two
phases have different hardware optima, which motivates disaggregation.
At batch size 1 on an H100, a 13B model generates tokens roughly every 8 ms; batching to 32 costs 2 
latency but delivers 16 throughput-the autoscaler must understand this curve.
Prefix-hash-aware routing is the single highest-leverage router optimization: it converts redundant prefill
work into cache hits with no accuracy cost.
Continuous batching and admission control (capping inflight sequences by KV capacity) are non-negotiable
for production; static batching and reactive scaling will both fail under real traffic patterns.
```

```
29.1 Reference Architecture
```
**29.1.2 KV-Cache-Aware Scheduling**
A scheduler that treats GPU memory as a black box will, under real traffic, either starve low-latency re-
quests waiting behind long-context ones or thrash the KV cache into a pattern of constant eviction and re-prefill.
Both failure modes show up as P99 TTFT spikes that no amount of extra hardware fixes. KV-cache-aware
scheduling is the discipline of making dispatch, admission, and eviction decisions that account for exactly how
many physical KV blocks each in-flight sequence holds and how much capacity each candidate replica has left.
It is a systems question that appears at senior and staff interviews whenever the conversation moves from “how
does inference work” to “how do you run it at scale.”
The KV cache is the dominant memory consumer during decode. For each in-flight sequence the system
must store one key tensor and one value tensor per layer, per head, per token seen so far. In BF16 the per-token
cost per layer is:
bytes per token per layer= 2NkvH 2

whereNkvis the number of key/value heads,His the head dimension, and the leading factor of 2 counts both
K and V. Summed overLlayers, a sequence of lengthToccupies 2 NkvHLT 2 bytes. Because this
scales linearly withT, a single 32k-token sequence can consume as much KV memory as dozens of 1k-token
sessions.
The core insight of KV-cache-aware scheduling is that _admitting a new request is an irreversible memory
commitment until the sequence finishes or is explicitly preempted_. A scheduler that does not track block occu-
pancy will over-admit, forcing the system to either stall (waiting for a slot to free) or evict a partially-decoded
sequence and re-prefill it from scratch, wasting the compute already spent. The PagedAttention abstraction
(used in vLLM and its successors) makes the accounting tractable: KV memory is partitioned into fixed-size
_blocks_ (typically 16 tokens wide), and the scheduler tracks a free-block count rather than raw bytes. A request
is admitted only when enough free blocks exist to hold its full worst-case KV footprint, or when a preemption
policy frees sufficient blocks first.
Prefix caching extends this further. Many requests share a common prefix-a system prompt, a RAG context,
or a few-shot template. If the KV blocks for that prefix are already resident on a replica, the prefill cost for the
shared portion is zero. The scheduler therefore maintains a _prefix hash table_ : a mapping from a rolling hash of
the token sequence to the physical block addresses that hold the corresponding KV vectors. When a new request
arrives, the scheduler computes its prefix hash and routes it to the replica with the longest matching cached
prefix, turning prefill into a cache hit.
_Admission control, block-level eviction policy, and prefix-aware routing are three levers that together de-
termine whether the KV cache operates near its theoretical eﬀiciency or wastes the majority of its capacity on
redundant computation._
The alternative-FIFO dispatch without block accounting-fails in two characteristic ways. First, a long-
context request admitted at the front of the queue holds tens of thousands of blocks for minutes; shorter requests
queue behind it even though the GPU has cycles to spare on a smaller batch. Second, when total block occupancy
approaches the physical limit, a naively greedy system must either halt new admissions (starving throughput) or
evict and re-prefill the longest resident sequence (wastingO(T)compute that has already been paid).
Block-level accounting solves the first problem by decoupling scheduling from request order: the dispatcher
picks from the ready queue whichever request best fills available block capacity without over-committing. It
solves the second by making eviction explicit and policy-driven. The standard policy is a modified LRU over
_logical sequences_ : when blocks must be freed, the scheduler selects the sequence with the lowest priority score


```
29.1 Reference Architecture
```
(often a combination of elapsed wait time, sequence length, and whether the sequence has a live client connec-
tion). In practice, background batch jobs are prime eviction candidates; interactive sessions are protected.
Prefix caching compounds the gains. A system-prompt block that is reused across 1000 sessions is com-
puted exactly once. Without prefix routing, each session independently prefills that prompt, turning a constant
cost into a cost proportional to request rate. At 10k requests per minute with a 2k-token system prompt at 8 ms
per prefill, unrouted sessions waste roughly 10 , 000  8 / 60  1 , 333 GPU-ms per minute on a single replica-
compute that otherwise could have served decode steps.

= 31, 744 blocks
```
A request with a 4k-token prompt plus a 1k-token max completion requiresd 5000 / 16 e= 313blocks at
peak. The scheduler can safely admitb 31 , 744 / 313 c= 101such requests before the H100 is fully committed.
Admitting request 102 without eviction forces an out-of-memory stall.
Now add prefix caching. Suppose all requests share a 1k-token system prompt (d 1000 / 16 e= 63blocks).
After the first request warms those blocks, every subsequent request needs onlyd 4000 / 16 e= 250blocks for
its unique portion. Effective capacity rises tob(31, 744 63)/ 250 c= 126concurrent requests-a 25% capacity
gain with no hardware change.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Block size is a latency-fragmentation tradeoff. Smaller blocks (8 tokens) reduce internal fragmentation
but increase block-table overhead and TLB pressure. Larger blocks (32 tokens) cut overhead but waste
memory when sequences end mid-block. Most production systems settle at 16 tokens; drop to 8 only for
extreme short-context workloads where fragmentation dominates.
Set admission headroom, not a hard limit. Admitting up to the last block is dangerous: decode steps
allocate one new block per step per sequence, so a fully-packed batch will OOM mid-step. Reserve a
safety margin of 5-10% of total blocks for in-flight growth. The scheduler should refuse new admissions
when free blocks fall below this watermark, not when they reach zero.
Preemption policy must match your SLO tier. For interactive users, never preempt; instead, queue
the incoming request. For batch jobs, preempt aggressively using swap-to-CPU (slower but preserves
progress) or full eviction (faster but wastes prefill). Implement priority tiers at the request level and wire
them into the eviction comparator.
Prefix hash granularity determines cache hit rate. Hashing at the full-prompt level misses partial prefix
matches. Hash at block granularity: compute a rolling hash after each block boundary and store a hit for
```

```
29.1 Reference Architecture
```
```
every prefix length that is a multiple of the block size. This maximises reuse when system prompts vary
by a few appended tokens, which is common in multi-turn conversations.
Disaggregated prefill changes the scheduler contract. When prefill workers are separate from decode
workers, the scheduler must coordinate a handoff: the prefill worker streams KV blocks for the prompt into
shared memory or over NVLink, and the decode worker picks up from there. The decode-side scheduler
must reserve the necessary blocks before the handoff begins, or the arriving blocks have nowhere to land.
Reserve-then-transfer, not transfer-then-find-space.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“How does vLLM prevent out-of-memory errors at high load?” Strong answers explain PagedAt-
tention block accounting: the scheduler maintains a free-block counter and refuses admission when the
counter minus the safety watermark is less than the worst-case block requirement of the incoming request.
Eviction policy (LRU over logical sequences, swap vs. discard) should be named. Weak answers say “it
manages memory better.”
“Two replicas are available. How do you route an incoming request?” The strong answer: compute
the prefix hash of the request’s prompt, check each replica’s prefix hash table for the longest matching
cached prefix, and route to the winner. If neither has a match, route to the replica with the most free
blocks. Fall back to round-robin only if block counts are equal and no prefix match exists. Naming the
cost of a wrong routing decision-a full re-prefill-makes the answer concrete.
“Your P99 TTFT spikes every few minutes on an otherwise healthy cluster. What’s your diagnosis?”
The candidate should describe a KV eviction storm: the decode batch fills available blocks, admission
control kicks in, new requests queue, and when a batch of long sessions finally completes it releases a
burst of blocks that triggers a flood of newly admitted requests whose prefills saturate the prefill stage
simultaneously. The fix is admission rate limiting: spread re-admissions over multiple scheduling steps
rather than unblocking the entire queue at once.
Senior follow-up: “How would you implement prefix caching across replicas, not just within one?”
The senior answer introduces a distributed prefix store-a fast key/value service (Redis Cluster or a custom
shard-by-hash service) mapping prefix hashes to the replica ID that holds the warm blocks. On cache
hit across replicas, the router either redirects the request or triggers a block migration via RDMA. Block
migration is worthwhile only when the shared prefix exceeds a threshold (roughly 512 tokens) because
migration latency amortizes over the TTFT saving. Below that threshold, local re-prefill is faster.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
KV memory is block-granular and grows linearly with sequence length; the scheduler must track free
blocks explicitly and refuse admission before-not after-the last block is consumed.
Prefix caching converts repeated prefill work into cache hits; a Llama-3-8B H100 instance gains roughly
25% effective concurrency when a 1k-token system prompt is shared across all sessions.
Eviction policy must respect SLO tiers: interactive sessions are never preempted; batch jobs are the first
candidates for swap-to-CPU or full eviction.
Block-granular prefix hashing maximises cache hit rate for multi-turn conversations where prompts differ
only in appended tokens.
In disaggregated prefill/decode deployments, block reservation must happen on the decode worker before
```

```
KV blocks are transferred from the prefill worker; the reverse order causes mid-transfer OOM and wastes
the prefill compute.

### 29.2 Capacity Planning

**29.2.1 Estimating Tokens-Per-Second per GPU**
Capacity planning for a production serving system begins with a single derivable number: how many output
tokens per second can one GPU produce for your model and workload? Every downstream decision-fleet size,
cost projection, SLA commitment-anchors to this estimate. In interviews at frontier labs, the question arrives
within the first ten minutes: “We need to serve a 70B model at 1,000 requests per second with p95 latency
under 100 ms. How many H100s?” Candidates who reach for benchmark sheets fail; candidates who derive the
answer from the physics of memory bandwidth on the whiteboard pass. This is a senior-level question because
it requires internalizing why generation is fundamentally different from training.
Autoregressive generation is memory-bandwidth-bound. Every time the model generates a single token,
the GPU must sweep all model weights from high-bandwidth memory (HBM) into registers, execute the forward
pass, and write effectively nothing back-a deeply asymmetric, read-dominated workload. For a 13B-parameter
model in BF16, that sweep transfers 13  109 2 = 26GB per token, per batch step, regardless of batch size.
To generate a token for a batch ofBconcurrent sequences, the GPU must also read each sequence’s KV
cache. In BF16, the KV cache for one sequence of lengthS(tokens already generated or prefilled) is:

```
Cseq(S) = 4LKHS bytes
```
whereLis the number of transformer layers,Kis the number of KV heads,His the head dimension, and the
factor of 4 combines 2 bytes per element (BF16) with 2 tensors (key and value). The total bytes transferred per
generation step for a batch of sizeBis:

```
M(B, S) = 2P+BCseq(S)
```
wherePis the parameter count. Given hardware memory bandwidthW(bytes per second), the per-step latency
isM(B, S)/W, and batch throughput in tokens per second is:

```

WhenBCseq 2 P-large batch, KV cache dominates-TPS saturates at the ceilingW/Cseq(S), independent
of any further increase inB.
_To maximize GPU utilization during generation, the primary lever is batch size_ B _; every generated token
forces a full sweep of model weights and all per-sequence KV caches from HBM._
The root cause is arithmetic intensity: the ratio of floating-point operations to bytes transferred. For an
MLP projection with weight matrix of shapeDF, processing a batch ofBtokens requires 2 BDFFLOPs

Attention layers are worse. Each sequence maintains its own KV cache, so unlike MLP weights-shared
across all batch members-the KV data scales withB. The arithmetic intensity of one attention step during

the same hardware cost.

**29.2.2 Budgeting for Long-Context Workloads**
Teams that extend their serving context window from 4K to 32K tokens routinely discover their GPU fleet
is suddenly undersized by an order of magnitude. The capacity estimate that held last quarter is now wrong by a
factor of eight or more. Context length is not a dial you can turn freely after sizing your fleet; it restructures the

than adds. Interviewers at infrastructure-focused teams probe this directly: “If we double context length, how

## Chapter 30 Designing a Pre-Training Run from Scratch

### 30.1 From Compute Budget to Architecture.

**30.1.1 Choosing Model Size, Token Count, and Schedule**
You have a fixed compute budget - say 1023 FLOPs - and you need to decide, before writing a single line of
training code, how many parameters your model should have and how many tokens to train on. Get this wrong in
either direction and you either leave capability on the table or burn money training a model that costs too much
to serve. This decision comes up in system design interviews at every frontier lab, typically framed as “givenX
H100-days, design the training run.” The answer is not a guess; it follows directly from isoFLOP analysis and
the Chinchilla scaling law, two tools you can derive from small proxy runs well before committing to the full
job.
Every transformer training run consumes roughly
C 6 N D

tokens. The factor of 6 accounts for the forward pass ( 2 N D) plus the backward pass ( 4 N Dincluding the
parameter gradient and the activation gradient). This approximation holds within 10% for most dense decoder
architectures in the regimeD

The Chinchilla paper (Hoffmann et al., 2022) posits that cross-entropy loss follows a joint scaling law of
the form

whereL∞is the irreducible error of the data distribution andα, β 0. 34 empirically. Both the model-size
term and the data term decay as independent power laws; the optimal allocation sets their marginal contributions
equal.
The practical procedure is the _isoFLOP sweep_ : fix a compute budgetC, then train a grid of models with
differentNwhile adjustingD=C/(6N)to keep total FLOPs constant. Each model reaches a different terminal
loss. Fitting a quadratic to those losses and reading off the minimum gives youN∗andD∗ = C/(6N∗)
simultaneously. Repeating this at several compute scales reveals that the optimal ratioD∗/N∗follows its own
power law, and at the scales studied by Chinchilla the ratio stabilizes near 20 tokens per parameter.
The punchline that every engineer should be able to state under pressure: _At a fixed compute budget,
training-optimal model size and token count scale as_ C^0.^5 _each; the ratio of tokens to parameters determines
how the budget is split, and that ratio has climbed steadily from 20:1 (Chinchilla) toward 40-700:1 in modern
inference-optimized runs._
The reason the power law form is so robust is that language modeling at scale is essentially a high-
dimensional nonparametric regression problem. Classical theory predicts error should decay asn−^1 /dwhered
is the intrinsic dimensionality of the task. For natural language,dis large, which yields exponents much smaller
than 0.5 and explains why empirical slopes around 0.1-0.3 are consistently observed rather than then−^1 orn−^0.^5
rates you would expect for simple function classes.
The training-optimal versus inference-optimal distinction is where modern practice diverges most sharply
from the original Chinchilla result. When the Chinchilla paper was written, LLMs were research artifacts and in-


```
30.1 From Compute Budget to Architecture
```
ference cost was irrelevant. The training-optimal answer minimizes loss per FLOP spent training. The inference-
optimal answer minimizes loss per FLOP spent _serving_ the model, which means accepting higher training cost
in exchange for a permanently smaller model. Once models become products, inference cost dominates because
you pay training cost once and serving cost for every query indefinitely. This is why Llama 3 trained at roughly
39 tokens per parameter, why recent Qwen models trained on 30 trillion tokens, and why the modern rule of
thumb has moved well above 20:1.
The Kaplan (2020) paper estimated a lower ratio - closer to 5-10 tokens per parameter - because its analysis
used models trained to a fixed step count rather than to full convergence with a cosine cooldown. A cosine
learning rate schedule cannot be truncated early; the cooldown phase is responsible for a substantial fraction of
the final loss reduction. Models stopped mid-cosine are not valid samples on the training-optimal frontier, which
caused Kaplan to underestimate the token contribution systematically. Chinchilla corrected this by training every
model to its natural termination point.

quadratic to the terminal losses and confirm the minimum. If the minimum shifts consistently toward smallerN,
the data suggests an inference-optimal regime; if it aligns near the Chinchilla ratio, training-optimal dominates.
This proxy sweep costs about 1% of the full budget and de-risks the entire run.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Pick the token-to-parameter ratio based on deployment, not theory. If you will serve the model at
scale, lean toward 40-200:1 or higher. If this is a research artifact unlikely to see heavy traffic, 20:1 is fine.
Never default to Chinchilla’s 20:1 for a production model without thinking through the serving economics.
Use the WSD (warmup-stable-decay) learning rate schedule. A cosine schedule requires committing
to a fixed endpoint before training starts; early checkpoints are incomparable because they have different
cooldown trajectories. WSD holds the learning rate flat during the stable phase, letting you branch off
cooldown ramps at arbitrary token counts. This turns the Chinchilla isoFLOP analysis from anO(n^2 )
training experiment into roughly anO(n)one.
```

Exclude embedding parameters from N when fitting scaling laws. Embedding layers have a different
scaling behavior than the attention and MLP blocks. Including them distorts the log-linear fit and produces
a visible kink in the scaling curve. Always report and fit non-embedding parameter counts.
The critical batch size grows as your target loss shrinks. As training progresses and loss decreases,
gradient signal becomes more precise and you can productively use larger batches. Llama 3 increased
batch size mid-run for exactly this reason. Plan for at least one batch-size ramp in your training schedule.
If you are tuning learning rate and batch size without mu-P, fit a scaling law on them. Without
maximal update parameterization, the optimal learning rate shifts roughly as 1 /width as the model grows.
Train five-plus proxy runs at different scales, find the optimal learning rate at each, and fit the resulting
scaling law to extrapolate the optimal rate for your target model. Do not transplant the learning rate from
a small run without this correction; it will be too high and the large model will diverge or converge to a
suboptimal loss.
```

**30.1.2 Picking a Parallelism Strategy for Your Cluster**
Once you have fixed your model size and token count, the next design decision is how to distribute the
work across your GPU cluster. This question shows up in system design interviews as “you have a 70B model
and 512 H100s, how do you parallelize training?” The answer requires knowing which axes of parallelism exist,
what hardware constraints bound each one, and how to compose them into a configuration that fits in memory
and keeps GPU utilization high. Getting this wrong means either hitting an OOM before the first forward pass
or spending half your compute budget waiting on communication rather than doing math.
Modern LLM training uses a combination of three parallelism axes, typically composed multiplicatively:
**Tensor parallelism (TP)** : splits individual weight matrices across GPUs within a layer. An all-reduce
is required after every matrix multiply, so TP ranks must be connected by NVLink or an equivalently
high-bandwidth interconnect. TP degree is almost always set to the number of GPUs per node (typically
8).
**Pipeline parallelism (PP)** : partitions the model’s layers into sequential stages, one stage per PP rank.
GPUs in different stages communicate only at stage boundaries via point-to-point sends. This communi-
cation uses slower inter-node links (InfiniBand) but is much less frequent than TP all-reduces.
**Data parallelism (DP)** : replicates the full model (or a TPPP shard of it) across independent groups that
each process a different micro-batch. Gradients are aggregated with an all-reduce across DP ranks after
each backward pass.
The total GPU count decomposes cleanly:
Total GPUs=TPPPDP.
Within the DP dimension, _ZeRO_ (Zero Redundancy Optimizer) shards optimizer states, gradients, and
optionally parameters across the DP group rather than replicating them. ZeRO stage 1 shards only optimizer
states, stage 2 adds gradient sharding, and stage 3 shards parameters as well. Each stage reduces memory
proportionally to the DP degree at the cost of additional all-gather communication.
_The standard recipe is: fill TP within a node (TP_ = _GPUs per node), fill PP across nodes to get the model
into memory, then fill the rest of your cluster with DP to increase throughput._
The hierarchy follows the hardware topology directly. NVLink bandwidth inside a node is typically 600-
900 GB/s all-reduce aggregate, whereas InfiniBand between nodes is one to two orders of magnitude slower
per link. Tensor parallelism inserts an all-reduce after every matrix multiply in every transformer layer - for
a 70B model that is hundreds of all-reduces per forward-backward pass. Those collectives must complete in
microseconds to not bottleneck compute, which means they can only run efficiently over NVLink. Placing TP
ranks on separate nodes would stall the entire pipeline waiting for slow cross-node traffic.
Pipeline parallelism, by contrast, only sends a single activation tensor at each stage boundary once per
micro-batch. The communication volume is small (hidden dimensionsequence lengthmicro-batch size in
BF16) and the timing is predictable, so it tolerates the higher latency of inter-node links.
The main cost of pipeline parallelism is the _pipeline bubble_ : at the start and end of each pipeline flush, some
stages are idle. Withpstages andmmicro-batches per flush, the bubble fraction is approximately(p1)/m.
The interleaved pipeline schedule (used by Megatron-LM) reduces this to(p/v1)/mby assigningv > 1
non-contiguous layer chunks to each rank, at the cost ofvmore point-to-point messages per micro-batch. As

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Set TP equal to GPUs per node, almost always. For H100 nodes with 8 GPUs, TP= 8. Going cross-
node with TP (TP= 16, 32 ) is technically possible but the NVLink advantage disappears and latency on

and doubles the number of inter-node point-to-point messages. If ZeRO-3 across DP gets the model into

MoE layers. Set EP degree equal to the number of experts (or a divisor of it) such that each EP rank holds
exactly one expert. The total GPU count becomes TPPPDPEP, but DP and EP share the same
physical dimension in most implementations (EP is implemented as DP over the expert dimension).
Match your global batch size to the critical batch size. The critical batch size scales predictably with
the inverse of the target loss. For a 7B model targeting a terminal loss around 2.0 nats, empirical estimates
put the critical batch size near 1-4M tokens. Below that threshold, adding more DP replicas (more GPUs)
is nearly as efficient as taking more steps. Above it, extra DP replicas produce diminishing gradient signal.
Design your TPPPDP product so that the resulting global batch lands at or just below the critical
batch size; then grow the batch size in stages as loss improves mid-training.
```

“When would you use ZeRO-3 instead of pipeline parallelism for a 70B model?” Strong answer:

DP group within a fat-tree fabric; PP wins when pipeline stages fit on separate chassis with limited cross-
chassis bandwidth.
Senior follow-up: “How does sequence parallelism change this analysis for a 1M-token context
model?” Sketch of the senior answer: at long sequence lengths, activations (which scale as sequence
lengthbatchdmodel) dominate over parameter memory. Sequence parallelism (SP) shards the se-
quence dimension across TP ranks, reducing activation memory by the TP degree. You need all-gather
before the QKV projection and reduce-scatter after the output projection, exactly replacing the TP all-
reduces. For a 1M-token context, SP is mandatory: activations without SP can exceed 10 GB per layer
per GPU even at micro-batch= 1, making the model impossible to fit at TP= 8without aggressive
activation recomputation.

```
Total GPUs=TPPPDP; set TP to the NVLink-connected group size (typically 8), use PP to get the
model into memory, fill remaining capacity with DP.
Pipeline bubble fraction is(p1)/mfor the basic schedule and(p/v1)/mfor the interleaved schedule;
keep it below 15% by ensuringmp.
ZeRO-3 is often preferable to PP for single-node-scale models (up to30B) when the DP group is large;
PP is necessary when parameters plus optimizer states exceed per-node memory even after TP sharding.
```

```
The global batch size produced by your parallelism configuration must stay at or below the critical batch
size; ramp the batch size mid-training as the terminal loss decreases.
For MoE models, add expert parallelism as a fourth axis; for ultra-long-context models, add sequence
parallelism within the TP group to manage activation memory.

### 30.2 Operations and Failure Modes

**30.2.1 Checkpointing, Fault Tolerance, and Silent Data Corruption**
When Meta trained Llama 3, they logged over 50 job interruptions from hardware failures across the full
run - roughly one every few days at production scale. Training a frontier model across thousands of GPUs is
a distributed system in the reliability-engineering sense: components will fail, and your design must make the
run survivable. Checkpointing strategy appears in senior-level design interviews precisely because the right
answer is not simply “save every N steps.” It requires async I/O pipelines, rolling retention policies, cross-
replica validation, and a concrete plan for the failure mode that inflicts the most damage: a GPU that silently
produces wrong results without crashing or throwing an error.
A checkpoint must capture everything needed to resume training from an exact point: model parameters,
optimizer state (momentum and variance tensors for Adam), the data loader cursor, the random number generator
state for both Python and CUDA, and the current global step counter. Miss any of these and a resumed run
diverges from the original trajectory - sometimes immediately, sometimes subtly over thousands of steps.
At scale, a synchronous checkpoint blocks the entire training loop. For a 70B-parameter model in ZeRO-3
across 512 H100s, the full checkpoint size is approximately:

(^70) | B{z (^2) }
bf16 params
+ 70| B(4 + 4 + 4){z }
fp32 opt. state (master weights,m,v)
= 140GB+ 840GB= 980GB total.
Sharded across 512 workers that is about 1.9 GB per rank. An NVMe RAID writing at 10 GB/s can
flush each shard in under 200 ms - but only if you do not wait for every rank serially. The standard solution is
_asynchronous checkpointing_ : each GPU serializes its shard into host DRAM (fast, under 100 ms), the training
loop resumes immediately, and a background CPU thread drains that buffer to persistent storage. The GPU never
stalls waiting for disk.
Rolling checkpoints address a second failure mode: a checkpoint file that is itself corrupted mid-write.
Keep the three most recent sharded saves (at stepsN,Nδ,N 2 δ) and delete the oldest only after the newest
has been checksum-validated. This gives you two rollback opportunities if the most recent save is bad.
_A checkpoint is not a save file - it is the full resumable state of a distributed computation, and its reliability
is a product of every component in that chain._
Asynchronous saves overlap I/O with compute so that checkpointing overhead approaches zero at reason-
able intervals (every 200-1,000 steps). The host-RAM staging buffer absorbs the burst, and the background
thread handles the slower NVMe write while training continues. Blocking the GPU until the file is flushed
wastes expensive accelerator time for no algorithmic benefit.
Rolling policies with post-write validation address the corruption-during-write failure mode. A naively
overwritten single checkpoint is worse than no checkpoint at all: you lose your fallback. A three-generation
rolling policy with per-shard checksum provides both recency and a verified fallback, at the cost of roughly 3 
the checkpoint storage.


```
30.2 Operations and Failure Modes
```
_Silent data corruption_ (SDC) is the harder case and the one that teams are often underprepared for. ECC
memory catches single-bit DRAM errors, but multi-bit errors, PCIe link faults, and rare CUDA kernel bugs
can produce numerically plausible but incorrect gradient values. The training loss does not spike - the model
simply learns the wrong thing, gradually. The detection strategy that works in practice is maintaining a frozen
_canary batch_ : a small fixed set of held-out examples whose loss is evaluated separately every 100 steps. A
canary loss that drifts upward while training loss looks healthy is an early SDC signal. For ZeRO-1 or ZeRO-2,
where all replicas hold identical parameters after each reduce, you can also compute the global gradient norm
independently on two separate ranks and compare; a sustained disagreement beyond numerical tolerance flags
a corrupted reduce.

**A Worked Example**

```
Consider a 7B model training on 64 H100s under FSDP (ZeRO-3). Each GPU holds roughly:
```
7 B(2 + 12)bytes
64 ^1.^5 GB per rank.
Checkpointing every 500 steps with async saves adds negligible overhead. At 800K tokens per step, 500
steps equals 400M tokens of training - the maximum exposure window for any hardware failure.
At step 8,200 a single GPU develops a flaky NVLink lane that silently biases its contribute to the reduce-
scatter by0.1% per step. No NaN appears; the training loss trends normally. At step 10,300, the canary batch
loss is 0.09 nats above its expected trajectory - 3.2 standard deviations from the rolling baseline. The run is
paused.
Rolling back to the step-8,000 checkpoint (the last clean save before the anomaly), swapping the affected
GPU, and resuming costs 300 steps of recompute across 64 GPUs. Without the canary, the team would have
continued for weeks and discovered the problem only during post-training evaluation, losing the entire run.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Checkpoint interval. Every 200-500 steps is the practical range for large runs. Too frequent and async
I/O cannot keep up with training throughput; too infrequent and a single GPU failure costs hours of
recompute. At 500 steps, 1M tokens/step, and 512 H100s at $3/hour, one failure costs roughly $3,000 of
wasted compute.
Rolling vs. permanent snapshots. Keep three rolling checkpoints for fast rollback, plus permanent snap-
shots at fixed milestones (e.g., every 10K steps). Permanent snapshots let you restart mid-training exper-
iments - if you changed the data mix at step 50K, you can re-evaluate from that exact checkpoint without
rerunning from scratch.
Validate every save before deleting the previous generation. After the background thread flushes to
disk, read back the shard header and compare a checksum. A corrupted save that silently passes is worse
than a failed save that triggers a retry. Track per-rank validation status in a distributed metadata store.
Canary batch sizing. 512-2,048 held-out examples is sufficient. Evaluate every 100 training steps. Alert
if the canary loss deviates by more than two standard deviations from a 500-step rolling mean. This adds
roughly 0.1% overhead at a 128K-token canary batch.
Save the full data cursor. Record the shard index, file offset, and shuffle seed alongside model state.
Without these, a resumed run either replays already-seen data or skips data, introducing distribution shifts
```

```

```
```
that are nearly impossible to diagnose later. This is the most commonly omitted element in naive check-
point implementations.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“Walk me through how you would checkpoint a 70B model training run across 512 GPUs with
FSDP.” Strong answer: describe ZeRO-3 sharding, async host-RAM staging, background flush to NVMe,
per-rank checksum validation, and a three-generation rolling retention policy. Mention that optimizer state
dominates checkpoint size and that the data loader cursor and RNG state must be saved alongside model
weights.
“What is silent data corruption and why is it particularly dangerous during training?” Strong an-
swer: SDC produces numerically plausible but incorrect gradient values - no crash, no NaN - so the
training loss can look healthy while the model learns from a corrupted signal for thousands of steps. De-
tection requires out-of-band validation (canary batch or cross-replica gradient comparison), not in-band
loss monitoring alone.
Senior follow-up: “You are 20 days into a 30-day run and discover a GPU has been silently corrupt-
ing gradients since day 5. What do you do?” Senior answer: quantify the contamination window by
comparing canary loss to its expected trajectory - if divergence is small and within two standard devia-
tions of noise, the model may be salvageable from a day-5 checkpoint with a targeted rerun. If the drift is
large, a 15-day rollback may be unavoidable. In either case: isolate and quarantine the affected hardware,
verify the day-5 checkpoint with an independent forward pass on a clean reference node, add cross-replica
gradient audits before resuming, and file a hardware incident report so the vendor can diagnose the root
cause.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Asynchronous checkpointing stages weights to host RAM first so training resumes before the file hits disk
```
- overhead approaches zero at 200-500 step intervals.
Keep three rolling checkpoints plus permanent milestone snapshots; validate each save with a checksum
before deleting the previous generation.
Save optimizer state, data loader cursor, and RNG seeds alongside model parameters - a resume without
these is not a true resume.
Silent data corruption produces no NaN and no crash; detect it with a frozen canary batch evaluated every
~100 steps, or via cross-replica gradient comparison on ZeRO-1/2 runs.
At Llama-3 scale, hardware failures are a statistical certainty; a fault-tolerant checkpoint strategy limits
blast radius to hundreds of steps rather than days of recompute.

**30.2.2 Monitoring Loss Spikes and Divergence**
Three hours into a 21-day training run, the per-step loss plot jumps from 2.8 to 11.3. The gradient norm has
been climbing for 50 steps. Do you roll back and resume, wait for self-recovery, or stop the run entirely? Getting
this decision wrong in either direction wastes GPU-months. The judgment call itself - and the instrumentation
that makes it reliable - comes up in system design interviews at every lab that trains models at scale, because it
tests whether you understand training dynamics at the level of individual steps rather than epoch averages.


```
30.2 Operations and Failure Modes
```
A training run produces two qualitatively different instability modes. A _spike_ is a transient loss increase that
recovers within a few hundred steps; the optimizer has encountered an anomalous gradient and the momentum
terms absorb the shock. _Divergence_ is a non-recovering increase - the optimizer has entered a region from
which gradient descent cannot escape, usually because the gradient scale has overwhelmed the learning rate or
the Adam second-moment estimate has underflowed.
Distinguishing these two in the first minutes of a suspected event requires per-step instrumentation, not
epoch-level averages. The canonical metrics to log at every training step are:
Training loss (cross-entropy in nats)
Globalℓ 2 gradient norm _before_ clipping
Effective learning rate (scheduler output at this step)
Hardware throughput (tokens per second per GPU, as a hardware health proxy)
And, evaluated on a fixed held-out set everyK= 100steps:
Canary batch loss (orthogonal signal independent of in-distribution training data)
Gradient norm is the leading indicator. During stable pre-training on a well-filtered dataset, the unclipped
global norm rarely exceeds 2 the gradient clipping threshold. When the unclipped norm crosses 5 - 10 the
clipping value, a bad batch or a numerical instability has already started to propagate - the loss spike will follow
10-50 steps later. This lead time is your intervention window.
_Per-step gradient norm is the earliest warning signal; training loss is the lagging indicator._
Logging at step granularity rather than epoch granularity catches transient events before they compound.
A single corrupted document that appears once may spike the loss for five steps and then recover; logged only
at epoch boundaries, you never see it, and you cannot correlate the event with a data cursor position to filter the
offending sample from future training.
The canary batch provides an orthogonal signal that distinguishes two very different root causes. If training
loss spikes but canary loss stays flat, the model is healthy and the event is almost certainly a data artifact -
something in the current batch that is anomalous relative to the rest of the distribution. If both training loss
and canary loss spike, or if canary loss drifts upward over hundreds of steps while training loss looks normal,
the model’s learned representations are degrading, which points toward a more serious problem: silent data
corruption, a numerical instability in a specific layer, or a bug in the optimizer implementation.
Epoch-level averaging destroys this signal entirely. A brief loss spike that resolves within 200 steps is
invisible in a per-epoch summary, yet the data cursor position that caused it can still be identified and the bad
document filtered, preventing recurrence.

**A Worked Example**

A 13B model is training on 128 H100s. The stable phase runs from step 12,000 to 14,900: training loss
 2. 2 nats, gradient norm 1. 3 , clipping threshold 1.0.
At step 14,950 the unclipped gradient norm climbs to 4.1 - roughly 3 above the rolling baseline. At step
14,960 it reaches 9.7. Gradient clipping fires, but the Adam second-moment estimate has already been updated
with the squared large gradient, depressing the effective learning rate for affected parameters for the next several
steps. At step 14,963 the training loss reads 5.4; at step 14,967 it reads 9.1.
Decision protocol:

1. Check the canary batch loss at step 14,950 through 14,967: it reads 2. 21 - completely flat. This is a data
    artifact, not model divergence.


```
30.2 Operations and Failure Modes
```
2. Pull the data loader cursor from the step-14,900 checkpoint: shard index 312, document offset 8,192.
3. Inspect documents at that offset. Find a 380,000-token sequence that was incorrectly chunked: a single
    training sample with no EOS token, heavy Unicode encoding errors, and near-zero perplexity on most
    tokens (a repeated byte pattern).
4. Roll back to the step-14,900 checkpoint. Add the document hash to the dataset blocklist. Reprocess the
    shard. Resume.
5. Recovery: within 60 steps, loss returns to 2. 2. The canary loss never deviated.
    Total cost: 100 steps of recompute plus 30 minutes of investigation. The alternative - running forward
10,000 steps hoping for self-recovery - would have consumed 80 GPU-hours and produced a model degraded
on the specific domain of that corrupted document.

**What You Actually Decide in Practice**

```
Spike vs. divergence threshold. If training loss has not returned to within 5% of its pre-spike value
within 200 steps, roll back. Self-recovery beyond 200 steps is rare for data-artifact spikes and almost
never happens for true divergence. Waiting longer only compounds the optimizer state corruption from
the large Adam second-moment update.
Gradient norm alert threshold. Set an automated alert at unclipped grad norm exceeding 5 the 1,000-
step rolling mean. At this level you have an intervention window before the loss visibly spikes. At 100 
the rolling mean, you have a bad batch; pause immediately and inspect the data cursor before resuming.
Do not adjust the learning rate as a recovery mechanism. Reducing LR mid-spike to “stabilize” the
run introduces a new instability: the Adam momentum vectors accumulated under the original LR are
now mismatched. The preferred recovery is a checkpoint rollback to before the anomaly. LR adjustments
belong in the schedule, not in ad hoc responses to individual spikes.
Build a bad-document filter as a continuous background job. Every time a spike investigation iden-
tifies a pathological document, add it to a blocklist and re-process the affected data shard offline. After
three or four spike investigations, patterns emerge (mislabeled code samples, HTML artifacts, very long
sequences with zero semantic content) that can be caught by a rule-based pre-filter, preventing the spike
entirely rather than just recovering from it.
Alert on canary divergence, not just training loss. If canary loss deviates by more than two standard
deviations from a 500-step rolling mean, page the on-call engineer. This catches slow model degrada-
tion - from silent data corruption, optimizer bugs, or data distribution drift - that step-level training loss
monitoring misses because the signal is spread across thousands of steps.
```
**How This Shows Up in Interviews**

```
“You are training a 30B model and the loss spikes mid-run. How do you decide whether to roll
back or continue?” Strong answer: check gradient norm trajectory (leading indicator - was it climbing
before the loss jumped?), check canary batch loss (data artifact vs. model degradation), correlate spike
timestamp with data loader cursor position to identify a candidate document, wait at most 200 steps for
self-recovery, then roll back to the most recent clean checkpoint if loss has not recovered.
“What metrics do you log during pre-training and at what granularity?” Strong answer: per-step
training loss, unclipped global gradient norm, effective learning rate, and hardware throughput; canary
batch loss every 100 steps. Epoch-level averages are insufficient because they mask transient spikes that
```

```
30.2 Operations and Failure Modes
```
```
are often correlated with specific, identifiable data artifacts.
Senior follow-up: “Your gradient norm alert fires, but when you inspect the documents at the data
cursor position you find nothing obviously wrong. What else could be causing the spike?” Senior
answer: the list of candidates in rough order of frequency: (1) silent data corruption where the gradient
is numerically plausible but wrong - cross-replica gradient norm comparison would reveal a discrepancy;
(2) a learning rate scheduler bug that momentarily emitted an incorrect LR value - check the per-step
LR log; (3) an out-of-memory event that silently fell back to lower precision in one kernel - check GPU
memory logs around the affected steps; (4) a numerical instability in a specific attention head triggered
by an unusually long sequence - profile the attention patterns on the documents near the spike. Work
from most common to most exotic and do not assume the data is the problem until you have ruled out the
infrastructure.
```
**Key Takeaways**

```
Log training loss, unclipped gradient norm, effective learning rate, and GPU throughput at every step -
epoch-level averages hide transient spikes that are correlated with specific, filterable bad documents.
Gradient norm is the leading indicator: it typically begins rising 10-50 steps before the training loss visibly
spikes, giving you an intervention window.
A fixed canary batch evaluated every 100 steps distinguishes data artifacts (canary unaffected) from true
model degradation (canary also drifts), which determines the correct response.
Correlate every spike with the data loader cursor position to identify and filter the offending document -
this is almost always faster and cheaper than rolling back without root-cause investigation.
If training loss has not recovered within 200 steps, roll back to the most recent checkpoint; do not reduce
the learning rate mid-spike, as this corrupts the optimizer momentum state accumulated under the original
schedule.
```

## Chapter 31 Designing a Fine-Tuning and Alignment Pipeline

### 31.1 Scoping the Problem

**31.1.1 Choosing Between SFT, DPO, and RLVR**
When an interviewer asks you to design a post-training pipeline from scratch, the very first decision sepa-
rates candidates who have shipped these systems from those who have only read about them: which optimiza-
tion objective do you reach for? Supervised fine-tuning, DPO, and RL from verifiable rewards (RLVR) are not
interchangeable-each one assumes a different answer to the question of what signal you have and what behavior
you are trying to unlock. This question appears at senior and staff levels at every frontier lab. Getting the choice
wrong at scoping time wastes months of compute and annotator budget before a single evaluation number tells
you something went sideways.
All three methods share the same goal: given a pre-trained base modelπbase, produce a policyπθthat
behaves better on your target task. They differ in what “better” means and how that signal is delivered.
**SFT** treats post-training as distribution matching. You collect a setD=f(xi, y∗i)gof prompt-completion
pairs from experts or high-quality sources and minimize:

But it does not reliably teach new knowledge. If the SFT targety∗references facts the base model does not
